# 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A Questions (3 Marks Each)

**Q1. [KTU University Exam — May 2024 Model Question]** Define pineapple leaf fiber (PALF). List any four important properties that make it suitable as a reinforcement in polymer composites.

**Model Answer:**
Pineapple Leaf Fiber (PALF) is a lignocellulosic natural fiber extracted from the leaves of *Ananas comosus*. It is composed of cellulose (70–82%), hemicellulose (15–20%), and lignin (5–12%).

**Important properties:**
1. **High tensile strength (413–1043 MPa)** — comparable to E-glass fiber on a per-weight basis.
2. **Low density (1.44 g/cm³)** — provides high **specific strength** (strength-to-weight ratio).
3. **High cellulose content (~80%)** — gives excellent stiffness and crystallinity.
4. **Low microfibrillar angle (~14°)** — promotes efficient axial load transfer.
5. *Bonus:* Renewable, biodegradable, low cost, and abundantly available as agro-waste.

**(3 marks: 1 for definition + 2 for properties)**

---

**Q2. [KTU University Exam — Dec 2023 Model Question]** Why is chemical treatment (alkali/mercerization) essential for PALF before composite fabrication? State the chemical reaction involved.

**Model Answer:**
Raw PALF is **hydrophilic** due to free hydroxyl (–OH) groups in cellulose and hemicellulose. Most polymer matrices (epoxy, polyester, PP) are **hydrophobic**. This mismatch causes poor interfacial adhesion and weak composites.

**Alkali treatment** removes surface impurities (lignin, wax, pectin), increases surface roughness, and converts –OH groups into alkoxide ions, thereby reducing hydrophilicity and improving matrix–fiber bonding.

**Chemical reaction:**
$$\text{Cell–OH} + \text{NaOH} \longrightarrow \text{Cell–O}^-\text{Na}^+ + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**(3 marks: 1 for problem statement + 1 for treatment explanation + 1 for reaction)**

---

## 5.2 Part B Questions (14 Marks — Internal Choice)

### **Question A (14 Marks)**

**(a)** Explain in detail the various methods of extracting pineapple leaf fiber from pineapple leaves. Compare the advantages and disadvantages of each method. **(7 marks)**

**Model Answer:**

**Method 1 — Mechanical Decortication**
- Fresh leaves are passed through a **decorticator** (raspador machine) that scrapes the waxy epidermal layer using rotating blades.
- Extracted fibers are washed and sun-dried.
- *Advantages:* Fast, eco-friendly, no chemical use, suitable for industrial scale-up.
- *Disadvantages:* May damage fibers, produces uneven fiber length, leaves some epidermal residue.

**Method 2 — Water Retting (Biological)**
- Leaves are immersed in **slow-running water ponds** for 7–14 days.
- Microbial action breaks down pectin and lignin that bind fibers to the leaf matrix.
- Fibers are then manually separated, washed, and dried.
- *Advantages:* Produces soft, fine, high-quality fibers; low energy input.
- *Disadvantages:* Time-consuming; produces polluted water; weather-dependent; emits foul odor.

**Method 3 — Chemical Retting**
- Leaves are treated with **NaOH (5–10%)** at elevated temperature (60–80 °C) for 1–3 hours.
- Alkali dissolves lignin, hemicellulose, and pectin, releasing the fibers.
- Fibers are neutralized, washed, and oven-dried.
- *Advantages:* Fastest method; produces clean fibers.
- *Disadvantages:* Risk of cellulose degradation if alkali concentration/temperature is excessive; chemical handling hazards.

**Comparison Table (KTU board expects this):**

| Parameter | Mechanical | Water Retting | Chemical Retting |
|---|---|---|---|
| Time | Hours | 7–14 days | 1–3 hours |
| Fiber quality | Coarse | Fine, soft | Clean, strong |
| Cost | Medium | Low | High (chemicals) |
| Environmental impact | Low | High (water pollution) | Medium (effluents) |
| Industrial viability | High | Low | Medium |

**(7 marks: 2 for each method description + 1 for comparison table)**

---

**(b)** Discuss the effect of **alkali treatment (mercerization)** on the mechanical properties of PALF and its epoxy composites. Use experimental observations to support your answer. **(7 marks)**

**Model Answer:**

**Effect on PALF Fiber Alone:**
1. **Cellulose crystallinity increases** — Removal of amorphous hemicellulose and lignin exposes more crystalline cellulose regions, increasing stiffness.
2. **Fiber diameter decreases** — typically from 60 μm (raw) to 40 μm (treated), improving aspect ratio.
3. **Surface roughness increases** — Creates mechanical interlocking sites for the matrix.
4. **Hydrophilicity decreases** — Reduced –OH groups improve compatibility with hydrophobic polymers.
5. **Tensile strength** increases by ~15–30% after optimal treatment (4–6% NaOH, 1–4 hr).

**Effect on PALF/Epoxy Composites:**
1. **Tensile strength** increases by 20–40% compared to untreated PALF composites.
2. **Young's modulus** increases by 15–25%.
3. **Interfacial shear strength (IFSS)** measured by single-fiber pull-out test shows significant improvement (typically doubles).
4. **Water absorption** decreases by 30–50% — improves long-term durability.
5. **Flexural strength** and **impact strength** also improve.

**Experimental Evidence (KTU board expects numbers):**
- Raw PALF: $E_f \approx 35$ GPa; Alkali-treated PALF: $E_f \approx 45$ GPa.
- Raw PALF/epoxy (30% Vf): $E_c \approx 4.8$ GPa; Treated PALF/epoxy (30% Vf): $E_c \approx 6.2$ GPa.

**Note:** Over-treatment (>8% NaOH or >6 hr) degrades cellulose and reduces fiber strength — an important **optimum** exists.

**(7 marks: 2 for fiber effect + 3 for composite effect + 2 for experimental evidence)**

---

### **Question B (14 Marks)**

**(a)** State the assumptions involved in deriving the **rule of mixtures** for a unidirectional fiber-reinforced composite. Derive the expression for longitudinal Young's modulus and tensile strength. **(7 marks)**

**Model Answer:**

**Assumptions:**
1. Fibers are **continuous, uniform, and aligned** parallel to the loading axis.
2. **Perfect bonding** between fiber and matrix (no slip at interface).
3. Both fiber and matrix experience the **same strain** (iso-strain or Voigt condition).
4. The composite is **macroscopically homogeneous** and **free of voids**.
5. Loads are applied **along the fiber direction only** (no transverse loading).

**Derivation of $E_c$:**

Under iso-strain condition:
$$\varepsilon_c = \varepsilon_f = \varepsilon_m = \varepsilon$$

Total load carried by composite:
$$P_c = P_f + P_m$$
$$\sigma_c A_c = \sigma_f A_f + \sigma_m A_m$$

Dividing by $A_c$ and noting $A_f/A_c = V_f$, $A_m/A_c = V_m$:
$$\sigma_c = \sigma_f V_f + \sigma_m V_m$$

Using Hooke's law ($\sigma = E \varepsilon$) with iso-strain:
$$E_c \varepsilon = E_f \varepsilon V_f + E_m \varepsilon V_m$$
$$\boxed{E_c = E_f V_f + E_m V_m}$$

**Derivation of $\sigma_c$:** Directly from the iso-strain loading step (ultimate tensile condition):
$$\boxed{\sigma_c = \sigma_f V_f + \sigma_m V_m}$$

**(7 marks: 2 for assumptions + 3 for $E_c$ derivation + 2 for $\sigma_c$ derivation)**

---

**(b)** A short, randomly oriented PALF/PP composite contains **35% volume fraction of alkali-treated PALF**. Given:
- $E_f = 55$ GPa, $E_m = 1.5$ GPa
- $\sigma_f = 500$ MPa, $\sigma_m = 30$ MPa
- $\rho_f = 1.44$ g/cm³, $\rho_m = 0.91$ g/cm³
- $\eta_l = 0.85$, $\eta_o = 0.2$

**Calculate:**
(i) Density of composite
(ii) Modified longitudinal Young's modulus
(iii) Modified longitudinal tensile strength
(iv) Weight fraction of PALF
**(7 marks)**

**Model Solution:**

**(i) Density of Composite:**
$$\rho_c = \rho_f V_f + \rho_m V_m = (1.44)(0.35) + (0.91)(0.65)$$
$$\rho_c = 0.504 + 0.5915 = \boxed{1.0955 \text{ g/cm}^3}$$

**(ii) Modified Young's Modulus:**
$$E_c = \eta_l \, \eta_o \, E_f V_f + E_m V_m$$
$$E_c = (0.85)(0.2)(55)(0.35) + (1.5)(0.65)$$
$$E_c = 3.2725 + 0.975 = \boxed{4.2475 \text{ GPa}}$$

**(iii) Modified Tensile Strength:**
$$\sigma_c = \eta_l \, \eta_o \, \sigma_f V_f + \sigma_m V_m$$
$$\sigma_c = (0.85)(0.2)(500)(0.35) + (30)(0.65)$$
$$\sigma_c = 29.75 + 19.50 = \boxed{49.25 \text{ MPa}}$$

**(iv) Weight Fraction of PALF:**
$$W_f = \frac{\rho_f V_f}{\rho_c} = \frac{(1.44)(0.35)}{1.0955} = \frac{0.504}{1.0955} = \boxed{0.4601 \text{ or } 46.01\%}$$

**(7 marks: ~1.75 marks per sub-part)**

---

> [!WARNING]
> **⚠️ KTU Examiner's Valuation Pitfall Callout**
> **Three Most Common Mistakes That Cost Marks:**
>
> 1. **Forgetting correction factors** $\eta_l$ and $\eta_o$ in numerical problems. For **short, random** PALF fibers, the **modified rule of mixtures MUST be used**. Writing $E_c = E_f V_f + E_m V_m$ directly will give a wildly wrong answer (often 5–10× the correct value).
>
> 2. **Mixing up $\rho_c$ formula** with $\rho_c = 1/(W_f/\rho_f + W_m/\rho_m)$ (which is for filler-loaded systems where $V_f$ is unknown). For known $V_f$, **always use** $\rho_c = \rho_f V_f + \rho_m V_m$.
>
> 3. **Not stating assumptions explicitly** in the derivation part. KTU board examiners allocate **at least 2 marks** for clearly listing assumptions. Write them in a bulleted list, not as a paragraph.

---

## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember 📝

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Rapid-Revision Checklist for KTU Exam Day**

- ✅ PALF = **Pineapple Leaf Fiber**; extracted from leaves of *Ananas comosus*.
- ✅ Composition: **Cellulose 70–82%**, Hemicellulose 15–20%, Lignin 5–12%.
- ✅ Density: **1.44 g/cm³** | Tensile strength: **413–1043 MPa** | $E_f$: **6.21–34.5 GPa**.
- ✅ Microfibrillar angle: **14°** (lower than sisal, coir → higher stiffness).
- ✅ Three extraction methods: **Mechanical Decortication**, **Water Retting**, **Chemical (NaOH) Retting**.
- ✅ Alkali (mercerization) treatment with **4–6% NaOH for 1–4 hr** is the most common surface modification.
- ✅ Chemical reaction: Cell–OH + NaOH → Cell–O⁻Na⁺ + H₂O.
- ✅ Rule of mixtures (continuous, aligned): $E_c = E_f V_f + E_m V_m$.
- ✅ Modified ROM (short, random): $E_c = \eta_l \eta_o E_f V_f + E_m V_m$.
- ✅ For 3-D random fibers: $\eta_o \approx 0.2$; for 2-D random: $\eta_o \approx 0.375$; aligned: $\eta_o = 1$.
- ✅ Density formula: $\rho_c = \rho_f V_f + \rho_m V_m$.
- ✅ Weight–volume relation: $W_f = \dfrac{\rho_f V_f}{\rho_f V_f + \rho_m V_m}$.
- ✅ Applications: automotive (door panels, dashboards), construction (panels), packaging, sports goods.
- ✅ Advantages over glass fiber: renewable, biodegradable, low cost, low density, less abrasive to processing equipment.
- ✅ Disadvantages: hydrophilic nature → moisture absorption, poor fire resistance, variability in fiber quality.
- ✅ Common ASTM test standards: **D3039** (tensile), **D790** (flexural), **D256** (impact), **D570** (water absorption).
- ✅ Always mention **assumptions** before any derivation — examiners award 2 marks just for that.

---

topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME** > - **Course:** PCPOL607 - PCPOL607 > - **Module:** Module Experiment 2 > - **Topic:** jute # JUTE — Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview > [!IMPORTANT] > **KTU 2024 Syllabus Definition (PCPOL607):** > *Jute* is a **lignocellulosic natural fiber** obtained from the stem/bast of plants belonging to the genus *Corchorus* (family Tiliaceae), primarily *Corchorus capsularis* (white jute) and *Corchorus olitorius* (tossa jute). Chemically, it is a **natural composite** of cellulose microfibrils embedded in a matrix of **hemicellulose and lignin**, and it is studied in polymer science as one of the most important **renewable, biodegradable reinforcing fibers** for polymer composites. ## Intuitive Analogy — "The Rope of Nature" Imagine a **steel-reinforced concrete pillar**. The **steel rods** carry the load (tension), while the **concrete** holds them together and transfers stress. Jute fiber works on the exact same principle, but nature builds it from plants: | Component in Concrete | Equivalent in Jute | Role | |---|---|---| | Steel rods (rebars) | **Cellulose microfibrils** | Provide tensile strength | | Concrete matrix | **Hemicellulose + Lignin** | Bind fibrils, transfer load | | Cement paste | **Pectins & waxes** | Lubricate and protect | > [!NOTE] > **Key KTU Highlight:** Jute is called a **"golden fiber"** because of its golden-silk luster, low cost (~**₹40–60/kg**), and high specific strength (strength-to-weight ratio comparable to glass fiber). ## Botanical & Chemical Origin - **Botanical source:** Bast (stem) fibers of *Corchorus capsularis* and *Corchorus olitorius*. - **Harvesting age:** 4–6 months (one of the fastest-growing crop fibers). - **Yield:** ~**2 tonnes/hectare** of dry fiber. - **Position in the stem:** Lies between the outer epidermis (skin) and the inner woody core, held together by pectin. ## Standard Composition of Jute Fiber (KTU Board-Standard Values) | Component | Composition (% by weight) | Function | |---|---|---| | **Cellulose (α-cellulose)** | **58–63 %** | Main load-bearing biopolymer | | **Hemicellulose** | **20–24 %** | Matrix binder, hydrophilic | | **Lignin** | **12–15 %** | Rigid aromatic matrix, UV resistance | | **Pectin** | **0.2–0.5 %** | Holds fiber bundles together | | **Wax & fat** | **0.4–0.8 %** | Surface lubrication | | **Ash & minerals** | **0.5–1.2 %** | Inorganic content | | **Moisture content** | **12–14 %** | At standard atmospheric condition | > [!TIP] > **Remember for KTU exams:** Jute has the **lowest cellulose content** and **highest lignin content** among common bast fibers (flax, hemp, kenaf). High lignin makes it **stiff but less flexible** and more **UV-degradable** than flax. # Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet ## 1. Hierarchical Structure of Jute Fiber Jute exhibits a **multi-level hierarchical architecture**, which is critical for understanding its mechanical behaviour in polymer composites: ``` Level 1: Stem (plant) → Several cm Level 2: Fiber bundle (tow) → 1–5 mm diameter Level 3: Technical fiber → 50–200 µm diameter Level 4: Ultimate fiber → 5–25 µm diameter Level 5: Microfibril → 0.1–0.5 µm Level 6: Cellulose chain → ~1 nm (β-1,4-linked D-glucose) ``` ## 2. Chemistry of the Three Main Constituents ### (a) Cellulose — The Load Bearer Cellulose is a **linear, syndiotactic homopolymer of β-D-glucopyranose** units linked by **β-(1→4) glycosidic bonds**. $$\text{Repeat unit: } (C_6H_{10}O_5)_n$$ Degree of polymerisation (DP) in jute cellulose ≈ **700–900** (much lower than cotton ≈ 10,000). Each glucose unit carries **three free –OH groups** (at C2, C3, and C6), enabling extensive **inter- and intra-molecular hydrogen bonding** that gives jute its high tensile strength. ### (b) Hemicellulose — The Compatibiliser Matrix - A **branched, heterogeneous polysaccharide** (xylan backbone in jute). - Contains many **–OH and –COOH groups** → highly **hydrophilic** → responsible for jute's moisture absorption. - Acts as a **coupling bridge** between cellulose and lignin. ### (c) Lignin — The Rigid Aromatic Glue - A **complex three-dimensional aromatic copolymer** of **phenylpropanoid units**: *p-coumaryl alcohol*, *coniferyl alcohol*, and *sinapyl alcohol*. - Provides **rigidity, compressive strength, and resistance to microbial attack**. - Contains both **aliphatic and aromatic –OH groups** → reactive sites for chemical modification. ## 3. KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet > [!NOTE] > The following equations are the **most-asked formulas** in KTU ESE/IA exams on natural fibers. | # | Quantity / Concept | Formula | Units | Notes | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | Degree of Polymerisation | $DP = \dfrac{M_n}{M_0}$ | dimensionless | $M_0$ = molar mass of repeat unit (162 g/mol for cellulose) | | 2 | Density of jute fiber | $\rho_f \approx 1.3\text{–}1.5$ | g/cm³ | Used for specific-strength calculations | | 3 | Specific tensile strength | $\sigma_{sp} = \dfrac{\sigma_t}{\rho_f}$ | $\dfrac{N \cdot m}{kg}$ | Compare with E-glass: ~**1400** vs jute ~**2600** | | 4 | Moisture Regain (MR) | $MR = \dfrac{W_{wet} - W_{dry}}{W_{dry}} \times 100$ | % | Jute MR ≈ **12–14 %** | | 5 | Fiber Volume Fraction (rule of mixtures) | $V_f = \dfrac{W_f / \rho_f}{W_f/\rho_f + W_m/\rho_m}$ | dimensionless | Used in composite micromechanics | | 6 | Composite tensile strength (ROM) | $\sigma_c = \sigma_f V_f + \sigma_m (1 - V_f)$ | MPa | Assumes perfect fiber–matrix bonding | | 7 | Young's modulus (ROM) | $E_c = E_f V_f + E_m (1 - V_f)$ | GPa | Voigt model (isostrain) | | 8 | Inverse rule of mixtures | $\dfrac{1}{E_c} = \dfrac{V_f}{E_f} + \dfrac{(1-V_f)}{E_m}$ | GPa | Reuss model (isostress) | | 9 | Cellulose content (Kürschner-Hoffer method) | $\%\,Cell = \dfrac{W_{residue}}{W_{sample}} \times 100$ | % | Alcohol–nitric acid digestion | | 10 | Hydrophilicity (water uptake) | $WU = \dfrac{W_{sat} - W_{dry}}{W_{dry}} \times 100$ | % | Jute can absorb **>30 %** of its dry weight | > [!WARNING] > In KTU answer sheets, **never** confuse **Moisture Regain (MR)** with **Moisture Content (MC)**. MR is based on dry weight; MC is based on original (wet) weight: > $MC = \dfrac{W_{wet} - W_{dry}}{W_{wet}} \times 100$ — a common board-exam trap. ## 4. Why Jute is a "Natural Composite" (KTU Conceptual Hook) A jute fiber is **already a composite before we even reinforce a polymer with it**: - **Cellulose fibrils** = high-modulus anisotropic reinforcement (E ≈ **10–30 GPa** along fibril axis). - **Hemicellulose + lignin matrix** = isotropic, low-modulus binder (E ≈ **2–4 GPa**). - The cell wall has a **multi-ply laminate structure** (primary wall → S1 → S2 → S3), with microfibrils wound at a **helix angle (microfibrillar angle, MFA)** of **~8–12°** in the S2 layer of jute. > The **lower the MFA**, the **higher the tensile strength and stiffness** — this is why jute's S2-dominated structure gives it strength comparable to flax. # Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix ## Derivation 1 — Degree of Polymerisation (DP) of Jute Cellulose The molecular weight of jute cellulose is experimentally determined via **viscometry (Mark–Houwink equation)** or **osmometry**. Given the molecular weight, DP is calculated as follows: $$\text{Step 1: Identify the repeat unit of cellulose}$$ Cellulose repeat unit = one **anhydroglucose unit (AGU)**, formula $C_6H_{10}O_5$. $$\text{Step 2: Calculate molar mass of the AGU}$$ $$\begin{aligned} M_0 &= 6 \times M_C + 10 \times M_H + 5 \times M_O \\ &= 6(12.01) + 10(1.008) + 5(16.00) \\ &= 72.06 + 10.08 + 80.00 \\ &= 162.14 \text{ g/mol} \end{aligned}$$ $$\text{Step 3: Apply the definition of DP}$$ $$\begin{aligned} DP &= \dfrac{M_n}{M_0} \\ &= \dfrac{M_n \text{ (g/mol of cellulose chain)}}{162.14 \text{ g/mol}} \end{aligned}$$ $$\text{Step 4: Numerical example (KTU-style problem)}$$ **Given:** Viscosity-average molecular weight of jute cellulose $M_v = 1.2 \times 10^5$ g/mol. $$\begin{aligned} DP &= \dfrac{1.2 \times 10^5}{162.14} \\ &= 740.0 \approx 740 \end{aligned}$$ **Interpretation:** A DP of ~740 means each jute cellulose chain has approximately **740 glucose units** linked by β-1,4-glycosidic bonds. This is **10–14 times lower** than cotton, explaining jute's comparatively **lower flexibility** but still high tensile strength due to dense H-bonding. --- ## Derivation 2 — Rule of Mixtures for Jute–PP Composite **Problem:** A jute fiber-reinforced polypropylene composite contains 30 % jute fiber by weight. Calculate the longitudinal tensile strength. Given: - $\sigma_f$ (jute fiber) = **400 MPa** - $\sigma_m$ (polypropylene) = **30 MPa** - $\rho_f$ (jute) = **1.45 g/cm³** - $\rho_m$ (PP) = **0.91 g/cm³** $$\text{Step 1: Convert weight fraction to volume fraction}$$ $$\begin{aligned} V_f &= \dfrac{W_f / \rho_f}{W_f/\rho_f + W_m/\rho_m} \\ &= \dfrac{0.30 / 1.45}{0.30/1.45 + 0.70/0.91} \\ &= \dfrac{0.2069}{0.2069 + 0.7692} \\ &= \dfrac{0.2069}{0.9761} \\ &= 0.2120 \approx 0.21 \end{aligned}$$ $$\text{Step 2: Apply the rule of mixtures (longitudinal tensile strength)}$$ $$\begin{aligned} \sigma_c &= \sigma_f \cdot V_f + \sigma_m \cdot (1 - V_f) \\ &= (400)(0.21) + (30)(0.79) \\ &= 84.0 + 23.7 \\ &= 107.7 \text{ MPa} \end{aligned}$$ $$\text{Step 3: Interpretation}$$ The composite strength (≈ **108 MPa**) is **3.6× higher** than neat PP and is a direct consequence of jute's high fiber strength being transferred efficiently to the matrix. > [!IMPORTANT] > This is the **theoretical maximum**. Actual strengths are **30–50 % lower** because of (a) weak fiber–matrix interface, (b) fiber agglomeration, and (c) moisture-induced voids. KTU examiners love asking the **"why actual strength < theoretical"** part. --- ## Derivation 3 — Specific Strength Comparison (Jute vs E-Glass) **Definition:** Specific strength = strength ÷ density. $$\begin{aligned} \text{E-Glass: } \sigma_{sp}^{glass} &= \dfrac{2400 \text{ MPa}}{2.55 \text{ g/cm}^3} = 941 \text{ kN·m/kg} \\ \text{Jute: } \sigma_{sp}^{jute} &= \dfrac{400 \text{ MPa}}{1.45 \text{ g/cm}^3} = 2759 \text{ kN·m/kg} \end{aligned}$$ **Result:** Jute has a **specific strength ~3× higher** than E-glass. This is the **headline reason** jute is studied as a sustainable alternative to glass fiber. --- ## Analytical Matrix — Jute vs Other Natural Fibers (KTU Comparison Table) | Property | **Jute** | Flax | Hemp | Sisal | Cotton | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Cellulose (%) | 58–63 | 70–75 | 70–78 | 60–67 | 88–96 | | Lignin (%) | 12–15 | 2–5 | 3–5 | 8–12 | <1 | | Density (g/cm³) | 1.3–1.5 | 1.4–1.5 | 1.4–1.5 | 1.3–1.5 | 1.5–1.6 | | Tensile strength (MPa) | 400–800 | 800–1500 | 600–1100 | 500–900 | 300–700 | | Young's modulus (GPa) | 10–30 | 50–70 | 30–70 | 10–25 | 5–12 | | Elongation (%) | 1.0–1.8 | 1.5–3.3 | 1.5–3.5 | 3–7 | 6–9 | | Microfibril angle (°) | 8–12 | 5–10 | 6–12 | 18–25 | 25–45 | | Moisture regain (%) | 12–14 | 8–12 | 8–10 | 10–12 | 7–8 | | Cost (USD/kg) | 0.4–0.8 | 1.5–2.5 | 1.0–2.0 | 0.6–1.0 | 1.5–2.5 | > [!TIP] > **Board Tip:** The inverse correlation between **microfibril angle (MFA)** and **modulus** is a recurring viva question. Jute's **low MFA (8–12°)** is what enables its competitive stiffness despite low cellulose content. # Structural Diagrams & Schematics ## Diagram 1 — Hierarchical Structure of Jute (Block-Level Functional Architecture Flow) ```mermaid flowchart TD A["STEM OF CORCHORUS PLANT"] --> B["BUNDLE OF BAST FIBERS"] B --> C["TECHNICAL FIBER STRAND"] C --> D["ULTIMATE CELL SINGLE FIBER"] D --> E["CELL WALL LAYERS S1 S2 S3"] E --> F["CELLULOSE MICROFIBRIL"] F --> G["CELLULOSE POLYMER CHAIN"] G --> H["BETA 1 4 D GLUCOSE REPEAT UNIT"] I["LIGNIN MATRIX"] --> E J["HEMICELLULOSE BRIDGE"] --> E K["PECTIN INTERFACE"] --> D L["CHEMICAL TREATMENT NAOH SILANE"] -.-> F M["PHYSICAL TREATMENT PLASMA CORONA"] -.-> D ``` ## Diagram 2 — Cell Wall Architecture (Lignocellulosic Composite Model) ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph CW["CELL WALL OF JUTE FIBER"] direction TB PW["PRIMARY WALL Pectin and loose cellulose"] S1["S1 LAYER Thin, random MFA"] S2["S2 LAYER Thickest, low MFA 8 to 12 degrees, max load bearing"] S3["S3 LAYER Inner lining, smooth"] end PW --> S1 --> S2 --> S3 subgraph ML["MATRIX LIGNIN AND HEMICELLULOSE"] MA["Binds microfibrils, transfers stress"] end S2 -.is reinforced by.-> ML note["MF = Microfibrils of cellulose
MFA = Microfibrillar Angle
Lower MFA = Higher Strength"]:::note ``` ## Diagram 3 — Jute-Polymer Composite Processing Flow ```mermaid flowchart TD R["RAW JUTE BAST"] --> R1["RETING 14 to 21 days in water"] R1 --> R2["STRIPPING AND WASHING"] R2 --> R3["DRYING Sun or oven 60 to 80 C"] R3 --> S["SURFACE TREATMENT Alkali NaOH 5 percent Silane Plasma"] S --> C1["COMPRESSION MOULDING 150 to 180 C"] S --> C2["INJECTION MOULDING 180 to 200 C"] S --> C3["HAND LAYUP WITH THERMOSET"] S --> C4["EXTRUSION WITH THERMOPLASTIC"] C1 --> P1["JUTE PP COMPOSITE SHEET"] C2 --> P2["JUTE PP COMPOSITE PART"] C3 --> P3["JUTE EPOXY COMPOSITE LAMINATE"] C4 --> P4["JUTE PE COMPOSITE PROFILE"] classDef proc fill:#f9e79f,stroke:#7d6608,color:#000; classDef prod fill:#a9dfbf,stroke:#1e8449,color:#000; classDef treat fill:#f5b7b1,stroke:#922b21,color:#000; class S,C1,C2,C3,C4 treat; class P1,P2,P3,P4 prod; class R,R1,R2,R3 proc; ``` ## Diagram 4 — Chemical Modification of Jute – OH Groups ```mermaid flowchart LR A["CELLULOSE OH"] --> B["ALKALI TREATMENT NaOH"] B --> C["CELL O NA plus Na plus OH removed"] C --> D["SURFACE ROUGHNESS INCREASED"] D --> E["BETTER MATRIX ADHESION"] A2["CELLULOSE OH"] --> F["SILANE TREATMENT R Si OR 3"] F --> G["SILOXANE BRIDGE Si O Si"] G --> H["COUPLING WITH POLYMER MATRIX"] A3["CELLULOSE OH"] --> I["ACETYLATION CH3COOH"] I --> J["CELL O CO CH3"] J --> K["HYDROPHOBIC SURFACE LOWER MOISTURE"] classDef ch fill:#d6eaf8,stroke:#1f618d,color:#000; class A,A2,A3,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,I,J,K ch; ``` > [!NOTE] > **Mermaid compilation note:** All node IDs are alphanumeric (`A`, `B`, `S1`, etc.), no reserved keywords are used, and node labels contain only raw uppercase/lowercase alphanumeric text with hyphens to preserve diagram integrity. ## Diagram 5 — Stress Transfer Mechanism at Fiber–Matrix Interface ```mermaid flowchart TD LOAD["APPLIED TENSILE LOAD"] --> MATRIX["POLYMER MATRIX PP or Epoxy"] MATRIX --> IFACE["INTERFACIAL SHEAR STRESS tau"] IFACE --> FIBER["JUTE FIBER LOAD BEARING"] FIBER -.fiber fracture or pull out.-> FAIL["COMPOSITE FAILURE"] MOD["MODIFICATIONS Alkali Silane Maleic Anhydride"] -.enhance.-> IFACE ``` # KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap ## Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each) ### Q1. `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]` **List the major chemical constituents of jute fiber and state the function of each.** **Model Answer (3 marks):** Jute is composed of three major constituents: 1. **Cellulose (58–63 %)** – a linear polymer of β-D-glucose units linked by β-1,4-glycosidic bonds; provides **tensile strength and stiffness** to the fiber (1 mark). 2. **Hemicellulose (20–24 %)** – a branched polysaccharide; acts as a **matrix binder** between cellulose and lignin and is responsible for moisture absorption (1 mark). 3. **Lignin (12–15 %)** – an aromatic copolymer of phenylpropanoid units; imparts **rigidity, UV resistance and compressive strength** (1 mark). --- ### Q2. `[KTU University Exam - May 2024]` **Why is jute considered a "natural composite"?** **Model Answer (3 marks):** Jute is inherently a **fiber-reinforced biocomposite** at the cell-wall level: - The **cellulose microfibrils** act as the **reinforcement** phase, providing high axial strength and modulus (≈10–30 GPa) (1 mark). - The **lignin and hemicellulose** form the **matrix** phase, transferring stress and binding the fibrils together (1 mark). - The cell wall has a **multi-ply laminate structure (S1, S2, S3)** with cellulose fibrils wound at a low microfibrillar angle (~8–12°), making it structurally analogous to a synthetic fiber-reinforced composite (1 mark). --- ## Part B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks, with Internal Choice) ### **Question A (14 Marks)** `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2022]` **(a)** Explain in detail the **hierarchical structure of jute fiber** from the macroscopic stem level down to the cellulose polymer chain. Sketch the chemical structure of the cellulose repeat unit. **(7 marks)** **(b)** Discuss the **merits and demerits of jute fiber** as a reinforcing material in polymer composites. Compare its specific strength with E-glass fiber. **(7 marks)** #### Model Solution **(a) Hierarchical structure (7 marks):** The jute bast fiber exhibits six hierarchical levels: 1. **Stem** → plant of genus *Corchorus*, harvested at 4–6 months (0.5 mark). 2. **Fiber bundle (tow)** → 1–5 mm thick, consists of many technical fibers glued by pectin (0.5 mark). 3. **Technical fiber** → 50–200 µm in diameter, the commercial unit used in composites (0.5 mark). 4. **Ultimate fiber (single cell)** → 5–25 µm diameter, polygonal cross-section, hollow lumen (0.5 mark). 5. **Cell wall layers** → Primary wall + S1 + S2 + S3; S2 is thickest with cellulose fibrils wound helically at **MFA = 8–12°** (1 mark). 6. **Cellulose polymer chain** → linear β-1,4-linked D-glucopyranose units; DP ≈ 700–900 (1 mark). **Chemical structure of cellulose repeat unit (anhydroglucose unit):** $$\text{Cellulose repeat unit: } (C_6H_{10}O_5)_n$$ The β-D-glucopyranose ring contains: - **Three –OH groups** at C2, C3 and C6 — responsible for hydrogen bonding. - **One ring oxygen** between C1 and C5. - **β-1,4 glycosidic linkage** connecting adjacent units (1 mark). **Intra-chain H-bond** between C3–OH and the ring oxygen of the adjacent unit stabilises the chain. **Inter-chain H-bonds** between C6–OH of one chain and C3–OH of the neighbouring chain form the sheets that give cellulose its high axial stiffness (1 mark). **(b) Merits & Demerits (7 marks):** **Merits (3.5 marks):** 1. **Low density (1.3–1.5 g/cm³)** → very high specific strength (3× E-glass) (1 mark). 2. **Renewable and biodegradable** → eco-friendly, carbon-neutral (0.5 mark). 3. **Low cost (₹40–60/kg)** → economical vs glass (₹200+/kg) (0.5 mark). 4. **High specific modulus** and good acoustic/thermal insulation (0.5 mark). 5. **Non-abrasive** to processing machinery → less wear on extruders (0.5 mark). **Demerits (2.5 marks):** 1. **High moisture absorption (12–14 %)** → poor fiber–matrix adhesion, swelling, voids (0.5 mark). 2. **Poor fiber–matrix bonding** with non-polar thermoplastics like PP and PE (0.5 mark). 3. **Low thermal stability** → degrades above 200 °C, limiting processing options (0.5 mark). 4. **Variability** in properties due to soil, climate, retting conditions (0.5 mark). 5. **Microbial degradation** over time → poor long-term durability (0.5 mark). **Specific strength comparison (1 mark):** $$\sigma_{sp}^{jute} = \dfrac{400}{1.45} \approx 2759 \text{ kN·m/kg}$$ $$\sigma_{sp}^{E\text{-}glass} = \dfrac{2400}{2.55} \approx 941 \text{ kN·m/kg}$$ ∴ Jute is **~3× superior** to E-glass in specific strength, making it attractive for **lightweight structural applications** in automotive and packaging. --- ### **Question B (14 Marks)** `[KTU University Exam - May 2023]` **(a)** Describe **chemical modification methods** used to improve the interfacial adhesion between jute fiber and a hydrophobic polymer matrix. Give one example reaction in each case. **(7 marks)** **(b)** A jute–PP composite is fabricated with **40 wt % jute fiber**. Using the rule of mixtures, calculate the **longitudinal tensile strength** and **Young's modulus** of the composite. Given: $\sigma_f = 450$ MPa, $\sigma_m = 32$ MPa, $E_f = 25$ GPa, $E_m = 1.5$ GPa, $\rho_f = 1.45$ g/cm³, $\rho_m = 0.91$ g/cm³. **(7 marks)** #### Model Solution **(a) Chemical modification methods (7 marks):** | # | Method | Reagent | Reaction (key change) | Effect (1 mark each) | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | **Alkali (mercerisation)** | 5 % NaOH | $Jute\text{-}OH + NaOH \rightarrow Jute\text{-}O^-Na^+ + H_2O$ | Removes hemicellulose, wax, lignin; increases surface roughness; exposes –OH for bonding | | 2 | **Silane coupling** | Trialkoxy silanes (e.g., 3-aminopropyl-triethoxysilane, APTES) | $Jute\text{-}OH + R\text{-}Si(OR')_3 \rightarrow Jute\text{-}O\text{-}Si\text{-}R + 3R'OH$ | Forms siloxane bridge, makes surface hydrophobic, covalent bond with polymer | | 3 | **Acetylation** | Acetic anhydride / glacial acetic acid | $Jute\text{-}OH + (CH_3CO)_2O \rightarrow Jute\text{-}O\text{-}COCH_3 + CH_3COOH$ | Replaces hydrophilic –OH with hydrophobic acetyl group; reduces moisture regain | | 4 | **Maleic anhydride grafting (MAPP)** | Maleic anhydride grafted PP (MAPP) | Anhydride ring opens; esterifies with jute –OH | Acts as a **compatibiliser** between non-polar PP and polar jute (most widely used commercially) | | 5 | **Benzoylation / peroxide treatment** | Benzoyl chloride, dicumyl peroxide | Benzoyl groups grafted onto cellulose | Improves surface energy match with polymer | Brief write-up of any two (each ~1.5 marks = 3 marks); remaining 4 marks for the table and the *MAPP* example, which is the **industry standard** for jute–PP composites. > [!IMPORTANT] > KTU examiners particularly appreciate the **maleic anhydride grafted PP (MAPP)** example — it is the most widely used compatibiliser in jute–polyolefin composites and is a **favourite viva question**. **(b) Numerical problem (7 marks):** **Given:** $W_f = 0.40$, $W_m = 0.60$, $\sigma_f = 450$ MPa, $\sigma_m = 32$ MPa, $E_f = 25$ GPa, $E_m = 1.5$ GPa, $\rho_f = 1.45$ g/cm³, $\rho_m = 0.91$ g/cm³. **Step 1 (1.5 marks): Volume fraction of fiber** $$\begin{aligned} V_f &= \dfrac{W_f/\rho_f}{W_f/\rho_f + W_m/\rho_m} \\ &= \dfrac{0.40/1.45}{0.40/1.45 + 0.60/0.91} \\ &= \dfrac{0.2759}{0.2759 + 0.6593} \\ &= \dfrac{0.2759}{0.9352} \\ &= 0.2950 \approx 0.30 \end{aligned}$$ **Step 2 (1.5 marks): Volume fraction of matrix** $$V_m = 1 - V_f = 1 - 0.30 = 0.70$$ **Step 3 (2 marks): Longitudinal tensile strength (Rule of Mixtures)** $$\begin{aligned} \sigma_c &= \sigma_f V_f + \sigma_m V_m \\ &= (450)(0.30) + (32)(0.70) \\ &= 135.0 + 22.4 \\ &= 157.4 \text{ MPa} \end{aligned}$$ **Step 4 (2 marks): Young's modulus (Rule of Mixtures — Voigt isostrain model)** $$\begin{aligned} E_c &= E_f V_f + E_m V_m \\ &= (25)(0.30) + (1.5)(0.70) \\ &= 7.50 + 1.05 \\ &= 8.55 \text{ GPa} \end{aligned}$$ **Result:** - Longitudinal tensile strength $\sigma_c \approx \mathbf{157.4 \text{ MPa}}$ - Young's modulus $E_c \approx \mathbf{8.55 \text{ GPa}}$ > [!WARNING] > **KTU Examiner's Valuation Pitfall:** > 1. **Wrong conversion** of wt % to vol % → check density values. Most students forget this step. > 2. **Confusion between ROM and inverse ROM** — ROM ($\sigma_c = \sigma_f V_f + \sigma_m V_m$) is for **isostrain (longitudinal)**, inverse ROM is for **isostress (transverse)**. Wrong formula → lose 2 marks. > 3. **Unit mismatch** — strength in MPa, modulus in GPa. Mixing them → 0 marks for the final answer. > 4. **Rounding** errors beyond 3 decimals — KTU allows ±2 % tolerance. --- ## 📋 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember > [!TIP] > **Last-minute revision checklist for KTU exams:** - [x] Jute = **lignocellulosic natural fiber** from *Corchorus* sp.; "**golden fiber**" of India & Bangladesh. - [x] Composition: **Cellulose 58–63 %, Hemicellulose 20–24 %, Lignin 12–15 %**, plus minor pectin, wax, ash. - [x] Cellulose repeat unit = **β-D-glucopyranose** with **β-1,4-glycosidic bonds**; DP ≈ **700–900**. - [x] Jute is **inherently a composite**: cellulose fibrils (reinforcement) in lignin/hemicellulose matrix. - [x] **Microfibrillar angle (MFA) ≈ 8–12°** → low MFA = high stiffness. - [x] Density = **1.3–1.5 g/cm³**; specific strength ≈ **3× E-glass**. - [x] **MR ≈ 12–14 %** (high moisture absorption → poor adhesion with hydrophobic polymers). - [x] Degrades above **200 °C** → limited thermoplastic processing window. - [x] Key treatments: **Alkali (NaOH), Silane (APTES), Acetylation, MAPP** (most important commercial compatibiliser). - [x] **Rule of mixtures:** $\sigma_c = \sigma_f V_f + \sigma_m V_m$ — valid only for *longitudinal* loading. - [x] **MR ≠ MC** — Moisture Regain uses dry weight as base; Moisture Content uses original wet weight. - [x] Compared to flax/hemp, jute has **lower cellulose, higher lignin** → less flexible, more UV-sensitive. - [x] Applications: **automotive door panels, geotextiles, packaging, roofing, carpet backing, reinforced PP/PE composites**. > **All the best for your KTU 2024 Scheme examination! 🌾**

> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME** > - **Course:** PCPOL607 - Polymer Chemistry & Technology > - **Module:** Module Experiment 2 > - **Topic:** Silk - Identification, Properties, and Chemical Analysis of a Natural Protein Fiber # 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview ## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition **Silk** is a continuous, natural **proteinaceous filament** secreted by certain arthropods, most notably the larvae of the *Bombyx mori* (domesticated mulberry silkworm), and is classified within polymer science as a **natural polypeptide biopolymer**. Chemically, silk is composed of two principal protein components: 1. **Fibroin** (~75%) – the structural, fibrous core protein that imparts tensile strength. 2. **Sericin** (~25%) – the globular, gummy protein that binds the fibroin filaments together (the "silk gum"). The repeating monomeric units in fibroin are predominantly the amino acids **glycine (Gly)**, **alanine (Ala)**, and **serine (Ser)**, arranged in the characteristic antiparallel **β-pleated sheet** configuration, which gives silk its remarkable mechanical strength. > [!IMPORTANT] > **KTU 2024 Syllabus Highlight (PCPOL607 – Experiment 2):** > Students are expected to perform qualitative identification of silk using **burning test, solubility test, microscopic examination, and chemical spot tests** (e.g., Millon's reagent, Biuret test, Ninhydrin test). Silk is benchmarked against other natural and synthetic fibers as part of fiber identification protocols. ## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Intuition Imagine a **construction crane cable** made of thousands of fine steel wires twisted together — no single wire is strong, but together they can lift enormous loads. Silk works on the exact same principle: - The **β-pleated sheets** of fibroin are like the "steel wires" (highly ordered, crystalline). - The **amorphous regions** of fibroin and the surrounding sericin act like the **twisting/braiding** that holds everything together and gives flexibility. - The **antiparallel hydrogen bonding** between adjacent protein chains is the "glue" that resists pulling forces. When a silkworm spins its cocoon, it is essentially extruding a **pre-engineered, nano-composite biopolymer cable** that is tougher, gram-for-gram, than many steels — a true masterpiece of natural materials engineering. > [!NOTE] > **Key physical constant to remember:** > - Density of silk: **ρ ≈ 1.30 – 1.38 g/cm³** > - Tenacity (dry): **0.35 – 0.55 N/tex** (≈ 3.5 – 5.5 g/denier) > - Moisture regain (standard): **11.0 %** --- # 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet ## 2.1 Hierarchical Structure of Silk Silk's properties arise from a **four-level hierarchical architecture**, a concept that KTU examiners frequently test in 14-mark questions. ### Level 1 — Primary Structure (Amino Acid Sequence) - Dominated by the simple, small amino acids **Gly (43.7 %)**, **Ala (28.8 %)**, and **Ser (11.9 %)**. - The repetitive motif is **(-Gly-Ala-Gly-Ala-Gly-Ser-)_n**. - Small side groups (H, CH₃, CH₂OH) → allow **close chain packing**. ### Level 2 — Secondary Structure (β-Sheets) - Chains align in an **antiparallel β-pleated sheet** stabilized by **inter-chain hydrogen bonds** (C=O···H–N). - Two crystalline polymorphs: - **Silk I** (water-soluble, helical) — the freshly spun form. - **Silk II** (insoluble, β-sheet) — the stable, spun form. ### Level 3 — Tertiary Structure (Microfibrils) - β-Sheets stack into **crystalline microfibrils** (≈ 3–5 nm diameter) embedded in a less-ordered matrix. - This is a natural **semi-crystalline polymer composite**. ### Level 4 — Quaternary Structure (Filament) - Two **brins** (fibroin filaments) are cemented by sericin to form a single **bave** (silk thread). - Typical bave diameter: **10 – 25 μm**. ## 2.2 Why Each Step Matters (The "Why & How") - **Why so much glycine and alanine?** Because their tiny R-groups (–H and –CH₃) allow chains to pack tightly, maximizing hydrogen bonding and crystallinity. - **How does silk achieve both strength and elasticity?** The **crystalline β-sheet domains** bear the load (high strength, high modulus), while the **amorphous tie-chains** between them allow extension and energy dissipation (toughness). - **How is sericin removed?** By **degumming** — boiling the cocoons in an alkaline soap solution (e.g., 0.5 – 1.0 % Na₂CO₃, 95–100 °C, 30–60 min). This step is the **first stage of silk processing in the textile industry**. ## 2.3 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet > [!IMPORTANT] > The following table is a **high-yield reference** for KTU Polymer Chemistry numerical problems. Memorize the units carefully — examiners award ½ mark for correct units. | # | Parameter / Quantity | Formula | Standard Value (Silk) | Unit | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | Degree of Polymerization (DP) | $\mathrm{DP} = \dfrac{\overline{M}_n}{M_0}$ | ≈ 2 000 – 4 000 (fibroin) | dimensionless | | 2 | Moisture Regain (MR) | $\mathrm{MR} = \dfrac{W_w - W_d}{W_d} \times 100$ | 11.0 | % | | 3 | Moisture Content (MC) | $\mathrm{MC} = \dfrac{W_w - W_d}{W_w} \times 100$ | 9.91 | % | | 4 | Tenacity (T) | $T = \dfrac{F}{L \times \rho}$ | 0.35 – 0.55 | N/tex | | 5 | Specific Stress | $\sigma_{sp} = \dfrac{F \cdot L_0 \cdot \rho_f}{L_f \cdot m}$ | — | N/tex | | 6 | Elongation at Break | $\varepsilon = \dfrac{L_f - L_0}{L_0} \times 100$ | 18 – 25 | % | | 7 | Crystallinity Index (X_c) | $X_c = \dfrac{I_c}{I_c + I_a} \times 100$ | 40 – 50 (silk II) | % | | 8 | Glass Transition (T_g) | Empirical Fox relation | ≈ 175 – 220 | °C | | 9 | Decomposition Temperature | DSC/TGA peak | ≈ 300 – 320 | °C | | 10 | Density (ρ) | $\rho = \dfrac{m}{V}$ | 1.30 – 1.38 | g/cm³ | > [!NOTE] > **Engineering Utility:** The same β-sheet architecture seen in silk fibroin is the inspiration behind modern **regenerated silk fibroin biomaterials** used in tissue-engineering scaffolds, biodegradable sutures, and flexible bioelectronics — making this topic a high-value link between traditional textile chemistry and advanced biomaterials engineering. --- # 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix ## 3.1 Worked Example 1 — Moisture Regain of a Silk Sample **Problem:** A 5.00 g sample of raw mulberry silk is conditioned at 65 % RH and weighed as $W_w = 5.55$ g. The sample is then oven-dried at 105 °C to constant weight $W_d = 5.00$ g. Calculate **(a)** Moisture Regain and **(b)** Moisture Content. ### Part (a) — Moisture Regain $$ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{MR} &= \frac{W_w - W_d}{W_d} \times 100 \\[6pt] &= \frac{5.55\,\text{g} - 5.00\,\text{g}}{5.00\,\text{g}} \times 100 \\[6pt] &= \frac{0.55}{5.00} \times 100 \\[6pt] &= 11.0\,\% \end{aligned} $$ **Logic row 1:** The numerator represents the mass of water lost on drying, expressed as a fraction of the **oven-dry mass** (the international convention for textile testing, ISO 6741). **Logic row 2:** The result matches the **standard regain of silk (11.0 %)** — confirming proper conditioning. ### Part (b) — Moisture Content $$ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{MC} &= \frac{W_w - W_d}{W_w} \times 100 \\[6pt] &= \frac{0.55}{5.55} \times 100 \\[6pt] &= 9.91\,\% \end{aligned} $$ **Logic row 3:** MC uses the **original wet mass** in the denominator, so it is always numerically smaller than MR for the same sample. MC is used in **commercial trade**, MR in **scientific specification**. --- ## 3.2 Worked Example 2 — Degree of Polymerization of Fibroin **Problem:** The number-average molecular weight of a silk fibroin sample is $\overline{M}_n = 392\,000$ g/mol. The fibroin repeat unit has the average amino-acid residue mass $M_0 = 98$ g/mol (average of Gly-Ala-Gly-Ala-Gly-Ser). Estimate the **degree of polymerization**. $$ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{DP} &= \frac{\overline{M}_n}{M_0} \\[6pt] &= \frac{392\,000\,\text{g/mol}}{98\,\text{g/mol}} \\[6pt] &= 4\,000 \end{aligned} $$ **Logic row 1:** $M_0$ is the average residue mass because the sequence is a near-regular alternation of Gly and Ala with occasional Ser. **Logic row 2:** A DP of 4 000 is consistent with **native B. mori fibroin** (literature range 2 000 – 4 000). --- ## 3.3 Worked Example 3 — Crystallinity Index from XRD **Problem:** From the X-ray diffractogram of a degummed silk sample, the integrated intensity of the crystalline peak (at $2\theta \approx 20.5°$) is $I_c = 1\,820$ counts, and the amorphous halo area is $I_a = 2\,680$ counts. Compute the crystallinity index $X_c$. $$ \begin{aligned} X_c &= \frac{I_c}{I_c + I_a} \times 100 \\[6pt] &= \frac{1\,820}{1\,820 + 2\,680} \times 100 \\[6pt] &= \frac{1\,820}{4\,500} \times 100 \\[6pt] &= 40.4\,\% \end{aligned} $$ **Logic row 1:** The crystalline peak at $2\theta \approx 20.5°$ corresponds to the **(020) reflection of silk II β-sheets**. **Logic row 2:** A crystallinity of ~40 % confirms the **semi-crystalline nature** of silk — the amorphous regions are responsible for its elasticity, while the crystalline domains provide strength. --- ## 3.4 Analytical Matrix — Quick Comparison vs Other Natural Fibers | Property | Silk | Wool (Protein) | Cotton (Cellulose) | |---|---|---|---| | Dominant Monomer | Amino acids (Gly, Ala) | Amino acids (Cys-rich) | Glucose (β-1,4) | | Secondary Structure | β-pleated sheet | α-helix + disulfide bonds | — | | Polymer Class | Polypeptide (Fibroin) | Polypeptide (Keratin) | Polysaccharide | | Moisture Regain (%) | 11.0 | 14 – 18 | 8.5 | | Density (g/cm³) | 1.34 | 1.31 | 1.52 | | Crystallinity (%) | 40 – 50 | ~30 | 60 – 70 | | Burning Test | Burns slowly, self-extinguishes, smells of burnt hair (protein) | Same as silk | Burns rapidly, paper-like smell (cellulose) | | Solubility in 70 % H₂SO₄ | Dissolves | Dissolves | Insoluble (carbonizes) | | Key Spot Test | Millon's → red; Ninhydrin → purple | Millon's → red; Ninhydrin → purple | Iodine/H₂SO₄ → blue-black | > [!NOTE] > **Examiner Tip:** In a fiber-identification question, always justify the test outcome by linking the **chemical nature of the polymer** to the **observed response** — not just stating the result. This is how full marks are secured. --- # 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics ## 4.1 Mermaid Flowchart — Hierarchical Structure of Silk ```mermaid flowchart TD node1["Level 1 Primary Structure
Amino Acid Sequence
Gly Ala Gly Ala Gly Ser"] node2["Level 2 Secondary Structure

3 to 5 nanometer diameter"] node4["Level 4 Quaternary Structure
Two Brins plus Sericin equals Bave
10 to 25 micrometer diameter"] node5["Final Product
Silk Filament or Fabric"] node6["Amorphous Tie Chains
Provide Flexibility and Toughness"] node7["Sericin Gum
Globular Binding Protein"] node1 --> node2 node2 --> node3 node3 --> node4 node4 --> node5 node2 -.intercalated with.-> node6 node4 -.bound by.-> node7 ``` ## 4.2 Mermaid Block Diagram — Silk Processing & Identification Experiment ```mermaid flowchart LR nodeA["Silk Cocoon
Bombyx mori"] nodeB["Stifling and Sorting
Hot air or steam kills pupa"] nodeC["Reeling

0.35 to 0.55 N per tex"] pA --aligned against--> pB pA --donates H bond--> pC pB --donates H bond--> pD pC --> pE pD --> pE pE --> pF ``` > [!NOTE] > **Why this diagram matters:** The β-sheet architecture is the **single most testable concept** in the silk module. Drawing a clearly antiparallel arrangement (opposite arrow directions) and labeling the hydrogen bonds explicitly is worth **at least 3 marks** in any silk-related KTU 14-mark question. --- # 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap ## 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each) ### Q1. [KTU University Exam – Dec 2023, Model Paper] **Differentiate between fibroin and sericin in silk with respect to their chemical nature, function, and solubility.** **Model Answer (10 lines, 3 marks):** | Feature | Fibroin | Sericin | |---|---|---| | Nature | Fibrous, structural protein | Globular, amorphous protein | | Function | Provides tensile strength | Cements fibroin filaments (brins) | | Secondary structure | Antiparallel β-pleated sheet | Random coil | | Solubility in hot water | Insoluble | Soluble | | Proportion in raw silk | ~75 % | ~25 % | **Memory anchor:** *"Fibroin = the fiber; Sericin = the sticker."* --- ### Q2. [KTU University Exam – June 2024, Supple Paper] **Why does silk give the smell of burnt hair on burning? Name the chemical test that confirms its protein nature.** **Model Answer (4 lines, 3 marks):** - Silk, being a **polypeptide (protein)**, on thermal decomposition yields volatile amines, H₂S, and other nitrogenous fragments that produce the **characteristic odour of burnt hair/feathers** — a universal signature of protein fibers. - **Confirmatory spot test:** **Millon's reagent** gives a **red / brick-red precipitate** (with tyrosine residues), and **Ninhydrin** gives a **purple / Ruhemann's violet** colour. - These tests collectively confirm the protein backbone of silk, distinguishing it from cellulose (cotton) and synthetic fibers. --- ## 5.2 Part B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks Each, Internal Choice) > **[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023, Main Paper, Module 2 Experiment]** ### Question A (14 Marks) — *Choose either A or B* **(a)** With a neat labelled diagram, describe the **hierarchical structure of mulberry silk (B. mori)** from the amino acid level to the final filament. Highlight the role of **β-pleated sheets** in determining the mechanical properties. **(7 marks)** **(b)** Explain the **principle, procedure, and chemical basis** of the following identification tests for silk: (i) **Burning test** (ii) **Millon's test** (iii) **Solubility in 70 % H₂SO₄**. For each test, write the **observation and inference**. **(7 marks)** --- #### Model Solution — Question A **Part (a) — Hierarchical Structure of Silk (7 marks)** - **Level 1 – Primary structure:** The polypeptide fibroin chain is composed predominantly of the amino acid sequence **(-Gly-Ala-Gly-Ala-Gly-Ser-)ₙ**, where Gly ≈ 43.7 %, Ala ≈ 28.8 %, Ser ≈ 11.9 %. The small R-groups permit close chain packing. **(1.5 marks)** - **Level 2 – Secondary structure (β-sheets):** Adjacent chains align in an **antiparallel β-pleated sheet** configuration. The C=O and N–H groups of neighbouring chains form **inter-chain hydrogen bonds** (C=O···H–N), which act as the "molecular crosslinks" of the fiber. This is the **silk II** polymorph, the water-insoluble, mechanically strong form. **(2 marks)** - **Level 3 – Tertiary structure:** Stacks of β-sheets assemble into **crystalline microfibrils** (≈ 3–5 nm diameter), interspersed with **amorphous tie-chains** of less-ordered fibroin segments. **(1.5 marks)** - **Level 4 – Quaternary structure:** Two **brins** (fibroin filaments) are held together by a sericin sheath to form a single **bave** (≈ 10–25 μm diameter) — the actual silk thread. **(1 mark)** - **Role in mechanical properties:** The crystalline β-sheets bear the tensile load, giving **high tenacity (0.35–0.55 N/tex)** and **high Young's modulus**; the amorphous regions allow **chain sliding and energy dissipation**, producing **toughness and ~20 % elongation**. **(1 mark)** > *[Refer to the Mermaid block diagram in Section 4.1 for the schematic.]* **Part (b) — Identification Tests (7 marks)** | Test | Principle | Procedure | Observation | Inference | |---|---|---|---|---| | **Burning Test** | Proteins decompose to release volatile N-compounds (amines, H₂S) | Hold a few fibers near a flame | Burns slowly, **self-extinguishes** when flame removed, curls away from flame, **emits smell of burnt hair** | Confirms **proteinaceous / polypeptide** nature (distinguishes from cellulose & synthetics) | | **Millon's Test** | Mercuric nitrate + nitrous acid reacts with the **phenolic –OH of tyrosine** residues | Treat fiber with Millon's reagent, warm gently | **Red / brick-red precipitate or coloration** | Confirms presence of **tyrosine-bearing protein** (i.e., a protein fiber); both silk and wool give positive | | **70 % H₂SO₄ Solubility** | Concentrated H₂SO₄ hydrolyses peptide bonds, dissolving the fiber | Immerse fiber in 70 % H₂SO₄ at room temperature | **Dissolves completely** (in 2–3 min) | Confirms protein; **distinguishes from cotton** (insoluble, chars) and from synthetics (insoluble) | > *Mnemonic: "**B**urn → **M**illon → **S**ulphuric" = **BMS** — the tri-test for silk. (Examiner award 1 mark for using neat tabulation.)* **Valuation cues:** 7 marks = (a) 1.5 + 2 + 1.5 + 1 + 1 for hierarchical + role = perfect 7; (b) 2 marks for principle+procedure of each, 1 mark for observation+inference. Tabular format gets bonus 0.5 mark. --- ### Question B (14 Marks) — *Alternative Choice* **(a)** Describe the **chemical composition, degumming process, and physical properties** of mulberry silk. Why is degumming essential before dyeing? **(7 marks)** **(b)** A **5.00 g sample of raw silk** is conditioned at 65 % RH, giving $W_w = 5.55$ g. After oven-drying to constant weight, $W_d = 5.00$ g. Calculate: (i) **Moisture Regain (MR)** and **Moisture Content (MC)** (ii) If the same sample shows an X-ray crystallinity index of 42.5 % and density 1.34 g/cm³, comment on the **suitability of this fiber for high-strength textile applications** based on its structure–property correlation. **(7 marks)** --- #### Model Solution — Question B **Part (a) — Chemical Composition, Degumming & Properties (7 marks)** - **Chemical composition of raw silk:** Two proteins — **fibroin (~75 %, structural)** and **sericin (~25 %, gummy binder)**. Trace amounts of waxes, fats, mineral salts and natural pigments (e.g., flavonoids giving yellow tint to mulberry silk). **(1.5 marks)** - **Degumming process:** Cocoons (or yarn) are treated in a hot **alkaline soap solution** (Na₂CO₃ 0.5–1.0 %, 95–100 °C, 30–60 min). This **hydrolyses sericin** into water-soluble peptides, which are washed away. **(2 marks)** - **Why degumming is essential before dyeing:** Sericin forms a **hydrophobic, impermeable layer** that blocks dye molecules from reaching the fibroin. Removal of sericin exposes the **reactive amino (–NH₂) and carboxyl (–COOH) groups** of fibroin, allowing **acid, reactive and direct dyes** to form ionic / covalent bonds with the fiber. Degumming also improves **lustre, handle, and whiteness**. **(2 marks)** - **Physical properties of degummed silk:** Tenacity 0.35–0.55 N/tex, elongation 18–25 %, moisture regain 11.0 %, density 1.34 g/cm³, thermal decomposition ≈ 300 °C, excellent drape, soft handle, natural lustre. **(1.5 marks)** **Part (b) — Numerical & Conceptual (7 marks)** **(i) MR and MC Calculation (4 marks):** $$ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{MR} &= \frac{5.55 - 5.00}{5.00} \times 100 = 11.0\,\% \\[6pt] \mathrm{MC} &= \frac{5.55 - 5.00}{5.55} \times 100 = 9.91\,\% \end{aligned} $$ Both values are within standard specifications for mulberry silk (MR = 11.0 %). **(ii) Structure–Property Comment (3 marks):** - A crystallinity of **42.5 %** places the sample in the **upper range of native silk II** (40–50 %), implying a high proportion of load-bearing β-sheets. - Combined with the **low density of 1.34 g/cm³**, the fiber offers an **excellent strength-to-weight ratio**. - **Conclusion:** This silk is **highly suitable for high-strength textile applications** such as parachute fabric, surgical sutures, and light-weight protective garments. - A higher crystallinity (>50 %) would make the fiber stiffer and less comfortable; a lower value (<35 %) would compromise strength. The 42.5 % value is therefore **optimum**. > [!WARNING] > **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Pitfalls** > 1. **Conflating MR and MC** — They are *not* interchangeable. MR uses $W_d$ in the denominator; MC uses $W_w$. Mixing them up costs **1 full mark** in numerical questions. > 2. **Forgetting the factor of 100** when reporting percentages — leads to a wrong order of magnitude. > 3. **Writing "silk is strong because of its protein nature"** — this is too vague. Always specify the **β-pleated sheet, hydrogen bonding, and crystallinity** to earn the structural mark. > 4. **Confusing Silk I and Silk II** — Silk I is the *freshly-spun, water-soluble, helical* form; Silk II is the *stable, β-sheet, water-insoluble* form. Examiners are fond of this trap. > 5. **Omitting the labelled diagram** in 7-mark structural questions — a clean block diagram is worth **at least 1 mark** by itself. --- ## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember - **Silk = protein fiber = polypeptide = fibroin (structural) + sericin (gum)**. - **Chemical signature:** Gly–Ala–Gly–Ala–Gly–Ser repeat; **β-pleated sheet (Silk II)**; **antiparallel** chain orientation; **inter-chain H-bonds**. - **Key constants (commit to memory):** density 1.30–1.38 g/cm³, moisture regain 11.0 %, tenacity 0.35–0.55 N/tex, elongation 18–25 %, crystallinity 40–50 %, T_decomp ≈ 300 °C. - **Degumming** with alkaline soap removes sericin → essential for dyeing, improves lustre and handle. - **Identification tri-test (BMS):** **B**urning (burnt hair smell) + **M**illon's (red) + **S**ulphuric acid 70 % (dissolves) → confirm protein, rule out cellulose and synthetics. - **Why silk is strong:** β-sheets + H-bonds + crystallinity + low density → exceptional specific strength. - **Why silk is tough:** Amorphous tie-chains between crystalline microfibrils allow energy dissipation. - **Engineering relevance:** Inspiration for **regenerated silk fibroin biomaterials** — sutures, scaffolds, flexible bioelectronics, regenerative tissue engineering. - **Trap to avoid:** Silk I (fresh, soluble, helical) vs Silk II (stable, β-sheet, insoluble). - **Formula drill:** $\mathrm{MR} = \frac{W_w - W_d}{W_d}\times 100$ ; $\mathrm{MC} = \frac{W_w - W_d}{W_w}\times 100$ ; $\mathrm{DP} = \frac{\overline{M}_n}{M_0}$ ; $X_c = \frac{I_c}{I_c + I_a}\times 100$. ---
