# SECTION 5: KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

---

## PART A — 3-Mark Questions (Short Answer)

### **Q1. [KTU University Exam – May 2024]**
**Define the term "weave crimp" and explain its effect on the strength of a fiber-reinforced polymer composite.**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**
Weave crimp refers to the **undulation (waviness)** of warp and weft yarns as they pass over and under each other in a woven fabric reinforcement. As the crimp angle $\theta$ increases, the effective load-carrying direction of the fiber deviates from the applied load direction. A first-order correction gives a strength reduction factor of $\cos^2 \theta$. In a typical plain weave, crimp can reduce in-plane strength by **10–25 %** compared to a unidirectional reinforcement. (3 marks)

---

### **Q2. [KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]**
**List any three bonding mechanisms at the fiber–matrix interface. Which is the most important prerequisite for the others to be effective?**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**
The four bonding mechanisms are:
1. Mechanical interlocking
2. Chemical bonding
3. Physical (van der Waals) adsorption
4. Thermodynamic wetting

**Wetting is the most important prerequisite.** If the matrix does not wet the fiber (high contact angle, poor spreading), it cannot penetrate into micropores (so no mechanical interlocking) and cannot establish molecular contact for chemical or physical bonding. (3 marks)

---

## PART B — 14-Mark Questions (ESE Module Internal Choice)

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout**
> - ❌ **Do not** confuse **fiber volume fraction** with **fiber weight fraction** — show the conversion step.
> - ❌ **Do not** write only the final number in 14-mark numerical problems; **every substitution must be shown** for full marks.
> - ❌ **Do not** omit the **assumption of perfect bonding** when applying the rule of mixtures — it is the most-tested concept.
> - ❌ **Do not** interchange **IFSS (interfacial shear strength)** with **ILSS (interlaminar shear strength)** — they are different tests (single-fiber pull-out vs. short-beam shear).
> - ❌ **Do not** forget to state **units** for every numerical answer — KTU examiners often deduct 0.5 mark for missing units.

---

### **Question A (14 Marks)**
**[KTU University Exam – Model Question, ESE Pattern]**

> **(a)** With neat sketches, explain the **three primary weave patterns** (plain, twill, satin) used in polymer composite reinforcements. Compare their relative merits in terms of **crimp, drapability, and in-plane strength**. **(7 marks)**
>
> **(b)** A unidirectional glass-fiber reinforced epoxy composite has a fiber volume fraction of **0.55**. Given: $\sigma_f = 2200$ MPa, $\sigma_m = 55$ MPa, $E_f = 72$ GPa, $E_m = 3.5$ GPa, $\rho_f = 2.54$ g/cm³, $\rho_m = 1.15$ g/cm³. Calculate:
> (i) Longitudinal tensile strength
> (ii) Longitudinal Young's modulus
> (iii) Transverse Young's modulus (using inverse rule of mixtures)
> (iv) Composite density
> **(7 marks)**

#### **Model Solution to Question A**

**(a) Weave patterns — 7 marks**

| Weave | Schematic (description) | Crimp | Drapability | In-plane strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Plain (1/1)** | Each warp over 1 weft, under 1 weft; "checkerboard" appearance | Highest (8–12 %) | Fair | Moderate (fiber undulation reduces efficiency) |
| **Twill (2/2)** | Each warp over 2 wefts, under 2; diagonal twill line visible | Medium (4–7 %) | Good | High (lower crimp, better alignment under load) |
| **Satin (5HS)** | Each warp over 4 wefts, under 1; no visible diagonal | Lowest (2–4 %) | Excellent | Highest (fibers almost straight, near-UD efficiency) |

> *Award 2 marks for plain weave, 2 marks for twill, 2 marks for satin, 1 mark for the comparison table.*

**(b) Numerical solution — 7 marks**

**(i) Longitudinal tensile strength** (Rule of mixtures):

$$
\sigma_{cL} = V_f \sigma_f + (1 - V_f) \sigma_m
$$

$$
\sigma_{cL} = (0.55 \times 2200) + (0.45 \times 55)
$$

$$
\sigma_{cL} = 1210 + 24.75 = 1234.75 \approx \mathbf{1234.75 \text{ MPa}}
$$

*2 marks*

**(ii) Longitudinal Young's modulus** (Rule of mixtures — Voigt model):

$$
E_{cL} = V_f E_f + (1 - V_f) E_m
$$

$$
E_{cL} = (0.55 \times 72) + (0.45 \times 3.5)
$$

$$
E_{cL} = 39.6 + 1.575 = \mathbf{41.18 \text{ GPa}}
$$

*2 marks*

**(iii) Transverse Young's modulus** (Inverse rule of mixtures — Reuss model):

$$
\dfrac{1}{E_{cT}} = \dfrac{V_f}{E_f} + \dfrac{(1-V_f)}{E_m}
$$

$$
\dfrac{1}{E_{cT}} = \dfrac{0.55}{72} + \dfrac{0.45}{3.5} = 0.007639 + 0.128571 = 0.136210 \text{ GPa}^{-1}
$$

$$
E_{cT} = \dfrac{1}{0.136210} = \mathbf{7.34 \text{ GPa}}
$$

*2 marks*

**(iv) Composite density**:

$$
\rho_c = V_f \rho_f + (1 - V_f) \rho_m
$$

$$
\rho_c = (0.55 \times 2.54) + (0.45 \times 1.15)
$$

$$
\rho_c = 1.397 + 0.5175 = \mathbf{1.9145 \text{ g/cm}^3}
$$

*1 mark*

> **Final answer box**: $\sigma_{cL} = 1234.75$ MPa, $E_{cL} = 41.18$ GPa, $E_{cT} = 7.34$ GPa, $\rho_c = 1.91$ g/cm³.

---

### **Question B (14 Marks) — Alternative Choice**

**[KTU University Exam – Model Question, ESE Pattern]**

> **(a)** Explain the **four major mechanisms of fiber–matrix bonding** in polymer composites. What is the role of **silane coupling agents** in improving the bond between glass fibers and epoxy resin? **(7 marks)**
>
> **(b)** Derive the expression for **critical fiber length** $l_c$. A carbon fiber of diameter **8 μm** and tensile strength **4500 MPa** is embedded in an epoxy matrix with an interfacial shear strength of **45 MPa**. Compute the critical fiber length and comment on whether a woven fabric of this fiber would achieve full strength translation efficiency. **(7 marks)**

#### **Model Solution to Question B**

**(a) Four bonding mechanisms — 7 marks**

1. **Mechanical interlocking (2 marks):** The polymer matrix, when cured, conforms to the surface roughness and micro-pores of the fiber. The "anchor-and-loop" mechanical coupling requires good matrix flow during processing (low viscosity, proper wetting). Most significant for carbon fibers with their characteristic grooved surface and for sized glass fibers.

2. **Chemical bonding (2 marks):** Covalent, ionic, or hydrogen bonds form between reactive functional groups on the fiber surface (–OH, –COOH, –NH₂) and the matrix (e.g., epoxide rings of epoxy). This is the strongest form of bonding and is the primary purpose of fiber surface treatments.

3. **Physical (van der Waals) adsorption (1 mark):** Weak, short-range London dispersion forces act between matrix molecules and the fiber surface. Always present; magnitude depends on molecular contact area, which is governed by wetting.

4. **Thermodynamic wetting (1 mark):** A low contact angle $\theta$ ensures the matrix spreads spontaneously, maximizing contact. Wetting is the **prerequisite** for the other three mechanisms.

**Silane coupling agents (1 mark):** Silanes such as γ-aminopropyltriethoxysilane have a dual functionality:
- The **alkoxy (–O–Si) end** hydrolyzes and reacts with –OH groups on the glass surface to form a stable **Si–O–Si** covalent bridge.
- The **organic functional group (–NH₂)** reacts with the epoxy resin during cure.
This creates a **molecular bridge** between the inorganic fiber and the organic matrix, dramatically improving IFSS and moisture resistance.

**(b) Critical fiber length derivation — 7 marks**

**Derivation (4 marks)**:

Force balance on a short fiber of diameter $d$ and embedded length $l_e$:

$$
\sigma_f \cdot \dfrac{\pi d^2}{4} = \tau_i \cdot \pi d \cdot \dfrac{l_c}{2}
$$

Simplify:

$$
\sigma_f \cdot \dfrac{d}{4} = \tau_i \cdot \dfrac{l_c}{2}
$$

$$
\boxed{\;l_c = \dfrac{\sigma_f \, d}{2 \, \tau_i}\;}
$$

**Numerical computation (2 marks)**:

$$
l_c = \dfrac{4500 \times 8 \times 10^{-3}}{2 \times 45} = \dfrac{36}{90} = \mathbf{0.40 \text{ mm}}
$$

**Comment (1 mark)**:

A typical woven fabric is made from **continuous filament tows** where the effective fiber length $l$ is many kilometers ($\gg l_c$). Therefore, $l \gg l_c$ and the fiber efficiency factor $\eta_l \to 1$. The woven fabric will achieve **near-full strength translation efficiency**, provided the bonding is adequate (good wetting and silane treatment).

---

## Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!TIP]
> **Rapid-Revision Checklist for KTU University Exam**

- ✅ **Weaving** = interlacing warp (0°) and weft (90°) yarns. Three patterns: **plain, twill, satin**.
- ✅ **Crimp** reduces effective fiber strength by a factor of $\cos^2 \theta$. Lower crimp → higher in-plane strength.
- ✅ **Plain weave** = most stable, highest crimp. **Satin** = smoothest, lowest crimp, best for aerospace.
- ✅ **Bonding** has 4 mechanisms: mechanical, chemical, physical, wetting — and **wetting is the prerequisite**.
- ✅ **Silane coupling agents** form Si–O–Si bridges between glass and epoxy (dual functionality).
- ✅ **Rule of mixtures** (longitudinal): $\sigma_{cL} = V_f \sigma_f + (1-V_f)\sigma_m$.
- ✅ **Inverse rule of mixtures** (transverse modulus): $\frac{1}{E_{cT}} = \frac{V_f}{E_f} + \frac{1-V_f}{E_m}$.
- ✅ **Critical fiber length**: $l_c = \dfrac{\sigma_f \, d}{2 \tau_i}$. Continuous woven fibers → $l \gg l_c$ → full strength.
- ✅ **IFSS** (interfacial shear strength) measured by **single-fiber pull-out test**: $\tau_i = \dfrac{F_{max}}{\pi d l_e}$.
- ✅ **Work of adhesion** (Dupré): $W_a = \gamma_{lv}(1 + \cos\theta)$ — higher when $\theta$ is low.
- ✅ **Surface treatments**: silane (glass), oxidation (carbon), alkali (natural fibers).
- ✅ **Volume fraction vs weight fraction**: $V_f = \dfrac{\rho_m W_f}{\rho_f W_f + \rho_m W_m}$.
- ✅ **Assumption for rule of mixtures to hold**: perfect bonding + iso-strain + aligned continuous fibers.
- ✅ **Units must be stated** for every numerical answer (MPa, GPa, g/cm³, mm).
- ✅ **ASTM standards** relevant: D3039 (tension), D7264 (flexion), D2344 (short-beam shear), D5229 (conditioning).

# 🧵 Properties of Yarns — Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition

In polymer and textile engineering, a **yarn** is a continuous assembly of interlocked, twisted, or otherwise cohesively bound fibers, filaments, or other linear material units, primarily used in weaving, knitting, braiding, sewing, and the production of technical textiles. The **properties of yarns** constitute the quantitative and qualitative characteristics that govern their processability, structural integrity, aesthetic performance, and end-use suitability. These properties are conventionally classified into three principal engineering domains:

1. **Geometric Properties** — Linear density (yarn count), diameter, cross-sectional shape, and twist characteristics.
2. **Mechanical Properties** — Tensile strength, tenacity, elongation at break, modulus, and fatigue behavior.
3. **Surface & Aesthetic Properties** — Evenness (CV%), hairiness, luster, friction, and moisture regain.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Syllabus Highlight:** As per the KTU 2024 Scheme (NEP 2020) for PCPOL607, Module Experiment 2 requires the student to *experimentally determine* yarn properties using standard testing protocols (IS, ASTM, and BIS standards). Theoretical understanding must be coupled with hands-on testing of linear density, twist, tensile strength, and evenness.

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Plain-English Intuition

Think of a yarn like a **rope made of many tiny strings twisted together** — just as the strength, thickness, and smoothness of a rope depend on how the strings are twisted and how many there are, the **properties of a yarn depend on the fiber composition, twist level, and uniformity of fiber distribution**.

- **Twist** is like wringing a wet towel — the more you twist, the tighter the fibers bind, but too much twist can make the yarn harsh and weak.
- **Yarn count** is the "thickness rating" of a yarn — a higher number means thinner yarn, and vice versa.
- **Evenness** is how uniformly the fibers are distributed along the yarn — like a well-mixed cup of coffee vs. one with lumps of powder.

> [!NOTE]
> **Standard Units Used in Yarn Testing (BIS / IS Standards):**
> - **Yarn Count:** Tex, Denier, Metric (Nm), English (Ne)
> - **Twist:** Turns per meter (TPM) or Turns per inch (TPI)
> - **Tensile Strength:** Gram-force (gf) or Centi-Newton (cN)
> - **Tenacity:** cN/tex or gf/tex
> - **Evenness:** CV% (Coefficient of Variation of mass per unit length)

---

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# 🔬 Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 Geometric Properties of Yarn

### 2.1.1 Yarn Count (Linear Density)

Yarn count defines the **mass per unit length** of the yarn. It is the most fundamental geometric property because it directly influences the fabric's weight, cover factor, and hand-feel.

There are two major systems of yarn count expression:

**(a) Indirect System** (length per unit weight — *higher number = finer yarn*)
- **English Count (Ne):** Number of 840-yard lengths per pound.
- **Metric Count (Nm):** Number of 1-meter lengths per gram.
- **Worsted Count, Linen Count, Cotton Count** — all indirect systems used for specific fiber types.

**(b) Direct System** (weight per unit length — *higher number = coarser yarn*)
- **Tex:** Weight in grams of 1000 meters of yarn.
- **Denier (Td):** Weight in grams of 9000 meters of yarn.
- **Decitex (dtex):** Weight in grams of 10,000 meters of yarn.

### 2.1.2 Twist

Twist is the **number of turns per unit length** inserted into the yarn to bind the constituent fibers/filaments together. It is the principal factor giving yarn its **cohesion, strength, and handle**.

- **Direction of Twist:**
  - **S-Twist:** Fibers follow the direction of the central part of the letter "S".
  - **Z-Twist:** Fibers follow the direction of the central part of the letter "Z".
- **Twist Multiplier (TM):** A normalized measure of twist intensity, independent of yarn count. Higher TM → harder, more compact yarn.

### 2.1.3 Diameter

The diameter of a yarn is inversely related to its linear density. For circular cross-section assumption:

$$d = \sqrt{\frac{4 \times 10^{6}}{\pi \times \rho \times N}} \;\; \text{(micrometers)}$$

where $\rho$ is yarn density in g/cm³ and $N$ is the yarn count (Nm).

## 2.2 Mechanical Properties of Yarn

### 2.2.1 Tensile Strength

The maximum tensile force a yarn can sustain before rupture, measured in gf or cN. Measured on a **C.R.E. (Constant Rate of Extension) tensile tester** (e.g., Instron, Statimat) as per **IS 1671** and **ASTM D2256**.

### 2.2.2 Tenacity

Specific strength — tensile strength normalized by linear density. This makes comparison between yarns of different counts meaningful.

$$\text{Tenacity} = \frac{\text{Breaking Force}}{\text{Linear Density}}$$

### 2.2.3 Elongation at Break

The percentage extension of a yarn at the moment of rupture, indicating its **ductility** and **stretch behavior** during processing.

### 2.2.4 Modulus and Work of Rupture

Initial modulus reflects the yarn's resistance to elastic deformation. Work of rupture (toughness) is the total energy absorbed before breakage.

## 2.3 Surface Properties

### 2.3.1 Evenness (C.V.%)

Measured using a **Uster Evenness Tester** as per **IS 13679**. Imperfections are classified as:
- **Thin places** (−50% of mean mass)
- **Thick places** (+50% of mean mass)
- **Neps** (+200% of mean mass, < 4 mm length)

### 2.3.2 Hairiness

Protruding fiber ends on the yarn surface, measured by **Zweigle Hairiness Tester** or **Uster Hairiness Module (H value)**.

### 2.3.3 Friction and Abrasion

Important for downstream processing like knitting and weaving. Measured by the **Yarn Friction Tester (e.g., Lawson-Hemphill)**.

---

## 2.4 📋 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

| # | Property | Formula | Unit | Standard |
|---|----------|---------|------|----------|
| 1 | Tex | $\text{Tex} = \dfrac{W_{(g)}}{L_{(m)}} \times 1000$ | g/km | — |
| 2 | Denier | $\text{Denier} = \dfrac{W_{(g)}}{L_{(m)}} \times 9000$ | g/9 km | — |
| 3 | Metric Count | $N_m = \dfrac{L_{(m)}}{W_{(g)}}$ | m/g | — |
| 4 | English Count | $N_e = \dfrac{L_{(yds)}}{W_{(lbs)} \times 840}$ | — | — |
| 5 | Conversion | $1 \text{ Tex} = 9 \text{ Denier} = \dfrac{1000}{N_m} = \dfrac{590.5}{N_e}$ | — | — |
| 6 | Twist Multiplier (Cotton) | $TM = \dfrac{TPI}{\sqrt{N_e}}$ | — | — |
| 7 | Twist Multiplier (Metric) | $TM = \dfrac{TPM}{\sqrt{N_m}}$ | — | — |
| 8 | Tenacity | $\text{Tenacity} = \dfrac{\text{Breaking Force (cN)}}{\text{Tex}}$ | cN/tex | IS 1671 |
| 9 | C.V.% of Evenness | $CV\% = \dfrac{\sigma}{\bar{x}} \times 100$ | % | IS 13679 |
| 10 | Yarn Diameter (approx) | $d = \sqrt{\dfrac{4 \times 10^{6}}{\pi \rho N_m}}$ | µm | — |
| 11 | Elongation % | $\epsilon\% = \dfrac{L_{break} - L_{initial}}{L_{initial}} \times 100$ | % | ASTM D2256 |
| 12 | Moisture Regain | $R = \dfrac{W_{wet} - W_{dry}}{W_{dry}} \times 100$ | % | IS 199 |

> [!NOTE]
> **Engineering Utility:** Yarn properties are critical for:
> - **Weaving/knitting machine settings** (tension, speed, yarn guides)
> - **Fabric weight calculation** (e.g., GSM = $\dfrac{\text{Tex} \times \text{EPI} \times \text{PPI}}{1000}$)
> - **Quality control in spinning mills** (Uster Statistics benchmarking)
> - **Technical textile design** (composites, geotextiles, filtration)

# ⚙️ Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Worked Derivation: Relationship Between Tex, Denier, and Metric Count

**Given:**
- 1 km of yarn weighs $W$ grams.
- Linear density in Tex: $\text{Tex} = W$ (since 1000 m = 1 km).

### Step 1 — Derive Tex in terms of grams per meter

A yarn of 1 Tex weighs 1 gram per 1000 meters.

$$
1 \, \text{Tex} = \frac{1 \, \text{g}}{1000 \, \text{m}} = 10^{-3} \, \text{g/m}
$$

### Step 2 — Express Denier in the same units

$$
1 \, \text{Denier} = \frac{1 \, \text{g}}{9000 \, \text{m}} = \frac{10^{-3}}{9} \, \text{g/m}
$$

### Step 3 — Compute the Tex-to-Denier ratio

$$
\frac{1 \, \text{Tex}}{1 \, \text{Denier}} = \frac{10^{-3} \, \text{g/m}}{10^{-3}/9 \, \text{g/m}} = 9
$$

$$
\boxed{\text{Denier} = 9 \times \text{Tex}}
$$

### Step 4 — Relate Tex and Metric Count

Metric Count $N_m$ is the number of meters per gram:

$$
N_m = \frac{L_{(m)}}{W_{(g)}}
$$

For a yarn weighing 1 gram in 1000 m: $N_m = 1000$, and Tex $= 1$. Therefore:

$$
\text{Tex} = \frac{1000}{N_m}
$$

### Step 5 — Relate Tex and English Count

For 1 Tex: $W = 1$ g per 1000 m.
- Length in yards: $1000 \times 1.0936 = 1093.6$ yards.
- Weight in pounds: $1 \, g = 1/453.59$ lbs $= 2.205 \times 10^{-3}$ lbs.

$$
N_e = \frac{1093.6}{2.205 \times 10^{-3} \times 840} \approx 590.5
$$

$$
\boxed{N_e = \frac{590.5}{\text{Tex}}}
$$

## 3.2 Worked Numerical Example — Yarn Count & Tenacity

> **Problem:** A 100 m sample of polyester yarn weighs 1.5 g. The breaking load on a tensile tester is found to be 450 cN. Calculate the yarn count in Tex, Denier, and Metric Count, and the tenacity.

**Step 1 — Tex**

$$
\text{Tex} = \frac{W_{(g)}}{L_{(m)}} \times 1000 = \frac{1.5}{100} \times 1000 = 15 \, \text{Tex}
$$

**Step 2 — Denier**

$$
\text{Denier} = 9 \times \text{Tex} = 9 \times 15 = 135 \, \text{D}
$$

**Step 3 — Metric Count**

$$
N_m = \frac{L_{(m)}}{W_{(g)}} = \frac{100}{1.5} = 66.67 \, \text{m/g}
$$

**Step 4 — Tenacity**

$$
\text{Tenacity} = \frac{450 \, \text{cN}}{15 \, \text{Tex}} = 30 \, \text{cN/tex}
$$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Result Interpretation:** A 15 Tex, 30 cN/tex yarn is a **medium-fine polyester filament yarn** of good tenacity — typical of apparel-grade applications. Tenacity above 25 cN/tex qualifies as **high-tenacity**, used in technical textiles.

## 3.3 Worked Numerical Example — Twist Multiplier & Fabric GSM

> **Problem:** A cotton yarn of $N_e = 40$ has a measured TPI of 20. Find (a) Twist Multiplier, and (b) GSM of a plain-weave fabric with EPI = 60 and PPI = 50.

**Step 1 — Twist Multiplier**

$$
TM = \frac{TPI}{\sqrt{N_e}} = \frac{20}{\sqrt{40}} = \frac{20}{6.3246} \approx 3.16
$$

**Step 2 — Convert Ne to Tex**

$$
\text{Tex} = \frac{590.5}{N_e} = \frac{590.5}{40} = 14.76 \, \text{Tex}
$$

**Step 3 — GSM of the fabric**

$$
GSM = \frac{\text{Tex} \times (EPI + PPI)}{1000} = \frac{14.76 \times (60 + 50)}{1000} = \frac{14.76 \times 110}{1000} = 1.624 \, \text{g/m}^2
$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Correction Note (KTU Examiner Tip):** The standard formula for fabric weight (woven) using Tex is:
> $$ GSM = \frac{(Tex_{warp} \times EPI) + (Tex_{weft} \times PPI)}{1000} $$
> If warp and weft are of the same yarn (as above), the formula simplifies correctly. If they differ, the examiner expects the student to sum them **separately**.

---

## 3.4 📊 Analytical Matrix — Properties vs. Test Methods

| Property | Instrument | Standard | Typical Range (Apparel) |
|----------|-----------|----------|------------------------|
| Yarn Count (Tex) | Wrap Reel + Balance | IS 1315 | 10–50 Tex |
| Twist | Twist Tester (Manual/Auto) | IS 832 | 5–30 TPI |
| Tensile Strength | CRE Tensile Tester | IS 1671 | 200–600 cN |
| Tenacity | Derived from above | IS 1671 | 15–35 cN/tex |
| Elongation | CRE Tensile Tester | ASTM D2256 | 8–25 % |
| Evenness (CV%) | Uster Evenness Tester | IS 13679 | 12–18 % |
| Hairiness (H) | Zweigle / Uster | ISO 16549 | 3–8 |
| Moisture Regain | Oven Dry Method | IS 199 | 4–13 % (fiber-dependent) |

This counter-twisting locks the fibers in place and produces a **balanced, stable yarn** that resists untwisting and snarling — a critical requirement for high-quality sewing threads and weaving yarns.

# 📝 KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## PART A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

### Q1. **[KTU University Exam — June 2024]** Define **yarn count**. Differentiate between **direct** and **indirect** systems of yarn count with one example each.

**Model Answer:**

**Yarn count** is a numerical expression of the linear density (mass per unit length) or fineness of a yarn, and is the most fundamental geometric property used in textile engineering.

| Aspect | Direct System | Indirect System |
|--------|---------------|-----------------|
| Definition | Weight per unit length | Length per unit weight |
| Higher number means | Coarser yarn | Finer yarn |
| Example: Tex | Weight in g of 1000 m | — |
| Example: Denier | Weight in g of 9000 m | — |
| Example: Metric Nm | — | m/g |
| Example: English Ne | — | 840 yds/lb |

(3 marks)

---

### Q2. **[KTU University Exam — Dec 2023]** Explain the difference between **S-twist** and **Z-twist** yarns. Why is twist direction important in plied yarn construction?

**Model Answer:**

- **S-Twist:** Fibers follow the direction of the central portion of the letter "S". On the yarn surface, the diagonal lines run from lower-left to upper-right when the yarn is held vertically.
- **Z-Twist:** Fibers follow the direction of the central portion of the letter "Z". Diagonal lines run from upper-left to lower-right.

**Importance in plied yarn:**
The plies are usually twisted in the **opposite direction** to the singles. This counter-twist action binds the singles together, **balances the torque**, and prevents the yarn from snarling or untwisting. For example, two Z-twist singles are plied with an S-twist.

(3 marks)

---

## PART B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks Each, Choice Based)

### 📌 Question A (14 Marks)

**[KTU University Exam — Model Paper 2024, Module Experiment 2]**

**(a) [7 Marks]** Describe with neat diagrams the **method for determination of yarn count (Tex)** as per **IS 1315**. List the apparatus required and the precautions to be taken.

**(b) [7 Marks]** A cotton yarn sample of length 120 m weighs 2.4 g. The yarn has 18 TPI. Calculate:
  (i) Yarn count in Tex, Denier, English Count (Ne), and Metric Count (Nm)
  (ii) Twist Multiplier
  (iii) Tenacity, if the breaking load is 480 cN

**Model Solution:**

#### (a) Determination of Yarn Count (Tex) — IS 1315

**Apparatus Required:**
- Wrap reel (1 m or 1.5 m circumference)
- Analytical balance (accuracy 0.001 g)
- Conditioning chamber (standard atmosphere: 65 ± 2 % RH, 27 ± 2 °C)
- Yarn package holder

**Procedure:**
1. Condition the yarn sample for **24 hours** in a standard atmosphere (as per IS 6359).
2. Mount the yarn package on the creel and thread it through the wrap reel guides.
3. Wind **100 wraps** of 1 m each = **100 m of yarn** onto the wrap reel.
4. Carefully remove the yarn skein and weigh it accurately on the analytical balance.
5. Record the mass $W$ in grams.
6. Calculate Tex as:

$$
\text{Tex} = \frac{W_{(g)}}{L_{(m)}} \times 1000
$$

7. Repeat for **at least 5 samples** and take the mean.

**Precautions:**
- Yarn must be conditioned to standard moisture equilibrium.
- Tension during wrapping must be uniform and low.
- Skein must be weighed immediately after removal to avoid moisture fluctuation.
- Multiple measurements should be averaged to minimize random error.

#### (b) Numerical Solution

**Given:** $L = 120$ m, $W = 2.4$ g, TPI $= 18$, Breaking load $= 480$ cN.

**(i) Yarn Count:**

- Tex:
$$
\text{Tex} = \frac{2.4}{120} \times 1000 = 20 \, \text{Tex}
$$

- Denier:
$$
\text{Denier} = 9 \times 20 = 180 \, \text{D}
$$

- Metric Count:
$$
N_m = \frac{120}{2.4} = 50 \, \text{m/g}
$$

- English Count:
$$
N_e = \frac{590.5}{20} = 29.53
$$

**(ii) Twist Multiplier:**

$$
TM = \frac{TPI}{\sqrt{N_e}} = \frac{18}{\sqrt{29.53}} = \frac{18}{5.434} \approx 3.31
$$

**(iii) Tenacity:**

$$
\text{Tenacity} = \frac{480}{20} = 24 \, \text{cN/tex}
$$

**Result:** The yarn is a 20 Tex, 24 cN/tex cotton yarn with a moderate twist level — suitable for medium-weight apparel fabric.

(14 marks)

---

### 📌 Question B (14 Marks) — Alternative Choice

**[KTU University Exam — Model Paper 2024, Module Experiment 2]**

**(a) [7 Marks]** Explain the **Uster Evenness Test** for yarns. Discuss the parameters CV%, thin places, thick places, and neps with reference to **IS 13679**.

**(b) [7 Marks]** Discuss the factors affecting **tenacity of a spun yarn** and explain the role of **fiber length, fineness, and twist** in determining yarn strength.

**Model Solution:**

#### (a) Uster Evenness Test — IS 13679

**Principle:** A known length of yarn is drawn at constant speed through a capacitive or optical sensing head. Mass variations cause proportional changes in capacitance/optical density, recorded as a voltage signal.

**Parameters Measured:**

1. **Mean Linear Density ($\bar{x}$):** Average mass per unit length (mg/m or ktex).
2. **Coefficient of Variation (CV%):**
$$
CV\% = \frac{\sigma}{\bar{x}} \times 100
$$
where $\sigma$ is the standard deviation of mass per unit length. **Lower CV% = more even yarn.**

3. **Imperfections per 1000 m:**
   - **Thin places:** −50% of mean (sensitive to fabric appearance).
   - **Thick places:** +50% of mean (cause uneven dyeing).
   - **Neps:** +200% of mean, length < 4 mm (affect fabric surface smoothness).

4. **Spectrogram & Variance-Length Curve:** Diagnostic tools to identify sources of variation (drafting wave, periodic fault, random error).

**Acceptance:** Compared against **Uster Statistics** (industry benchmark) for grading yarn into categories (5%, 25%, 50%, 75% levels).

#### (b) Factors Affecting Tenacity of Spun Yarn

1. **Fiber Length:** Longer fibers provide more contact points and better grip through twist. Longer staple → higher tenacity (up to a limit).

2. **Fiber Fineness:** Finer fibers offer more fibers per cross-section → better load distribution → higher tenacity. However, very fine fibers increase spinning breaks.

3. **Twist:** Increases inter-fiber friction and cohesion. Tenacity rises with twist up to an **optimum twist** (critical twist), beyond which it drops because:
   - Excessive twist reduces fiber alignment with yarn axis.
   - Higher torsional stress reduces tensile efficiency.

4. **Fiber Strength:** Intrinsic fiber tenacity is the upper limit of yarn tenacity.

5. **Friction & Surface Properties:** Higher fiber friction → better cohesion → higher yarn strength (up to a point).

6. **Yarn Structure:** Ring-spun > Rotor-spun > Air-jet-spun in tenacity (in general).

7. **Moisture:** Slight moisture plasticizes fibers and increases tenacity; excess moisture reduces it.

(14 marks)

---

> [!WARNING]
> **🚨 KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout:**
> - **Common Mistake 1:** Confusing $N_m$ and $N_e$ — *always check the units*. $N_m$ uses meters and grams; $N_e$ uses yards and pounds. A student writing $N_m$ in place of $N_e$ loses **2 marks instantly**.
> - **Common Mistake 2:** In Tex calculation, forgetting the factor of 1000 — students often write $W/L$ directly, which is **wrong** (that gives g/m, not Tex).
> - **Common Mistake 3:** In Twist Multiplier, students apply the **wrong denominator** — use $\sqrt{N_e}$ for cotton TPI; use $\sqrt{N_m}$ for metric TPM. Mixing them is a **favourite trap** of KTU paper setters.
> - **Common Mistake 4:** Not mentioning the **standard atmosphere** (65% RH, 27°C) during yarn testing. Examiners deduct marks for missing this precondition.
> - **Common Mistake 5:** In Uster evenness questions, writing "**C.V. is calculated as standard deviation × 100**" — without the division by mean — is treated as a **conceptual error** and costs 1 mark.

---

## 🧠 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember (Rapid Revision Checklist)

- **Yarn Count** is the **single most important** yarn property. Master all four units: **Tex, Denier, Nm, Ne**. Memorize conversions: $1 \, \text{Tex} = 9 \, \text{D} = 1000/N_m = 590.5/N_e$.
- **Twist** is a *necessary evil* — it gives strength but reduces softness and luster. Always distinguish **S** vs **Z** twist.
- **Twist Multiplier (TM)** normalizes twist across yarn counts. **Optimum TM for cotton ≈ 3.5–4.5** (ring-spun).
- **Tenacity** is the **specific strength** — always report in **cN/tex** for cross-yarn comparison. Above 25 cN/tex = high tenacity.
- **C.V.% of Evenness** is the **gold standard** for yarn quality. Uster Evenness Tester is the industry tool.
- **Three imperfections** to memorize: **Thin places (−50%), Thick places (+50%), Neps (+200%, <4 mm)**.
- **IS Standards** to remember: **IS 1315** (count), **IS 832** (twist), **IS 1671** (tensile), **IS 13679** (evenness), **IS 199** (moisture).
- **Standard Atmosphere** for yarn testing: **65 ± 2 % RH, 27 ± 2 °C** (Tropical conditions as per BIS).
- **Elongation** is reported in **%** — typical cotton: 6–10%, polyester filament: 15–25%.
- **Hairiness** is measured by **Zweigle H-value** — affects fabric pilling, print clarity, and handle.
- **Plied yarn twist direction** is **opposite** to singles — this balance prevents snarling.
- **Higher twist = higher tenacity (up to optimum), higher hairiness, lower luster, harder hand-feel**.
- **Lower twist = softer feel, higher luster, but weaker yarn and pilling-prone fabrics**.
- **For 14-mark questions**, always structure the answer as: **Definition → Principle/Apparatus → Procedure → Calculation → Result/Conclusion**.

---

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
# 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition

**Yarn Numbering System** is a standardized numerical expression that quantitatively defines the *linear density* (i.e., fineness or coarseness) of a yarn by establishing a precise mathematical relationship between its **mass** and **length**. In the context of KTU 2024 Scheme textile and polymer processing modules, yarn numbering is treated as a fundamental metrological parameter that governs yarn pricing, fabric construction, process control in spinning, weaving, knitting, and quality assurance.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Syllabus Highlight:**
> Yarn Numbering = The numerical ratio expressing the *linear density* of a yarn, used universally to specify yarn fineness across cotton, worsted, woolen, jute, filament, and synthetic fiber systems.

The two principal philosophical approaches are:

1. **Indirect Numbering System** — The count number is inversely proportional to the linear density. A *higher* number means a *finer* (thinner) yarn.
   - Examples: English Cotton Count $\left(N_e\right)$, Metric Count $\left(N_m\right)$, Worsted Count, Woolen (Yorkshire) Count.

2. **Direct Numbering System** — The count number is directly proportional to the linear density. A *higher* number means a *coarser* (thicker) yarn.
   - Examples: Tex, Denier (Td), Decitex (dtex), Jute Count.

> [!NOTE]
> **Standard Conversion Constants Used in KTU Examinations:**
> - $1 \text{ pound (lb)} = 453.6 \text{ grams (g)}$
> - $1 \text{ yard (yd)} = 0.9144 \text{ meters (m)}$
> - $1 \text{ inch} = 0.0254 \text{ m}$

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Real-World Intuition

Imagine you are a shopkeeper measuring pasta. You could measure pasta in two ways:

- **Method A (Indirect):** *"How many 50-cm long strands make 1 kg of pasta?"* — If more strands fit into 1 kg, the pasta is thin. This is the **Indirect System** (higher number = finer).

- **Method B (Direct):** *"What is the weight in grams of a fixed 1000 m length of pasta?"* — If the strand is thick, the 1000 m sample will be heavy. This is the **Direct System** (higher number = coarser).

> [!NOTE]
> **Real-World Mapping:** A $30^s$ cotton yarn is finer than a $10^s$ cotton yarn (Indirect). A 50 Tex yarn is coarser than a 20 Tex yarn (Direct). The same physical yarn will have a *small* number in Indirect but a *large* number in Direct.

## 1.3 Physical Significance

Yarn numbering determines:

- **Cost per unit length** (finer yarns cost more per kg but more kg is required per meter of fabric).
- **Fabric handle, drape, and GSM** (grams per square meter).
- **Process parameters** in ring spinning, rotor spinning, and air-jet spinning.
- **Quality control** tolerances in modern textile mills.

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 Logical Foundation — The "Why" Behind Each System

### 2.1.1 Indirect Yarn Numbering Systems

The philosophy of indirect systems is rooted in **historical industry practice**, where the spinner wanted to know *"How much yarn can I get from one pound of raw material?"*

> [!NOTE]
> **Definition Recap:** Indirect count = $\dfrac{\text{Length of yarn}}{\text{Unit weight of yarn}}$

#### (a) English Cotton Count $\left(N_e\right)$

$N_e$ is defined as **the number of 840-yard hanks** that weigh **1 pound (avoirdupois)**.

- $1$ hank (cotton) $= 840 \text{ yards} = 768.1 \text{ m}$
- If $N_e = 30$, then $30 \times 840 = 25{,}200$ yards of yarn weigh $1 \text{ lb}$.

#### (b) Metric Count $\left(N_m\right)$

$N_m$ is defined as **the number of meters** of yarn that weigh **1 gram**.

- If $N_m = 50$, then $50 \text{ m}$ of yarn weighs $1 \text{ g}$ (or $50{,}000 \text{ m/kg}$).

#### (c) Worsted Count

Worsted count is the number of **560-yard** hanks per pound (used for long-staple combed yarns like wool).

#### (d) Woolen (Yorkshire) Count

Woolen (Yorkshire) count is the number of **256-yard** skeins per pound (used for short-staple woolen yarns).

### 2.1.2 Direct Yarn Numbering Systems

Direct systems are scientifically cleaner and globally preferred for **man-made filament yarns** (polyester, nylon, viscose).

#### (a) Tex System

Tex = **weight in grams of 1000 meters** of yarn. If a yarn has Tex $= 25$, then 1000 m of that yarn weighs 25 g.

- Recommended by the **International Organization for Standardization (ISO)**.

#### (b) Denier System

Denier = **weight in grams of 9000 meters** of yarn. Predominantly used for **filament silk and synthetic filament yarns**.

#### (c) Decitex (dtex)

Decitex = **weight in grams of 10,000 meters** of yarn. Used for finer filament yarns (hosiery, microfibers).

#### (d) Jute Count (Lb/spy)

Jute count is the **weight in pounds of 14,400 yards** of yarn (or length in yards per pound × 14,400). Specifically used for **jute industry**.

## 2.2 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Master these conversion constants. They are the most-marks-bearing part of every KTU question on this topic.**

| System | Type | Master Formula | Definition Statement | Used For |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- | :--- |
| $N_e$ (English Cotton) | Indirect | $N_e = \dfrac{L \text{ (yards)}}{W \text{ (lb)} \times 840}$ | No. of 840-yd hanks per lb | Cotton, spun yarns |
| $N_m$ (Metric) | Indirect | $N_m = \dfrac{L \text{ (m)}}{W \text{ (g)}}$ | No. of meters per gram | Cotton, blends, hosiery |
| Worsted | Indirect | $N_w = \dfrac{L \text{ (yd)}}{W \text{ (lb)} \times 560}$ | No. of 560-yd hanks per lb | Worsted wool |
| Woolen (Yorkshire) | Indirect | $N_{y} = \dfrac{L \text{ (yd)}}{W \text{ (lb)} \times 256}$ | No. of 256-yd skeins per lb | Woolen spun yarns |
| Tex | Direct | $\text{Tex} = \dfrac{W \text{ (g)} \times 1000}{L \text{ (m)}}$ | Grams per 1000 m | All yarn types (ISO) |
| Denier | Direct | $\text{Denier} = \dfrac{W \text{ (g)} \times 9000}{L \text{ (m)}}$ | Grams per 9000 m | Filament silk, synthetics |
| Decitex (dtex) | Direct | $\text{dtex} = \dfrac{W \text{ (g)} \times 10000}{L \text{ (m)}}$ | Grams per 10000 m | Fine filament, microfibers |
| Jute Count (Lb/spy) | Direct | $J = \dfrac{W \text{ (lb)} \times 14400}{L \text{ (yd)}}$ | Pounds per 14400 yd | Jute yarn |

### 2.3 Critical Conversion Formulas (KTU High-Yield)

> [!NOTE]
> **All these identities assume the SAME physical yarn — only the units of expression change.**

$$
\begin{aligned}
N_e \times \text{Tex} &= 590.5 \\[4pt]
N_m \times \text{Tex} &= 1000 \\[4pt]
\text{Denier} &= 9 \times \text{Tex} \\[4pt]
\text{dtex} &= 10 \times \text{Tex} \\[4pt]
N_m &= 1.693 \times N_e \\[4pt]
\text{dtex} &= \dfrac{9}{10} \times \text{Denier}^{-1} \cdot 10 = 1.111 \times \text{Denier} \\[4pt]
1 \text{ Denier} &= 1.111 \text{ dtex}
\end{aligned}
$$

| From $\rightarrow$ To | Multiplication Factor |
| :--- | :---: |
| $N_e \rightarrow N_m$ | $\times \; 1.693$ |
| $N_m \rightarrow N_e$ | $\times \; 0.5905$ |
| $N_e \rightarrow \text{Tex}$ | $590.5 \;\big/\; N_e$ |
| $\text{Tex} \rightarrow N_e$ | $590.5 \;\big/\; \text{Tex}$ |
| $N_m \rightarrow \text{Tex}$ | $1000 \;\big/\; N_m$ |
| $\text{Tex} \rightarrow N_m$ | $1000 \;\big/\; \text{Tex}$ |
| $\text{Tex} \rightarrow \text{Denier}$ | $\times \; 9$ |
| $\text{Tex} \rightarrow \text{dtex}$ | $\times \; 10$ |
| $\text{Denier} \rightarrow \text{dtex}$ | $\times \; 1.111$ |
| $\text{dtex} \rightarrow \text{Denier}$ | $\times \; 0.9$ |

## 2.4 Real-World Engineering Utility

1. **Process Selection:** A $60^s$ $N_e$ cotton yarn requires ring spinning; a 1000 dtex polypropylene tape is made by extrusion.
2. **Quality Control:** GSM (grams per square meter) of fabric is calculated from the Tex of warp and weft yarns.
3. **International Trade:** Tex is the legal ISO standard for export-import documentation of textile raw materials.
4. **Costing:** Indirect count aids spinners (more yarn from raw material); Direct count aids weavers (predictable weight per fabric length).

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Derivation: Why $N_e \times \text{Tex} = 590.5$

We start with the definitions and convert from imperial to metric.

**Step 1 — Write the imperial definition of $N_e$:**
$$
N_e = \frac{L_{\text{yd}}}{W_{\text{lb}} \times 840}
$$

**Step 2 — Write the metric definition of Tex:**
$$
\text{Tex} = \frac{W_{\text{g}} \times 1000}{L_{\text{m}}}
$$

**Step 3 — Convert the imperial units to metric:**

Length in yards to meters:
$$
L_{\text{m}} = L_{\text{yd}} \times 0.9144
$$

Weight in pounds to grams:
$$
W_{\text{g}} = W_{\text{lb}} \times 453.6
$$

**Step 4 — Substitute into the Tex expression:**
$$
\text{Tex} = \frac{W_{\text{lb}} \times 453.6 \times 1000}{L_{\text{yd}} \times 0.9144}
$$

**Step 5 — Simplify the numerical coefficient:**
$$
\frac{453.6 \times 1000}{0.9144} = \frac{453600}{0.9144} = 496{,}063
$$

Wait, let us compute this more carefully:
$$
453.6 \div 0.9144 = 496.063
$$

Thus, $\text{Tex} = \dfrac{496.063 \times W_{\text{lb}} \times 1000}{L_{\text{yd}} \times 1000}$ — actually, simply:
$$
\text{Tex} = \frac{W_{\text{lb}}}{L_{\text{yd}}} \times \frac{453.6}{0.9144} \times 1000
$$

The conversion ratio:
$$
\frac{453.6}{0.9144} = 496.063
$$

So:
$$
\text{Tex} = \frac{W_{\text{lb}}}{L_{\text{yd}}} \times 496.063 \times 1000
$$

**Step 6 — Take the product $N_e \times \text{Tex}$:**
$$
N_e \times \text{Tex} = \frac{L_{\text{yd}}}{W_{\text{lb}} \times 840} \times \frac{W_{\text{lb}}}{L_{\text{yd}}} \times 496.063 \times 1000
$$

**Step 7 — Cancel the $L_{\text{yd}}$ and $W_{\text{lb}}$ terms:**
$$
N_e \times \text{Tex} = \frac{496.063 \times 1000}{840}
$$

**Step 8 — Final evaluation:**
$$
\frac{496.063 \times 1000}{840} = \frac{496063}{840} = 590.55
$$

Therefore, $N_e \times \text{Tex} = 590.5$ (rounded to one decimal). $\blacksquare$

## 3.2 Derivation: Why $N_m \times \text{Tex} = 1000$

**Step 1 — Write definitions:**
$$
N_m = \frac{L_{\text{m}}}{W_{\text{g}}}, \quad \text{Tex} = \frac{W_{\text{g}} \times 1000}{L_{\text{m}}}
$$

**Step 2 — Multiply them:**
$$
N_m \times \text{Tex} = \frac{L_{\text{m}}}{W_{\text{g}}} \times \frac{W_{\text{g}} \times 1000}{L_{\text{m}}}
$$

**Step 3 — Cancel $L_{\text{m}}$ and $W_{\text{g}}$:**
$$
N_m \times \text{Tex} = 1000 \quad \blacksquare
$$

## 3.3 Derivation: Denier $= 9 \times$ Tex

**Step 1 — Write both definitions:**
$$
\text{Tex} = \frac{W_{\text{g}} \times 1000}{L_{\text{m}}}, \quad \text{Denier} = \frac{W_{\text{g}} \times 9000}{L_{\text{m}}}
$$

**Step 2 — Take the ratio:**
$$
\frac{\text{Denier}}{\text{Tex}} = \frac{W_{\text{g}} \times 9000 \;/\; L_{\text{m}}}{W_{\text{g}} \times 1000 \;/\; L_{\text{m}}} = \frac{9000}{1000} = 9
$$

Therefore, $\text{Denier} = 9 \times \text{Tex}$. $\blacksquare$

## 3.4 Analytical Matrix — Comprehensive Numerical Example

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Examiner Tip:** This type of "convert the count" question appears almost every KTU exam. Master this framework.

**Given:** A cotton yarn of length $2520 \text{ m}$ weighs $50 \text{ g}$. Find:
(i) $N_e$, (ii) $N_m$, (iii) Tex, (iv) Denier, (v) dtex.

### Solution

**Step 1 — Convert length to yards and weight to pounds for $N_e$:**
$$
L_{\text{yd}} = 2520 \div 0.9144 = 2755.91 \text{ yd}
$$
$$
W_{\text{lb}} = 50 \div 453.6 = 0.11023 \text{ lb}
$$

**Step 2 — Compute $N_e$:**
$$
N_e = \frac{L_{\text{yd}}}{W_{\text{lb}} \times 840} = \frac{2755.91}{0.11023 \times 840} = \frac{2755.91}{92.59}
$$
$$
N_e = 29.76 \approx 30^s
$$

**Step 3 — Compute $N_m$:**
$$
N_m = \frac{L_{\text{m}}}{W_{\text{g}}} = \frac{2520}{50} = 50.4
$$

**Step 4 — Compute Tex:**
$$
\text{Tex} = \frac{W_{\text{g}} \times 1000}{L_{\text{m}}} = \frac{50 \times 1000}{2520} = 19.84 \text{ Tex}
$$

**Step 5 — Compute Denier:**
$$
\text{Denier} = 9 \times \text{Tex} = 9 \times 19.84 = 178.57 \text{ Denier}
$$

**Step 6 — Compute dtex:**
$$
\text{dtex} = 10 \times \text{Tex} = 10 \times 19.84 = 198.4 \text{ dtex}
$$

### 3.4.1 Verification Matrix (Cross-Check Using Conversion Constants)

| Quantity | Direct Calculation | Cross-Check | Match? |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| $N_e$ | 29.76 | $590.5 / 19.84 = 29.76$ | $\checkmark$ |
| $N_m$ | 50.4 | $1000 / 19.84 = 50.40$ | $\checkmark$ |
| $N_m$ from $N_e$ | — | $1.693 \times 29.76 = 50.39$ | $\checkmark$ |
| Denier | 178.57 | $9 \times 19.84 = 178.56$ | $\checkmark$ |
| dtex | 198.4 | $10 \times 19.84 = 198.4$ | $\checkmark$ |
| dtex from Denier | — | $1.111 \times 178.57 = 198.37$ | $\checkmark$ |

> [!NOTE]
> **Conclusion:** The yarn is approximately $30^s$ $N_e$ (or 50 $N_m$ or 20 Tex), a typical count for medium-count cotton shirting fabric.

## 3.5 Second Worked Example — Synthetic Filament Yarn

**Given:** A polyester filament yarn has Tex $= 16.7$. Find: (i) Denier, (ii) dtex, (iii) $N_m$, (iv) $N_e$.

### Solution

**Step 1 — Denier:**
$$
\text{Denier} = 9 \times 16.7 = 150.3 \text{ Denier (commonly written 150D)}
$$

**Step 2 — dtex:**
$$
\text{dtex} = 10 \times 16.7 = 167 \text{ dtex}
$$

**Step 3 — $N_m$:**
$$
N_m = \frac{1000}{16.7} = 59.88
$$

**Step 4 — $N_e$:**
$$
N_e = \frac{590.5}{16.7} = 35.36^s
$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Industry Note:** A 150 Denier polyester filament yarn (commonly called 150D/48F where 48F = 48 filaments) is the standard yarn for sportswear, light-weight suiting, and ladies' dress material.

<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->
# 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics

## 4.1 Block-Level Functional Architecture of Yarn Numbering Systems

The diagram below maps the *interaction and inter-conversion pathways* between various yarn numbering systems. Each node represents a counting system; the edges indicate the mathematical relationship used during conversion.

```mermaid
graph TD
    Root[Yarn Numbering System] --> Direct[Direct Systems]
    Root --> Indirect[Indirect Systems]

    Direct --> TexNode[Tex]
    Direct --> DenNode[Denier]
    Direct --> DtexNode[Decitex dtex]
    Direct --> JuteNode[Jute Count]

    Indirect --> NeNode[English Cotton Ne]
    Indirect --> NmNode[Metric Nm]
    Indirect --> WorNode[Worsted 560 yd]
    Indirect --> WolNode[Woolen Yorkshire 256 yd]

    TexNode -- "9x" --> DenNode
    TexNode -- "10x" --> DtexNode
    DenNode -- "x 1.111" --> DtexNode
    TexNode -- "1000 / x" --> NmNode
    TexNode -- "590.5 / x" --> NeNode
    NeNode -- "x 1.693" --> NmNode
    WorNode -- "560 by 840 ratio" --> NeNode
    WolNode -- "256 by 840 ratio" --> NeNode

    AppA[Application: Filament Silk, Nylon] --> DenNode
    AppB[Application: Microfiber Hosiery] --> DtexNode
    AppC[Application: Cotton Spun Yarn] --> NeNode
    AppD[Application: Worsted Wool] --> WorNode
    AppE[Application: Jute Sacking] --> JuteNode
    AppF[Application: ISO Standard Export] --> TexNode
```

## 4.2 Inter-Conversion Reference Flowchart

The schematic below illustrates the **decision logic** an engineer follows when converting between arbitrary yarn numbering systems.

```mermaid
graph TD
    Start[Given Yarn Count] --> Step1[Identify the Source System]
    Step1 --> Step2{Convertible via Tex?}
    Step2 -- Yes --> Step3[Convert to Tex as the Hub Unit]
    Step2 -- No --> Step4[Convert via Imperial Metric Bridge]
    Step3 --> Step5[From Tex to Target System]
    Step4 --> Step5
    Step5 --> Step6[Apply Multiplication or Division Factor]
    Step6 --> Step7[Verify with Reverse Calculation]
    Step7 --> End[Final Converted Count]
```

## 4.3 Physical Interpretation of Indirect vs. Direct Systems

| Feature | Direct System (Tex / Denier) | Indirect System ($N_e$ / $N_m$) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Higher count means | Coarser yarn | Finer yarn |
| Mathematical nature | Weight per unit length | Length per unit weight |
| SI / ISO alignment | Tex is the official ISO standard | Non-SI, industry-specific |
| Typical use | Filament yarns (synthetic, silk) | Spun staple yarns (cotton, wool) |
| Sample calculation | 30 Tex = 30 g / 1000 m | $30^s$ $N_e$ = 25,200 yd / lb |

> [!NOTE]
> **Memory Aid (KTU Mnemonic):** *"DIRECT = Dense"* (high number = thick). *"INDIRECT = Inverse"* (high number = thin).

<!-- SECTION_4_END -->

# 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A Questions (3 Marks Each)

### Question 1 `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]`

**Define yarn numbering system. Differentiate between direct and indirect numbering systems with suitable examples.**

**Model Answer:**

Yarn numbering system is a numerical expression that defines the linear density (fineness or coarseness) of a yarn by expressing the ratio between its weight and length.

| Aspect | Direct System | Indirect System |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Definition | Weight per fixed length | Length per fixed weight |
| Relation | Count $\propto$ weight | Count $\propto$ length |
| Finer yarn | Lower number | Higher number |
| Examples | Tex, Denier, dtex | $N_e$, $N_m$, Worsted, Woolen |
| Common use | Filament yarns | Spun staple yarns |

### Question 2 `[KTU University Exam - May 2024]`

**State and explain the Tex system of yarn numbering. Why is Tex considered the international standard?**

**Model Answer:**

The Tex system expresses yarn count as the **weight in grams of 1000 meters** of yarn.

$$
\text{Tex} = \frac{W_{\text{g}}}{L_{\text{m}}} \times 1000
$$

Tex is the official ISO standard for linear density of textile fibers and yarns because:
1. It is based on the SI unit system (grams and meters).
2. It is a direct system, so higher number unambiguously means coarser yarn.
3. It is universally applicable to all fiber types (natural, regenerated, synthetic, filament, spun).
4. It eliminates confusion arising from country-specific indirect systems.

---

## 5.2 Part B Questions (14 Marks Each) — Internal Choice

### Question A (14 Marks) `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]`

**(a) A yarn of length 1680 yards weighs 1 pound. Calculate its count in (i) English Cotton Count ($N_e$), (ii) Tex, and (iii) Denier. (7 marks)**

**Model Solution:**

**Step 1 — Compute $N_e$:**
$$
N_e = \frac{L_{\text{yd}}}{W_{\text{lb}} \times 840} = \frac{1680}{1 \times 840} = 2
$$

**Step 2 — Convert imperial to metric for Tex:**
$$
L_{\text{m}} = 1680 \times 0.9144 = 1536.19 \text{ m}
$$
$$
W_{\text{g}} = 1 \times 453.6 = 453.6 \text{ g}
$$

**Step 3 — Compute Tex:**
$$
\text{Tex} = \frac{453.6 \times 1000}{1536.19} = 295.25 \text{ Tex}
$$

**Step 4 — Cross-check using $N_e \times \text{Tex} = 590.5$:**
$$
\text{Tex} = \frac{590.5}{2} = 295.25 \text{ Tex} \quad \checkmark
$$

**Step 5 — Compute Denier:**
$$
\text{Denier} = 9 \times 295.25 = 2657.25 \text{ Denier}
$$

| Quantity | Value |
| :---: | :---: |
| $N_e$ | $2^s$ |
| Tex | $295.25$ |
| Denier | $2657.25$ |

**(b) Convert 30 Ne cotton count to (i) Metric Count ($N_m$), (ii) Tex, (iii) Denier, and (iv) Decitex (dtex). (7 marks)**

**Model Solution:**

**Step 1 — Compute $N_m$:**
$$
N_m = 1.693 \times N_e = 1.693 \times 30 = 50.79
$$

**Step 2 — Compute Tex:**
$$
\text{Tex} = \frac{590.5}{N_e} = \frac{590.5}{30} = 19.68 \text{ Tex}
$$

**Step 3 — Compute Denier:**
$$
\text{Denier} = 9 \times 19.68 = 177.12 \text{ Denier}
$$

**Step 4 — Compute dtex:**
$$
\text{dtex} = 10 \times 19.68 = 196.8 \text{ dtex}
$$

| System | Value |
| :---: | :---: |
| $N_m$ | $50.79$ |
| Tex | $19.68$ |
| Denier | $177.12$ |
| dtex | $196.8$ |

---

### Question B (14 Marks) `[KTU University Exam - May 2024]` (Internal Alternative)

**(a) Explain in detail the various direct yarn numbering systems with their formulas and applications. (7 marks)**

**Model Answer:**

Direct yarn numbering systems express count as the **weight per unit length** of yarn. The four main direct systems are:

1. **Tex System:** Weight in grams of 1000 m of yarn. Formula: $\text{Tex} = \dfrac{W_{\text{g}} \times 1000}{L_{\text{m}}}$. Used for all yarn types as per ISO standard.

2. **Denier System:** Weight in grams of 9000 m of yarn. Formula: $\text{Denier} = \dfrac{W_{\text{g}} \times 9000}{L_{\text{m}}}$. Used for filament silk and synthetic filament yarns (nylon, polyester).

3. **Decitex (dtex):** Weight in grams of 10,000 m of yarn. Formula: $\text{dtex} = \dfrac{W_{\text{g}} \times 10000}{L_{\text{m}}}$. Used for microfibers, hosiery, and fine filament yarns.

4. **Jute Count (Lb/spy):** Weight in pounds of 14,400 yards of yarn. Formula: $J = \dfrac{W_{\text{lb}} \times 14400}{L_{\text{yd}}}$. Used exclusively for jute industry (hessian cloth, sacking).

**Key Relationships:**
- $\text{Denier} = 9 \times \text{Tex}$
- $\text{dtex} = 10 \times \text{Tex}$
- $1 \text{ dtex} = 1.111 \text{ Denier}$

**(b) A yarn measures 5000 meters in length and weighs 75 grams. Find its count in $N_m$, Tex, Denier, and dtex. (7 marks)**

**Model Solution:**

**Step 1 — Compute $N_m$:**
$$
N_m = \frac{L_{\text{m}}}{W_{\text{g}}} = \frac{5000}{75} = 66.67
$$

**Step 2 — Compute Tex:**
$$
\text{Tex} = \frac{W_{\text{g}} \times 1000}{L_{\text{m}}} = \frac{75 \times 1000}{5000} = 15 \text{ Tex}
$$

**Step 3 — Compute Denier:**
$$
\text{Denier} = 9 \times 15 = 135 \text{ Denier}
$$

**Step 4 — Compute dtex:**
$$
\text{dtex} = 10 \times 15 = 150 \text{ dtex}
$$

| System | Value |
| :---: | :---: |
| $N_m$ | $66.67$ |
| Tex | $15$ |
| Denier | $135$ |
| dtex | $150$ |

**Step 5 — Cross-check via $N_m \times \text{Tex} = 1000$:**
$$
66.67 \times 15 = 1000.05 \approx 1000 \quad \checkmark
$$

---

## 5.3 KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Student Mistakes That Cost Marks:**
> 
> 1. **Unit Confusion in $N_e$ formula:** Students frequently write $N_e = \dfrac{L_{\text{yd}}}{W_{\text{lb}}}$ forgetting to multiply the denominator by 840. This error alone costs 2 to 3 marks per question.
> 
> 2. **Wrong Denier-Tex Relation:** Many students write $\text{Denier} = \dfrac{\text{Tex}}{9}$ instead of $\text{Denier} = 9 \times \text{Tex}$. The ratio $\dfrac{9000}{1000} = 9$ must be memorized.
> 
> 3. **Forgetting to convert between yards and meters:** A direct substitution of yards into the Tex formula gives a wildly incorrect result. Always convert to **meters and grams** before applying Tex.
> 
> 4. **Mixing up $N_e$ and $N_m$ conversion factor:** The factor is $N_m = 1.693 \times N_e$, **not** 1.5 or 1.7. The exact value is $\dfrac{453.6}{0.9144 \times 0.84} \times 0.001 \times 1000 = 1.693$. Using an approximate value may lose fractional marks.
> 
> 5. **Not showing cross-verification:** KTU examiners award bonus partial credit when students verify the result using a different conversion path (e.g., checking $N_e \times \text{Tex} = 590.5$). Skipping this is a missed opportunity.
> 
> 6. **Confusing Jute Count with other systems:** Jute count is a *direct* system but uses *pounds per 14,400 yards* — a unique unit. Do not apply the $840$-yard hank logic of $N_e$ to jute.

---

## 5.4 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember (Rapid Revision Checklist)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Pre-Exam Rapid-Fire Revision — Pin These to Your Wall.**

- [ ] **Indirect Systems (Length per unit weight):** $N_e$, $N_m$, Worsted, Woolen — *higher number = finer yarn*.
- [ ] **Direct Systems (Weight per unit length):** Tex, Denier, dtex, Jute — *higher number = coarser yarn*.
- [ ] **English Cotton $N_e$:** $\dfrac{L_{\text{yd}}}{W_{\text{lb}} \times 840}$ — based on **840-yard hank per pound**.
- [ ] **Metric $N_m$:** $\dfrac{L_{\text{m}}}{W_{\text{g}}}$ — based on **meters per gram**.
- [ ] **Tex:** $\dfrac{W_{\text{g}} \times 1000}{L_{\text{m}}}$ — ISO standard; **grams per 1000 m**.
- [ ] **Denier:** $\dfrac{W_{\text{g}} \times 9000}{L_{\text{m}}}$ — **grams per 9000 m**; for filament yarns.
- [ ] **dtex:** $\dfrac{W_{\text{g}} \times 10000}{L_{\text{m}}}$ — **grams per 10,000 m**; for microfibers.
- [ ] **Jute Count:** $\dfrac{W_{\text{lb}} \times 14400}{L_{\text{yd}}}$ — for jute industry.
- [ ] **Master Conversion 1:** $N_e \times \text{Tex} = 590.5$.
- [ ] **Master Conversion 2:** $N_m \times \text{Tex} = 1000$.
- [ ] **Master Conversion 3:** $\text{Denier} = 9 \times \text{Tex}$.
- [ ] **Master Conversion 4:** $\text{dtex} = 10 \times \text{Tex}$.
- [ ] **Master Conversion 5:** $N_m = 1.693 \times N_e$.
- [ ] **Imperial-to-Metric Constants:** $1 \text{ lb} = 453.6 \text{ g}$, $1 \text{ yd} = 0.9144 \text{ m}$.
- [ ] **Always show two-step verification** in KTU numerical answers to score full marks.
- [ ] **Tex is the universal hub** for converting between any two yarn numbering systems.
- [ ] **Cross-check identity** $\text{Tex} \times N_m = 1000$ must hold for every yarn — use it as a sanity check.

## SECTION 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### 1.1 Yarn Spinning — The Formal Definition

**Yarn Spinning** is the mechanical process of converting staple fibres (short-length fibres) or filament tow into a continuous, twisted, and cohesive yarn suitable for weaving, knitting, or other fabric-forming operations. In the context of cotton and cotton-blend yarns, spinning transforms the loose, disordered fibre assembly — after preparatory processes like blowroom, carding, drawing, and roving — into a uniform linear assembly of parallelised, twisted fibres held together by inter-fibre friction and twist-induced lateral pressure.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Syllabus Highlight:** For cotton yarn manufacture, the most industrially dominant route is the **ring spinning system**, accounting for over **80%** of global short-staple yarn production. Modern variants like compact, rotor, and air-jet spinning are considered extensions of this fundamental conversion philosophy.

### 1.2 Brief Idea About Spinning of Cotton Yarns

The journey of a cotton fibre from bale to finished yarn passes through a sequence of unit operations. The spinning process itself typically refers to the **final twist insertion and winding stage** that converts a drafted fibre ribbon (roving or sliver) into yarn.

**Stages of Conventional Cotton Yarn Manufacturing:**

1. **Blowroom:** Opening, cleaning, and mixing of cotton bales; removal of trash, dust, and micro-dust particles.
2. **Carding:** Individualisation of fibres, removal of remaining impurities, and formation of a carded sliver.
3. **Drawing (Breaker + Finisher Draw Frames):** Doubling of slivers for longitudinal blending, parallelisation, and drafting to improve evenness.
4. **Roving (Speed Frame / Simplex):** Drafting of drawn sliver, insertion of a small amount of protective twist, and packaging onto a bobbin.
5. **Ring Spinning (the actual "spinning" stage):** Final drafting, twist insertion via a traveller rotating around a stationary ring, and winding onto a cop.
6. **Winding / Clearing / Conditioning:** Transfer of yarn from ring cops to larger packages, electronic yarn clearing for fault removal, and waxing.

> [!NOTE]
> **Conceptual Analogy:** Think of cotton spinning as making a "rope" out of millions of tiny cotton staples. Imagine you have a pile of short, fuzzy strings of different lengths. Spinning is the process of pulling them straight (drafting), laying them parallel (parallelisation), twisting them together (twisting), and rolling the result onto a holder (winding) — much like twisting individual blades of grass between your palms to form a string, except done at industrial speeds with micron-level precision.

### 1.3 Brief Idea About Spinning of Blends

**Yarn blending** refers to the deliberate mixing of two or more fibre types (e.g., cotton + polyester) during the yarn manufacturing process to obtain a yarn that combines the desirable properties of each constituent fibre.

**Common Examples of Blend Yarns:**

| Blend Composition | Common Abbreviation | Key Advantage |
|---|---|---|
| Polyester / Cotton | P/C or PC | Strength of polyester + comfort of cotton |
| Cotton / Viscose | C/V | Soft handle + moisture absorbency |
| Cotton / Modal | C/M | Enhanced softness + lustre |
| Cotton / Linen | C/L | Strength + cool handle |

**Common Methods of Blending:**

- **Bale Blending** (at blowroom): Layers of different fibre bales are laid out in a pattern and plucked in vertical sections.
- **Sliver / Draw Frame Blending:** Two or more slivers of different fibres are fed together at the draw frame; the most precise and widely used method.
- **Roving Blending:** Done at the speed frame; less common due to quality constraints.
- **Yarn Blending (Doubling):** Two or more spun yarns of different fibres are twisted together in the plied yarn stage.

> [!NOTE]
> **Conceptual Analogy:** Yarn blending is exactly like making a salad. You can mix the lettuce and tomatoes *before* dressing (fibre-level blending), or you can have separate bowls of each and mix at the table (yarn-level blending). Each method gives a slightly different "taste" — i.e., final yarn properties.

### 1.4 Yarn Count and Yarn Appearance — Formal Definitions

**Yarn Count (also called Yarn Number):** A numerical expression that indicates the **linear density (fineness or coarseness)** of a yarn — i.e., the relationship between its weight and its length. It is the single most important parameter that defines the "thickness" of a yarn.

**Yarn Appearance:** A visual quality descriptor that includes the **evenness, smoothness, cleanliness, neatness, and freedom from faults (slubs, neps, thick-thin places, fly waste, etc.)** of a yarn when viewed as a wound package (cone, cheese) or as a fabric surface.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Yarn Count Systems — Two Fundamental Types:**
> - **Indirect (Length-weight) System:** Higher the count number, *finer* the yarn. Example: **English Cotton Count (Ne)**.
> - **Direct (Weight-length) System:** Higher the count number, *coarser* the yarn. Examples: **Tex, Denier, Metric Count (Nm) used in inverse form**.

---

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
## SECTION 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### 2.1 Detailed Mechanics of Ring Spinning (Most Common Cotton System)

Ring spinning remains the **workhorse** of the cotton yarn industry due to its versatility and superior yarn quality. The process can be decomposed into the following concurrent operations occurring at the spindle:

1. **Drafting Zone:** The roving passes through drafting rollers (apron or roller drafting system), which attenuate it to the final yarn linear density.
2. **Twist Insertion Zone:** A rotating spindle drives the traveller around a stationary ring. The yarn is led through the traveller, which rotates at a slightly slower speed than the spindle, causing **twist to propagate upward** from the yarn balloon into the fibres just below the front drafting roller.
3. **Winding Zone:** The yarn is wound onto the cop (yarn package on the spindle) at a rate that matches the difference between the spindle speed and the traveller speed.

**Twist Equation:**

$$T_{per\ metre} = \frac{N_{spindle} - N_{traveller}}{V_{delivery}}$$

Where:
- $N_{spindle}$ = Spindle rotational speed (rpm)
- $N_{traveller}$ = Traveller rotational speed (rpm)
- $V_{delivery}$ = Linear delivery speed of front drafting roller (m/min)

**Twist Multiplier (TM) — Used to Design Twist Levels for a Given Count:**

$$TM = \frac{T_{per\ inch} \times \sqrt{Ne}}{\sqrt{\text{constant}}}$$

In simplified engineering form (for cotton):

$$TPI = TM \times \sqrt{Ne}$$

Where TPI = Twist Per Inch, Ne = English Cotton Count.

> [!TIP]
> **Why twist?** Twist converts the loosely held parallel fibre assembly into a load-bearing structure. The frictional grip between adjacent fibres, enhanced by twist-induced radial pressure, allows the yarn to withstand tensile loads. **Higher TM = stronger but harsher and less lustrous yarn.**

### 2.2 Modern Spinning Variants for Cotton and Blends

| Spinning System | Key Principle | Yarn Properties | Typical Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Ring Spinning** | Traveller-ring twist | Strong, fine, hairy | Premium woven/knit |
| **Compact Spinning** | Pneumatic condensation of fibre strand | Reduced hairiness, stronger | High-quality woven |
| **Rotor (Open-End) Spinning** | Twist inserted by rotor groove | Bulkier, less hairy, even | Denim, towels, knit |
| **Air-Jet Spinning** | Twisting by vortex air streams | Very low hairiness | Shirting, suiting |
| **Friction Spinning** | Two rotating drums twist fibres | Coarse, soft, low strength | Industrial, blankets |
| **Vortex Spinning** | High-speed air vortex | Fine, low hairiness, even | Apparel |

### 2.3 Detailed Blending Methodology

**The Draw Frame Blending (Preferred Industrial Method):**

- 4 to 8 slivers of one fibre (say polyester) and 4 to 8 slivers of another fibre (say cotton) are fed simultaneously at the back of a draw frame.
- They are drafted and doubled, producing a thoroughly homogenised blend sliver.
- **Intimate blending** is achieved at the fibre level — critical for dye uptake and handle uniformity.

**Blend Ratio Verification — The Dissolution Test:**

For a P/C blend, the polyester component is dissolved using **sulphuric acid (75%)** or **ortho-chlorophenol**, and the cotton residue is weighed. The blend ratio is computed as:

$$\%P = \frac{W_P}{W_P + W_C} \times 100 \quad ; \quad \%C = \frac{W_C}{W_P + W_C} \times 100$$

Where $W_P$ and $W_C$ are the masses of polyester and cotton, respectively.

### 2.4 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

| # | Formula / Concept | Expression | Units | Remarks |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | English Cotton Count (Ne) | $Ne = \dfrac{L_{yards}}{W_{lbs}}$ | — | Indirect system; higher Ne = finer |
| 2 | Tex (Tt) | $Tt = \dfrac{W_{grams}}{L_{km}}$ | g/km | Direct system; higher Tex = coarser |
| 3 | Denier (Td) | $Td = \dfrac{W_{grams}}{L_{9000m}}$ | g/9000m | Direct; used for filament |
| 4 | Metric Count (Nm) | $Nm = \dfrac{L_{metres}}{W_{kg}}$ | m/kg | Indirect |
| 5 | Conversion: Tex ↔ Ne | $Tex = \dfrac{590.5}{Ne}$ | g/km | Standard cotton |
| 6 | Conversion: Tex ↔ Denier | $Denier = 9 \times Tex$ | — | Direct relationship |
| 7 | Conversion: Ne ↔ Nm | $Nm = 1.69 \times Ne$ | — | For cotton-type |
| 8 | Twist Per Inch (TPI) | $TPI = \dfrac{TM}{\sqrt{Ne}}$ | twists/inch | TM = Twist Multiplier |
| 9 | Twist Per Metre (TPM) | $TPM = TPI \times 39.37$ | twists/m | Conversion |
| 10 | Yarn Linear Density (g/m) | $g/m = \dfrac{Tex}{1000}$ | g/m | From Tex |
| 11 | Blend Component (%) | $\%X = \dfrac{W_X}{W_{total}} \times 100$ | % | Dissolution test |
| 12 | Standard twist TM (cotton) | $TM = 3.0$ to $4.2$ | — | Depends on end-use |
| 13 | Hairiness Index | $H = \dfrac{L_{hair}}{L_{base}} \times 100$ | % | Lower = cleaner yarn |
| 14 | CV% of count (evenness) | $CV\% = \dfrac{\sigma}{\bar{x}} \times 100$ | % | Lower = more even |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Critical Conversion to Memorise for KTU Board Exams:**
> - **Tex = 590.5 / Ne** (for cotton)
> - **1 Denier = 1/9 Tex**
> - **1 metre = 1.0936 yards**

### 2.5 Yarn Appearance — Detailed Components

Yarn appearance is a **multi-dimensional quality attribute** evaluated visually and instrumentally:

1. **Evenness (CV% of mass):** Variation in linear density along the yarn length. Measured by **Uster Evenness Tester** (capacitance method).
2. **Cleanliness / Faults:** Number of thick places (+50%), thin places (-50%), and neps (+200%) per km.
3. **Hairiness:** Protruding fibre ends from the yarn body. Measured by **Zweigle Hairiness Meter** (S3, S2, S1 zones).
4. **Lustre:** Specular reflection of light from the yarn surface.
5. **Neatness of Package:** Winding pattern, surface integrity of cone/cheese.

> [!NOTE]
> **Uster Statistics** are the global industry benchmark for yarn evenness. Lower U% and CV% indicate higher-quality yarn. For example, a premium combed cotton ring-spun yarn of Ne 40s should typically have CV% < 13% and thin places/km < 15.

---

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
## SECTION 3: Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

### 3.1 Derivation of the Yarn Count Conversion (Tex to English Cotton Count, Ne)

**Starting Definition of English Cotton Count:**

$$Ne = \frac{L_{yards}}{W_{lbs}}$$

**Starting Definition of Tex:**

$$Tt = \frac{W_{grams}}{L_{km}}$$

**Step 1: Convert Length Units**

We need to express Tex in terms of yards. Since 1 yard = 0.0009144 km, we have:

$$1 \text{ km} = \frac{1}{0.0009144} \text{ yards} = 1093.6 \text{ yards}$$

**Step 2: Convert Mass Units**

We need to express Tex (grams per km) in pounds per yard. Since 1 pound (lb) = 453.592 grams, we have:

$$1 \text{ gram} = \frac{1}{453.592} \text{ lb} = 2.2046 \times 10^{-3} \text{ lb}$$

**Step 3: Substitute into the Tex Definition**

$$Tt = \frac{W_{grams}}{L_{km}} = \frac{W_{lb} \times 453.592}{L_{yards} \times 0.0009144}$$

$$Tt = \frac{453.592}{0.0009144} \times \frac{W_{lb}}{L_{yards}}$$

**Step 4: Evaluate the Numerical Constant**

$$Tt = 496055 \times \frac{W_{lb}}{L_{yards}}$$

But since $Ne = \dfrac{L_{yards}}{W_{lb}}$, we can write:

$$\frac{W_{lb}}{L_{yards}} = \frac{1}{Ne}$$

**Step 5: Final Relationship**

$$Tt = \frac{496055}{Ne} \approx \frac{590.5}{Ne}$$

> [!TIP]
> The factor 590.5 is a **practical textile constant** for cotton (assumes standard moisture regain of 8.5%). For other fibres like wool (with higher regain ~18%), the factor is approximately 885.5.

---

### 3.2 Worked Numerical Example — KTU Board Exam Style

**Problem:** A yarn package weighs 250 g and contains 5000 metres of yarn. Calculate: (a) Tex, (b) English count (Ne), and (c) Denier. (Assume 590.5 constant.)

**Solution:**

**(a) Calculation of Tex:**

$$Tt = \frac{W_{grams}}{L_{km}} = \frac{250 \text{ g}}{5 \text{ km}} = 50 \text{ Tex}$$

**(b) Calculation of Ne:**

$$Ne = \frac{590.5}{Tt} = \frac{590.5}{50} = 11.81$$

So the yarn is approximately **Ne 12s** — a medium-coarse cotton yarn suitable for towel or knit fabric.

**(c) Calculation of Denier:**

$$Denier = 9 \times Tt = 9 \times 50 = 450 \text{ Denier}$$

This is a **medium-denier** yarn.

> [!NOTE]
> **KTU-Style Quick Verification:** A 50 Tex cotton yarn is roughly the thickness of a typical sweater yarn. Finer shirt yarn would be around 15–20 Tex (Ne 30s–40s); very fine shirting is 7–10 Tex (Ne 60s–80s).

---

### 3.3 Derivation of the Twist Multiplier Relation

**Starting Point: Twist Per Inch (TPI):**

$$TPI = \frac{\text{Number of twists}}{\text{Length in inches}}$$

**Empirical Engineering Relation (Peirce / Munden):**

For a given yarn diameter, the optimum twist is found to be inversely proportional to the square root of the count (since yarn diameter ∝ 1/√Ne for indirect system). Therefore:

$$TPI = \frac{K}{\sqrt{Ne}}$$

Where $K$ is the **Twist Multiplier (TM)** — a fibre- and end-use-dependent constant.

**Re-arranging to find TM:**

$$TM = TPI \times \sqrt{Ne}$$

**Worked Example:** A Ne 30s cotton yarn is spun with 20 TPI. Calculate TM.

$$TM = 20 \times \sqrt{30} = 20 \times 5.477 = 109.55$$

For cotton, typical TM values range between **3.0 to 4.2** when twist is in **TPI** and Ne is in standard cotton form. The dimensionless TM helps **standardise twist design across counts**.

---

### 3.4 Analytical Matrix — Spinning Methods vs. Yarn Properties

| Yarn Property | Ring | Compact | Rotor | Air-Jet | Vortex |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Strength (CSP) | High | Highest | Medium | Medium | Medium |
| Hairiness | High | Low | Medium | Lowest | Lowest |
| Evenness (CV%) | 12–15 | 11–13 | 13–16 | 13–16 | 12–15 |
| Production Speed | Low | Low | Very High | High | High |
| Yarn Cost | High | Highest | Low | Medium | Medium |
| Count Range (Ne) | 6s–200s | 30s–200s | 6s–40s | 20s–80s | 20s–60s |

> [!TIP]
> **Rule of Thumb for KTU Viva:** "Rotor is for bulk and speed; Ring is for fineness and quality; Compact is the premium ring; Air-jet/vortex is for hairiness-critical end-uses like suiting."

## SECTION 5: KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

### 5.1 Part A Questions (3 Marks Each)

---

**Q1. [KTU University Exam – May 2024]**
**Define English Cotton Count (Ne) and Tex. Give the conversion formula between them.**

**Model Answer:**
English Cotton Count (Ne) is defined as the number of 840-yard lengths per pound of yarn:

$$Ne = \frac{L_{yards}}{W_{lbs} \times 840}$$

Tex is the weight in grams of 1000 metres (1 km) of yarn:

$$Tt = \frac{W_{grams}}{L_{km}}$$

The conversion is:

$$Tex = \frac{590.5}{Ne}$$

(3 marks: 1 mark each for definition + 1 for conversion formula)

---

**Q2. [KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]**
**Briefly explain the term "yarn appearance" and list four factors on which it depends.**

**Model Answer:**
Yarn appearance is a visual quality attribute describing the surface uniformity, evenness, hairiness, and freedom from faults of a yarn as observed on a wound package or fabric surface.

**Four Key Factors:**
1. Fibre evenness and uniformity of the roving/sliver.
2. Twist level and twist distribution.
3. Spinning system (ring/rotor/air-jet — each gives distinct appearance).
4. Fibre finish, hairiness, and neps.

(3 marks: 1 mark for definition + 2 marks for four factors)

---

### 5.2 Part B Questions (14 Marks Each) — KTU ESE Module Internal Choice

---

#### **Question A (14 Marks) [KTU University Exam – Dec 2024 Model]**

**(a)** With a neat labelled flow diagram, explain the **conventional ring spinning process** for cotton yarns. List the main preparatory stages leading up to the ring frame. (7 marks)

**(b)** A cotton yarn has English count Ne 40s. Calculate (i) Tex, (ii) Denier, and (iii) the **TPM (twists per metre)** if the Twist Multiplier (TM) is 3.8. (7 marks)

**Model Solution:**

**(a) Ring Spinning Process (7 marks):**

The conventional ring spinning process converts roving into finished yarn through the following stages:

1. **Blowroom (1 mark):** Bale opening, mixing, cleaning, and removal of trash.
2. **Carding (1 mark):** Fibre individualisation, removal of short fibres and neps, formation of carded sliver.
3. **Draw Frame – Breaker (0.5 mark):** Doubling of 6–8 carded slivers for longitudinal blending and parallelisation.
4. **Draw Frame – Finisher (0.5 mark):** Further drafting and evenness improvement.
5. **Speed Frame / Simplex (1 mark):** Attenuates drawn sliver into roving with protective twist wound on a bobbin.
6. **Ring Spinning Frame (2 marks):**
   - Final drafting by front rollers.
   - Twist insertion via traveller rotating around ring (driven by spindle).
   - Winding of twisted yarn onto cop.
7. **Autoconer (Winding) (1 mark):** Transfer to larger package; electronic yarn clearing; waxing.

*(Diagram expected: refer to Section 4.1 above for typical flow.)*

**(b) Calculations (7 marks):**

**Given:** Ne = 40, TM = 3.8

**(i) Tex Calculation (2 marks):**

$$Tex = \frac{590.5}{Ne} = \frac{590.5}{40} = 14.76 \text{ Tex}$$

**(ii) Denier Calculation (2 marks):**

$$Denier = 9 \times Tex = 9 \times 14.76 = 132.86 \text{ Denier}$$

**(iii) TPM Calculation (3 marks):**

First find TPI:

$$TPI = \frac{TM}{\sqrt{Ne}} = \frac{3.8}{\sqrt{40}} = \frac{3.8}{6.324} = 0.601 \text{ TPI}$$

> *Note: The convention in Indian textile practice is TM = TPI × √Ne for cotton, so TPI = 3.8/√40 = 0.60. This is unusually low and indicates that for finer yarns TM is often expressed differently. The correct industrial formula for twist is:*

$$TPI = TM \times \sqrt{Ne} = 3.8 \times \sqrt{40} = 3.8 \times 6.324 = 24.03 \text{ TPI}$$

Converting TPI to TPM:

$$TPM = TPI \times 39.37 = 24.03 \times 39.37 = 946.1 \text{ TPM}$$

**Final Answers:** Tex = 14.76, Denier = 132.86, TPM = 946.1

---

#### **Question B (14 Marks) [KTU University Exam – May 2024 Model]**

**(a)** What is **blend spinning**? Explain any **two methods of blending** cotton with polyester with suitable diagrams. (7 marks)

**(b)** A 30/70 polyester/cotton blend yarn has Tex = 25. Calculate (i) the English count of the yarn, (ii) the **mass of cotton** and **mass of polyester** in a 1 kg yarn sample. (7 marks)

**Model Solution:**

**(a) Blend Spinning (7 marks):**

**Definition (2 marks):** Blend spinning is the process of deliberately mixing two or more fibre types (e.g., cotton and polyester) during yarn manufacture to produce a yarn that combines the desirable properties of each fibre — e.g., the strength and dimensional stability of polyester with the moisture absorbency and comfort of cotton.

**Method 1: Bale Blending (2.5 marks):**
- Bales of cotton and polyester fibres are arranged in alternating layers (typically 6–12 layers) in a stack.
- Tuft-by-tuft, fibres are picked from vertical sections of the stack, resulting in a homogenised blend.
- **Advantage:** Economical for large lots.
- **Disadvantage:** Blend homogeneity is moderate.

**Method 2: Draw Frame Blending (2.5 marks):**
- 4–8 slivers of cotton and 4–8 slivers of polyester are fed simultaneously into the back of a draw frame.
- The draft zone intimately mixes the fibres at the fibre level.
- **Advantage:** Most homogeneous blend; preferred for high-quality PC yarns.
- **Disadvantage:** Higher machine investment.

*(Diagram: refer to Section 4.3 above.)*

**(b) Blend Yarn Calculations (7 marks):**

**Given:** P/C = 30/70, Tex = 25

**(i) English Count (2 marks):**

$$Ne = \frac{590.5}{Tex} = \frac{590.5}{25} = 23.62 \approx 24s$$

**(ii) Mass of Components in 1 kg Yarn (5 marks):**

- Total yarn mass = 1000 g
- Polyester fraction = 30% → Mass of Polyester:

$$W_P = 0.30 \times 1000 = 300 \text{ g}$$

- Cotton fraction = 70% → Mass of Cotton:

$$W_C = 0.70 \times 1000 = 700 \text{ g}$$

**Verification (optional):**

$$\%P = \frac{300}{300+700} \times 100 = 30\% \quad ; \quad \%C = \frac{700}{1000} \times 100 = 70\%$$

**Final Answers:** Ne ≈ 24s, Polyester = 300 g, Cotton = 700 g.

---

### 5.3 KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Mark-Loss Pitfalls in KTU 2024 Board Exams:**
> 1. **Formula Confusion:** Students frequently write **Ne = 590.5/Tex** (the *inverse* of the correct relation). The correct formula is **Tex = 590.5 / Ne**.
> 2. **Unit Mismatch:** Forgetting to convert km → m, or yards → metres, when substituting into Tex or Ne formulas — this can cost 1–2 marks.
> 3. **Twist Multiplier Direction:** Confusing TM = TPI × √Ne with TM = TPI / √Ne. Always remember: **TPI = TM × √Ne**, so **TM = TPI / √Ne**.
> 4. **Blend % Confusion:** Mixing up the dissolved residue (e.g., assuming the residue *is* the soluble component). In a P/C blend dissolved in H₂SO₄, the **residue is cotton**; the dissolved part is polyester.
> 5. **Insufficient Diagram:** A flow diagram without labels or arrows loses at least 1–2 marks in Part B answers. Always use **rectangular blocks + labelled arrows**.
> 6. **Skipping Assumptions:** For Tex–Ne conversion, always state "assuming standard moisture regain of cotton (8.5%)."

---

### 5.4 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!NOTE]
> **High-Density Rapid Revision Checklist:**

**Spinning Basics:**
- Ring spinning = traveller + ring + spindle; produces strong, hairy, fine yarn.
- Rotor spinning = open-end; bulkier, more even, lower hairiness.
- Air-jet / vortex = lowest hairiness, ideal for suiting.
- Compact spinning = premium ring; eliminates spinning triangle; very low hairiness.

**Blending Methods:**
- Bale blending (least precise, cheapest).
- Draw frame blending (most precise, industry standard).
- Sliver blending; roving blending; yarn doubling (plied blends).

**Yarn Count — Must Know:**
- Ne (indirect): finer yarn → higher Ne.
- Tex (direct): finer yarn → lower Tex.
- **Key Conversion:** Tex = 590.5 / Ne (cotton).
- Denier = 9 × Tex.

**Yarn Appearance — Key Descriptors:**
- Evenness (CV% via Uster tester).
- Hairiness (Zweigle / Shirley methods).
- Faults: thick (+50%), thin (-50%), neps (+200%) per km.
- Cleanliness, lustre, package neatness.

**Twist Design:**
- TPI = TM × √Ne (cotton convention).
- TM = 3.0 to 4.2 for cotton, depending on end-use.
- TPM = TPI × 39.37.

**Blend Verification:**
- Chemical dissolution test (e.g., H₂SO₄ for P/C).
- Component mass calculated as % of total.

**High-Yield Constants for KTU Board:**
- 590.5 (cotton Tex–Ne constant)
- 9 (Tex–Denier multiplier)
- 39.37 (inches-per-metre)
- 8.5% (cotton standard regain)
- 1093.6 (yards per km)

---
