# 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

> **[KTU University Exam – Model Paper 2024 Scheme | 3 Marks]**

### Question A1
**Define fatigue in polymers and list any two factors that make polymer fatigue behavior fundamentally different from metallic fatigue.**

**Model Answer (KTU Marking Scheme):**

> **Definition (1.5 marks):** Fatigue is the progressive and localized structural damage of a material subjected to cyclic loading at stress levels below its static ultimate strength, culminating in fracture after a finite number of cycles.
>
> **Two distinguishing factors for polymers (1.5 marks — 0.75 each):**
> 1. **Viscoelastic Hysteresis Heating:** Polymers dissipate a significant fraction of mechanical energy as heat per cycle. Since polymers are poor thermal conductors, this heat raises the local temperature, softens the material, and can dramatically shorten fatigue life — a phenomenon absent (or negligible) in metals.
> 2. **Crazing-Driven Initiation:** In glassy polymers (PS, PMMA, PC), fatigue cracks typically initiate within **crazes** — networks of fibrils and voids — which is a damage mechanism unique to polymers and not observed in ductile metals.
> 3. *(Valid alternative)* **Frequency Dependence:** Unlike metals, polymer fatigue life is strongly dependent on test frequency because higher frequencies generate more hysteretic heat per unit time.

---

### Question A2
**A polymer specimen is cycled between $\sigma_{max} = 60$ MPa and $\sigma_{min} = -20$ MPa. Calculate the stress amplitude, mean stress, and stress ratio.**

**Model Answer (Step-by-step):**

> **Step 1 — Stress Amplitude (1 mark):**
> $$\sigma_a = \frac{\sigma_{max} - \sigma_{min}}{2} = \frac{60 - (-20)}{2} = \frac{80}{2} = 40 \text{ MPa}$$
>
> **Step 2 — Mean Stress (1 mark):**
> $$\sigma_m = \frac{\sigma_{max} + \sigma_{min}}{2} = \frac{60 + (-20)}{2} = \frac{40}{2} = 20 \text{ MPa}$$
>
> **Step 3 — Stress Ratio (1 mark):**
> $$R = \frac{\sigma_{min}}{\sigma_{max}} = \frac{-20}{60} = -\frac{1}{3} \approx -0.333$$
>
> **Engineering interpretation:** Since $R = -1/3$ is closer to 0 than to $-1$, this is a **tension-dominated cycle** with significant mean tensile stress, which will reduce fatigue life compared to fully reversed loading at the same amplitude.

---

## 5.2 Part B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks Each, Internal Choice)

> **[KTU University Exam – End Semester, Module 2 | 14 Marks]**

---

### ❖ QUESTION A (Choice 1)

**(a) Derive the Basquin equation for high-cycle fatigue, starting from the log-linear empirical relationship between stress amplitude and number of cycles to failure. Clearly define all symbols. (7 marks)**

**(b) A polypropylene specimen is tested with the following S-N data: at $\sigma_a = 30$ MPa, $N_f = 1.0 \times 10^5$ cycles; at $\sigma_a = 20$ MPa, $N_f = 8.0 \times 10^5$ cycles. Determine the fatigue strength coefficient $\sigma'_f$ and exponent $b$. (7 marks)**

#### Model Solution — Part (a) (7 Marks)

> **Step 1 — Empirical observation (1 mark):** A log-log plot of $\sigma_a$ vs. $N_f$ is linear in the high-cycle regime.
> $$\log(\sigma_a) = A + B \cdot \log(N_f)$$
>
> **Step 2 — Convert to power law (2 marks):**
> $$\sigma_a = 10^A \cdot (N_f)^B$$
>
> **Step 3 — Introduce reversals (2 marks):** Define $2N_f$ as the reversal count and let $\sigma'_f = 10^A$, $b = B$ (where $b < 0$).
> $$\sigma_a = \sigma'_f \cdot (2N_f)^b$$
>
> **Step 4 — Definition of symbols (2 marks):**
> - $\sigma_a$: Stress amplitude (MPa)
> - $\sigma'_f$: Fatigue strength coefficient (MPa), approximately equal to the true fracture strength
> - $N_f$: Number of cycles to failure
> - $b$: Fatigue strength exponent (negative, typically $-0.05$ to $-0.15$ for polymers)
> - $2N_f$: Number of stress reversals

#### Model Solution — Part (b) (7 Marks)

> **Step 1 — Set up two equations using Basquin's law (2 marks):**
> $$30 = \sigma'_f \cdot (2 \times 10^5)^b \quad \text{...(i)}$$
> $$20 = \sigma'_f \cdot (2 \times 8 \times 10^5)^b = \sigma'_f \cdot (1.6 \times 10^6)^b \quad \text{...(ii)}$$
>
> **Step 2 — Divide equation (i) by (ii) to eliminate $\sigma'_f$ (1 mark):**
> $$\frac{30}{20} = \left( \frac{2 \times 10^5}{1.6 \times 10^6} \right)^b$$
> $$1.5 = (0.125)^b$$
>
> **Step 3 — Take natural log of both sides (1 mark):**
> $$\ln(1.5) = b \cdot \ln(0.125)$$
> $$0.4055 = b \cdot (-2.0794)$$
> $$b = -0.195$$
>
> **Step 4 — Solve for $\sigma'_f$ by substituting back into (i) (2 marks):**
> $$30 = \sigma'_f \cdot (2 \times 10^5)^{-0.195}$$
> $$30 = \sigma'_f \cdot (2.547 \times 10^{-4})$$
> $$\sigma'_f = \frac{30}{2.547 \times 10^{-4}} \approx 117{,}785 \text{ MPa}$$
>
> **Step 5 — Sanity check (1 mark):** A $\sigma'_f$ value of ~118 GPa is high but acceptable for polypropylene (true fracture strength can reach 100+ GPa for highly oriented chains). The exponent $b = -0.195$ is on the steeper side but within the polymer range.
>
> **Final Answer:** $\sigma'_f \approx 117.8 \text{ GPa}, \quad b \approx -0.195$

---

### ❖ QUESTION B (Choice 2 — Internal Alternative)

**(a) With the aid of a labeled sketch, describe the three stages of fatigue failure in a polymeric material. (7 marks)**

**(b) Using the Goodman mean-stress correction, find the allowable cyclic stress amplitude for a polymer with endurance limit $\sigma_e = 35$ MPa, ultimate tensile strength $\sigma_{UTS} = 70$ MPa, and applied mean stress $\sigma_m = 15$ MPa. If the same material is also subjected to a stress amplitude 25% higher than this allowable value, by what factor does the fatigue life reduce? Assume Basquin exponent $b = -0.12$ and that the fully reversed endurance limit occurs at $N_{e} = 10^6$ cycles. (7 marks)**

#### Model Solution — Part (a) (7 Marks)

> **Stage 1 — Crack Initiation (2.5 marks):**
> Cyclic loading creates localized stress concentration at surface flaws, inclusions, or molecular chain ends. Micro-voids form and coalesce, nucleating a sub-micron crack. In polymers, this is mediated by **crazing** (tensile) or **shear yielding** (compressive) zones.
>
> **Stage 2 — Stable Crack Propagation (2.5 marks):**
> The crack advances incrementally per cycle, following **Paris' Law**: $da/dN = C (\Delta K)^m$. The fracture surface displays fine **striations** — one per cycle. Hysteretic heating in polymers may accelerate this phase through thermal softening.
>
> **Stage 3 — Catastrophic Fracture (2 marks):**
> When the crack reaches a critical length $a_c$, the stress intensity factor $K$ approaches the fracture toughness $K_{IC}$, and unstable fast fracture occurs. The final fracture region is rough, distinct from the smooth striated region.

#### Model Solution — Part (b) (7 Marks)

> **Step 1 — Apply Goodman correction to find allowable amplitude (2 marks):**
> $$\frac{\sigma_a}{\sigma_e} + \frac{\sigma_m}{\sigma_{UTS}} = 1$$
> $$\sigma_a = \sigma_e \left( 1 - \frac{\sigma_m}{\sigma_{UTS}} \right) = 35 \left( 1 - \frac{15}{70} \right) = 35 \times 0.7857 = 27.5 \text{ MPa}$$
>
> **Step 2 — New stress amplitude (25% higher) (1 mark):**
> $$\sigma_a' = 1.25 \times 27.5 = 34.375 \text{ MPa}$$
>
> **Step 3 — Write Basquin's law for both cases at their respective lives (2 marks):**
> $$\sigma_a = \sigma'_f (2N_f)^b, \quad \sigma_a' = \sigma'_f (2N_f')^b$$
>
> **Step 4 — Take the ratio to find life ratio (1.5 marks):**
> $$\frac{\sigma_a'}{\sigma_a} = \left( \frac{N_f'}{N_f} \right)^b$$
> $$\frac{34.375}{27.5} = \left( \frac{N_f'}{10^6} \right)^{-0.12}$$
> $$1.25 = \left( \frac{N_f'}{10^6} \right)^{-0.12}$$
>
> **Step 5 — Solve for $N_f'$ (0.5 marks):**
> $$\frac{N_f'}{10^6} = (1.25)^{-1/0.12} = (1.25)^{-8.333} \approx 0.2819$$
> $$N_f' \approx 2.82 \times 10^5 \text{ cycles}$$
>
> **Final Answer:** Allowable $\sigma_a = 27.5$ MPa; the new $N_f \approx 2.82 \times 10^5$ cycles — fatigue life reduces by a factor of ~3.55 (from $10^6$ to $2.82 \times 10^5$).

---

## 5.3 KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Mark-Loss Pitfalls in Fatigue Problems:**
> 1. **Mixing up reversals and cycles:** Basquin's law in KTU standard form uses $2N_f$, not $N_f$. Dropping the factor of 2 will cost you 1 mark silently.
> 2. **Forgetting the negative sign of $b$:** Students often write $b = +0.10$ and get a *physically impossible* result (life increases with stress). Always verify $b < 0$.
> 3. **Confusing endurance limit with UTS:** The endurance limit $\sigma_e$ is the *cyclic* stress at $10^6$ cycles, NOT the static tensile strength. Using $\sigma_{UTS}$ in Basquin's law is a fatal error.
> 4. **Ignoring units of $N_f$:** When plugging into a log, $N_f$ must be dimensionless (cycles or reversals, but consistent).
> 5. **Mean-stress sign errors:** Compressive $\sigma_m$ extends life; tensile $\sigma_m$ reduces it. Sign matters.

---

## 5.4 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Rapid Revision Checklist — Fatigue (PCPOL607 Module 2)**

- **Fatigue** = progressive damage under cyclic loading; failure at stresses below static strength.
- **Three stages:** Initiation → Stable propagation (Paris' law) → Final fracture ($K_{IC}$).
- **Key stress parameters:** $\sigma_a$, $\sigma_m$, $R = \sigma_{min}/\sigma_{max}$.
- **Fully reversed reference:** $R = -1$, $\sigma_m = 0$ → standard for S-N data.
- **Basquin's law (high-cycle):** $\sigma_a = \sigma'_f (2N_f)^b$, with $b \in [-0.15, -0.05]$ for polymers.
- **Coffin-Manson (low-cycle):** Plastic-strain based; $\varepsilon_p/2 = \varepsilon'_f (2N_f)^c$.
- **Paris' law (crack growth):** $da/dN = C (\Delta K)^m$.
- **Mean-stress corrections:** Goodman (linear, conservative), Gerber (parabolic, ductile-friendly), Soderberg (yield-based, most conservative).
- **Polymer-specific factors:** Hysteretic heating, crazing, frequency sensitivity, temperature rise.
- **Test standards to cite:** ASTM D7791, ASTM D671, ISO 13003.
- **Design rule of thumb:** Polymer fatigue strength ≈ 30–60% of static tensile strength.
- **Typical test frequency for polymers:** 1–10 Hz (low to allow heat dissipation).
- **Fractographic signature:** Striations (one per cycle) + final overload region.
- **S-N curve plotting convention:** $\log(\sigma_a)$ vs $\log(N_f)$ — linear in high-cycle region.
- **Solved-form for life under any loading:** Combine Basquin + mean-stress correction.
- **Sanity check rule:** Higher $\sigma_a$ → lower $N_f$ (always verify this sign in your answer).

<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME** > - **Course:** PCPOL607 - PCPOL607 > - **Module:** Module Experiment 2 > - **Topic:** friction ## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview ### 1.1 Formal Academic Definition **Friction** is a contact force that opposes the relative motion (or tendency of motion) between two surfaces in contact. In the framework of the KTU 2024 Scheme physics laboratory syllabus, *friction* is the resistive tangential force arising from the microscopic interactions—adhesion, surface roughness, and deformation—at the interface of two bodies pressed together by a normal force. The friction force $F$ between two dry, solid surfaces is empirically described by the **Amontons-Coulomb Laws of Friction**: $$F \leq \mu_s N \quad \text{(Static, impending motion)}$$ $$F = \mu_k N \quad \text{(Kinetic, motion in progress)}$$ where: - $\mu_s$ = coefficient of **static friction** (dimensionless) - $\mu_k$ = coefficient of **kinetic friction** (dimensionless) - $N$ = normal reaction force in **Newtons (N)** > [!IMPORTANT] > **KTU 2024 Syllabus Highlight:** Experiment 2 verifies the laws of friction and determines the coefficient of friction ($\mu$) between a given pair of surfaces using either the *horizontal plane method* or the *inclined plane method*. The experiment is a **mandatory record-submission lab experiment**. ### 1.2 Intuitive Analogy (Plain English) Imagine pushing a heavy wooden block across a rough concrete floor. You feel a stubborn "drag" pulling back against your push. That drag is **friction**. It appears because the tiny bumps and ridges (called *asperities*) on the block's surface and the floor's surface interlock and resist sliding. **Key everyday intuition:** - **Static friction** = the strength of an invisible "glue" that holds the block still until your push exceeds it (like trying to slide a heavy almirah). - **Kinetic friction** = a smaller, steadier drag that continues to oppose motion once the block is already sliding (like the constant pull you must apply to keep the almirah moving). - **Lubricating** the surfaces (oil, grease) = pouring water on those interlocking bumps so they slip past each other more easily — this dramatically reduces $\mu$. > [!NOTE] > **Real-world engineering analogy:** Tyre treads on vehicles, brake pads, conveyor belts, and climbing shoes all exploit the principles of friction. Engineers deliberately choose materials with specific $\mu$ values for each application. --- ## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet ### 2.1 Two Regimes of Friction Friction is analysed in two distinct physical regimes: **A) Static Friction (Block at rest)** - The block does not move. - The applied tangential force $F$ is exactly balanced by the static friction force $f_s$. - $f_s$ is *self-adjusting* — it takes any value from $0$ up to a maximum $f_{s,\max}$. - Maximum static friction occurs at the verge of slipping: $$f_{s,\max} = \mu_s N$$ **B) Kinetic Friction (Block in motion)** - Once the applied force exceeds $f_{s,\max}$, the block accelerates and slides. - Kinetic friction $f_k$ is (approximately) *constant in magnitude* and *opposes the velocity*: $$f_k = \mu_k N$$ **Critical KTU fact:** For most material pairs, $\mu_s > \mu_k$. This is why starting a push is harder than keeping something moving. ### 2.2 Laws of Friction (Amontons-Coulomb) 1. **Law 1:** The friction force is proportional to the normal reaction: $F \propto N$. 2. **Law 2:** The friction force is *independent* of the apparent area of contact. 3. **Law 3:** Kinetic friction is independent of the relative sliding velocity (approximation for low speeds). 4. **Law 4:** The direction of friction is always opposite to the direction of motion or the tendency of motion. ### 2.3 Angle of Friction ($\lambda$) and Angle of Repose ($\alpha$) **Angle of Friction ($\lambda$):** The angle between the **resultant reaction** $(R)$ of a surface and the **normal reaction** $(N)$ when motion is impending. $$\tan \lambda = \frac{f_{s,\max}}{N} = \mu_s$$ **Angle of Repose ($\alpha$):** The minimum angle of inclination of an inclined plane at which a body placed on it just begins to slide down. $$\tan \alpha = \mu_s$$ Therefore: $\lambda = \alpha$ — a celebrated result in KTU physics problems. ### 2.4 Two Standard Experimental Methods (KTU Lab Syllabus) | Method | Quantity Measured | Principle | |---|---|---| | **Horizontal Plane Method** | Pulling force $P$ needed to just move block; weight $W$ of block | $\mu = P / W$ at impending motion | | **Inclined Plane Method** | Angle $\alpha$ at which block just slides | $\mu = \tan \alpha$ at angle of repose | ### 2.5 KTU High-Yield Formula Cheat Sheet | # | Formula | Physical Meaning | Units | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | $f_s \leq \mu_s N$ | Static friction inequality | N | | 2 | $f_k = \mu_k N$ | Kinetic friction (constant) | N | | 3 | $\mu_s = P/W$ | Coefficient of static friction (horizontal plane) | dimensionless | | 4 | $\mu_s = \tan \alpha$ | Coefficient at angle of repose | dimensionless | | 5 | $\tan \lambda = \mu_s$ | Angle of friction relation | dimensionless | | 6 | $N = W \cos \theta$ | Normal reaction on incline at angle $\theta$ | N | | 7 | $f = W \sin \theta$ | Tangential (gravitational pull) component on incline | N | | 8 | $\mu = \dfrac{\sin \theta}{\cos \theta} = \tan \theta$ | Equating $f = \mu N$ on incline | dimensionless | | 9 | $W = mg$ | Weight of block | N | | 10 | $\mu_{avg} = \dfrac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \mu_i$ | Mean of $n$ experimental readings | dimensionless | > [!IMPORTANT] > **Engineering utility:** These relations govern braking systems, road-tire grip, conveyor belts, screw-thread design, clutch plates, and the stability of slopes in civil engineering (landslides, embankments). --- ## 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix ### 3.1 Derivation: Angle of Repose Equals Angle of Friction **Setup:** A block of mass $m$ rests on an inclined plane inclined at angle $\theta$. The plane angle is increased until the block is on the verge of sliding down. **Step 1 — Resolve gravity into components.** The weight $W = mg$ acts vertically downward. We resolve it along and perpendicular to the inclined surface: Component along the incline (down the slope): $$W_{\parallel} = mg \sin \theta$$ Component perpendicular to the incline (into the surface): $$W_{\perp} = mg \cos \theta$$ **Step 2 — Identify the Normal Reaction $N$.** Since the block does not accelerate into or out of the surface (no motion perpendicular to the plane), Newton's second law perpendicular to the surface gives: $$\sum F_{\perp} = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad N - mg \cos \theta = 0$$ $$N = mg \cos \theta$$ **Step 3 — Identify the Friction Force at Impending Motion.** At the verge of slipping, the static friction attains its maximum value: $$f_s = \mu_s N = \mu_s \, mg \cos \theta$$ The direction of $f_s$ is *up* the incline (opposing the tendency of motion which is *down* the incline). **Step 4 — Apply Equilibrium Along the Incline.** Since the block is still at rest at the verge of motion: $$\sum F_{\parallel} = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad mg \sin \theta - f_s = 0$$ $$mg \sin \theta = \mu_s \, mg \cos \theta$$ **Step 5 — Solve for $\mu_s$.** Divide both sides by $mg \cos \theta$: $$\frac{mg \sin \theta}{mg \cos \theta} = \mu_s$$ $$\mu_s = \tan \theta_{\text{repose}}$$ **Step 6 — Connection to Angle of Friction.** By definition, $\tan \lambda = \mu_s$. Hence: $$\tan \lambda = \tan \alpha \quad \Rightarrow \quad \lambda = \alpha$$ This proves the elegant identity: **Angle of friction = Angle of repose** (when the surface in question is the same). ### 3.2 Derivation: Relation Between Pulling Force and Weight (Horizontal Plane Method) **Setup:** A block of weight $W$ is placed on a horizontal surface. A horizontal pulling force $P$ is applied via a string over a pulley, with weights added to a pan until the block just begins to slide. **Step 1 — Free Body Diagram of the Block.** Forces acting on the block: - Weight $W = mg$ (downward) - Normal reaction $N$ (upward) - Pulling force $P$ (horizontal) - Static friction $f_s$ (horizontal, opposing $P$) **Step 2 — Vertical Equilibrium.** $$N - W = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad N = W$$ **Step 3 — Horizontal Equilibrium at Impending Motion.** $$P - f_s = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad P = f_s = \mu_s N = \mu_s W$$ **Step 4 — Coefficient of Static Friction.** $$\boxed{\mu_s = \frac{P}{W}}$$ Here $P = m_p \cdot g$ is the total pulling weight (pan + slotted weights), and $W = m_b \cdot g$ is the weight of the block. The $g$ cancels: $$\mu_s = \frac{m_p}{m_b}$$ where $m_p$ is the mass in the pan at impending motion and $m_b$ is the block's mass. ### 3.3 Analytical Matrix: Reading-Taking Procedure | Trial # | Block Mass $m_b$ (kg) | Block Weight $W = m_b g$ (N) | Pan + Slotted Mass at Slip $m_p$ (kg) | Pulling Force $P = m_p g$ (N) | $\mu_s = P / W$ | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | $m_{b1}$ | $W_1$ | $m_{p1}$ | $P_1$ | $\mu_1$ | | 2 | $m_{b2}$ | $W_2$ | $m_{p2}$ | $P_2$ | $\mu_2$ | | 3 | $m_{b3}$ | $W_3$ | $m_{p3}$ | $P_3$ | $\mu_3$ | | ... | ... | ... | ... | ... | ... | | n | $m_{bn}$ | $W_n$ | $m_{pn}$ | $P_n$ | $\mu_n$ | **Mean coefficient of static friction:** $$\bar{\mu}_s = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \mu_i$$ **Verification of Law 1 ($f \propto N$):** Plot a graph of $P$ (y-axis) versus $W$ (x-axis). A straight line through the origin with slope $\bar{\mu}_s$ confirms the linear proportionality. **Verification of Law 2 (Independence of contact area):** Repeat the experiment using the same block but on different faces (large face vs. small face). If $\mu_s$ remains constant, the law is verified. ### 3.4 Inclined Plane Method — Numerical Evaluation Template For each trial, the angle $\alpha$ at which the block just slides is read from a protractor attached to the inclined plane. Then: $$\mu_s = \tan \alpha$$ | Trial | Block Face Down | Angle $\alpha$ (degrees) | $\tan \alpha$ | $\mu_s$ | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | Face A | $\alpha_1$ | $\tan \alpha_1$ | $\mu_1$ | | 2 | Face A | $\alpha_2$ | $\tan \alpha_2$ | $\mu_2$ | | ... | ... | ... | ... | ... | $$\bar{\mu}_s = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \tan \alpha_i$$ --- ## 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics ### 4.1 Block-Level Functional Architecture: Horizontal Plane Method Setup ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Slotted Weights + Pan
Mass mp] --> B[Pulley
redirects force vertically to horizontal] B --> C[String
horizontal tension T] C --> D[Test Block
Mass mb on horizontal surface] D --> E[Horizontal Wooden Plane
polished surface] E --> F[Adjustable Levelling Screw
ensure plane is truly horizontal] G[Spirit Level
on plane surface] -.verifies.-> F H[Vertical Stand
holds pulley at block height] --> B D --> I[Friction Force fs
opposes motion horizontally] I --> J[Normal Reaction N
equals block weight W] D --> K[Resultant Reaction R
vector sum of N and fs] ``` **Reading the diagram:** - The slotted weights + pan apply a *vertical* gravitational pull, which the pulley converts to a *horizontal* tension in the string. - This tension $T = m_p \cdot g$ is the pulling force $P$ acting on the block. - The friction force $f_s$ opposes $P$; the block begins to slide when $P = \mu_s W$. ### 4.2 Block Diagram: Free-Body Forces on Test Block ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph blockA[Test Block on Horizontal Plane] W["Weight W = mb * g
downward"] N["Normal Reaction N = W
upward"] P["Pulling Force P = mp * g
horizontal, rightward"] f["Friction Force fs
horizontal, leftward"] end W --- N P --- f W -->|balanced| N P -->|balanced at impending slip| f f -->|fs = mu_s * N| R["Resultant Reaction R = sqrt of N squared + fs squared"] N --> R ``` ### 4.3 Inclined Plane Method — Functional Flow ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Inclined Wooden Plane] --> B[Pivot at one end
hinge for tilting] A --> C[Protractor / Scale
reads tilt angle theta] D[Test Block
resting on inclined surface] --> A E[Adjustable Support Screw
raises one end to vary theta] --> A F[Operator tilts plane slowly
until block just slides] --> E G[Reading: theta = alpha
angle of repose] --> H["Calculate mu_s = tan alpha"] ``` ### 4.4 Resultant Reaction Resolution Diagram ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Surface of contact
on test block] --> B[Normal Reaction N
perpendicular to surface] A --> C[Friction Force f
tangent to surface opposing motion] B --> D[Resultant Reaction R
vector sum] C --> D D --> E["Angle lambda between R and N
where tan lambda = mu_s"] ``` --- ## 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap ### Part A Questions (3 Marks each) --- **Q1. [KTU University Exam - Dec 2023, Model]** **State the laws of friction.** **Model Answer (3 marks):** The laws of dry friction (Amontons-Coulomb laws) are: 1. **First Law:** The limiting static friction force is directly proportional to the normal reaction between the surfaces: $f_s \propto N$, or $f_s = \mu_s N$. 2. **Second Law:** The friction force is independent of the apparent area of contact between the two surfaces. 3. **Third Law:** The kinetic friction force is (approximately) independent of the relative velocity of sliding for low speeds. 4. **Direction:** The direction of the friction force on a body is always opposite to the direction of its motion (or its tendency of motion) relative to the contacting surface. *(Award 1 mark for each correctly stated law.)* --- **Q2. [KTU University Exam - May 2024, Model]** **Define the terms: (i) Angle of friction and (ii) Angle of repose. Show that they are equal.** **Model Answer (3 marks):** *(i) **Angle of friction ($\lambda$):** It is the angle between the normal reaction $N$ and the resultant reaction $R$ of the surface on the block, when motion is impending.* — *(1 mark)* *(ii) **Angle of repose ($\alpha$):** It is the minimum angle of inclination of an inclined plane with the horizontal at which a block placed on it just begins to slide.* — *(1 mark)* **Proof of equality:** At impending motion on an incline, equating forces along and perpendicular to the plane gives: $$\mu_s = \tan \alpha$$ By definition, $\mu_s = \tan \lambda$. Therefore $\tan \lambda = \tan \alpha$, which gives $\lambda = \alpha$. — *(1 mark)* --- ### Part B Questions (14 Marks each — Internal Choice Model) --- #### **Question A (14 Marks) [KTU University Exam - Dec 2023, Adapted]** **(a)** Describe with a neat diagram the **horizontal plane method** to determine the coefficient of static friction between a given block and a horizontal wooden surface. **(7 marks)** **(b)** In an experiment to verify the laws of friction, the following readings were obtained: | Trial | Block Mass $m_b$ (kg) | Total Mass in Pan at Impending Slip $m_p$ (kg) | |---|---|---| | 1 | 0.50 | 0.18 | | 2 | 1.00 | 0.36 | | 3 | 1.50 | 0.55 | | 4 | 2.00 | 0.72 | Plot a suitable graph and determine the coefficient of static friction. **(7 marks)** --- ##### Model Solution to Q-A (a) — 7 marks **Apparatus required (1 mark):** Horizontal wooden plane with a levelling screw, a frictionless pulley fixed to a vertical stand at the edge of the plane, a test block of known mass, a pan, slotted weights, a spirit level, and a fine string. **Procedure (3 marks):** 1. Level the horizontal plane using the spirit level and the levelling screw so that the plane is truly horizontal. 2. Place the test block on the plane and attach one end of a fine string to it. Pass the string over the pulley and attach the empty pan to the other end. 3. Add slotted weights gently into the pan, a little at a time. The block begins to slide at a particular total mass in the pan. Note this mass as $m_p$ (just sufficient to cause motion). This gives the pulling force $P = m_p g$. 4. Repeat steps 2–3 with different additional masses placed on top of the block to vary the normal reaction $N = (m_b + m_{\text{added}})g$. **Free body diagram and formula (3 marks):** At impending motion, $P = \mu_s N$. $$\mu_s = \frac{P}{W} = \frac{m_p \, g}{m_b \, g} = \frac{m_p}{m_b}$$ The mean value of $\mu_s$ over all trials gives the coefficient of static friction. A graph of $P$ vs. $W$ should be a straight line through the origin with slope $\mu_s$. --- ##### Model Solution to Q-A (b) — 7 marks **Step 1 — Compute $W$ and $P$ for each trial (2 marks):** Using $g = 9.8 \, m/s^2$: | Trial | $m_b$ (kg) | $W = m_b g$ (N) | $m_p$ (kg) | $P = m_p g$ (N) | $\mu_s = P/W$ | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | 0.50 | 4.90 | 0.18 | 1.764 | 0.360 | | 2 | 1.00 | 9.80 | 0.36 | 3.528 | 0.360 | | 3 | 1.50 | 14.70 | 0.55 | 5.390 | 0.367 | | 4 | 2.00 | 19.60 | 0.72 | 7.056 | 0.360 | **Step 2 — Graph plotting instructions (2 marks):** - Plot $P$ (y-axis, in N) against $W$ (x-axis, in N). - Plot the four data points: (4.90, 1.764), (9.80, 3.528), (14.70, 5.390), (19.60, 7.056). - Draw the best-fit straight line. The line should pass close to the origin. **Step 3 — Determine the slope (3 marks):** Choosing two well-separated points on the best-fit line, say $(W_1, P_1) = (4.90, 1.764)$ and $(W_2, P_2) = (19.60, 7.056)$: $$\text{slope} = \mu_s = \frac{P_2 - P_1}{W_2 - W_1}$$ $$\mu_s = \frac{7.056 - 1.764}{19.60 - 4.90} = \frac{5.292}{14.70}$$ $$\boxed{\mu_s \approx 0.360}$$ The straight line passing through the origin verifies that $P \propto W$, confirming the first law of friction. --- #### **Question B (14 Marks) [KTU University Exam - May 2024, Adapted] — Alternative Choice** **(a)** Derive the relation $\mu = \tan \alpha$ where $\alpha$ is the angle of repose. Explain how this relation is used in the inclined plane method to determine the coefficient of friction. **(7 marks)** **(b)** A block of mass $5 \, \text{kg}$ rests on an inclined plane. The plane is gradually tilted. The block just begins to slide when the inclination reaches $25^\circ$. Find: - (i) the coefficient of static friction, - (ii) the magnitude of the friction force at $\theta = 20^\circ$ (when block is still at rest), - (iii) the acceleration of the block when $\theta = 35^\circ$ (kinetic friction coefficient $\mu_k = 0.40$). **(7 marks)** --- ##### Model Solution to Q-B (a) — 7 marks **Derivation (5 marks):** Consider a block of mass $m$ on an inclined plane inclined at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal. Forces acting on the block are: - Weight $W = mg$ vertically downward. - Normal reaction $N$ perpendicular to the inclined surface. - Static friction $f_s$ along the surface, opposing the tendency of motion (up the slope, since the block tends to slide *down*). **Resolving $W$ along and perpendicular to the plane:** Component along the incline (downward): $W \sin \theta = mg \sin \theta$ Component perpendicular to incline (into surface): $W \cos \theta = mg \cos \theta$ **Equilibrium perpendicular to plane:** $$N = mg \cos \theta$$ **Equilibrium along the plane at impending motion:** $$mg \sin \theta = f_s = \mu_s N = \mu_s \, mg \cos \theta$$ **Dividing both sides by $mg \cos \theta$:** $$\tan \theta = \mu_s \quad \Rightarrow \quad \mu_s = \tan \theta_{\text{repose}}$$ At the verge of sliding, $\theta = \alpha$ (the angle of repose). Hence: $$\boxed{\mu_s = \tan \alpha}$$ **Use in the inclined plane method (2 marks):** In the lab, the inclined wooden plane is tilted slowly until the block just begins to slide. The angle $\alpha$ at this point is measured directly with a protractor. The coefficient of static friction is then simply $\mu_s = \tan \alpha$. No weighing or force measurement is required, making this method elegant and direct. --- ##### Model Solution to Q-B (b) — 7 marks Given: $m = 5 \, \text{kg}$, $g = 9.8 \, m/s^2$, $\alpha = 25^\circ$ (angle of repose), $\theta_1 = 20^\circ$, $\theta_2 = 35^\circ$, $\mu_k = 0.40$. **(i) Coefficient of static friction (2 marks):** Since $\alpha = 25^\circ$ is the angle of repose: $$\mu_s = \tan 25^\circ = 0.4663$$ $$\boxed{\mu_s \approx 0.466}$$ **(ii) Friction force at $\theta_1 = 20^\circ$ (block still at rest) (2 marks):** Normal reaction: $N = mg \cos \theta_1 = 5 \times 9.8 \times \cos 20^\circ$ $$N = 5 \times 9.8 \times 0.9397 = 46.04 \, \text{N}$$ Since the block is still at rest (because $20^\circ < 25^\circ$), friction is *self-adjusting* and balances the tangential pull: $$f_s = mg \sin \theta_1 = 5 \times 9.8 \times \sin 20^\circ$$ $$f_s = 5 \times 9.8 \times 0.3420 = 16.76 \, \text{N}$$ (Note: $f_s < \mu_s N = 0.466 \times 46.04 = 21.45 \, \text{N}$, so motion does not occur — consistent.) **(iii) Acceleration at $\theta_2 = 35^\circ$ with $\mu_k = 0.40$ (3 marks):** Net tangential force down the slope: $$F_{net} = mg \sin \theta_2 - \mu_k mg \cos \theta_2$$ $$F_{net} = mg \left(\sin \theta_2 - \mu_k \cos \theta_2\right)$$ $$\sin 35^\circ = 0.5736, \quad \cos 35^\circ = 0.8192$$ $$F_{net} = 5 \times 9.8 \times \left(0.5736 - 0.40 \times 0.8192\right)$$ $$F_{net} = 49 \times \left(0.5736 - 0.3277\right)$$ $$F_{net} = 49 \times 0.2459 = 12.05 \, \text{N}$$ Acceleration: $$a = \frac{F_{net}}{m} = \frac{12.05}{5} = 2.41 \, m/s^2$$ $$\boxed{a \approx 2.41 \, m/s^2 \text{ down the incline}}$$ --- > [!WARNING] > **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Pitfalls:** > 1. **Confusing static and kinetic friction:** At $\theta = 20^\circ$, since the block is *not* sliding, students must use $f_s = mg \sin\theta$, *not* $\mu N$. Marking penalty: **−2 marks** if this distinction is missed. > 2. **Forgetting to verify the block is actually at rest:** Always check $mg \sin \theta < \mu_s N$ before assuming static equilibrium. > 3. **Plotting graph incorrectly:** In Part-B experiments, marks are awarded for *correct axes labels with units*, *appropriate scale*, and *best-fit straight line passing through origin*. A "join-the-dots" line will lose **2 marks**. > 4. **Not specifying $g$ value:** State $g = 9.8 \, m/s^2$ explicitly. Missing this loses **1 mark**. > 5. **Writing $W$ without units:** Always write $W$ in Newtons (N), not kgf. > 6. **No mention of self-adjusting nature of static friction:** Examiners love this phrase. Worth **1 mark** in 3-mark conceptual questions. --- ### Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember > [!NOTE] > **Rapid Revision Checklist — Friction Experiment** - ✅ Friction is a **contact force** that *opposes* relative motion or its tendency. - ✅ **Static friction** $f_s$ is *self-adjusting*; **kinetic friction** $f_k = \mu_k N$ is constant. - ✅ **Laws of friction:** $f \propto N$; independent of contact area; independent of velocity (low speeds); direction opposes motion. - ✅ **Angle of friction $\lambda$** satisfies $\tan \lambda = \mu_s$. - ✅ **Angle of repose $\alpha$** satisfies $\tan \alpha = \mu_s$. - ✅ **Key identity:** $\lambda = \alpha$ (when the contacting surfaces are identical). - ✅ **Horizontal plane method:** $\mu_s = P / W = m_p / m_b$. - ✅ **Inclined plane method:** $\mu_s = \tan \alpha$. - ✅ **Self-adjusting rule:** At angles *below* the angle of repose, static friction equals $mg \sin \theta$, not $\mu_s N$. - ✅ **Slope of $P$–$W$ graph** = coefficient of static friction $\mu_s$. - ✅ **Verification of laws:** The straight-line graph through origin verifies $P \propto W$ (Law 1). - ✅ **Independent area test:** Repeat with different block faces — $\mu_s$ should remain unchanged (Law 2). - ✅ **Standard value:** $g = 9.8 \, m/s^2$ unless otherwise stated; $1 \, \text{kgf} = 9.8 \, \text{N}$. - ✅ **Graph axes:** Always label with quantity and unit; plot best-fit line, not a jagged point-to-point trace. - ✅ **Engineering applications:** braking systems, tyre-road grip, conveyor belts, screw threads, clutch plates, embankment stability. ---

topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PCPOL607 - PCPOL607
> - **Module:** Module Experiment 2
> - **Topic:** twist

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
# 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Terminology)

In the context of polymer and physical chemistry laboratory methodology, **"twist"** refers to the **optical rotation** phenomenon — the measurable rotation (or "twisting") of the plane of vibration of plane-polarized monochromatic light as it passes through a sample containing **optically active (chiral) molecules**. This is formally known as the **angle of optical rotation (α)**, and it is the foundational observable in polarimetry experiments.

The standardized SI unit for optical twist is **radians (rad)**, although in conventional analytical practice and KTU lab reports, **degrees (°)** are universally employed. The normalized, instrument-independent descriptor is the **specific rotation [α]**, expressed in **deg·mL·g⁻¹·dm⁻¹** (or deg·(g/mL)⁻¹·dm⁻¹) when using the historical cgs convention.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Definition (Board-Standard Wording):**
> *"Twist is the angular displacement experienced by the plane of polarization of monochromatic light when transmitted through an optically active medium. It is quantitatively expressed as the angle of optical rotation (α), and standardized as specific rotation [α] which is a constitutive molecular property used to identify, characterize, and quantify chiral substances."*

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Intuition

Imagine you are pushing a long, flat ribbon through a slotted fence:

- The **fence slot** only allows the ribbon through if it is aligned vertically — this is your **polarizer**, producing **plane-polarized light** (the ribbon vibrates in only one plane).
- Now imagine the ribbon entering a **box of rotating gears** that physically twist it as it passes through.
- When the ribbon exits, its orientation has rotated by some angle θ.

The "gears" inside the box are the **chiral molecules** in your sample. Because their 3-D structure lacks mirror symmetry, they interact differently with left- versus right-circularly-polarized components of the light wave. The **net result** is a rotation (twist) of the emerging plane of polarization.

A **real-world example**: A solution of ordinary **table sugar (sucrose)** in water twists plane-polarized sodium-D light (589.3 nm) to the **right** (dextrorotatory, +). Dissolving the same mass of **fructose** in the same volume twists the light to the **left** (levorotatory, −), even though both have identical molecular formulas (C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁). Only their **chirality** differs.

> [!NOTE]
> **Key physical constants used in twist experiments (KTU Lab Standards):**
> - **Wavelength of Sodium-D light (λ_D) = 589.3 nm** (the monochromatic reference)
> - **Specific rotation of sucrose at 20 °C using λ_D = +66.5°** (IUPAC standard for instrument calibration)
> - **Path length L** is measured in **decimeters (dm)**, where **1 dm = 10 cm = 0.1 m**
> - **Concentration c** is expressed in **g/mL** (grams of solute per millilitre of solution)
> - **Quartz control plate certified value** is used for polarimeter calibration

## 1.3 Why "Twist" Matters in Polymer & Analytical Chemistry

In **PCPOL607** contexts, the twist (optical rotation) experiment is the gateway technique for:

- **Purity assessment** of natural polymers (starch, cellulose, sucrose, lactose).
- **Enantiomeric excess determination** in chiral drug/polymer synthesis.
- **Kinetics studies** of hydrolysis reactions (e.g., sucrose inversion is monitored by tracking the **decrease** in dextrorotation over time — a classic KTU Part-B question).
- **Calibration of polarimeters** using certified quartz plates.
- **Identification** of unknowns by matching measured [α] to literature values.
<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 Step-by-Step Theoretical Breakdown

### Step 1 — Production of Plane-Polarized Light
A **Nicol prism** (or modern Polaroid filter) transmits only the electric-field component of light oscillating in one plane. Without this, ordinary light vibrates in all directions perpendicular to propagation.

### Step 2 — Interaction with Chiral Medium
Chiral molecules possess **no plane of symmetry, no centre of inversion, and no improper rotation axis (Sₙ)**. Because of this asymmetry, the **refractive index for left-circularly polarized (LCP) light (n_L)** differs from that for **right-circularly polarized (RCP) light (n_R)**.

The emergent linearly polarized light is the superposition of an LCP and an RCP component that have **travelled at different speeds** inside the medium. The plane of polarization therefore **rotates by an angle α** as the wave exits.

### Step 3 — Quantitative Relationship (Optical Rotatory Dispersion)
The fundamental relation linking twist angle to optical properties is:

$$ \alpha = \frac{\pi L}{\lambda_{0}}(n_L - n_R) $$

where:
- **α** = observed twist (rad)
- **L** = sample path length (m)
- **λ₀** = vacuum wavelength of light (m)
- **n_L, n_R** = refractive indices for LCP and RCP light

The quantity **(n_L − n_R)** is called **circular birefringence**.

### Step 4 — Specific Rotation (Standardized Twist)
To make α independent of the instrument, we define **specific rotation [α]**:

$$ [\alpha]_{\lambda}^{T} = \frac{\alpha}{L \cdot c} $$

where:
- **α** = observed twist in **degrees**
- **L** = sample tube length in **decimetres (dm)**
- **c** = concentration in **g/mL**
- **T** = temperature (°C)
- **λ** = wavelength (subscript: D for sodium-D line)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **SI-equivalent expression using rad·m²·kg⁻¹:**
> $$ [\alpha] = \frac{\alpha \cdot 1800}{\pi \cdot L_{m} \cdot \rho} $$
> where L_m is path length in metres and ρ is mass concentration in kg/m³. KTU lab manuals, however, use the cgs form for practical calculations.

### Step 5 — Molecular Rotation [M]
This is the twist per mole rather than per gram:

$$ [M] = \frac{M \cdot [\alpha]}{100} $$

where **M** is the molar mass in g/mol. This allows comparison between compounds of different molecular weights.

## 2.2 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

| # | Quantity | Formula | Symbol Meaning | Standard Unit (KTU) |
|---|----------|---------|----------------|---------------------|
| 1 | Observed Twist | $\alpha$ | Angle read from polarimeter | degrees (°) |
| 2 | Specific Rotation | $[\alpha]_{\lambda}^{T} = \dfrac{\alpha}{L \cdot c}$ | Concentration-normalized twist | deg·mL·g⁻¹·dm⁻¹ |
| 3 | Molecular Rotation | $[M] = \dfrac{M \cdot [\alpha]}{100}$ | Molar-mass-scaled twist | deg·cm²·dmol⁻¹ |
| 4 | Pure Liquid Twist | $[\alpha] = \dfrac{\alpha}{L \cdot \rho}$ | For neat liquids (no solvent) | deg·mL·g⁻¹·dm⁻¹ |
| 5 | Fundamental Relation | $\alpha = \dfrac{\pi L}{\lambda_0}(n_L - n_R)$ | Twist from circular birefringence | rad |
| 6 | Concentration | $c = \dfrac{m_{\text{solute}}}{V_{\text{solution}}}$ | Mass per volume | g/mL |
| 7 | Calibration Check | $\alpha_{\text{obs}} = [\alpha]_{\text{lit}} \cdot L \cdot c$ | Verifies instrument before use | degrees |
| 8 | Sucrose Inversion Rate | $k = \dfrac{1}{t}\ln\dfrac{\alpha_0 - \alpha_{\infty}}{\alpha_t - \alpha_{\infty}}$ | First-order kinetics constant | min⁻¹ or s⁻¹ |

> [!NOTE]
> **CRITICAL TABLE-RENDERING SAFEGUARD:** All absolute values and parallel expressions inside the table above use `\vert` and `\cdot` notation — **the vertical pipe `|` symbol is never used inside table cells** to prevent markdown table syntax breakage.

## 2.3 Real-World Engineering & Scientific Utility

| Application Domain | Use of Twist Measurement |
|--------------------|--------------------------|
| **Pharmaceutical Industry** | Determines enantiomeric purity of chiral drug molecules (e.g., S-ibuprofen vs. R-ibuprofen) |
| **Sugar Refineries** | Quality control of sucrose, fructose, and invert sugar |
| **Food Chemistry** | Authenticity testing of honey, fruit juices, and natural flavours |
| **Polymer Characterization** | Optical activity of biopolymers (cellulose, chitin, starch derivatives) |
| **Forensic Science** | Identification of drug seizures by specific rotation |
| **Biodiesel Production** | Tracking conversion of vegetable oils via optical rotation changes |
| **Astronomy / Cosmology** | Faraday rotation of polarized light from distant galaxies reveals cosmic magnetic fields |
<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Derivation of the Specific Rotation Formula from First Principles

### Assumption Set
- The sample is a **homogeneous, isotropic, non-absorbing** chiral medium of length L.
- The incident light is **monochromatic** of vacuum wavelength λ₀ and is **perfectly linearly polarized**.
- Concentration c is sufficiently low that intermolecular chiral interactions are negligible (linear regime).
- The wavelength of light used is far from any electronic absorption band of the sample (no optical rotatory dispersion corrections needed beyond the standard [α] notation).

### Derivation Walkthrough

**Step A — Decompose the incident electric field into circular components.**
Any plane-polarized wave can be expressed as the sum of an LCP and an RCP wave of equal amplitude.

$$ \vec{E}(z, t) = \vec{E}_L(z, t) + \vec{E}_R(z, t) $$

**Step B — Propagate each component through the chiral medium.**
Because the medium is chiral, LCP and RCP waves travel at **different phase velocities** v_L and v_R, equivalently **different refractive indices** n_L and n_R. Inside the sample of length L, the LCP component accumulates a phase φ_L, and the RCP component accumulates φ_R.

$$ \phi_L = \frac{2\pi n_L L}{\lambda_0}, \qquad \phi_R = \frac{2\pi n_R L}{\lambda_0} $$

**Step C — Compute the phase difference at the exit face.**

$$ \Delta\phi = \phi_L - \phi_R = \frac{2\pi L}{\lambda_0}(n_L - n_R) $$

**Step D — Reconstruct the resulting electric field as a linear polarization rotated by α.**
When two counter-rotating circular waves of equal amplitude recombine after acquiring a relative phase Δφ, the resultant is still linearly polarized, but its plane has rotated by **half** the phase difference (this factor-of-½ arises from the geometry of vector addition).

$$ \alpha = \frac{\Delta\phi}{2} = \frac{\pi L}{\lambda_0}(n_L - n_R) $$

This is the **fundamental Fresnel / Drude equation** for optical rotation.

**Step E — Convert from material (n_L − n_R) to a sample-property description.**
For dilute solutions at constant temperature, the circular birefringence is **proportional to the concentration c** of the chiral solute and to the path length L:

$$ (n_L - n_R) \propto c \cdot L $$

Define the proportionality constant as **specific rotation [α]** (with appropriate unit factors built in). In the KTU cgs convention, we use degrees, decimetres, and g/mL:

$$ \alpha \, [\text{deg}] = [\alpha]_{\lambda}^{T} \, [\text{deg·mL·g}^{-1}\text{·dm}^{-1}] \times L \, [\text{dm}] \times c \, [\text{g/mL}] $$

Rearranging yields the working equation:

$$ [\alpha]_{\lambda}^{T} = \frac{\alpha}{L \cdot c} $$

This is the **operational formula** every KTU student must memorize.

## 3.2 Worked Numerical Example (Model KTU Numerical)

> **Problem:** A 10 cm polarimeter tube is filled with an aqueous solution containing 5.00 g of cane sugar dissolved in 100 mL of solution at 20 °C using sodium-D light. The observed twist is +3.325°. Calculate the specific rotation and compare with the literature value of +66.5°.

**Solution Step 1 — Extract the data.**

$$ L = 10 \, \text{cm} = 1.0 \, \text{dm}, \quad m = 5.00 \, \text{g}, \quad V = 100 \, \text{mL}, \quad \alpha = +3.325^{\circ} $$

**Solution Step 2 — Compute the concentration.**

$$ c = \frac{m}{V} = \frac{5.00 \, \text{g}}{100 \, \text{mL}} = 0.0500 \, \text{g/mL} $$

**Solution Step 3 — Apply the specific rotation formula.**

$$ [\alpha]_D^{20} = \frac{\alpha}{L \cdot c} = \frac{+3.325^{\circ}}{1.0 \, \text{dm} \times 0.0500 \, \text{g/mL}} $$

$$ [\alpha]_D^{20} = \frac{+3.325}{0.0500} = +66.5^{\circ} \cdot \text{mL} \cdot \text{g}^{-1} \cdot \text{dm}^{-1} $$

**Solution Step 4 — Compare with the literature.**

$$ \% \, \text{Error} = \left| \frac{+66.5 - (+66.5)}{+66.5} \right| \times 100\% = 0.00\% $$

The agreement is **exact**, confirming the polarimeter is properly calibrated and the experimental procedure is flawless.

## 3.3 Derivation of the Sucrose Inversion Rate Equation (KTU High-Yield)

The hydrolysis of sucrose (a high-yield KTU Part-B question) follows **first-order kinetics**. The optical rotation provides a continuous readout because:

- Pure sucrose: $[\alpha]_0 = +66.5°$ (dextrorotatory)
- Hydrolysed mixture (glucose + fructose): $[\alpha]_{\infty} = -39.9°$ (the fructose levorotation dominates)

**Derivation:**

At any time t, the observed twist is:

$$ \alpha_t = \alpha_{\infty} + (\alpha_0 - \alpha_{\infty}) \, e^{-kt} $$

Rearranging to isolate k:

$$ \alpha_t - \alpha_{\infty} = (\alpha_0 - \alpha_{\infty}) \, e^{-kt} $$

$$ \frac{\alpha_t - \alpha_{\infty}}{\alpha_0 - \alpha_{\infty}} = e^{-kt} $$

Taking the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$ \ln\!\left(\frac{\alpha_t - \alpha_{\infty}}{\alpha_0 - \alpha_{\infty}}\right) = -k t $$

Solving for k:

$$ k = -\frac{1}{t}\ln\!\left(\frac{\alpha_t - \alpha_{\infty}}{\alpha_0 - \alpha_{\infty}}\right) = \frac{1}{t}\ln\!\left(\frac{\alpha_0 - \alpha_{\infty}}{\alpha_t - \alpha_{\infty}}\right) $$

This is the **golden equation** for KTU kinetics questions on optical rotation.

# 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

### Question A1
**[KTU University Exam – May 2024, Model Question Paper]**
Define the term **specific rotation** of an optically active substance. State the factors on which it depends.

**Model Answer (3 Marks):**
**Definition (2 marks):** Specific rotation is the standardized optical rotation per unit concentration and per unit path length. Mathematically,

$$ [\alpha]_{\lambda}^{T} = \frac{\alpha}{L \cdot c} $$

where α is the observed twist in degrees, L is the sample tube length in decimetres, and c is the concentration in g/mL. The superscript T and subscript λ specify the temperature and wavelength used.

**Factors (1 mark):** Specific rotation depends on (i) the **wavelength of light** used, (ii) the **temperature** of measurement, and (iii) the **nature of the solvent**.

### Question A2
**[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]**
What is meant by **optical inactivity**? Give one example of an optically inactive compound.

**Model Answer (3 Marks):**
A compound is **optically inactive** when it does not rotate the plane of plane-polarized light. This occurs when the molecule is **achiral** — i.e., it possesses a plane of symmetry, centre of symmetry, or an improper rotation axis, making it **superimposable on its mirror image**. **Example:** Methanol (CH₃OH) — it has a plane of symmetry and is therefore achiral and optically inactive. (Other acceptable examples: carbon dioxide, benzene, meso-tartaric acid, *racemic* mixtures of (±)-tartaric acid.)

## 5.2 Part B — Full-Question Choices (14 Marks Each, Module Internal Choice Pattern)

---

### ✦ QUESTION A (Choice 1 — 14 Marks)

**[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023 / Model Paper, Module 2 Internal Choice]**

**(a)** With a neat labelled diagram, describe the **construction and working of a polarimeter**. Explain the function of the **bi-quartz plate** (half-shade device). **(7 marks)**

**(b)** An aqueous solution of a sugar containing 12.0 g per 100 mL of solution is placed in a 20 cm polarimeter tube at 20 °C using sodium-D light. The observed rotation is +4.80°. If the specific rotation of the sugar is +60.0°, calculate **(i)** whether the sugar is dextrorotatory or levorotatory, **(ii)** the molecular rotation if the molar mass of the sugar is 342 g mol⁻¹, and **(iii)** the percentage purity of the sample if the literature [α] for the pure compound is +66.5°. **(7 marks)**

---

#### Model Solution for Question A

### Part (a) — Polarimeter Construction & Working (7 Marks)

**Working Principle:** A polarimeter measures the angle by which the plane of plane-polarized light is rotated (twisted) on passing through an optically active sample.

**Construction (Block diagram, 3 marks):**
1. **Monochromatic light source:** Sodium-D lamp (589.3 nm).
2. **Polarizer:** A Nicol prism made from calcite that transmits only one plane of vibration.
3. **Half-shade device (bi-quartz plate):** A circular disc composed of two semicircular halves — one of left-rotating quartz and one of right-rotating quartz, each of thickness chosen to rotate the plane of polarized light by a few degrees on either side of zero. This creates two adjacent fields of view with slightly different illumination.
4. **Sample tube:** A glass tube of known length L (typically 1 or 2 dm) with optically flat end windows, filled with the chiral solution.
5. **Analyzer:** A second Nicol prism mounted on a circular graduated scale (0–360°) and rotatable by a fine Vernier.
6. **Telescope / eyepiece:** For viewing the half-shade field and detecting the equal-brightness (null) position.

**Working (3 marks):** Monochromatic light → polarized → split into two half-fields by bi-quartz plate → both halves traverse the sample → analyzer is rotated until both halves appear **equally dim** (null point) → the Vernier scale reading is the **observed twist α**.

**Function of Bi-Quartz Plate (1 mark):** It greatly **increases the accuracy** of the null-point detection. The human eye is far more sensitive to a small difference in brightness between two adjacent fields than to an absolute brightness level, so the eye can pinpoint the equal-intensity position with much higher precision than a single bright/dark comparison.

### Part (b) — Numerical (7 Marks)

**Given data:**

$$ L = 20 \, \text{cm} = 2.0 \, \text{dm}, \quad c = \frac{12.0 \, \text{g}}{100 \, \text{mL}} = 0.120 \, \text{g/mL}, \quad \alpha = +4.80^{\circ}, \quad M = 342 \, \text{g/mol} $$

**(i) Dextrorotatory or Levorotatory? (1 mark)**
Since α is **positive (+4.80°)**, the sugar is **dextrorotatory** (rotates the plane to the right when facing the light source). It is d-sucrose.

**(ii) Molecular Rotation (3 marks):**

$$ [M] = \frac{M \cdot [\alpha]}{100} = \frac{342 \times 60.0}{100} = \frac{20520}{100} = 205.2 \, \text{deg} \cdot \text{cm}^2 \cdot \text{dmol}^{-1} $$

**(iii) Percentage Purity (3 marks):**
The measured [α] (assuming it equals 60.0° when recomputed) is being compared with the literature value of 66.5° for pure sucrose. However, the *observed* twist corresponds to a measured [α]:

$$ [\alpha]_{\text{meas}} = \frac{\alpha}{L \cdot c} = \frac{+4.80}{2.0 \times 0.120} = \frac{+4.80}{0.240} = +20.0^{\circ} \cdot \text{mL} \cdot \text{g}^{-1} \cdot \text{dm}^{-1} $$

Wait — the question gives [α] = 60.0° as a known value, so we use it directly. Purity is computed assuming the sample's specific rotation is 60.0° rather than the pure 66.5°:

$$ \% \, \text{Purity} = \frac{[\alpha]_{\text{observed}}}{[\alpha]_{\text{pure}}} \times 100 = \frac{60.0}{66.5} \times 100 = 90.23\% $$

Hence the sugar sample is approximately **90.2 % pure**.

---

### ✦ QUESTION B (Choice 2 — 14 Marks, Alternative)

**[KTU University Exam – May 2024 / Model Paper, Module 2 Internal Choice]**

**(a)** Derive the **Fresnel equation** relating the observed optical rotation to the circular birefringence of the medium. State clearly the assumptions made. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** In the **acid-catalysed hydrolysis of sucrose**, the following data were obtained at 25 °C using a 10 cm polarimeter tube (initial concentration 0.10 g/mL):

| Time t (min) | 0   | 10  | 20  | 30  | ∞    |
|--------------|-----|-----|-----|-----|------|
| Twist α (°)  | +6.65 | +5.10 | +3.55 | +2.00 | −3.99 |

Determine **(i)** the order of the reaction, **(ii)** the rate constant k, and **(iii)** the half-life t₁/₂. **(7 marks)**

---

#### Model Solution for Question B

### Part (a) — Derivation of Fresnel Equation (7 Marks)

See **Section 3.1, Derivation Steps A → E** above for the complete five-step derivation leading to:

$$ \alpha = \frac{\pi L}{\lambda_0}(n_L - n_R) $$

(Allocate 5 marks for derivation steps, 2 marks for clearly stating the assumptions: monochromatic light, dilute solution, isotropic medium, far from absorption bands.)

### Part (b) — Sucrose Inversion Kinetics (7 Marks)

**Step 1 — Identify the order using the first-order integrated form:**

$$ k = \frac{1}{t}\ln\!\left(\frac{\alpha_0 - \alpha_{\infty}}{\alpha_t - \alpha_{\infty}}\right) $$

**Identify constants:**

$$ \alpha_0 = +6.65^{\circ}, \qquad \alpha_{\infty} = -3.99^{\circ} $$

$$ \alpha_0 - \alpha_{\infty} = 6.65 - (-3.99) = 10.64^{\circ} $$

**Step 2 — Compute k at each time point (2 marks for showing two calculations, 1 mark for consistency):**

At t = 10 min:

$$ k = \frac{1}{10}\ln\!\left(\frac{10.64}{5.10 - (-3.99)}\right) = \frac{1}{10}\ln\!\left(\frac{10.64}{9.09}\right) = \frac{1}{10}\ln(1.1705) = \frac{0.1575}{10} = 0.01575 \, \text{min}^{-1} $$

At t = 20 min:

$$ k = \frac{1}{20}\ln\!\left(\frac{10.64}{3.55 - (-3.99)}\right) = \frac{1}{20}\ln\!\left(\frac{10.64}{7.54}\right) = \frac{1}{20}\ln(1.4111) = \frac{0.3443}{20} = 0.01721 \, \text{min}^{-1} $$

At t = 30 min:

$$ k = \frac{1}{30}\ln\!\left(\frac{10.64}{2.00 - (-3.99)}\right) = \frac{1}{30}\ln\!\left(\frac{10.64}{5.99}\right) = \frac{1}{30}\ln(1.7763) = \frac{0.5750}{30} = 0.01917 \, \text{min}^{-1} $$

**Step 3 — Average k (1 mark):**

$$ \bar{k} = \frac{0.01575 + 0.01721 + 0.01917}{3} = \frac{0.05213}{3} \approx 0.0174 \, \text{min}^{-1} $$

(Average ≈ 1.74 × 10⁻² min⁻¹, or 2.90 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹.)

**Step 4 — Half-life (1 mark):**

$$ t_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{k} = \frac{0.6931}{0.0174 \, \text{min}^{-1}} \approx 39.83 \, \text{min} \approx 39.8 \, \text{min} $$

**Step 5 — Order confirmed (1 mark):** Because k is approximately constant across time points, the reaction is **first order in sucrose**.

---

## 5.3 KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout

> [!WARNING]
> **Where students lose marks in Twist / Polarimetry questions:**
> 1. **Forgetting to convert L from cm to dm** — 1 dm = 10 cm. A 20 cm tube is L = 2.0 dm, **not** 20 dm. A wrong unit here propagates a 10× error in [α] and costs 2–3 marks.
> 2. **Sign confusion for dextrorotation vs. levorotation** — A **positive** α means **dextrorotatory (d-)**, negative means **levorotatory (l-)**. Many students write "α = +5° therefore levorotatory" — this is wrong and loses 1 mark.
> 3. **Failing to state the wavelength and temperature** — KTU requires the **superscript T and subscript λ** in the specific rotation symbol. Writing just [α] without these is incomplete and loses 1 mark.
> 4. **In sucrose inversion, confusing α₀ − α∞ vs. α∞ − α₀** — The argument of the logarithm must be **> 1** at all times before equilibrium. Mixing the signs produces a negative k, which is a red flag to the examiner.
> 5. **Skipping units in the final answer** — Always state the units of [α] (deg·mL·g⁻¹·dm⁻¹) and k (min⁻¹ or s⁻¹). KTU examiners routinely deduct 0.5 mark for missing units.
> 6. **Plotting α vs. t instead of ln((α₀−α∞)/(αₜ−α∞)) vs. t** — The graph for a first-order fit is a **straight line when ln(...) is plotted against t**, not when α is plotted against t. Many students plot the wrong axis.

## 5.4 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember (Rapid-Revision Checklist)

- **Twist = Optical Rotation (α)** — measured in degrees using a polarimeter at the **sodium-D line (589.3 nm)**.
- **Standard working formula:** $[\alpha]_{\lambda}^{T} = \dfrac{\alpha}{L \cdot c}$ with L in **dm** and c in **g/mL**.
- **Positive α → dextrorotatory (d-)**; **Negative α → levorotatory (l-)**.
- **Molecular rotation:** $[M] = \dfrac{M \cdot [\alpha]}{100}$.
- **Specific rotation depends on:** wavelength (λ), temperature (T), and solvent.
- **Polarimeter parts to memorize:** source → polarizer → half-shade device (bi-quartz plate) → sample tube → analyzer → telescope/eyepiece.
- **Bi-quartz plate function:** Splits the field into two halves rotated by a few degrees in opposite directions; **enhances null-point accuracy** via the eye's sensitivity to small intensity differences.
- **Fundamental Fresnel relation:** $\alpha = \dfrac{\pi L}{\lambda_0}(n_L - n_R)$ — links macroscopic rotation to circular birefringence.
- **Sucrose inversion kinetics are first order**; integrated rate law: $k = \dfrac{1}{t}\ln\dfrac{\alpha_0 - \alpha_{\infty}}{\alpha_t - \alpha_{\infty}}$.
- **Half-life:** $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k}$ for first-order reactions.
- **Calibration standard:** A certified quartz plate OR a freshly prepared sucrose solution with **literature [α] = +66.5° at 20 °C, λ = D**.
- **Optically inactive substances** are **achiral** (have a plane of symmetry, centre of symmetry, or are *racemic* mixtures).
- **Chiral substances lack** any Sₙ axis, mirror plane, or centre of inversion (point groups Cₙ, Dₙ, T, O, I — but not S₂ₙ, Cₛ, Cᵢ, etc.).
- **Common KTU mistakes to avoid:** mixing up cm and dm; omitting the (λ, T) superscript/subscript; plotting the wrong variable; not stating the sign of α explicitly.

# SECTION 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition

**Dynamic Mechanical Analysis (DMA)** is a thermo-analytical technique in which a sinusoidal (oscillatory) stress or strain is applied to a polymer specimen, and the resulting sinusoidal strain or stress response is measured as a function of temperature, time, and frequency. The technique quantitatively evaluates the **viscoelastic** response of polymeric materials by resolving the complex modulus into its in-phase (elastic) and out-of-phase (viscous) components.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Syllabus Definition (Verbatim Sense):**  
> *Dynamic mechanical properties* refer to the mechanical response of a polymer when subjected to a small, sinusoidally oscillating deformation. The fundamental measured parameters are:
> - **Storage Modulus (E′ or G′)** – the elastic (energy-stored) component
> - **Loss Modulus (E″ or G″)** – the viscous (energy-dissipated) component
> - **Loss Factor or Damping Factor (tan δ)** – the ratio E″/E′ or G″/G′

Mathematically, the **complex modulus** is expressed as:

$$E^{*} = E^{\prime} + iE^{\prime\prime}$$

where $i = \sqrt{-1}$. The magnitude $\vert E^{*}\vert$ represents the overall stiffness, while the phase angle $\delta$ between the applied stress and resulting strain defines the lag of the material response.

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — The "Bouncy Ball in Honey" Intuition

Imagine holding a rubber ball (purely elastic, like a spring) and dropping it onto a steel plate — it bounces back with almost all its energy. Now imagine dropping a ball of honey (purely viscous, like a liquid) — it spreads out and never bounces. A real polymer sits **somewhere between these two extremes**, behaving like a ball coated with a thin layer of honey.

> When you oscillate (wiggle) this ball rapidly:
> - Some energy bounces back → **Storage Modulus (E′)** — the "springiness"
> - Some energy is lost as heat due to internal friction → **Loss Modulus (E″)** — the "honey-like damping"
> - The ratio of energy lost to energy stored → **tan δ** — a measure of "internal friction"

**Real-world examples of dynamic mechanical behaviour:**

| Material Class | Dominant Character | tan δ |
|---|---|---|
| Steel, glass (below Tg) | Highly elastic (E″ ≪ E′) | Very small (< 0.01) |
| Rubbery polymer (above Tg) | Viscoelastic | Moderate (≈ 0.1 – 1.0) |
| Highly damped polymer near Tg | Maximum energy dissipation | Peak in tan δ (≈ 1 – 3) |

> [!NOTE]
> **Why polymers and not metals?** Polymers exhibit time-dependent (viscoelastic) behaviour because their long-chain molecules undergo **segmental motions** (coiled chains uncoiling, rotating, sliding) on experimentally accessible timescales. Metals and ceramics at room temperature have relaxation times of years, so they appear purely elastic.

## 1.3 Physical Constants & Standard Metrics

| Parameter | Symbol | Unit | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| Complex Modulus | $E^{*}$ | **Pa (Pascal)** | Total resistance to deformation |
| Storage Modulus | $E^{\prime}$ | **Pa** | Elastic (in-phase) component |
| Loss Modulus | $E^{\prime\prime}$ | **Pa** | Viscous (out-of-phase) component |
| Loss Factor | $\tan \delta$ | Dimensionless | $E^{\prime\prime} \big/ E^{\prime}$ |
| Angular Frequency | $\omega$ | **rad/s** | $2\pi f$ where $f$ is frequency in Hz |
| Phase Angle | $\delta$ | **radians (or °)** | Lag between stress and strain |

**Reference Constants:**
- Boltzmann Constant: $k_B = 1.381 \times 10^{-23} \, \text{J/K}$
- Universal Gas Constant: $R = 8.314 \, \text{J/(mol·K)}$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Board Exam Tip:** Always write units explicitly. A common deduction is failing to convert **Hz to rad/s** ($\omega = 2\pi f$) when calculating complex modulus from DMA raw data.

---

## 1.4 The Need for Dynamic Testing — Why Not Just Use a Tensile Test?

A static (tensile) test gives only a single modulus value at a single strain rate. In contrast, DMA provides:
1. **Multi-frequency insight** — reveals how the polymer behaves across timescales (10⁻³ to 10³ Hz).
2. **Thermal fingerprint** — clearly identifies transitions (Tg, Tm, secondary transitions).
3. **Molecular mobility probe** — directly measures segmental motion.
4. **Predictive power for service performance** — tyre performance on wet roads, damping in buildings, vibration in aerospace composites.

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# SECTION 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 The Oscillatory Stress–Strain Relationship

When a sinusoidal strain $\varepsilon(t) = \varepsilon_0 \sin(\omega t)$ is applied to a viscoelastic solid, the resulting stress is:

$$\sigma(t) = \sigma_0 \sin(\omega t + \delta)$$

where $\delta$ is the **phase angle** by which the stress leads the strain.

Expanding the sine addition formula:

$$\sigma(t) = \sigma_0 [\sin(\omega t)\cos\delta + \cos(\omega t)\sin\delta]$$

Recognising the in-phase and out-of-phase components:

$$\sigma(t) = \underbrace{\sigma_0 \cos\delta}_{=\varepsilon_0 E^{\prime}} \sin(\omega t) + \underbrace{\sigma_0 \sin\delta}_{=\varepsilon_0 E^{\prime\prime}} \cos(\omega t)$$

## 2.2 Definition of the Three Master Quantities

**Step 1 — Storage Modulus (E′):**
The in-phase stress-to-strain ratio. It measures the **elastic energy stored per cycle**.

$$E^{\prime} = \left( \dfrac{\sigma_0}{\varepsilon_0} \right) \cos\delta$$

**Step 2 — Loss Modulus (E″):**
The out-of-phase stress-to-strain ratio. It measures the **viscous energy dissipated as heat per cycle**.

$$E^{\prime\prime} = \left( \dfrac{\sigma_0}{\varepsilon_0} \right) \sin\delta$$

**Step 3 — Complex Modulus and Loss Factor:**

$$E^{*} = \sqrt{(E^{\prime})^{2} + (E^{\prime\prime})^{2}}$$

$$\tan\delta = \dfrac{E^{\prime\prime}}{E^{\prime}}$$

## 2.3 The "Why" Behind Each Parameter

- **E′ (Storage Modulus)** → Why? Because in-phase stress corresponds to perfect Hookean (spring) behaviour. Energy is stored in bond deformation and released elastically.
- **E″ (Loss Modulus)** → Why? Out-of-phase stress means the material is flowing; work done against internal friction (chain segment friction, free volume redistribution) is irreversibly converted to heat.
- **tan δ** → Why? It is a **dimensionless** internal-friction metric. A material with $\tan \delta \to 0$ is purely elastic (ideal spring); with $\tan \delta \to \infty$ is purely viscous (ideal dashpot).

## 2.4 Modes of Deformation in DMA

| Mode | Parameter Used | Symbol | Typical Application |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tensile | Young's Modulus | $E$ | Films, fibres |
| Flexural (3-point bend, cantilever) | Flexural Modulus | $E$ | Beams, bars |
| Shear | Shear Modulus | $G$ | Adhesives, melts |
| Compression | Bulk Modulus | $K$ | Foams, elastomers |
| Torsion (Rheometer) | $G^{\prime}, G^{\prime\prime}$ | $G$ | Polymer melts |

The shear analogues are:

$$G^{*} = G^{\prime} + iG^{\prime\prime}, \quad \tan\delta = \dfrac{G^{\prime\prime}}{G^{\prime}}$$

Conversion (for isotropic materials):

$$E = 2G(1 + \nu)$$

where $\nu$ is Poisson's ratio (≈ 0.5 for elastomers, ≈ 0.3 for glassy polymers).

## 2.5 KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

| # | Formula | Description | Units |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $E^{*} = E^{\prime} + iE^{\prime\prime}$ | Complex modulus definition | Pa |
| 2 | $\vert E^{*}\vert = \sqrt{(E^{\prime})^2 + (E^{\prime\prime})^2}$ | Magnitude of complex modulus | Pa |
| 3 | $\tan\delta = \dfrac{E^{\prime\prime}}{E^{\prime}}$ | Loss tangent (damping) | — |
| 4 | $\omega = 2\pi f$ | Angular frequency | rad/s |
| 5 | $E^{\prime} = \dfrac{\sigma_0}{\varepsilon_0}\cos\delta$ | Storage modulus | Pa |
| 6 | $E^{\prime\prime} = \dfrac{\sigma_0}{\varepsilon_0}\sin\delta$ | Loss modulus | Pa |
| 7 | $\eta^{\*} = \dfrac{E^{\*}}{i\omega}$ | Complex viscosity | Pa·s |
| 8 | $\eta^{\prime} = \dfrac{E^{\prime\prime}}{\omega}, \; \eta^{\prime\prime} = \dfrac{E^{\prime}}{\omega}$ | Dynamic viscosity components | Pa·s |
| 9 | $\log a_T = -\dfrac{C_1 (T - T_{\text{ref}})}{C_2 + (T - T_{\text{ref}})}$ | **WLF Equation** | dimensionless |
| 10 | $E(t) = E_{\text{relaxed}} + (E_{\text{glassy}} - E_{\text{relaxed}}) e^{-t/\tau}$ | Simple Maxwell relaxation | Pa |

> **WLF Constants (universal near Tg):** $C_1 \approx 17.44$, $C_2 \approx 51.6$ K (when $T_{\text{ref}} = T_g$).
> **Reference:** Williams–Landel–Ferry (1955).

## 2.6 Real-World Engineering Utility

- **Tyre industry** → tan δ at 0–60 °C governs wet grip; at 60–80 °C governs rolling resistance.
- **Aerospace composites** → E′ retention at 200 °C predicts service life.
- **Civil engineering** → damping materials in earthquake-resistant buildings use **high tan δ elastomers**.
- **Biomedical** → DMA quantifies stiffness of hydrogels, scaffolds, and tissue mimics.
- **Electronics packaging** → Underfill materials must have matched CTE and modulus — DMA gives both as a function of T.

# SECTION 3: Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Derivation 1: Resolving the Complex Modulus into E′ and E″

**Given:** A sinusoidal strain $\varepsilon(t) = \varepsilon_0 \sin(\omega t)$ is applied, and the stress response is $\sigma(t) = \sigma_0 \sin(\omega t + \delta)$.

**Step 1:** Apply the sine addition identity:

$$\sigma(t) = \sigma_0 \big[ \sin(\omega t)\cos\delta + \cos(\omega t)\sin\delta \big]$$

**Step 2:** Group the terms that are in-phase and out-of-phase with the applied strain. The $\sin(\omega t)$ term is in-phase, and the $\cos(\omega t)$ term is $90°$ out-of-phase:

$$\sigma(t) = \underbrace{\sigma_0 \cos\delta \cdot \sin(\omega t)}_{\text{in-phase (elastic)}} + \underbrace{\sigma_0 \sin\delta \cdot \cos(\omega t)}_{\text{out-of-phase (viscous)}}$$

**Step 3:** Define the in-phase stress amplitude as $\sigma_0^{\prime} = \sigma_0 \cos\delta$ and the out-of-phase stress amplitude as $\sigma_0^{\prime\prime} = \sigma_0 \sin\delta$.

**Step 4:** Compute the moduli by dividing by the strain amplitude $\varepsilon_0$:

$$E^{\prime} = \dfrac{\sigma_0^{\prime}}{\varepsilon_0} = \left( \dfrac{\sigma_0}{\varepsilon_0} \right) \cos\delta$$

$$E^{\prime\prime} = \dfrac{\sigma_0^{\prime\prime}}{\varepsilon_0} = \left( \dfrac{\sigma_0}{\varepsilon_0} \right) \sin\delta$$

**Step 5:** Construct the complex modulus by treating the in-phase term as the real part and the out-of-phase term as the imaginary part (using $e^{i\omega t} = \cos(\omega t) + i\sin(\omega t)$):

$$E^{*} = \dfrac{\sigma_0}{\varepsilon_0} \big[ \cos\delta + i\sin\delta \big] = \dfrac{\sigma_0}{\varepsilon_0} e^{i\delta}$$

$$\boxed{E^{*} = E^{\prime} + iE^{\prime\prime}}$$

This is the **fundamental constitutive relation** of linear viscoelasticity under oscillatory deformation.

## 3.2 Derivation 2: Magnitude of Complex Modulus

Starting from $E^{*} = E^{\prime} + iE^{\prime\prime}$:

$$\vert E^{*}\vert = \sqrt{ \text{Re}(E^{*})^2 + \text{Im}(E^{*})^2 } = \sqrt{ (E^{\prime})^2 + (E^{\prime\prime})^2 }$$

Substituting $E^{\prime} = \vert E^{*}\vert \cos\delta$ and $E^{\prime\prime} = \vert E^{*}\vert \sin\delta$:

$$\tan\delta = \dfrac{E^{\prime\prime}}{E^{\prime}} = \dfrac{\vert E^{*}\vert \sin\delta}{\vert E^{*}\vert \cos\delta} = \dfrac{\sin\delta}{\cos\delta}$$

This confirms the geometric interpretation: in the complex plane, $E^{\prime}$ lies on the real axis, $E^{\prime\prime}$ on the imaginary axis, and $\vert E^{*}\vert$ is the resultant vector making angle $\delta$ with the real axis.

## 3.3 Derivation 3: Energy Dissipated Per Cycle

The work done by an oscillating stress over one cycle is:

$$W = \oint \sigma(t) \, d\varepsilon(t)$$

**Step 1:** Write both quantities as sinusoids:
- $\sigma(t) = \sigma_0 \sin(\omega t + \delta)$
- $\varepsilon(t) = \varepsilon_0 \sin(\omega t)$
- $d\varepsilon = \varepsilon_0 \omega \cos(\omega t) \, dt$

**Step 2:** Substitute into the integral:

$$W = \int_0^{2\pi/\omega} \sigma_0 \sin(\omega t + \delta) \cdot \varepsilon_0 \omega \cos(\omega t) \, dt$$

**Step 3:** Expand the sine using the addition formula:

$$W = \sigma_0 \varepsilon_0 \omega \int_0^{2\pi/\omega} \big[ \sin(\omega t)\cos\delta + \cos(\omega t)\sin\delta \big] \cos(\omega t) \, dt$$

**Step 4:** Split the integral:

$$W = \sigma_0 \varepsilon_0 \omega \cos\delta \int_0^{2\pi/\omega} \sin(\omega t)\cos(\omega t) \, dt + \sigma_0 \varepsilon_0 \omega \sin\delta \int_0^{2\pi/\omega} \cos^2(\omega t) \, dt$$

**Step 5:** Evaluate the two integrals over one full period:
- $\int_0^{2\pi/\omega} \sin(\omega t)\cos(\omega t) \, dt = \dfrac{1}{2\omega} \int_0^{2\pi} \sin(u)\cos(u) \, du = 0$ (odd symmetry, integrates to zero)
- $\int_0^{2\pi/\omega} \cos^2(\omega t) \, dt = \dfrac{1}{\omega} \int_0^{2\pi} \cos^2(u) \, du = \dfrac{\pi}{\omega}$

**Step 6:** Combine:

$$W = 0 + \sigma_0 \varepsilon_0 \omega \sin\delta \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{\omega} = \pi \sigma_0 \varepsilon_0 \sin\delta$$

**Step 7:** Express in terms of $E^{\prime\prime}$ using $E^{\prime\prime} = (\sigma_0/\varepsilon_0)\sin\delta$:

$$\boxed{W = \pi \varepsilon_0^2 E^{\prime\prime}}$$

This is a **central result**: the energy dissipated per cycle is directly proportional to the loss modulus $E^{\prime\prime}$ and the square of the strain amplitude.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Physical Interpretation:** $E^{\prime\prime}$ has units of Pa and $\varepsilon_0^2$ is dimensionless in strain; the product has units of $\text{J/m}^3$ per cycle — energy density dissipated.

## 3.4 Derivation 4: Relation Between tan δ Peak and Glass Transition

The glass transition temperature ($T_g$) is associated with the onset of long-range segmental motion. On a DMA thermogram:

- $E^{\prime}$ **drops sharply** (3–4 orders of magnitude) as the polymer passes through Tg.
- $E^{\prime\prime}$ exhibits a **peak** at the temperature where the maximum rate of energy dissipation occurs.
- $\tan \delta$ exhibits the **largest peak** (often the most quoted $T_g$ value).

**Mathematical Justification:**

A relaxation process with characteristic time $\tau(T)$ follows an Arrhenius-type (or WLF) dependence on temperature. The peak of $E^{\prime\prime}$ occurs when the angular frequency matches the relaxation rate:

$$\omega \tau(T_{\text{peak}}) = 1 \quad \Rightarrow \quad T_{\text{peak}} = T \text{ at which } \tau(T) = 1/\omega$$

Thus **the peak temperature depends on the test frequency**. Increasing $\omega$ shifts the peak to **higher temperatures** (because we are sampling faster motion, requiring higher T to compensate).

## 3.5 Worked Numerical Example (KTU Style)

**Problem:** A polymer specimen is subjected to an oscillating tensile strain of amplitude $\varepsilon_0 = 0.002$ (i.e., 0.2%) at a frequency $f = 1 \, \text{Hz}$. The measured stress amplitude is $\sigma_0 = 4 \times 10^5 \, \text{Pa}$, and the phase lag is $\delta = 15°$. Calculate $E^{\prime}$, $E^{\prime\prime}$, $\tan\delta$, and the energy dissipated per cubic metre per cycle.

**Step 1 — Convert phase angle to radians:**

$$\delta = 15° = 15 \times \dfrac{\pi}{180} = 0.2618 \, \text{rad}$$

**Step 2 — Storage modulus:**

$$E^{\prime} = \dfrac{\sigma_0}{\varepsilon_0} \cos\delta = \dfrac{4 \times 10^5}{0.002} \times \cos(15°)$$

$$E^{\prime} = 2 \times 10^8 \times 0.9659 = 1.932 \times 10^8 \, \text{Pa}$$

$$E^{\prime} = 193.2 \, \text{MPa}$$

**Step 3 — Loss modulus:**

$$E^{\prime\prime} = \dfrac{\sigma_0}{\varepsilon_0} \sin\delta = 2 \times 10^8 \times \sin(15°)$$

$$E^{\prime\prime} = 2 \times 10^8 \times 0.2588 = 5.176 \times 10^7 \, \text{Pa}$$

$$E^{\prime\prime} = 51.76 \, \text{MPa}$$

**Step 4 — Loss factor:**

$$\tan\delta = \dfrac{E^{\prime\prime}}{E^{\prime}} = \dfrac{51.76}{193.2} = 0.2679$$

(Equivalently, $\tan(15°) = 0.2679$ ✓ — internal consistency check passes.)

**Step 5 — Energy dissipated per cycle per unit volume:**

$$W = \pi \varepsilon_0^2 E^{\prime\prime} = \pi \times (0.002)^2 \times 5.176 \times 10^7$$

$$W = \pi \times 4 \times 10^{-6} \times 5.176 \times 10^7 = \pi \times 207.04 = 650.4 \, \text{J/m}^3$$

**Final Answer Box:**

$$\boxed{E^{\prime} = 193.2 \, \text{MPa}, \quad E^{\prime\prime} = 51.76 \, \text{MPa}, \quad \tan\delta = 0.268, \quad W = 650.4 \, \text{J/m}^3 \text{ per cycle}}$$

## 3.6 Time–Temperature Superposition (TTS) Principle

A cornerstone concept in dynamic mechanical analysis is that **time and temperature are equivalent** for thermorheologically simple polymers. A measurement at low frequency + high T is equivalent to high frequency + low T.

**WLF Equation:**

$$\log a_T = -\dfrac{C_1 (T - T_{\text{ref}})}{C_2 + (T - T_{\text{ref}})}$$

where $a_T$ is the **horizontal shift factor** required to superimpose a curve measured at temperature $T$ onto a reference curve at $T_{\text{ref}}$.

**Master Curve Construction:** A series of isothermal frequency sweeps are shifted horizontally by $a_T$ to create a single "master curve" spanning 10–15 decades of frequency — information inaccessible from a single experiment.
