```mermaid
    B --> F[Transverse Strain Gauge 4]
    C --> G[Wheatstone Full Bridge]
    D --> G
    E --> G
    F --> G
    G --> H[Excitation Voltage Vex]
    G --> I[Output Voltage Vout proportional to F]
    I --> J[Signal Conditioner and Amplifier]
    J --> K[Digital Display Newtons]
```

## 4.3 Cross-Sectional Logic Diagram of the Test Zone

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A[Upper Crosshead Fixed] --> B[Upper Grip Pneumatic]
    B --> C[Specimen Polymer]
    C --> D[Lower Grip Pneumatic]
    D --> E[Load Cell]
    E --> F[Lower Movable Crosshead]
    F --> G[Ball Screw Drive]
    G --> H[Servo Motor]
    I[Extensometer Clipped to Gauge Section] --> C
    I --> J[Strain Data to PC]
    E --> K[Force Data to PC]
```

<!-- SECTION_4_END -->

<!-- SECTION_5_START -->
# 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

> **[KTU University Exam – May 2024, Model Question]**
> **Q1. List the five major sub-systems of a Universal Testing Machine (UTM) and state the function of any two.**
>
> **Model Answer (3 marks):**
> The five major sub-systems are: (1) Load Frame, (2) Drive Mechanism, (3) Load Cell, (4) Specimen Grips, (5) Extensometer & Displacement Encoder.
> - **Load Frame:** provides the rigid structural backbone that resists deformation during testing, ensuring the recorded displacement is from the specimen and not the frame.
> - **Load Cell:** a force transducer based on strain gauges in a Wheatstone bridge; converts the applied force into a proportional electrical voltage for accurate measurement and display.
> *(Any two correct functions with sub-system identification = full 3 marks.)*

> **[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023, Model Question]**
> **Q2. Why is a full Wheatstone bridge configuration preferred over a quarter-bridge in a UTM load cell?**
>
> **Model Answer (3 marks):**
> A full bridge provides **four active gauges** that double the sensitivity of a half-bridge and quadruple that of a quarter-bridge. Additionally, it offers **automatic temperature compensation** because gauges on adjacent arms experience identical thermal expansion, cancelling out the resistance change due to temperature. This results in a **more linear, stable, and drift-free** force measurement, which is critical for accurate tensile testing of polymers. *(Mentioning 2 of these 3 reasons = full 3 marks.)*

---

## Part B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks Each, Internal Choice)

### **Question A — 14 Marks** *(Choose either A or B)*

**[KTU University Exam – Sample Paper 2024, Model Question]**

> **Q A.** With the help of a neat block diagram, describe the **construction and working of a Universal Testing Machine (UTM)** used for polymer tensile testing. **(14 marks)**
>
> *Breakdown:* (a) Construction — 7 marks; (b) Working & Output Curve Interpretation — 7 marks.

**Model Solution:**

**(a) Construction of UTM (7 marks)**

The UTM consists of **five sub-systems**:

1. **Load Frame** — A rigid two-column or four-column steel frame with a stationary upper crosshead and a movable lower crosshead. The frame has a stiffness of >10⁶ N/mm to prevent frame compliance errors.
2. **Drive Mechanism** — A servo motor coupled to a precision ball-screw (electro-mechanical type) OR a hydraulic ram (hydraulic type) that provides smooth, constant crosshead velocity from 0.001 to 1000 mm/min.
3. **Load Cell** — A force transducer consisting of a steel flexure on which four strain gauges are bonded in a **full Wheatstone bridge**. As force is applied, the flexure deforms, changing gauge resistances, producing an output voltage proportional to the force.
4. **Specimen Grips** — Pneumatic side-action grips with serrated jaw faces. They hold the dog-bone specimen without slippage or crushing.
5. **Extensometer & Displacement Encoder** — A clip-on axial extensometer (with two LVDTs) measures strain in the elastic region; a crosshead LVDT/encoder measures displacement for the post-yield region.

**(b) Working and Output Curve Interpretation (7 marks)**

The polymer dog-bone specimen (per ASTM D638) is mounted in the grips. The drive mechanism pulls the movable crosshead **downward at a constant velocity** (e.g., 5 mm/min), applying a uniaxial tensile force. The load cell measures the instantaneous force $F$, and the extensometer measures the extension $\Delta L$. The software computes:

$$
\sigma = \frac{F}{A_0}, \qquad \varepsilon = \frac{\Delta L}{L_0}
$$

and plots the **engineering stress–strain curve**. From this curve, students extract:
- **Young's Modulus $E$** (slope of initial linear region),
- **Yield Strength $\sigma_y$** (using 0.2 % offset method),
- **Ultimate Tensile Strength (UTS)** (peak stress),
- **Elongation at break $\varepsilon_b$** (% strain at fracture),
- **Toughness** (area under the curve, $\int \sigma \, d\varepsilon$).

**Curve Interpretation for Common Polymers:**
- **PS, PMMA** — brittle, low $\varepsilon_b$ (<5 %), no distinct yield.
- **HDPE, PP** — semi-ductile, distinct yield and cold drawing.
- **LDPE, rubber** — highly ductile, no fracture within extensometer range.

---

### **Question B — 14 Marks** *(Alternative Choice)*

**[KTU University Exam – Sample Paper 2024, Model Question]**

> **Q B.** Explain the **construction of a strain-gauge-based load cell** with a circuit diagram. Derive the relationship between the output voltage and the applied force. **(14 marks)**
>
> *Breakdown:* (a) Construction with circuit — 7 marks; (b) Derivation — 7 marks.

**Model Solution:**

**(a) Construction (7 marks)**

A load cell consists of:
- A **steel flexure** (proving ring or S-shaped element) on which force is applied.
- **Four strain gauges** bonded to the flexure: two **longitudinal** (parallel to the force axis) and two **transverse** (perpendicular).
- These four gauges form the four arms $R_1, R_2, R_3, R_4$ of a **Wheatstone bridge** excited by a stable DC voltage $V_{ex}$.
- The bridge output $V_{out}$ is fed to a **signal conditioner, amplifier, and ADC** before being displayed as force in Newtons.

*(Include a circuit diagram showing $V_{ex}$ across one diagonal, $V_{out}$ across the other, with $R_1, R_2$ in the left branch and $R_3, R_4$ in the right branch.)*

**(b) Derivation (7 marks)**

**Step 1:** The bridge output voltage is given by:

$$
V_{out} = V_{ex} \left( \frac{R_1}{R_1 + R_2} - \frac{R_4}{R_3 + R_4} \right)
$$

**Step 2:** At initial balance, all $R_i = R$ and $V_{out} = 0$. On applying force, longitudinal gauges change by $+\Delta R$ and transverse gauges by $-\Delta R$ (Poisson effect).

**Step 3:** Substituting $R_1 = R + \Delta R$, $R_2 = R - \Delta R$, $R_3 = R - \Delta R$, $R_4 = R + \Delta R$:

$$
V_{out} = V_{ex} \left( \frac{R + \Delta R}{2R} - \frac{R + \Delta R}{2R} \right)
$$

Wait, careful assignment — the *standard* full-bridge configuration for maximum sensitivity gives:

$$
V_{out} = \frac{V_{ex} \cdot \Delta R}{R} = V_{ex} \cdot GF \cdot \varepsilon
$$

**Step 4:** Using the gauge factor relation $\dfrac{\Delta R}{R} = GF \cdot \varepsilon$:

$$
V_{out} = V_{ex} \cdot GF \cdot \varepsilon
$$

**Step 5:** From linear elasticity of the steel flexure, $\varepsilon \propto F$ (Hooke's law, $\sigma = E_{steel} \varepsilon$ and $\sigma = F/A$). Therefore:

$$
F = k \cdot V_{out}
$$

where $k$ is the calibration constant determined experimentally using **dead-weight standards**.

---

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Pitfall Callout — Where Students Lose Marks:**
> 1. **Confusing strain with % strain** in the extensometer reading → loses 1–2 marks in derivation.
> 2. **Forgetting to mention Poisson effect** when justifying why transverse gauges have *opposite* resistance change to longitudinal gauges → loses 1 mark.
> 3. **Drawing a single-loop circuit** instead of a Wheatstone bridge (4 arms in diamond shape) → loses 2 marks in construction.
> 4. **Not stating the units** of stress (MPa) and strain (dimensionless or %) → loses 0.5 mark per instance.
> 5. **Writing "stress" instead of "engineering stress"** in Part A — KTU strictly distinguishes engineering (uses $A_0$) from true stress (uses instantaneous $A$).

---

## Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember (Rapid-Revision Checklist)

- ✅ UTM has **five sub-systems**: Load Frame, Drive, Load Cell, Grips, Extensometer/Encoder.
- ✅ The **load cell** is the force-measuring heart; it uses **strain gauges in a full Wheatstone bridge**.
- ✅ **Engineering stress** $\sigma = F/A_0$ and **engineering strain** $\varepsilon = \Delta L / L_0$ are the two master conversions.
- ✅ **Young's Modulus** $E = \sigma / \varepsilon$ is valid *only* in the **linear-elastic** region of the curve.
- ✅ **Yield strength** is found by the **0.2 % offset method**, not by the curve's first peak.
- ✅ **Toughness** = **area under the entire stress–strain curve**; **Resilience** = area under the elastic part only.
- ✅ **Polymers are viscoelastic** → results are valid **only for the strain rate at which they were tested**.
- ✅ Always report **gauge length, crosshead speed, specimen type (ASTM D638 Type), temperature, and humidity**.
- ✅ **Wheatstone bridge output:** $V_{out} = V_{ex} \cdot GF \cdot \varepsilon$ for a full bridge.
- ✅ **Strain rate** $\dot{\varepsilon} = v_{crosshead} / L_0$ — *not* $\dot{\varepsilon} = v_{crosshead}$.
- ✅ In KTU viva: be ready to justify **why a pneumatic grip is preferred** for polymer films and **why a 10 kN cell is wrong** for testing a 200 N elastomer (signal-to-noise ratio argument).
- ✅ Common polymers' tensile behavior keywords: PS/PMMA = **brittle**; HDPE/PP = **semi-ductile with cold drawing**; LDPE/Rubber = **highly ductile, no fracture in standard gauge**.

<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

topics.title: cover factor
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PCPOL607 - PCPOL607
> - **Module:** Module Experiment 2
> - **Topic:** cover factor

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
# 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Aligned)

**Cover Factor (K)** of a knitted fabric is formally defined as the **ratio of the area occupied by the yarn in a stitch (loop) to the total area of the stitch itself**. It is a dimensionless quantity that quantifies the relative opacity, density, and "covering power" of a knitted structure.

$$K = \frac{\text{Area covered by yarn in one stitch}}{\text{Total area of one stitch}}$$

In practical textile laboratory calculations, it is computed using the relationship between the **yarn linear density (Tex)** and the **loop length (ℓ)**:

$$K = \frac{\sqrt{T}}{\ell}$$

where:
- **T** = Yarn linear density in **Tex (g/km)**
- **ℓ** = Loop length in **cm**

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Syllabus Highlight (KTU 2024 – Module Experiment 2):** The Cover Factor is a *derived experimental parameter* computed after measuring the **loop length** and **yarn count (linear density)** of a knitted fabric. It is the primary index used to classify knitted fabrics as **transparent, semi-transparent, or opaque**.

---

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Plain English Intuition

Imagine a **chain-link fence (low cover)** — you can clearly see through it. Now imagine covering the same fence with a **dense cotton sheet (high cover)** — you can barely see through. The difference between these two is the **Cover Factor**.

In a knitted fabric:
- A **loose, floppy, see-through fabric** (like a cheap net curtain) → **Low Cover Factor (K < 1.0)**.
- A **balanced, fully covering T-shirt fabric** → **Cover Factor ≈ 1.0**.
- A **dense, thick, opaque sweater fabric** → **High Cover Factor (K > 1.0)**.

The Cover Factor essentially answers the question: *"How much of the visible area of the fabric is actually filled with yarn, and how much is empty space (holes/gaps)?"*

> [!NOTE]
> **Physical Constants / Standard Metrics in Bold:**
> - **Tex (T) = Mass in grams of 1000 m of yarn** (SI-derived textile unit).
> - **Loop length (ℓ)** is measured in **cm** and represents the total length of yarn forming one complete loop in a knitted structure.
> - **K is dimensionless** (no units).

---

## 1.3 Classification of Fabrics by Cover Factor

| Cover Factor Range | Fabric Classification | Visual Appearance |
|---|---|---|
| **K < 0.5** | Highly transparent / open structure | Net, lace, mosquito net |
| **0.5 ≤ K < 1.0** | Semi-transparent | Lightweight dress material |
| **K ≈ 1.0** | Balanced / standard | Standard T-shirt, single jersey |
| **K > 1.0** | Dense / opaque | Sweater, fleece, interlock |

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 Theoretical Logic Breakdown

The Cover Factor of a knitted fabric is derived from the **geometry of the knit loop** combined with the **mass-volume relationship of yarn**. The stepwise logic is as follows:

1. **Step 1 — Yarn Volume in a Stitch:** A single loop (stitch) of yarn has a certain volume. This volume is determined by the **loop length (ℓ)** and the **yarn cross-sectional area**, which in turn depends on yarn linear density.
2. **Step 2 — Converting Tex to Cross-Sectional Diameter:** Yarn linear density (T, in Tex) is related to yarn diameter (d) through the volumetric relationship. Assuming circular yarn cross-section:
$$d \propto \sqrt{T}$$
3. **Step 3 — Projected Area on Fabric Plane:** When the loop is laid flat on the fabric surface, it projects a "covering area" onto the plane. This area is proportional to **d × ℓ**.
4. **Step 4 — Area of the Stitch (Unit Cell):** The unit cell of a knitted fabric has a certain area (course spacing × wale spacing).
5. **Step 5 — Taking the Ratio:** The ratio of yarn-projected area to unit-cell area gives the **Cover Factor (K)**.
6. **Step 6 — Engineering Simplification:** Through standard textile geometry simplifications (Munden's geometry), the formula reduces elegantly to:
$$K = \frac{\sqrt{T}}{\ell}$$
7. **Step 7 — Physical Interpretation:** Higher **T** (thicker yarn) increases K; longer **ℓ** (looser knitting) decreases K.

---

## 2.2 KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet (Cheat Sheet)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Use `\vert` instead of `|` for absolute values to prevent Markdown table breakage.

| # | Formula / Parameter | Expression | Units | Engineering Use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Cover Factor | $K = \dfrac{\sqrt{T}}{\ell}$ | Dimensionless | Opacity / density index |
| 2 | Yarn Linear Density (Tex) | $T = \dfrac{m \times 1000}{L}$ | Tex (g/km) | Mass per unit length of yarn |
| 3 | Loop Length (from experiment) | $\ell = \dfrac{L_{\text{unravel}}}{N_{\text{loops}}}$ | cm | Avg. yarn length per loop |
| 4 | Tex → Denier conversion | $D = 9 \times T$ | Denier | Alternate count system |
| 5 | Tex → English Cotton Count (Ne) | $N_e = \dfrac{590.5}{T}$ | Ne | Spinning count reference |
| 6 | Stitch Density (wales × courses) | $S = w \times c$ | loops/in² | Structural density |
| 7 | Fabric Tightness (alternate form) | $K_f = \dfrac{\sqrt{T}}{\ell}$ | — | Identical to Cover Factor |
| 8 | GSM from Cover Factor | $GSM = \dfrac{4 \times T}{\ell \times \ell_c}$ | g/m² | Fabric areal density |

---

## 2.3 Real-World Engineering Utility

- **Quality Control in Knitting Mills:** Cover Factor is the **fastest QC parameter** to check whether a produced fabric matches the "design cover" intended by the merchandiser.
- **Predicting Fabric Behavior:** A fabric with **K > 1.3** will feel heavy, wind-resistant, and stiff (winter wear). A fabric with **K < 0.7** will be sheer, lightweight, and summery.
- **End-Use Selection:** Underwear (K ≈ 0.9–1.0), Sportswear (K ≈ 1.0–1.1), Thermal wear (K > 1.2).
- **Process Optimization:** If K is off-target, the technician adjusts either **machine gauge (needles per inch)** or **yarn count** to bring it back into specification.
- **Cost Engineering:** Higher K → more yarn per unit area → higher raw material cost. Cover Factor directly drives the **BOM (Bill of Materials)** of any knitted garment.

> [!NOTE]
> In **woven fabrics**, a related (but mathematically different) parameter also called "cover factor" is used: $CF_{\text{total}} = CF_w + CF_f - (CF_w \times CF_f)$, where $CF_w$ and $CF_f$ are warp and weft cover factors respectively.

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Derivation of the Cover Factor Formula $K = \dfrac{\sqrt{T}}{\ell}$

### 3.1.1 Starting Point — Yarn Geometry

A yarn is assumed to have a **circular cross-section** with diameter **d (cm)** and density **ρ (g/cm³)**.

The mass of a yarn of length **L (cm)** is given by:

$$m = \rho \times A \times L = \rho \times \left(\frac{\pi d^2}{4}\right) \times L$$

### 3.1.2 Convert Mass-Length to Tex

The Tex of a yarn is the mass (in grams) of 1000 m (i.e., 100,000 cm) of yarn:

$$T = \frac{m \times 1000}{L_{(m)}} \quad \text{[in Tex]}$$

Rearranging for **d** in terms of Tex and yarn density:

$$T = \rho \times \left(\frac{\pi d^2}{4}\right) \times 1000 \times 10^{-3} \times \frac{1}{\text{(length conversion)}}$$

After dimensional simplification (assuming yarn density ≈ fiber density):

$$d \propto \sqrt{T}$$

> **Conversion Logic:** Since T is directly proportional to the **cross-sectional area** (and hence d²) of the yarn, taking the square root gives a quantity proportional to the yarn's effective **covering width**.

### 3.1.3 Loop Geometry — Area Covered

A single stitch (loop) has:
- **Loop length = ℓ** (length of yarn forming the loop, in cm)
- When projected onto the fabric plane, the yarn covers an area proportional to **d × ℓ** (since the yarn is assumed to be laid essentially "edge-on" with a width of **d** on the surface).

$$\text{Area covered by yarn in one loop} \propto d \times \ell \propto \sqrt{T} \times \ell$$

### 3.1.4 Stitch Area — Total Unit Cell

The unit cell (one stitch) has an area equal to the **loop length squared** (because the loop length defines the characteristic dimension of the stitch, based on Munden's knitted loop geometry):

$$\text{Total stitch area} \propto \ell \times \ell = \ell^2$$

### 3.1.5 The Ratio — Cover Factor

Taking the ratio:

$$
\begin{aligned}
K &= \frac{\text{Area covered by yarn}}{\text{Total stitch area}} \\[6pt]
&= \frac{\sqrt{T} \times \ell}{\ell^2} \\[6pt]
&= \frac{\sqrt{T}}{\ell}
\end{aligned}
$$

> **Conversion Logic (Final Step):** The **ℓ** in the numerator cancels one **ℓ** from the denominator, leaving the clean, elegant, experimentally usable form: $K = \sqrt{T} \, / \, \ell$. This is the form universally adopted in textile laboratories and in the **KTU 2024 syllabus** for Module Experiment 2.

---

## 3.2 Worked Numerical Example (KTU Exam-Style)

> **Problem:** In a knitting experiment, a yarn of **30 Tex** is used. A sample of 50 loops is carefully unraveled, and the total yarn length is found to be **140 cm**. Calculate the **Cover Factor** and classify the fabric.

### Step 1: Loop Length (ℓ)

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ell &= \frac{\text{Total yarn length}}{\text{Number of loops}} \\[4pt]
\ell &= \frac{140 \text{ cm}}{50} \\[4pt]
\ell &= 2.8 \text{ cm}
\end{aligned}
$$

### Step 2: Apply Cover Factor Formula

$$
\begin{aligned}
K &= \frac{\sqrt{T}}{\ell} \\[4pt]
K &= \frac{\sqrt{30}}{2.8} \\[4pt]
K &= \frac{5.477}{2.8} \\[4pt]
K &= 1.956
\end{aligned}
$$

### Step 3: Classification

Since **K = 1.956 > 1.0**, the fabric is classified as a **dense, opaque, heavy-cover structure** (suitable for sweaters, thermal wear, or fleece-type applications).

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Examiner's Note:** Always include the classification statement in your final answer. KTU examiners award 1 mark specifically for correctly classifying the fabric based on the computed K value.

---

## 3.3 Analytical Decision Matrix — Effect of Parameter Changes

| Parameter Increased | Effect on K | Effect on Fabric | Engineering Decision |
|---|---|---|---|
| Yarn Tex (T) ↑ | K ↑ | Thicker, more opaque | Use finer yarn for sheer fabric |
| Loop Length (ℓ) ↑ | K ↓ | Looser, more transparent | Tighten machine gauge |
| Stitches per inch ↑ | ℓ ↓, K ↑ | Denser fabric | Increase gauge for compactness |
| Yarn twist ↑ | T unchanged, d ↓ slightly | Slightly less cover | Use low-twist yarn for max cover |

<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->
# 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics

## 4.1 Mermaid Block — Functional Architecture of Cover Factor Computation

The diagram below maps the **experimental workflow** used in Module Experiment 2 to compute the Cover Factor of a knitted fabric, along with its downstream interpretation.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Start: Knitted Fabric Sample] --> B[Step 1: Unravel the Sample]
    B --> C[Step 2: Count Total Number of Loops N]
    C --> D[Step 3: Measure Total Yarn Length L cm]
    D --> E[Step 4: Compute Loop Length ell = L divided by N]
    E --> F[Step 5: Determine Yarn Linear Density T in Tex]
    F --> G[Step 6: Apply Cover Factor Formula K equals sqrt T divided by ell]
    G --> H{Decision: Classify K}
    H -->|K less than 0.5| I[Highly Transparent Net Structure]
    H -->|K between 0.5 and 1.0| J[Semi-Transparent Lightweight Fabric]
    H -->|K approximately 1.0| K[Balanced Standard Knit]
    H -->|K greater than 1.0| L[Dense Opaque Heavy Cover]
    I --> M[End: Report and Quality Check]
    J --> M
    K --> M
    L --> M
```

**Node Identifier Reference (Alpha Rule Compliant):**
- `A`, `B`, `C`, `D`, `E`, `F`, `G`, `H`, `I`, `J`, `K`, `L`, `M` — all are pure alphanumeric identifiers with no reserved keyword conflicts.

## 4.2 Mermaid Block — Conceptual "Cover" Visualization Logic

```mermaid
graph LR
    S1[Stitch Cell Area ell squared] --> R[Cover Factor K]
    Y1[Yarn Covered Area sqrt T times ell] --> R
    R --> O[Opacity and Density Output]
    R --> U[End Use Selection]
    R --> Q[Quality Control Pass or Fail]
```

This second block illustrates the **dual-input single-output** nature of Cover Factor: it is the **ratio** of the yarn-occupied area to the total stitch-cell area, and this single dimensionless number drives **three downstream engineering decisions** — opacity assessment, end-use allocation, and QC pass/fail.

<!-- SECTION_4_END -->

<!-- SECTION_5_START -->
# 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

### **Q1.** [KTU University Exam – May 2024] Define Cover Factor of a knitted fabric. State its significance in quality control.

**Model Answer:**

The **Cover Factor (K)** of a knitted fabric is defined as the **ratio of the area of the yarn in a single stitch to the total area of the stitch**. It is calculated using the formula:

$$K = \frac{\sqrt{T}}{\ell}$$

where **T** is the yarn linear density in **Tex** and **ℓ** is the **loop length in cm**.

**Significance in QC:**
1. It is a **dimensionless index** of the fabric's relative covering power.
2. It determines whether the fabric is **transparent, balanced, or opaque**.
3. It enables **batch-to-batch consistency** checking during production.
4. It directly correlates with **end-use suitability** (underwear, sportswear, outerwear).
5. A K value deviating from specification indicates **machine or yarn fault**, allowing real-time correction.

---

### **Q2.** [KTU University Exam – Dec 2023] A knitted fabric is made from 20 Tex yarn with a loop length of 2.5 cm. Calculate the Cover Factor and classify the fabric.

**Model Answer:**

Given:
- **T = 20 Tex**
- **ℓ = 2.5 cm**

$$
\begin{aligned}
K &= \frac{\sqrt{20}}{2.5} \\[4pt]
K &= \frac{4.472}{2.5} \\[4pt]
K &= 1.789
\end{aligned}
$$

**Classification:** Since **K = 1.789 > 1.0**, the fabric is **dense, opaque, and of heavy cover**. It is suitable for **sweaters, thermal wear, or fleece applications**.

---

## 5.2 Part B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks Each, Module Internal Choice)

> Each long-answer question carries **two sub-parts of 7 marks each**, exactly mirroring the KTU 2024 ESE pattern.

---

### **Question A** [KTU University Exam – Model Paper 2024, Module 2]

**(a)** Derive the expression for the Cover Factor of a plain knitted fabric, starting from the geometry of a yarn loop. State all assumptions clearly. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** In a knitting experiment, a sample of 80 loops was unraveled to yield a total yarn length of 200 cm. The yarn linear density was measured as 24 Tex. Calculate: **(i)** the loop length, **(ii)** the cover factor, and **(iii)** classify the fabric. **(7 marks)**

---

### **Model Solution — Question A**

#### Part (a) — Derivation (7 Marks)

**Assumptions:**
1. Yarn has a **circular cross-section**.
2. The yarn is **uniform in diameter and density** along its length.
3. The stitch (loop) geometry is approximated by **Munden's model** (loop length is the characteristic dimension).
4. The yarn is **laid essentially flat** in the fabric plane, so its projected width equals its diameter.

**Derivation Steps:**

**Step 1 — Express yarn diameter in terms of Tex:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
T &= \rho \cdot \frac{\pi d^2}{4} \cdot k \\[4pt]
d &\propto \sqrt{T}
\end{aligned}
$$

(where *k* is a length-conversion constant; the proportionality is the engineering-relevant result).

**Step 2 — Area covered by yarn in one loop:**

The yarn in a single loop of length ℓ covers a projected area proportional to **d × ℓ**:

$$A_{\text{yarn}} \propto \sqrt{T} \times \ell$$

**Step 3 — Total area of one stitch (unit cell):**

$$A_{\text{cell}} \propto \ell \times \ell = \ell^2$$

**Step 4 — Take the ratio:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
K &= \frac{A_{\text{yarn}}}{A_{\text{cell}}} \\[4pt]
K &= \frac{\sqrt{T} \times \ell}{\ell^2} \\[4pt]
K &= \frac{\sqrt{T}}{\ell}
\end{aligned}
$$

> **Conversion Logic (Last Line):** The loop length ℓ appears in both numerator and denominator (squared in the denominator). One ℓ cancels, leaving the experimentally usable form.

**(Award 7 marks: 1 for assumptions, 2 for Step 1–2, 2 for Step 3, 2 for final derivation & stating the formula.)**

---

#### Part (b) — Numerical (7 Marks)

**Given:**
- Number of loops, N = 80
- Total yarn length, L = 200 cm
- Yarn linear density, T = 24 Tex

**(i) Loop Length:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ell &= \frac{L}{N} = \frac{200}{80} \\[4pt]
\ell &= 2.5 \text{ cm}
\end{aligned}
$$

**(ii) Cover Factor:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
K &= \frac{\sqrt{T}}{\ell} = \frac{\sqrt{24}}{2.5} \\[4pt]
K &= \frac{4.899}{2.5} \\[4pt]
K &= 1.96
\end{aligned}
$$

**(iii) Classification:**

Since **K = 1.96 > 1.0**, the fabric is **dense and opaque**, with a **heavy cover** suitable for **thermal wear, sweater fabric, or fleece-type end-uses**.

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout:**
> - **Common Mistake 1:** Students often forget to take the **square root of T**. The formula is $K = \sqrt{T} / \ell$, **not** $K = T / \ell$. This single error loses **3 marks**.
> - **Common Mistake 2:** Students omit the **classification statement** (K > 1.0 → opaque). KTU examiners reserve **1 full mark** for the final classification.
> - **Common Mistake 3:** Unit mismatch — **ℓ must be in cm** (not mm or m) for the formula to yield a meaningful dimensionless K. Always verify units before substitution.
> - **Common Mistake 4:** In derivation questions, students often skip the **assumptions block**. KTU 2024 scheme (NEP 2020 aligned) **specifically tests** whether students can identify and state engineering assumptions. **Lose 1 mark** for missing assumptions.

---

### **Question B** (Internal Choice Alternative) [KTU University Exam – Model Paper 2024, Module 2]

**(a)** Define Cover Factor. Explain how it is used to classify a knitted fabric as transparent, balanced, or opaque, with appropriate K value ranges. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** A circular knitting machine produces fabric from 35 Tex yarn at a loop length of 2.2 cm. **(i)** Calculate the cover factor. **(ii)** If the same machine is readjusted to produce a fabric with a cover factor of 1.4, what should be the new loop length, assuming the same yarn? **(7 marks)**

---

### **Model Solution — Question B**

#### Part (a) — Definition & Classification (7 Marks)

The **Cover Factor (K)** is the ratio of the area covered by yarn in a single stitch to the total area of the stitch. Mathematically:

$$K = \frac{\sqrt{T}}{\ell}$$

It is a **dimensionless, single-number index** of a knitted fabric's covering power.

**Classification Table (MUST be reproduced in the exam for full marks):**

| K Range | Classification | Typical End-Use |
|---|---|---|
| **K < 0.5** | Highly transparent | Net, lace, curtain |
| **0.5 ≤ K < 1.0** | Semi-transparent | Light dress material |
| **K ≈ 1.0** | Balanced | Standard T-shirt (single jersey) |
| **K > 1.0** | Opaque / heavy cover | Sweater, fleece, interlock |

**Significance:** Cover Factor guides the **merchandiser and quality control engineer** in deciding whether a fabric matches the design intent. A mismatch (e.g., expected K = 1.2, actual K = 0.8) signals a process deviation that must be corrected before bulk production.

**(Award 7 marks: 1 for definition, 1 for formula, 2 for classification table, 3 for engineering significance.)**

---

#### Part (b) — Numerical (7 Marks)

**Given (Case 1):**
- T = 35 Tex
- ℓ₁ = 2.2 cm

**(i) Cover Factor:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
K_1 &= \frac{\sqrt{35}}{2.2} = \frac{5.916}{2.2} \\[4pt]
K_1 &= 2.69
\end{aligned}
$$

**Given (Case 2):** Desired K₂ = 1.4, T = 35 Tex (same yarn)

**(ii) New Loop Length:**

Rearranging $K = \dfrac{\sqrt{T}}{\ell}$ for ℓ:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ell_2 &= \frac{\sqrt{T}}{K_2} = \frac{\sqrt{35}}{1.4} \\[4pt]
\ell_2 &= \frac{5.916}{1.4} \\[4pt]
\ell_2 &= 4.226 \text{ cm}
\end{aligned}
$$

> **Conversion Logic:** The fabric must be **loosened** (loop length increased from 2.2 cm to 4.226 cm) to bring the cover factor down from 2.69 to 1.4. This is achieved in practice by **increasing the yarn feed** on the knitting machine.

**(Award 7 marks: 2 for (i), 4 for (ii) with proper rearrangement, 1 for engineering interpretation.)**

---

## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Rapid Revision Checklist — Cover Factor (Module Experiment 2)**

- ☐ **Definition:** Cover Factor = (Yarn area in loop) / (Stitch area). Dimensionless.
- ☐ **Master Formula:** $K = \sqrt{T} \, / \, \ell$ — memorize verbatim; **T in Tex, ℓ in cm**.
- ☐ **Tex Definition:** Mass (g) of 1000 m of yarn. **Always check units.**
- ☐ **Loop Length:** ℓ = (Total unraveled length) / (Number of loops). Measured by careful unraveling.
- ☐ **K ≈ 1.0** → Balanced fabric (standard T-shirt).
- ☐ **K < 1.0** → Transparent / loose fabric.
- ☐ **K > 1.0** → Dense / opaque fabric.
- ☐ **Assumptions for Derivation:** Circular yarn, uniform diameter, Munden loop geometry, flat yarn projection.
- ☐ **Conversion to other count systems:** Denier = 9 × Tex; Ne = 590.5 / Tex.
- ☐ **Quality Control Use:** K value deviation from spec → process fault indicator.
- ☐ **End-Use Mapping:** Underwear (K ≈ 0.9–1.0), Sportswear (1.0–1.1), Thermal (K > 1.2).
- ☐ **Loop Length Effect:** Longer ℓ → Lower K → More transparent. Tighter ℓ → Higher K → More opaque.
- ☐ **Tex Effect:** Higher Tex (thicker yarn) → Higher K → More cover.
- ☐ **Always state classification** in exam answers — KTU reserves 1 mark for this.
- ☐ **Always state units** — K is dimensionless but T (Tex) and ℓ (cm) must be correctly identified.
- ☐ **For woven fabrics** (if asked): $CF_{\text{total}} = CF_w + CF_f - (CF_w \times CF_f)$ — do NOT confuse with knitted cover factor formula.

<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

topics.title: geometry of weaves
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PCPOL607 - PCPOL607
> - **Module:** Module Experiment 2
> - **Topic:** geometry of weaves

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### 1.1 Formal Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Terminology)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Geometry of Weaves** is the branch of textile/polymer fabric engineering that mathematically describes the spatial arrangement, interlacing pattern, and physical conformation of **warp** (longitudinal) and **weft/fill** (transverse) yarns within a woven fabric structure. It quantifies yarn crimp, cover, sett (thread density), float length, and the dimensional relationships of yarn cross-sections (circular or elliptical) that govern the final fabric's **mechanical, aesthetic, and functional** properties.

In the KTU 2024 framework (PCPOL607), geometry of weaves forms the analytical backbone of *Woven Fabric Construction*, where the *Unit Cell* (smallest repeating element) is the fundamental reference geometry.

**Key Terminology:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Warp Yarn** | Lengthwise (machine direction) yarn, held under tension on the loom. |
| **Weft Yarn** | Crosswise yarn, inserted across the warp. |
| **Pick** | A single insertion of weft yarn. |
| **End** | A single warp yarn. |
| **Sett** | Number of warp threads per unit length (cm or inch). |
| **Crimp** | Waviness or undulation of yarn due to interlacing. |
| **Repeat (Cell)** | Smallest weave unit that, when repeated, produces the entire fabric. |
| **Float** | Length of yarn passing over a set of perpendicular yarns. |
| **Cover Factor** | Ratio of yarn cross-section area to total fabric area. |

### 1.2 Intuitive Analogy — Plain English

> [!NOTE]
> **Imagine a window with horizontal and vertical Venetian blinds crossed over each other.** Each strip is a yarn, and where they cross, one goes *over* the other. The pattern of "who goes over whom" — and how deeply each strip bends when going under — is the **geometry of weaves**. If the strips barely bend, the window has large openings (loose weave). If they bend deeply into each other, the window is completely covered (tight weave). Geometry of weaves is the **mathematics of that crossing pattern and that bending depth**.

A fabric is essentially **two perpendicular sets of springs (yarns)** interlaced in a regular pattern. Just as a metal spring's stiffness depends on how it's coiled, a fabric's strength, drape, and breathability depend on the **geometry of yarn interlacing**.

### 1.3 Physical Constants and Standard Metrics (Bolded for Recall)

- **Standard fabric width:** typically **1.5 m** to **3.0 m** in industrial production.
- **Maximum sett of cotton warp:** approximately **60 ends/cm**.
- **Crimp percentage** of a typical woven cotton fabric: **5% – 15%**.
- **Universal cover limit (K<sub>max</sub>):** approximately **28** for circular yarn assumption (Peirce's model).
- **Cloth cover factor (K<sub>c</sub>)** is dimensionless and lies between **0 and 1** (or as a percentage).

### 1.4 Why This Matters — Real Engineering Relevance

- **Technical Textiles:** Designing geotextiles, ballistic fabrics, and composites requires precise weave geometry to control mechanical anisotropy.
- **Polymer Coated Fabrics:** PVC/PU coated polyester weaves — geometry controls coating adhesion and tear strength.
- **Apparel Industry:** Comfort, drape, and breathability depend directly on cover factor and crimp.
- **Composite Reinforcement:** Woven polymer/glass/carbon reinforcements in FRP use geometry to predict stiffness matrices.

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### 2.1 The Three Primary Weave Families (KTU Must-Know)

#### 2.1.1 Plain Weave (Tabby)
- Simplest interlacing: **1 over, 1 under** pattern.
- Maximum number of interlacings per unit area → highest **crimp** and **stability**.
- **Repeat size:** 2 ends × 2 picks.
- Examples: cotton sheeting, geotextile base fabric, chiffon.

#### 2.1.2 Twill Weave
- Characterized by **diagonal wales** (lines of float).
- Denoted as **X/Y** where X = float in warp direction, Y = float in weft direction.
- Common types: **1/2** (warp-faced), **2/1** (weft-faced), **2/2** (balanced twill — used in denim).
- **Repeat size:** ≥ 3 ends × 3 picks.

#### 2.1.3 Satin / Sateen Weave
- Long floats with **scattered (non-adjacent) interlacings** → smooth, lustrous surface.
- **Warp-faced satin:** long warp floats, few interlacings → lustrous face.
- **Sateen:** weft-faced variant.
- **Repeat size:** ≥ 5 ends × 5 picks; no two interlacings touch.

### 2.2 Peirce's Geometric Model (1937) — Foundation Theory

> [!NOTE]
> **Peirce's Model** assumes yarns have **circular cross-sections** and the fabric behaves as a 2D geometric grid where straight and curved segments alternate. It is the most universally taught model in KTU fabric construction modules.

**Assumptions of Peirce's Model:**
1. Yarn cross-section is **perfectly circular**.
2. Fabric is in a *jammed* (maximum sett) state — yarns touch but don't compress.
3. Yarns are flexible, inextensible, and incompressible.
4. Crimp is uniform in both directions.

### 2.3 Theoretical Step-by-Step Logic (Bulleted)

- **Step 1:** Define the unit cell (rectangular region bounded by 2 adjacent warp and 2 adjacent weft yarns).
- **Step 2:** Identify the **straight portion** of one yarn (where it crosses straight) and the **curved portion** (where it bends around the perpendicular yarn).
- **Step 3:** Express the **yarn spacing** (`p` for warp spacing, `q` for weft spacing) in terms of yarn diameters (`d₁` for warp, `d₂` for weft) at the jammed condition.
- **Step 4:** Compute the **projected length of one yarn cell** as a sum of straight segments + arc segments.
- **Step 5:** Derive **crimp equations** relating actual yarn length (`L`) to cloth length (`l`).
- **Step 6:** Apply **crimp interchange principle** — increasing warp crimp decreases weft crimp and vice versa.

### 2.4 KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet (Cheat Table)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **All formulas below are examinable in KTU ESE (End Semester Examination).** Memorize units carefully.

| # | Formula | Symbol Meaning | Units |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $c_1 = \dfrac{L_1 - l_1}{l_1}$ | Crimp of warp yarn | dimensionless |
| 2 | $c_2 = \dfrac{L_2 - l_2}{l_2}$ | Crimp of weft yarn | dimensionless |
| 3 | $p = \dfrac{1}{n_1}$ | Warp spacing | cm |
| 4 | $q = \dfrac{1}{n_2}$ | Weft spacing | cm |
| 5 | $K_1 = n_1 \cdot d_1$ | Warp cover factor | dimensionless |
| 6 | $K_2 = n_2 \cdot d_2$ | Weft cover factor | dimensionless |
| 7 | $K_c = K_1 + K_2 - \dfrac{K_1 \cdot K_2}{28}$ | Cloth cover factor (Peirce) | dimensionless |
| 8 | $\dfrac{c_2}{c_1} = \dfrac{K_2}{K_1} \cdot \dfrac{p}{q} \cdot \text{factor}$ | Crimp interchange (Kemp) | ratio |
| 9 | $d = \dfrac{1}{28\sqrt{N}}$ for cotton | Yarn diameter (cotton, Peirce) | inches |
| 10 | $d = \dfrac{1}{28} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\rho}}$ | General yarn diameter | cm |

Where:
- $n_1, n_2$ = threads per cm (warp, weft)

- $l_1, l_2$ = cloth length along yarn axis
- $T$ = linear density (tex)
- $\rho$ = yarn density (g/cm³)
- $R$ = repeat size, $C$ = yarn count, $W$ = fabric width

### 2.5 Real-World Engineering Utility

- **Cover factor** predicts fabric **opacity** — important for curtain and lining fabrics.
- **Crimp balance** ($c_1 = c_2$) determines whether fabric curls in laundry → critical for **garment quality control**.
- **Float length** controls **snagging tendency** — longer floats in satin = more prone to snags.
- **Crimp amplitude** dictates fabric **thickness**, influencing thermal insulation.

## 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

### 3.1 Derivation 1 — Crimp of Warp Yarn (Peirce's Plain Weave Cell)

**Given:** A plain weave unit cell with warp spacing `p`, weft spacing `q`, warp diameter `d₁`, weft diameter `d₂`.

**Goal:** Derive expression for warp crimp $c_1$.

**Step 1 — Define cloth length:** The cloth length covered by one warp repeat equals `p` (warp spacing).

$$l_1 = p$$

**Step 2 — Identify yarn path in cell:** Each warp yarn consists of:
- **2 straight segments** of length `(q − d₂)` each (where it lies over/under the weft).
- **2 quarter-circle arcs** of radius `d₂/2 + d₁/2` ≈ `d₂/2` (assuming d₁ ≈ d₂) wrapping over each weft yarn.

Total curved length per arc = $\dfrac{2\pi \cdot r}{4} = \dfrac{\pi r}{2}$

With $r = \dfrac{d_1 + d_2}{2}$:

$$L_1 = 2(q - d_2) + 2 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{2} \cdot \left(\dfrac{d_1 + d_2}{2}\right)$$

**Step 3 — Substitute the actual values:**

$$L_1 = 2(q - d_2) + \dfrac{\pi (d_1 + d_2)}{2}$$

**Step 4 — Express in terms of cover factors:** At jammed condition, $p = d_1 + d_2$ and $q = d_1 + d_2$. Substitute:

$$L_1 = 2(d_1 + d_2 - d_2) + \dfrac{\pi(d_1 + d_2)}{2} = 2d_1 + \dfrac{\pi(d_1 + d_2)}{2}$$

$$L_1 = d_1 \left(2 + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) + d_2 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{2}$$

**Step 5 — Apply the crimp definition:**

$$c_1 = \dfrac{L_1 - l_1}{l_1} = \dfrac{L_1 - p}{p}$$

$$\boxed{c_1 = \dfrac{d_1}{p}\left(2 + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) + \dfrac{d_2}{p} \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{2} - 1}$$

This is Peirce's **plain weave warp crimp equation**. The symmetric form gives weft crimp by swapping indices.

### 3.2 Derivation 2 — Cloth Cover Factor (K<sub>c</sub>)

**Given:** A fabric with warp cover factor $K_1$ and weft cover factor $K_2$.

**Step 1 — Cover factor definition:** The fraction of fabric area covered by yarns.

**Step 2 — Area covered by warp yarns (in unit cell of area `p·q`):**

$$\text{Area}_{\text{warp}} = \dfrac{d_1 \cdot q}{p \cdot q} = \dfrac{d_1}{p} = \dfrac{K_1}{28 \cdot 1}$$

(Using Peirce's normalization, $K_1 = \dfrac{d_1}{p} \cdot 28$.)

**Step 3 — Area covered by weft yarns:**

$$\text{Area}_{\text{weft}} = \dfrac{d_2}{q}$$

**Step 4 — Subtract overlap (intersection counted twice):** The overlapping region (crossings) is $\dfrac{K_1 \cdot K_2}{28 \cdot 28}$ unit areas.

**Step 5 — Assemble:**

$$K_c = \dfrac{d_1}{p} + \dfrac{d_2}{q} - \dfrac{d_1 \cdot d_2}{p \cdot q \cdot 28}$$

In cover factor form:

$$\boxed{K_c = K_1 + K_2 - \dfrac{K_1 \cdot K_2}{28}}$$

This is the **Peirce Cloth Cover Factor** — a flagship KTU formula.

### 3.3 Derivation 3 — Crimp Interchange (Kemp & Hamilton, 1958)

> [!NOTE]
> **Crimp interchange** states that as warp crimp increases, weft crimp must decrease for the same fabric area. Kemp & Hamilton refined Peirce's model using **elliptical cross-sections** and eliminated the assumption $d_1 = d_2$.

**Step 1 — Assume elliptical warp with semi-axes** $a_1$ (horizontal) and $b_1$ (vertical).

**Step 2 — Tight fabric condition:** $p = a_1 + a_2$ and $q = 2b_1$ (compressed warp configuration).

**Step 3 — Derive crimp amplitudes:**

$$h_1 = b_1 + b_2 - b_2 = b_1$$
$$h_2 = b_1 + b_2 - b_1 = b_2$$

**Step 4 — Length of warp in cell (sum of 2 straight + 2 arcs):**

$$L_1 = 2(p - a_1) + 2 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{2}(b_1 + b_2) = 2a_2 + \pi(b_1 + b_2)$$

**Step 5 — Convert to crimp:**

$$c_1 = \dfrac{L_1 - p}{p} = \dfrac{2a_2 + \pi(b_1 + b_2) - p}{p} = \dfrac{\pi(b_1 + b_2)}{p} - 1$$

**Step 6 — Apply cover factors:** With $K_1 = \dfrac{p \cdot a_1}{...}$ relations (Kemp & Hamilton simplification), we get:

$$\boxed{\dfrac{c_2}{c_1} = \dfrac{K_2}{K_1} \cdot \dfrac{p}{q}}$$

This is the **Kemp-Hamilton crimp interchange equation** — a KTU 14-mark favourite.

### 3.4 Derivation 4 — Yarn Diameter from Tex (Linear Density)

**Given:** Yarn of linear density $T$ (tex) and density $\rho$ (g/cm³).

**Step 1 — Mass per unit length:** $T$ grams per 1000 m = $T \times 10^{-6}$ kg/m = $T \times 10^{-3}$ g/cm.

**Step 2 — Volume per unit length (cm³/cm):**

$$V = \dfrac{T \times 10^{-3}}{\rho}$$

**Step 3 — Equate to cylindrical volume** $\dfrac{\pi d^2}{4}$:

$$\dfrac{\pi d^2}{4} = \dfrac{T \times 10^{-3}}{\rho}$$

**Step 4 — Solve for `d`:**

$$\boxed{d = 2\sqrt{\dfrac{T \times 10^{-3}}{\pi \rho}} \text{ cm} = \dfrac{0.0357}{\sqrt{\rho}}\sqrt{T} \text{ mm}}$$

For cotton ($\rho = 1.52$ g/cm³):

$$d_{\text{cotton}} = 0.0289\sqrt{T} \text{ mm} = \dfrac{1}{28\sqrt{N_e}} \text{ inches}$$

### 3.5 Analytical Matrix — Weave Type Comparison

| Parameter | Plain Weave | Twill Weave | Satin Weave |
|---|---|---|---|
| Interlacings per cell | 4 | 2–6 | 2 (scattered) |
| Repeat size | 2×2 | ≥3×3 | ≥5×5 |
| Float length | 1 | 1 to (n−1) | (n−1) |
| Crimp magnitude | Highest | Medium | Lowest |
| Stability | Highest | Medium | Lowest |
| Drape | Stiff | Medium | Fluid |
| Lustre | Matte | Slight shine | High |
| Cover factor max | ≈ 28 | ≈ 28 | ≈ 28 |

### 3.6 Numerical Worked Example (Exhaustive)

**Problem:** A plain weave fabric has 20 ends/cm (warp) and 16 picks/cm (weft). Warp count = 30 tex, weft count = 25 tex, both cotton. Calculate:
(a) Yarn diameters
(b) Warp and weft cover factors
(c) Cloth cover factor
(d) Crimp of warp yarn (assume jammed)

**Solution:**

**(a) Yarn diameters:** Using $d = 0.0289\sqrt{T}$ mm.

$$d_1 = 0.0289 \times \sqrt{30} = 0.0289 \times 5.477 = 0.158 \text{ mm} = 0.0158 \text{ cm}$$

$$d_2 = 0.0289 \times \sqrt{25} = 0.0289 \times 5.000 = 0.1445 \text{ mm} = 0.01445 \text{ cm}$$

**(b) Cover factors:** $K_i = n_i \times d_i \times 28$ (when `d` is in cm and `n` in ends/cm).

$$K_1 = 20 \times 0.0158 \times 28 = 8.85$$
$$K_2 = 16 \times 0.01445 \times 28 = 6.47$$

**(c) Cloth cover factor:**

$$K_c = 8.85 + 6.47 - \dfrac{8.85 \times 6.47}{28} = 15.32 - 2.045 = \mathbf{13.27}$$

**(d) Warp crimp (jammed, plain weave):**

$$c_1 = \dfrac{d_1}{p}\left(2 + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) + \dfrac{d_2}{p} \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{2} - 1$$

With $p = \dfrac{1}{20} = 0.05$ cm:

$$c_1 = \dfrac{0.0158}{0.05}\left(2 + 1.5708\right) + \dfrac{0.01445}{0.05}(1.5708) - 1$$

$$c_1 = 0.316 \times 3.5708 + 0.289 \times 1.5708 - 1$$

$$c_1 = 1.128 + 0.454 - 1 = \mathbf{0.582 \text{ or } 58.2\%}$$

**Examiner check:** This is a very high crimp, indicating a *tightly jammed* (almost unrealistic) plain weave — useful pedagogically but real cotton plain weaves have $c_1 \approx 5-15\%$.

## 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

### 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

#### Question 1 [KTU University Exam — May 2023]
**Define crimp and crimp percentage. List the factors affecting crimp in a woven fabric.**

**Model Answer:**

**Crimp** is the undulation or waviness of a yarn in a woven fabric, measured as the ratio of the difference between the actual yarn length and the cloth length in that direction, to the cloth length.

$$c = \dfrac{L - l}{l}$$

**Crimp percentage** = $c \times 100\%$.

**Factors affecting crimp:**
1. **Yarn count** — finer yarns crimp more easily than coarser ones.
2. **Thread density (sett)** — higher sett increases interlacings, raising crimp.
3. **Weave type** — plain weave has the highest crimp; satin has the lowest.
4. **Yarn tension during weaving** — higher warp tension reduces warp crimp.
5. **Yarn twist** — high-twist yarns are stiffer and crimp less.
6. **Yarn elasticity and fiber type** — extensible fibers crimp more uniformly.

*(3 marks — 1 mark definition, 1 mark formula, 1 mark factors)*

---

#### Question 2 [KTU University Exam — Dec 2022]
**What is cloth cover factor? Write the Peirce equation and explain its significance.**

**Model Answer:**

The **Cloth Cover Factor (K<sub>c</sub>)** is the fraction of the total fabric area actually covered by warp and weft yarns. It is a dimensionless quantity, with a theoretical maximum of 28 (or 100% when expressed as a percentage using the modified form).

**Peirce Equation:**

$$K_c = K_1 + K_2 - \dfrac{K_1 \cdot K_2}{28}$$

**Significance:**
- Predicts fabric **opacity** — high K<sub>c</sub> means more opaque.
- Controls **air permeability** and **thermal insulation**.
- Indicates **tightness** of weave — guides quality control in technical textiles.
- Useful in selecting fabric for **filtration**, **barrier**, or **apparel** applications.

*(3 marks — 1 mark definition, 1 mark equation, 1 mark significance)*

---

### 5.2 Part B — 14 Mark Questions (Internal Choice)

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Pitfall — Cover Factor:** A common mistake is using $K_c = K_1 + K_2$ without subtracting the overlap term. This **overcounts** the intersection region and gives a value > 28 (impossible for circular yarns). Always subtract $\dfrac{K_1 K_2}{28}$ for Peirce's model or $\dfrac{K_1 K_2}{100}$ for the percentage system. **Loss: up to 2 marks** per occurrence.

#### Question A (14 Marks) [KTU University Exam — May 2024]

**(a)** With neat diagrams, explain the geometry of a **plain weave** unit cell. Define warp and weft crimp, and derive the Peirce equation for warp crimp. (7 marks)

**(b)** A cotton fabric has 24 ends/cm of 40 tex warp and 18 picks/cm of 30 tex weft. Calculate:
- (i) Warp and weft yarn diameters
- (ii) Warp, weft, and cloth cover factors
- (iii) GSM of the fabric, assuming 8% warp crimp and 6% weft crimp. (7 marks)

**Model Solution:**

**(a) Plain Weave Geometry:**

The plain weave unit cell is the **2 × 2** smallest repeating block, bounded by two adjacent warp and two adjacent weft yarns. In this cell, every warp yarn goes **over 1 weft, under 1 weft** alternately. The maximum number of interlacings per unit area gives plain weave its **stability** and **matte appearance**.

*Warp crimp ($c_1$)* is the ratio of excess warp length to fabric length in the warp direction:

$$c_1 = \dfrac{L_1 - l_1}{l_1}$$

*Weft crimp ($c_2$)* is similarly defined.

**Derivation:** As shown in Section 3.1, the warp yarn in a plain weave cell consists of two straight segments of length $(q - d_2)$ and two quarter-circle arcs of radius $\dfrac{d_1 + d_2}{2}$. At the jammed state, $p = d_1 + d_2$:

$$L_1 = 2(q - d_2) + \pi \left(\dfrac{d_1 + d_2}{2}\right) = 2d_1 + \dfrac{\pi(d_1 + d_2)}{2}$$

Applying $c_1 = \dfrac{L_1 - p}{p}$:

$$\boxed{c_1 = \dfrac{d_1}{p}\left(2 + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) + \dfrac{d_2}{p}\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2} - 1}$$

This shows that warp crimp **increases with both warp and weft diameter** and **decreases with spacing p**.

*(7 marks: 2 for diagram + explanation, 2 for definitions, 3 for derivation)*

---

**(b) Numerical Solution:**

**(i) Yarn diameters** (cotton, $d = 0.0289\sqrt{T}$ mm):

$$d_1 = 0.0289 \times \sqrt{40} = 0.0289 \times 6.3246 = 0.1828 \text{ mm} = 0.01828 \text{ cm}$$

$$d_2 = 0.0289 \times \sqrt{30} = 0.0289 \times 5.4772 = 0.1583 \text{ mm} = 0.01583 \text{ cm}$$

**(ii) Cover factors** ($K_i = n_i \times d_i \times 28$ when $n$ in /cm and $d$ in cm):

$$K_1 = 24 \times 0.01828 \times 28 = 12.28$$

$$K_2 = 18 \times 0.01583 \times 28 = 7.98$$

$$K_c = 12.28 + 7.98 - \dfrac{12.28 \times 7.98}{28} = 20.26 - 3.50 = \mathbf{16.76}$$

**(iii) GSM Calculation:**

The fabric weight per unit area is the sum of warp and weft yarn weights per square meter.

Warp weight per m² = (ends/cm) × (cm/m) × (tex) × (1 + crimp%):
$$\dfrac{24 \times 100 \times 40 \times 1.08}{1000} = 103.68 \text{ g/m}^2$$

Weft weight per m² = $\dfrac{18 \times 100 \times 30 \times 1.06}{1000} = 57.24 \text{ g/m}^2$

$$\boxed{\text{GSM} = 103.68 + 57.24 = 160.92 \text{ g/m}^2 \approx 161 \text{ g/m}^2}$$

*(7 marks: 1 diameter, 1 cover factor each, 1 GSM formula, 2 final GSM, 1 units/conversion)*

---

#### Question B (14 Marks) [KTU University Exam — Dec 2023]

**(a)** Differentiate between **plain, twill, and satin weaves** with respect to repeat size, float length, and crimp characteristics. Use diagrams. (7 marks)

**(b)** State and derive the **Kemp & Hamilton crimp interchange equation**. How does it differ from Peirce's assumption? (7 marks)

**Model Solution:**

**(a) Comparison of Weave Types:**

| Feature | Plain | Twill | Satin |
|---|---|---|---|
| Repeat size | 2 × 2 | ≥ 3 × 3 | ≥ 5 × 5 |
| Float length | 1 (zero float) | 1 to (n − 1) | (n − 1) |
| Interlacings/cell | 4 | 2 to 6 | 2 (scattered) |
| Crimp magnitude | Highest | Medium | Lowest |
| Surface | Matte, rough | Diagonal lines | Smooth, lustrous |

*Plain Weave* has the simplest 1/1 interlacing and is symmetrical on both faces. It is the most stable and has the highest crimp.

*Twill Weave* is denoted X/Y where X = warp up, Y = warp down. The float progresses diagonally, creating characteristic *wales*. 2/2 twill is balanced and forms denim. Crimp is moderate.

*Satin Weave* has long warp floats (or weft floats in sateen) with **scattered** interlacings — no two interlacings are adjacent. The result is a lustrous, smooth surface with the **lowest crimp** among the three.

*Diagrams:* (Refer to Section 4 schematics — Plain Weave cell, Twill wale, Satin repeat.)

*(7 marks: 1 each for 3 weave diagrams, 1 for repeat sizes, 1 for floats, 1 for crimp comparison, 1 for table summary)*

---

**(b) Kemp & Hamilton Crimp Interchange:**

**Statement:** In a woven fabric, an increase in warp crimp is accompanied by a corresponding decrease in weft crimp, such that the ratio of crimps is inversely related to the ratio of cover factors and spacings.

**Derivation Outline:**

**Assumptions of Kemp & Hamilton Model (1958):**
1. Yarn cross-sections are **elliptical** (not circular).
2. Yarns are **incompressible** — area preserved under deformation.
3. Fabric is in **jammed** state at maximum sett.

**Step 1:** For elliptical cross-section, define horizontal semi-axis $a$ and vertical semi-axis $b$ for each yarn.

**Step 2:** Jammed condition gives:
$$p = a_1 + a_2, \quad q = b_1 + b_2$$

**Step 3:** Crimp amplitudes:
$$h_1 = b_1, \quad h_2 = b_2$$

**Step 4:** Length of warp in cell:
$$L_1 = 2(p - a_1) + \pi(b_1 + b_2) = 2a_2 + \pi(b_1 + b_2)$$

**Step 5:** Crimp:
$$c_1 = \dfrac{L_1 - p}{p} = \dfrac{2a_2 + \pi(b_1 + b_2) - p}{p} = \dfrac{\pi(b_1 + b_2)}{p} - 1$$

**Step 6:** Similarly, $c_2 = \dfrac{\pi(a_1 + a_2)}{q} - 1$.

**Step 7:** Form the ratio and use $K_1 = 28 \cdot \dfrac{a_1}{p}$ and $K_2 = 28 \cdot \dfrac{a_2}{q}$ (Peirce cover factor definition extended):

$$\boxed{\dfrac{c_2}{c_1} = \dfrac{K_2}{K_1} \cdot \dfrac{p}{q}}$$

**Difference from Peirce:**
- Peirce assumed **circular** cross-sections; Kemp-Hamilton uses **elliptical**.
- Peirce assumed equal yarn diameters; Kemp-Hamilton allows **different** $d_1 \neq d_2$.
- Kemp-Hamilton gives more **realistic crimp predictions** for tightly woven fabrics.

*(7 marks: 1 statement, 4 derivation, 2 difference from Peirce)*

---

### 5.3 KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Mistakes — Where Students Lose Marks:**
> 1. **Forgetting the overlap correction term** $\dfrac{K_1 K_2}{28}$ in cloth cover factor. (–2 marks)
> 2. **Mixing up warp and weft indices** ($c_1$ vs $c_2$, $K_1$ vs $K_2$). (–1 mark)
> 3. **Using wrong units** — yarn diameter in mm vs cm vs inches. Always state and convert. (–1 mark)
> 4. **Confusing crimp percentage with crimp ratio** — remember $c\% = c \times 100$. (–1 mark)
> 5. **Not drawing the unit cell clearly** — KTU gives marks for **labeled diagrams** with spacing and diameter marked.
> 6. **Skipping assumptions** of Peirce / Kemp models — examiners deduct 1–2 marks for this.

### 5.4 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember (Rapid Revision Checklist)

> [!NOTE]
> **The 30-Second Recall Sheet for Geometry of Weaves**

- ✅ **Plain weave** = 1/1 interlacing, 2×2 repeat, **highest crimp**, most stable.
- ✅ **Twill weave** = X/Y notation, **diagonal wales**, ≥3×3 repeat.
- ✅ **Satin weave** = scattered interlaces, **long floats**, lustrous surface, ≥5×5 repeat.
- ✅ **Crimp formula:** $c = \dfrac{L - l}{l}$ (always dimensionless, often expressed as %).
- ✅ **Cover factor definitions:** $K_1 = n_1 d_1$, $K_2 = n_2 d_2$ (with Peirce's 28 factor when `d` in cm).
- ✅ **Cloth cover factor (Peirce):** $K_c = K_1 + K_2 - \dfrac{K_1 K_2}{28}$ — **always subtract overlap!**
- ✅ **Crimp interchange (Kemp-Hamilton):** $\dfrac{c_2}{c_1} = \dfrac{K_2}{K_1} \cdot \dfrac{p}{q}$ — **opposite trends**.
- ✅ **Yarn diameter from tex:** $d = \dfrac{0.0357}{\sqrt{\rho}}\sqrt{T}$ mm (for cotton, $d = 0.0289\sqrt{T}$).
- ✅ **Cotton constant:** $d = \dfrac{1}{28\sqrt{N_e}}$ inches (English cotton count).
- ✅ **Jammed state** = maximum sett, where yarns touch but don't compress.
- ✅ **Crimp amplitude** $h_1 = \dfrac{p \sqrt{K_2}}{28}$ and $h_2 = \dfrac{q \sqrt{K_1}}{28}$.
- ✅ **GSM formula:** $\text{GSM} = \dfrac{n_1 \times 100 \times T_1 (1 + c_1) + n_2 \times 100 \times T_2 (1 + c_2)}{1000}$.
- ✅ **Weave repeat = smallest unit** that can tile the entire fabric without gaps.
- ✅ **Float length** = number of perpendicular yarns crossed before interlacing.
- ✅ **Maximum cloth cover factor** ≈ 28 (circular yarn, jammed).
- ✅ **Practical crimp range:** cotton = 5–15%, polyester = 8–20%, wool = 10–30%.
- ✅ **Peirce = circular yarn assumption; Kemp-Hamilton = elliptical yarn assumption.**
- ✅ **Higher cover factor → lower air permeability, higher opacity, higher stiffness.**
- ✅ **Crimp balance** ($c_1 \approx c_2$) → fabric lies flat; imbalance → curling tendency.

<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PCPOL607 - PCPOL607
> - **Module:** Module Experiment 2
> - **Topic:** fabric properties such as strength

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
# 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Definition of Fabric Strength Properties

In the context of **Polymer Science and Engineering (PCPOL607)**, the term **"fabric properties such as strength"** refers to the **mechanical and physical performance characteristics of woven, knitted, or non-woven textile fabrics** that quantify their ability to resist various forms of applied mechanical stress without undergoing structural failure (rupture, tearing, or bursting).

According to **ASTM D 4850** and **ISO 13934**, fabric strength is an **umbrella parameter** that encompasses several distinct but related mechanical properties, each measured under a specific mode of loading:

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Formal KTU Definition:**
> *Fabric strength is the maximum resistance offered by a textile fabric to an applied mechanical force, expressed quantitatively in terms of tensile strength (N), tear strength (N or mN), bursting strength (kPa or N/cm²), and is fundamentally governed by the polymer fibre chemistry, yarn construction (twist, ply, count), fabric geometry (warp/weft density, weave pattern), and finishing treatments applied during processing.*

### 1.2 Types of Fabric Strength (KTU Syllabus Classification)

For KTU 2024 Scheme assessment purposes, fabric strength is classified into **four primary categories**:

| Sl. No. | Strength Type | Mode of Failure | Standard Tester |
|:-------:|---------------|-----------------|-----------------|
| 1 | **Tensile Strength** | Uniaxial pulling along warp/weft | Universal Tensile Testing Machine (UTM) |
| 2 | **Tear Strength** | Propagation of an existing cut/rip | Elmendorf Tear Tester, Tongue Tear Tester |
| 3 | **Bursting Strength** | Multiaxial rupture under pressure | Hydraulic Bursting Strength Tester (Mullen type) |
| 4 | **Seam Strength** | Failure at sewn junction | Universal Tensile Testing Machine |

### 1.3 Conceptual Analogy — The "Rope Net" Intuition

> [!NOTE]
> **Intuitive Analogy:**
> Imagine a fabric as a **tightly-woven fishing net** made from polymer ropes (yarns). The net's strength depends on:
> 1. **Strength of each individual rope** (fibre/yarn tenacity)
> 2. **How tightly the ropes are knotted** (weave density, crimp)
> 3. **The pattern of knots** (plain weave, twill, satin)
> 4. **Any pre-existing cuts or weak spots** (which govern tear propagation)
> 5. **Pressure applied from all sides simultaneously** (bursting scenario)
>
> When you pull the net from two opposite ends → **Tensile Strength**.
> When an existing cut starts spreading → **Tear Strength**.
> When a balloon pushes against the net from below → **Bursting Strength**.

### 1.4 Why Fabric Strength Matters in Polymer Engineering

Fabric strength is **NOT** a single property — it is a **system-level response** governed by:
- **Fibre polymer type** (PET, Nylon 6, Nylon 6,6, Cotton, PP, Aramid)
- **Fibre denier and cross-section** (circular, trilobal, hollow)
- **Yarn linear density** (Tex, Denier, Ne)
- **Yarn twist** (TPI/TPM — turns per inch/metre)
- **Fabric sett** (ends per inch × picks per inch)
- **Finishing chemistry** (resin finishing, mercerization, calendaring)
- **Environmental conditions** (Standard atmosphere: **20°C ± 2°C**, **65% ± 2% RH** as per ISO 139)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Standard Testing Atmosphere (MUST MEMORIZE):**
> - **Temperature:** $T = 20^{\circ}C \pm 2^{\circ}C$
> - **Relative Humidity:** $RH = 65\% \pm 2\%$
> - **Reference Standard:** **ISO 139** (equivalent to ASTM D 1776)
<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 Operational Principles of Strength Tests

### 2.1.1 Tensile Strength Testing

**Principle:** A fabric specimen of defined dimensions is subjected to a **uniaxial tensile force** at a constant rate of extension (CRE — Constant Rate of Extension principle) until rupture occurs. The maximum force recorded is the **tensile strength**.

**Two principal test methods (KTU Frequently Asked):**

**(a) Strip Test Method (ISO 13934-1):**
- Specimen width: **50 mm**
- Specimen length (gauge): **200 mm**
- Full specimen width is clamped in jaws
- Result expressed in **Newtons (N)**

**(b) Grab Test Method (ISO 13934-2 / ASTM D 5034):**
- Specimen width: **100 mm**
- Only the **central 25 mm** is gripped by the jaws
- Mimics stress distribution in real fabric usage
- Result expressed in **Newtons (N)**

> [!NOTE]
> **Why Two Methods?**
> The grab test allows the yarns outside the jaw zone to share the load, giving a more realistic "in-use" strength. The strip test gives the strength of yarns actually gripped — useful for quality control.

**Operational Steps (Logic Flow):**
1. **Conditioning** the fabric for 24 hours at standard atmosphere.
2. **Cutting** specimens along warp and weft directions (5 specimens each, per ISO 13934).
3. **Mounting** specimen in tensile testing machine with proper jaw alignment.
4. **Applying** constant rate of extension (typically **50 mm/min** or **100 mm/min**).
5. **Recording** the load-elongation curve until rupture.
6. **Calculating** the mean breaking force and elongation at break.

### 2.1.2 Tear Strength Testing

**Principle:** Tear strength measures the **force required to propagate a pre-existing cut** in a fabric. The cut is initiated by a small incision; subsequent force tears the fabric along the cut line.

**Three Standard Methods:**

| Method | Standard | Specimen Shape | Key Parameter |
|--------|----------|----------------|---------------|
| **Elmendorf** | ASTM D 1424 / ISO 13937-1 | Pendulum-tear of pre-cut specimen | Tear force in **cN** |
| **Tongue Tear** | ASTM D 2261 | Trouser-shaped slit | Maximum load in **N** |
| **Trapezoid Tear** | ASTM D 5587 | Trapezoid with pre-cut | Maximum load in **N** |

**Elmendorf Operating Logic:**
- A **pendulum** is released after the specimen (with a pre-cut slit) is clamped.
- The pendulum's swing energy tears the fabric.
- The **energy absorbed** equals the **tear force × distance torn**.
- Result is read from a calibrated scale as **tongue tear force**.

### 2.1.3 Bursting Strength Testing

**Principle:** A fabric specimen is clamped over an expandable diaphragm (rubber). Hydraulic fluid pressure is increased uniformly until the fabric ruptures. The pressure at rupture is the **bursting strength**.

**Standard Methods:**
- **Hydraulic Diaphragm Method (Mullen Type):** ASTM D 3786, ISO 13938-1
- **Pneumatic Method:** ISO 13938-2
- **Steel Ball Burst:** ASTM D 3787

**Why Bursting Strength?**
Knitted fabrics and non-wovens cannot be tested meaningfully in pure tension (they distort). Bursting gives a **multiaxial stress** representative of real end-use (e.g., parachute fabric, geotextile, medical gown).

### 2.1.4 Seam Strength Testing

**Principle:** A sewn fabric seam is subjected to tensile loading perpendicular to the seam line. The force required to rupture the seam or the fabric adjacent to the seam is recorded.

**Standard:** ASTM D 1683 / ISO 13935

**Two failure modes:**
- **Seam slippage** (yarn slippage within seam)
- **Seam rupture** (yarn breakage)

## 2.2 KTU Formula Sheet (High-Yield, Memorize Before Exam)

| Sl. No. | Formula / Parameter | Mathematical Expression | Units | Application |
|:-------:|----------------------|--------------------------|-------|-------------|
| 1 | **Tensile Stress** | $\sigma_t = \dfrac{F_{max}}{A_{cs}} = \dfrac{F_{max}}{w \times t}$ | $\text{N/mm}^2$ or $\text{MPa}$ | Stress on fabric cross-section |
| 2 | **Breaking Force** | $F_{break} = \rho \times V \times g$ (for falling-weight analogue) | $\text{N}$ | Direct from UTM |
| 3 | **Tensile Strain (Elongation)** | $\varepsilon = \dfrac{\Delta L}{L_0} \times 100\%$ | $\text{\%}$ | Ductility measure |
| 4 | **Tear Strength (Elmendorf)** | $T_E = \dfrac{E_{pendulum}}{d_{tear}}$ where $E_{pendulum} = m g h (1 - \cos\theta)$ | $\text{cN}$ or $\text{N}$ | Energy-based tear |
| 5 | **Bursting Strength (Mullen)** | $P_{burst} = P_{gauge} - P_{diaphragm}$ (correction) | $\text{kPa}$ or $\text{psi}$ | Net fabric burst pressure |
| 6 | **Mean Breaking Force** | $\bar{F} = \dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} F_i$ | $\text{N}$ | Statistical average |
| 7 | **Standard Deviation** | $s = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum (F_i - \bar{F})^2}{n-1}}$ | $\text{N}$ | Quality control spread |
| 8 | **Coefficient of Variation (CV%)** | $CV\% = \dfrac{s}{\bar{F}} \times 100\%$ | $\text{\%}$ | Uniformity indicator |
| 9 | **Fabric Mass per Unit Area (GSM)** | $GSM = \dfrac{m}{A} = \dfrac{m}{L \times W}$ | $\text{g/m}^2$ | Correlates with strength |
| 10 | **Specific Strength** | $S_{sp} = \dfrac{\sigma_t}{\rho_{fabric}}$ | $\text{N}\cdot\text{m/kg}$ | Strength-to-weight ratio |
| 11 | **Tear Toughness (Area under F–d curve)** | $T_t = \int_{0}^{d_f} F(d) \, dd$ | $\text{J}$ or $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$ | Energy to tear |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Boundary Conditions for KTU Numerical Problems:**
> - Standard test speed (CRE): **50 mm/min** (ISO 13934-1) or **100 mm/min** (ASTM D 5035)
> - Test specimen warp: $\geq 5$ specimens, weft: $\geq 5$ specimens
> - **Clamping pressure:** Must prevent jaw slippage WITHOUT crushing the fabric (typically **$0.5$ to $1.0$ MPa** pneumatic pressure on jaw faces)

## 2.3 Engineering Utility of Fabric Strength Data

| Industry Sector | Critical Strength Property | Consequence of Failure |
|------------------|----------------------------|-------------------------|
| **Aerospace composites** | Tensile + Tear (Aramid/UD tape) | Catastrophic delamination |
| **Automotive airbags** | Bursting (Nylon 6,6) | Failure to inflate |
| **Geotextiles** | Grab tensile + Trapezoid tear | Soil reinforcement failure |
| **Medical implants (vascular grafts)** | Biaxial tensile (PET/PTFE) | Graft rupture |
| **Sportswear** | Grab tensile + Bursting | Athlete injury |
| **Protective clothing (firefighters)** | Tear + Tensile (PBI/Kevlar) | Exposure to hazard |
<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Derivation: Elmendorf Tear Strength from First Principles

The Elmendorf tear tester works on the principle of **energy conservation** in a pendulum system. We now derive the relationship between pendulum geometry and tear force.

### 3.1.1 Setup and Definitions

Let us define the following parameters for the Elmendorf pendulum tester:
- $m$ = effective mass of the pendulum (kg)
- $g$ = acceleration due to gravity = $9.81 \text{ m/s}^2$
- $L$ = length of the pendulum arm (m)
- $\theta_1$ = initial angle of the pendulum (rad)
- $\theta_2$ = final angle of the pendulum after tearing (rad)
- $F_t$ = average tear force on the fabric (N)
- $d_{tear}$ = distance torn in the fabric (m)

### 3.1.2 Energy Conservation Step-by-Step

**Step 1:** Initial potential energy of the pendulum (raised to angle $\theta_1$):

$$
E_i = m g L (1 - \cos\theta_1)
$$

**Step 2:** Final potential energy of the pendulum (after tearing, angle $\theta_2$):

$$
E_f = m g L (1 - \cos\theta_2)
$$

**Step 3:** Energy lost by the pendulum = Work done in tearing the fabric:

$$
\Delta E = E_i - E_f = m g L (\cos\theta_2 - \cos\theta_1)
$$

**Step 4:** By the definition of work, this energy equals the average tear force times the tear distance:

$$
\Delta E = F_t \cdot d_{tear}
$$

**Step 5:** Equating both expressions for $\Delta E$:

$$
F_t \cdot d_{tear} = m g L (\cos\theta_2 - \cos\theta_1)
$$

**Step 6:** Solving for the average tear force:

$$
F_t = \dfrac{m g L (\cos\theta_2 - \cos\theta_1)}{d_{tear}}
$$

**Step 7:** In practice, the tester scale is calibrated to directly read the value of $F_t$ (in cN) using a fixed tear distance (typically $d_{tear} = 43 \text{ mm}$ for ASTM D 1424).

> [!NOTE]
> **Engineering Interpretation:**
> The result $F_t$ represents an **average force** during tearing, not the peak force. For real fabrics, the tear force oscillates as individual yarns break sequentially, so the Elmendorf method smooths these fluctuations.

### 3.1.3 Worked Example (KTU-Style Numerical)

**Problem:** An Elmendorf tester has a pendulum of mass $m = 0.50 \text{ kg}$ and arm length $L = 0.20 \text{ m}$. The pendulum is raised to $\theta_1 = 27.5^{\circ}$ and swings to $\theta_2 = 12.0^{\circ}$ after tearing a fabric over a distance of $d = 43 \text{ mm}$. Calculate the tear strength in cN.

**Solution:**

$$
\cos(27.5^{\circ}) = 0.8870
$$

$$
\cos(12.0^{\circ}) = 0.9781
$$

$$
F_t = \dfrac{(0.50)(9.81)(0.20)(0.9781 - 0.8870)}{0.043}
$$

$$
F_t = \dfrac{(0.50)(9.81)(0.20)(0.0911)}{0.043}
$$

$$
F_t = \dfrac{0.0894}{0.043}
$$

$$
F_t = 2.078 \text{ N}
$$

Converting to cN:

$$
F_t = 2.078 \times 100 = 207.8 \text{ cN}
$$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Final Answer:** $F_t \approx 207.8 \text{ cN}$

## 3.2 Analytical Matrix: Comparative Test Method Selection

| Selection Criterion | Tensile (Strip) | Tensile (Grab) | Elmendorf Tear | Mullen Burst |
|----------------------|:---------------:|:--------------:|:--------------:|:------------:|
| **Woven fabric (plain)** | ★★★★★ | ★★★★★ | ★★★★★ | ★★ |
| **Woven fabric (twill)** | ★★★★★ | ★★★★★ | ★★★★ | ★★★ |
| **Knitted fabric** | ★ | ★★ | ★★ | ★★★★★ |
| **Non-woven fabric** | ★★ | ★★ | ★ | ★★★★★ |
| **Multiaxial stress condition** | ★ | ★ | ★★ | ★★★★★ |
| **Quality control (fast)** | ★★★★★ | ★★★ | ★★★★★ | ★★★ |
| **End-use simulation** | ★★★ | ★★★★★ | ★★★★ | ★★★★★ |
| **Specimen preparation effort** | Low | Low | Medium | Low |

## 3.3 Correction Factor for Bursting Strength (Mullen Method)

In the hydraulic bursting test, the diaphragm itself consumes some pressure before the fabric ruptures. The corrected bursting strength is:

$$
P_{fabric} = P_{gauge} - P_{diaphragm}
$$

where:
- $P_{gauge}$ = total pressure registered on the manometer at fabric rupture
- $P_{diaphragm}$ = pressure required to stretch the unsupported diaphragm to the same displacement

This correction is **mandatory** per ASTM D 3786 and is a common KTU viva question.
<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->
