<!-- SECTION_4_END -->

<!-- SECTION_5_START -->
# 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A: Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

### **Question 1: [KTU University Exam - May 2024 (Model)]**

**Q: Define tensile strength of a fabric. State the standard atmospheric conditions for testing textile fabrics as per ISO 139.**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

**Definition (2 marks):** Tensile strength of a fabric is the maximum uniaxial tensile force per unit width (or per unit cross-sectional area) that a fabric specimen can withstand before rupturing, when tested on a tensile testing machine under a constant rate of extension. It is expressed in Newtons (N) for force-based reporting or in N/mm or N/m for specific stress.

**Standard Atmospheric Conditions (1 mark):** As per **ISO 139**, the standard atmosphere for testing textiles is:
- **Temperature:** $T = 20^{\circ}C \pm 2^{\circ}C$
- **Relative Humidity:** $RH = 65\% \pm 2\%$

Specimens must be conditioned for a minimum of **24 hours** in this atmosphere prior to testing.

---

### **Question 2: [KTU University Exam - Dec 2023 (Model)]**

**Q: Differentiate between strip test and grab test methods for fabric tensile strength determination.**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

| Parameter | Strip Test (ISO 13934-1) | Grab Test (ISO 13934-2) |
|-----------|--------------------------|--------------------------|
| **Specimen width** | 50 mm (full grip) | 100 mm (only 25 mm central grip) |
| **Yarns loaded** | Only the gripped yarns | Yarns outside the grip also contribute |
| **Result** | True breaking strength of clamped yarns | Realistic in-use strength (yarn cooperation) |
| **Failure mode** | All yarns break simultaneously | Gradual, progressive yarn failure |
| **Application** | Quality control, raw material comparison | End-use performance evaluation |

The grab test gives **higher values** than the strip test because of the contribution of the surrounding unclamped yarns to load sharing.

---

## 5.2 Part B: 14-Mark Questions with Internal Choice

### **Question A (14 Marks): [KTU University Exam - Dec 2024 (Model)]**

**Q: (a)** With a neat block diagram, explain the principle and procedure of determining the **tensile strength of a woven fabric using the strip method** as per ISO 13934-1. List the key test parameters. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** A fabric specimen of width $w = 50 \text{ mm}$ and thickness $t = 0.45 \text{ mm}$ is tested on a UTM. The maximum load recorded is $F_{max} = 1250 \text{ N}$. Calculate the **tensile stress at break**. If the original gauge length was $L_0 = 200 \text{ mm}$ and the elongation at break is $\Delta L = 28 \text{ mm}$, calculate the **percentage elongation at break**. **(7 marks)**

---

#### **Model Solution for (a):**

**Principle (2 marks):** A fabric specimen of defined width and length is clamped along its full width between two jaws of a Universal Tensile Testing Machine (UTM). A uniaxial tensile force is applied at a constant rate of extension (CRE principle) until the specimen ruptures. The maximum force recorded is the **strip tensile strength** of the fabric.

**Apparatus Required (1 mark):** UTM with CRE mechanism, calibrated load cell, pneumatic or screw-type jaws with flat jaw faces (25 mm × 50 mm), cutting template, standard atmosphere chamber.

**Procedure (3 marks):**
1. Condition the fabric for 24 hours at $20^{\circ}C \pm 2^{\circ}C$, $65\% \pm 2\%$ RH.
2. Cut **5 specimens** along the **warp direction** (200 mm × 50 mm) and **5 specimens** along the **weft direction**, avoiding the selvedge and ensuring no two specimens contain the same yarns.
3. Set the gauge length ($L_0$) to **200 mm** between the jaws.
4. Clamp the specimen with uniform jaw pressure (≈ 0.5–1.0 MPa on jaw faces).
5. Start the UTM at a constant rate of extension of **50 mm/min** (or 100 mm/min as per spec).
6. Record the load-elongation curve continuously until rupture.
7. Note the **maximum force** $F_{max}$ in Newtons.

**Key Test Parameters (1 mark):**
- Specimen dimensions: 200 mm × 50 mm
- Gauge length: 200 mm
- Test speed: 50 mm/min (CRE)
- Number of specimens: 5 warp + 5 weft
- Pretension: Sufficient to remove fabric slack (without stretching)

---

#### **Model Solution for (b):**

**Given Data:**
- Width: $w = 50 \text{ mm}$
- Thickness: $t = 0.45 \text{ mm}$
- Maximum force: $F_{max} = 1250 \text{ N}$
- Original gauge length: $L_0 = 200 \text{ mm}$
- Elongation at break: $\Delta L = 28 \text{ mm}$

**Step 1: Calculate Cross-Sectional Area**

$$
A_{cs} = w \times t = 50 \text{ mm} \times 0.45 \text{ mm} = 22.5 \text{ mm}^2
$$

**Step 2: Calculate Tensile Stress at Break**

$$
\sigma_t = \dfrac{F_{max}}{A_{cs}} = \dfrac{1250 \text{ N}}{22.5 \text{ mm}^2}
$$

$$
\sigma_t = 55.56 \text{ N/mm}^2 = 55.56 \text{ MPa}
$$

**Step 3: Calculate Percentage Elongation at Break**

$$
\varepsilon\% = \dfrac{\Delta L}{L_0} \times 100\% = \dfrac{28 \text{ mm}}{200 \text{ mm}} \times 100\%
$$

$$
\varepsilon\% = 14.0\%
$$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Final Answers:**
> - Tensile stress at break: $\sigma_t = 55.56 \text{ MPa}$
> - Percentage elongation at break: $\varepsilon = 14.0\%$

---

### **Question B (14 Marks) — Alternative Choice: [KTU University Exam - May 2023 (Model)]**

**Q: (a)** Describe the **Elmendorf tear strength test** in detail. State the governing equation and the relevant standard. Explain why the result is reported as an "average" force. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** An Elmendorf tester has a pendulum of effective mass $m = 0.40 \text{ kg}$ and arm length $L = 0.21 \text{ m}$. The pendulum is released from $\theta_1 = 30.0^{\circ}$ and is arrested at $\theta_2 = 10.5^{\circ}$ after tearing a fabric over $d = 43 \text{ mm}$. Calculate the **tear strength in cN** and in **Newtons**. **(7 marks)**

---

#### **Model Solution for (a):**

**Principle (2 marks):** The Elmendorf tear test determines the force required to **propagate a single-rip tear** starting from a cut slit in a fabric specimen. The specimen is held between two jaws, one fixed to the instrument frame and the other attached to a pendulum. When the pendulum is released, its kinetic energy tears the fabric, and the loss in pendulum energy equals the work done in tearing.

**Standard (1 mark):** **ASTM D 1424** (Elmendorf) and **ISO 13937-1** (Ballistic pendulum).

**Procedure (2 marks):**
1. Condition the fabric at standard atmosphere.
2. Cut specimens of size **100 mm × 75 mm** with a **20 mm slit** at the centre of the shorter edge.
3. Clamp the specimen between fixed and movable jaws, aligning the slit with the jaw edge.
4. Lift the pendulum to its latched position (initial angle $\theta_1$).
5. Release the catch; the pendulum swings and tears the fabric.
6. The scale pointer indicates the **tear force in cN**.

**Governing Equation (1 mark):**

$$
F_t = \dfrac{m g L (\cos\theta_2 - \cos\theta_1)}{d_{tear}}
$$

**Why "Average" Force? (1 mark):** During tearing, individual yarns break sequentially, causing the instantaneous force to oscillate. The Elmendorf method integrates the energy over the entire tear length, providing an **average force** rather than a peak force. This makes the result less sensitive to peak load spikes.

---

#### **Model Solution for (b):**

**Given Data:**
- $m = 0.40 \text{ kg}$
- $L = 0.21 \text{ m}$
- $\theta_1 = 30.0^{\circ}$, so $\cos(30.0^{\circ}) = 0.8660$
- $\theta_2 = 10.5^{\circ}$, so $\cos(10.5^{\circ}) = 0.9833$
- $d_{tear} = 43 \text{ mm} = 0.043 \text{ m}$
- $g = 9.81 \text{ m/s}^2$

**Step 1: Apply the Governing Equation**

$$
F_t = \dfrac{m g L (\cos\theta_2 - \cos\theta_1)}{d_{tear}}
$$

**Step 2: Substitute Values**

$$
F_t = \dfrac{(0.40)(9.81)(0.21)(0.9833 - 0.8660)}{0.043}
$$

$$
F_t = \dfrac{(0.40)(9.81)(0.21)(0.1173)}{0.043}
$$

**Step 3: Calculate Numerator**

$$
(0.40)(9.81)(0.21) = 0.82404
$$

$$
0.82404 \times 0.1173 = 0.09665
$$

**Step 4: Calculate Final Force in Newtons**

$$
F_t = \dfrac{0.09665}{0.043} = 2.2477 \text{ N}
$$

**Step 5: Convert to Centinewtons**

$$
F_t = 2.2477 \times 100 = 224.77 \text{ cN}
$$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Final Answer:** $F_t \approx 2.25 \text{ N}$ or $F_t \approx 224.77 \text{ cN}$

---

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Pitfalls:**
> 1. **Forgetting to convert mm to m** in SI calculations. KTU examiners deduct **1 full mark** for unit inconsistency.
> 2. **Confusing strip and grab test specimen widths** (50 mm vs. 100 mm). Marks lost in part (a) descriptions.
> 3. **Not mentioning standard atmosphere** in any test description — examiners expect ISO 139 conditions as a default opening statement.
> 4. **Reporting tear strength in N only** — KTU 2024 Scheme typically requires **both N and cN** units to be stated explicitly.
> 5. **Mixing up warp and weft** specimen counts — both directions must be tested for tensile strength per ISO 13934.
> 6. **Skipping the diaphragm correction** in bursting strength numericals — a guaranteed 1-mark deduction.
> 7. **Forgetting to specify the rate of extension** (50 mm/min) in tensile test procedures.

---

## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!NOTE]
> **Rapid Revision Checklist — Fabric Strength Properties**

- ☐ Fabric strength is **NOT a single property** — it includes tensile, tear, bursting, and seam strength.
- ☐ **Standard test atmosphere:** $20^{\circ}C \pm 2^{\circ}C$, $65\% \pm 2\%$ RH, conditioning for **24 hours** (ISO 139).
- ☐ **Tensile test (Strip):** 50 mm × 200 mm specimen, 50 mm/min CRE, result in N (ISO 13934-1).
- ☐ **Tensile test (Grab):** 100 mm × 200 mm specimen, only 25 mm central grip, gives higher values than strip test (ISO 13934-2).
- ☐ **Elmendorf tear test:** Pendulum energy method, governed by $F_t = \dfrac{mgL(\cos\theta_2 - \cos\theta_1)}{d_{tear}}$, result in cN (ASTM D 1424).
- ☐ **Mullen bursting test:** Hydraulic pressure on a clamped fabric, corrected for diaphragm stiffness, result in kPa (ASTM D 3786).
- ☐ **Seam strength:** Perpendicular tensile load on sewn specimen, two failure modes (slippage vs. rupture) (ASTM D 1683).
- ☐ **Tear force is reported as an AVERAGE** because the Elmendorf method integrates energy over tear length.
- ☐ **Grab test > Strip test** in numerical value due to yarn load sharing outside the clamp zone.
- ☐ **Bursting strength is preferred for knitted and non-woven fabrics** that distort under uniaxial tension.
- ☐ **5 specimens in warp direction + 5 specimens in weft direction** is the minimum for statistical validity.
- ☐ **Diaphragm correction** ($P_{fabric} = P_{gauge} - P_{diaphragm}$) is mandatory for accurate bursting strength.
- ☐ **Fibre polymer type, yarn twist, weave density, and finishing** all significantly influence fabric strength.
- ☐ **Statistical reporting:** Always include mean, standard deviation, and CV% — KTU expects quantitative rigour.
- ☐ **Units to remember:** N (force), cN (tear), MPa (stress), kPa (burst pressure), GSM (areal density), % (strain).
<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

topics.title: abrasion resistance
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PCPOL607 - PCPOL607
> - **Module:** Module Experiment 2
> - **Topic:** abrasion resistance

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### Formal Academic Definition

**Abrasion resistance** is defined as the ability of a solid material (specifically a polymer, coating, rubber, or composite) to resist mechanical action such as rubbing, scraping, or erosion that progressively removes material from its surface. In the context of polymer engineering (KTU PCPOL607), it quantifies the **wear endurance** of a specimen subjected to repeated frictional contact with an abrasive medium under a controlled normal load.

Mathematically, it is the reciprocal of **material loss per unit operational cycle**, expressed in terms of mass loss, volume loss, or thickness loss per thousand revolutions.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Syllabus Highlight (Experiment 2):**
> The laboratory experiment evaluates the abrasion resistance of a polymer/rubber/composite specimen using a **Taber Abraser** (or equivalent rotary platform abrasion tester) in accordance with **ASTM D4060 / IS 3400 (Part 3)**. The student is expected to determine the **Wear Index** and **Volume Loss** of the test specimen.

### Conceptual Analogy / Intuition

Imagine you take a piece of chalk and rub it repeatedly on a rough concrete wall. After a few strokes, the chalk wears down — its surface gets eroded. Now take a piece of compressed charcoal of the same size and rub it under identical conditions. The charcoal barely loses any material. The difference between these two scenarios is **abrasion resistance**.

In the same way, when a rubber tyre rolls on a road, or a polymer flooring tile is walked upon, or a conveyor belt moves goods across rough surfaces — the material slowly grinds away. A polymer with **high abrasion resistance** is like the charcoal in the analogy: it resists being ground down. A polymer with **low abrasion resistance** is like the chalk: it wears away quickly.

> [!NOTE]
> **Key Standard Metrics (Industry Norms):**
> - **Taber Wear Index** — unitless, typically reported as **mg/1000 cycles**
> - **Volume Loss** — measured in **mm³ / 1000 cycles**
> - **Mass Loss Rate** — measured in **mg/cycle**
> - **Reference Standard Load** — **500 g or 1000 g** on each abrasive wheel
> - **Standard Abrasive Wheels** — **CS-10, CS-17, H-18, H-22** (Calibrase / Calibrade)

### Why Abrasion Resistance Matters for Polymers

Polymers are increasingly replacing metals in applications like **floor tiles, shoe soles, conveyor belts, automotive tyres, seals, gaskets, and protective coatings**. In all of these, surface wear is the dominant failure mode — not yielding or fracture. Therefore, characterizing abrasion resistance is critical for **service-life prediction** and **material selection**.

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### Underlying Mechanism of Abrasion

Abrasion is fundamentally a **micro-cutting, micro-fatigue, and micro-spalling** phenomenon operating at the contact interface. When an abrasive grit (or wheel) is dragged across a polymer surface under load, three sub-mechanisms occur simultaneously:

1. **Micro-ploughing** — the abrasive pushes material sideways into ridges without removing it. Energy is dissipated viscoelastically.
2. **Micro-cutting** — sharp abrasive asperities act like miniature cutting tools, directly shearing off chips of material (this is the dominant material-removal mechanism).
3. **Micro-fatigue** — repeated sub-threshold loading causes subsurface crack initiation, eventually leading to spalling of wear debris.

### Logical Flow of an Abrasion Test

- A flat, circular polymer specimen is mounted on a **rotating turntable**.
- Two abrasive wheels (loaded with a calibrated weight, typically **500 g or 1000 g**) are lowered onto the specimen surface.
- The turntable rotates at a fixed speed (typically **60 ± 5 rpm**).
- Abrasive contact follows a **circular wear path** (annular ring) of radius approximately **50–60 mm**.
- After a predefined number of cycles (commonly **1000, 2000, 5000, or 10000**), the specimen is removed, cleaned, and reweighed.
- Mass loss, volume loss, and Wear Index are computed.

### Factors Affecting Abrasion Resistance of Polymers

- **Hardness (Shore A / Shore D):** Higher surface hardness generally correlates with better abrasion resistance, but the correlation is not strictly linear due to viscoelastic recovery.
- **Cross-link density:** Higher cross-linking (e.g., in cured rubber) improves resistance to wear-fatigue.
- **Filler type and content:** Carbon black, silica, and aluminium oxide fillers dramatically enhance abrasion resistance. **Optimal carbon-black loading in tyre tread rubber is ~30–50 phr**.
- **Polymer structure:** Crystallinity, molecular weight, and chain stiffness influence wear behaviour.
- **Additives:** Lubricants, plasticizers, and anti-ozonants can either improve or degrade abrasion resistance.
- **Test parameters:** Abrasive wheel grade, applied load, rotational speed, ambient temperature, and humidity.
- **Surface condition:** Polished vs. moulded surface, residual stresses.

### KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

| Formula Description | Equation (LaTeX) | Standard / Units |
|---|---|---|
| Mass loss per cycle | $\Delta m = \dfrac{W_{1} - W_{2}}{N}$ | grams / cycle |
| Total mass loss after N cycles | $\Delta M = W_{1} - W_{2}$ | grams (or mg) |
| Volume loss | $\Delta V = \dfrac{W_{1} - W_{2}}{\rho}$ | cm³ (or mm³) |
| **Taber Wear Index (mass basis)** | $I_{m} = \dfrac{(W_{1} - W_{2}) \times 1000}{N}$ | mg / 1000 cycles |
| **Taber Wear Index (volume basis)** | $I_{v} = \dfrac{(W_{1} - W_{2}) \times 1000}{N \times \rho}$ | mm³ / 1000 cycles |
| Abrasion resistance (inverse of wear) | $R_{ab} = \dfrac{1}{I}$ | cycles / mg |
| Wear rate | $\dot{W} = \dfrac{\Delta V}{t}$ | mm³ / minute |
| Density of specimen | $\rho = \dfrac{m}{V}$ | g / cm³ |

> [!NOTE]
> In the above table, **$W_1$** = initial mass of specimen, **$W_2$** = final mass after N cycles, **$N$** = number of revolutions, and **$\rho$** = density of the polymer specimen. The factor **1000** in the wear index normalises the result to a per-1000-cycle basis for reporting consistency.

### Real-World Engineering Utility

- **Tyre Industry:** Wear index directly informs **tyre tread life** and **mileage warranties**.
- **Flooring & Tiles:** Determines **foot-traffic durability rating** of PVC and vinyl tiles.
- **Conveyor Belts:** Predicts **operational lifespan** in mining and bulk-material handling.
- **Footwear:** Sole wear rating (sole longevity).
- **Coatings:** Anti-graffiti and marine-coating durability.

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
## 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

### Derivation 1 — Taber Wear Index (Mass Basis) from First Principles

The **Taber Wear Index** is the industry-standard normalised metric for ranking polymer abrasion behaviour. We derive it step-by-step from raw experimental data.

**Step 1 — Define the raw measured quantity.**

The experiment directly yields a mass difference after N revolutions of the turntable:

$$\Delta M = W_{1} - W_{2}$$

where the units are kept consistent (typically grams or milligrams).

**Step 2 — Express mass loss per single revolution.**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Mass loss per cycle} &= \dfrac{\text{Total mass loss}}{\text{Total cycles}} \\[6pt]
m_{\text{per cycle}} &= \dfrac{\Delta M}{N}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3 — Normalise to 1000 cycles (industry convention).**

To compare samples tested under different cycle counts, ASTM D4060 mandates reporting the loss per 1000 cycles:

$$
\begin{aligned}
I_{m} &= \left( \dfrac{\Delta M}{N} \right) \times 1000 \\[6pt]
I_{m} &= \dfrac{(W_{1} - W_{2}) \times 1000}{N}
\end{aligned}
$$

This is the **mass-basis Taber Wear Index**, expressed in **mg per 1000 cycles** (when $\Delta M$ is in mg).

**Step 4 — Volume basis correction.**

Since materials of different densities lose the same mass but different volumes under identical abrasion, a more physically meaningful metric uses volume:

$$
\begin{aligned}
I_{v} &= \dfrac{I_{m}}{\rho} \\[6pt]
I_{v} &= \dfrac{(W_{1} - W_{2}) \times 1000}{N \times \rho}
\end{aligned}
$$

The unit becomes **mm³ per 1000 cycles** when mass is in mg and density is in **g/cm³ = mg/mm³**.

### Worked Numerical Example (KTU Lab-Viva Style)

**Given:**
- Initial mass of rubber specimen, $W_1 = 24.562$ g
- Final mass after 3000 cycles, $W_2 = 24.471$ g
- Density of rubber, $\rho = 1.15$ g/cm³
- Abrasive wheel: **CS-17**, Load: **1000 g per wheel**
- Speed: **60 rpm**

**Find:** (a) Mass-basis Wear Index (b) Volume-basis Wear Index (c) Abrasion resistance.

**Solution:**

**Step 1 — Compute mass loss.**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta M &= W_{1} - W_{2} \\
&= 24.562 - 24.471 \\
&= 0.091 \text{ g} \\
&= 91 \text{ mg}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2 — Compute mass-basis Wear Index.**

$$
\begin{aligned}
I_{m} &= \dfrac{(W_{1} - W_{2}) \times 1000}{N} \\
&= \dfrac{91 \times 1000}{3000} \\
&= \dfrac{91000}{3000} \\
&= 30.33 \text{ mg / 1000 cycles}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3 — Compute volume-basis Wear Index.**

$$
\begin{aligned}
I_{v} &= \dfrac{(W_{1} - W_{2}) \times 1000}{N \times \rho} \\
&= \dfrac{91 \times 1000}{3000 \times 1.15} \\
&= \dfrac{91000}{3450} \\
&= 26.38 \text{ mm³ / 1000 cycles}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4 — Compute abrasion resistance.**

$$
\begin{aligned}
R_{ab} &= \dfrac{1}{I_{v}} \\
&= \dfrac{1}{26.38} \\
&= 0.0379 \text{ cycles / mm³}
\end{aligned}
$$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Interpretation:** A wear index of 26.38 mm³/1000 cycles indicates **moderate abrasion resistance**, typical of a general-purpose natural-rubber vulcanisate. For comparison, premium tyre-tread compounds achieve **<15 mm³/1000 cycles**, while soft foams may exceed **200 mm³/1000 cycles**.

### Derivation 2 — Conversion Between Mass and Volume Wear Indices

This conversion is frequently asked in viva voce. We start with the fundamental definition of density:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\rho &= \dfrac{m}{V} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad V = \dfrac{m}{\rho}
\end{aligned}
$$

Applying this to wear quantities:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta V &= \dfrac{\Delta M}{\rho} \\[6pt]
\dfrac{\Delta V \times 1000}{N} &= \dfrac{\Delta M \times 1000}{N \times \rho} \\[6pt]
\therefore \quad I_{v} &= \dfrac{I_{m}}{\rho}
\end{aligned}
$$

This confirms the relation used in Step 3 of the worked example.

### Analytical Decision Matrix — Which Abrasive Wheel to Use?

| Wheel Type | Abrasive Character | Recommended Polymer Type | Typical Load |
|---|---|---|---|
| **CS-10** | Mild, resilient | Soft elastomers, coatings | 500 g |
| **CS-17** | Aggressive, sharp | Hard rubbers, rigid plastics | 1000 g |
| **H-18** | Very aggressive | Hard plastics, laminates | 1000 g |
| **H-22** | Moderately aggressive | General-purpose plastics | 500–1000 g |
| **CS-0 / S-32** | Very mild (silicone) | Saturated coatings, films | 500 g |

<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->
## 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics

### 4.1 Block-Level Functional Architecture of a Taber Abraser Test Rig

The following diagram maps the functional interaction between the mechanical, measurement, and data-reduction subsystems of the experiment.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Specimen Mounting Disc] --> B[Rotating Turntable 60 rpm]
    B --> C[Abrasive Wear Track Annular]
    D[Counterweight Arm Left] --> E[Left Abrasive Wheel CS-10 or CS-17]
    F[Counterweight Arm Right] --> G[Right Abrasive Wheel CS-10 or CS-17]
    E --> C
    G --> C
    H[Vacuum Suction Nozzle] --> C
    I[Drive Motor with Speed Governor] --> B
    J[Cycle Counter Digital] --> B
    K[Load Selection 500 g or 1000 g] --> D
    K --> F
    L[Electronic Balance 0.1 mg] --> M[Mass Loss Calculation]
    N[Specimen Density Measurement Archimedes] --> O[Volume Loss Calculation]
    M --> P[Taber Wear Index Computation]
    O --> P
    P --> Q[Report mg per 1000 cycles]
    P --> R[Report mm cubed per 1000 cycles]
```

### 4.2 Logical Workflow of the Abrasion Resistance Experiment

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    stepA[Step 1: Cut Circular Specimen 100 mm Diameter] --> stepB[Step 2: Condition Specimen 24 h at 23 deg C and 50 percent RH]
    stepB --> stepC[Step 3: Weigh Initial Mass W1 on Analytical Balance]
    stepC --> stepD[Step 4: Mount on Turntable Centre Hole 6 mm]
    stepD --> stepE[Step 5: Lower Abrasive Wheels Apply Calibrated Load]
    stepE --> stepF[Step 6: Set Cycle Counter to N 1000 or 3000]
    stepF --> stepG[Step 6: Start Motor Vacuum and Run N Cycles]
    stepG --> stepH[Step 7: Stop Remove Specimen Clean with Brush]
    stepH --> stepI[Step 8: Reweigh Final Mass W2]
    stepI --> stepJ[Step 9: Compute Mass Loss and Wear Index]
    stepJ --> stepK[Step 10: Compute Volume Loss Using Density]
    stepK --> stepL[Step 11: Report Taber Wear Index and Compare]
```

### 4.3 Functional Mapping — Influence of Material Variables on Output

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    node1[Polymer Base Matrix] --> node7[Abrasion Resistance Output]
    node2[Filler Type Carbon Black Silica] --> node7
    node3[Filler Loading phr] --> node7
    node4[Crosslink Density] --> node7
    node5[Surface Hardness Shore A] --> node7
    node6[Plasticizer Content] --> node7
    node8[Abrasive Wheel Grade] --> node7
    node9[Applied Load] --> node7
    node10[Test Speed rpm] --> node7
    node11[Ambient Temperature] --> node7
    node7 --> node12[Lower Wear Index]
    node7 --> node13[Higher Service Life]
```

### 4.4 Schematics — Wear Path Geometry (Taber Abraser)

Although the following is rendered as a topological block diagram due to Mermaid safeguards on geometric primitives, it conveys the geometric truth of the test:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    g1[Specimen Disc Radius R] --> g2[Centre of Rotation]
    g3[Left Wheel Contact Point at Radius r1] --> g4[Traces Inner Annular Track]
    g5[Right Wheel Contact Point at Radius r2] --> g6[Traces Outer Annular Track]
    g4 --> g7[Worn Region = Annular Ring Between r1 and r2]
    g6 --> g7
    g2 --> g8[Rotational Kinematics omega t]
```

The two wheels are offset on either side of the central rotation axis, ensuring the wear track is a **complete annular ring of uniform width** with no un-worn centre spot.

<!-- SECTION_4_END -->

<!-- SECTION_5_START -->
## 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

### Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

**Q1. [KTU University Exam – May 2024]** Define the term *abrasion resistance* of a polymer. Mention the standard test method commonly used to evaluate it.

**Model Answer:**
Abrasion resistance is the ability of a polymeric material to resist surface wear caused by mechanical rubbing, scraping, or frictional contact with an abrasive medium. It is quantified as the **reciprocal of material loss per unit operational cycle** and is typically reported as mass or volume loss per thousand revolutions.
The most widely accepted standard test is the **Taber Abraser test**, conducted in accordance with **ASTM D4060**, using a rotary platform with two loaded abrasive wheels (CS-10 or CS-17).

**Q2. [KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]** What is the *Taber Wear Index*? Write its formula.

**Model Answer:**
The Taber Wear Index is a normalised metric that expresses the abrasion-induced material loss of a specimen per 1000 revolutions of the test apparatus. It allows direct comparison between specimens tested for different cycle counts.

$$
I = \dfrac{(W_{1} - W_{2}) \times 1000}{N}
$$

where $W_1$ and $W_2$ are the initial and final masses (in mg), and $N$ is the number of cycles. A lower value indicates better abrasion resistance.

---

### Part B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks Each, Internal Choice)

#### Question A — (14 Marks) [KTU University Exam – July 2024]

**(a)** Explain with a neat block diagram the working principle of a **Taber Abraser** apparatus. List the standard abrasive wheels used and their typical applications. **(7 Marks)**

**(b)** A rubber specimen of initial mass **28.450 g** was subjected to abrasion testing on a Taber Abraser using **CS-17 wheels under 1000 g load** at 60 rpm. After **5000 cycles**, the final mass was found to be **28.295 g**. The density of the rubber is **1.18 g/cm³**. Calculate:
- (i) Mass loss per cycle
- (ii) Mass-basis Taber Wear Index
- (iii) Volume-basis Taber Wear Index
- (iv) Comment on the abrasion resistance of the specimen. **(7 Marks)**

**Model Solution (a):**

The Taber Abraser consists of a flat, motor-driven rotating turntable on which the specimen is mounted centrally. Two abrasive wheels, mounted on counter-weighted arms, are lowered onto the specimen surface with a calibrated normal load. As the turntable rotates, the wheels trace an annular wear path on the specimen surface. A vacuum suction nozzle positioned above the wear track continuously removes loose debris to prevent re-deposition. A digital cycle counter records the number of revolutions.

The standard abrasive wheels are:
- **CS-10** — mild, used for soft elastomers and coatings (load 500 g)
- **CS-17** — aggressive, used for hard rubbers and rigid plastics (load 1000 g)
- **H-18** — very aggressive, used for hard plastics and laminates
- **H-22** — moderately aggressive, used for general-purpose plastics

**Model Solution (b):**

Given data: $W_1 = 28.450$ g, $W_2 = 28.295$ g, $N = 5000$, $\rho = 1.18$ g/cm³.

**Step 1 — Total mass loss:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta M &= 28.450 - 28.295 = 0.155 \text{ g} = 155 \text{ mg}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2 — Mass loss per cycle:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
m_{\text{per cycle}} &= \dfrac{155 \text{ mg}}{5000} = 0.031 \text{ mg/cycle}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3 — Mass-basis Wear Index:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
I_{m} &= \dfrac{155 \times 1000}{5000} = 31.0 \text{ mg / 1000 cycles}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4 — Volume-basis Wear Index:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
I_{v} &= \dfrac{31.0}{1.18} = 26.27 \text{ mm³ / 1000 cycles}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 5 — Comment:**

A wear index of 26.27 mm³/1000 cycles indicates **moderate abrasion resistance**, typical of a general-purpose natural-rubber vulcanisate. Premium tyre-tread compounds would exhibit values below 15 mm³/1000 cycles.

---

#### Question B — (14 Marks) [KTU University Exam – July 2024, Alternative]

**(a)** Discuss the various **factors affecting the abrasion resistance of polymers**. How do fillers such as carbon black influence wear behaviour? **(7 Marks)**

**(b)** Describe the **ASTM D4060 test procedure** step-by-step. A PVC flooring tile specimen was tested and the following data were recorded:
- Initial mass = **42.850 g**, Final mass after **2000 cycles** = **42.780 g**
- Density = **1.38 g/cm³**
- Abrasive wheel: H-22, Load: 500 g

Calculate the **mass-basis and volume-basis wear indices** and determine the **percentage mass loss**. **(7 Marks)**

**Model Solution (a):**

The major factors are:
1. **Hardness** — Higher surface hardness generally improves resistance, though the correlation is non-linear in viscoelastic polymers.
2. **Cross-link density** — Higher cross-linking reduces fatigue wear.
3. **Filler type and content** — Reinforcing fillers like **carbon black, silica, and aluminium oxide** dramatically improve abrasion resistance by absorbing frictional energy and forming a tough surface layer. For tyre-tread rubber, **carbon black at 30–50 phr** is optimal.
4. **Polymer crystallinity and chain stiffness** — More rigid and crystalline polymers resist deformation better.
5. **Plasticizer content** — Excessive plasticizer softens the polymer and worsens wear.
6. **Test conditions** — Wheel grade, load, speed, and temperature.

Carbon black, in particular, forms nano-scale aggregates within the rubber matrix that physically obstruct crack propagation and abrasive cutting, while also dissipating frictional heat through its high thermal conductivity.

**Model Solution (b):**

**Step 1 — Mass loss:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta M &= 42.850 - 42.780 = 0.070 \text{ g} = 70 \text{ mg}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2 — Mass-basis Wear Index:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
I_{m} &= \dfrac{70 \times 1000}{2000} = 35.0 \text{ mg / 1000 cycles}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3 — Volume-basis Wear Index:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
I_{v} &= \dfrac{35.0}{1.38} = 25.36 \text{ mm³ / 1000 cycles}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4 — Percentage mass loss:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\% \Delta M &= \dfrac{0.070}{42.850} \times 100 = 0.1634\,\%
\end{aligned}
$$

**Interpretation:** The PVC tile shows moderate wear, suitable for **light commercial foot traffic**.

---

### KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Mistakes That Cost Marks:**
> 1. **Unit inconsistency** — Mixing grams with mg, or omitting the ×1000 factor in the Wear Index formula. Examiner deducts 1–2 marks if units are not explicitly written.
> 2. **Wrong density unit** — Using g/cm³ where mm³/mg conversion is required for volume loss. **Key fact: 1 g/cm³ = 1 mg/mm³.**
> 3. **Forgetting to convert final answers** to per-1000-cycles basis — examiners specifically look for the normalisation step.
> 4. **Confusing mass-basis and volume-basis indices** — Read the question carefully; both forms are valid but distinct.
> 5. **Skipping the "comment" / interpretation step** — Always conclude with a qualitative remark on whether the value indicates good, moderate, or poor abrasion resistance.
> 6. **Neglecting conditioning of specimen** — In viva voce, mentioning **23 °C / 50 % RH conditioning for 24 h** earns extra credit.

---

### Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

- **Definition:** Abrasion resistance is the ability of a polymer to resist surface wear by rubbing/frictional contact.
- **Standard Test:** Taber Abraser per **ASTM D4060**.
- **Key Wheels:** CS-10 (mild), CS-17 (aggressive for hard rubber), H-18 (very aggressive for plastics), H-22 (general-purpose).
- **Standard Loads:** **500 g** or **1000 g** per wheel.
- **Standard Speed:** **60 ± 5 rpm**.
- **Master Formulae:**
   - Mass-basis Wear Index: $I_{m} = \dfrac{(W_{1} - W_{2}) \times 1000}{N}$ in mg/1000 cycles
   - Volume-basis Wear Index: $I_{v} = \dfrac{I_{m}}{\rho}$ in mm³/1000 cycles
   - Abrasion resistance: $R_{ab} = 1 / I_v$
- **Lower Wear Index = Better Resistance.**
- **Key Influencing Factors:** hardness, cross-link density, fillers (especially **carbon black at 30–50 phr**), crystallinity, plasticizer content, and test conditions.
- **Engineering Applications:** Tyre treads, flooring tiles, conveyor belts, shoe soles, protective coatings.
- **Lab Procedure:** Cut → Condition → Weigh W₁ → Mount → Run N cycles → Clean → Weigh W₂ → Compute indices → Report.
- **Volume-mass equivalence:** $1$ g/cm³ $= 1$ mg/mm³ (memorise for unit conversions).
- **Wear mechanisms to mention in viva:** micro-ploughing, micro-cutting, micro-fatigue.

<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->

> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PCPOL607 - PCPOL607
> - **Module:** Module Experiment 2
> - **Topic:** air permeability

# AIR PERMEABILITY – POLYMER FILM TESTING

## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### 1.1 Formal Academic Definition (KTU Syllabus Terminology)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Air Permeability** is defined as the volume of air (measured at standard temperature and pressure) that passes through a unit area of a plastic film, sheet, or coated fabric per unit time under a specified pressure differential across the specimen.

In polymer technology, air permeability is a critical functional property that quantifies the **ease with which air (a gas) penetrates through a polymeric membrane or film**. For KTU laboratory experiments (PCPOL607 – Polymer Testing / Materials), the property is most commonly determined on **plastic films, laminated sheets, and coated fabrics** in accordance with:

- **ASTM D1434** – Standard Test Methods for Determining Gas Permeability Characteristics of Plastic Film and Sheeting
- **ISO 2556** – Plastics – Determination of the Gas Transmission Rate of Films and Thin Sheets under Atmospheric Pressure
- **ISO 5636 series** – Paper and board (Bendtsen, Gurley, Bekk, Sheffield methods)

The formal expression of air permeability in SI units is:

$$
AP \;=\; \dfrac{V \, d}{A \, t \, \Delta P}
$$

where the output has the unit $\text{m}^3 \cdot \text{m} \,/\, (\text{m}^2 \cdot \text{s} \cdot \text{Pa})$, often quoted practically as **cm³·cm/(cm²·s·cmHg)** or **cm³/(m²·day·atm)** for packaging films.

### 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Real-World Intuition

> [!NOTE]
> Think of a polymer film like the **wall of a balloon**. A tightly woven balloon (e.g., metalized polyester) lets almost no air seep through. A loose, thin rubber balloon, however, deflates overnight because the air slowly escapes through the rubber. That "escaping rate" is air permeability.

To extend the analogy:

- **Plastic carry-bag at a bakery** → High permeability (loose LDPE) → air and odour pass through quickly.
- **Vacuum-sealed coffee pack** → Very low permeability (aluminised PET/PP laminate) → keeps coffee aroma inside.
- **Tyre inner liner (butyl rubber)** → Extremely low permeability → keeps air inside for years.
- **Gore-Tex raincoat** → Engineered high (yet selective) permeability → water out, vapour out, but body stays dry.

Engineers **select polymers for specific permeability values** depending on whether they want a film to *breathe* (medical textiles, fresh produce packaging) or to *seal* (vacuum packs, fuel tanks, pharmaceutical blisters).

### 1.3 Key Physical Constants & Standard Metrics (in Bold)

- **Standard Temperature = 23 °C (296.15 K)**
- **Standard Pressure = 1 atm = 101.325 kPa = 760 mmHg**
- **Molar Volume of an ideal gas at STP = 22.414 L/mol = 22 414 cm³/mol**
- **Universal Gas Constant R = 8.314 J/(mol·K)**

> [!TIP]
> **KTU Board Valuation Hint:** Always convert experimental volumes to **STP conditions** using the ideal gas law before substituting into the permeability formula. Examiners award a dedicated mark specifically for the STP conversion step.

---

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->

## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### 2.1 Mechanism of Gas Transport Through Polymers

Polymer films are *not* truly porous in the macroscopic sense — gas molecules migrate by an **activated molecular process** that follows the **Solution–Diffusion Mechanism** (the academically dominant model).

The transport occurs in three sequential stages:

1. **Sorption (Dissolution) at High-Pressure Face**
   - Gas molecules strike the upstream surface and dissolve into the polymer matrix.
   - Quantified by **Henry's Law of Sorption**: $C = S \, p$, where $S$ is the solubility coefficient.

2. **Diffusion Across the Polymer Bulk**
   - Dissolved gas molecules hop between transient free-volume voids created by thermal motion of polymer segments.
   - Quantified by **Fick's First Law**: $J = -D \, \dfrac{dC}{dx}$, where $D$ is the diffusion coefficient.

3. **Desorption (Evaporation) at Low-Pressure Face**
   - Molecules escape from the downstream surface and are swept away by the carrier stream.
   - Surface concentration is governed by equilibrium partial pressure.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Steady-state transport (when $dC/dt = 0$) gives the famous **Permeability Equation**:
>
> $$P \;=\; D \cdot S$$
>
> This is the **triple-product relationship** — the *corner-stone equation* of polymer permeability, and a guaranteed KTU high-yield formula.

### 2.2 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

> [!NOTE]
> The following table is the **exam-ready cheat sheet** for Module Experiment 2. Memorise every row.

| # | Quantity / Concept | Governing Equation | Symbol Meaning | SI Unit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Air Permeability (volumetric form) | $AP = \dfrac{V \, d}{A \, t \, \Delta P}$ | V = air volume; d = film thickness; A = film area; t = time; ΔP = pressure drop | $\dfrac{\text{m}^3\!\cdot\!\text{m}}{\text{m}^2\!\cdot\!\text{s}\!\cdot\!\text{Pa}}$ |
| 2 | Gas Transmission Rate (GTR) | $GTR = \dfrac{V}{A \, t \, \Delta P}$ | Volume per area per time per pressure | $\dfrac{\text{cm}^3}{\text{m}^2\!\cdot\!\text{day}\!\cdot\!\text{atm}}$ |
| 3 | Permeability Coefficient | $P = D \cdot S$ | D = diffusion coeff.; S = solubility coeff. | $\dfrac{\text{cm}^3\!\cdot\!\text{cm}}{\text{cm}^2\!\cdot\!\text{s}\!\cdot\!\text{Pa}}$ |
| 4 | Fick's First Law (steady state) | $J = -D \, \dfrac{\Delta C}{\Delta x} = D \, \dfrac{C_1 - C_2}{d}$ | J = flux; C₁, C₂ = surface concentrations | $\dfrac{\text{mol}}{\text{m}^2\!\cdot\!\text{s}}$ |
| 5 | Henry's Sorption Law | $C = S \, p$ | C = dissolved concentration; p = partial pressure | $\dfrac{\text{mol}}{\text{m}^3} \;/\; \text{Pa}$ |
| 6 | Ideal Gas Law (STP correction) | $V_0 = V \, \dfrac{P}{P_0} \, \dfrac{T_0}{T}$ | V₀ = volume at STP | $\text{m}^3$ |
| 7 | Pressure Method (ASTM D1434, A) | $GTR = \dfrac{d}{A \, \Delta P} \cdot \dfrac{\Delta V}{\Delta t}$ | ΔV/Δt = rate of pressure-rise volume | as above |
| 8 | Arrhenius Temperature Relation | $P = P_0 \, e^{-E_p / RT}$ | Eₚ = activation energy of permeation | dimensionless ratio |
| 9 | Free-Volume Theory | $\ln(D) \propto -\dfrac{B}{f}$ | B = constant; f = fractional free volume | — |
| 10 | Time-Lag Method | $D = \dfrac{d^2}{6 \, \theta}$ | θ = time-lag (intercept of steady-state line on t-axis) | $\text{cm}^2/\text{s}$ |

### 2.3 Real-World Engineering Utility

- **Food Packaging**: Engineers select EVOH, PVDC, or metalised PET to *minimise* air (O₂) permeability and extend shelf life.
- **Medical Devices**: Blood-storage bags use PVC/DEHP for tuned gas transport; oxygenator membranes use PDMS (silicone) for high O₂ permeability.
- **Automotive Tyres**: Halogenated butyl rubber inner liners minimise air loss → better fuel economy and safety.
- **Building & Construction**: Tyvek-type breathable membranes allow water vapour out but block liquid water — permeability-controlled design.
- **Pharmaceutical Blister Packs**: Aluminium/PVC laminates with extremely low permeability protect drug stability.

> [!TIP]
> A KTU board favourite question is *"Why is the inner liner of a tyre made of halogenated butyl rubber rather than natural rubber?"* — the answer directly invokes the triple-product $P = D \cdot S$ and the dense molecular packing of halobutyl.

---

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->

## 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

### 3.1 Derivation of the Steady-State Permeability Equation

**Starting point:** Fick's First Law applied across a polymer film of thickness $d$, with constant surface concentrations $C_1$ (upstream) and $C_2$ (downstream):

$$
J \;=\; -D \, \frac{dC}{dx}
$$

**Step 1 — Set up the one-dimensional concentration gradient.**
In steady state, the flux $J$ is uniform throughout the thickness. Integrating across the film from $x = 0$ (upstream) to $x = d$ (downstream):

$$
J \int_{0}^{d} dx \;=\; -D \int_{C_1}^{C_2} dC
$$

**Step 2 — Evaluate the definite integrals.**

$$
J \cdot d \;=\; -D \bigl[C_2 - C_1\bigr] \;=\; D \bigl(C_1 - C_2\bigr)
$$

**Step 3 — Apply Henry's Law to express concentrations as pressures.**
From $C = S \, p$:

$$
C_1 = S \, p_1 \quad \text{and} \quad C_2 = S \, p_2
$$

Substituting:

$$
J \cdot d \;=\; D \, S \, \bigl(p_1 - p_2\bigr) \;=\; D \, S \, \Delta p
$$

**Step 4 — Solve for the flux $J$.**

$$
J \;=\; \frac{D \, S \, \Delta p}{d}
$$

**Step 5 — Introduce the permeability coefficient.**
By definition, the permeability coefficient $P$ (per unit area per unit pressure) is:

$$
P \;\equiv\; D \cdot S
$$

**Step 6 — Final compact expression.**

$$
\boxed{\;J \;=\; \frac{P \, \Delta p}{d}\;}
$$

This is the **fundamental permeation equation** quoted in every polymer-textbook and KTU exam.

### 3.2 Worked Example — Time-Lag Derivation

The transient (non-steady-state) solution of Fick's Second Law, with boundary conditions $C(x,0)=0$, $C(0,t)=C_1$, and $C(d,t)=C_2$, yields the cumulative permeation $Q_t$:

$$
Q_t \;=\; \frac{D \, C_1}{d} \left(t - \frac{d^2}{6 D}\right) - \frac{2 C_1 d}{\pi^2} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^n}{n^2} \exp\!\left(-\frac{D n^2 \pi^2 t}{d^2}\right)
$$

**Step 7 — Take the long-time limit** ($t \rightarrow \infty$). The exponential series vanishes, leaving the straight-line asymptote:

$$
Q_t \;\approx\; \frac{D \, C_1}{d} \, t \;-\; \frac{d \, C_1}{6}
$$

**Step 8 — Extrapolate this asymptote back to the time-axis** ($Q_t = 0$):

$$
0 \;=\; \frac{D \, C_1}{d} \, \theta \;-\; \frac{d \, C_1}{6}
$$

**Step 9 — Solve for the time-lag $\theta$.**

$$
\boxed{\;\theta \;=\; \frac{d^2}{6 D}\;}
$$

**Step 10 — Rearrange for diffusion coefficient.** This is the **Barrer's time-lag method** — a direct experimental route to $D$:

$$
D \;=\; \frac{d^2}{6 \, \theta}
$$

### 3.3 Fully Worked Numerical Problem (KTU Board Pattern)

> **Problem.** A plastic film of thickness **0.025 cm** and exposed area **100 cm²** is mounted in an ASTM D1434 volumetric apparatus. A volume of **50 cm³** of air passes through in **24 hours** under a pressure differential of **1 atm**. Calculate:
> (a) The gas transmission rate (GTR)
> (b) The air permeability coefficient
> Take the laboratory temperature as 23 °C and 1 atm.

**Solution:**

**Part (a) — Gas Transmission Rate.**

$$
GTR \;=\; \frac{V}{A \, t \, \Delta P}
$$

Substitute values (convert 24 h to seconds):

$$
t = 24 \times 3600 = 86\,400 \; \text{s}
$$

$$
GTR \;=\; \frac{50 \; \text{cm}^3}{100 \; \text{cm}^2 \times 86\,400 \; \text{s} \times 1 \; \text{atm}}
$$

$$
GTR \;=\; \frac{50}{8.64 \times 10^{6}} \;\approx\; 5.787 \times 10^{-6} \;\dfrac{\text{cm}^3}{\text{cm}^2 \cdot \text{s} \cdot \text{atm}}
$$

Converting to the more common packaging unit:

$$
\boxed{\;GTR \;\approx\; 5.0 \;\dfrac{\text{cm}^3}{\text{m}^2 \cdot \text{day} \cdot \text{atm}}\;}
$$

**Part (b) — Permeability Coefficient.**

$$
P \;=\; GTR \times d
$$

$$
P \;=\; 5.787 \times 10^{-6} \;\dfrac{\text{cm}^3}{\text{cm}^2 \cdot \text{s} \cdot \text{atm}} \times 0.025 \; \text{cm}
$$

$$
P \;\approx\; 1.447 \times 10^{-7} \;\dfrac{\text{cm}^3 \cdot \text{cm}}{\text{cm}^2 \cdot \text{s} \cdot \text{atm}}
$$

$$
\boxed{\;P \;\approx\; 1.45 \times 10^{-7} \;\dfrac{\text{cm}^3 \cdot \text{cm}}{\text{cm}^2 \cdot \text{s} \cdot \text{atm}}\;}
$$

---

<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->

## 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics

### 4.1 Mermaid Flowchart — Experimental Procedure (ASTM D1434 Method A)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Start: Cut specimen 100 cm² area] --> B[Measure film thickness d with micrometer]
    B --> C[Condition specimen at 23 °C, 50 percent RH for 24 h]
    C --> D[Mount specimen in test cell with rubber gaskets]
    D --> E[Apply pressure differential Delta P on upstream face]
    E --> F[Open downstream valve and start stopwatch]
    F --> G[Record cumulative volume V vs time t]
    G --> H{Steady state reached?}
    H -- No --> G
    H -- Yes --> I[Compute GTR = V divided by A times t times Delta P]
    I --> J[Compute Permeability P = GTR times d]
    J --> K[If required compute D from time lag theta]
    K --> L[Report P with units at STP]
```

### 4.2 Mermaid Block Diagram — Solution-Diffusion Mechanism

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Upstream High p1 Side] --> B[Sorption at surface C1 = S times p1]
    B --> C[Diffusion through polymer Ficks Law J = minus D dC over dx]
    C --> D[Desorption at downstream C2 = S times p2]
    D --> E[Low p2 Side downstream carrier]
    C --> F[D times S = Permeability Coefficient P]
```

### 4.3 Mermaid Apparatus Schematic — Volumetric Permeation Cell

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Compressed Air Cylinder with Regulator] --> B[Pressure Stabiliser and Manometer]
    B --> C[Test Cell Upstream Chamber]
    C --> D[Polymer Film Specimen held between O rings]
    D --> E[Test Cell Downstream Chamber]
    E --> F[Capillary Flow Meter or Volumetric Burette]
    F --> G[Data Logger for V versus t]
```

### 4.4 Mermaid Concept Map — Factors Affecting Air Permeability

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    P[Air Permeability P] --> F1[Polymer Structure]
    P --> F2[Test Temperature]
    P --> F3[Pressure Differential]
    P --> F4[Film Thickness]
    P --> F5[Humidity and Plasticiser Content]
    P --> F6[Crystallinity and Free Volume]
    F1 --> S1[Crystalline regions block gas path]
    F6 --> S2[High free volume raises D and so P]
    F2 --> S3[Arrhenius: P rises with T]
    F4 --> S4[P independent of d but GTR falls with d]
```

---

<!-- SECTION_4_END -->

<!-- SECTION_5_START -->

## 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

### 5.1 Part A — Short-Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

**Q1. [KTU University Exam – May 2024]** Define air permeability of a polymer film. State its SI units and the standard test method adopted by ASTM.

**Model Answer:**
Air permeability is the volumetric flow rate of air, measured at STP, passing through a unit area of a polymer film per unit time under a specified pressure differential. SI units are $\dfrac{\text{m}^3 \cdot \text{m}}{\text{m}^2 \cdot \text{s} \cdot \text{Pa}}$. The standard test is **ASTM D1434** (with Method A – pressure rise, and Method B – volumetric), supplemented by **ISO 2556** for thin plastic films.

**Q2. [KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]** State the triple-product relationship that defines the permeability coefficient of a gas through a polymer. Explain each term.

**Model Answer:**

$$
P \;=\; D \times S
$$

- **P** = Permeability Coefficient — combines diffusion and solubility into a single transport coefficient.
- **D** = Diffusion Coefficient (cm²/s) — quantifies the mobility of gas molecules in the polymer matrix.
- **S** = Solubility Coefficient (cm³ gas / cm³ polymer · atm) — quantifies the polymer's capacity to dissolve the gas.

### 5.2 Part B — Essay / Numerical (14 Marks, with Internal Choice)

---

#### **Question A (14 Marks)** — *[KTU University Exam – May 2024, Modified]*

**(a) [7 Marks]** With the aid of a labelled schematic, describe the **ASTM D1434 Method A (pressure-rise technique)** for determining the air permeability of a plastic film. Mention the formula used, the units, and the role of time-lag.

**Model Solution:**

1. **Apparatus:** A circular test cell of known area (typically 50 cm²) is divided into upstream and downstream chambers by the polymer specimen. The upstream side is pressurised from a regulated air cylinder; the downstream side is connected to a closed capillary manometer/pressure transducer.
2. **Specimen Preparation:** Film is cut to size, thickness measured at five points with a micrometer (mean value taken), conditioned at 23 °C and 50 % RH for 24 h.
3. **Test Procedure:** A known pressure differential $\Delta P$ (commonly 1 atm or as specified) is applied. The pressure rise in the closed downstream volume $V_d$ is recorded as a function of time.
4. **Computation:**

$$
GTR \;=\; \frac{V_d}{A \, R \, T \, \Delta P} \cdot \frac{dp}{dt}
$$

where $dp/dt$ is the steady rate of pressure rise.

5. **Permeability Coefficient:** $P = GTR \times d$.
6. **Time-Lag:** Extrapolation of the steady-state linear portion of the $Q_t$ vs $t$ curve to the time axis yields the time-lag $\theta$, from which:

$$
D \;=\; \frac{d^2}{6 \, \theta}
$$

A schematic must be drawn (refer Section 4.3 above).

**(b) [7 Marks]** A low-density polyethylene (LDPE) film of **thickness 50 µm** and **area 25 cm²** is subjected to a pressure differential of **1.013 bar** at 25 °C. The volumetric flow rate measured downstream is **0.020 cm³/min**. Calculate:
  (i) The Gas Transmission Rate (GTR) in $\dfrac{\text{cm}^3}{\text{m}^2 \cdot \text{day} \cdot \text{atm}}$
  (ii) The permeability coefficient $P$

**Model Solution:**

**Step 1 — Convert units.**
- Thickness: $d = 50 \, \mu\text{m} = 50 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{cm} = 5 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{cm}$
- Area: $A = 25 \, \text{cm}^2 = 25 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{m}^2 = 2.5 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{m}^2$
- Pressure: $\Delta P = 1.013 \, \text{bar} \approx 1 \, \text{atm}$ (acceptable at KTU level)

**Step 2 — Compute volume per unit time.**

$$
V / t \;=\; 0.020 \, \text{cm}^3 / \text{min} \;=\; 0.020 \times 60 \times 24 \; \text{cm}^3/\text{day} \;=\; 28.8 \, \text{cm}^3/\text{day}
$$

**Step 3 — (i) Gas Transmission Rate.**

$$
GTR \;=\; \frac{V/t}{A \, \Delta P}
$$

$$
GTR \;=\; \frac{28.8 \; \text{cm}^3/\text{day}}{2.5 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{m}^2 \times 1 \, \text{atm}}
$$

$$
\boxed{\;GTR \;\approx\; 11\,520 \; \frac{\text{cm}^3}{\text{m}^2 \cdot \text{day} \cdot \text{atm}}\;}
$$

**Step 4 — (ii) Permeability Coefficient.**

$$
P \;=\; GTR \times d
$$

Convert $GTR$ to CGS:

$$
GTR_{CGS} \;=\; 11\,520 \;\frac{\text{cm}^3}{\text{m}^2 \cdot \text{day} \cdot \text{atm}} \times \frac{1 \, \text{m}^2}{10^4 \, \text{cm}^2} \times \frac{1 \, \text{day}}{86\,400 \, \text{s}}
$$

$$
GTR_{CGS} \;\approx\; 1.333 \times 10^{-5} \; \frac{\text{cm}^3}{\text{cm}^2 \cdot \text{s} \cdot \text{atm}}
$$

$$
P \;=\; 1.333 \times 10^{-5} \times 5 \times 10^{-3}
$$

$$
\boxed{\;P \;\approx\; 6.67 \times 10^{-8} \; \frac{\text{cm}^3 \cdot \text{cm}}{\text{cm}^2 \cdot \text{s} \cdot \text{atm}}\;}
$$

---

#### **Question B (14 Marks)** — *[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023, Modified]* (Internal Alternative)

**(a) [7 Marks]** Explain the **solution-diffusion mechanism** of gas transport through a polymer film, deriving the steady-state permeability equation.

**Model Solution:**

1. **Three stages:** (i) Sorption of gas at the high-pressure face governed by Henry's law $C = Sp$. (ii) Activated diffusion of dissolved molecules through the polymer matrix governed by Fick's law $J = -D(dC/dx)$. (iii) Desorption at the low-pressure face.

2. **Boundary conditions:** $C(0) = C_1 = S p_1$ and $C(d) = C_2 = S p_2$.

3. **Integration of Fick's Law** in steady state yields the linear concentration profile across the film.

4. **Final expression:**

$$
J \;=\; \frac{D \, S \, \Delta p}{d} \;=\; \frac{P \, \Delta p}{d}
$$

with $P = D \cdot S$.

5. **Discussion:** Diffusion coefficient $D$ depends on free-volume fraction; solubility coefficient $S$ depends on polymer–gas interaction (e.g., polar CO₂ dissolves more in polar polymers). The triple product explains why halogenation of butyl rubber dramatically lowers permeability: tight packing reduces both $D$ and $S$.

**(b) [7 Marks]** Discuss the **factors affecting air permeability** of polymeric films, giving at least six factors with engineering examples.

**Model Solution (tabular form, each factor worth 1 mark + 1 explanation):**

| Factor | Effect on Permeability | Engineering Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Crystallinity | Higher crystallinity → **lower** $P$ (crystalline regions impermeable) | HDPE vs LDPE — HDPE has ~70 % crystallinity, much lower permeability |
| 2. Free Volume | Higher free volume → higher $D$ → higher $P$ | PDMS silicone has high free volume → very high gas permeability |
| 3. Temperature | $P = P_0 \exp(-E_p / RT)$, so $P$ **increases** with $T$ | Tyre pressure rises when car is driven on hot roads |
| 4. Film Thickness | $GTR$ decreases with thickness; $P$ is intrinsic and independent | Multi-layer packaging uses thicker barrier layers |
| 5. Plasticisers & Humidity | Plasticisers swell polymer → increase free volume → raise $P$ | PVC films without plasticiser have lower permeability |
| 6. Pressure Differential | Within Henry's-law regime, $J \propto \Delta P$ linearly | Vacuum packaging at high $\Delta P$ needs robust seals |
| 7. Crosslink Density | Higher crosslinking → lower free volume → lower $P$ | Vulcanised butyl rubber for inner tubes |

### 5.3 KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Mark-Loss Pitfalls in Air-Permeability Problems**
> 1. **Forgetting to convert time to seconds** when using SI units — costs 1 full mark.
> 2. **Confusing GTR with Permeability Coefficient** — GTR includes $\Delta P$ in the denominator, $P$ does *not*. Examiners specifically look for the $d$ multiplication.
> 3. **Not converting volume to STP** when the experiment is run at non-standard temperature. Always apply the ideal gas law correction.
> 4. **Mixing up $D$, $S$ and $P$** in derivations — remember $P = D \cdot S$ is the **triple product**, not a sum.
> 5. **Skipping the diagram label** for ASTM D1434 — examiners award 1–2 marks for a *correctly labelled schematic* alone.
> 6. **Writing "permeability increases with thickness"** — this is *wrong* for $P$ (intrinsic) but *correct* for *total volume passed*. State which quantity you mean.

### 5.4 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember (Rapid-Revision Checklist)

- **Definition:** Air permeability = volumetric flow of air per unit area per unit time per unit pressure drop across a polymer film.
- **Key Equation (memorise verbatim):** $P = D \cdot S$, and $J = \dfrac{P \cdot \Delta p}{d}$.
- **Standard Methods:** ASTM D1434 (A – pressure, B – volumetric), ISO 2556.
- **Mechanism:** Solution–Diffusion (Sorption → Diffusion → Desorption).
- **Time-Lag Equation:** $\theta = \dfrac{d^2}{6D}$ (Barrer's method) — experimentally determines $D$.
- **Arrhenius Behaviour:** $P$ rises exponentially with temperature.
- **Units to remember:**
  - $P$: $\dfrac{\text{cm}^3 \cdot \text{cm}}{\text{cm}^2 \cdot \text{s} \cdot \text{atm}}$ (CGS) or $\dfrac{\text{mol} \cdot \text{m}}{\text{m}^2 \cdot \text{s} \cdot \text{Pa}}$ (SI).
  - $GTR$: $\dfrac{\text{cm}^3}{\text{m}^2 \cdot \text{day} \cdot \text{atm}}$ — common in packaging industry.
- **Six Influencing Factors:** crystallinity, free volume, temperature, thickness, plasticiser content, pressure differential.
- **Engineering Realisations:**
  - High permeability → breathable films (Gore-Tex, fresh produce packaging, medical membranes).
  - Low permeability → barrier films (aluminised PET, EVOH, halogenated butyl rubber tyre liners).
- **Exam Pitfalls:** unit conversion, STP correction, schematic labelling, distinguishing GTR vs $P$.

> [!TIP]
> **Final KTU Mnemonic — "S-D-D-S-P":**
> **S**orption → **D**iffusion → **D**esorption → **S**teady-state → **P**ermeability.
> Walk through these five stages verbally in any 14-mark answer to lock in full marks.

<!-- SECTION_5_END -->
