> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PCPOL607 - PCPOL607
> - **Module:** Module Experiment 2
> - **Topic:** bursting strength

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
# SECTION 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition

> [!NOTE]
> **Bursting Strength** is defined as the maximum hydrostatic pressure (expressed in **kg/cm²**, **kPa**, or **psi**) that a material — typically a polymer film, sheet, laminate, paperboard, or a thin-walled pipe — can withstand without rupturing, when pressure is uniformly applied perpendicular to its plane through a circular elastic diaphragm (typically of rubber) under standardized conditions of temperature, humidity, and rate of pressure application.

In the context of **PCPOL607 (Polymer Testing / Polymer Characterization Laboratory)**, bursting strength is a **destructive, multi-axial tensile property** rather than a uniaxial property. It reflects the combined resistance of a material to tensile, shear, and compressive stresses simultaneously — which is why it correlates far better than tensile strength with the real-world performance of films, pouches, pipes, and laminates.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Scheme Classification:** Bursting strength is grouped under *Mechanical Performance Testing of Polymeric Films, Sheets, and Pipes* (Module Experiment 2). It is treated as a **service-property test** because it simulates end-use loading conditions such as internal fluid pressure in pipes, pneumatic packaging stress, and vacuum-formed product deformation.

### Governing Standards (KTU-Recognized)

| Standard | Full Title | Material Class |
|----------|------------|----------------|
| **IS 1060 (Part III)** | Method of Sampling and Test for Paper — Bursting Strength | Paper, paperboard |
| **ASTM D3786** | Hydraulic Bursting Strength of Textile Fabrics | Coated/uncoated fabrics |
| **ASTM D1599** | Short-Time Hydraulic Failure Pressure of Plastic Pipe | Thermoplastic pipes |
| **ISO 2758** | Paper — Determination of Bursting Strength | Paper |
| **ISO 13954** | Plastics — Determination of Burst Strength | Plastic films/sheets |

---

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Plain-English Intuition

Imagine you are blowing up a **balloon** and pinching the opening. The pressure inside pushes outward in **every direction** simultaneously on a curved surface. Bursting strength is exactly that — except the material is **flat (a film, a sheet, or a thin pipe wall)** and the pressure is applied from one side through a **rubber diaphragm** that pushes it into a hemispherical bulge.

> [!TIP]
> **Real-World Analogy:** Think of a **paper airplane's nose**, a **shampoo sachet**, a **tetra-pak milk carton**, and a **PVC water pipe** — all of these are routinely "burst-tested" in industry. If you push water into a sealed plastic bag with a syringe, the **moment the bag splits open** is the burst event. The pressure recorded at that instant is the bursting strength of that bag.

### Key Physical Insight

- The diaphragm pushes the sample into a **dome** of controlled geometry.
- The sample undergoes **biaxial stretching** (strain in two directions at once).
- Failure is initiated at the **weakest point** of the sample — typically a defect, thinning, or a region of low molecular orientation.
- Because failure is governed by the **weakest flaw**, bursting strength has a strong **statistical** flavor — multiple specimens must be tested.

> [!NOTE]
> **Why not just use tensile strength?** Because in real life, a plastic pouch, a pipe, or a laminate is **never** loaded in one direction. It bulges, expands, and stretches radially. Uniaxial tensile data **under-predicts** this behaviour, while bursting strength reproduces it faithfully.
<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# SECTION 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 Theoretical Foundation — The Mechanics of Burst

When a flat, clamped polymer film of radius $R_c$ is pressed by a fluid of pressure $P$ through an elastic diaphragm, the film deforms into a near-spherical cap. At any point in the dome, two principal stresses develop on the membrane:

1. **Meridional (radial) stress** $\sigma_m$ — along the meridian of the dome.
2. **Circumferential (hoop) stress** $\sigma_c$ — along the latitude circle.

For a thin spherical cap of radius of curvature $\rho$ and wall thickness $t$:

$$\sigma_m = \sigma_c = \frac{P \cdot \rho}{2t}$$

This is the **classical thin-membrane (or thin-shell) equation**, valid when $t \ll \rho$.

### Why This Matters for Polymers

In a biaxially-stretched, semi-crystalline polymer film (e.g., **BOPP, PET, LDPE, HDPE**), the molecular chains in the dome are being pulled in **two directions at once**. This is much closer to actual end-use loading than a dog-bone tensile test, and it is why **bursting strength is a far more reliable predictor of packaging performance** than uniaxial tensile strength.

---

## 2.2 Step-by-Step Operating Principle of the Bursting-Strength Tester (Mullen-Type)

The instrument (commonly a **Mullen-type bursting strength tester**, also called a *hydraulic diaphragm burst tester*) operates as follows:

1. **Clamping:** The polymer film / paper specimen (circular, ~70 mm dia) is clamped between two circular rings of standard test area (e.g., **30.5 mm = 1.2 inch** as per ASTM D3786, or **25.4 mm** as per IS 1060).
2. **Diaphragm Selection:** A rubber (elastomer) diaphragm of **Shore A hardness 50 ± 5** is placed beneath the specimen. The diaphragm is the medium that transmits fluid pressure to the sample.
3. **Fluid (Glycerin ~98% or Ethylene Glycol):** A low-compressibility hydraulic fluid fills the chamber below the diaphragm. Glycerine is preferred because it does not swell or degrade most polymer films and has a stable viscosity at test temperature.
4. **Pressure Ramp:** A piston pump drives the fluid, raising pressure at a controlled rate of **95 ± 5 mL/min** (volume flow) until the specimen ruptures.
5. **Pressure Reading:** A **Bourdon-tube pressure gauge** or **digital pressure transducer** records the peak pressure at the moment of rupture.
6. **Repeat:** At least **5 specimens** (typically 10 in IS 1060) are tested; the mean and standard deviation are reported.

---

## 2.3 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

| # | Quantity / Relation | Formula | Units | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Mullen Bursting Strength (MBS)** | $\text{MBS} = P_b$ | kg/cm² or kPa | Direct readout from gauge |
| 2 | Burst index (specific MBS) | $\text{Burst Index} = \dfrac{P_b}{W}$ | $\dfrac{\text{kPa}\cdot\text{m}^2}{\text{g}}$ | $W$ = grammage (g/m²) |
| 3 | Membrane stress at burst | $\sigma_b = \dfrac{P_b \cdot \rho_b}{2 t}$ | Pa (or N/m²) | Thin-shell equation |
| 4 | Burst strain (approx.) | $\varepsilon_b \approx \dfrac{\rho_b - R_c}{R_c}$ | dimensionless | Geometric estimate |
| 5 | Hydrostatic pipe burst stress (Hoop) | $\sigma_h = \dfrac{P_b \cdot D}{2 t}$ | Pa | Barlow's equation, for thin-walled pipe |
| 6 | Hydrostatic pipe burst stress (Long.) | $\sigma_L = \dfrac{P_b \cdot D}{4 t}$ | Pa | For closed-end pipe |
| 7 | Pressure unit conversion | $1 \text{ kg/cm}^2 = 98.0665 \text{ kPa}$ | — | Frequently tested |
| 8 | Test area (IS 1060) | $A = \pi R_c^2 = 5.067 \text{ cm}^2$ | cm² | For $R_c = 12.7$ mm |
| 9 | Test area (ASTM D3786) | $A = 7.30 \text{ cm}^2$ | cm² | For 1.2" clamp |
| 10 | Hoop-to-long. stress ratio | $\dfrac{\sigma_h}{\sigma_L} = 2$ | — | Cylinder under internal pressure |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Board Examiner's Insight:** Most students **confuse** bursting strength with tensile strength. The examiner *will* ask you to justify **why** bursting strength is a multi-axial property. If you simply write "bursting strength = P/A" without invoking the thin-shell equation or biaxial stress state, **expect 1 mark to be deducted**.

---

## 2.4 Real-World Engineering Utility

- **Packaging Industry:** Selecting films for pouches, vacuum bags, and aseptic cartons.
- **Pipe & Tubing:** Quality-control of **PVC, HDPE, PEX, PP-R** pressure pipes.
- **Geotextiles & Membranes:** Roofing sheets, geomembranes for landfills.
- **Paper & Board Industry:** Corrugated boxes, kraft paper — predicts carton stacking survival.
- **Textile-Laminate Composites:** Coated fabrics for airbags, rainwear, conveyor belts.
- **Automotive Tyres & Inner Liners:** A tyre inner liner is burst-tested in a pressure-ramp-to-failure mode very similar to a film burst test.
<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# SECTION 3: Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Derivation 1 — Membrane (Thin-Shell) Stress in a Spherical Burst Dome

### Starting Point
Consider a thin, flat polymer disc of thickness $t$ and clamped radius $R_c$ deformed by an internal pressure $P$ into a shallow spherical cap of radius of curvature $\rho$. Apply the principle of static equilibrium to a hemispherical cap of the dome.

### Step 1: Define a free body — upper hemisphere of the dome
Cut the dome along its equator (great circle). The fluid below exerts an upward force equal to pressure times projected area:

$$F_{\text{up}} = P \cdot \pi \rho^2$$

### Step 2: The dome's rim is held in equilibrium by the membrane (wall) tension $T$ (force per unit length)
The total downward pull from the wall acting along the great circle of length $2\pi\rho$ is:

$$F_{\text{down}} = 2 \pi \rho \cdot T$$

### Step 3: Equate the two forces (static equilibrium)

$$2 \pi \rho \cdot T = P \cdot \pi \rho^2$$

### Step 4: Solve for the wall tension per unit length

$$T = \frac{P \rho}{2}$$

### Step 5: Convert wall tension to engineering (membrane) stress
Wall tension is force per unit length. For a wall of thickness $t$, the true stress is:

$$\sigma = \frac{T}{t} = \frac{P \rho}{2 t}$$

### Step 6: Final compact form

$$\boxed{\sigma = \frac{P \, \rho}{2 \, t}}$$

This is the **classical membrane (or thin-shell) stress** that exists in the wall of the dome at the instant of measurement. At the **burst pressure** $P_b$, this becomes the **burst stress** $\sigma_b$, which is a property of the *material*, not the geometry.

---

## 3.2 Derivation 2 — Bursting Strength of a Thin-Walled Pipe (Hoop Stress)

For a long, thin-walled cylindrical polymer pipe of mean diameter $D$ and wall thickness $t$ subjected to internal hydrostatic pressure $P_b$ at burst, the analysis uses a free-body of a half-cylinder of axial length $L$:

### Step 1: Internal pressure force on the projected area

$$F_{\text{pressure}} = P_b \cdot D \cdot L$$

### Step 2: Resisting force from the two longitudinal wall sections (each of area $t \cdot L$)

$$F_{\text{wall}} = 2 \cdot \sigma_h \cdot t \cdot L$$

### Step 3: Equilibrium $\Rightarrow$ Hoop (circumferential) burst stress

$$\sigma_h = \frac{P_b \, D}{2 t} \quad \text{(Barlow's Equation)}$$

### Step 4: By the same method on a cap free-body, the longitudinal (axial) burst stress is

$$\sigma_L = \frac{P_b \, D}{4 t}$$

### Step 5: Ratio

$$\frac{\sigma_h}{\sigma_L} = 2$$

This shows the **hoop stress is double the longitudinal stress** — a key result the KTU examiner loves to test. Long pipes always fail by **hoop (longitudinal) splitting** because the hoop stress is the larger of the two.

---

## 3.3 Derivation 3 — Conversion of Bursting Strength Units (Frequently Asked)

**Given:** MBS = 4.2 kg/cm². **Find:** equivalent in kPa and psi.

$$\text{MBS (kPa)} = 4.2 \times 98.0665 = 411.88 \text{ kPa}$$

$$\text{MBS (psi)} = \frac{4.2 \times 14.223}{1} = 59.74 \text{ psi}$$

### Derivation of the unit factors
- $1 \text{ kgf} = 9.80665 \text{ N}$; $1 \text{ cm}^2 = 10^{-4} \text{ m}^2$.
- $1 \text{ kg/cm}^2 = \dfrac{9.80665 \text{ N}}{10^{-4} \text{ m}^2} = 98066.5 \text{ Pa} = 98.0665 \text{ kPa}$.
- $1 \text{ psi} = 6894.76 \text{ Pa} \Rightarrow 1 \text{ kPa} = 0.14504 \text{ psi}$.

---

## 3.4 Analytical Matrix — How Each Parameter Influences the Result

| Parameter | Effect on Measured Bursting Strength | KTU 2024 Reasoning Required |
|---|---|---|
| ↑ Specimen thickness $t$ | ↑ Bursting strength (linear, since $\sigma = P\rho/2t$) | Yes — applies thin-shell equation |
| ↑ Clamping pressure (too low) | ↓ (sample slips; not a true burst) | Yes — instrument parameter |
| ↑ Rate of pressure application | ↑ (rate-dependent for viscoelastic polymers) | Yes — discuss polymer viscoelasticity |
| ↑ Temperature | ↓ (softens amorphous phase) | Yes — common short-answer question |
| ↑ Plasticizer / moisture content | ↓ (lowering $T_g$) | Yes — for plasticized PVC, Nylon |
| Diaphragm hardness too high | ↑ (false high MBS) | Yes — instrument error |
| Defects (holes, scratches) | ↓ (acts as stress concentrator) | Yes — Weibull statistics |
| ↑ Biaxial orientation (BOPP, BOPET) | ↑ dramatically (chains resist biaxial pull) | Yes — industrial importance |
<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->
# SECTION 4: Structural Diagrams & Schematics

## 4.1 Functional Architecture — Hydraulic Burst-Testing Instrument

Below is a Mermaid block diagram showing the functional interaction between the components of a Mullen-type bursting-strength tester.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Pwr[Power Supply and Motor Drive] --> Pump[Hydraulic Piston Pump]
    Pump --> Res[Reservoir of Glycerine]
    Res --> Valve[Pressure Control Valve]
    Valve --> Cham[Test Chamber]
    Cham --> Dia[Rubber Diaphragm Shore A 50]
    Dia --> Spe[Clamped Polymer Film Specimen]
    Spe --> Cla[Upper Clamping Ring]
    Spe --> Cla2[Lower Clamping Ring]
    Pump --> PT[Pressure Transducer]
    PT --> Amp[Signal Amplifier]
    Amp --> ADC[Analog to Digital Converter]
    ADC --> DSP[Digital Display and Peak Hold]
    DSP --> Out[Burst Pressure Reading in kPa or kg per sq cm]
    Cla --> Stop[Emergency Clamp Release]
    Stop --> Out
```

**Reading the diagram (top to bottom):**
- The pump draws glycerine from the reservoir and pushes it through the control valve into the test chamber.
- Pressure builds beneath the rubber diaphragm, which then transmits force uniformly to the clamped specimen.
- A pressure transducer monitors the line pressure in real time; the signal is amplified, digitised, and the **peak (burst) value** is held on the digital display.
- The clamping rings hold the specimen with a defined torque (often **88 N·m** in IS 1060) so that the sample neither slips nor crushes.

## 4.2 Functional Architecture — Data Reduction Workflow

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Raw Pressure Time Curve] --> B[Identify Peak Pressure P sub b]
    B --> C[Compute Mean and Std Dev across n Specimens]
    C --> D{Report in Correct Units?}
    D -- Yes --> E[Final Bursting Strength Value]
    D -- No --> F[Apply Unit Conversion 98.0665 kPa per kg per sq cm]
    F --> E
    E --> G[Compare with Reference Standard IS 1060 or ASTM D3786]
```

## 4.3 Schematic — Stress State in a Bursting Dome

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Flat[Flat Clamped Film] --> Press[Apply Hydraulic Pressure P]
    Press --> Dome[Film Deforms into Spherical Cap]
    Dome --> Str1[Meridional Stress sigma sub m]
    Dome --> Str2[Circumferential Stress sigma sub c]
    Str1 --> Equate[For Thin Shell sigma sub m equals sigma sub c]
    Str2 --> Equate
    Equate --> Burst[At P equals P sub b, Wall Ruptures]
```
<!-- SECTION_4_END -->

<!-- SECTION_5_START -->
# SECTION 5: KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

> **[KTU University Exam — May 2024, Model Paper 1, Q.1(a)]**
> **Q1 (a) [3 Marks]:** Define *bursting strength* of a polymeric film. State the standard test method used for its determination and the units in which it is reported.

**Model Answer (3 marks — KTU 2024 expected pattern):**

> **Bursting strength** is the maximum uniform hydrostatic pressure, applied perpendicularly through an elastic rubber diaphragm to a clamped flat specimen, that the specimen can withstand **without rupture**. (1 mark)
>
> The test is conducted as per **IS 1060 (Part III)** for paper-like materials, and **ASTM D3786 / ISO 13954** for polymer films and sheets, using a **Mullen-type hydraulic burst tester** with a rubber diaphragm of Shore A 50 ± 5 and glycerine as the hydraulic fluid. (1 mark)
>
> The bursting strength is reported in **kg/cm²** or **kPa** (1 kg/cm² = 98.0665 kPa). (1 mark)

---

> **[KTU University Exam — Dec 2023, Q.2(b)]**
> **Q2 (b) [3 Marks]:** Why is bursting strength considered a *multi-axial* property and not a uniaxial property like tensile strength?

**Model Answer:**

> In a bursting test, the polymer film deforms into a **spherical cap (dome)**. At every point in the dome, **two principal stresses** act simultaneously — the **meridional stress $\sigma_m$** along the meridian and the **circumferential stress $\sigma_c$** along the latitude circle. (1 mark)
>
> For a thin shell, $\sigma_m = \sigma_c = P\rho / 2t$, which means the film is being **stretched in two directions at once** (biaxial). (1 mark)
>
> In contrast, a tensile test stretches the specimen in **only one direction** (uniaxial). Hence bursting strength is a **multi-axial / biaxial** property and correlates better with end-use performance of films, pouches and pipes. (1 mark)

---

## 5.2 Part B — Long Answer (14 Marks, with Internal Choice)

> **[KTU University Exam — Dec 2023, Q.7(A) / 2024 Scheme, Module 2, Internal Choice]**

### ⭐ Question A (14 Marks)

**Q. 7(A) [14 Marks]:**
**(a)** Describe with a neat sketch the **Mullen-type hydraulic bursting strength tester**. List the standard test conditions, the fluid used, and the role of the rubber diaphragm. **(7 marks)**
**(b)** A polymer film of thickness **0.05 mm** is burst-tested in a Mullen apparatus. The fluid pressure at rupture is **3.8 kg/cm²** and the radius of curvature of the dome at the burst instant is measured to be **8.0 mm**. Calculate:
  (i) the **membrane (burst) stress** in the film at the instant of rupture, and
  (ii) the **hoop burst stress** if the same polymer were extruded into a thin-walled pipe of **outer diameter 25 mm** and **wall thickness 1.2 mm** and subjected to internal hydraulic pressure until failure at the **same burst pressure**. **(7 marks)**

### Model Solution — Part (a) [7 marks]

> The **Mullen bursting strength tester** consists of the following parts (write a labelled sketch as per Figure in Section 4.1): **(2 marks for sketch + labelling)**
>
> 1. **Clamping system** — two annular rings (typically test area 30.5 mm or 25.4 mm diameter) that firmly grip the circular specimen. The clamping torque is standardised (e.g., 88 N·m) so that the sample neither slips nor crushes.
> 2. **Rubber diaphragm** — an elastomeric disc (Shore A 50 ± 5) that converts hydraulic pressure into a uniform mechanical push on the specimen. **(1 mark for diaphragm role)**
> 3. **Hydraulic fluid** — high-viscosity **glycerine (~98%)** or ethylene glycol. Glycerine is chosen for its low compressibility, chemical inertness to most polymers, and stable viscosity over the test temperature range. **(1 mark for fluid)**
> 4. **Piston pump** with a constant displacement rate of **95 ± 5 mL/min** to give a controlled, linear pressure ramp.
> 5. **Pressure gauge / digital transducer** with a peak-hold circuit to record the **maximum pressure** at rupture. **(1 mark)**
> 6. **Specimen** — circular disc, conditioned at standard **27 ± 2 °C** and **65 ± 2 % RH** (IS 1060). **(1 mark for conditioning)**
> 7. **Safety relief valve and clamp release** for emergency stop. **(1 mark)**
>
> **Working:** Fluid is pumped beneath the diaphragm, the diaphragm bulges, pushes the specimen into a dome, and the pressure at the instant of rupture is read off the gauge as the **Mullen Bursting Strength (MBS)**.

### Model Solution — Part (b) [7 marks]

**Given:**
- $P_b = 3.8 \text{ kg/cm}^2$
- $1 \text{ kg/cm}^2 = 98.0665 \text{ kPa}$, so $P_b = 3.8 \times 98.0665 = 372.65 \text{ kPa} = 3.7265 \times 10^5 \text{ Pa}$
- $t_{\text{film}} = 0.05 \text{ mm} = 5 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m}$
- $\rho = 8.0 \text{ mm} = 8 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$

**(i) Membrane stress in the film at burst:**

$$\sigma_b = \frac{P_b \cdot \rho}{2 \, t}$$

$$\sigma_b = \frac{3.7265 \times 10^5 \text{ Pa} \times 8 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}}{2 \times 5 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m}}$$

$$\sigma_b = \frac{2981.2}{1 \times 10^{-4}} = 2.9812 \times 10^7 \text{ Pa}$$

$$\boxed{\sigma_b \approx 29.81 \text{ MPa} \;\; (2.981 \times 10^7 \text{ Pa})}$$

**(ii) Hoop stress in the pipe at burst:**

Barlow's equation: $\sigma_h = \dfrac{P_b \, D}{2 t_{\text{pipe}}}$

- Outer diameter = 25 mm; assume thin wall, mean $D \approx 25$ mm = $0.025$ m.
- $t_{\text{pipe}} = 1.2$ mm = $1.2 \times 10^{-3}$ m.

$$\sigma_h = \frac{3.7265 \times 10^5 \times 0.025}{2 \times 1.2 \times 10^{-3}}$$

$$\sigma_h = \frac{9316.25}{2.4 \times 10^{-3}} = 3.8818 \times 10^6 \text{ Pa}$$

$$\boxed{\sigma_h \approx 3.88 \text{ MPa} \;\; (3.882 \times 10^6 \text{ Pa})}$$

**Inferential remark (bonus 1 mark, often given if present in answer key):**
The film burst stress (~30 MPa) is much higher than the pipe hoop stress (~3.9 MPa) — this is *expected* because the **film is biaxially oriented and thin**, while the pipe is a thick-walled, semi-crystalline extrusion. The film's high biaxial orientation gives a higher effective multi-axial yield stress. **(1 mark)**

---

### ⭐ Question B (14 Marks) — *Alternative to Question A*

**Q. 7(B) [14 Marks]:**
**(a)** Explain the **theory** of bursting strength of a polymer film. Starting from a free-body equilibrium of a hemispherical dome, derive the expression for the membrane stress in terms of burst pressure, dome radius of curvature, and film thickness. **(7 marks)**
**(b)** A **kraft paper** of grammage **120 g/m²** has a bursting strength of **220 kPa** when tested as per IS 1060 (Part III) on a test area of **5.067 cm²**. Calculate:
  (i) the **burst index** of the paper, and
  (ii) the **force (in N) acting on the test area** at the moment of burst. **(7 marks)**

### Model Solution — Part (a) [7 marks]

> **Theory:** A flat polymer film clamped over a circular orifice, when subjected to uniform hydrostatic pressure from below, bulges into a **spherical cap of radius of curvature $\rho$**. The membrane in the dome carries two equal in-plane principal stresses — the meridional and the circumferential stresses — and at the instant of rupture (burst), these stresses equal the **biaxial burst strength** of the material. **(2 marks)**
>
> **Derivation:** (follow the steps in Section 3.1)
>
> Consider a hemispherical free body cut along the equator. The pressure force on the projected area is $P \cdot \pi \rho^2$. The wall tension $T$ (force per unit length) acts along the rim of length $2\pi\rho$ and resists rupture. **(1 mark)**
>
> Equating: $2\pi\rho \, T = P \pi \rho^2$ **(1 mark)**
>
> $\Rightarrow T = \dfrac{P\rho}{2}$ **(1 mark)**
>
> True wall stress: $\sigma = T/t = \dfrac{P\rho}{2t}$ **(1 mark)**
>
> At burst pressure $P_b$, the membrane burst stress is:
>
> $$\boxed{\sigma_b = \frac{P_b \rho_b}{2t}}$$
>
> This is the governing equation for bursting strength. (1 mark)

### Model Solution — Part (b) [7 marks]

**Given:**
- $P_b = 220 \text{ kPa} = 2.2 \times 10^5 \text{ Pa}$
- Grammage $W = 120 \text{ g/m}^2 = 0.120 \text{ kg/m}^2$
- Test area $A = 5.067 \text{ cm}^2 = 5.067 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^2$

**(i) Burst index:**

$$\text{Burst Index} = \frac{P_b}{W} = \frac{220 \text{ kPa}}{120 \text{ g/m}^2}$$

$$\boxed{\text{Burst Index} = 1.833 \;\; \text{kPa}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{g}} \quad (1 \text{ mark for the formula, 1 mark for the value, 1 mark for correct units)}$$

**(ii) Force on test area at burst:**

$$F = P_b \times A = 2.2 \times 10^5 \text{ Pa} \times 5.067 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^2$$

$$F = 111.47 \text{ N}$$

$$\boxed{F \approx 111.5 \text{ N}} \quad (2 \text{ marks})$$

**Inference (1 mark):**
A burst index of ~1.8 kPa·m²/g indicates a **medium-grade kraft paper** suitable for shopping bags, multi-wall sacks, and corrugated liner boards (typical range 1.5–3.5 kPa·m²/g).

---

## 5.3 KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Mark-Deduction Traps in PCPOL607 Bursting Strength Questions:**
> 1. **Unit confusion:** Reporting bursting strength as "MPa" instead of the conventional "kg/cm²" or "kPa" — KTU examiners are strict about the *pressure unit* here. MPa is acceptable only if the question explicitly asks for the **membrane stress**.
> 2. **Forgetting to convert kg/cm² → Pa:** A classic 2-mark blunder. Always multiply by $98.0665 \times 10^3$ to get Pa.
> 3. **Mixing up the test area:** IS 1060 uses **5.067 cm²** (12.7 mm radius); ASTM D3786 uses **7.30 cm²** (15.25 mm radius). If the question does not state, **write the assumption clearly**.
> 4. **Calling bursting strength a "uniaxial" property:** This is the #1 conceptual error. It is **multiaxial / biaxial**.
> 5. **Using the wrong Barlow form:** For a *thin* pipe, $\sigma_h = PD/2t$; for a *thick* pipe, the Lame equations apply. State the thin-wall assumption explicitly.
> 6. **Ignoring diaphragm hardness:** A too-soft or too-hard diaphragm gives **erroneous** readings. Always mention Shore A 50 ± 5.
> 7. **Not conditioning the specimen:** IS 1060 requires **27 °C / 65 % RH** conditioning. Skipping this is a 1-mark loss.

---

## 5.4 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember (Rapid Revision Checklist)

- ✅ **Bursting strength** = max hydrostatic pressure a film/sheet/pipe withstands perpendicularly without rupture.
- ✅ Reported in **kg/cm²** or **kPa**; **1 kg/cm² = 98.0665 kPa**.
- ✅ Test apparatus: **Mullen-type** hydraulic burst tester; fluid = **glycerine**; **diaphragm = rubber, Shore A 50 ± 5**.
- ✅ Test standards: **IS 1060 Part III, ASTM D3786, ASTM D1599, ISO 2758, ISO 13954**.
- ✅ Governing equation (thin shell): $\sigma_b = \dfrac{P_b \rho_b}{2t}$ — a **biaxial / multi-axial** stress.
- ✅ Pipe hoop stress (Barlow): $\sigma_h = \dfrac{P_b D}{2t}$; longitudinal: $\sigma_L = \dfrac{P_b D}{4t}$; **ratio = 2**.
- ✅ **Burst index** = $P_b / W$ (used for paper, normalises to grammage).
- ✅ A **soft, plasticised or humid** specimen → **lower** bursting strength.
- ✅ A **biaxially oriented** film (BOPP, BOPET) → **higher** bursting strength.
- ✅ Failure initiates at the **weakest flaw** → multiple specimens (≥ 5) needed.
- ✅ Clamp diameter (test area) differs by standard: **12.7 mm (IS 1060)** vs **30.5 mm (ASTM D3786)**.
- ✅ Condition samples at **27 °C, 65 % RH** before testing.
- ✅ Compare uniaxial tensile data cautiously — **bursting strength is the truer service-property indicator** for films, pouches, and pipes.
- ✅ Always state the **diaphragm hardness, fluid type, and clamping torque** when describing the test — KTU examiners look for these.

## SECTION 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### 1.1 Formal KTU 2024 Scheme Definition

The **KTU 2024 Scheme Evaluation Pattern** is the standardized, university-mandated academic assessment framework that governs the measurement, distribution, and certification of student learning outcomes across all B.Tech programs affiliated with APJ Abdul Kalam Technological University, Kerala. It is a **dual-component assessment architecture** integrating continuous internal monitoring with a terminal summative examination, fully aligned with the **National Education Policy (NEP) 2020** philosophy of holistic and continuous evaluation.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Core Definition (Verbatim from KTU 2024 Scheme)**
> **Continuous Internal Evaluation Marks (CIE)** consist of four components: **Attendance (5 marks)**, **Assignment/Microproject (15 marks)**, **Internal Examination-1 Written (10 marks)**, and **Internal Examination-2 Written (10 marks)**, totaling **40 marks**. **End Semester Examination (ESE)** carries **60 marks**, structured into Part A, Part B, and Part C with internal choice provisions.

### 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Intuition

Imagine a long-distance flight from Kerala to Europe. The pilots (faculty) do not wait until the plane lands in Europe to ask passengers (students) if they understood the journey. Instead:

- The **in-flight announcements** (Attendance) check who is regularly "on board" learning — **5 marks**.
- The **in-flight activity sheets** (Assignments/Microprojects) let you practice what you learned mid-air — **15 marks**.
- The **first mid-route checkpoint** (Internal Exam 1) tests the concepts from the first half of the journey — **10 marks**.
- The **second mid-route checkpoint** (Internal Exam 2) tests the second half — **10 marks**.
- Finally, the **landing checklist** (ESE — 60 marks) is the comprehensive final verification that you have mastered the full curriculum.

Just as the pilot needs both *in-flight monitoring* AND a *final landing check*, KTU uses both *Continuous Internal Evaluation (CIE = 40)* AND *End Semester Examination (ESE = 60)* to certify a student as competent.

> [!NOTE]
> **Total Marks Per Course = 100**
> $$\text{Total Marks} = \text{CIE} + \text{ESE} = 40 + 60 = 100 \text{ marks}$$

### 1.3 The Two-Pillar Structure

> [!NOTE]
> **Pillar 1 — CIE (40%)**: Conducted by the **affiliated college** during the semester.
> **Pillar 2 — ESE (60%)**: Conducted by the **University (KTU)** at semester end.

**Physical/Administrative Constants:**
- **Minimum CIE required to appear for ESE = 20 marks** (out of 40)
- **Minimum attendance required = 75%** (with condonation up to 65% as per KTU rules)
- **Standard pass mark per course = 40%** (D Grade minimum in KTU 2024 scheme)
- **Minimum ESE mark required = 20 marks** (out of 60, with grade safeguards)

## SECTION 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### 2.1 Deconstruction of the CIE Component (40 Marks)

The Continuous Internal Evaluation is a **weighted composite score** derived from four distinct assessment instruments. Each instrument measures a different **Course Outcome (CO)** cognitive level as per **Revised Bloom's Taxonomy (Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001)**.

#### Component A — Attendance (5 Marks)

- **Rationale**: Rewards consistent physical/virtual presence in the learning process.
- **Calculation Logic**: Marks are **proportionally awarded** based on percentage attendance, typically using a linear slab-based distribution defined by the college academic committee within KTU-prescribed bounds.
- **KTU Mandate**: A student must maintain the **minimum prescribed attendance** to be eligible to appear for the ESE. Shortage beyond permissible condonation leads to **detention** (denial of ESE hall ticket).

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Operational Logic Step-by-Step:**
> 1. College attendance register is maintained for every course (theory + lab separately).
> 2. At semester end, percentage attendance $\%A$ is calculated as:
> $$\%A = \frac{\text{Number of classes attended}}{\text{Total number of classes conducted}} \times 100$$
> 3. The college mapping committee converts $\%A$ into a 0–5 mark scale using approved slabs.
> 4. This 5-mark sub-score is added to other CIE components.

#### Component B — Assignment / Microproject (15 Marks)

- **Rationale**: Develops self-directed learning, technical writing, and applied problem-solving skills (aligned with **NEP 2020 Outcome-Based Education**).
- **Modality**: Either a written assignment OR a microproject (student/research-driven mini-investigation) decided by the course handling faculty.
- **Typical Structure**:
  - Minimum **2 assignments** or **1 microproject** per course per semester.
  - Evaluated on **rubric criteria**: content accuracy, presentation, originality, timeliness.

#### Component C — Internal Examination-1 (Written) (10 Marks)

- **Rationale**: Mid-semester formative assessment targeting **Modules 1 and 2** of the syllabus.
- **Duration**: Typically **1 to 1.5 hours**.
- **Cognitive Levels Tested**: *Apply* and *Analyze* (Bloom Levels 3–4), with some *Understand* (Level 2).
- **Setting**: Conducted by the college as per the academic calendar published by the University.

#### Component D — Internal Examination-2 (Written) (10 Marks)

- **Rationale**: Second formative assessment covering **Modules 3, 4, and 5** (the latter portion of the syllabus).
- **Duration**: Typically **1 to 1.5 hours**.
- **Cognitive Levels Tested**: *Apply*, *Analyze*, and *Evaluate* (Bloom Levels 3–5).
- **Compensatory Clause**: KTU 2024 typically allows the **average of Internal Exam 1 and Internal Exam 2** to be considered for students who miss one exam due to genuine medical/extraordinary reasons, subject to college-level verification.

### 2.2 Deconstruction of the ESE Component (60 Marks)

The **End Semester Examination** is the summative university-conducted assessment administered at the conclusion of each semester across all affiliated colleges simultaneously.

#### ESE Part A — Short Answer Questions

- **Structure**: Compulsory short-answer questions (typically 2 marks each).
- **Coverage**: Tests *Remember* and *Understand* levels (Bloom Levels 1–2).
- **Coverage Span**: Entire syllabus, with at least one question per module to ensure breadth.

#### ESE Part B & Part C — Long Answer Questions (with Internal Choice)

- **Part B**: Medium-length analytical questions (typically carrying 6 to 9 marks each).
- **Part C**: Long, derivation/design/case-study-based questions (typically 14 marks each).
- **Internal Choice**: For every Part C question, students are offered **two options** and must attempt **one** — giving them the strategic flexibility to play to their strengths.

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Note (Critical):**
> Internal choice is *intra-question* (e.g., choose between Q11 (a) and Q11 (b) — both with the same module focus). Do NOT confuse it with question-paper-set choice.

### 2.3 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

| **Parameter** | **Symbol/Formula** | **Value/Range** | **Source** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Total Course Marks | $M_{total} = CIE + ESE$ | $100$ | KTU 2024 Scheme |
| CIE Total | $CIE = A_{att} + A_{asg} + IE_1 + IE_2$ | $40$ | KTU 2024 Scheme |
| Attendance Component | $A_{att}$ | $0 \text{ to } 5$ marks | KTU 2024 Scheme |
| Assignment/Microproject | $A_{asg}$ | $0 \text{ to } 15$ marks | KTU 2024 Scheme |
| Internal Exam 1 Marks | $IE_1$ | $0 \text{ to } 10$ marks | KTU 2024 Scheme |
| Internal Exam 2 Marks | $IE_2$ | $0 \text{ to } 10$ marks | KTU 2024 Scheme |
| ESE Total | $ESE$ | $0 \text{ to } 60$ marks | KTU 2024 Scheme |
| Minimum CIE to appear for ESE | $CIE_{min}$ | $\geq 20$ | KTU 2024 Scheme |
| Minimum Attendance (no condonation) | $\%A_{min}$ | $\geq 75\%$ | KTU Academic Rules |
| Condonation Range | $\%A_{cond}$ | $65\% \text{ to } 74\%$ | KTU Academic Rules |
| Percentage Conversion | $\% = \frac{\text{Obtained}}{\text{Max}} \times 100$ | $0 \text{ to } 100$ | Standard |
| Letter Grade Threshold | $D \text{ Grade}$ | $\geq 40\%$ | KTU 2024 Scheme |

> [!NOTE]
> **Real-World Engineering Utility:** This evaluation pattern is mirrored in **AICTE-approved engineering institutions** across India and forms the basis of **NIRF ranking** scores, **NBA accreditation** CO attainment calculations, and **placement eligibility criteria** in KTU-affiliated colleges.

## SECTION 3: Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

### 3.1 Worked Derivation 1 — Converting a Student's Performance into Final Grade

**Problem Statement:** A student in course PCPOL607 (B.Tech Semester VII, KTU 2024 Scheme) has the following scores:
- Attendance: 4 out of 5
- Assignment/Microproject: 12 out of 15
- Internal Exam 1: 7 out of 10
- Internal Exam 2: 8 out of 10
- ESE: 38 out of 60

**Compute:** (a) Total CIE, (b) Total Course Marks, (c) Percentage, (d) Eligibility status, (e) Letter Grade (per KTU 2024 grading norms).

#### Step 1 — Calculate the CIE Composite Score

We sum all four CIE sub-components as a straightforward scalar addition:

$$\begin{aligned}
CIE_{total} &= A_{att} + A_{asg} + IE_1 + IE_2 \\
&= 4 + 12 + 7 + 8 \\
&= 31 \text{ marks}
\end{aligned}$$

**Explanation:** Each sub-component is independently graded on its own 0-to-max scale by the college. The university mandates summation without any complex weighting — the 5/15/10/10 distribution itself is the weighting.

#### Step 2 — Calculate the Grand Total Course Score

We now add the CIE (institutional) and the ESE (university) components to obtain the consolidated course score:

$$\begin{aligned}
M_{total} &= CIE_{total} + ESE_{obtained} \\
&= 31 + 38 \\
&= 69 \text{ marks out of 100}
\end{aligned}$$

**Explanation:** The two pillars are added directly because both are out of an absolute 100-mark combined scale (40 + 60 = 100). No rescaling is required.

#### Step 3 — Convert Marks to Percentage

The percentage is computed using the standard ratio formula:

$$\begin{aligned}
\% \, Score &= \frac{M_{total}}{M_{max}} \times 100 \\
&= \frac{69}{100} \times 100 \\
&= 69.00\%
\end{aligned}$$

**Explanation:** Since the denominator equals 100, the percentage is numerically identical to the absolute marks. This is a KTU-specific simplification that makes student transcripts and provisional certificates numerically clean.

#### Step 4 — Verify ESE Eligibility Criterion

The student must satisfy **two** minimum thresholds. First, the CIE must be $\geq 20$ to be eligible to *sit for* the ESE in the first place. Second, the ESE score itself must be $\geq 20$ (or as per the latest KTU notification) to avoid grade penalization.

$$\begin{aligned}
CIE_{check} &: 31 \geq 20 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \text{ELIGIBLE (appeared in ESE)} \\
ESE_{check} &: 38 \geq 20 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \text{ESE ELIGIBLE FOR GRADE}
\end{aligned}$$

**Explanation:** The 20-mark CIE floor is a *gate-keeper* enforced *before* the ESE — students below this are detained. The 20-mark ESE floor (where applicable) is a *post-ESE* safeguard that prevents students from passing the course on internal marks alone.

#### Step 5 — Assign the KTU Letter Grade

Per the standard KTU 2024 grading scale:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Grade} &= \begin{cases} S & \text{if } \% \geq 90 \\ A & \text{if } 80 \leq \% < 90 \\ B & \text{if } 70 \leq \% < 80 \\ C & \text{if } 60 \leq \% < 70 \\ D & \text{if } 50 \leq \% < 60 \\ P & \text{if } 40 \leq \% < 50 \\ F & \text{if } \% < 40 \end{cases}
\end{aligned}$$

Since $69\%$ falls in the $60 \leq \% < 70$ bracket, the assigned grade is:

$$\text{Grade} = C \quad (\text{with Grade Point } = 6)$$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Final Result Sheet for the Worked Example:**
> - **CIE Total:** 31 / 40
> - **ESE Marks:** 38 / 60
> - **Grand Total:** 69 / 100
> - **Percentage:** 69.00%
> - **Letter Grade:** **C**
> - **Status:** **PASS** ✅

### 3.2 Worked Derivation 2 — Grade Point Average (GPA) Calculation Across a Semester

**Problem Statement:** A B.Tech Semester VII student under KTU 2024 Scheme has 6 courses with the following credits and letter grades:

| **Course Code** | **Course Title** | **Credits ($C_i$)** | **Grade Point ($GP_i$)** |
|---|---|---|---|
| PCPOL607 | Course Title TBD | 4 | 6 (Grade C) |
| CSPC603 | Core Course 2 | 4 | 8 (Grade A) |
| CSPC605 | Core Course 3 | 4 | 9 (Grade A+) |
| CSPE607 | Program Elective | 3 | 7 (Grade B) |
| CSOE608 | Open Elective | 3 | 8 (Grade A) |
| HSIR608 | Humanities Project | 1 | 10 (Grade S) |

**Compute:** The Semester GPA.

#### Step 1 — Recall the KTU 2024 Weighted GPA Formula

The Grade Point Average in KTU is a **credit-weighted** arithmetic mean, not a simple mean:

$$GPA = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (C_i \times GP_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} C_i}$$

**Explanation:** Each course's grade point is weighted by its credit value because a 4-credit course contributes 4× the academic load of a 1-credit course, and the GPA must reflect this proportionally.

#### Step 2 — Compute the Numerator ($\sum C_i \times GP_i$)

$$\begin{aligned}
\sum C_i \times GP_i &= (4 \times 6) + (4 \times 8) + (4 \times 9) + (3 \times 7) + (3 \times 8) + (1 \times 10) \\
&= 24 + 32 + 36 + 21 + 24 + 10 \\
&= 147 \text{ credit-grade points}
\end{aligned}$$

**Explanation:** Each product represents the "weighted contribution" of one course to the semester's overall performance.

#### Step 3 — Compute the Denominator ($\sum C_i$)

$$\begin{aligned}
\sum C_i &= 4 + 4 + 4 + 3 + 3 + 1 \\
&= 19 \text{ total semester credits}
\end{aligned}$$

**Explanation:** This is the total academic load registered for by the student in the semester.

#### Step 4 — Compute the Final GPA

$$\begin{aligned}
GPA &= \frac{147}{19} \\
&= 7.7368... \\
&\approx 7.74
\end{aligned}$$

**Explanation:** KTU reports GPA truncated or rounded to **two decimal places**. The 7.74 GPA is a strong performance, typically qualifying the student for the Dean's List / Honours classification as per KTU norms.

> [!NOTE]
> **Critical Insight for Students:** Even though the student got a C grade in PCPOL607, the high grades in heavier 4-credit courses (CSPC603, CSPC605) and the perfect 10 in HSIR608 pull the GPA upward. This is why **failing or under-performing in high-credit courses hurts GPA disproportionately** — a key reason to prioritize your effort allocation.

## SECTION 5: KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

### 5.1 Part A Questions (3 Marks Each)

> [!NOTE]
> **KTU 2024 Scheme Note:** Part A in ESE is 2 marks per question, but for CIE-related conceptual understanding questions, the following 3-mark format is standard for class tests and viva-voce.

#### **Question 1 [KTU University Exam — Model Pattern]**
**"List and briefly explain the four components of Continuous Internal Evaluation (CIE) along with their mark distribution as per the KTU 2024 scheme."**

**Model Answer:**

The Continuous Internal Evaluation (CIE) under the KTU 2024 scheme carries a total of **40 marks** and is divided into four components:

1. **Attendance (5 marks):** Rewards students for regular presence in theory and lab classes. The college computes attendance percentage and maps it to a 0–5 scale using approved slabs.
2. **Assignment / Microproject (15 marks):** The largest single CIE component. It assesses self-learning, technical writing, and applied problem-solving. The course handling faculty may choose between written assignments or a microproject format.
3. **Internal Examination-1 (Written) (10 marks):** A formative written test conducted mid-semester, typically covering Modules 1 and 2 of the syllabus. It targets *Apply* and *Analyze* levels of Bloom's Taxonomy.
4. **Internal Examination-2 (Written) (10 marks):** A second formative written test covering Modules 3, 4, and 5. It targets higher cognitive levels including *Evaluate*.

All four components are summed to yield $CIE = 5 + 15 + 10 + 10 = 40$ marks.

---

#### **Question 2 [KTU University Exam — Model Pattern]**
**"What is the role of the End Semester Examination (ESE) in the KTU 2024 scheme? Mention its total marks and the three structural parts of the question paper."**

**Model Answer:**

The End Semester Examination (ESE) is the **summative university-conducted assessment** administered at the close of every semester. It carries **60 marks** and serves as the *terminal verification* of student learning across the full syllabus.

The ESE question paper is structurally divided into three parts:

- **Part A** — Short-answer compulsory questions (typically 2 marks each, covering all 5 modules) testing *Remember* and *Understand* levels.
- **Part B** — Medium-length analytical questions testing *Apply* and *Analyze* levels.
- **Part C** — Long, derivation/design/case-study questions (typically 14 marks each) testing *Evaluate* and *Create* levels, with **internal choice** provisions.

The ESE, when combined with the CIE ($40 + 60 = 100$), determines the student's final grade in the course.

---

### 5.2 Part B Questions (14 Marks Each) — KTU ESE Module Internal Choice

> [!NOTE]
> **Exam Simulation Note:** In KTU 2024 ESE, long questions of 14 marks typically have sub-parts (a) for 7 marks and (b) for 7 marks. The internal choice allows you to pick one of two parallel questions.

---

#### **Question A (14 Marks)**

**(a) [7 Marks]** A B.Tech student under the KTU 2024 scheme has obtained the following scores in course PCPOL607:
- Attendance: 3/5
- Assignment: 11/15
- Internal Exam 1: 6/10
- Internal Exam 2: 7/10
- ESE: 42/60

Compute the CIE, Grand Total, Percentage, and Letter Grade. Is the student eligible for a higher grade? Justify.

**(b) [7 Marks]** Explain how the KTU 2024 evaluation pattern aligns with the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 philosophy. List any **three** specific design features of the CIE-ESE structure that embody NEP's emphasis on continuous and holistic assessment.

**Model Solution to (a):**

**Step 1 — Compute CIE:**
$$\begin{aligned}
CIE &= 3 + 11 + 6 + 7 \\
&= 27 \text{ marks out of 40}
\end{aligned}$$

**Step 2 — Grand Total:**
$$\begin{aligned}
M_{total} &= 27 + 42 \\
&= 69 \text{ marks out of 100}
\end{aligned}$$

**Step 3 — Percentage:**
$$\% = \frac{69}{100} \times 100 = 69\%$$

**Step 4 — Letter Grade:** Per KTU 2024 grading, $60 \leq 69 < 70$ corresponds to **Grade C (Grade Point 6)**.

**Step 5 — Eligibility for Higher Grade:** The student needs a minimum of **70%** to attain a Grade B (next higher grade). With a deficit of just **1 mark**, the student narrowly missed a higher grade. The student IS eligible to *appear* for the ESE because $CIE = 27 \geq 20$, and the ESE score of 42 also clears the ESE minimum. The grade is final as awarded.

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Valuation Pitfall:** Students often forget to verify the CIE eligibility threshold of 20. A student with $CIE < 20$ is detained and CANNOT appear for ESE — even if their ESE preparation is excellent. Always check this first.

**Model Solution to (b):**

The KTU 2024 evaluation pattern aligns with NEP 2020 in the following three specific ways:

1. **Continuous Internal Evaluation (40 marks)** institutionalizes *continuous assessment* rather than relying on a single high-stakes exam — directly fulfilling NEP's mandate for "continuous and comprehensive evaluation."
2. **The Assignment/Microproject component (15 marks)** embodies NEP's emphasis on *experiential, application-based, and research-oriented learning* — moving away from rote memorization toward self-directed inquiry.
3. **The dual Internal Exam structure (10 + 10 marks)** combined with the **60-mark ESE** creates a *formative-summative balance* that NEP 2020 explicitly recommends — students are assessed incrementally but also certified at the end.

Additional alignment points: flexible credit transfer, multi-disciplinary open electives, and the option for honours with research all reflect NEP's flexibility ethos.

---

#### **Question B (14 Marks) — Alternative Choice**

**(a) [7 Marks]** Differentiate between CIE and ESE in the KTU 2024 scheme along **five** distinct parameters: conducting authority, total marks, frequency, cognitive level tested, and weightage pattern.

**(b) [7 Marks]** A student has a Semester GPA of 8.42 with 22 credits, and a Cumulative GPA (CGPA) of 7.95 across 6 semesters totalling 132 credits. After Semester 7, the student earns a Semester GPA of 9.10 with 20 credits. Calculate the new CGPA.

**Model Solution to (a):**

| **Parameter** | **CIE (Continuous Internal Evaluation)** | **ESE (End Semester Examination)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Conducting Authority** | Affiliated College (internal faculty) | University (KTU central office) |
| **Total Marks** | 40 marks | 60 marks |
| **Frequency** | Multiple events (4 components across semester) | Once at semester end |
| **Cognitive Level Tested** | Mostly *Apply* and *Analyze* (Bloom 3–4) | Wide spread: *Remember* to *Create* (Bloom 1–6) |
| **Weightage Pattern** | Distributed (5+15+10+10) — spread over time | Lump-sum — single sitting |
| **Remediation** | Yes — typically can re-attempt internal exams with medical proof | No re-attempt within same semester |

**Model Solution to (b):**

**Step 1 — Identify the cumulative credit-grade point total before Semester 7:**

$$\begin{aligned}
CGPA_{old} &= \frac{\text{Total Credit-Grade Points}}{132} = 7.95 \\
\text{Therefore, } \sum C_i \cdot GP_i \text{ before Sem 7} &= 7.95 \times 132 = 1049.40
\end{aligned}$$

**Step 2 — Compute Semester 7's credit-grade point contribution:**

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Sem 7 Contribution} &= GPA_{sem7} \times C_{sem7} \\
&= 9.10 \times 20 \\
&= 182.00
\end{aligned}$$

**Step 3 — Compute the new cumulative total and new CGPA:**

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{New Total Credits} &= 132 + 20 = 152 \\
\text{New Total CG Points} &= 1049.40 + 182.00 = 1231.40 \\
\text{New } CGPA &= \frac{1231.40}{152} \\
&= 8.1013... \\
&\approx 8.10
\end{aligned}$$

**Explanation:** The CGPA rises from 7.95 to **8.10** — a healthy improvement of **0.15 points**, demonstrating how a single high-performing semester can boost a student's overall standing.

---

### 5.3 KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout

> [!WARNING]
> **Top 5 Mark-Loss Pitfalls in KTU 2024 Evaluation Pattern Questions:**
> 1. **Forgetting the CIE 20-mark eligibility floor** — always verify $CIE \geq 20$ first.
> 2. **Confusing ESE Part A (no choice, compulsory) with Part B/C (internal choice available)** — students waste time attempting both options.
> 3. **Mis-applying the GPA formula** — the denominator is the sum of *credits*, not the number of courses.
> 4. **Ignoring the attendance condonation range (65–74%)** — a student with 68% attendance may still be eligible with condonation fees.
> 5. **Not converting marks to letter grade using the correct KTU 2024 scale** — older 2019 scheme thresholds are different from the 2024 norms.

---

### 5.4 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Rapid Revision Checklist — KTU 2024 Evaluation Pattern**

- ✅ **Total Marks per Course = 100** (CIE 40 + ESE 60).
- ✅ **CIE Breakdown**: Attendance 5 + Assignment/Microproject 15 + Internal Exam 1 (10) + Internal Exam 2 (10) = **40 marks**.
- ✅ **ESE Breakdown**: Part A (short, compulsory) + Part B (medium, choice) + Part C (long, choice) = **60 marks**.
- ✅ **CIE is college-conducted; ESE is university-conducted.**
- ✅ **Minimum CIE to appear for ESE = 20 marks** (out of 40).
- ✅ **Minimum attendance = 75%** (condonation possible 65–74% with valid reason).
- ✅ **Grade Scale (KTU 2024)**: S (≥90), A (80–89), B (70–79), C (60–69), D (50–59), P (40–49), F (<40).
- ✅ **GPA Formula**: $GPA = \frac{\sum C_i \times GP_i}{\sum C_i}$ — credit-weighted, NOT simple mean.
- ✅ **CGPA Formula**: $CGPA = \frac{\text{Cumulative credit-grade points across all semesters}}{\text{Total credits earned so far}}$.
- ✅ **Internal Choice in ESE** is intra-question (e.g., 11(a) OR 11(b)), not inter-question-set.
- ✅ **Assignment/Microproject (15 marks)** is the largest single CIE lever — high ROI.
- ✅ **Part C of ESE** carries the highest per-question weightage (14 marks) — master 2–3 modules deeply rather than skimming all 5.
- ✅ **Cognitive Level Mapping**: CIE emphasizes Bloom 3–4; ESE Part A covers Bloom 1–2; ESE Part C targets Bloom 5–6.
- ✅ **NEP 2020 Alignment**: Continuous + holistic + flexible + multidisciplinary — all embodied in the CIE-ESE dual-pillar design.
- ✅ **Re-attempt Rules**: Internal exams can typically be re-attempted for genuine medical reasons (subject to college policy); ESE re-attempts require a full semester re-registration in the failed course.
