# Module Experiment 2: Testing and Applications of Fibres (Cognitive Level: K5 – Evaluate)

## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### 1.1 Formal Academic Definition

In the context of **Polymer Technology and Fibre Science (PCPOL607 – Polymer Characterization & Testing Laboratory)**, **fibre testing** refers to the systematic, standardized evaluation of physical, mechanical, chemical, and thermal properties of textile and industrial fibres to determine their **suitability, performance, durability, and end-use applications**. Under the KTU 2024 Scheme (NEP 2020 aligned), this experiment falls under **Module Experiment 2**, with the **Bloom's cognitive level K5 (Evaluate)**, meaning students are expected to **critically judge, compare, and justify** the use of various fibres for specific applications based on empirical test data.

The key fibre properties tested include:
- **Tensile Strength** (breaking force per unit linear density)
- **Elongation at Break** (%)
- **Tenacity** (gf/denier or cN/tex)
- **Fineness / Linear Density** (denier or tex)
- **Moisture Regain (MR%)** and **Moisture Content (MC%)**
- **Crimp**, **Lustre**, and **Density**
- **Thermal Stability** (Tg, Tm, LOI values)
- **Chemical Resistance** (acid, alkali, solvent)
- **Microscopic Identification** (cross-section, longitudinal view)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Syllabus Highlight:** Module Experiment 2 emphasizes the **application-oriented evaluation** of fibres. Students must not merely *list* properties but must **evaluate and justify** which fibre is appropriate for a given end-use (e.g., geotextiles, medical sutures, composite reinforcement, protective clothing).

### 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Intuition

> [!NOTE]
> **Real-World Analogy — "The Rope Quality Inspector"**
>
> Imagine you are a quality inspector at a factory that produces climbing ropes. Before any rope leaves the factory, you must test it: pull it until it breaks (tensile test), check how much it stretches (elongation), measure its thickness (denier), and verify it can withstand sunlight and water (UV & moisture tests). Only ropes passing all tests are certified for climbers. **Fibre testing in polymer technology is the same idea** — we "interview" each fibre through standardized scientific tests to determine its "resume" and then assign it the right job (application). A cotton fibre is "hired" for shirts, a Kevlar fibre for bulletproof vests, and a polyester fibre for seat belts.

### 1.3 Standard Metrics & Constants

| Metric | Symbol | Standard Value/Unit | Significance |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Linear Density** | $D$ or $T$ | **denier (den)** or **tex** | Weight of 9000 m (den) or 1000 m (tex) of fibre |
| **Tenacity** | $\tau$ | **gf/den** or **cN/tex** | Strength normalized to fineness |
| **Breaking Strength** | $F_b$ | **N** or **gf** | Maximum force fibre withstands |
| **Elongation** | $\varepsilon$ | **%** | Strain at break |
| **Moisture Regain** | $MR$ | **%** | Water uptake under standard conditions (65% RH, 20°C) |
| **Initial Modulus** | $E_i$ | **gf/den** | Resistance to initial deformation |
| **Density** | $\rho$ | **g/cm³** | Mass per unit volume |

> [!NOTE]
> **Key SI Unit Conversions (must memorize for KTU exams):**
> - $1 \text{ tex} = 1 \text{ g/1000 m} = 0.1111 \text{ denier}$
> - $1 \text{ gf/den} = 0.0882 \text{ cN/tex}$
> - $1 \text{ gf/den} \times \rho \,(\text{g/cm}^3) = 8.83 \times \text{ tenacity in gf/den}$ (specific strength relation)

---

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 Hierarchical Classification of Fibre Testing Methods

Fibre testing in the KTU 2024 curriculum is broadly divided into **four critical domains**, each addressing a specific engineering decision:

### A. Mechanical (Tensile) Testing
This evaluates the **load-bearing capacity** and **elastic behaviour** of fibres. The standard instrument is the **Universal Testing Machine (UTM)** with pneumatic or hydraulic clamps, operating per **ASTM D3822** (single-fibre tensile test) or **IS 2351** standards.

**Key Sub-Properties:**
- **Tenacity**: Strength per unit linear density → allows comparison between thick and thin fibres.
- **Initial Modulus**: Slope of the initial linear portion of the stress–strain curve → indicates **stiffness**.
- **Yield Point**: Stress at which plastic (permanent) deformation begins.
- **Toughness**: Area under the stress–strain curve → represents **energy absorbed** before rupture.
- **Work of Rupture**: Total energy (in joules) to break the fibre.

### B. Physical / Dimensional Testing
- **Fineness (Denier/Tex)**: Measured using a **Vibroscope** (ASTM D1577) or **gravimetric method**.
- **Crimp**: Number of crimps per unit length → critical for wool, acrylic bulk yarns.
- **Cross-sectional Shape**: Determined by **optical microscopy** or **SEM** — e.g., round (nylon), trilobal (polyester), kidney-shaped (cotton).

### C. Chemical / Environmental Testing
- **Moisture Regain**: Measured by **oven-dry method** (ASTM D2654).
- **Chemical Resistance**: Immersion in acids, alkalis, organic solvents.
- **UV Degradation**: Xenon arc or QUV accelerated weathering.
- **Flammability**: **Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI)** test (ASTM D2863) → % O₂ required to sustain combustion.
- **Dye Affinity**: Tests like **AATCC Test Method 8** for colour fastness.

### D. Thermal Testing
- **Glass Transition Temperature (Tg)** and **Melting Point (Tm)** via **DSC (Differential Scanning Calorimetry)**.
- **Thermal Decomposition Temperature** via **TGA (Thermogravimetric Analysis)**.
- **Shrinkage (%)**: Measured after exposure to hot air or boiling water.

## 2.2 Why and How Behind Each Testing Step

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Engineering "Why" Behind Fibre Testing:**
> Every test answers a specific **design question**:
> - "Will this rope hold a 100 kg load?" → **Tensile Test**
> - "Will this fabric be comfortable in humid Kerala weather?" → **Moisture Regain Test**
> - "Can this fibre survive sterilization in an autoclave (121°C)?" → **Thermal Test (Tg, Tm)**
> - "Is this fibre safe for a surgical implant?" → **Chemical Resistance & Biocompatibility Test**
> - "Will this curtain catch fire easily?" → **LOI / Flammability Test**

## 2.3 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

| # | Property | Formula | Variables & Units | Application Context |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Denier** | $D = \dfrac{W \times 9000}{L}$ | $W$ = weight (g), $L$ = length (m) | Fineness of synthetic fibres |
| 2 | **Tex** | $T = \dfrac{W \times 1000}{L}$ | $W$ = weight (g), $L$ = length (m) | Universal fineness unit |
| 3 | **Tenacity** | $\tau = \dfrac{F_b}{D} \times 9$ | $F_b$ = breaking force (gf), $D$ = denier | Fibre strength comparison |
| 4 | **Elongation %** | $\varepsilon = \dfrac{L_f - L_0}{L_0} \times 100$ | $L_0$ = original length, $L_f$ = final length | Stretchability |
| 5 | **Initial Modulus** | $E_i = \dfrac{\Delta F / D}{\Delta \varepsilon}$ | $F$ = force, $D$ = denier, $\varepsilon$ = strain | Stiffness |
| 6 | **Moisture Regain** | $MR\% = \dfrac{W_w - W_d}{W_d} \times 100$ | $W_w$ = wet weight, $W_d$ = dry weight | Hygroscopic nature |
| 7 | **Moisture Content** | $MC\% = \dfrac{W_w - W_d}{W_w} \times 100$ | Same as above | Wet-basis analysis |
| 8 | **Density** | $\rho = \dfrac{m}{V}$ | $m$ = mass, $V$ = volume | Fibre identification |
| 9 | **Specific Strength** | $\sigma_{sp} = \dfrac{\tau}{\rho}$ | $\tau$ = tenacity, $\rho$ = density | Cross-material comparison |
| 10 | **LOI (Flammability)** | $LOI = \dfrac{[O_2]}{[O_2] + [N_2]} \times 100$ | Volume fractions of O₂ and N₂ | Fire resistance |
| 11 | **Conversion** | $D = 9 \times T$ | Denier = 9 × Tex | Unit conversion |
| 12 | **Conversion** | $1 \text{ gf/den} = 0.0882 \text{ cN/tex}$ | — | International standard reporting |

> [!NOTE]
> **KTU Examiner's Tip:** Questions on **unit conversion between denier and tex** and **moisture regain vs moisture content** appear almost every year. Memorize formulas 1, 2, 6, and 7.

## 2.4 Real-World Engineering Utility

Fibre testing is the **backbone of the textile, aerospace, biomedical, and composites industries**. Without standardized testing:
- A geotextile used in **Kerala's coastal road construction** could fail under monsoon stress.
- A **Kevlar vest** might not stop a bullet if its tenacity drops below the 22 gf/den threshold.
- A **dialysis membrane** (hollow polysulphone fibre) could rupture if tensile strength is miscalculated.
- A **firefighter's Nomex suit** must have LOI > 28 to self-extinguish.

---

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Derivation: Conversion Between Denier and Tex

### Background
The **denier system** defines the linear density of a fibre as the weight in grams of **9,000 metres** of that fibre. The **tex system** defines it as the weight in grams of **1,000 metres**.

### Step-by-Step Derivation

**Step 1:** Let $W$ grams be the weight of $L$ metres of fibre.

**Step 2:** By definition of denier:
$$
D = \frac{W \times 9000}{L}
$$

**Step 3:** By definition of tex:
$$
T = \frac{W \times 1000}{L}
$$

**Step 4:** Dividing the two equations to eliminate $W/L$:
$$
\frac{D}{T} = \frac{(W \times 9000)/L}{(W \times 1000)/L} = \frac{9000}{1000} = 9
$$

**Step 5:** Therefore the conversion relations are:
$$
D = 9 \times T
$$
$$
T = \frac{D}{9}
$$

**Step 6:** Numerical verification: A nylon fibre weighing 50 g per 9000 m has denier = 50. Its tex = 50/9 ≈ 5.56. Conversely, 50 g per 1000 m → tex = 50, and denier = 50 × 9 = 450.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Conversion Logic Summary:** Since denier is measured over a 9× longer length than tex, the same fibre will have a **denier value 9 times greater** than its tex value.

---

## 3.2 Derivation: Relationship Between Tenacity (gf/den) and Specific Strength

The **specific strength** allows comparison of fibres of different densities — it is the tenacity divided by density:

**Step 1:** Tenacity in engineering units (force/area):
$$
\sigma = \frac{F_b}{A}
$$
where $A$ is the cross-sectional area.

**Step 2:** Linear density in denier relates to mass per length:
$$
D = \rho \times A \times L \times 9 \times 10^5
$$
where $\rho$ = density (g/cm³), $A$ = cross-section (cm²), $L$ = length (cm), and $9 \times 10^5$ converts cm to 9000 m.

**Step 3:** Solving for $A$:
$$
A = \frac{D}{\rho \times L \times 9 \times 10^5}
$$

**Step 4:** Substituting into the stress equation:
$$
\sigma = \frac{F_b \times \rho \times L \times 9 \times 10^5}{D}
$$

**Step 5:** Since tenacity $\tau = F_b / D$, we obtain:
$$
\sigma = \tau \times \rho \times L \times 9 \times 10^5
$$

**Step 6:** For a 1 cm gauge length, **specific strength** is:
$$
\sigma_{sp} = \frac{\sigma}{\rho} = \tau \times 9 \times 10^5 \text{ (in cgs units)}
$$

**Practical use:** A Kevlar fibre with tenacity 22 gf/den and density 1.44 g/cm³ has $\sigma_{sp} = 22/1.44 \approx 15.3$ gf·den⁻¹·cm³·g⁻¹, which is **5× higher than steel** (≈ 2.7 gf·den⁻¹·cm³·g⁻¹ normalized). This justifies Kevlar's use in **ballistic protection**.

---

## 3.3 Analytical Matrix: Comparison of Common Fibres (K5 Evaluation Focus)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> This matrix is the **most exam-relevant** table in this module. KTU questions at the K5 level (Evaluate) typically ask: *"Justify why fibre X is preferred over fibre Y for application Z."* Use this matrix to construct your answers.

| Property | Cotton | Wool | Silk | Polyester | Nylon 6,6 | Kevlar 49 | Glass Fibre |

| **Tenacity (gf/den)** | 3.0–4.9 | 1.0–1.7 | 4.0–5.0 | 4.0–5.5 | 5.0–6.5 | 18–22 | 9–15 |

| **Initial Modulus (gf/den)** | 30–60 | 25–40 | 50–80 | 90–120 | 30–50 | 500–1000 | 250–400 |
| **Moisture Regain (%)** | 7–8.5 | 13–18 | 10–11 | 0.4 | 4.0–4.5 | 3.5 | 0 |
| **Density (g/cm³)** | 1.52 | 1.31 | 1.34 | 1.38 | 1.14 | 1.44 | 2.55 |
| **LOI (%)** | 18 | 25 | 23 | 20–22 | 20–22 | 28–30 | — |
| **Tg (°C)** | — | — | — | 70–80 | 50 | 250 (no Tg) | 700 (softens) |
| **Tm (°C)** | — | — | — | 255–265 | 255–265 | 560 (decomposes) | 800+ |
| **Acid Resistance** | Poor | Good | Moderate | Good | Poor | Moderate | Good |
| **Alkali Resistance** | Good | Poor | Poor | Moderate | Good | Good | Poor |
| **UV Resistance** | Good | Moderate | Poor | Excellent | Fair | Good | Excellent |
| **Cost (relative)** | Low | High | Very High | Low | Medium | Very High | Medium |
| **Best Application** | Apparel, towels | Winter wear, carpets | Luxury textiles | Apparel, seat belts | Carpets, hosiery | Bulletproof vests | Composites, FRP |

## 3.4 Worked Example: KTU-Style Numerical Problem (K5 Level)

**Problem:** A polyester fibre sample has a length of 30 cm and weighs 0.045 g. The breaking force recorded on a tensile tester is 180 gf. Calculate:
1. Denier
2. Tex
3. Tenacity in gf/den
4. Elongation at break if final length is 37.5 cm
5. Comment on its suitability for industrial conveyor belts (K5 evaluation).

### Step-by-Step Solution:

**Step 1 — Denier Calculation:**
Using $D = \dfrac{W \times 9000}{L}$, with $W = 0.045$ g and $L = 30$ cm $= 0.30$ m:
$$
D = \frac{0.045 \times 9000}{0.30} = \frac{405}{0.30} = 1350 \text{ denier}
$$

**Step 2 — Tex Calculation:**
$$
T = \frac{D}{9} = \frac{1350}{9} = 150 \text{ tex}
$$

**Step 3 — Tenacity Calculation:**
$$
\tau = \frac{F_b}{D} = \frac{180}{1350} = 0.1333 \text{ gf/den}
$$

**Step 4 — Elongation %:**
$$
\varepsilon = \frac{L_f - L_0}{L_0} \times 100 = \frac{37.5 - 30}{30} \times 100 = 25\%
$$

**Step 5 — K5 Evaluation for Conveyor Belts:**
- Tenacity of 0.133 gf/den is **extremely low** (industrial polyester is usually 4–5 gf/den). The sample is likely a **drawn, low-tenacity textile-grade yarn**.
- The 25% elongation is **acceptable** for textile use but **too high** for conveyor belts (which require <5% elongation for dimensional stability under load).
- **Verdict:** This sample is **NOT suitable** for industrial conveyor belts. A high-tenacity, low-shrinkage industrial polyester (e.g., Type 715, 8.5 gf/den) or a **Kevlar-reinforced composite** would be the correct engineering choice.

> [!NOTE]
> This worked example demonstrates **K5 evaluation**: the student must *judge* the suitability of data against application requirements, not merely compute numbers.

# 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A: Short-Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

### Q1. [KTU University Exam – May 2024]
**Define tenacity. Why is tenacity preferred over breaking strength as a measure of fibre strength?**

**Model Answer:**
**Tenacity** is defined as the **breaking force per unit linear density** of a fibre. It is expressed in **gf/den (grams-force per denier)** or **cN/tex (centinewtons per tex)**.

Mathematically:
$$
\tau = \frac{F_b}{D}
$$
where $F_b$ is the breaking force and $D$ is the denier.

**Why tenacity is preferred over breaking strength:**
1. **Normalisation:** Tenacity normalises strength with respect to fibre fineness, allowing direct comparison between fibres of different thicknesses.
2. **Cross-fibre comparison:** A fine fibre and a coarse fibre can both be ranked on the same scale.
3. **Design relevance:** In textile engineering, designers need to know strength *per unit weight*, not absolute force, because fabric weight is critical.
4. **Material-independent metric:** It removes the dependency on cross-sectional area variations due to spinning irregularities.

> [!NOTE]
> **Examiner's Note (1 mark):** Mention that tenacity has units of gf/den, not gf. Many students lose a mark by writing only the numerical force value.

---

### Q2. [KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]
**Distinguish between moisture regain (MR%) and moisture content (MC%). A cotton sample weighs 120 g in the wet state and 110 g in the oven-dry state. Calculate both MR% and MC%.**

**Model Answer:**

| Parameter | Moisture Regain (MR%) | Moisture Content (MC%) |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | Weight of water expressed as % of **dry weight** | Weight of water expressed as % of **wet weight** |
| Formula | $MR = \dfrac{W_w - W_d}{W_d} \times 100$ | $MC = \dfrac{W_w - W_d}{W_w} \times 100$ |
| Basis | Oven-dry weight (common in textile trade) | Wet weight (common in engineering) |

**Calculation:**
Given: $W_w = 120$ g, $W_d = 110$ g.

Weight of water:
$$
W_w - W_d = 120 - 110 = 10 \text{ g}
$$

**Moisture Regain:**
$$
MR\% = \frac{10}{110} \times 100 = 9.09\%
$$

**Moisture Content:**
$$
MC\% = \frac{10}{120} \times 100 = 8.33\%
$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Examiner's Note (1 mark):** State clearly that MR% > MC% for the same sample because the denominator (dry weight) is smaller than the wet weight.

---

## 5.2 Part B: Long-Answer Questions (14 Marks Each — Internal Choice)

### Question A (Option 1) — [KTU University Exam – July 2024]

**Q. (a) Describe the procedure for determining the tensile properties of a single fibre using a Universal Testing Machine (UTM) as per ASTM D3822. List the precautions to be taken during sample preparation and testing.** **[7 Marks]**

**Model Answer:**

**1. Apparatus Required (1 mark):**
- Universal Testing Machine (UTM) with constant rate of extension (CRE) mechanism
- Pneumatic or capstan-type fibre grips
- Load cell of appropriate range (typically 10 N or 50 N)
- Vernier calliper for sample length measurement
- Standard atmosphere chamber (65% RH, 20°C)
- Computer with data acquisition software

**2. Sample Preparation (2 marks):**
1. Condition the fibre sample in a **standard atmosphere (65% RH, 20°C) for 24 hours** as per ASTM D1776.
2. Cut a single filament of **30 cm gauge length** using a sharp blade to avoid micro-damage.
3. Inspect under a microscope to ensure **no visible defects, bends, or crimping irregularities**.
4. Mount the fibre on a **paper tab frame** to ensure straight alignment and to prevent damage during grip insertion.

**3. Testing Procedure (3 marks):**
1. Set the UTM to a **constant rate of extension (CRE) of 100% per minute** of the gauge length (i.e., 300 mm/min for 30 cm sample).
2. Fix the fibre in the upper grip first, then the lower grip, ensuring **zero slack** but no initial tension.
3. Start the crosshead and record force-extension data continuously.
4. The test continues until **fibre rupture**.
5. The software generates the **stress–strain (force–elongation) curve** automatically.
6. Read the **breaking force** from the peak of the curve.
7. Calculate **tenacity** = $F_b / D$ and **elongation %** = $(L_f - L_0)/L_0 \times 100$.

**4. Precautions (1 mark):**
- Use **capstan grips** for high-tenacity fibres to prevent jaw breakage.
- Maintain **constant temperature and humidity** throughout.
- Discard results where fibre breaks **at or inside the grip** (premature failure).
- Test at least **25–30 samples** for statistical reliability.
- Calibrate load cell and crosshead speed before each batch.

---

**(b) The following data were obtained for a Nylon 6 fibre sample. The breaking force is 450 gf, denier is 70, original length is 30 cm, and final length at break is 42 cm. Calculate the tenacity, elongation %, and initial modulus (given slope of initial linear region: 9 gf per 1% strain). Comment on the suitability of this fibre for parachute canopies (K5 evaluation).** **[7 Marks]**

**Model Answer:**

**Step 1 — Tenacity:**
$$
\tau = \frac{F_b}{D} = \frac{450}{70} = 6.43 \text{ gf/den}
$$

**Step 2 — Elongation %:**
$$
\varepsilon = \frac{42 - 30}{30} \times 100 = 40\%
$$

**Step 3 — Initial Modulus:**
The slope is 9 gf per 1% strain on a 70 denier fibre.
$$
E_i = \frac{9 \text{ gf}}{70 \text{ den} \times 0.01} = \frac{9}{0.7} = 12.86 \text{ gf/den}
$$

**Step 4 — K5 Evaluation for Parachute Canopies:**

| Property | Nylon 6 Value | Parachute Requirement | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tenacity | 6.43 gf/den | 4.0–5.0 gf/den minimum | ✅ Excellent |
| Elongation | 40% | 20–30% (controlled stretch) | ⚠️ Slightly high |
| Initial Modulus | 12.86 gf/den | 30–50 gf/den (moderate stiffness) | ⚠️ Too compliant |

**Engineering Justification:**
- **Strength** is more than adequate to withstand the opening shock of a parachute (typically 3–5 g of payload weight).
- **Elongation of 40% is borderline** — it provides good shock absorption (preventing bone-jarring opening) but may cause excessive drift and slower descent stabilisation.
- **Low initial modulus** means the canopy may balloon excessively and lose aerodynamic shape.

**Verdict (K5):** The fibre is **acceptable but not optimal**. A **ripstop Nylon 6,6 with a higher modulus (40 gf/den) and slightly lower elongation (25–30%)** would be a superior choice. A blend with **Dyneema (UHMWPE)** could further improve dimensional stability.

---

### Question B (Option 2) — [KTU University Exam – July 2024]

**Q. (a) Explain the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) test for fibres as per ASTM D2863. Why is LOI a critical parameter for fibres used in protective clothing?** **[7 Marks]**

**Model Answer:**

**1. Definition (1 mark):**
The **Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI)** is defined as the **minimum concentration of oxygen (expressed as volume percentage) in a mixture of oxygen and nitrogen** that will just support the combustion of a specimen under specified test conditions.

$$
LOI = \frac{[O_2]}{[O_2] + [N_2]} \times 100
$$

**2. Apparatus and Procedure (3 marks):**
- A **vertical glass column** (chimney) with a controlled gas-mixing system.
- The specimen is mounted vertically in the holder at the centre of the column.
- A mixture of O₂ and N₂ is passed through the column at a controlled flow rate.
- The top of the specimen is **ignited with a pilot flame**.
- The O₂ concentration is **progressively reduced** until the specimen **self-extinguishes within 3 minutes** or burns less than 50 mm of its length.
- The O₂ concentration at this point is the LOI.

**3. Classification of Fibres by LOI (2 marks):**

| LOI Range | Behaviour | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| < 21% | Highly flammable (burns in air) | Cotton (18), Polypropylene (18) |
| 21–28% | Combustible but self-extinguishing limited | Polyester (20–22), Nylon (20–22), Wool (25) |
| > 28% | Self-extinguishing, fire-resistant | Kevlar (28–30), Nomex (28–30), PBI (41), PTFE (95) |

**4. Importance for Protective Clothing (1 mark):**
- **Firefighter suits** require LOI > 28 to prevent flashover injuries.
- **Industrial workers** in oil refineries, electrical substations, and chemical plants must wear LOI > 30 garments.
- **Aerospace and military** applications mandate LOI > 30 with low smoke and toxic gas emission.
- LOI correlates directly with **survival time** in a fire — higher LOI = more time to escape.

> [!NOTE]
> **Atmospheric oxygen is 21%.** Any fibre with LOI > 21 will not sustain combustion in normal air, making it inherently flame-retardant.

---

**(b) With the help of a comparative property matrix, evaluate the suitability of (i) cotton, (ii) polyester, (iii) Nomex, and (iv) Kevlar 49 for use in (a) everyday T-shirts, (b) firefighter jackets, and (c) bulletproof vests. Justify your selections with specific property data.** **[7 Marks]**

**Model Answer:**

**Comparative Property Matrix (3 marks):**

| Property | Cotton | Polyester | Nomex | Kevlar 49 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tenacity (gf/den) | 3.0–4.9 | 4.0–5.5 | 4.0–5.0 | 18–22 |
| Elongation (%) | 6–9 | 15–30 | 15–22 | 2.5–3.5 |
| LOI (%) | 18 | 20–22 | 28–30 | 28–30 |
| Moisture Regain (%) | 7–8.5 | 0.4 | 4.5 | 3.5 |
| Density (g/cm³) | 1.52 | 1.38 | 1.38 | 1.44 |
| Cost (₹/kg approx) | 200 | 180 | 2500 | 5000 |

**Application (a) — Everyday T-Shirts: COTTON ✅ (2 marks)**
- **Justification:**
  - Highest **moisture regain (7–8.5%)** among the four — absorbs sweat, keeping the wearer cool in Kerala's humid climate.
  - **Soft hand feel** and **hypoallergenic**.
  - **Low LOI (18)** is acceptable since T-shirts are not safety-critical.
  - **Low cost** makes it commercially viable.
  - Polyester would be too **hydrophobic (MR = 0.4%)** and uncomfortable in humid weather.
  - Nomex and Kevlar are **over-engineered and prohibitively expensive** for casual wear.

**Application (b) — Firefighter Jackets: NOMEX ✅ (1 mark)**
- **Justification:**
  - **LOI of 28–30%** is critical — it self-extinguishes in air and prevents burn injuries.
  - **Good thermal stability** (Tg ~ 275°C, does not melt — chars at 400°C), unlike polyester which melts at 260°C and causes severe skin adhesion burns.
  - **Adequate tenacity (4–5 gf/den)** to withstand physical stress.
  - Kevlar has higher tenacity but **too low elongation (2.5–3.5%)** — it would be brittle under flexing.
  - Cotton has **LOI of 18** — it would ignite and continue burning — UNACCEPTABLE for firefighting.

**Application (c) — Bulletproof Vests: KEVLAR 49 ✅ (1 mark)**
- **Justification:**
  - **Exceptionally high tenacity (18–22 gf/den)** — 5× that of cotton, sufficient to absorb bullet kinetic energy.
  - **Very high initial modulus (500–1000 gf/den)** — resists deformation on impact, distributing force over a wider area.
  - **Low density (1.44 g/cm³)** — lighter than glass fibre and most metals.
  - **High LOI (28–30%)** — does not ignite on impact friction.
  - Cotton, polyester, and Nomex all have **tenacities below 6 gf/den** — they would tear on bullet impact and provide NO ballistic protection.

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Pitfalls:**
> 1. **Confusing LOI and Tg:** LOI is flammability (oxygen required); Tg is a thermal transition. Do not interchange them.
> 2. **Using breaking strength instead of tenacity:** Tenacity (gf/den) is the normalized parameter; using gf alone loses 1 mark.
> 3. **Ignoring the application context:** K5 questions demand *justification*. Merely listing properties without linking to the application is graded at K2/K3 level, not K5.
> 4. **Wrong unit conversions:** $1 \text{ tex} = 9 \text{ den}$ is the most tested conversion. Get this wrong and lose 1 mark.
> 5. **Mixing up MR% and MC%:** A common error is using wet weight for MR% — remember, MR% is based on **dry weight**.

---

## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **High-Density Rapid Revision Checklist for KTU 2024 Exam — Module Experiment 2**

### Core Definitions to Memorize
- **Fibre:** A textile material with length >> diameter, flexible, and having a length-to-diameter ratio > 1000:1.
- **Filament:** A continuous fibre of indefinite length (e.g., silk, synthetic).
- **Staple:** Short fibre of finite length (e.g., cotton, wool — usually 1–10 cm).
- **Denier:** Weight in grams of 9000 m of fibre.
- **Tex:** Weight in grams of 1000 m of fibre.
- **Tenacity:** Breaking force per unit linear density (gf/den or cN/tex).
- **Moisture Regain (MR%):** Water weight as % of dry weight.
- **Moisture Content (MC%):** Water weight as % of wet weight.
- **LOI:** Minimum O₂ % to sustain combustion.
- **Tg:** Glass transition temperature — onset of segmental motion.
- **Tm:** Melting temperature — crystalline phase transition.

### Critical Conversions (Lose marks if forgotten)
- $1 \text{ tex} = 9 \text{ den}$
- $1 \text{ gf/den} = 0.0882 \text{ cN/tex}$
- $1 \text{ gf} = 0.00981 \text{ N}$
- $MR\% = \dfrac{MC\%}{100 - MC\%} \times 100$ and vice versa

### Testing Standards to Recall
- **ASTM D3822:** Single-fibre tensile test
- **ASTM D1577:** Linear density (Vibroscope)
- **ASTM D2654:** Moisture regain
- **ASTM D2863:** LOI flammability
- **IS 2351:** Indian standard for fibre tensile test
- **AATCC 8:** Colour fastness

### Application Justifications (K5 Quick-Reference)
| Application | Best Fibre | Critical Property |
|---|---|---|
| Everyday apparel | Cotton | High MR% (comfort) |
| Winter wear | Wool | High MR% + low thermal conductivity |
| Seat belts | High-tenacity polyester | High tenacity + low elongation |
| Bulletproof vests | Kevlar 49 / Dyneema | Ultra-high tenacity + high modulus |
| Firefighter suits | Nomex / PBI | High LOI + high Tg |
| Marine ropes | Nylon 6,6 | High elongation (shock absorption) |
| Aircraft composites | Carbon / Glass fibre | High specific strength |
| Medical sutures | Polyglycolide / Silk | Biocompatibility + controlled degradation |
| Hot gas filtration | PPS / PTFE | Thermal + chemical resistance |

### Common Pitfalls to Avoid
1. ❌ Confusing denier with tex — denier is 9× tex.
2. ❌ Using breaking strength instead of tenacity.
3. ❌ Reporting elongation as a fraction instead of a percentage.
4. ❌ Confusing LOI with Tg.
5. ❌ Failing to justify the application in K5-level questions.
6. ❌ Forgetting to specify units (gf/den vs N vs cN/tex).
7. ❌ Not conditioning samples at 65% RH, 20°C before testing.
8. ❌ Reporting tenacity without including the linear density in the denominator.

### Final K5 Evaluation Mantra
> *"Every fibre has a unique property fingerprint. The test data tells you what the fibre **CAN** do. The application requirement tells you what the fibre **MUST** do. K5 evaluation is the bridge between these two — you must **judge** whether the fibre's capabilities meet the application's demands, and **justify** your decision with quantitative data."*

# 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Introduction to Textile Fibres

A **fibre** is defined as a slender, thread-like natural or manufactured (synthetic/regenerated) material that possesses a high length-to-diameter ratio (typically > 1000:1) and can be spun into yarn or directly converted into fabric. According to KTU 2024 scheme, fibres are the fundamental **polymeric building blocks** of the textile industry, characterized by properties such as **tenacity (strength)**, **flexibility**, **elasticity**, and **cohesion**.

> [!NOTE]
> **Syllabus Highlight (CO3):** A fibre must possess a minimum length of approximately **5 mm to 15 mm** (for staple/spun yarns) and a length-to-width ratio of at least **1000:1** to be considered spinnable into yarn.

### 1.2 Classification of Fibres (CO3 - K2 Level: Understand & Analyse)

Fibres are broadly classified into **two main categories** based on their origin and chemical composition. This classification is a fundamental analytical concept tested in KTU examinations.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Essential Fibre Property Requirements:**
> - **Length** : Minimum 5 mm (staple) or continuous (filament)
> - **Tenacity** : ≥ 2 g/denier (grams per denier)
> - **Flexibility** : Ability to bend without breaking
> - **Cohesion** : Surface friction to hold fibres together
> - **Uniformity** : Consistent cross-section and density

### 1.3 Detailed Classification of Fibres

#### **A. Natural Fibres**
Fibres obtained from natural sources (plants, animals, minerals).

| Sub-Category | Source | Examples | Key Property |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cellulosic (Plant)** | Seed, Bast, Leaf, Fruit | Cotton, Jute, Flax, Coir, Sisal | Hydrophilic, biodegradable |
| **Protein (Animal)** | Hair, Silk secretion | Wool, Silk, Cashmere | Elastic, hygroscopic |
| **Mineral** | Rock/ore | Asbestos (obsolete) | Heat resistant, hazardous |

#### **B. Manufactured Fibres (Man-Made Fibres)**
Fibres produced by chemical/physical processing of natural or synthetic polymers.

| Sub-Category | Origin | Examples | Polymer Base |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Regenerated** | Natural polymer + chemical treatment | Viscose Rayon, Modal, Lyocell, Acetate | Cellulose (natural) |
| **Synthetic** | Petrochemical monomers | Polyester, Nylon 6,6, Acrylic, Spandex | Synthetic polymer |
| **Inorganic** | Minerals/glass | Glass fibre, Carbon fibre, Ceramic | Silica/carbon |

### 1.4 Conceptual Analogy / Intuition

> **Real-World Analogy (The Building Blocks Concept):**
> Think of fibres as the **bricks** of a house. Just as a house cannot be built without bricks, fabric cannot be created without fibres.
> - **Natural fibres** = Bricks made from naturally occurring clay (mud bricks).
> - **Man-made/synthetic fibres** = Bricks manufactured in a factory with a specific mould (engineered for uniform strength and size).
> - **Spinning** = The process of binding small bricks together using cement/mortar to form a long column (yarn).
> - **Fabric making** = Arranging these columns (yarns) in a structured pattern to form a wall (cloth).
> This analogy helps us visualize the journey from **fibre → yarn → fabric → garment**.

### 1.5 Identification Tests for Fibres (Burn Test)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Burn Test Characteristics (Frequently Asked in KTU):**
> - **Cotton/Linen (Cellulose)** : Burns quickly, yellow flame, paper/wood smell, fine grey ash.
> - **Wool/Silk (Protein)** : Burns slowly, sizzles, black bead, hair/feather smell.
> - **Polyester/Nylon (Synthetic)** : Melts and drips, black smoke, chemical/sweet smell, hard black bead.
> - **Acetate/Rayon (Regenerated)** : Burns rapidly, chemical smell, irregular black bead.

# 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 Theoretical Basis of Fibre Classification

The classification of fibres is rooted in their **polymer chemistry** and **origin**. The fundamental understanding requires analysing fibres at the **molecular level**.

### 2.2 Polymer Structure-Based Analysis

**Natural Cellulosic Fibres (e.g., Cotton)**
- Composed of **cellulose**: A linear polymer of β-D-glucose units linked by β(1→4) glycosidic bonds.
- Polymer chain orientation and crystallinity determine the fibre strength.

**Natural Protein Fibres (e.g., Wool)**
- Composed of **keratin** (wool) or **fibroin** (silk): Polypeptides formed by amino acid condensation.
- Wool contains **disulphide bonds (-S-S-)** that provide elasticity and resilience.

**Synthetic Fibres (e.g., Polyester - PET)**
- Composed of **polyethylene terephthalate**: A condensation polymer of ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid.
- Linear polymer chains with high crystallinity give high tenacity.

### 2.3 Step-by-Step Analytical Logic for Fibre Classification

To classify a given fibre, the following logical steps are applied:

1. **Origin Analysis** : Determine whether the fibre is from natural (plant/animal/mineral) or manufactured source.
2. **Chemical Composition** : Test for presence of cellulose, protein, or synthetic polymer using burn test, microscopy, or chemical analysis.
3. **Morphology** : Examine cross-section and longitudinal structure under microscope (e.g., cotton has kidney-shaped cross-section, wool has circular).
4. **Performance Properties** : Test for tenacity, moisture regain, elasticity, and thermal behaviour.
5. **Final Classification** : Place the fibre in the appropriate category and sub-category.

### 2.4 Properties Comparison Table (KTU High-Yield)

| Property | Cotton | Wool | Polyester | Nylon 6,6 | Viscose Rayon |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Tenacity (g/den)** | 3.0–4.9 | 1.0–1.7 | 4.0–7.0 | 4.5–8.5 | 1.5–2.5 |
| **Elongation (%)** | 3–7 | 25–35 | 15–30 | 20–40 | 15–30 |
| **Moisture Regain (%)** | 7.0–8.5 | 14–18 | 0.2–0.5 | 3.5–5.0 | 11–13 |
| **Density (g/cm³)** | 1.54 | 1.32 | 1.38 | 1.14 | 1.50 |
| **Glass Transition Tg (°C)** | — | — | 70–80 | 50–60 | — |

> [!NOTE]
> **Units Used in Textile Testing:**
> - **Denier (den)** : Mass in grams of 9000 m of fibre/yarn.
> - **Tex** : Mass in grams of 1000 m of fibre/yarn.
> - **Moisture Regain (%)** = $\frac{W_w - W_d}{W_d} \times 100$, where $W_w$ = wet weight, $W_d$ = dry weight.

### 2.5 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

| # | Concept | Formula / Relation | Significance |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Denier** | $D = \frac{Mass (g)}{Length (m)} \times 9000$ | Measures linear density |
| 2 | **Tex** | $T = \frac{Mass (g)}{Length (m)} \times 1000$ | SI-like linear density unit |
| 3 | **Tenacity** | $T_n = \frac{Breaking\ Strength\ (g)}{Denier}$ | Strength per unit weight |
| 4 | **Moisture Regain** | $MR(\%) = \frac{W_w - W_d}{W_d} \times 100$ | Hygroscopicity measure |
| 5 | **Moisture Content** | $MC(\%) = \frac{W_w - W_d}{W_w} \times 100$ | Alternative moisture measure |
| 6 | **Conversion Tex → Denier** | $1\ Tex = 9\ Denier$ | Unit conversion |
| 7 | **Yarn Count (English Cotton)** | $Ne = \frac{Length\ (840\ yds)}{Weight\ (lb)}$ | Indirect yarn numbering |
| 8 | **Yarn Count (Metric)** | $Nm = \frac{Length\ (m)}{Weight\ (g)}$ | Indirect yarn numbering |

### 2.6 Real-World Engineering Utility

The classification system enables:
- **Quality control** in textile manufacturing.
- **Blending decisions** (e.g., polyester-cotton blend for shirting fabric).
- **Process selection** (e.g., wet spinning for viscose, melt spinning for polyester).
- **End-use prediction** (e.g., aramid fibre for bulletproof vests, glass fibre for composites).

# 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Numerical Analysis

## 3.1 Derivations of Key Unit Conversions

### Derivation 1: Relationship between Tex and Denier

By definition:
- $1\ Denier = \frac{1\ gram}{9000\ metres}$ of fibre.
- $1\ Tex = \frac{1\ gram}{1000\ metres}$ of fibre.

For the same fibre of mass $m$ grams and length $L$ metres:

$$
D = \frac{m}{L} \times 9000
$$

$$
T = \frac{m}{L} \times 1000
$$

Dividing the equation for $D$ by the equation for $T$:

$$
\frac{D}{T} = \frac{9000}{1000} = 9
$$

Therefore:

$$
D = 9 \times T \quad \text{or} \quad T = \frac{D}{9}
$$

**Conclusion:** $1\ Tex = 9\ Denier$ is the conversion factor for linear density of fibres.

### Derivation 2: Relationship between Moisture Regain and Moisture Content

Let the dry weight of the fibre be $W_d$ and the wet weight (containing moisture) be $W_w$.

By definition:
- Moisture Regain is based on dry weight:

$$
MR = \frac{W_w - W_d}{W_d} \times 100
$$

- Moisture Content is based on wet weight:

$$
MC = \frac{W_w - W_d}{W_w} \times 100
$$

To convert $MR$ to $MC$, substitute $W_w = W_d \left(1 + \frac{MR}{100}\right)$:

$$
MC = \frac{W_w - W_d}{W_w} \times 100 = \frac{W_d \left(1 + \frac{MR}{100}\right) - W_d}{W_d \left(1 + \frac{MR}{100}\right)} \times 100
$$

Simplifying the numerator:

$$
MC = \frac{\frac{MR}{100}}{1 + \frac{MR}{100}} \times 100
$$

$$
\boxed{MC(\%) = \frac{100 \times MR}{100 + MR}}
$$

Similarly, the reverse conversion is:

$$
\boxed{MR(\%) = \frac{100 \times MC}{100 - MC}}
$$

### Derivation 3: Yarn Twist Multiplier and Twist Angle

The twist angle $\theta$ of a yarn is related to the twist turns per metre ($T$) and yarn linear density.

For a yarn of diameter $d$ (in mm), the surface twist angle is given by:

$$
\tan \theta = \frac{\pi \cdot d \cdot T}{1000}
$$

Where:
- $T$ = turns per metre.
- $d$ = yarn diameter in mm.

This derivation is used in determining the optimum twist for a given yarn count.

### 3.2 Worked Numerical Example (KTU Board Exam Style)

**Problem:** A cotton fibre sample has a wet weight of 110 g and a dry weight of 95 g. Calculate (a) Moisture Regain, and (b) Moisture Content.

**Solution:**

Given:
- $W_w = 110\ g$
- $W_d = 95\ g$

**Part (a): Moisture Regain**

Using the formula:

$$
MR(\%) = \frac{W_w - W_d}{W_d} \times 100
$$

Substituting values:

$$
MR(\%) = \frac{110 - 95}{95} \times 100 = \frac{15}{95} \times 100
$$

$$
MR(\%) = 15.79\%
$$

**Part (b): Moisture Content**

Using the formula:

$$
MC(\%) = \frac{W_w - W_d}{W_w} \times 100
$$

Substituting values:

$$
MC(\%) = \frac{110 - 95}{110} \times 100 = \frac{15}{110} \times 100
$$

$$
\boxed{MC(\%) = 13.64\%}
$$

**Verification using the derived conversion formula:**

$$
MC = \frac{100 \times 15.79}{100 + 15.79} = \frac{1579}{115.79} = 13.64\%
$$

The values match, confirming the correctness of the derivation.

### 3.3 Analytical Matrix for Spinning Operation Selection

# 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A: Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

### **Question 1** [KTU University Exam - May 2024]

**"Classify textile fibres with suitable examples. Briefly describe the burn test characteristics of natural and synthetic fibres."** (3 Marks)

### **Model Answer:**

Textile fibres are classified into two main categories:

**1. Natural Fibres** : Fibres obtained from natural sources.
- *Cellulosic (Plant)*: Cotton, Jute, Flax — *Burn test*: Burns quickly with yellow flame, smell of burning paper, produces fine grey ash.
- *Protein (Animal)*: Wool, Silk — *Burn test*: Burns slowly with sizzling sound, smell of burning hair, leaves a crushable black bead.

**2. Manufactured Fibres** : Fibres produced by chemical processing.
- *Regenerated*: Viscose Rayon, Acetate — *Burn test*: Burns rapidly with chemical odour, leaves irregular black bead.
- *Synthetic*: Polyester, Nylon, Acrylic — *Burn test*: Melts and drips, black smoke, sweet chemical smell, leaves hard black bead.

---

### **Question 2** [KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]

**"Explain the difference between staple fibres and filament fibres with two examples each."** (3 Marks)

### **Model Answer:**

| Property | Staple Fibres | Filament Fibres |
|---|---|---|
| **Length** | Short, finite length (mm to cm) | Continuous, infinite length |
| **Spinning** | Requires spinning into yarn | Can be used directly as yarn |
| **Examples** | Cotton, Wool, Jute, Flax | Silk (natural), Polyester, Nylon (synthetic) |
| **Feel** | Softer, fuzzy surface | Smooth, lustrous surface |

Staple fibres must undergo **staple spinning** operations (blowroom, carding, drawing, roving, ring spinning) to form yarn, while filament fibres can be used directly or texturized for fabric formation.

---

## 5.2 Part B: Long Answer Questions (14 Marks - Module Internal Choice)

### **Question A (Choice 1)** [KTU University Exam - May 2024]

**(a) Explain in detail the classification of textile fibres with suitable examples. Compare the properties of natural and synthetic fibres. (7 Marks)**

**(b) Describe the Melt Spinning process for synthetic fibre production with a neat block diagram. List four polymers produced by this method. (7 Marks)**

### **Model Answer (a):**

Textile fibres are broadly classified based on their origin into **Natural Fibres** and **Manufactured Fibres**.

**1. Natural Fibres** are obtained from natural sources and are further divided into:
- **Cellulosic (Plant) Fibres**: Cotton (from seed), Jute, Flax, Hemp, Sisal (from bast/stem). Polymer: Cellulose.
- **Protein (Animal) Fibres**: Wool (from sheep fleece), Silk (from silkworm cocoons). Polymer: Keratin / Fibroin.
- **Mineral Fibres**: Asbestos (now obsolete due to health hazards).

**2. Manufactured Fibres** are produced by industrial processes and include:
- **Regenerated Fibres**: Viscose Rayon, Modal, Lyocell, Acetate. Polymer source: Natural cellulose chemically modified.
- **Synthetic Fibres**: Polyester (PET), Nylon 6,6, Acrylic (PAN), Spandex, Polypropylene. Polymer source: Petrochemicals.
- **Inorganic Fibres**: Glass fibre, Carbon fibre, Ceramic fibre. Used in composites.

**Comparison of Natural vs Synthetic Fibres:**

| Property | Natural Fibres | Synthetic Fibres |
|---|---|---|
| **Source** | Plants/Animals | Petrochemicals |
| **Moisture Absorption** | High (e.g., cotton 8%, wool 16%) | Low (e.g., polyester 0.4%) |
| **Strength** | Moderate | High |
| **Wrinkle Resistance** | Poor (cotton), Good (wool) | Excellent |
| **Biodegradability** | Yes | No (most) |
| **Cost** | Variable | Generally lower at scale |
| **Dyeability** | Easy | Requires special dyes |

**Conclusion**: Natural fibres are valued for comfort and biodegradability, while synthetic fibres offer superior strength, durability, and ease of maintenance.

### **Model Answer (b):**

**Melt Spinning Process:**

Melt spinning is the most economical and widely used spinning method for thermoplastic polymers. The process steps are:

1. **Polymer Feed**: Polymer chips (e.g., PET, Nylon) are fed into an extruder.
2. **Melting Zone**: The chips are melted in a heated extruder at a temperature **above the polymer's melting point (Tm)** but below the degradation temperature.
3. **Metering Pump**: A metering pump delivers a precise, uniform flow of the polymer melt.
4. **Filter Pack**: Removes impurities and gels to ensure clean extrusion.
5. **Spinneret**: The polymer melt is forced through a spinneret containing hundreds of fine holes (0.1–0.4 mm diameter).
6. **Quenching Chamber**: The extruded filaments are solidified by a stream of cool air.
7. **Finish Application**: Spin finish is applied to provide lubrication, antistatic, and cohesion properties.
8. **Drawing Zone**: Filaments are stretched (draw ratio 3:1 to 6:1) to orient the molecular chains, increasing tenacity.
9. **Winding**: The continuous filament yarn is wound on packages.

**Block Diagram:**

```
Polymer Chips → Extruder (Melting) → Metering Pump → Filter → Spinneret
    → Quenching Air Chamber → Finish Applicator → Drawing Godets → Winder
```

**Four Polymers Produced by Melt Spinning:**
1. **Polyester (PET)** – for apparel, home textiles.
2. **Nylon 6,6** – for hosiery, carpets, parachutes.
3. **Polypropylene (PP)** – for industrial textiles, geotextiles.
4. **Polyethylene (PE)** – for industrial applications.

---

### **Question B (Choice 2)** [KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]

**(a) Discuss the various methods of spinning synthetic fibres. Compare Dry Spinning and Wet Spinning processes. (7 Marks)**

**(b) Explain the different operations involved in making fabric. Describe the Weaving process with its preparatory steps. (7 Marks)**

### **Model Answer (a):**

**Methods of Spinning Synthetic Fibres:**

The major spinning methods are:

1. **Melt Spinning**: Used for thermoplastics (PET, Nylon, PP). Polymer is melted and extruded.
2. **Dry Spinning**: Polymer dissolved in a volatile solvent (e.g., PAN in DMF). Solvent evaporates in a hot chamber.
3. **Wet Spinning**: Polymer solution is extruded into a coagulation bath (e.g., Viscose into H₂SO₄).
4. **Dry-Jet Wet Spinning**: Used for liquid crystalline polymers (e.g., Aramid/Kevlar).
5. **Emulsion Spinning**: Polymer in dispersed form is spun.
6. **Electrospinning**: Used for producing nanofibres.

**Comparison of Dry Spinning vs Wet Spinning:**

| Parameter | Dry Spinning | Wet Spinning |
|---|---|---|
| **Polymer State** | Solution in volatile solvent | Solution in non-volatile solvent |
| **Solidification** | By solvent evaporation in hot air | By chemical reaction in coagulation bath |
| **Spinneret Position** | Above the bath | Inside the bath |
| **Filament Speed** | Higher (200–800 m/min) | Lower (5–50 m/min) |
| **Polymers** | Acrylic, Spandex, Modacrylic | Viscose Rayon, Cuprammonium, Lyocell |
| **Solvent Recovery** | Required and economical | Complex, requires recovery system |
| **Capital Cost** | Moderate | High |
| **Yarn Quality** | Softer, less hairy | Stiffer, requires after-treatment |

**Conclusion**: Dry spinning is faster and suitable for heat-sensitive polymers, while wet spinning is essential for polymers requiring chemical regeneration.

### **Model Answer (b):**

**Fabric Making Operations:**

Fabric is produced from yarn (or directly from fibres) through various processes:

1. **Weaving** : Interlacing of two sets of yarns (warp and weft) at right angles on a loom.
2. **Knitting** : Interlooping of a single set of yarn to form loops (courses and wales).
3. **Non-Woven Fabric** : Bonding of fibres by mechanical, thermal, or chemical means.
4. **Braiding** : Diagonal interlacing of yarns to form flat or tubular structures.
5. **Lace Making** : Decorative openwork fabric.
6. **Tufting** : Insertion of yarn into a base fabric (mainly carpets).
7. **Felting** : Matting of fibres using heat, moisture, and pressure (wool).

**Weaving Process and Preparatory Steps:**

**Preparatory Steps (Warp Preparation):**
1. **Winding**: Transferring yarn from spinning packages to larger packages (cones).
2. **Warping**: Assembling hundreds of warp yarns from creel in parallel form onto a warp beam.
3. **Sizing/Slashing**: Applying a protective coating (size) of starch/PVA to warp yarns to improve strength and reduce abrasion during weaving.
4. **Drawing-In**: Passing warp yarns through the heald eyes and reed.

**Actual Weaving Process (Loom Operations):**
1. **Shedding**: Raising and lowering warp yarns to form a shed (opening).
2. **Picking**: Inserting the weft (filling) yarn through the shed using a shuttle, projectile, rapier, or air jet.
3. **Beat-up**: Pushing the newly inserted weft yarn into the fell of the cloth.
4. **Take-up**: Winding the woven fabric onto a cloth roll.

**Modern Weaving Machines:** Air-jet loom, Water-jet loom, Rapier loom, Projectile loom — all offer higher speed and reduced noise compared to traditional shuttle looms.

---

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout:**
> 1. **Confusing Staple and Filament**: Students often interchange "staple spinning" with "fibre classification." Remember: *staple spinning* refers to the process, while *staple fibre* refers to the type of fibre.
> 2. **Melt Spinning is NOT applicable to acrylic or viscose**: Many students write "acrylic is melt spun" — this is wrong. Acrylic decomposes before melting; it must be **dry spun**. Viscose must be **wet spun**.
> 3. **Skip the Yarn Stage in Non-Woven**: Non-woven fabrics are made directly from fibres, bypassing the yarn stage. Mentioning "weaving" for non-woven is a common error.
> 4. **Always draw the Block Diagram**: In spinning questions, KTU examiners award 1–2 marks specifically for labelled block diagrams. Omitting them leads to significant mark loss.
> 5. **Weaving vs Knitting**: Do not confuse the two. *Weaving* = interlacing; *Knitting* = interlooping. A single sentence error here can cost up to 2 marks.

---

## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Rapid Revision Checklist (Must Memorize for KTU Exam):**

### **Fibre Classification (CO3)**
- ⭐ Fibres are classified into **Natural** and **Manufactured** (Man-made).
- ⭐ Natural fibres include **Cellulosic** (cotton, jute), **Protein** (wool, silk), and **Mineral** (asbestos).
- ⭐ Manufactured fibres include **Regenerated** (viscose), **Synthetic** (polyester, nylon), and **Inorganic** (glass, carbon).
- ⭐ Burn test is a key identification tool: cellulose burns with paper smell, protein with hair smell, synthetic melts.

### **Spinning Operations (CO4)**
- ⭐ **Melt spinning** is used for thermoplastics: **Polyester, Nylon, Polypropylene, Polyethylene**.
- ⭐ **Dry spinning** is used for heat-sensitive polymers: **Acrylic (PAN), Spandex, Modacrylic**.
- ⭐ **Wet spinning** is used for cellulose-derived polymers: **Viscose Rayon, Lyocell, Cuprammonium**.
- ⭐ **Dry-jet wet spinning** is used for liquid crystalline polymers: **Aramid (Kevlar, Nomex)**.
- ⭐ Each spinning method requires **draw-down, cooling/precipitation, drawing, and winding** stages.

### **Fabric Making Operations (CO5)**
- ⭐ Major fabric forming methods: **Weaving, Knitting, Non-woven, Braiding, Lace, Tufting, Felting**.
- ⭐ **Weaving** is interlacing of warp and weft; preparatory steps are **winding, warping, sizing, drawing-in**.
- ⭐ **Knitting** is interlooping; types are **weft knit** and **warp knit**.
- ⭐ **Non-woven** skips the yarn stage; bonding methods are **mechanical, thermal, chemical**.

### **Key Formulas to Memorize**
- ⭐ $1\ Tex = 9\ Denier$
- ⭐ $MR(\%) = \frac{W_w - W_d}{W_d} \times 100$
- ⭐ $MC(\%) = \frac{W_w - W_d}{W_w} \times 100$
- ⭐ $MC = \frac{100 \times MR}{100 + MR}$ (conversion formula)

### **Key Properties to Compare**
- ⭐ Cotton: Hydrophilic, comfortable, weak when wet.
- ⭐ Wool: Elastic, hygroscopic, shrinks on washing.
- ⭐ Polyester: Strong, hydrophobic, wrinkle-resistant, low moisture regain.
- ⭐ Nylon 6,6: Highest tenacity among common fibres, elastic.
- ⭐ Viscose Rayon: Highly absorbent, soft, but weak when wet.

> [!NOTE]
> **Final Exam Tip for KTU 2024 Scheme:**
> - Part A questions (3 marks) usually test definitions, classifications, or simple comparisons — answer in 5–6 lines with a small table if possible.
> - Part B questions (14 marks) require **detailed explanation + diagrams + examples**. Always include a labelled block diagram and at least 2 examples.
> - For CO-based questions, **map your answer to the CO statement** explicitly (e.g., "This demonstrates CO3: classification of fibres").

# MODULE EXPERIMENT 2 — K3 (APPLY) COMPETENCY FRAMEWORK

> [!NOTE]
> **KTU 2024 Scheme — Revised Bloom's Taxonomy Mapping**
> The tag **K3 – Apply** is not a content topic. It is a **cognitive level descriptor** drawn from Anderson & Krathwohl's Revised Bloom's Taxonomy. In the KTU 2024 Outcome-Based Education (OBE) framework, every Course Outcome (CO) is tagged with a cognitive level (K1–K6). Module Experiment 2 is mapped to **K3**, meaning the student must demonstrate the ability to **execute, implement, and use** a procedure, formula, or methodology in a new but similar situation.

## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **K3 — APPLY (Cognitive Domain)**
> *Executing a procedure in a given situation; using a known rule, formula, principle, or method in a concrete, novel context. The learner carries out or applies a procedure to a problem that was not memorized verbatim.*

In KTU 2024 OBE terminology, the verb-descriptors for **K3** (Apply) are:

- **Execute** a standard procedure
- **Implement** a known formula into numerical data
- **Modify** an existing process to fit a new set of inputs
- **Use** a theorem, law, or protocol to obtain a result
- **Demonstrate** correct procedural sequencing
- **Solve** structured (closed-ended) problems using taught methods

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — Plain English Intuition

> [!NOTE]
> **Analogy: The "Recipe → New Dish" Model**
> - **K1 (Remember):** You read the recipe and can recall the ingredients.
> - **K2 (Understand):** You can explain *why* baking soda makes the cake fluffy.
> - **K3 (Apply):** You take that same recipe and successfully bake the cake in a *different oven*, with *slightly different ingredients*, and it still comes out edible. The procedure is the same, the context is new.
> - **K4 (Analyze):** You taste the cake, identify it is too sweet, and diagnose the cause.
> - **K5 (Evaluate):** You compare this cake to a market cake and judge which is better.
> - **K6 (Create):** You invent a brand-new pastry using the underlying principles.

**K3 is the "First-Hand Use" level.** The student is no longer just recalling or explaining — they are *doing* the experiment, *running* the calculation, or *operating* the instrument with their own hands. In Module Experiment 2, K3 means the student must take a known experimental protocol and physically/analytically execute it.

## 1.3 The OBE Mapping Triangle

| Course Outcome Tag | Bloom Level | Verb in Question Paper | Expected Student Behaviour |
|---|---|---|---|
| **CO2 / CO3** | K3 – Apply | Apply, Execute, Compute, Determine, Illustrate, Solve | Picks the right formula, plugs in values, computes the answer, validates units |
| CO1 | K2 – Understand | Explain, Describe, State | Restates a principle in own words |
| CO4 | K4 – Analyze | Compare, Differentiate, Examine | Breaks a result into cause-and-effect components |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Module Experiment 2 (K3) is worth the maximum cognitive weight in your internal lab assessment (typically 20–30 marks per experiment). Mastering K3 separates a "pass" student from a "distinction" student in KTU B.Tech.**

# DEEP THEORETICAL ANALYSIS — THE K3 COGNITIVE ENGINE

## 2.1 Anatomy of an "Apply-Level" Experiment

Every K3 experiment in your PCPOL607 lab course contains **four universal operational phases**. Mastery of these phases is what the examiner is actually testing.

### Phase 1 — **Identify the Governing Principle**
> Before touching any apparatus, the student must recognize *which* theoretical principle the experiment demonstrates. This is the bridge from K2 (Understand) to K3 (Apply).

- Read the experiment objective.
- Recall the **standard metric / physical constant** involved (e.g., molecular weight, viscosity coefficient, glass transition temperature).
- State the **governing equation** that links the measured quantities to the target result.

### Phase 2 — **Sequence the Procedural Steps**
> The student must arrange the experimental workflow in a logical, hazard-free order.

- Calibration of instruments
- Sample preparation
- Controlled application of stimulus (heat, load, shear)
- Data capture at defined intervals
- Controlled termination of the experiment

### Phase 3 — **Execute with Data**
> The actual *doing* — this is where K3 lives. The student:

- Records **raw observations** (mass, time, temperature, deflection, current).
- Substitutes raw values into the governing equation.
- Performs unit conversions and arithmetic.

### Phase 4 — **Verify and Report**
> The student cross-checks the result against expected ranges, computes % error, and writes a formal lab report in the KTU-prescribed format.

## 2.2 The KTU Formula Sheet for K3-Level Problem Solving

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Universal K3 Formula Toolkit**
> While each specific experiment (tensile testing, melt flow index, viscosity measurement, etc.) has its own governing equation, the *meta-equations* that govern how an Apply-level question is graded are constant. Memorize this table.

| # | K3 Meta-Operation | Governing Expression | Unit Logic | When Used |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Percentage Error** | $\%E = \dfrac{\vert O - T \vert}{T} \times 100$ | Dimensionless % | Comparing experimental vs. standard value |
| 2 | **Mean (Average) of N readings** | $\bar{x} = \dfrac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i$ | Same as $x$ | Reducing random error |
| 3 | **Standard Deviation** | $\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{N-1} \sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}$ | Same as $x$ | Quantifying repeatability |
| 4 | **Linear Regression (Best-Fit Slope)** | $m = \dfrac{N \sum xy - \sum x \sum y}{N \sum x^2 - (\sum x)^2}$ | $\frac{y}{x}$ unit | Graph-based result extraction |
| 5 | **Propagation of Error (Sum/Diff)** | $\Delta z = \sqrt{(\Delta x)^2 + (\Delta y)^2}$ | Same as $z$ | Adding measured quantities |
| 6 | **Propagation of Error (Product/Quotient)** | $\dfrac{\Delta z}{z} = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\Delta x}{x}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{\Delta y}{y}\right)^2}$ | Dimensionless | Multiplying measured quantities |
| 7 | **Significant Figure Rounding** | Round to lowest sig-fig of inputs | — | Final answer presentation |
| 8 | **Logarithmic Interpolation** | $y = y_1 + \dfrac{(y_2 - y_1)}{\log(x_2) - \log(x_1)} \cdot [\log(x) - \log(x_1)]$ | Same as $y$ | Reading values from log-scale graphs |
| 9 | **Unit Conversion Master Equation** | $Q_{\text{desired}} = Q_{\text{given}} \times \prod \left(\dfrac{\text{old unit}}{\text{new unit}}\right)^{\pm 1}$ | Target unit | Converting MPa ↔ psi, cP ↔ Pa·s, etc. |
| 10 | **Reynolds Number (flow regime check)** | $Re = \dfrac{\rho v D}{\mu}$ | Dimensionless | Validating laminar flow assumption |

> [!NOTE]
> **Engineering Utility:** These 10 meta-equations appear in **every** KTU B.Tech laboratory discipline — Mechanical, Civil, Polymer, Chemical, Electrical. They are the "operating system" on which every experiment-specific formula runs. Internal examiners award up to **2 marks** in K3 questions purely for correct unit handling and error analysis.

## 2.3 The K3 Decision Flowchart — How a Student Picks the Right Formula

```
[Read the question]
       ↓
[Identify the target quantity] → e.g., "Find the Young's Modulus"
       ↓
[Identify the measured quantities] → e.g., "Load (N), Elongation (mm), Cross-section (mm²), Gauge length (mm)"
       ↓
[Recall the governing principle] → Hooke's Law: σ = E · ε
       ↓
[Map measured quantities to principle] → σ = F/A, ε = ΔL/L₀
       ↓
[Compose the working formula] → E = (F · L₀) / (A · ΔL)
       ↓
[Check unit consistency] → F [N], L₀ [m], A [m²], ΔL [m] → E [Pa]
       ↓
[Substitute and compute]
       ↓
[Apply sig-fig rule and report]
```

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **The Examiner's Eye:** When a KTU examiner marks a K3 answer, they run this exact flowchart in their head. If your answer is wrong, they will trace *which step* failed. Most students fail at the **unit consistency** or **formula composition** step — both are *preventable* errors.

# STEP-BY-STEP DERIVATION WORKBENCH — SOLVING K3 PROBLEMS

## 3.1 The Master Derivation: From Governing Principle to Working Equation

The hallmark of a K3 answer is that the student **derives the working formula from the governing principle** before plugging in numbers. Below is the exhaustive step-by-step procedure, using the generic stress-strain Hooke's Law as the canonical K3 example.

### Derivation 1 — Young's Modulus from Raw Tensile Data

**Given Governing Principle (Hooke's Law, K2 input):**

$$\sigma = E \cdot \varepsilon$$

where $\sigma$ is engineering stress, $E$ is Young's modulus, and $\varepsilon$ is engineering strain.

**Step 1: Decompose $\sigma$ into measurable quantities**

By definition, engineering stress is the axial force per unit original cross-sectional area:

$$\sigma = \dfrac{F}{A_0}$$

**Step 2: Decompose $A_0$ into measurable quantities**

For a specimen of width $w$ and thickness $t$:

$$A_0 = w \cdot t$$

**Step 3: Decompose $\varepsilon$ into measurable quantities**

Engineering strain is the change in length per unit original length:

$$\varepsilon = \dfrac{\Delta L}{L_0} = \dfrac{L - L_0}{L_0}$$

**Step 4: Substitute (2) and (3) into (1)**

$$E = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon} = \dfrac{F / A_0}{\Delta L / L_0}$$

**Step 5: Algebraic simplification — the Working Formula**

$$E = \dfrac{F \cdot L_0}{A_0 \cdot \Delta L}$$

This is the equation the student uses for computation.

**Step 6: Unit consistency check**

- $F$: Newton $[\text{N}] = [\text{kg} \cdot \text{m} \cdot \text{s}^{-2}]$
- $L_0$: metre $[\text{m}]$
- $A_0$: square metre $[\text{m}^{2}]$
- $\Delta L$: metre $[\text{m}]$

$$[E] = \dfrac{[\text{N}] \cdot [\text{m}]}{[\text{m}^{2}] \cdot [\text{m}]} = \dfrac{\text{N}}{\text{m}^{2}} = \text{Pa} \;\checkmark$$

> The dimensional analysis confirms the result is in Pascals, the SI unit of modulus.

---

### Derivation 2 — Propagation of Error for a Product

**Given:** $E = \dfrac{F \cdot L_0}{A_0 \cdot \Delta L}$ where $F$, $L_0$, $A_0$, and $\Delta L$ are each measured with finite precision.

**Step 1: Take natural log of both sides**

$$\ln E = \ln F + \ln L_0 - \ln A_0 - \ln(\Delta L)$$

**Step 2: Differentiate both sides**

$$\dfrac{dE}{E} = \dfrac{dF}{F} + \dfrac{dL_0}{L_0} - \dfrac{dA_0}{A_0} - \dfrac{d(\Delta L)}{\Delta L}$$

**Step 3: Replace infinitesimals with absolute uncertainties and apply root-sum-square rule**

$$\dfrac{\Delta E}{E} = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\Delta F}{F}\right)^{2} + \left(\dfrac{\Delta L_0}{L_0}\right)^{2} + \left(\dfrac{\Delta A_0}{A_0}\right)^{2} + \left(\dfrac{\Delta(\Delta L)}{\Delta L}\right)^{2}}$$

**Step 4: Solve for absolute uncertainty**

$$\Delta E = E \cdot \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\Delta F}{F}\right)^{2} + \left(\dfrac{\Delta L_0}{L_0}\right)^{2} + \left(\dfrac{\Delta A_0}{A_0}\right)^{2} + \left(\dfrac{\Delta(\Delta L)}{\Delta L}\right)^{2}}$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Examination Tip:** For a K3 problem, you are **not** required to derive the propagation-of-error equation in the exam hall. You are only required to **state** the equation and **apply** it to the numerical data. The derivation above is for *understanding* so that you remember the rule intuitively.

---

### Derivation 3 — The Percentage Error Convention

**Given:** Observed value $O$ and True/Standard value $T$.

**Step 1: Define absolute error**

$$E_{\text{abs}} = \vert O - T \vert$$

**Step 2: Normalize by the true value to obtain a dimensionless ratio**

$$E_{\text{rel}} = \dfrac{E_{\text{abs}}}{T}$$

**Step 3: Convert to percentage**

$$\%E = E_{\text{rel}} \times 100 = \dfrac{\vert O - T \vert}{T} \times 100$$

**Step 4: Worked numerical example**

Suppose a student measures the viscosity of glycerol at 25 °C and obtains $\eta_{\text{obs}} = 1.42 \; \text{Pa} \cdot \text{s}$. The handbook value is $\eta_{\text{std}} = 1.49 \; \text{Pa} \cdot \text{s}$.

$$\begin{aligned}
\%E &= \dfrac{\vert 1.42 - 1.49 \vert}{1.49} \times 100 \\
&= \dfrac{0.07}{1.49} \times 100 \\
&= 4.698 \;\%
\end{aligned}$$

**Step 5: Significant figure discipline**

The input $1.49$ has 3 significant figures, so the final answer must be reported as:

$$\%E \approx 4.70 \;\%$$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Convention:** A percentage error between **0–5%** is considered **excellent**, **5–10%** is **acceptable**, and **>10%** is flagged for **repeat-of-experiment**. Examiners deduct marks only for errors **>10%** if the student has documented the procedure correctly.

# KTU 2024 SCHEME EXAMINATION QUESTION BANK

## 5.1 PART A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

> **[KTU University Exam – May 2024 Style]**

### **Q1. [3 Marks]**
*"Distinguish between K2 (Understand) and K3 (Apply) cognitive levels with one laboratory-based example each."*

**Model Answer:**

K2 (Understand) involves restating a known principle in the learner's own words without necessarily using it. **Example:** A student can verbally explain that *viscosity of a polymer melt decreases with increasing temperature* without performing any test.

K3 (Apply) involves executing a known procedure or formula in a concrete, novel situation. **Example:** A student actually measures the viscosity of a polymer melt at three different temperatures using a Brookfield viscometer, plots the data, and computes the activation energy of flow.

The key distinction is **active execution versus passive comprehension**. K3 demands a numerical or physical outcome derived from the procedure; K2 demands only a verbal or written explanation.

---

### **Q2. [3 Marks]**
*"List the four universal operational phases of any K3 (Apply) laboratory experiment. State the governing meta-equation for percentage error."*

**Model Answer:**

The four universal operational phases of a K3 experiment are:

1. **Identify the Governing Principle** — recognize which theoretical law the experiment demonstrates.
2. **Sequence the Procedural Steps** — arrange the experimental workflow in a logical, safe order.
3. **Execute with Data** — record raw observations and substitute into the governing equation.
4. **Verify and Report** — cross-check the result, compute error, and submit the lab report.

The governing meta-equation for percentage error is:

$$\%E = \dfrac{\vert O - T \vert}{T} \times 100$$

where $O$ is the observed value and $T$ is the true (standard) value.

---

## 5.2 PART B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks Each, Internal Choice)

> **Note:** As per KTU 2024 Scheme, Module-2 carries a 14-mark question with internal choice. Two alternatives are provided below.

---

### **QUESTION A — 14 Marks**
**[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023 Style]**

> *"A polymer tensile-test specimen of original gauge length 50 mm and rectangular cross-section 10 mm × 4 mm is subjected to an axial tensile load of 4800 N. The elongation at this load is 0.85 mm.*
>
> *(a) Compute the Young's Modulus of the material, expressing the result in GPa with appropriate significant figures. [7 marks]*
>
> *(b) If the true cross-sectional area is 5% smaller than the measured value due to surface roughness, recalculate the corrected modulus and determine the percentage correction. [7 marks]"*

#### **Model Solution — Part (a) [7 Marks]**

**Step 1: State the governing equation**

$$E = \dfrac{F \cdot L_0}{A_0 \cdot \Delta L}$$

**Step 2: Identify the measured quantities and their units**

- $F = 4800 \; \text{N}$
- $L_0 = 50 \; \text{mm} = 0.050 \; \text{m}$
- Width $w = 10 \; \text{mm} = 0.010 \; \text{m}$
- Thickness $t = 4 \; \text{mm} = 0.004 \; \text{m}$
- $\Delta L = 0.85 \; \text{mm} = 0.00085 \; \text{m}$

**Step 3: Compute the original cross-sectional area**

$$A_0 = w \cdot t = 0.010 \times 0.004 = 4.0 \times 10^{-5} \; \text{m}^{2}$$

**Step 4: Substitute into the working equation**

$$\begin{aligned}
E &= \dfrac{4800 \times 0.050}{4.0 \times 10^{-5} \times 0.00085} \\
&= \dfrac{240}{3.4 \times 10^{-8}} \\
&= 7.0588 \times 10^{9} \; \text{Pa}
\end{aligned}$$

**Step 5: Convert to GPa and apply sig-fig rule**

$$E = 7.0588 \; \text{GPa} \approx 7.1 \; \text{GPa} \quad \text{(2 sig figs, since } \Delta L \text{ has 2 sig figs)}$$

**Final Answer:** $\boxed{E = 7.1 \; \text{GPa}}$

#### **Model Solution — Part (b) [7 Marks]**

**Step 1: Express the corrected area**

$$A_{\text{true}} = A_0 \times (1 - 0.05) = 0.95 \cdot A_0 = 0.95 \times 4.0 \times 10^{-5} = 3.8 \times 10^{-5} \; \text{m}^{2}$$

**Step 2: Recompute the corrected modulus $E_{\text{corr}}$**

$$\begin{aligned}
E_{\text{corr}} &= \dfrac{F \cdot L_0}{A_{\text{true}} \cdot \Delta L} \\
&= \dfrac{4800 \times 0.050}{3.8 \times 10^{-5} \times 0.00085} \\
&= \dfrac{240}{3.23 \times 10^{-8}} \\
&= 7.4300 \times 10^{9} \; \text{Pa} \\
&= 7.43 \; \text{GPa}
\end{aligned}$$

**Step 3: Calculate the percentage correction**

$$\begin{aligned}
\%\text{Correction} &= \dfrac{\vert E_{\text{corr}} - E \vert}{E} \times 100 \\
&= \dfrac{\vert 7.43 - 7.06 \mid}{7.06} \times 100 \\
&= \dfrac{0.37}{7.06} \times 100 \\
&= 5.24 \; \%
\end{aligned}$$

**Step 4: Interpret the result**

A **5% under-estimation** in cross-sectional area leads to a **5.24% over-estimation** in Young's modulus. This is a **systematic error** that propagates inversely through the modulus formula.

**Final Answer:** $\boxed{E_{\text{corr}} = 7.43 \; \text{GPa}, \quad \%\text{Correction} = 5.24 \; \%}$

---

### **QUESTION B — 14 Marks** (Internal Choice Alternative)
**[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023 Style]**

> *"A capillary rheometer is used to measure the viscosity of a polymer melt at a constant temperature of 200 °C. The capillary has radius $R = 1.0 \; \text{mm}$ and length $L = 20 \; \text{mm}$. A pressure drop of $\Delta P = 5.0 \times 10^{5} \; \text{Pa}$ drives the melt through the capillary at a volumetric flow rate $Q = 1.5 \times 10^{-7} \; \text{m}^{3}/\text{s}$.*
>
> *(a) Using the Hagen-Poiseuille equation, calculate the apparent viscosity of the melt. [7 marks]*
>
> *(b) Compute the wall shear stress, the apparent shear rate, and verify whether the flow regime is laminar by computing the Reynolds number. Assume melt density $\rho = 950 \; \text{kg/m}^{3}$. [7 marks]"*

#### **Model Solution — Part (a) [7 Marks]**

**Step 1: State the Hagen-Poiseuille equation for a circular capillary**

$$Q = \dfrac{\pi R^{4} \Delta P}{8 \eta L}$$

**Step 2: Rearrange to solve for viscosity**

$$\eta = \dfrac{\pi R^{4} \Delta P}{8 Q L}$$

**Step 3: Identify and substitute values**

- $R = 1.0 \times 10^{-3} \; \text{m}$, so $R^{4} = 1.0 \times 10^{-12} \; \text{m}^{4}$
- $\Delta P = 5.0 \times 10^{5} \; \text{Pa}$
- $Q = 1.5 \times 10^{-7} \; \text{m}^{3}/\text{s}$
- $L = 20 \times 10^{-3} \; \text{m} = 0.020 \; \text{m}$

**Step 4: Compute the numerator**

$$\pi R^{4} \Delta P = 3.1416 \times 1.0 \times 10^{-12} \times 5.0 \times 10^{5} = 1.5708 \times 10^{-6}$$

**Step 5: Compute the denominator**

$$8 Q L = 8 \times 1.5 \times 10^{-7} \times 0.020 = 2.4 \times 10^{-8}$$

**Step 6: Divide**

$$\begin{aligned}
\eta &= \dfrac{1.5708 \times 10^{-6}}{2.4 \times 10^{-8}} \\
&= 65.45 \; \text{Pa} \cdot \text{s}
\end{aligned}$$

**Final Answer:** $\boxed{\eta = 65.5 \; \text{Pa} \cdot \text{s}}$

#### **Model Solution — Part (b) [7 Marks]**

**Step 1: Wall shear stress** — given by the force balance on a cylindrical element:

$$\tau_w = \dfrac{R \cdot \Delta P}{2 L}$$

**Step 2: Substitute values**

$$\begin{aligned}
\tau_w &= \dfrac{(1.0 \times 10^{-3}) \times (5.0 \times 10^{5})}{2 \times 0.020} \\
&= \dfrac{500}{0.040} \\
&= 1.25 \times 10^{4} \; \text{Pa} \\
&= 12.5 \; \text{kPa}
\end{aligned}$$

**Step 3: Apparent shear rate** — for a power-law fluid in a capillary, the apparent (Newtonian) shear rate is:

$$\dot{\gamma}_{\text{app}} = \dfrac{4 Q}{\pi R^{3}}$$

**Step 4: Compute the denominator**

$$\pi R^{3} = 3.1416 \times (1.0 \times 10^{-3})^{3} = 3.1416 \times 10^{-9} \; \text{m}^{3}$$

**Step 5: Compute the shear rate**

$$\begin{aligned}
\dot{\gamma}_{\text{app}} &= \dfrac{4 \times 1.5 \times 10^{-7}}{3.1416 \times 10^{-9}} \\
&= \dfrac{6.0 \times 10^{-7}}{3.1416 \times 10^{-9}} \\
&= 190.99 \; \text{s}^{-1} \\
&\approx 191 \; \text{s}^{-1}
\end{aligned}$$

**Step 6: Reynolds number check**

$$Re = \dfrac{\rho v D}{\mu} = \dfrac{\rho \cdot 2v_{\text{avg}} \cdot 2R}{\eta}$$

where $v_{\text{avg}} = Q / (\pi R^{2})$:

$$v_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{1.5 \times 10^{-7}}{3.1416 \times 10^{-6}} = 4.77 \times 10^{-2} \; \text{m/s}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
Re &= \dfrac{950 \times 4.77 \times 10^{-2} \times 2 \times 10^{-3}}{65.45} \\
&= \dfrac{0.0907}{65.45} \\
&= 1.39 \times 10^{-3}
\end{aligned}$$

**Step 7: Interpret the result**

$$Re \approx 1.4 \times 10^{-3} \ll 2100 \quad \therefore \; \text{Flow is firmly LAMINAR} \;\checkmark$$

**Final Answer:** $\boxed{\tau_w = 12.5 \; \text{kPa}, \quad \dot{\gamma}_{\text{app}} \approx 191 \; \text{s}^{-1}, \quad Re \approx 1.4 \times 10^{-3} \; (\text{Laminar})}$

---

## 5.3 KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning & Pitfall Callout

> [!WARNING]
> **Where KTU Students Lose Marks on K3 Questions:**
> 1. **Unit Inconsistency (–2 marks):** Mixing mm with m, or N with kgf, without conversion. Always convert to SI base units *before* substituting.
> 2. **Skipping the Working Formula (–1 mark):** Writing only the final number. Examiners reward the **derivation path**, not just the answer.
> 3. **Sig-Fig Negligence (–1 mark):** Reporting 7.0588 GPa when the input has only 2 sig figs. Always round at the end.
> 4. **No Error Analysis (–2 marks):** Skipping the percentage error / uncertainty section. A K3 answer is **incomplete** without it.
> 5. **Confusing $A_0$ and $A_{\text{true}}$ (–2 marks):** Tensile stress uses *original* area, not *instantaneous* area. Many students mix this up.
> 6. **Verbal description only, no equation (–3 marks):** A K3 answer *must* contain at least one **explicit mathematical expression**. Pure prose = K2, not K3.

---

## 5.4 TOPIC RECAP & RAPID-REVISION CHECKLIST

> [!NOTE]
> **K3 — APPLY: 30-Second Revision Drill**

- [x] **K3 = Execute a known procedure in a *new but similar* situation** — not recall, not analyze, not create.
- [x] **Four operational phases:** Identify Principle → Sequence Steps → Execute with Data → Verify and Report.
- [x] **Master equation for grading:** Hooke's Law for stress-strain, Hagen-Poiseuille for capillary flow, Arrhenius for temperature dependence.
- [x] **Always state the governing equation first**, then derive the working formula, *then* substitute.
- [x] **SI unit discipline:** Convert mm → m, °C → K, cP → Pa·s **before** substituting.
- [x] **Percentage Error formula:** $\%E = \dfrac{\vert O - T \vert}{T} \times 100$ — a 0–5% error is excellent.
- [x] **Propagation of error** uses root-sum-square for products/quotients, simple sum-of-squares for sums/differences.
- [x] **Significant figures:** Report to the *least* precise input measurement.
- [x] **K3 answer must contain math** — prose alone is K2 level and will be downgraded.
- [x] **Reynolds number < 2100 = laminar; > 4000 = turbulent** — always validate the flow-regime assumption.
- [x] **Lab report must have 8 sections:** Aim, Theory, Apparatus, Procedure, Observation, Calculation, Result, Discussion.
- [x] **KTU OBE mark weight:** K3 carries **maximum** cognitive weight in lab internal assessments — mastery here translates directly to grade improvement.
