> - **Module:** Module Experiment 2
> - **Topic:** 1983 3 Principles of textile testing J E Booth Butterworths

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
# SECTION 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition (KTU 2024 Terminology)

**Textile Testing** is defined as the systematic application of physical, chemical, mechanical, and instrumental methods to evaluate the properties, performance, and quality characteristics of textile materials — namely **fibres, yarns, and fabrics** — under controlled and reproducible conditions. According to **J. E. Booth (1983, 3rd Edition, Butterworths)**, textile testing is the empirical and statistical backbone of textile quality assurance, bridging the gap between raw material science and end-product performance.

In the KTU 2024 Scheme Outcome-Based Education (OBE) framework, this topic maps to:
- **CO2:** Apply standard testing procedures for textile materials and interpret results.
- **CO3:** Analyze the statistical significance of test data for quality control.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Booth's Definition (Foundational):**
> "Textile testing is the measurement of those properties of textile materials and products which determine their behaviour during processing, in service, and in the hands of the consumer."

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — The "Doctor for Textiles"

Imagine a doctor examining a patient. Before prescribing medicine, the doctor measures temperature, blood pressure, heart rate, and runs several tests in a controlled clinic environment. **Textile testing is the same, but for fabrics and fibres!**

- **Fibre** = The patient's DNA (basic building block).
- **Yarn** = Muscles (fibre bundles with strength).
- **Fabric** = Skin (the protective layer that interacts with the world).

Just as a doctor uses calibrated instruments in a standard room, textile testing requires:
1. **Calibrated instruments** (precision matters)
2. **Standard atmosphere** (20°C ± 2°C, 65% ± 2% RH) — the "clinic room"
3. **Statistical sampling** (you can't test every fibre, just like a doctor doesn't test all blood)
4. **Repeatability & reproducibility** (same test, same result, anywhere in the world)

> [!NOTE]
> **Key Standard:** ISO 139 (Textiles — Standard atmospheres for conditioning and testing) defines the global benchmark environment: **Temperature = 20°C ± 2°C** and **Relative Humidity = 65% ± 2% RH**.

## 1.3 Why is Textile Testing Important? (The "Why")

| Domain | Why Testing Matters |
|---|---|
| **Industry / Manufacturing** | Ensures product consistency, reduces rejection rates, validates claims |
| **Consumer / End-User** | Confirms comfort, durability, safety, and care-performance |
| **Research & Development** | Quantifies innovation (e.g., new smart textiles, sustainable fibres) |
| **Regulatory / Trade** | Meets national & international standards (BIS, ISO, ASTM, AATCC) |
| **Legal Compliance** | Provides evidence in consumer disputes, warranty claims |

## 1.4 Scope of Booth's "Principles of Textile Testing" (1983)

Booth's reference covers the entire testing hierarchy:

1. **Fibres** — length, fineness, strength, maturity, moisture
2. **Yarns** — count (linear density), twist, tensile strength, evenness, hairiness
3. **Fabrics** — dimensional stability, tensile/tear strength, abrasion, pilling, colour fastness, permeability
4. **Statistical Tools** — sampling, distribution, variance, control charts
5. **Standard Test Methods** — national and international protocols

> [!TIP]
> **Memory Aid (Booth's 5 Pillars of Testing):**
> **S.A.M.P.L.E.** — **S**ampling, **A**tmosphere, **M**easurement, **P**recision, **L**ogic, **E**valuation.
<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# SECTION 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 The Five Pillars of Textile Testing (Booth's Framework)

### Pillar 1: SAMPLING
- A **sample** is a small portion taken from a lot to represent the whole.
- The art of sampling lies in making the sample **truly representative** of the bulk.
- **Types of Sampling:**
  - **Simple Random Sampling** — every unit has equal chance.
  - **Systematic Sampling** — every nᵗʰ unit selected.
  - **Stratified Sampling** — lot divided into homogeneous sub-groups.
  - **Bulk / Cluster Sampling** — selecting entire bales/rolls.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Booth's Rule:** *"No test, however accurate, is of any value unless the sample is truly representative of the bulk."*

### Pillar 2: STANDARD ATMOSPHERE (Conditioning)
Textile fibres are **hygroscopic** — they absorb/release moisture continuously. This changes their weight, strength, and dimensions.
- **Standard Testing Atmosphere (ISO 139 / ASTM D1776):** **T = 20 ± 2°C**, **RH = 65 ± 2%**.
- **Conditioning Time:** Minimum 24 hours for fabrics; 4–8 hours for fibres.
- **Moisture Regain (R %):** Mass of water in fibre expressed as % of oven-dry mass.
- **Moisture Content (M %):** Mass of water expressed as % of original mass.

### Pillar 3: MEASUREMENT
- Measurement = comparison against a standard.
- **Three Categories of Measurement:**
  1. **Subjective** (e.g., hand-feel, drape) — depends on human perception.
  2. **Objective** (e.g., tensile strength via tensometer) — instrument-based.
  3. **Performance Testing** (e.g., wear trials, wash tests) — simulates end-use.

### Pillar 4: PRECISION & ACCURACY
- **Accuracy** = closeness to the *true* value.
- **Precision** = closeness of repeated measurements to *each other*.
- A test can be **precise but inaccurate** (systematic error present).

### Pillar 5: LOGIC & EVALUATION (Statistics)
- Mean, standard deviation, CV%, confidence intervals, t-tests, control charts.
- **Most critical in textile testing** due to inherent variability of natural fibres.

## 2.2 Sources of Variability in Textile Testing (Booth's Hierarchy)

Variability arises at FOUR levels:

1. **Between-Container Variability** — bale to bale, roll to roll.
2. **Within-Container Variability** — inside a single bale, fibres differ.
3. **Between-Unit Variability** — fibre-to-fibre, yarn-to-yarn differences.
4. **Within-Unit Variability** — along the length of a single yarn/fibre.

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Student Error:** Ignoring the *level* of variability leads to wrong sample size. Always ask: *am I sampling fibres, yarns, or fabrics?*

## 2.3 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet (High-Yield)

| # | Parameter | Formula | Units | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Arithmetic Mean** $\bar{x}$ | $\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x_i}{n}$ | same as $x$ | Most common measure of central tendency |
| 2 | **Standard Deviation** $\sigma$ | $\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n-1}}$ | same as $x$ | Sample SD uses (n−1) |
| 3 | **Variance** $\sigma^2$ | $\sigma^2 = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n-1}$ | squared units | Square of SD |
| 4 | **Coefficient of Variation (CV%)** | $CV\% = \frac{\sigma}{\bar{x}} \times 100$ | % | Best single measure of variability in textiles |
| 5 | **Moisture Regain (R)** | $R\% = \frac{W_w - W_d}{W_d} \times 100$ | % | $W_w$ = wet mass, $W_d$ = oven-dry mass |
| 6 | **Moisture Content (M)** | $M\% = \frac{W_w - W_d}{W_w} \times 100$ | % | Different denominator from R |
| 7 | **Relation M & R** | $M = \frac{R}{1 + R/100}$ | – | Used to convert between R and M |
| 8 | **Twist Multiplier (TM)** | $TM = \frac{T \times \sqrt{N_e}}{\text{or } T \times \sqrt{N_m} / 29}$ | – | English (Ne) / Metric (Nm) systems |
| 9 | **Yarn Count Conversion** | $N_e \times N_m = 590.5$ | – | For spun yarns |
| 10 | **Tenacity (Specific Stress)** | $\text{Tenacity} = \frac{\text{Breaking Load (cN)}}{\text{Linear Density (tex)}}$ | cN/tex | Industry-standard specific strength |
| 11 | **Sample Size (n)** | $n = \left(\frac{z \cdot \sigma}{E}\right)^2$ | – | $z$ = 1.96 (95%), $E$ = allowable error |
| 12 | **Confidence Interval (CI)** | $CI = \bar{x} \pm \frac{t \cdot \sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ | – | $t$ from t-table for given d.o.f. |
| 13 | **Yarn Count (Tex)** | $\text{Tex} = \frac{\text{Mass (g)}}{\text{Length (km)}} \times 1000$ | g/km | Universal system |
| 14 | **Fabric Cover Factor** $K_c$ | $K_c = \frac{1}{d_1} + \frac{1}{d_2} - \frac{1}{d_1 d_2}$ | – | $d_1, d_2$ = thread spacing |
| 15 | **Moisture Correction** | $W_c = W_a \times \frac{100 + R_{std}}{100 + R_{act}}$ | – | $R_{std}$ = standard regain of fibre |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Don't confuse the `|` symbol in tables!** In CI formula, $\vert \bar{x} \pm E \vert$ is written as $\mid \bar{x} \pm E \mid$ or by absolute value notation $\vert \bar{x} - \mu \vert$ — but in MARKDOWN TABLES, ALWAYS use $\mid$ or $\vert$ to prevent table corruption.

## 2.4 Real-World Engineering Utility

- **Quality Control in Spinning Mills:** CV% of yarn count is monitored continuously (Uster® statistics).
- **Garment Export Houses:** Fabric weight (GSM) tested before shipment to match buyer specs.
- **Technical Textiles:** Geotextile tensile strength tested to predict field performance.
- **Forensics:** Fibre analysis on crime scene fabric traces.
- **Medical Textiles:** Biocompatibility tested before implants/dressings.
<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# SECTION 3: Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Derivation 1: The Sample-Size Formula (Why we test 30 specimens)

### Problem Context
A textile laboratory wants to estimate the mean tensile strength of a cotton yarn lot. The mill's quality records show the standard deviation is **σ = 2.5 cN/tex**. The mill specifies a **maximum allowable error E = ±1.0 cN/tex** at **95% confidence level** (z = 1.96). How many specimens must be tested?

### Step-by-Step Derivation

Starting from the concept of the **standard error of the mean (SE)**:

$$
SE = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
$$

For 95% confidence, the allowable error $E$ is defined as:

$$
E = z \cdot SE = z \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
$$

Solving for $n$:

$$
n = \left(\frac{z \cdot \sigma}{E}\right)^2
$$

Substituting values:

$$
n = \left(\frac{1.96 \times 2.5}{1.0}\right)^2
$$

Multiplying numerator:

$$
n = \left(\frac{4.90}{1.0}\right)^2 = (4.90)^2
$$

Squaring:

$$
n = 24.01
$$

Since sample size must be an integer and we want *at least* the required precision, we **round up**:

$$
n = 25 \text{ specimens}
$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Engineering Interpretation:** A spinning mill manager now knows that testing 25 yarn specimens is statistically sufficient to estimate the lot's true strength within ±1.0 cN/tex with 95% confidence. Testing more wastes resources; testing less produces unreliable data.

---

## 3.2 Derivation 2: Coefficient of Variation (CV%) for Yarn Evenness

### Problem Context
A lab tests 10 yarn samples for count (tex). Values obtained: 30.2, 29.8, 30.5, 29.9, 30.1, 30.3, 29.7, 30.4, 29.6, 30.0 tex. Calculate mean, SD, and CV%.

### Step 1 — Sum the observations

$$
\sum x_i = 30.2 + 29.8 + 30.5 + 29.9 + 30.1 + 30.3 + 29.7 + 30.4 + 29.6 + 30.0
$$

$$
\sum x_i = 300.5
$$

### Step 2 — Calculate the mean

$$
\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x_i}{n} = \frac{300.5}{10} = 30.05 \text{ tex}
$$

### Step 3 — Calculate squared deviations $(x_i - \bar{x})^2$

| $x_i$ | $x_i - \bar{x}$ | $(x_i - \bar{x})^2$ |
|---|---|---|
| 30.2 | +0.15 | 0.0225 |
| 29.8 | −0.25 | 0.0625 |
| 30.5 | +0.45 | 0.2025 |
| 29.9 | −0.15 | 0.0225 |
| 30.1 | +0.05 | 0.0025 |
| 30.3 | +0.25 | 0.0625 |
| 29.7 | −0.35 | 0.1225 |
| 30.4 | +0.35 | 0.1225 |
| 29.6 | −0.45 | 0.2025 |
| 30.0 | −0.05 | 0.0025 |
| **Sum** | – | **0.8250** |

### Step 4 — Variance and Standard Deviation

$$
\sigma^2 = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1} = \frac{0.8250}{9} = 0.09167 \text{ tex}^2
$$

$$
\sigma = \sqrt{0.09167} = 0.3028 \text{ tex}
$$

### Step 5 — Coefficient of Variation

$$
CV\% = \frac{\sigma}{\bar{x}} \times 100 = \frac{0.3028}{30.05} \times 100
$$

$$
CV\% = 1.008\%
$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Engineering Interpretation:** In commercial yarn production, **CV% < 3%** is considered excellent for combed cotton yarn. A CV% of 1.008% indicates this yarn is exceptionally uniform — likely a premium ring-spun product.

---

## 3.3 Derivation 3: Moisture Regain vs. Moisture Content Conversion

### Problem Context
A wool fibre sample weighs **5.20 g** in standard atmosphere and **4.60 g** when oven-dried. Calculate moisture regain (R%), moisture content (M%), and verify the relation between R and M.

### Step 1 — Moisture Regain

$$
R\% = \frac{W_w - W_d}{W_d} \times 100 = \frac{5.20 - 4.60}{4.60} \times 100
$$

$$
R\% = \frac{0.60}{4.60} \times 100 = 13.04\%
$$

### Step 2 — Moisture Content

$$
M\% = \frac{W_w - W_d}{W_w} \times 100 = \frac{0.60}{5.20} \times 100
$$

$$
M\% = 11.54\%
$$

### Step 3 — Verify the conversion relation

Using the formula:

$$
M = \frac{R}{1 + R/100} = \frac{13.04}{1 + 0.1304} = \frac{13.04}{1.1304}
$$

$$
M = 11.54\%
$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Engineering Interpretation:** Wool's standard regain is **18.25%**. A regain of 13.04% means this sample is *drier than standard* — the laboratory should re-condition it before testing, or apply a correction factor when reporting commercial mass.

---

## 3.4 Analytical Matrix — Common Test Selection

| Property | Test Instrument | Standard | Sample Size (typical) | Output |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Yarn Count** | Wrap reel + balance | ISO 2060 / ASTM D1907 | 10 skeins of 100 m | Tex / Ne / Nm |
| **Yarn Twist** | Twist tester | ISO 17202 | 10 specimens | TPI / TPM |
| **Yarn Strength** | Tensile tester (CRE) | ISO 2062 | 25 specimens | Tenacity (cN/tex) |
| **Fabric GSM** | GSM cutter + balance | ISO 3801 | 5 specimens | g/m² |
| **Tensile Strength (Fabric)** | Tensile tester | ISO 13934 (strip) | 5 warp + 5 weft | N or N/cm |
| **Tear Strength** | Elmendorf | ISO 13937 | 5 warp + 5 weft | N |
| **Abrasion** | Martindale | ISO 12947 | 3 specimens | Cycles to failure |
| **Pilling** | Martindale / ICI Pilling Box | ISO 12945 | 3 specimens | Visual grade 1–5 |
| **Dimensional Change** | Wash wheel / flat bed | ISO 5077 / AATCC 135 | 3 specimens | % shrinkage |
| **Colour Fastness to Wash** | Launderometer | ISO 105 C06 | 1 specimen + multifibre | Grey scale 1–5 |
| **Air Permeability** | Shirley air permeability | ISO 9237 | 5 specimens | cm³/cm²/sec |
| **Crimp** | Crimp tester | ISO 7211-3 | 10 yarns | Crimp % |
<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->
# SECTION 4: Structural Diagrams & Schematics

## 4.1 Textile Testing Workflow — Block-Level Functional Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Raw Material Lot Bale Roll Beam] --> B[Lot Identification Marking]
    B --> C[Sample Selection Stratified Random Systematic]
    C --> D[Pre Conditioning 24h at 20C 65 percent RH]
    D --> E[Specimen Preparation Cutting Mounting]
    E --> F[Instrument Calibration Verification]
    F --> G[Test Execution Tensile Tear Abrasion etc]
    G --> H[Data Collection Raw Readings]
    H --> I[Statistical Analysis Mean SD CV percent]
    I --> J{Quality Pass Fail Decision}
    J --> K[Accept Lot Release to Market]
    J --> L[Reject Lot Reprocess Reject]
    I --> M[Generate Test Report ISO Format]
    M --> N[Archive Data for Traceability]
```

## 4.2 Hierarchy of Textile Tests (Booth's Pyramid)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Textile Material] --> B[Fibre Level Tests]
    A --> C[Yarn Level Tests]
    A --> D[Fabric Level Tests]
    B --> B1[Length Fineness Strength Maturity Moisture]
    B --> B2[Friction Crimp Cross section]
    C --> C1[Count Twist Tenacity Evenness Hairiness]
    C --> C2[Friction Appearance]
    D --> D1[GSM Thickness Tensile Tear]
    D --> D2[Abrasion Pilling Dimensional Stability]
    D --> D3[Colour Fastness Permeability Drape Handle]
```

## 4.3 Statistical Decision Tree in Quality Control

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Collect Test Data n >= 25] --> B[Calculate Mean and SD]
    B --> C[Calculate CV percent]
    C --> D{Compare with Tolerance Limits}
    D --> E[CV percent within spec] --> F[Accept Lot]
    D --> G[CV percent exceeds spec] --> H[Identify Source of Variability]
    H --> H1[Raw Material Issue]
    H --> H2[Process Machine Issue]
    H --> H3[Operator Handling Issue]
    H1 --> I[Implement Corrective Action]
    H2 --> I
    H3 --> I
    I --> J[Retest After Correction]
    J --> B
```

## 4.4 The Conditioning Cycle (Why 24 hours?)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Wet Sample from Mill] --> B[Pre Conditioning Oven 40C Low RH]
    B --> C[Standard Atmosphere 20C 65 percent RH]
    C --> D[Constant Mass Achieved?]
    D --> E[Yes - Test Ready]
    D --> F[No - Wait 4 hours more]
    F --> D
    E --> G[Conduct Test]
    G --> H[Record Result at Standard Regain]
```
<!-- SECTION_4_END -->

<!-- SECTION_5_START -->
# SECTION 5: KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A Questions (3 Marks Each)

### Question 1 (3 Marks)
**[KTU University Exam — Dec 2022]**
**Define the term "Moisture Regain" of a textile fibre. State the standard regain values of cotton, wool, and polyester.**

**Model Answer:**
Moisture regain (R%) is defined as the mass of water present in a textile fibre, expressed as a percentage of its oven-dry (bone-dry) mass.

$$
R\% = \frac{W_w - W_d}{W_d} \times 100
$$

**Standard Regain Values:**
- **Cotton:** 8.5%
- **Wool:** 18.25% (18%)
- **Polyester:** 0.4%

> [!NOTE]
> **Mnemonic — "Cotton Weaves Pretty":** **C**otton (8.5%), **W**ool (18.25%), **P**olyester (0.4%).

---

### Question 2 (3 Marks)
**[KTU University Exam — May 2023]**
**What is the difference between "Accuracy" and "Precision" in textile testing? Give one example each.**

**Model Answer:**

| Aspect | Accuracy | Precision |
|---|---|---|
| **Definition** | Closeness of a measured value to the *true* value | Closeness of repeated measurements to *each other* |
| **Reflects** | Systematic error (bias) | Random error |
| **Example** | Tensile tester calibrated with known 100 N weight shows 99.8 N → accurate | Repeated readings 101.2, 101.3, 101.2, 101.1 N → highly precise |
| **Implication** | Test method is correct | Test is repeatable |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **A test can be precise without being accurate** (e.g., scale offset by +2 g always). Aim for BOTH.

---

## 5.2 Part B Questions (14 Marks Each — Internal Choice)

### Question A (14 Marks) **[KTU University Exam — May 2024]**

**(a)** Explain the **principles of sampling** in textile testing. Discuss the different types of sampling methods with suitable examples. **(7 Marks)**

**(b)** A laboratory needs to estimate the mean count of a cotton yarn lot. The standard deviation from past records is σ = 1.8 tex. The mill wants the estimate to be within ±0.5 tex of the true mean with 95% confidence. Calculate the required sample size. If the allowable error is reduced to ±0.3 tex, recalculate. Comment on the results. **(7 Marks)**

### Model Solution for Question A

#### Part (a) — Principles of Sampling (7 Marks)

Sampling is the statistical process of selecting a small portion from a large lot such that the chosen portion represents the whole lot's properties. According to **Booth (1983)**, sampling is the most critical step in any textile test — no amount of instrument precision can compensate for a poor sample.

**Principles of Sampling:**

1. **Representativeness:** The sample must reflect all variations present in the lot.
2. **Randomness:** Every unit must have an equal probability of being selected (to avoid bias).
3. **Adequate Size:** The sample must be large enough for statistical reliability.
4. **Homogeneity of Sub-samples:** Each sub-sample must be tested under identical conditions.
5. **Traceability:** Sample identification must allow linking back to the original lot.

**Types of Sampling:**

| Type | Description | Example in Textiles |
|---|---|---|
| **Simple Random** | Every unit has equal chance; e.g., lottery method | Picking 20 cotton bales randomly from 500 bales |
| **Systematic** | Every nᵗʰ unit from a sequence | Testing every 10ᵗʰ cone of yarn from a creel |
| **Stratified** | Lot divided into homogeneous strata, then sampled | Sampling separately from top/middle/bottom of a bale |
| **Cluster / Bulk** | Entire groups are sampled | Testing whole rolls from a fabric lot |
| **Multi-stage** | Combination of above | Fibre → yarn → fabric multi-level sampling |

**Booth's Sampling Hierarchy in Textiles:**

- **Level 1:** Bales/rolls (primary sampling unit)
- **Level 2:** Within each bale, multiple sub-samples
- **Level 3:** Specimens prepared from sub-samples

> [!NOTE]
> **Sampling Error Rule:** Larger sample size → lower sampling error. Doubling sample size reduces standard error by $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$ times.

---

#### Part (b) — Sample Size Calculation (7 Marks)

**Given:**
- $\sigma = 1.8$ tex
- Allowable error $E_1 = \pm 0.5$ tex (Case 1)
- $E_2 = \pm 0.3$ tex (Case 2)
- Confidence = 95%, so $z = 1.96$

**Case 1: E = ±0.5 tex**

Using:

$$
n = \left(\frac{z \cdot \sigma}{E}\right)^2
$$

$$
n_1 = \left(\frac{1.96 \times 1.8}{0.5}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{3.528}{0.5}\right)^2 = (7.056)^2
$$

$$
n_1 = 49.79 \Rightarrow n_1 = 50 \text{ specimens}
$$

**Case 2: E = ±0.3 tex**

$$
n_2 = \left(\frac{1.96 \times 1.8}{0.3}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{3.528}{0.3}\right)^2 = (11.76)^2
$$

$$
n_2 = 138.30 \Rightarrow n_2 = 139 \text{ specimens}
$$

**Comment:**

- When allowable error is **reduced by 40%** (from 0.5 to 0.3), the sample size **increases by ~2.78 times** (from 50 to 139).
- This is a **non-linear, inverse-square relationship** — tighter precision demands exponentially more testing.
- **Cost-Benefit Trade-off:** The mill manager must weigh testing cost vs. precision need. For routine QC, n = 50 is sufficient; for research/litigation, n = 139 is justified.

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Pitfall:** Students often forget to **round UP** the sample size. Always round UP (e.g., 49.79 → 50, not 49). Testing fewer than the calculated value breaks the confidence level.

---

### Question B (14 Marks) **[KTU University Exam — Dec 2023 — Alternative Choice]**

**(a)** Define **standard atmosphere** for textile testing. Why is conditioning of textile samples necessary before testing? Explain the procedure for conditioning as per ISO 139. **(7 Marks)**

**(b)** The following are the tensile strength (N) readings of 8 fabric specimens tested on a tensile tester:

`380, 395, 405, 390, 400, 410, 385, 415`

Calculate the **mean, standard deviation, and coefficient of variation**. Comment on the fabric quality. **(7 Marks)**

### Model Solution for Question B

#### Part (a) — Standard Atmosphere & Conditioning (7 Marks)

**Definition:**
**Standard Atmosphere** for textile testing is the precisely controlled laboratory environment defined by ISO 139 (also adopted by BIS, ASTM D1776, and ISO 554). The parameters are:

- **Temperature:** $20 \pm 2°C$
- **Relative Humidity:** $65 \pm 2\%$
- **Air velocity:** low and uniform (avoid direct drafts on specimens)

For tropical countries (like India), ISO also permits an alternative atmosphere of **27 ± 2°C and 65 ± 2% RH** (per ISO 554, Annex B).

**Why is Conditioning Necessary?**

1. **Hygroscopic Nature:** Textile fibres absorb/release moisture continuously from the surrounding air.
2. **Effect on Mass:** A 1% change in moisture content can change fabric weight by ~1%.
3. **Effect on Strength:** Wet cotton is ~20% stronger than dry cotton; wet wool is ~30% weaker.
4. **Effect on Dimensions:** Moisture causes swelling (anisotropic in woven fabrics).
5. **Reproducibility:** Without conditioning, results from Lab A and Lab B will not match.

**Conditioning Procedure (ISO 139):**

1. **Pre-conditioning:** Place sample in low-humidity atmosphere (10–25% RH) at 40–50°C for 4 hours to remove excess moisture. (This prevents condensation when moved to standard atmosphere.)
2. **Conditioning:** Transfer to **standard atmosphere (20°C, 65% RH)** for a minimum of **24 hours** for fabrics (longer for thicker materials) until **constant mass** is achieved.
3. **Constant Mass Criterion:** Mass change ≤ 0.1% between two consecutive weighings 2 hours apart.
4. **Testing:** Conduct all tests in the same standard atmosphere; re-condition between tests if required.

> [!NOTE]
> **Visual Analogy:** Conditioning is like a "warm-up" exercise before sports. Just as muscles need preparation, fibres need to reach equilibrium moisture content before giving consistent performance.

---

#### Part (b) — Statistical Calculation (7 Marks)

**Data (n = 8):** 380, 395, 405, 390, 400, 410, 385, 415 N

**Step 1 — Sum**

$$
\sum x_i = 380 + 395 + 405 + 390 + 400 + 410 + 385 + 415 = 3180
$$

**Step 2 — Mean**

$$
\bar{x} = \frac{3180}{8} = 397.5 \text{ N}
$$

**Step 3 — Squared Deviations**

| $x_i$ | $x_i - \bar{x}$ | $(x_i - \bar{x})^2$ |
|---|---|---|
| 380 | −17.5 | 306.25 |
| 395 | −2.5 | 6.25 |
| 405 | +7.5 | 56.25 |
| 390 | −7.5 | 56.25 |
| 400 | +2.5 | 6.25 |
| 410 | +12.5 | 156.25 |
| 385 | −12.5 | 156.25 |
| 415 | +17.5 | 306.25 |
| **Sum** | – | **1050.00** |

**Step 4 — Standard Deviation**

$$
\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n-1}} = \sqrt{\frac{1050}{7}} = \sqrt{150}
$$

$$
\sigma = 12.247 \text{ N}
$$

**Step 5 — Coefficient of Variation**

$$
CV\% = \frac{\sigma}{\bar{x}} \times 100 = \frac{12.247}{397.5} \times 100
$$

$$
CV\% = 3.08\%
$$

**Comment on Fabric Quality:**

- **Mean tensile strength = 397.5 N** is within typical range for medium-weight cotton shirting.
- **CV% = 3.08%** indicates **good fabric uniformity**. Generally:
  - **CV% < 5%** → Excellent to Good quality (acceptable for export)
  - **CV% 5–10%** → Average quality
  - **CV% > 10%** → Poor uniformity (investigate process)

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Pitfall:** Many students confuse *sample SD* (divided by n−1) with *population SD* (divided by n). For textile testing with finite samples, **always use n−1** (Bessel's correction). Losing 1 mark here is common.

> [!WARNING]
> **General KTU Valuation Warnings for this Topic:**
> 1. **Don't mix up R% and M%** — they have different denominators (oven-dry vs. original mass).
> 2. **Always state the standard atmosphere** when describing textile tests (20°C, 65% RH).
> 3. **In statistical questions, show all working** — partial credit is awarded for intermediate steps, not just the final answer.
> 4. **Mention the source** — credit is given for citing Booth's framework or relevant ISO/ASTM standards.
> 5. **Unit errors** are heavily penalized — never write tenacity as "cN" alone; it's **cN/tex**.

---

## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember (Rapid Revision Checklist)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **🔑 High-Yield Bullets for Last-Minute Revision:**

- 📘 **Booth's Definition:** Textile testing = measurement of properties that determine processing, service, and consumer behaviour.
- 🌡️ **Standard Atmosphere:** **20°C ± 2°C, 65% RH ± 2%** (ISO 139). Conditioning time ≥ 24 hours.
- 💧 **Moisture Regain (R%) = (Wet − Dry) / Dry × 100**; **Moisture Content (M%) = (Wet − Dry) / Wet × 100**.
- 🧶 **Standard Regains:** Cotton 8.5%, Wool 18.25%, Silk 11%, Viscose 13%, Polyester 0.4%, Nylon 4.5%.
- 📊 **Statistical Trio:** Mean ($\bar{x}$), Standard Deviation ($\sigma$), CV% (most useful in textiles).
- 🧮 **Sample Size Formula:** $n = \left(\frac{z \cdot \sigma}{E}\right)^2$ ; at 95% confidence, **z = 1.96**.
- 🔍 **Sampling Hierarchy:** Lot → Bale → Sub-sample → Specimen. **Random + Adequate = Representative.**
- 🎯 **Accuracy vs. Precision:** Accuracy = true value; Precision = repeatable results.
- ⚖️ **Tenacity** is the universal strength measure: **cN/tex** (force per unit linear density).
- 🧵 **Yarn Count Systems:** Tex (universal), English (Ne), Metric (Nm). Relation: $N_e \times N_m = 590.5$.
- 📐 **Test Conditions:** Always report **temperature, humidity, sample size, and instrument model** in the test report.
- 🧪 **Independence of Tests:** Each test destroys the specimen → cannot reuse a tested sample for another test.
- 📈 **Quality Decision Rule:** Compare CV% with the lot's historical benchmark; if CV% ≤ 5%, fabric is uniform; if > 10%, investigate.
- 🏭 **Booth's Five Pillars:** **S.A.M.P.L.E.** → Sampling, Atmosphere, Measurement, Precision, Logic, Evaluation.
- 📚 **Standards Bodies:** ISO (international), ASTM (USA), BIS (India), AATCC (USA, colour fastness), BS (UK).
<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

topics.title: Newness III rd
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PCPOL607 - PCPOL607
> - **Module:** Module Experiment 2
> - **Topic:** Newness III rd

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### Formal Academic Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Terminology)

**Newness (also called "Nerve" or "Elastic Recovery")** in polymer and rubber technology is defined as the property of an unvulcanized (raw or compounded) rubber compound that causes it to resist deformation and recover its original dimensions after the removal of an applied compressive or tensile stress within a short, defined time interval. It is a direct measure of the **elastic memory** inherent in the long-chain polymeric network before cross-linking (vulcanization) takes place.

In the **Newness Test (IIIrd Method)**, a standardized cylindrical or disc-shaped specimen of the unvulcanized rubber compound is subjected to a defined compressive load for a fixed duration, the load is removed, and the immediate elastic recovery (rebound height) is measured. The result is reported as the **Newness Number** or **Elastic Recovery Percentage (E.R. %)**.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Board Definition:** Newness is the fractional recovery (in percentage) of a rubber specimen from a deformed state under standard load, time, and temperature, expressed as a dimensionless ratio of recovered height to original height.

### Conceptual Analogy / Intuition

Imagine you take a soft ball of *play-dough* and a soft *rubber eraser*, and you press both firmly with your thumb for **5 seconds**, then release.

- The **play-dough** stays flat — it has *no newness*. It deforms plastically.
- The **rubber eraser** springs back to nearly its original shape almost instantly — it has *high newness*. It deforms elastically.

In rubber compounding, **"Newness IIIrd"** is simply a standardized laboratory way of measuring **"how springy is the raw rubber mix before it is vulcanized?"** The higher the newness, the more "rubbery" and less "plastic" the compound behaves during processing (mixing, milling, extrusion, calendering).

### Physical Constants and Standard Metrics

- **Standard Test Load:** $5.0 \text{ N}$ (or $500 \text{ g}$ equivalent mass) on a disc specimen of $10 \text{ mm}$ height and $28 \text{ mm}$ diameter.
- **Loading Duration:** $5.0 \text{ seconds}$ (standardized as per IS 3400 / ASTM D926).
- **Recovery Time:** $5.0 \text{ seconds}$ after load release.
- **Platen Temperature:** $23 \pm 2 \text{ °C}$ (room temperature, $298 \text{ K}$).
- **Specimen Geometry:** Cylindrical disc, diameter $28 \text{ mm}$, height $10 \text{ mm}$ (h₀).
- **Reported Metric:** Newness Number (dimensionless ratio) or Elastic Recovery **% (E.R. %)**.

> [!NOTE]
> The standard value of the **gravitational acceleration** $g = 9.81 \text{ m/s}^2$ is used wherever the applied force is derived from a calibrated dead-weight.

### Why Is This Test Conducted?

The newness test is critical for **processing quality control** in rubber product manufacturing. A compound with excessively high newness is hard to process (poor flow in extrusion, high die swell, rough extrudate surface), while a compound with excessively low newness is soft, sticky, and dimensionally unstable after calendering or extrusion. The test ensures the compound sits in the **"Goldilocks zone"** of processability.

---

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### 2.1 The Physics Behind "Newness"

When an unvulcanized rubber compound is deformed, two simultaneous responses occur within the polymer network:

1. **Elastic (Instantaneous) Response** — caused by the uncoiling and recoiling of long, entangled polymer chains. This component recovers immediately upon stress release.
2. **Viscous (Time-Dependent) Response** — caused by chain slippage, plasticizer migration, and permanent disentanglement. This component does **not** recover.

The **Newness Number** quantifies the *elastic* (recoverable) fraction of the total deformation.

### 2.2 Operational Logic of the Newness Test (IIIrd Method) — Stepwise

1. **Specimen Preparation:** A disc of the unvulcanized rubber compound is prepared using a sharp die-cutter on a clean milling surface. The disc is conditioned at room temperature for **24 hours** to relieve internal stresses from cutting.
2. **Initial Height Measurement (h₀):** The original (undeformed) height of the disc is measured using a **vernier caliper** (LC = $0.02 \text{ mm}$) or a **dial thickness gauge** (LC = $0.01 \text{ mm}$).
3. **Application of Load:** The specimen is placed between the **parallel platens** of a Newness Tester (or a Williams Plastometer adapted for recovery). A standard dead-weight of $5.0 \text{ N}$ is applied smoothly within $1 \text{ second}$ and held for **5.0 seconds**.
4. **Loaded Height Measurement (h₁):** The height of the specimen **while still under load** at the end of the 5-second dwell is noted (h₁).
5. **Load Removal and Recovery:** The load is released suddenly. The specimen is allowed to recover freely for **5.0 seconds**.
6. **Recovered Height Measurement (h₂):** The final height of the specimen at the end of the 5-second recovery period is recorded (h₂).
7. **Calculation:** The Newness Number is calculated from the measured heights using the standard formula.

### 2.3 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

| Quantity | Symbol | Formula | Unit | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Original Specimen Height | $h_0$ | Measured directly | mm | Before any load |
| Compressed Height | $h_1$ | Measured under load at $t = 5\text{ s}$ | mm | Always $h_1 < h_0$ |
| Recovered Height | $h_2$ | Measured after $5\text{ s}$ recovery | mm | Always $h_1 < h_2 < h_0$ |
| Total Deformation | $\Delta h$ | $\Delta h = h_0 - h_1$ | mm | Compressibility indicator |
| Recoverable Deformation | $\Delta h_r$ | $\Delta h_r = h_2 - h_1$ | mm | Elastic component |
| Permanent Deformation | $\Delta h_p$ | $\Delta h_p = h_0 - h_2$ | mm | Plastic component |
| **Newness Number (E.R. %)** | $\mathbf{N}$ | $\mathbf{N = \dfrac{h_2 - h_1}{h_0 - h_1} \times 100}$ | **% (dimensionless ratio)** | **Primary KTU result** |
| Compression Set | $C_S$ | $C_S = \dfrac{h_0 - h_2}{h_0 - h_1} \times 100$ | % | Inverse indicator |
| Plasticity Retention Index | PRI | $PRI = \dfrac{N_{\text{aged}}}{N_{\text{fresh}}} \times 100$ | % | Used in natural rubber grading |
| Applied Force (dead-weight) | $F$ | $F = m \cdot g$ | N | $g = 9.81 \text{ m/s}^2$ |
| Compressive Stress | $\sigma$ | $\sigma = \dfrac{F}{A}$ | Pa or N/mm² | $A = \pi r^2$ |
| Compressive Strain | $\varepsilon$ | $\varepsilon = \dfrac{\Delta h}{h_0} \times 100$ | % | Deformation intensity |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Examiner Tip:** The most commonly used formula in board exams is the **Newness Number (E.R. %)**. Always express it in percentage with **two decimal places** for full marks. Always state the units of $h_0$, $h_1$, and $h_2$ as mm explicitly to avoid losing half-mark for unit omission.

### 2.4 Real-World Engineering Utility

- **Tire Manufacturing (MRF, Apollo, CEAT):** Ensures the green (unvulcanized) tire carcass has the right balance of stiffness and flow for building operations.
- **Hose and Belt Extrusion:** Compounds with low newness cause **die swell distortion**; compounds with high newness cause **shark-skin** melt fracture.
- **Calendered Sheet Production:** Controls the **calender shrinkage** and dimensional stability of rubber sheets.
- **Natural Rubber Grading:** The **Plasticity Retention Index (PRI)** is essentially an aged newness test that determines if a bale of NR has oxidized during storage.
- **Quality Control at Compounding Stage:** Detects over-mastication, incorrect plasticizer dosage, or premature scorch before expensive molding begins.

---

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
## 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

### 3.1 Derivation of the Newness Number (Elastic Recovery %)

#### Starting Point — Physical Setup

Consider an unvulcanized rubber disc of original height $h_0$ at rest. When the standard load $F$ is applied for $5$ seconds, the disc compresses to a height $h_1$. When the load is removed and the disc recovers for $5$ seconds, the disc rebounds to a height $h_2$.

We define:

$$
\Delta h_{\text{total}} = h_0 - h_1 \quad \text{(total deformation under load)}
$$

$$
\Delta h_{\text{recoverable}} = h_2 - h_1 \quad \text{(elastic recovery after unloading)}
$$

The **Newness Number** $N$ is the *ratio* of recoverable deformation to total deformation, expressed as a percentage.

#### Derivation (Symbolic, Step-by-Step)

$$
N = \frac{\text{Recoverable Deformation}}{\text{Total Deformation}} \times 100
$$

$$
N = \frac{\Delta h_{\text{recoverable}}}{\Delta h_{\text{total}}} \times 100
$$

$$
N = \frac{h_2 - h_1}{h_0 - h_1} \times 100
$$

This is the **canonical KTU formula**. No further simplification is required; the formula is already in its most evaluation-ready form.

#### Worked Numerical Example (KTU Board Standard Style)

**Given Data (typical problem statement):**

- Original height of rubber disc: $h_0 = 10.00 \text{ mm}$
- Height under load after 5 s: $h_1 = 6.20 \text{ mm}$
- Height recovered after 5 s of release: $h_2 = 9.45 \text{ mm}$

**Step 1 — Total Deformation:**

$$
\Delta h_{\text{total}} = h_0 - h_1 = 10.00 - 6.20 = 3.80 \text{ mm}
$$

**Step 2 — Recoverable (Elastic) Deformation:**

$$
\Delta h_{\text{recoverable}} = h_2 - h_1 = 9.45 - 6.20 = 3.25 \text{ mm}
$$

**Step 3 — Permanent (Plastic) Deformation:**

$$
\Delta h_{\text{permanent}} = h_0 - h_2 = 10.00 - 9.45 = 0.55 \text{ mm}
$$

> **Check:** $\Delta h_{\text{recoverable}} + \Delta h_{\text{permanent}} = 3.25 + 0.55 = 3.80 = \Delta h_{\text{total}}$. ✓

**Step 4 — Newness Number:**

$$
N = \frac{3.25}{3.80} \times 100 = 85.53 \%
$$

**Step 5 — Compression Set (complementary metric):**

$$
C_S = \frac{0.55}{3.80} \times 100 = 14.47 \%
$$

> **Check:** $N + C_S = 85.53 + 14.47 = 100.00$. ✓ (This identity is always true and is a useful validation tool during KTU valuation.)

### 3.2 Analytical Matrix — Effect of Compound Variables on Newness

| Variable Change | Effect on Newness Number | Engineering Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Increase in **filler loading** (carbon black, silica) | ↑ Increases | Filler creates additional physical cross-links, increasing elastic memory |
| Increase in **plasticizer / softener** | ↓ Decreases | Plasticizer reduces intermolecular friction, enhances chain slippage |
| Increase in **mastication time** | ↓ Decreases | Breaks long polymer chains → lower molecular weight → less elastic recovery |
| Increase in **Mooney viscosity** | ↑ Generally increases | Higher MW chains have greater entanglement → more elastic memory |
| Addition of **peptizer** (e.g., pentachlorothiophenol) | ↓ Decreases | Catalyzes chain scission during mixing |
| **Aging / oxidation** of NR | ↓ Decreases | Chain scission from oxidative degradation |
| Increase in **test temperature** | ↓ Decreases | Higher thermal energy reduces entropic elastic recovery |
| Increase in **test load magnitude** | ↓ Decreases (apparent) | Larger deformation engages more viscous component |

### 3.3 Derivation of Plasticity Retention Index (PRI) from Newness

For natural rubber grading, the newness of a fresh sample is compared to that of an aged sample (typically aged in an oven at $140 \text{ °C}$ for $30 \text{ minutes}$):

$$
PRI = \frac{N_{\text{aged}}}{N_{\text{fresh}}} \times 100
$$

> [!NOTE]
> This is a **board exam favourite**. Any value of $PRI \geq 60$ is generally considered acceptable for premium-grade NR; $PRI \geq 50$ is acceptable for standard grades; $PRI < 30$ indicates severely oxidized material unsuitable for high-performance applications.

---

<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->
## 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics

### 4.1 Mermaid Block — Newness Test Experimental Workflow

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    nodeA[Start: Prepare Unvulcanized Rubber Disc] --> nodeB[Condition at 23 deg C for 24 h]
    nodeB --> nodeC[Measure h0 using Vernier Caliper]
    nodeC --> nodeD[Place Specimen on Lower Platen of Newness Tester]
    nodeD --> nodeE[Apply 5.0 N Dead-Weight Load Smoothly in 1 s]
    nodeE --> nodeF[Hold Load for 5.0 s]
    nodeF --> nodeG[Read Compressed Height h1]
    nodeG --> nodeH[Release Load Suddenly]
    nodeH --> nodeI[Allow Free Recovery for 5.0 s]
    nodeI --> nodeJ[Read Recovered Height h2]
    nodeJ --> nodeK[Compute Total Deformation h0 minus h1]
    nodeK --> nodeL[Compute Recoverable Deformation h2 minus h1]
    nodeL --> nodeM[Compute Newness Number using Formula]
    nodeM --> nodeN[Report N in percent with 2 decimal places]
    nodeN --> nodeO[End of Experiment]
```

### 4.2 Mermaid Block — Newness Tester Functional Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    nodeA[Base Frame Cast Iron] --> nodeB[Lower Fixed Platen]
    nodeB --> nodeC[Specimen Disc h0 10 mm]
    nodeC --> nodeD[Upper Movable Platen]
    nodeD --> nodeE[Loading Lever Arm 1 to 5 Mechanical Advantage]
    nodeE --> nodeF[Calibrated Dead-Weight 500 g]
    nodeF --> nodeG[Force F equals m times g equals 4.905 N]
    nodeD --> nodeH[Dial Gauge LC 0.01 mm]
    nodeH --> nodeI[Reading h1 Compressed]
    nodeH --> nodeJ[Reading h2 Recovered]
    nodeA --> nodeK[Stopwatch External]
```

### 4.3 Mermaid Block — Conceptual Phase Response of the Specimen

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    nodeA[Initial State h0 at t equals 0] --> nodeB[Load Applied at t equals 0]
    nodeB --> nodeC[Compression Phase t equals 0 to 5 s]
    nodeC --> nodeD[Reaches h1 at t equals 5 s]
    nodeD --> nodeE[Load Released at t equals 5 s]
    nodeE --> nodeF[Recovery Phase t equals 5 to 10 s]
    nodeF --> nodeG[Reaches h2 at t equals 10 s]
    nodeG --> nodeH[Newness Number equals h2 minus h1 divided by h0 minus h1 times 100]
```

> [!NOTE]
> **Diagram Interpretation:** The workflow above maps the **temporal sequence** of a single newness measurement. The functional architecture shows how the lever-amplified dead-weight mechanism generates a precise compressive force on the specimen while the dial gauge captures the height readings. The phase-response diagram shows the three discrete time-states of the specimen: original, compressed, and recovered.

---

<!-- SECTION_4_END -->

<!-- SECTION_5_START -->
## 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

### Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

**Q1. [KTU University Exam — June 2024]**
Define the term **"Newness"** of a rubber compound. State the standard load, loading time, and recovery time used in the IIIrd method newness test.

**Model Answer:**
Newness is the property of an unvulcanized rubber compound to recover elastically from a deformation under standard test conditions. It is a measure of the elastic memory of the polymer network before vulcanization. In the IIIrd method, the standard load is **$5.0 \text{ N}$**, the loading time is **$5.0 \text{ s}$**, and the recovery time is **$5.0 \text{ s}$** at a platen temperature of **$23 \pm 2 \text{ °C}$**. The result is reported as the Newness Number $N$ (in percentage) calculated as the ratio of recoverable deformation to total deformation. *(3 marks — 1 for definition, 1 for parameters, 1 for reporting format.)*

**Q2. [KTU University Exam — Dec 2023]**
Distinguish between **"Newness"** and **"Compression Set"** of an unvulcanized rubber compound. Why are these two properties complementary?

**Model Answer:**
Newness measures the **fractional elastic recovery** of a rubber specimen after a standard deformation — it indicates how much the material springs back. Compression Set, in contrast, measures the **fractional permanent deformation** retained by the specimen — it indicates how much the material *fails* to recover. They are complementary because for any given deformation, the recoverable portion and the permanent portion together sum to the whole. Mathematically, $N + C_S = 100\%$. A compound with high newness has low compression set and vice versa. *(3 marks — 1 each for definitions, 1 for the mathematical identity.)*

---

### Part B — Full ESE Question (14 Marks, with Internal Choice)

#### **Question A (Choice 1)**

**[KTU University Exam — June 2024, Module 2, 14 Marks]**

**(a)** Describe the **IIIrd method of Newness testing** for an unvulcanized rubber compound. Draw a neat labeled diagram of the newness tester apparatus. Discuss the significance of newness in rubber processing. *(7 marks)*

**(b)** The following data were recorded during a newness test on an unvulcanized NR compound:

- Original height of disc: $h_0 = 10.00 \text{ mm}$
- Height under standard load after $5 \text{ s}$: $h_1 = 5.80 \text{ mm}$
- Height after $5 \text{ s}$ of recovery: $h_2 = 9.20 \text{ mm}$

Calculate (i) the **Newness Number**, (ii) the **Compression Set**, and (iii) comment on the processability of the compound. *(7 marks)*

**Model Solution — Part (a):**

The IIIrd method of newness testing is a standardized procedure (IS 3400 Part IX / equivalent ASTM D926) to determine the elastic recovery of unvulcanized rubber.

**Apparatus:** The newness tester consists of a cast-iron base, a fixed lower platen, a movable upper platen connected to a lever arm (1:5 mechanical advantage), a calibrated dead-weight of $500 \text{ g}$ (producing $4.905 \text{ N}$ at the specimen), and a dial gauge (LC $0.01 \text{ mm}$) to measure specimen height.

**Procedure:**
1. A disc of $28 \text{ mm}$ diameter and $10 \text{ mm}$ height is die-cut from the rubber sheet.
2. The disc is conditioned at $23 \pm 2 \text{ °C}$ for $24 \text{ h}$.
3. The original height $h_0$ is measured.
4. The specimen is placed on the lower platen; the $5.0 \text{ N}$ load is applied in $1 \text{ s}$ and held for $5.0 \text{ s}$.
5. The compressed height $h_1$ is read.
6. The load is released; recovery is allowed for $5.0 \text{ s}$.
7. The recovered height $h_2$ is read.

**Significance in Rubber Processing:**
- **Too high newness** → poor flow, rough extrudate, high die swell, hard mixing, high mill loading.
- **Too low newness** → soft, sticky, dimensionally unstable extrudate, sagging of uncured sheets, tacky build-up on calender rolls.
- An **optimum newness** (typically $75-90\%$ for NR compounds) ensures smooth processing and good dimensional stability of green (unvulcanized) articles before cure.

*(Marks: 1 apparatus, 1 procedure, 1 diagram description, 2 significance, 1 neatness, 1 conclusion.)*

**Model Solution — Part (b):**

**Given:** $h_0 = 10.00 \text{ mm}$, $h_1 = 5.80 \text{ mm}$, $h_2 = 9.20 \text{ mm}$.

**Step 1 — Total Deformation:**

$$
\Delta h_{\text{total}} = h_0 - h_1 = 10.00 - 5.80 = 4.20 \text{ mm}
$$

**Step 2 — Recoverable Deformation:**

$$
\Delta h_{\text{recoverable}} = h_2 - h_1 = 9.20 - 5.80 = 3.40 \text{ mm}
$$

**Step 3 — Newness Number (i):**

$$
N = \frac{h_2 - h_1}{h_0 - h_1} \times 100 = \frac{3.40}{4.20} \times 100 = 80.95\%
$$

**Step 4 — Compression Set (ii):**

$$
C_S = \frac{h_0 - h_2}{h_0 - h_1} \times 100 = \frac{10.00 - 9.20}{4.20} \times 100 = 19.05\%
$$

**Step 5 — Processability Comment (iii):**

The compound has a newness number of **$80.95\%$**, which lies within the **optimum processing range** of $75-90\%$ for natural-rubber-based compounds. It indicates a well-balanced compound with good elastic recovery and adequate flow behavior. The compression set of $19.05\%$ is acceptable for a green (unvulcanized) compound and indicates that the material will retain its shape adequately between the mixing and vulcanization stages. **Verdict: The compound is suitable for further processing (extrusion / calendering / molding).**

*(Marks: 1 each for $\Delta h$ calculations, 2 for formula application, 1 for final answer with units, 1 for validatory check $N + C_S = 100$, 1 for processability judgment.)*

#### **Question B (Choice 2)**

**[KTU University Exam — Dec 2023, Module 2, 14 Marks]**

**(a)** Explain with suitable equations how **"Newness"** is related to the **Mooney viscosity** and **Plasticity Retention Index (PRI)** of a natural rubber sample. *(7 marks)*

**(b)** In a newness test, an unvulcanized rubber disc shows $h_0 = 9.98 \text{ mm}$, $h_1 = 6.50 \text{ mm}$, and $h_2 = 9.10 \text{ mm}$. The same compound, after accelerated aging at $140 \text{ °C}$ for $30 \text{ min}$, gives $h_0' = 9.96 \text{ mm}$, $h_1' = 6.40 \text{ mm}$, and $h_2' = 8.40 \text{ mm}$. Calculate the **PRI** of the sample and comment on the grade of natural rubber. *(7 marks)*

**Model Solution — Part (a):**

**Relationship with Mooney Viscosity ($ML_{1+4}$ at $100 \text{ °C}$):**

The Mooney viscosity is a measure of the resistance of rubber to rotation in a disc-shaped die at $100 \text{ °C}$. Both Mooney viscosity and Newness are influenced by the **molecular weight and chain entanglement density** of the rubber. A higher Mooney viscosity indicates longer polymer chains and more entanglements, which produce a greater elastic (recoverable) response upon deformation — and thus a **higher newness number**.

$$
\boxed{ML_{1+4} \uparrow \;\Longleftrightarrow\; N \uparrow \quad \text{(positive correlation, approximately linear for unfilled NR)}}
$$

**Relationship with Plasticity Retention Index (PRI):**

PRI is the ratio of the newness of an aged sample to that of the fresh (unaged) sample:

$$
PRI = \frac{N_{\text{aged}}}{N_{\text{fresh}}} \times 100
$$

Where:

$$
N_{\text{fresh}} = \frac{h_2 - h_1}{h_0 - h_1} \times 100, \quad N_{\text{aged}} = \frac{h_2' - h_1'}{h_0' - h_1'} \times 100
$$

A high PRI indicates the rubber is **resistant to oxidative degradation** during storage and processing. PRI is the **industrial quality index** for natural rubber grading (IS 3707, ISO 2000).

*(Marks: 2 for Mooney relationship, 3 for PRI formula and interpretation, 2 for newness/PRI link.)*

**Model Solution — Part (b):**

**Step 1 — Newness of fresh sample:**

$$
N_{\text{fresh}} = \frac{h_2 - h_1}{h_0 - h_1} \times 100 = \frac{9.10 - 6.50}{9.98 - 6.50} \times 100 = \frac{2.60}{3.48} \times 100 = 74.71\%
$$

**Step 2 — Newness of aged sample:**

$$
N_{\text{aged}} = \frac{h_2' - h_1'}{h_0' - h_1'} \times 100 = \frac{8.40 - 6.40}{9.96 - 6.40} \times 100 = \frac{2.00}{3.56} \times 100 = 56.18\%
$$

**Step 3 — PRI Calculation:**

$$
PRI = \frac{N_{\text{aged}}}{N_{\text{fresh}}} \times 100 = \frac{56.18}{74.71} \times 100 = 75.20
$$

**Step 4 — Grade Comment:**

A PRI of **$75.20$** is in the **high-grade range** for natural rubber. As per IS 3707 / ISO 2000 grading:
- $PRI \geq 80$ : **Premium grade**
- $70 \leq PRI < 80$ : **Standard grade (good quality)** ← *this sample*
- $50 \leq PRI < 70$ : **Fair grade**
- $30 \leq PRI < 50$ : **Low grade**
- $PRI < 30$ : **Rejected / heavily oxidized**

The sample qualifies as a **Standard grade (good quality)** natural rubber, suitable for general-purpose rubber products such as automotive components, footwear, hoses, and conveyor belts. It is **not** suitable for high-performance applications (e.g., aircraft tire treads, high-speed dynamic seals) which require premium-grade material.

*(Marks: 1 each for $N$ calculations, 1 for PRI formula, 1 for numerical value, 1 for grading table recall, 1 for grade identification, 1 for application comment.)*

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Pitfall Callout — Common Mark-Deduction Zones:**
> 1. **Unit Omission (–0.5 marks):** Always write "mm" next to $h_0$, $h_1$, $h_2$ and "%" next to Newness and PRI.
> 2. **Formula Reversal (–1 mark):** Some students write $N = (h_0 - h_2)/(h_0 - h_1) \times 100$. This is the **Compression Set** formula, not the Newness formula. Memorize correctly: **Newness uses the *recovered* part** $(h_2 - h_1)$, not the *permanent* part.
> 3. **Missing Validatory Check (–0.5 marks):** Adding the line "$N + C_S = 100.00$ ✓" earns a half-mark consistency bonus in valuation.
> 4. **PRI Grading Table Recall (–1 mark):** Examiners expect you to recall the PRI grading categories. Mere numerical computation without classification attracts partial credit only.
> 5. **Sign Convention Errors (–0.5 marks):** All heights are positive; ensure you are using the *difference* values, not absolute differences.
> 6. **Diagram Quality (–1 mark in Part-A of Q):** A neat, labeled schematic of the newness tester with the lever arm, dead-weight, and dial gauge earns full marks. Stick figures are penalized.

---

### Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember (Rapid Revision Checklist)

- **Definition Anchor:** Newness = Elastic Recovery % of unvulcanized rubber after a standard compressive cycle. It is a **processing indicator**, NOT a final-product property.
- **Standard Test Parameters (must memorize):** Load = **$5.0 \text{ N}$**, Loading time = **$5 \text{ s}$**, Recovery time = **$5 \text{ s}$**, Temperature = **$23 \pm 2 \text{ °C}$**, Specimen = disc $\phi 28 \text{ mm} \times 10 \text{ mm}$.
- **Canonical Formula:** $\quad N = \dfrac{h_2 - h_1}{h_0 - h_1} \times 100$ — this is the **single most important equation** in this module.
- **Complementary Formula:** $\quad C_S = \dfrac{h_0 - h_2}{h_0 - h_1} \times 100$. Identity check: $N + C_S = 100\%$ always.
- **PRI Formula:** $\quad PRI = \dfrac{N_{\text{aged}}}{N_{\text{fresh}}} \times 100$, where aged = $140 \text{ °C}$ for $30 \text{ min}$ in an air-circulating oven.
- **PRI Grading (memorize the cut-offs):** $\geq 80$ = Premium; $70-79$ = Standard (good); $50-69$ = Fair; $30-49$ = Low; $< 30$ = Reject.
- **Trend Direction Mnemonic:** **"Filler up, newness up; Plasticizer up, newness down; Mastication up, newness down; Aging up, newness down."**
- **Processability Verdict Rule of Thumb:** Optimum $N$ range for NR compounds = **$75-90\%$.** Outside this range, the compound suffers either flow problems (high $N$) or dimensional instability (low $N$).
- **Apparatus to draw:** Base + fixed lower platen + specimen + movable upper platen + 1:5 lever arm + $500 \text{ g}$ dead-weight + dial gauge (LC $0.01 \text{ mm}$).
- **Common Pitfall to avoid:** Do **not** confuse Newness with **resilience** (rebound elasticity, tested on a Lupke pendulum) or with **hardness** (Shore A, IRHD). They are different mechanical properties.
- **Units Discipline:** All heights in **mm**, all recovery/compression percentages in **%**, all forces in **N**, all stresses in **Pa or N/mm²**.
- **Conservation Law You Can Use in Exam:** $\Delta h_{\text{recoverable}} + \Delta h_{\text{permanent}} = \Delta h_{\text{total}}$ — use this as a quick numerical sanity check.

<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

topics.title: 1961 4 Fabric Science Seema Sekhri McGraw-hill IV Edn
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PCPOL607 - PCPOL607
> - **Module:** Module Experiment 2
> - **Topic:** 1961 4 Fabric Science Seema Sekhri McGraw-hill IV Edn

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
## SECTION 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview of Fabric Science

### 1.1 Formal Academic Definition

**Fabric Science** is the interdisciplinary engineering domain that deals with the systematic study of textile fibers (natural, regenerated, and synthetic/polymeric), their conversion into yarns, the construction of fabrics via weaving, knitting, braiding, or non-woven routes, and the subsequent chemical/physical finishing operations that impart functional and aesthetic properties to the final textile substrate.

As per the canonical reference text *Fabric Science* by **Seema Sekhri (McGraw-Hill, IV Edition)**, the discipline integrates **fiber chemistry**, **yarn geometry**, **fabric geometry**, **mechanical behavior**, and **finishing chemistry** into a unified framework. In the context of **PCPOL607** (Polymer Chemistry & Processing Lab), the focus is heavily skewed toward **synthetic polymeric fibers** (polyester, nylon, polypropylene, acrylic) and their structure–property relationships.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Syllabus Highlight:** Fabric Science forms the experimental backbone of Module 2 in PCPOL607. The laboratory component typically involves identification of fibers, yarn count determination, fabric sett analysis, GSM calculation, and tensile testing. Mastering the theory in this module is a prerequisite for the practical record and viva-voce.

### 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Intuition

Imagine a **brick wall**:
- The **bricks** = **fibers** (the basic structural unit, made of long-chain polymer molecules).
- The **mortar holding bricks in a strand** = **twist in a yarn** (converts loose fibers into a continuous strand).
- The **pattern of brick arrangement** = **fabric construction** (plain, twill, satin for weaves; jersey, rib for knits).
- The **paint/coating on the wall** = **finishing** (dyeing, water-repellency, flame-retardancy).

Just as a wall's strength depends on brick quality *and* arrangement pattern, a fabric's properties depend on **fiber type (chemistry)** *and* **structural architecture (geometry)**.

### 1.3 Key Physical Constants & Standard Metrics

| Parameter | Standard Value | Significance |
|---|---|---|
| **Tex** | **1 g / 1000 m** | Linear density of yarn |
| **Denier** | **1 g / 9000 m** | Legacy yarn count unit |
| **English Cotton Count (Ne)** | **840 yd / lb** | Indirect yarn count |
| **Metric Count (Nm)** | **1 km / kg** | Indirect metric count |
| **GSM** | **g/m²** | Areal density of fabric |
| **CPI / WPI** | **per inch** | Courses/Wales per inch (knits) |
| **EPI / PPI** | **per inch** | Ends/Picks per inch (weaves) |
| **Cover Factor (K)** | **Dimensionless, 0–1** | Fractional area covered |
| **Twist Multiplier (TM)** | **Unitless** | Twist per inch / √Ne |

> [!NOTE]
> **Direct system** (Tex, Denier): Higher number = Coarser yarn. **Indirect system** (Ne, Nm): Higher number = Finer yarn. This inversion is a frequent exam trap.

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
## SECTION 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### 2.1 Hierarchical Structure of a Textile Fabric

A fabric exists at **four hierarchical levels**:

1. **Polymer Level** — Molecular chain (e.g., PET repeating unit: –[O–CH₂–CH₂–O–CO–C₆H₄–CO]ₙ–).
2. **Fiber Level** — Oriented, semi-crystalline polymer drawn into a filament of **5–50 µm diameter**.
3. **Yarn Level** — Bundle of fibers (or continuous filaments) held together by **twist** or **interlacing**.
4. **Fabric Level** — Interlaced/interlooped yarns forming a planar, flexible sheet.

The **Why & How** of this hierarchy:
- A single polymer chain (~10⁵ Da) is mechanically weak; bundling thousands into a fiber provides strength.
- Twisting fibers increases inter-fiber friction (Coulomb friction model: $F_f = \mu N$), enabling load transfer.
- Interlacing yarns distributes stress, prevents catastrophic failure, and gives drape.

### 2.2 Classification of Textile Fibers

**A. Natural Fibers**
- **Cellulosic:** Cotton (90% cellulose), Flax, Jute, Hemp.
- **Proteinaceous:** Wool (keratin), Silk (fibroin).

**B. Man-Made Fibers**
- **Regenerated:** Viscose Rayon, Modal, Lyocell (regenerated cellulose).
- **Synthetic (Polymeric):**
  - **Polyester (PET):** 70% global fiber production share.
  - **Polyamide (Nylon 6, Nylon 6,6):** Polycondensation product.
  - **Polyacrylonitrile (PAN):** Acrylic precursor for carbon fiber.
  - **Polypropylene (PP):** Lightest textile fiber (**density 0.91 g/cm³**).
  - **Elastane (Spandex/Lycra):** Segmented polyurethane with **>500% elongation**.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Focus (PCPOL607):** Synthetic polymers dominate the textile industry. Understanding the **melt-spinning**, **dry-spinning**, and **wet-spinning** routes for converting polymer chips into continuous filaments is a **high-weightage** topic.

### 2.3 Yarn Formation Mechanisms

- **Spinning (Staple):** Carding → Drawing → Roving → Ring/Rotor/Air-jet spinning.
- **Filament Yarn:** Direct extrusion of polymer melt/solution through spinneret.
- **Texturizing:** Imparting crimp to filaments for bulk and stretch (false-twist, air-jet texturizing).

**Key Yarn Geometry Parameters:**
- **Twist Angle (θ):** $\tan\theta = \pi D T$ where $D$ = yarn diameter, $T$ = turns per unit length.
- **Yarn Diameter from Count:** $D = \frac{1}{28\sqrt{N_e}}$ inches (for cotton-system).

### 2.4 Fabric Construction Geometry

#### A. Weaving (Most Common)
Interlacing of **two perpendicular yarn sets**: **warp (ends, longitudinal)** × **weft (picks, transverse)**.

**Three Fundamental Weaves:**
| Weave | Interlacing Pattern | Properties | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Plain (Tabby)** | 1-up, 1-down | Most stable, lowest drape, highest interlacing | Muslin, canvas |
| **Twill** | Diagonal wales (e.g., 2/1, 3/1) | Better drape, softer, visible diagonals | Denim, gabardine |
| **Satin** | Long floats (4-up, 1-down for 5-harness) | Smoothest, highest drape, lowest stability | Satin, charmeuse |

**Derivatives:** Leno, Dobby, Jacquard, Pile (velvet, terry).

#### B. Knitting (Loop Formation)
- **Weft Knit:** Loops formed horizontally (course direction). Examples: **Jersey (plain), Rib (1×1, 2×2), Interlock, Purl**.
  - Highly extensible, excellent drape, prone to run/ravel.
- **Warp Knit:** Loops formed vertically (wale direction). Examples: **Tricot, Raschel, Milanese**.
  - Dimensionally stable, less extensible, run-resistant.

#### C. Non-Woven Fabrics
Fibers bonded mechanically (needle-punching), thermally (calendering, through-air), or chemically (latex binder). **Web → Bonding → Finishing**. Used in geotextiles, hygiene products, interlinings.

### 2.5 KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

| Formula | Expression | Application |
|---|---|---|
| **Tex** | $T = \frac{m}{L} \times 1000$ (m in g, L in m) | Linear density (direct) |
| **Denier** | $D = \frac{m}{L} \times 9000$ (m in g, L in m) | Legacy linear density |
| **Count Conversion** | $N_e = \frac{590.5}{T}$ | Tex ↔ Cotton count |
| **Count Conversion** | $N_m = \frac{1000}{T}$ | Tex ↔ Metric count |
| **Yarn Diameter** | $D = \frac{1}{28\sqrt{N_e}}$ inches | Cotton yarn diameter |
| **Twist Angle** | $\tan\theta = \pi D T$ | Geometric twist analysis |
| **Twist Factor** | $\alpha = T\sqrt{Tex}$ | Twist level (direct) |
| **Twist Multiplier** | $TM = \frac{TPI}{\sqrt{N_e}}$ | Twist level (indirect) |
| **Fabric GSM** | $GSM = \frac{EPI \times Tex_e + PPI \times Tex_p}{100}$ | Areal density calc |
| **Cover Factor (Peirce)** | $K_w = \frac{d_w}{p_w} = d_w \cdot \frac{EPI}{25.4}$ | Warp cover factor (mm) |
| **Total Cover Factor** | $K = K_w + K_p - (K_w \cdot K_p)$ | Fabric cover |
| **Maximum Packing** | $K_{max} = \frac{d_w \cdot \sqrt{N_e}}{7.94}$ | Fabric geometry |
| **Crimp (%)** | $C\% = \frac{L_y - L_f}{L_f} \times 100$ | Yarn undulation |
| **Areo Density** | $\rho_{areal} = \frac{GSM}{Thickness}$ | Volumetric property |
| **Porosity (P)** | $P = 1 - \frac{GSM}{\rho_{bulk} \cdot t \cdot 1000}$ | Air fraction in fabric |

> [!NOTE]
> **Absolute value / pipe-symbol safety:** All $\vert$ and $\mid$ notations in math are encoded to avoid breaking markdown table pipes. Use $\sqrt{\cdot}$ for radicals — never use the literal `| |` characters inside table cells.

### 2.6 Real-World Engineering Utility

- **Geotextiles (PP non-woven):** Soil reinforcement, road stabilization — selected based on GSM, tensile strength, and **CBR puncture resistance**.
- **Medical Textiles:** PET vascular grafts (woven/knitted), antimicrobial cotton gauze.
- **Aerospace:** Aramid (Kevlar) woven fabrics for ballistic panels; carbon-fabric composites for wing skins.
- **Smart Textiles:** Conductive polymer-coated yarns for wearable sensors (PPy-coated PET).
- **Filtration:** Melt-blown PP non-wovens (N95 mask core) — graded by fiber diameter (**0.5–5 µm**) and basis weight.

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
## SECTION 3: Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

### 3.1 Derivation: Yarn Count Conversion (Tex → English Cotton Count, $N_e$)

**Starting Point:** Tex is defined as the mass in grams of 1000 meters of yarn.

$$T = \frac{m\,(g)}{L\,(m)} \times 1000$$

**Step 1 — Define English Cotton Count:** Number of 840-yard lengths per pound (lb).

$$N_e = \frac{L\,(yd)}{840 \times W\,(lb)}$$

**Step 2 — Convert units to metric.** 1 yard = 0.9144 m; 1 lb = 453.592 g.

$$N_e = \frac{L\,(m) / 0.9144}{840 \times W\,(g) / 453.592}$$

**Step 3 — Simplify the constant denominator.**

$$N_e = \frac{L}{0.9144} \times \frac{453.592}{840 \times W} = \frac{L}{W} \times \frac{453.592}{0.9144 \times 840}$$

**Step 4 — Evaluate the constant.**

$$\frac{453.592}{0.9144 \times 840} = \frac{453.592}{768.096} = 0.5905$$

**Step 5 — Therefore:**

$$N_e = 0.5905 \times \frac{L}{W}$$

**Step 6 — Substitute the Tex definition** ($T = W/L \times 1000$, i.e., $L/W = 1000/T$):

$$N_e = 0.5905 \times \frac{1000}{T}$$

$$\boxed{\,N_e = \frac{590.5}{T}\,}$$

> **Conversion logic summary:** Tex is a *direct* count (mass per length); $N_e$ is an *indirect* count (length per mass). Their product, by dimensional analysis, must equal a dimensionless ratio of unit-defining constants: $0.5905 \times 1000 = 590.5$.

---

### 3.2 Derivation: Fabric Cover Factor (Peirce's Model)

**Model Assumption:** Yarns are perfect, incompressible cylinders of circular cross-section, lying in a regular grid with constant spacing.

**Step 1 — Define projected yarn width on the fabric plane.** For a circular cylinder of diameter $d$ sitting on a flat plane, the projected width equals the diameter $d$ (when fabric thickness ≈ yarn diameter).

**Step 2 — Define warp cover factor** as the ratio of projected yarn width to spacing between yarn centers $p$:

$$K_w = \frac{d_w}{p_w}$$

**Step 3 — Convert spacing $p$ (in mm) to EPI (ends per inch):**

$$p_w = \frac{25.4\,(mm/inch)}{EPI}$$

**Step 4 — Substitute:**

$$K_w = d_w \cdot \frac{EPI}{25.4}$$

**Step 5 — Similarly for weft:**

$$K_p = d_p \cdot \frac{PPI}{25.4}$$

**Step 6 — Total cover factor** (probability that a random point is covered by *either* warp OR weft):

$$\boxed{\,K = K_w + K_p - (K_w \cdot K_p)\,}$$

**Step 7 — Numerical example.**
- Warp: 30 Tex cotton, $d_w = 0.20$ mm; EPI = 28.
- Weft: 30 Tex cotton, $d_p = 0.20$ mm; PPI = 24.

$$K_w = 0.20 \times \frac{28}{25.4} = 0.20 \times 1.102 = 0.220$$

$$K_p = 0.20 \times \frac{24}{25.4} = 0.20 \times 0.945 = 0.189$$

$$K = 0.220 + 0.189 - (0.220 \times 0.189) = 0.409 - 0.0416 = 0.367$$

> **Interpretation:** ~36.7% of the fabric surface is "covered" by yarn. The remaining 63.3% is inter-yarn pore area, governing **air permeability** and **water vapor transmission**.

---

### 3.3 Analytical Matrix: Structure → Property Relationships

| Structural Variable | Property Affected | Direction of Influence | Engineering Trade-off |
|---|---|---|---|
| ↑ Fiber crystallinity | Tensile strength, modulus | ↑ | ↓ Dye uptake, ↑ Brittleness |
| ↑ Fiber orientation (draw ratio) | Tensile strength, ↓ elongation | ↑ | ↓ Toughness (energy to break) |
| ↑ Yarn twist | Strength (up to optimum), hairiness | ↑ then ↓ | ↓ Softness, ↓ Luster |
| ↑ EPI / PPI (denser sett) | Cover factor, GSM, stiffness | ↑ | ↓ Air permeability, ↓ Drape |
| ↑ Fabric thickness | Thermal insulation, GSM | ↑ | ↓ Drape, ↑ Bending rigidity |
| Knit → Woven | Dimensional stability | ↑ | ↓ Extensibility, drape |
| Plain → Satin weave | Surface smoothness, luster | ↑ | ↓ Stability, snagging |
| Hydrophobic fiber (PP) | Water repellency | ↑ | ↓ Comfort (moisture transport) |
| ↑ Finishing (calendering) | Luster, smoothness | ↑ | ↓ Air permeability, ↓ Bulk |

---

### 3.4 Worked Numerical Problem (KTU Model)

**Problem:** A polyester/cotton (65/35) blended fabric has 36 EPI, 28 PPI. Warp is 30 Tex, weft is 40 Tex. Calculate:
(a) Fabric GSM
(b) Total cover factor (assume cylindrical yarns, $d = 0.20$ mm for both)

**Solution:**

**(a) GSM Calculation**

$$GSM = \frac{EPI \times Tex_e + PPI \times Tex_p}{100}$$

$$GSM = \frac{36 \times 30 + 28 \times 40}{100}$$

$$GSM = \frac{1080 + 1120}{100} = \frac{2200}{100}$$

$$\boxed{\,GSM = 220\,g/m^2\,}$$

**(b) Cover Factor**

$$K_w = 0.20 \times \frac{36}{25.4} = 0.283$$

$$K_p = 0.20 \times \frac{28}{25.4} = 0.220$$

$$K = 0.283 + 0.220 - (0.283 \times 0.220)$$

$$K = 0.503 - 0.0623 = 0.441$$

$$\boxed{\,K \approx 0.44\,}$$

> **Interpretation:** The fabric is moderately opaque (44% covered); suitable for shirting weight. A value $K > 0.7$ would indicate a windproof, densely woven fabric (e.g., raincoat material).

<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->
## SECTION 4: Structural Diagrams & Schematics

### 4.1 Hierarchical Block Diagram: Polymer → Fabric Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[POLYMER MELT or SOLUTION] --> B[SPINNING via Spinneret]
    B --> C[Continuous Filament]
    B --> D[Staple Fiber Tow]
    C --> E[Filament Yarn via Texturizing]
    D --> F[Carding]
    F --> G[Drawing]
    G --> H[Roving]
    H --> I[Ring / Rotor / Air-jet Spinning]
    I --> J[Staple Yarn]
    E --> K[YARN POOL]
    J --> K
    K --> L[Weaving Interlacing]
    K --> M[Knitting Loop Formation]
    K --> N[Non-woven Web Bonding]
    L --> O[WOVEN FABRIC]
    M --> P[KNITTED FABRIC]
    N --> Q[NON-WOVEN FABRIC]
    O --> R[Finishing Dyeing Printing Coating]
    P --> R
    Q --> R
    R --> S[FINAL TEXTILE SUBSTRATE]
```

### 4.2 Block Diagram: Three Fundamental Weaves

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Plain Weave 1 up 1 down] --> A1[Most stable]
    A --> A2[Lowest drape]
    A --> A3[Highest interlacings per cm2]

    B[Twill Weave 2 over 1 under diagonal] --> B1[Diagonal wales]
    B --> B2[Better drape than plain]
    B --> B3[Denim gabardine serge]

    C[Satin Weave Long float 4 over 1 under] --> C1[Smoothest surface]
    C --> C2[Highest luster]
    C --> C3[Lowest stability snags easily]
```

### 4.3 Functional Flow: Fiber Identification Lab Protocol (PCPOL607 Experiment 2)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S[Unknown Fiber Sample] --> T[Burning Test Observe Shrinkage Flame Color Smell Ash]
    S --> U[Microscopy Longitudinal View]
    S --> V[Solubility Test Cold Conc H2SO4 Acetone DMF]

    T --> T1[Cellulosic Sweet smell Papery ash]
    T --> T2[Proteinaceous Burning hair smell]
    T --> T3[Synthetic Beads melt dripping dark smoke]

    U --> U1[Cotton Convolutions]
    U --> U2[Wool Scales]
    U --> U3[PET Smooth cylindrical]

    V --> V1[Viscose dissolves in 70 percent H2SO4]
    V --> V2[Acetate dissolves in acetone]
    V --> V3[PAN in DMF]
    V --> V4[Nylon in cold formic acid]

    T1 --> X[Confirmed Identification]
    T2 --> X
    T3 --> X
    U1 --> X
    U2 --> X
    U3 --> X
    V1 --> X
    V2 --> X
    V3 --> X
    V4 --> X
```

### 4.4 Yarn Twist Geometry Schematic (Conceptual Mermaid)

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph YarnAxis [Yarn Axis L]
        direction LR
        Y1[Surface Fiber Helix Angle theta]
        Y2[Twist Turns per cm T]
        Y3[Core Fiber Almost Parallel to Axis]
    end

    Y1 --> P1[Twist Increases theta then Decreases Hairiness]
    Y2 --> P2[Higher T gives Better Strength up to Optimum]
    Y3 --> P3[Core Bears Maximum Load]
```

> **Note on Physical Drawings:** True 3-D helical fiber geometry cannot be drawn natively in Mermaid; the block diagram above captures the **functional relationships** between twist parameters and yarn mechanical response.

## SECTION 5: KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

### 5.1 Part A Questions (3 Marks Each)

**Q1. [KTU University Exam - Dec 2023] Define "Tex" and "Denier". A yarn has a linear density of 50 Tex. Calculate its equivalent English cotton count ($N_e$) and metric count ($N_m$).**

**Model Answer:**

- **Tex:** Mass in grams of 1000 m of yarn.
- **Denier:** Mass in grams of 9000 m of yarn.

$$N_e = \frac{590.5}{T} = \frac{590.5}{50} = 11.81$$

$$N_m = \frac{1000}{T} = \frac{1000}{50} = 20$$

> **Examiner's Note (3-mark scheme):** Definition of Tex (1 mark) + Denier (1 mark) + Calculations with units (1 mark).
