## 5.3 ⚠️ KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout

> [!WARNING]
> **Where Students Lose Marks in This Topic:**
>
> 1. **Confusing DPI and CPI.** DPI is a marketing term (Dots Per Inch), CPI is the technical term (Counts Per Inch). They are numerically equal, but examiners penalize loose terminology.
> 2. **Forgetting the blank line before/after LaTeX blocks** in the answer sheet rendering — handwritten scripts must show boxed formulas with a clear one-line gap.
> 3. **Mixing up the X and Y layer assignments** in resistive touchscreen derivations. Always state *which layer is being driven* and *which is being read*.
> 4. **Ignoring the Nyquist criterion** when justifying polling rates. A 1000 Hz polling rate must be defended with $f_s \ge 2 f_{\mathrm{max}}$ math, not a hand-wave.
> 5. **Drawing block diagrams without arrows.** Unconnected blocks receive *zero* marks in the diagram sub-question.
> 6. **Skipping engineering interpretation** after a numerical calculation. The KTU 2024 scheme follows Outcome-Based Education; numerical answers without context fail the CO (Course Outcome) mapping.

- [ ] **BCI devices** operate in the EEG band of **0.5 Hz – 100 Hz**.
- [ ] **PCAP touchscreens** cannot be activated with a gloved hand *unless* the glove is conductive (or the panel supports *glove mode*).
- [ ] **Report latency** = scan time + processing time + transmission time.
- [ ] **Touch sampling rate** of **240 Hz** is standard in flagship smartphones as of 2024.
- [ ] **Saw-tooth waveform** drives SAW touchscreens; **piezoelectric transducers** detect the acoustic disturbance.
- [ ] **IR touchscreens** use **retro-reflective arrays** around the bezel; interruption of beams = touch.
- [ ] **Force Touch / 3D Touch** uses capacitive sensors beneath the display to measure *pressure* in addition to position.
- [ ] **Eye trackers** use **Pupil Center Corneal Reflection (PCCR)** method with infrared illumination.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Last-Minute Mnemonics:**
> - **"I-S-O"** for Touchscreen types: **I**nfrared → **S**AW → **O**ptical (capacitive is *separate*).
> - **"DMA-C"** for input devices: **D**igitizer, **M**icrophone, **A**ccelerometer, **C**amera, (joystick).
> - **"FT-VR-K"** for output feedback: **F**orce (haptic), **T**hermal (rare), **V**isual, **R**umble (haptic), **K**inesthetic.

# 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition (KTU 2024 Terminology)

**Database Design** in the context of Polymer Composites Engineering is the systematic process of structuring a **logical and physical data architecture** that captures, stores, retrieves, and manages information about matrix materials, reinforcement fibers, fabrication processes, mechanical/thermal/chemical test results, and application domains of composite materials.

According to the **KTU 2024 Scheme** for Polymer Composites (PCPOL607), Module Experiment 2 mandates students to design a structured **Composite Materials Database (CMDB)** that supports the entire product life-cycle — from raw material selection to performance evaluation.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Syllabus Highlight (PCPOL607 – Module Experiment 2):**
> Students must design a relational database that models:
> (a) Matrix polymers and their grades
> (b) Reinforcement fibers (natural & synthetic)
> (c) Composite formulations / lay-up sequences
> (d) Mechanical, thermal, and chemical test outcomes
> (e) Processing methods and application mapping

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — The Library of Materials

Imagine a **vast engineering library** where every book represents a *composite material recipe* — its cover lists the title (material name), inside pages describe the chapter-wise contents (matrix, fiber, additives), and an index card at the back stores test results (tensile strength, impact resistance, glass transition temperature). The librarian (Database Management System) ensures:

- No two recipes are jumbled into the same book (**Data Integrity**)
- A reader can quickly locate any recipe using filters (**Query Optimization**)
- New recipes can be appended without disturbing old ones (**Scalability**)
- Books follow a standard cataloging system — Dewey Decimal — (**Normalization**)

This "library" is exactly what a Composite Materials Database is, and *designing* it means deciding **what shelves exist, what categories of books sit on each shelf, and how shelves reference each other**.

## 1.3 Key Entities in a Composite Materials Database (CMDB)

| # | Entity | Purpose |
|---|--------|---------|
| 1 | **Matrix Material** | Stores polymer resin information (Epoxy, Polyester, PEEK) |
| 2 | **Reinforcement** | Stores fiber data (Carbon, Glass, Aramid, Jute) |
| 3 | **Composite Formulation** | Maps matrix + reinforcement + additives + ratios |
| 4 | **Fabrication Process** | Records hand lay-up, RTM, filament winding parameters |
| 5 | **Test Result** | Stores mechanical, thermal, chemical outcomes |
| 6 | **Application** | Aerospace, automotive, marine, sports equipment mapping |
| 7 | **Supplier/Manufacturer** | Vendor details for traceability |

> [!NOTE]
> The **atomicity** of each entity follows KTU's NEP 2020 outcome-based learning — every data attribute must be *indivisible, unique, and functionally dependent* on its primary key.

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 The Three-Tier Database Design Architecture

Database design is universally taught in three sequential phases, each with a distinct deliverable:

### Tier 1 — Conceptual Design (ER Modeling)
- Identifies **entities**, **attributes**, and **relationships**
- Uses **Chen Notation** or **Crow's Foot Notation**
- Independent of any DBMS
- Output: **Entity-Relationship (ER) Diagram**

### Tier 2 — Logical Design (Relational Schema)
- Converts ER Diagram into **relations (tables)**
- Applies **Normalization Rules (1NF → 2NF → 3NF → BCNF)**
- Defines **Primary Keys, Foreign Keys, Candidate Keys**
- Output: **Relational Schema (set of tables with attributes)**

### Tier 3 — Physical Design (Implementation)
- Selects DBMS (MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle)
- Defines **data types, indexes, storage engines, partitioning**
- Considers **denormalization trade-offs** for query performance
- Output: **DDL scripts and live database**

## 2.2 Normalization — The Heart of Good Design

Normalization eliminates **data redundancy** and prevents **update, insertion, and deletion anomalies**.

### First Normal Form (1NF)
A relation is in **1NF** if and only if every cell contains a single, atomic value — no repeating groups or arrays.

$$\text{1NF} \iff \forall \, t \in R, \, \forall \, A_i \in t : A_i \text{ is atomic}$$

### Second Normal Form (2NF)
A relation is in **2NF** if it is in 1NF and every non-prime attribute is **fully functionally dependent** on the entire primary key (no partial dependencies).

$$R \in 2NF \iff R \in 1NF \;\land\; \nexists \, X \subset PK, \, A \notin PK : X \rightarrow A$$

### Third Normal Form (3NF)
A relation is in **3NF** if it is in 2NF and has **no transitive dependencies** for non-prime attributes.

$$R \in 3NF \iff \nexists \, X \rightarrow Y \rightarrow Z \; \text{where} \; Z \text{ is non-prime}$$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> KTU examiners expect students to demonstrate normalization up to **3NF** with worked examples from the composite materials domain.

## 2.3 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

| Design Phase | Key Concept | Formula / Rule | Engineering Use |
|--------------|-------------|----------------|-----------------|
| Conceptual | Cardinality | $1:1, \; 1:N, \; M:N$ | Defines how matrix ↔ reinforcement relate |
| Conceptual | Participation | Total / Partial | Mandatory vs optional join |
| Logical | Functional Dependency | $X \rightarrow Y$ | Determines keys and normalization |
| Logical | 1NF Condition | Atomic attributes only | Removes multivalued fields |
| Logical | 2NF Condition | Full FD on PK | Removes partial dependencies |
| Logical | 3NF Condition | No transitive FD | Removes derived attributes |
| Physical | Index Cardinality | $C = \dfrac{\text{Distinct values}}{\text{Total rows}}$ | Query speed optimization |
| Physical | Storage Estimate | $S = R \times W \times (1 + O)$ | Disk allocation planning |

Where:
- $R$ = number of records
- $W$ = row width in bytes
- $O$ = overhead factor (typically **0.3 to 0.5**)

> [!NOTE]
> **Standard Constants Used:**
> - Block size (InnoDB MySQL): **16 KB**
> - Page size (PostgreSQL): **8 KB**
> - Typical overhead factor $O$ for B-Tree indexes: **~0.4**

## 2.4 Real-World Engineering Utility

In the polymer composites industry, a well-designed CMDB enables:

1. **Materials Selection by Properties** — query "all composites with tensile strength > 500 MPa and density < 1.6 g/cc"
2. **Process-Property Correlation** — discover which fabrication parameters yield optimal glass transition temperature
3. **Cost Optimization** — rank alternatives by cost-to-performance ratio
4. **Regulatory Traceability** — REACH, RoHS compliance tracking
5. **Predictive Modeling Input** — feeds Machine Learning models for property prediction
6. **Failure Analysis Archive** — historical case data for root-cause analysis

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# 3. Step-by-Step Derivation & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Worked Example — Designing a Composite Materials Database

### Step 1: Identify Entities from Problem Statement

**Problem Statement (Typical KTU Lab Question):**
*"Design a database to store information about polymer composite materials. For each composite, record the matrix polymer, reinforcement fiber, fiber volume fraction, fabrication process, test results (tensile strength, flexural strength, impact strength, Tg), and target application."*

**Entities Extracted:**

| Entity Name | Identifier |
|-------------|------------|
| Matrix | `matrix_id` |
| Reinforcement | `fiber_id` |
| Process | `process_id` |
| TestResult | `test_id` |
| Application | `app_id` |
| Composite | `composite_id` |
| Supplier | `supplier_id` |

### Step 2: Define Attributes and Keys

**Matrix Table (M):**

$$\text{Matrix}(\underline{\text{matrix\_id}},\, \text{name},\, \text{type},\, \text{grade},\, T_g,\, \text{density})$$

Underline indicates **Primary Key**.

**Reinforcement Table (R):**

$$R(\underline{\text{fiber\_id}},\, \text{fiber\_name},\, \text{form},\, \text{density},\, \text{tensile\_modulus})$$

**Composite Formulation Table (C):**

$$C(\underline{\text{composite\_id}},\, \text{name},\, \text{matrix\_id}^{FK},\, V_f,\, \text{process\_id}^{FK},\, \text{app\_id}^{FK})$$

**TestResult Table (T):**

$$T(\underline{\text{test\_id}},\, \text{composite\_id}^{FK},\, \text{tensile\_strength},\, \text{flexural\_strength},\, \text{impact\_strength})$$

### Step 3: Establish Relationships and Cardinalities

| Relationship | Entities | Cardinality | Justification |
|--------------|----------|-------------|---------------|
| Uses | Matrix ↔ Composite | 1 : N | One matrix can be used in many composites |
| Reinforces | Reinforcement ↔ Composite | M : N | Composites can have hybrid fibers |
| ManufacturedBy | Process ↔ Composite | 1 : N | One process produces many composites |
| TestedUnder | Composite ↔ TestResult | 1 : N | Each composite has many tests |
| AppliedIn | Application ↔ Composite | 1 : N | One application uses many composites |

The **M:N relationship** between Reinforcement and Composite must be resolved by creating a junction (associative) entity:

$$RC(\underline{\text{composite\_id}^{FK},\, \text{fiber\_id}^{FK}},\, \text{fiber\_volume\_fraction})$$

### Step 4: Normalization Walk-through (1NF → 3NF)

**Initial Unnormalized Form (UNF) — Test Result with multi-valued attributes:**

| test_id | composite_name | fibers_used | strengths |
|---------|----------------|-------------|-----------|
| T01 | CFRP-A | Carbon, Glass | 550, 480 |

**Apply 1NF — atomicize:**

| test_id | composite_name | fiber | strength |
|---------|----------------|-------|----------|
| T01 | CFRP-A | Carbon | 550 |
| T01 | CFRP-A | Glass | 480 |

**Apply 2NF — remove partial dependency:**
Since `test_id → strength` (full dependency) and `fiber` depends on the combination `test_id + fiber`, the table must split:

$$T_1(\underline{\text{test\_id}},\, \text{composite\_id}^{FK},\, \text{tensile\_strength})$$

$$T_2(\underline{\text{test\_id}^{FK},\, \text{fiber\_id}^{FK}},\, \text{fiber\_contribution})$$

**Apply 3NF — remove transitive dependency:**
If `composite_name → application_area → cost_estimate`, then `cost_estimate` transitively depends on `composite_name` via `application_area`. Move `cost_estimate` to a separate `Application` table.

### Step 5: Final Relational Schema (3NF)

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Matrix} &(\underline{\text{matrix\_id}},\, \text{name},\, \text{type},\, T_g,\, \text{density}) \\[4pt]
\text{Reinforcement} &(\underline{\text{fiber\_id}},\, \text{fiber\_name},\, \text{form},\, \text{density}) \\[4pt]
\text{Composite} &(\underline{\text{composite\_id}},\, \text{name},\, \text{matrix\_id}^{FK},\, \text{process\_id}^{FK}) \\[4pt]
\text{Composite\_Fiber} &(\underline{\text{composite\_id}^{FK},\, \text{fiber\_id}^{FK}},\, V_f) \\[4pt]
\text{Process} &(\underline{\text{process\_id}},\, \text{process\_name},\, \text{parameters}) \\[4pt]
\text{TestResult} &(\underline{\text{test\_id}},\, \text{composite\_id}^{FK},\, \sigma_t,\, \sigma_f,\, \text{impact}) \\[4pt]
\text{Application} &(\underline{\text{app\_id}},\, \text{app\_name},\, \text{industry}) \\[4pt]
\text{Composite\_App} &(\underline{\text{composite\_id}^{FK},\, \text{app\_id}^{FK}}) \\[4pt]
\text{Supplier} &(\underline{\text{supplier\_id}},\, \text{name},\, \text{material\_id}^{FK})
\end{aligned}
$$

### Step 6: Sample Data Insertion (Composite)

| composite_id | name | matrix_id | process_id | $V_f$ (carbon) |
|--------------|------|-----------|------------|----------------|
| C001 | CFRP-A | M01 (Epoxy) | P02 (RTM) | 0.55 |
| C002 | GFRP-B | M02 (Polyester) | P01 (Hand layup) | 0.40 |

The corresponding **storage estimate** for a database of $R = 10,000$ composites with average row width $W = 256$ bytes:

$$
S = 10{,}000 \times 256 \times (1 + 0.4) = 3{,}584{,}000 \text{ bytes} \approx 3.42 \text{ MB}
$$

<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->

# 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A Questions (3 Marks Each)

### Question 1: Define Database Normalization. List the different normal forms. `[KTU University Exam - May 2024]`

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

**Definition (2 marks):** Database Normalization is a systematic process of organizing the attributes of a relation into multiple related tables to **minimize data redundancy** and avoid **insertion, update, and deletion anomalies**. It is based on the concept of *functional dependencies* between attributes.

**Normal Forms Listed (1 mark):**
1. First Normal Form (1NF)
2. Second Normal Form (2NF)
3. Third Normal Form (3NF)
4. Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF)
5. Fourth Normal Form (4NF)
6. Fifth Normal Form (5NF)

---

### Question 2: What is a Primary Key? Differentiate between Primary Key and Candidate Key. `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]`

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

**Primary Key (1.5 marks):** A Primary Key is a column (or set of columns) that **uniquely identifies each row** in a relation. It must be **non-null** and **unique** throughout the table. Each relation can have **only one** primary key.

**Candidate Key (1 mark):** A Candidate Key is any attribute (or minimal combination of attributes) that is *eligible* to be a primary key. A relation can have **multiple candidate keys**, but only one is chosen as the primary key; the rest become **alternate keys**.

| Feature | Primary Key | Candidate Key |
|---------|-------------|---------------|
| Quantity per table | One only | One or more |
| Uniqueness | Guaranteed | Guaranteed |
| Null values | Not allowed | Not allowed |
| Selection | Deliberately chosen | Eligible but unselected |

---

## 5.2 Part B Questions (14 Marks Each — Internal Choice)

### Question A — 14 Marks `[KTU University Exam - May 2024]`

**Question:** Design a database for a Polymer Composites Testing Laboratory. The database should store information about:
- (a) Composite samples received for testing (7 marks)
- (b) Tests conducted and the results obtained (7 marks)

Draw the ER diagram, convert it into a relational schema, and normalize up to 3NF.

#### Sub-Part (a) — Composite Sample Management (7 Marks)

**Step 1: Identify Entities and Attributes**

Entities:
- **Sample** (sample_id PK, name, date_received, supplier_id FK)
- **Supplier** (supplier_id PK, name, address, contact)
- **MatrixMaterial** (matrix_id PK, type, name)
- **FiberMaterial** (fiber_id PK, type, name)
- **SampleComposition** (sample_id FK, fiber_id FK, vf, layer_orientation)

**Step 2: ER Diagram Representation**

| Entity | Attributes | Key |
|--------|------------|-----|
| Sample | sample_id, name, date_received, supplier_id | PK = sample_id |
| Supplier | supplier_id, name, address, contact | PK = supplier_id |
| SampleComposition | sample_id, fiber_id, vf, orientation | PK = (sample_id, fiber_id) |

**Step 3: Cardinality**

- Supplier **1 : N** Sample (one supplier provides many samples)
- Sample **1 : N** SampleComposition (one sample may have hybrid fibers)

**Step 4: Normalization**

**UNF:**
| sample_id | name | suppliers | fibers | vf_list |
|-----------|------|-----------|--------|---------|

**1NF:** Split multi-valued `suppliers` and `fibers` into separate atomic rows.

**2NF:** Since `vf` depends fully on (sample_id, fiber_id) — already satisfied; but separate Sample and SampleComposition tables.

**3NF:** Move supplier address and contact to Supplier table (no transitive dependency via supplier_id).

**Final Schema (1 mark):**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Supplier} &(\underline{\text{supplier\_id}},\, \text{name},\, \text{address},\, \text{contact}) \\[2pt]
\text{Sample} &(\underline{\text{sample\_id}},\, \text{name},\, \text{date\_received},\, \text{supplier\_id}^{FK}) \\[2pt]
\text{SampleComposition} &(\underline{\text{sample\_id}^{FK},\, \text{fiber\_id}^{FK}},\, V_f,\, \text{orientation})
\end{aligned}
$$

#### Sub-Part (b) — Test Results and Normalization (7 Marks)

**Entities Identified:**
- **Test** (test_id PK, test_name, standard_code)
- **TestResult** (result_id PK, sample_id FK, test_id FK, value, unit, date_tested)
- **Equipment** (equipment_id PK, equipment_name, calibration_date)

**Functional Dependencies (1.5 marks):**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{test\_id} & \rightarrow \text{test\_name},\, \text{standard\_code} \\[2pt]
\text{result\_id} & \rightarrow \text{sample\_id},\, \text{test\_id},\, \text{value},\, \text{unit},\, \text{date\_tested} \\[2pt]
\text{equipment\_id} & \rightarrow \text{equipment\_name},\, \text{calibration\_date}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Normalization Steps (3.5 marks):**

1. **1NF:** All attributes atomic — no lists, no repeating groups
2. **2NF:** All non-key attributes fully depend on PK (no partial FD)
3. **3NF:** No transitive FD — `equipment_name` and `calibration_date` moved to separate Equipment table

**Final 3NF Schema (2 marks):**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Test} &(\underline{\text{test\_id}},\, \text{test\_name},\, \text{standard\_code}) \\[2pt]
\text{TestResult} &(\underline{\text{result\_id}},\, \text{sample\_id}^{FK},\, \text{test\_id}^{FK},\, \text{equipment\_id}^{FK},\, \text{value},\, \text{unit},\, \text{date\_tested}) \\[2pt]
\text{Equipment} &(\underline{\text{equipment\_id}},\, \text{equipment\_name},\, \text{calibration\_date})
\end{aligned}
$$

---

### Question B — 14 Marks (Alternative Choice) `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]`

**Question:** A polymer composite manufacturing company wishes to computerize its records. The system must handle:
- (a) Raw material inventory and supplier information (7 marks)
- (b) Production batches and quality control records (7 marks)

Design an appropriate database with ER diagram, schema, and 3NF normalization.

#### Sub-Part (a) — Raw Material & Supplier Module (7 Marks)

**Entities:**
- **RawMaterial** (rm_id PK, name, type, unit, current_stock, reorder_level)
- **Supplier** (supplier_id PK, name, contact, address)
- **PurchaseOrder** (po_id PK, po_date, supplier_id FK, total_amount)
- **PurchaseOrderItem** (po_id FK, rm_id FK, quantity, unit_price)

**Cardinality:**
- Supplier **1 : N** PurchaseOrder
- PurchaseOrder **1 : N** PurchaseOrderItem
- RawMaterial **1 : N** PurchaseOrderItem

**3NF Schema:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{RawMaterial} &(\underline{\text{rm\_id}},\, \text{name},\, \text{type},\, \text{unit},\, \text{current\_stock},\, \text{reorder\_level}) \\[2pt]
\text{Supplier} &(\underline{\text{supplier\_id}},\, \text{name},\, \text{contact},\, \text{address}) \\[2pt]
\text{PurchaseOrder} &(\underline{\text{po\_id}},\, \text{po\_date},\, \text{supplier\_id}^{FK},\, \text{total\_amount}) \\[2pt]
\text{PurchaseOrderItem} &(\underline{\text{po\_id}^{FK},\, \text{rm\_id}^{FK}},\, \text{quantity},\, \text{unit\_price})
\end{aligned}
$$

#### Sub-Part (b) — Production & QC Module (7 Marks)

**Entities:**
- **Batch** (batch_id PK, batch_date, operator, rm_id FK, quantity_produced)
- **QualityCheck** (qc_id PK, batch_id FK, parameter, measured_value, specification, pass_fail)

**Normalization (1NF → 3NF):**

**UNF Example:**
| batch_id | parameters_tested | values | pass_fail |
|----------|-------------------|--------|-----------|

**1NF:** Split rows so each parameter-value pair is atomic.

**2NF:** All non-key attrs functionally dependent on full PK.

**3NF:** Move `parameter` and `specification` to a Parameter table if reused.

**Final 3NF:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Batch} &(\underline{\text{batch\_id}},\, \text{batch\_date},\, \text{operator},\, \text{rm\_id}^{FK},\, \text{quantity\_produced}) \\[2pt]
\text{QualityCheck} &(\underline{\text{qc\_id}},\, \text{batch\_id}^{FK},\, \text{parameter},\, \text{measured\_value},\, \text{specification},\, \text{pass\_fail})
\end{aligned}
$$

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Pitfalls:**
> 1. **Forgetting the M:N junction table** between Reinforcement and Composite — students often place fiber_id directly inside Composite, violating 1NF (multi-valued attribute). **Loss: up to 2 marks.**
> 2. **Confusing 2NF and 3NF** — remember: 2NF deals with *partial* dependencies (composite key), while 3NF deals with *transitive* dependencies (non-key → non-key). Examiners frequently set trick questions on this. **Loss: 1.5 marks.**
> 3. **Missing Foreign Key notation** — always superscript FK on foreign key attributes in the schema (e.g., `matrix_id^{FK}`). Without this, the schema appears incomplete. **Loss: 1 mark.**
> 4. **Drawing the ER diagram with wrong cardinality symbols** — Crow's Foot "many" side must show the *crow's foot*, not just text. **Loss: 1 mark.**
> 5. **Not specifying the participation (total/partial)** in the ER diagram — KTU 2024 rubric specifically checks this. **Loss: 0.5 marks.**

---

## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Rapid Revision Checklist — Database Design for PCPOL607 Experiment 2**

- **Three design tiers:** Conceptual (ER) → Logical (Schema) → Physical (DBMS)
- **Always identify entities first**, then attributes, then relationships — this is the **top-down approach** KTU expects
- **Primary Key = unique + not null**; **Foreign Key = references another table's PK**
- **1NF = atomicity** — no lists, no multi-valued cells
- **2NF = full functional dependency on PK** — eliminate partial dependencies
- **3NF = no transitive dependencies** — eliminate indirect dependencies
- **M:N relationships** must be resolved via a **junction (associative) entity**
- **Cardinality notations:** `1:1`, `1:N`, `M:N` — use Crow's Foot symbols in ER diagrams
- **ER Diagram tools** accepted in KTU: draw.io, Lucidchart, Mermaid, or hand-drawn
- **Storage estimation formula:** $S = R \times W \times (1 + O)$ where $O \approx 0.4$
- **Composite-specific entities to always include:** Matrix, Reinforcement, Formulation, TestResult, Application
- **Composite-specific attributes:** $V_f$ (fiber volume fraction), $T_g$ (glass transition temperature), $\sigma_t$ (tensile strength), $\sigma_f$ (flexural strength), impact strength
- **Foreign Key relationships in CMDB:**
  - Composite → Matrix (many-to-one)
  - Composite_Fiber → Composite, Reinforcement (junction)
  - TestResult → Composite (many-to-one)
  - Composite_App → Composite, Application (junction)
- **Normalization is mandatory** — KTU awards full marks only when schema is in 3NF
- **Always use primary key notation** (underline) and **foreign key notation** (superscript FK) in the schema

# 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## Formal Academic Definition

**Graphic Standards** in the context of polymer science laboratory experiments refer to the universally accepted conventions, rules, and protocols governing the visual representation of experimental data. These standards ensure that all scientific figures — graphs, charts, spectra, and schematic diagrams — communicate information with **accuracy, reproducibility, and interpretive clarity**. 

In KTU-aligned polymer engineering labs, graphical standards are typically derived from international bodies such as **ASTM (American Society for Testing and Materials)**, **ISO (International Organization for Standardization)**, and **BIS (Bureau of Indian Standards)**. The core philosophy is encapsulated in the acronym **"MAPS"** — **M**eaningful, **A**ccurate, **P**recise, and **S**elf-contained.

> [!NOTE]
> **Syllabus Highlight:** A graph is not merely a "drawing" — it is a **mathematical model of a physical phenomenon**. Every graphical element (axis, scale, legend, symbol) must follow standardized conventions so that any polymer scientist in the world can interpret it identically.

## Conceptual Analogy / Intuition

Imagine you and a friend are in different countries trying to read the same map. If one map uses kilometers and another uses miles, communication breaks down. **Graphic Standards are the "universal language" of scientific charts** — they ensure that a tensile stress–strain curve drawn in Kerala can be read instantly by a polymer engineer in Germany, Japan, or the USA.

Think of a stress–strain plot for a polymer like HDPE (High-Density Polyethylene) as a "photo" of its mechanical personality. Graphic standards determine:
- The "frame" size of the photo (graph dimensions)
- The "language" written on it (SI units, English labels)
- The "clothing" of the data points (markers, line styles)
- The "caption" beneath it (figure number, title, conditions)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Core Definition for Exams:** *Graphic Standards are a codified set of rules that dictate the formatting of axes, scales, legends, units, line types, symbols, and annotations in the visual presentation of experimental data, ensuring unambiguous scientific communication across global polymer engineering communities.*

## Key Standardization Bodies (in Bold)

- **ASTM E380** — Standard for SI Units usage
- **ISO 80000** — Quantities and units
- **ASTM D638** — Tensile properties of plastics (graphical output standards)
- **ASTM D1238** — Melt flow rate reporting (graph conventions)
- **BIS IS 2267** — Indian standards for plastics testing graphics

## Fundamental Graphical Parameters

| Parameter | Standard Requirement | Example (Tensile Test) |
|---|---|---|
| **Axis Type** | Independent variable on X, dependent on Y | Strain (%) vs. Stress (MPa) |
| **Units** | SI units, parentheses | Stress **(MPa)** |
| **Gridlines** | Light, non-intrusive | Optional major gridlines |
| **Font** | Sans-serif (Arial/Helvetica) | 10–12 pt |
| **Line Width** | 0.5–1.5 pt | 0.75 pt recommended |
| **Marker Size** | Visible but not dominant | 4–6 pt |
| **Aspect Ratio** | Follows "Golden Rule" | ~1.6:1 width:height |
<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## Structured Logical Breakdown of Graphical Construction

A polymer experimental graph follows a **7-step construction protocol**:

### Step 1 — Identify the Relationship
Determine the physical/chemical relationship being plotted. For polymer experiments, common relationships include:
- Stress–Strain (mechanical)
- Viscosity–Shear Rate (rheological)
- Absorbance–Wavelength (spectroscopic)
- Conversion–Time (kinetic)
- Molecular Weight–Retention Time (chromatographic)

### Step 2 — Choose the Correct Coordinate System
- **Linear–Linear**: Used when both variables vary across a narrow range (e.g., 0–100 °C vs. 0–50 MPa).
- **Log–Log**: Used when data spans multiple orders of magnitude (e.g., viscosity vs. molecular weight, $M_w$ ranging from 10⁴ to 10⁶ g/mol).
- **Semi-Log**: Used for exponential decay/growth (e.g., stress relaxation modulus vs. time).
- **Polar/Categorical**: Used for anisotropic properties (e.g., orientation-dependent tensile strength).

### Step 3 — Determine the Scale Range
The scale must encompass **all data points with ~10% padding** on either side. The minimum scale interval should be 1, 2, 2.5, or 5 (multiples of these are preferred over 3, 7, or 9 for cleaner reading).

### Step 4 — Label Axes Rigorously
Each axis must display:
- **Variable name** (e.g., "Stress")
- **Symbol** in italics (e.g., *σ*)
- **Units in brackets** (e.g., [MPa])
- **Numerical scale** with major and minor tick marks

### Step 5 — Plot Data Points with Markers
Use distinguishable markers (●, ▲, ■, ◆, ★) for different datasets. Markers should be **larger than the line width** but not obscure the data.

### Step 6 — Draw the Best-Fit Curve
Use the **method of least squares** for linear regression. For non-linear data, polynomial or exponential fitting may be applied. Avoid connecting data points with straight lines (this is reserved for theoretical/computed plots).

### Step 7 — Annotate and Caption
Add a **legend** (top-right or outside plot area), a **figure number** (Fig. 2.1), and a **caption** below explaining conditions, sample ID, temperature, and test standard followed.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **"Why" and "How" Insight:** The reason SI units are mandated is rooted in the **Mètre-Convention of 1875** — the international treaty that unified measurement science. Using non-SI units (like kgf/cm²) without proper conversion factors introduces **systematic errors** of up to 0.2% in polymer tensile data reporting.

## KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

| **Formula / Rule** | **Expression** | **Application in Polymer Labs** |
|---|---|---|
| Linear Regression Slope | $m = \dfrac{n \sum xy - \sum x \sum y}{n \sum x^2 - (\sum x)^2}$ | Young's modulus from σ–ε curve |
| Linear Regression Intercept | $b = \dfrac{\sum y - m \sum x}{n}$ | Yield point offset calculation |
| Pearson Correlation Coefficient | $r = \dfrac{n \sum xy - \sum x \sum y}{\sqrt{[n \sum x^2 - (\sum x)^2][n \sum y^2 - (\sum y)^2]}}$ | Linearity check of calibration |
| Log-Log Slope (Power Law) | $n = \dfrac{\log y_2 - \log y_1}{\log x_2 - \log x_1}$ | Power-law index in $\eta = K\dot{\gamma}^{n-1}$ |
| Standard Error of Slope | $SE_m = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{(n-2)\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}}$ | Uncertainty in modulus |
| Logarithmic Strain | $\epsilon_{true} = \ln(1 + \epsilon_{eng})$ | Converting engineering to true strain |
| True Stress | $\sigma_{true} = \sigma_{eng}(1 + \epsilon_{eng})$ | Necking region of polymer |
| Arrhenius (log scale) | $\ln k = \ln A - \dfrac{E_a}{RT}$ | Cure kinetics plotting |
| Viscosity Average MW | $[\eta] = K M_v^a$ (Mark–Houwink) | Intrinsic viscosity from graph intercept |
| Decimal Reduction Rule | $D_{10} = \dfrac{t}{\log(N_0/N)}$ | Disinfection/sterilization graphics |

> [!WARNING]
> **Pipe-Symbol Safeguard Applied:** All absolute values in the formulas above are rendered using clear LaTeX notation. In your exam answer books, write them as $\vert x \vert$ — never use the literal `|` symbol in tables to avoid markdown/evaluation parsing errors.

## Real-World Engineering Utility

- **Quality Control Labs** in polymer manufacturing use standardized graphs to compare batch-to-batch consistency of HDPE, PP, and PVC.
- **Research Publications** in journals like *Polymer* and *Macromolecules* reject papers with non-standardized figures.
- **Patent Filings** require ASTM-compliant graphs for legal defensibility of property claims.
- **Regulatory Submissions** to FDA/BIS for medical-grade polymers demand ISO 80000-compliant data presentation.
- **Failure Analysis** in field returns uses standardized overlay plots to compare failed vs. nominal specimens.
<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## Derivation 1: Least-Squares Best-Fit Line (Foundation of All Linear Graphs)

The most fundamental graphical standard in polymer labs is the **linear regression line**, used to extract Young's modulus, calibration constants, and rate constants from raw data.

### Setting Up the Problem

Given $n$ experimental data points $(x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2), \ldots, (x_n, y_n)$, we seek a straight line:

$$
y = mx + b
$$

that **minimizes the sum of squared vertical deviations** (the "residuals"):

$$
S = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - mx_i - b)^2
$$

### Step 1 — Differentiate with Respect to $b$

$$
\frac{\partial S}{\partial b} = -2 \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - mx_i - b) = 0
$$

This gives the first normal equation:

$$
\sum y_i = m \sum x_i + nb
$$

### Step 2 — Differentiate with Respect to $m$

$$
\frac{\partial S}{\partial m} = -2 \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i (y_i - mx_i - b) = 0
$$

This gives the second normal equation:

$$
\sum x_i y_i = m \sum x_i^2 + b \sum x_i
$$

### Step 3 — Solve the 2×2 System

From the first equation, isolate $b$:

$$
b = \frac{\sum y_i - m \sum x_i}{n}
$$

Substitute into the second equation:

$$
\sum x_i y_i = m \sum x_i^2 + \left(\frac{\sum y_i - m \sum x_i}{n}\right) \sum x_i
$$

Multiply through by $n$:

$$
n \sum x_i y_i = mn \sum x_i^2 + \sum y_i \sum x_i - m (\sum x_i)^2
$$

Collect $m$ terms on the left:

$$
mn \sum x_i^2 - m (\sum x_i)^2 = n \sum x_i y_i - \sum y_i \sum x_i
$$

Factor out $m$:

$$
m \left[n \sum x_i^2 - (\sum x_i)^2\right] = n \sum x_i y_i - \sum x_i \sum y_i
$$

### Step 4 — Final Slope Expression

$$
m = \frac{n \sum x_i y_i - \sum x_i \sum y_i}{n \sum x_i^2 - (\sum x_i)^2}
$$

### Step 5 — Final Intercept Expression

$$
b = \frac{\sum y_i - m \sum x_i}{n}
$$

### Step 6 — Worked Numerical Example (Polymer Tensile Test)

Consider a polyethylene tensile test with the following data:

| Point | Strain $\epsilon$ (%) | Stress $\sigma$ (MPa) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.5 | 5.2 |
| 2 | 1.0 | 10.4 |
| 3 | 1.5 | 15.7 |
| 4 | 2.0 | 20.9 |
| 5 | 2.5 | 26.1 |

Here $n = 5$.

Compute the required sums:

$$
\sum x_i = 0.5 + 1.0 + 1.5 + 2.0 + 2.5 = 7.5
$$

$$
\sum y_i = 5.2 + 10.4 + 15.7 + 20.9 + 26.1 = 78.3
$$

$$
\sum x_i^2 = 0.25 + 1.00 + 2.25 + 4.00 + 6.25 = 13.75
$$

$$
\sum x_i y_i = 2.60 + 10.40 + 23.55 + 41.80 + 65.25 = 143.60
$$

Compute the slope $m$:

$$
m = \frac{5 \times 143.60 - 7.5 \times 78.3}{5 \times 13.75 - (7.5)^2}
$$

$$
m = \frac{718.00 - 587.25}{68.75 - 56.25} = \frac{130.75}{12.50} = 10.46 \text{ MPa/\%}
$$

Compute the intercept $b$:

$$
b = \frac{78.3 - 10.46 \times 7.5}{5} = \frac{78.3 - 78.45}{5} = \frac{-0.15}{5} = -0.03 \text{ MPa}
$$

### Step 7 — Interpret the Result for the Polymer Engineer

The slope of the stress–strain plot in the **elastic region** is the **Young's Modulus**, $E$. Since strain is in %, the modulus in MPa is the slope multiplied by 100:

$$
E = m \times 100 = 10.46 \times 100 = 1046 \text{ MPa} \approx 1.05 \text{ GPa}
$$

This value is **consistent with HDPE** (literature range: 0.5–1.5 GPa), validating both the experiment and the graphical method.

---

## Derivation 2: Log-Log Power-Law Plot for Viscosity (Ostwald–de Waele)

Polymer melts and concentrated solutions obey the **power-law model**:

$$
\eta = K \dot{\gamma}^{n-1}
$$

Taking $\log_{10}$ of both sides:

$$
\log \eta = \log K + (n-1) \log \dot{\gamma}
$$

This is a straight line on log-log axes with slope $(n-1)$ and intercept $\log K$.

### Step-by-Step Logic

- If $n = 1$ (Newtonian), slope = 0 → horizontal line.
- If $n < 1$ (shear-thinning, typical for polymers), slope is negative.
- If $n > 1$ (shear-thickening, rare), slope is positive.

For a typical LDPE melt, $n \approx 0.3$–$0.5$, meaning the slope of the log-log plot is approximately $-0.5$ to $-0.7$.

---

## Derivation 3: Standard Error of the Slope (Uncertainty Bars on Graphs)

The standard error of the regression slope is given by:

$$
SE_m = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{(n-2)\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \bar{x})^2}}
$$

This value defines the **error bar height** along the trendline — a graphical standard required by ASTM E177 for reporting polymer property uncertainty.

---

## Analytical Matrix: Choosing the Right Graph Type

| **Polymer Property Measured** | **Independent Variable (X)** | **Dependent Variable (Y)** | **Recommended Plot Type** | **Key Constant Extracted** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tensile Modulus | Strain (%) | Stress (MPa) | Linear | Young's Modulus $E$ |
| Melt Viscosity | Shear rate (s⁻¹) | Viscosity (Pa·s) | Log–Log | Power-law index $n$ |
| Glass Transition | Temperature (°C) | Storage modulus $E'$ | Semi-log | $T_g$ at inflection |
| Cure Kinetics | Time (min) | Conversion $\alpha$ | Linear (sigmoidal fit) | Rate constant $k$ |
| UV Absorbance | Wavelength (nm) | Absorbance (a.u.) | Linear (overlay spectra) | $\lambda_{max}$ |
| Molecular Weight | Elution volume (mL) | Detector response | Linear (chromatogram) | $M_w$, $M_n$ |
| Crystallinity | Temperature (°C) | Heat flow (W/g) | Linear (DSC thermogram) | $T_m$, $\Delta H_f$ |
| Creep Compliance | Time (s) | Strain (%) | Log–Log | Creep modulus |
<!-- SECTION_3_END -->
