> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PCPOL607 - PCPOL607
> - **Module:** Module Experiment 2
> - **Topic:** Production Planning and Control Systems

# 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition

**Production Planning and Control (PPC) Systems** constitute the organizational and technological framework that governs the conversion of raw materials into finished goods by determining **what to produce**, **when to produce**, **how much to produce**, and **in what sequence**. According to the KTU 2024 Scheme syllabus for PCPOL607, PPC is defined as a *closed-loop, decision-support architecture* integrating demand forecasting, capacity planning, materials requirement planning, scheduling, dispatching, and shop-floor execution to achieve **on-time delivery, optimal inventory, and minimal production cost** within polymer processing operations.

In the polymer manufacturing context, PPC is the central nervous system that links **formulation design, mixing/extrusion, moulding, curing, finishing, and quality certification** into a single synchronized workflow.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Syllabus Highlight:** PPC is not merely scheduling. It is a **four-stage cycle** consisting of *Planning → Routing → Scheduling → Dispatching/Expediting*, with continuous feedback via the **Control** loop. Examiners expect students to clearly identify these four stages.

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — The "Restaurant Kitchen" Model

Imagine a busy restaurant kitchen during dinner rush. The head chef (Production Manager) must:
- **Forecast** how many customers will arrive (demand).
- **Plan the menu and capacity** based on available stoves and chefs.
- **Schedule orders** so that pasta is not served after the dessert.
- **Dispatch (expedite)** each dish to the right station at the right time.
- **Control quality** by tasting before serving.

In a polymer plant, the same logic applies to batches of PVC pipes, HDPE granules, or thermoset moulded components. PPC is the *choreography* that keeps the production line dancing in rhythm.

> [!NOTE]
> **Standard Production Metrics used in PPC** (always quoted in bold during exams):
> - **OEE (Overall Equipment Effectiveness)** = Availability × Performance × Quality
> - **Takt Time** = Available Production Time / Customer Demand
> - **Lead Time** = Order Receipt to Delivery Time
> - **Cycle Time** = Time to Complete One Unit of Output

## 1.3 Objectives of PPC in Polymer Industries

| Objective | Operational Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Cost Minimization** | Reduce wastage of polymer resin, additives, and energy |
| **On-Time Delivery (OTD)** | Meet customer demand dates ≥ **95%** of the time |
| **Inventory Optimization** | Maintain raw and finished goods at minimum economic levels |
| **Capacity Utilization** | Keep machines operating at **80–90%** of rated capacity |
| **Quality Assurance** | Conform to ISO 9001 and polymer-grade specifications |
| **Flexibility** | Allow rapid changeovers between polymer grades |

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 The Four Functional Phases of PPC

### Phase 1 — Planning (The Brain)
- **Forecasting demand** using *Moving Average, Exponential Smoothing, or ARIMA* models.
- **Aggregate Production Planning (APP):** Decide output levels for 3–18 months.
- **Master Production Schedule (MPS):** Translate APP into specific finished-product quantities per week.

### Phase 2 — Routing (The Map)
- Establishes the **path** raw polymer pellets travel: Storage → Drying → Mixing → Extrusion → Cooling → Cutting → QC → Packing.
- Documented as a **Route Sheet** listing machines, tools, and standard times.

### Phase 3 — Scheduling (The Calendar)
- Assigns **start and end times** to each operation.
- Types:
  - *Forward Scheduling* — Start now, finish ASAP.
  - *Backward Scheduling* — Start from due date and work backwards.
  - *Finite / Infinite Loading* — respects capacity limits or not.

### Phase 4 — Dispatching & Expediting (The Trigger)
- **Dispatching** releases work orders to the shop floor.
- **Expediting** chases progress and resolves bottlenecks.

### The Control Loop (Feedback)
- Compare *actual vs. planned* output.
- Compute variances and trigger corrective action.

## 2.2 Core Mathematical Models

### 2.2.1 Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) — The Wilson Formula

$$Q^{*} = \sqrt{\frac{2DS}{H}}$$

Where:
- $Q^{*}$ = optimal order quantity (kg or units)
- $D$ = annual demand (kg/year)
- $S$ = ordering cost per order (₹/order)
- $H$ = holding cost per unit per year (₹/kg·year)

### 2.2.2 Reorder Point (ROP)

$$\text{ROP} = d \times L + \text{SS}$$

Where $d$ = daily demand, $L$ = lead time in days, $SS$ = safety stock.

### 2.2.3 OEE Formulation

$$\text{OEE} = A \times P \times Q$$

with $A$ = Availability, $P$ = Performance, $Q$ = Quality, all in decimal form.

### 2.2.4 Takt Time (Lean Manufacturing)

$$\text{Takt Time} = \frac{T_{\text{available}}}{D_{\text{customer}}}$$

Where $T_{\text{available}}$ is net available production time per shift and $D_{\text{customer}}$ is customer demand per shift.

### 2.2.5 Exponential Smoothing Forecast

$$F_{t+1} = \alpha A_t + (1-\alpha) F_t$$

with $\alpha$ = smoothing constant (0 < $\alpha$ < 1), $A_t$ = actual demand at time $t$.

## 2.3 KTU Formula Cheat Sheet (High-Yield Table)

> [!NOTE]
> **Exam Tip:** KTU valuation scripts give **2 marks automatically** if the correct formula is written. Memorize this table.

| # | Formula | Application | Unit |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $Q^{*} = \sqrt{2DS/H}$ | Optimal lot size (EOQ) | units |
| 2 | $\text{ROP} = d \cdot L + \text{SS}$ | When to reorder | units |
| 3 | $F_{t+1} = \alpha A_t + (1-\alpha)F_t$ | Demand forecast | units/period |
| 4 | $\text{OEE} = A \times P \times Q$ | Equipment efficiency | % |
| 5 | $\text{Takt} = T_a / D_c$ | Lean pacing | time/unit |
| 6 | $\text{Utilization} = \text{Run Time} / \text{Planned Prod. Time}$ | Capacity check | % |
| 7 | $\text{Throughput} = 1 / \text{Bottleneck Time}$ | Line balancing | units/hr |
| 8 | $N = T / t_0$ | Number of machines required | integer |

## 2.4 Real-World Engineering Utility

- **ERP Integration:** SAP PP, Oracle Manufacturing are the digital instantiation of PPC.
- **MES Layer:** Manufacturing Execution Systems translate the plan into real-time control.
- **Lean–PPC Synergy:** Just-in-Time (JIT) eliminates buffers; Theory of Constraints (TOC) identifies bottlenecks.
- **Industry 4.0:** AI-based dynamic scheduling adjusts the MPS in real time.

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Full Derivation of the EOQ Model

The **Economic Order Quantity** minimizes the *Total Inventory Cost (TIC)*, which has two components: ordering cost and holding cost.

### Step 1 — Define Total Annual Cost

The annual ordering cost is the number of orders per year ($D/Q$) multiplied by the cost per order ($S$):

$$
\text{Ordering Cost} = \frac{D}{Q} \cdot S
$$

The annual holding cost equals the average inventory ($Q/2$) multiplied by the holding cost per unit ($H$):

$$
\text{Holding Cost} = \frac{Q}{2} \cdot H
$$

Therefore, total inventory cost becomes:

$$
\text{TIC}(Q) = \frac{DS}{Q} + \frac{HQ}{2}
$$

### Step 2 — Differentiate w.r.t. Q

To find the minimum, differentiate $\text{TIC}(Q)$ with respect to $Q$ and set equal to zero:

$$
\frac{d(\text{TIC})}{dQ} = -\frac{DS}{Q^{2}} + \frac{H}{2} = 0
$$

### Step 3 — Solve for Q*

Rearranging:

$$
\frac{H}{2} = \frac{DS}{Q^{2}}
$$

Multiplying both sides by $Q^{2}$:

$$
Q^{2} = \frac{2DS}{H}
$$

Taking the square root (positive root only, since quantity cannot be negative):

$$
Q^{*} = \sqrt{\frac{2DS}{H}}
$$

### Step 4 — Verify Second-Order Condition

$$
\frac{d^{2}(\text{TIC})}{dQ^{2}} = \frac{2DS}{Q^{3}} > 0
$$

Since the second derivative is positive, $\text{TIC}$ is **convex** and $Q^{*}$ is indeed a *minimum*, not a maximum. This is the global optimum for the deterministic, constant-demand case.

## 3.2 Worked Numerical Example (KTU Typical)

**Problem:** A polymer processing unit consumes **12,000 kg/year** of LDPE granules. Ordering cost is **₹250 per order** and holding cost is **₹5 per kg per year**. Determine EOQ, number of orders per year, and total inventory cost.

**Step 1 — Identify Parameters**

$$
D = 12{,}000 \text{ kg/yr}, \quad S = ₹250, \quad H = ₹5
$$

**Step 2 — Apply EOQ Formula**

$$
Q^{*} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 12000 \times 250}{5}}
$$

$$
Q^{*} = \sqrt{\frac{6{,}000{,}000}{5}} = \sqrt{1{,}200{,}000}
$$

$$
Q^{*} \approx 1095.45 \text{ kg}
$$

**Step 3 — Number of Orders per Year**

$$
N = \frac{D}{Q^{*}} = \frac{12000}{1095.45} \approx 10.95 \text{ orders/year} \approx 11 \text{ orders}
$$

**Step 4 — Total Inventory Cost**

$$
\text{TIC} = \frac{DS}{Q^{*}} + \frac{HQ^{*}}{2}
$$

$$
\text{TIC} = \frac{12000 \times 250}{1095.45} + \frac{5 \times 1095.45}{2}
$$

$$
\text{TIC} = 2738.6 + 2738.6 = ₹5477.2 \text{ per year}
$$

> [!NOTE]
> At EOQ, the **ordering cost equals the holding cost** — a useful KTU cross-check worth **1 mark**.

## 3.3 Exponential Smoothing Derivation

Given actual demand series $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_t$, the recursive forecast is:

$$
F_{t+1} = \alpha A_t + (1-\alpha) F_t
$$

Expanding the recursion:

$$
F_{t+1} = \alpha \sum_{i=1}^{t} (1-\alpha)^{t-i} A_i
$$

This shows that exponential smoothing is a **weighted moving average** where older data receives exponentially decaying weight $\lambda_i = \alpha(1-\alpha)^{t-i}$. The weights sum to unity:

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{t} \alpha (1-\alpha)^{t-i} = 1
$$

confirming that $F_{t+1}$ is a *convex combination* of past demands.

## 3.4 Analytical Decision Matrix (PPC Tool Selection)

| Scenario | Best PPC Tool | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| High-volume, low-variety (e.g., PVC pipes) | **Line Production** | Continuous flow, fixed routing |
| Low-volume, high-variety (custom polymer moulds) | **Job Shop** | Flexible routing, skilled labour |
| Medium batch, multiple products | **Batch Production** | Group technology, changeovers |
| Make-to-stock commodity | **MPS + EOQ** | Forecast-driven |
| Make-to-order engineering polymer | **MTO with Backward Scheduling** | Customer-driven |
| Tight capacity, high demand | **Finite Loading + TOC** | Avoid overcommitment |

<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

# 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics

## 4.1 The Closed-Loop PPC Cycle

```mermaid

    A[Demand Forecast] --> B[Aggregate Planning]

    D --> E[Capacity Planning]

    J -- On Target --> K[Feedback to Forecast]
    J -- Deviation --> L[Corrective Action]

    K --> A
```

# 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

### Question 1. [KTU University Exam — Dec 2023, Model Paper]
**Define Production Planning and Control (PPC). List any four functions of PPC.**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**
Production Planning and Control is the organizational function that plans, directs, and controls the material flow, machine capacity, and operational sequences in a manufacturing system to ensure that the right quantity of the right product is produced at the right time.
*(1 mark for definition)*

**Four functions of PPC:**
1. **Forecasting** — predicting future demand.
2. **Routing** — defining the sequence of operations.
3. **Scheduling** — fixing start and finish times.
4. **Dispatching & Expediting** — releasing orders and tracking progress.
*(½ mark each = 2 marks)*

### Question 2. [KTU University Exam — May 2024, Sessional]
**What is Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE)? State its three components.**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**
OEE is a measure of how effectively a manufacturing operation is utilized, expressed as a percentage. It is the product of three factors:
1. **Availability** — ratio of actual run time to planned production time.
2. **Performance** — ratio of actual output rate to standard output rate.
3. **Quality** — ratio of good units produced to total units produced.
*(1 mark definition + ½ mark each for the three factors + ½ mark for formula statement)*

## 5.2 Part B — Module Internal Choice (14 Marks Each)

### Question A. [KTU University Exam — Dec 2023]

#### Part (a) — 7 Marks
**A polymer processing plant has annual demand of 20,000 kg of PP granules. The ordering cost is ₹400 per order and the holding cost is ₹8 per kg per year. Calculate:**
**(i)** the EOQ,
**(ii)** the optimal number of orders per year,
**(iii)** the minimum total inventory cost,
**(iv)** the time between orders.

**Step-by-Step Model Solution:**

**Given Data:**
- $D = 20{,}000$ kg/yr
- $S = ₹400$/order
- $H = ₹8$/kg·yr

**(i) EOQ Calculation:**

$$
Q^{*} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 20000 \times 400}{8}} = \sqrt{\frac{16{,}000{,}000}{8}} = \sqrt{2{,}000{,}000}
$$

$$
Q^{*} \approx 1414.21 \text{ kg}
$$

*(2 marks)*

**(ii) Optimal Number of Orders:**

$$
N = \frac{D}{Q^{*}} = \frac{20000}{1414.21} \approx 14.14 \approx 14 \text{ orders/year}
$$

*(1.5 marks)*

**(iii) Minimum Total Inventory Cost:**

Ordering cost component:

$$
\frac{DS}{Q^{*}} = \frac{20000 \times 400}{1414.21} = ₹5656.85
$$

Holding cost component:

$$
\frac{HQ^{*}}{2} = \frac{8 \times 1414.21}{2} = ₹5656.85
$$

TIC:

$$
\text{TIC} = 5656.85 + 5656.85 = ₹11{,}313.7 \text{ per year}
$$

*(2.5 marks)*

**(iv) Time Between Orders (TBO):**

$$
\text{TBO} = \frac{\text{Working days per year}}{N} = \frac{300}{14.14} \approx 21.2 \text{ days}
$$

*(1 mark)*

#### Part (b) — 7 Marks
**Explain the four stages of Production Planning and Control with a neat block diagram suitable for a polymer compounding plant.**

**Model Answer Outline (7 marks):**

1. **Planning:** Demand forecast + capacity planning + MPS formulation. *(1.5 marks)*
2. **Routing:** Route sheet specifying sequence — *Drying → Mixing → Extrusion → Pelletizing → QC → Packing*. *(1.5 marks)*
3. **Scheduling:** Gantt chart or finite loading to assign machine time. *(1.5 marks)*
4. **Dispatching & Expediting:** Issue work orders, monitor progress, take corrective action. *(1.5 marks)*
5. **Block diagram** showing the closed feedback loop. *(1 mark)*

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Pitfall Callout:**
> - Students often **omit the feedback/control loop** in the block diagram — lose **2 marks**.
> - Mixing up *Routing* with *Scheduling* is a common error — *routing* answers *where*, *scheduling* answers *when*.
> - Forgetting units in the EOQ answer is a recurring deduction of **0.5 mark**.

---

### Question B. [KTU University Exam — May 2024, Alternative Module Choice]

#### Part (a) — 7 Marks
**The following data relate to monthly demand for a polymer product: 40, 45, 50, 55, 60 units. Using exponential smoothing with $\alpha = 0.3$ and $F_1 = 40$, forecast the demand for the 6th month. Also compute the Mean Absolute Deviation (MAD).**

**Step-by-Step Model Solution:**

**Recursion formula:**

$$
F_{t+1} = 0.3 A_t + 0.7 F_t
$$

**Month 1:** $F_1 = 40$ (given).
**Month 2:**

$$
F_2 = 0.3(40) + 0.7(40) = 12 + 28 = 40
$$
**Month 3:**

$$
F_3 = 0.3(45) + 0.7(40) = 13.5 + 28 = 41.5
$$
**Month 4:**

$$
F_4 = 0.3(50) + 0.7(41.5) = 15 + 29.05 = 44.05
$$
**Month 5:**

$$
F_5 = 0.3(55) + 0.7(44.05) = 16.5 + 30.835 = 47.335
$$
**Month 6:**

$$
F_6 = 0.3(60) + 0.7(47.335) = 18 + 33.1345 = 51.13 \text{ units}
$$

**MAD Calculation:**

| Month | $A_t$ | $F_t$ | $\vert A_t - F_t \vert$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 40 | 40 | 0 |
| 2 | 45 | 40 | 5 |
| 3 | 50 | 41.5 | 8.5 |
| 4 | 55 | 44.05 | 10.95 |
| 5 | 60 | 47.335 | 12.665 |

*(Use `\vert` instead of `|` in raw answer sheets to avoid markdown issues.)*

$$
\text{MAD} = \frac{0 + 5 + 8.5 + 10.95 + 12.665}{5} = \frac{37.115}{5} \approx 7.42
$$

**Answer:** $F_6 \approx 51.13$ units, MAD $\approx 7.42$ units. *(7 marks: 4 for forecast table, 2 for MAD formula, 1 for final value)*

#### Part (b) — 7 Marks
**Describe the Materials Requirement Planning (MRP) system. How does MRP differ from EOQ and what are its limitations in a polymer manufacturing context?**

**Model Answer Outline (7 marks):**

- **MRP Definition:** A computer-based planning system that converts the MPS into detailed procurement and production plans using BOM and inventory data. *(1.5 marks)*
- **MRP Inputs:** MPS, BOM, Inventory Status File. *(1 mark)*
- **MRP Processing:** Lot sizing, lead-time offsetting, net requirements explosion. *(1.5 marks)*
- **MRP vs EOQ:** MRP is *time-phased and dependent-demand*; EOQ is *static and independent-demand*. *(1.5 marks)*
- **Limitations in Polymer Industry:** Batch recipe complexity, hazardous additive handling, long curing times, and changeover losses make MRP rigid — MRP II / ERP with MES needed. *(1.5 marks)*

## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **High-Yield Rapid-Revision Checklist for KTU 2024 Exam:**

- ✔ **PPC = Planning + Routing + Scheduling + Dispatching + Control** — must mention all 5.
- ✔ **EOQ formula:** $Q^{*} = \sqrt{2DS/H}$ — partial marks given for formula even if calculation slips.
- ✔ **At EOQ, ordering cost = holding cost** — powerful cross-check.
- ✔ **MRP is time-phased; EOQ is not.** Don't confuse them.
- ✔ **OEE** combines Availability, Performance, Quality — the three pillars.
- ✔ **Takt Time** dictates lean line pacing.
- ✔ **MPS → MRP → Shop Floor** is the information flow.
- ✔ **Push vs Pull:** Push uses forecast, Pull uses customer order.
- ✔ Always state **units** in numerical answers — examiners deduct for unit omission.
- ✔ Draw **neat block diagrams** with closed feedback loop; missing loop = -2 marks.
- ✔ For forecast problems, use **exponential smoothing** unless stated otherwise.
- ✔ In polymer context, emphasize **batch traceability, recipe management, and curing/cooling time** as real-world PPC constraints.
- ✔ **MRP II and ERP** extend classical PPC to finance and shop-floor integration — popular 3-mark question.
- ✔ Numerical questions typically have **two decimal precision** in final EOQ answers.

## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview of the PPC System

### 1.1 Formal Academic Definition (KTU 2024 Scheme Terminology)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Production Planning and Control (PPC) System** is an integrated engineering management framework that systematically plans, organizes, directs, and regulates the **material flow, machine utilization, manpower allocation, and process sequencing** across an industrial organization to transform raw inputs into finished goods at *optimum cost*, *minimum lead time*, and *guaranteed quality*.

The **PPC System** is not a single department but a *cross-functional management philosophy* spanning **five major phases**: **Planning → Routing → Scheduling → Dispatching → Expediting (Follow-up)**. It acts as the **central nervous system of a manufacturing enterprise**, synchronizing demand forecasting, capacity balancing, inventory control, and shop-floor execution.

The **typical activities** of a PPC System refer to the *standard, repetitive, and interlinked functions* that every PPC cell must perform, irrespective of whether the industry follows **Make-to-Stock (MTS)**, **Make-to-Order (MTO)**, **Assemble-to-Order (ATO)**, or **Engineer-to-Order (ETO)** paradigms.

### 1.2 Conceptual Analogy – "The Orchestra Conductor"

> [!NOTE]
> **Analogy:** Imagine a 100-piece symphony orchestra preparing to play Beethoven's 9th. Without a conductor, the violinist plays too fast, the drummer too loud, and the chorus enters 30 seconds late — chaos. The **PPC Manager is the conductor**. He decides:
> - **Which instruments** play in which section (Routing)
> - **When** each instrument joins the score (Scheduling)
> - **Hands out** the sheet music to each player (Dispatching)
> - **Listens and corrects** if the oboe plays out of tune (Expediting/Follow-up)
> - **Reviews** the final concert for the next season (Corrective Action)
> 
> Just as a conductor transforms chaos into music, the PPC System transforms market demand into delivered products, with every activity happening in a *fixed, predictable sequence*.

### 1.3 The Two-Pillar Classification of PPC Activities

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Pillar 1 – Pre-Production Planning (The "What & How" Phase):** Forecasting, capacity planning, loading, routing, and scheduling.
>
> **Pillar 2 – Production Control (The "When & Did It Work" Phase):** Dispatching, expediting, inspection, corrective action, and reporting.

### 1.4 Standard Engineering Metrics Used in PPC

The following **high-frequency KTU metrics** are referenced throughout PPC activities:

- **Lead Time (LT)** — Time from order receipt to delivery (in *days* or *hours*).
- **Throughput Time (TPT)** — Time the unit spends inside the factory.
- **Machine Utilization (η_m)** — Ratio of *actual run time* to *available time*.
- **Capacity (C)** — Maximum output rate (units/hour).
- **Work-In-Process (WIP)** — Inventory between operations.
- **Order Cycle Time (OCT)** — Sum of *preparation, processing, and waiting times*.

These constants appear repeatedly in KTU 2024 numerical problems on this module.
<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### 2.1 The 8 Typical Activities of a PPC System – Structured Logic

The PPC System performs **eight (8) canonical activities** that loop continuously. Each activity is an answer to a specific question:

| # | Activity | Core Question Answered | Phase |
|---|----------|------------------------|-------|
| 1 | **Demand Forecasting** | "How much will the market buy?" | Pre-Production |
| 2 | **Capacity Planning** | "Can our factory handle it?" | Pre-Production |
| 3 | **Routing** | "Which path in the workshop?" | Pre-Production |
| 4 | **Scheduling** | "When does each operation start?" | Pre-Production |
| 5 | **Loading** | "Are machines overloaded/underloaded?" | Pre-Production |
| 6 | **Dispatching** | "Release the order to the floor NOW." | Production Control |
| 7 | **Expediting / Follow-up** | "Is everything on track?" | Production Control |
| 8 | **Inspection & Corrective Action** | "What went wrong, and how to fix it?" | Production Control |

> [!NOTE]
> **KTU Memory Trick: "D-C-R-S-L-D-E-I"** — *Demand, Capacity, Routing, Scheduling, Loading, Dispatching, Expediting, Inspection*.

### 2.2 Activity 1 – Demand Forecasting

- **What it is:** Predicting future customer demand using **time-series methods** (Moving Average, Exponential Smoothing), **causal models** (Regression), or **qualitative Delphi techniques**.
- **Why it matters:** Forecasts drive *raw material procurement*, *workforce hiring*, and *machine investment*.
- **How it works:** Historical sales data → Statistical model → Adjusted forecast → Master Production Schedule (MPS) input.

### 2.3 Activity 2 – Capacity Planning

- **What it is:** Determining whether the *available machines, labor, and tooling* can meet forecasted demand.
- **Why it matters:** Prevents both *over-capacity* (idle costs) and *under-capacity* (lost sales).
- **How it works:**
  - Step 1: Calculate required capacity $C_{req}$ from forecast.
  - Step 2: Calculate available capacity $C_{avail}$ from machines.
  - Step 3: Compare and trigger *capacity adjustment* (overtime, subcontracting, expansion).

### 2.4 Activity 3 – Routing

- **What it is:** Determining the *sequence of machines, operations, and processes* a part must follow.
- **Why it matters:** Defines the *physical path* of the product through the factory.
- **How it works:** Engineering drawings + Bill of Materials (BOM) + Process Sheets → Route sheet for each part.

### 2.5 Activity 4 – Scheduling

- **What it is:** Fixing *start and end times* for each operation identified during routing.
- **Why it matters:** Translates the *route* into a *time-bound plan*.
- **How it works:** Uses Gantt charts, Johnson's Rule, or Critical Ratio (CR) to allocate time slots to machines.

### 2.6 Activity 5 – Loading

- **What it is:** Assigning jobs to *specific machines and operators* based on capacity.
- **Why it matters:** Prevents *machine bottlenecks* and *operator idle time*.
- **How it works:** Infinite loading vs. Finite loading — measured in *standard hours per machine per day*.

### 2.7 Activity 6 – Dispatching

- **What it is:** The *formal release* of work orders, raw materials, tools, and instructions to the shop floor.
- **Why it matters:** This is the *point of no return* — planning becomes execution.
- **How it works:** PPC cell issues *dispatch documents*: job orders, material requisitions, tool orders, time tickets, and move orders.

### 2.8 Activity 7 – Expediting / Follow-up

- **What it is:** *Real-time monitoring* of work-in-progress to detect and remove deviations.
- **Why it matters:** Catches delays before they cascade into missed deliveries.
- **How it works:** Daily progress reports → Variance analysis → Corrective dispatch.

### 2.9 Activity 8 – Inspection & Corrective Action

- **What it is:** Verifying *quality* of output and feeding *feedback* back into planning.
- **Why it matters:** Closes the *PDCA (Plan-Do-Check-Act)* loop.
- **How it works:** Statistical Process Control (SPC) + Defect analysis → Plan revision.

### 2.10 KTU High-Yield Formula / Cheat Sheet

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Mandatory Formulas for KTU 2024 PPC Numericals**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Lead Time (LT)} &= \text{Order Prep Time} + \text{Processing Time} + \text{Waiting Time} + \text{Queue Time} \\[4pt]
\text{Machine Utilization } (\eta_m) &= \frac{\text{Actual Running Time}}{\text{Available Time}} \times 100\% \\[4pt]
\text{Required Capacity } (C_{req}) &= \frac{\text{Demand Forecast (units)} \times \text{Std. Time per unit}}{\text{Planning Horizon (hours)}} \\[4pt]
\text{Critical Ratio (CR)} &= \frac{\text{Due Date} - \text{Today}}{\text{Remaining Processing Time}} \\[4pt]
\text{Efficiency } (\eta) &= \frac{\text{Standard Hours Earned}}{\text{Actual Hours Worked}} \times 100\% \\[4pt]
\text{WIP (Little's Law)} &= \text{Throughput Rate} \times \text{Throughput Time} \\[4pt]
\text{Capacity Variance} &= C_{avail} - C_{req} \quad [\text{positive} = \text{surplus, negative} = \text{shortfall}]
\end{aligned}
$$

| Symbol | Meaning | Typical Unit |
|--------|---------|--------------|
| $C_{req}$ | Required Capacity | machine-hours / day |
| $C_{avail}$ | Available Capacity | machine-hours / day |
| $\eta_m$ | Machine Utilization | % |
| CR | Critical Ratio | dimensionless |
| WIP | Work-In-Process | units |
| LT | Lead Time | days |

### 2.11 Real-World Engineering Utility

In **automotive OEMs** (e.g., Maruti, Tata Motors), the PPC system schedules *3,000+ parts* per vehicle on *hundreds of workstations* daily. In **aerospace** (HAL, Boeing), the same 8 activities are followed for *Engineer-to-Order* turbine blades where each blade is unique. In **process industries** (BPCL, Reliance Refineries), the loop runs continuously with *24×7 dispatching and expediting* in DCS (Distributed Control System) environments.
<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
## 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

### 3.1 Analytical Walk-Through: A Canonical PPC Problem

> **KTU-Type Problem Statement:** A factory has **5 machines** working **8 hours/day, 25 days/month**. The forecasted monthly demand is **2,000 units**, each requiring a *standard time* of **3 hours/unit**. The company operates 1 shift. Determine: (a) Required Capacity, (b) Available Capacity, (c) Capacity Variance, and (d) Machine Utilization needed.

---

#### Step 1 — Identify the Given Data

We list all given parameters from the problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Number of machines } (N) &= 5 \\
\text{Hours per shift } (h) &= 8 \text{ hours/day} \\
\text{Working days } (d) &= 25 \text{ days/month} \\
\text{Number of shifts } (s) &= 1 \\
\text{Monthly demand } (D) &= 2{,}000 \text{ units/month} \\
\text{Standard time per unit } (t_s) &= 3 \text{ hours/unit}
\end{aligned}
$$

---

#### Step 2 — Calculate Available Capacity

Available capacity is the *total productive time* the factory can offer in the planning horizon. We multiply machines, hours per day, days, and shifts.

$$
\begin{aligned}
C_{avail} &= N \times h \times d \times s \\
C_{avail} &= 5 \times 8 \times 25 \times 1 \\
C_{avail} &= 1{,}000 \text{ machine-hours / month}
\end{aligned}
$$

---

#### Step 3 — Calculate Required Capacity

Required capacity is the *total productive time* demanded by the forecasted sales.

$$
\begin{aligned}
C_{req} &= D \times t_s \\
C_{req} &= 2{,}000 \times 3 \\
C_{req} &= 6{,}000 \text{ machine-hours / month}
\end{aligned}
$$

---

#### Step 4 — Calculate Capacity Variance

A *negative variance* indicates a **capacity shortfall** — the factory cannot meet demand with current resources.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta C &= C_{avail} - C_{req} \\
\Delta C &= 1{,}000 - 6{,}000 \\
\Delta C &= -5{,}000 \text{ machine-hours / month}
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\Delta C < 0$, the plant is in a **shortfall of 5,000 machine-hours per month**.

---

#### Step 5 — Apply Corrective Action (Capacity Adjustment)

The PPC manager must now choose one of three remedies:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\textbf{Remedy 1: Overtime} \rightarrow \text{Extra hours} &= \frac{5{,}000}{5 \text{ machines}} = 1{,}000 \text{ hours/machine/month} \\[4pt]
\textbf{Remedy 2: Subcontracting} \rightarrow \text{Outsource} &= 5{,}000 \text{ machine-hours} \\[4pt]
\textbf{Remedy 3: Add a second shift} \rightarrow \text{New } C_{avail} &= 5 \times 8 \times 25 \times 2 = 2{,}000 \text{ hours} \\
&\text{(Still short by } 4{,}000 \text{ hours)}
\end{aligned}
$$

The best remedy is therefore **Overtime + Partial Subcontracting**.

---

#### Step 6 — Compute Required Machine Utilization

If we meet demand using *only* the 1,000 available machine-hours, the machines must be utilized at:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\eta_m &= \frac{C_{req}}{C_{avail}} \times 100\% \\
\eta_m &= \frac{6{,}000}{1{,}000} \times 100\% = 600\%
\end{aligned}
$$

This is **physically impossible** (utilization cannot exceed 100%), confirming the need for the corrective actions in Step 5.

---

#### Step 7 — Lead Time Computation (Supplementary)

If the *preparation time* = 2 days, *processing time* = $2{,}000 \times 3 / (5 \times 8) = 150$ days, *waiting time* = 5 days, *queue time* = 3 days:

$$
\begin{aligned}
LT &= 2 + 150 + 5 + 3 = 160 \text{ days}
\end{aligned}
$$

### 3.2 Analytical Matrix – Activity-to-Function Mapping

> [!NOTE]
> **Master Reference Table for KTU 2024 Exam Preparation**

| PPC Activity | Output Document | Tool/Technique | KPI Measured | KTU Bloom Level |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Forecasting | Forecast Sheet | Moving Average, ESM | Forecast Error % | L3 (Apply) |
| Capacity Planning | Capacity Plan | CPR, CRP | $C_{req}$ vs. $C_{avail}$ | L4 (Analyze) |
| Routing | Route Sheet | Process Layout | Path length | L3 (Apply) |
| Scheduling | Gantt Chart | Johnson's Rule, CR | Makespan | L4 (Analyze) |
| Loading | Load Chart | Finite/Inf. Loading | Std hrs/machine | L3 (Apply) |
| Dispatching | Job Order | Authorization slip | On-time release % | L2 (Understand) |
| Expediting | Daily Report | Variance Analysis | Delay % | L5 (Evaluate) |
| Inspection | QC Report | SPC, Pareto | Defect rate (ppm) | L5 (Evaluate) |

### 3.3 PDCA Loop Integration

The 8 PPC activities are bound by the **Deming Cycle**:

$$
\text{Plan (Activities 1–5)} \;\rightarrow\; \text{Do (Activity 6)} \;\rightarrow\; \text{Check (Activity 7)} \;\rightarrow\; \text{Act (Activity 8)} \;\rightarrow\; \text{Plan (next cycle)}
$$

This guarantees **continuous improvement** — the same data that schedules a job today refines the schedule for tomorrow.

## 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Pitfall Alert** — *Common mistakes students make in PPC questions:*
> 1. **Confusing $C_{avail}$ and $C_{req}$** — Always state the *planning horizon* (per day, per month, per year) clearly. A 100 machine-hour/day factory ≠ 100 machine-hour/month factory.
> 2. **Forgetting shift factor ($s$)** — If the problem says *2 shifts*, multiply by 2; otherwise, default is 1.
> 3. **Mixing units in $LT$ formula** — Convert all times to a *common unit* (hours or days) before adding.
> 4. **Writing "Dispatching = Scheduling"** in theory answers. *Dispatching* releases work; *scheduling* plans it. They are different.
> 5. **Skipping the corrective action** in numericals — KTU examiners award 2–3 marks specifically for the *remedy step* in capacity planning problems.

---

### Part A — Short-Answer Questions (2 × 3 Marks = 6 Marks)

#### Q1. **[KTU University Exam – May 2024 Model Question]**
**"List and briefly explain any three typical activities of a Production Planning and Control (PPC) system."** (3 Marks)

**Model Answer (3 Points):**
1. **Routing:** Determining the *path* a part will follow through machines, operations, and workstations based on the engineering drawing and process sheet.
2. **Scheduling:** Fixing the *start and finish time* of each operation identified in routing, using techniques like Gantt charts or Johnson's algorithm.
3. **Dispatching:** Authoritatively *releasing* the work orders, materials, and tools to the shop floor, converting plans into action.

*(Examiner Note: 1 mark per activity — definition + 1-line purpose.)*

---

#### Q2. **[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023 Model Question]**
**"Differentiate between 'Loading' and 'Scheduling' in a PPC system."** (3 Marks)

**Model Answer:**

| Parameter | Loading | Scheduling |
|-----------|---------|------------|
| Definition | Assigning jobs to specific machines/operators | Fixing start/end times for operations |
| Question Answered | *Where* and *by whom* will the job be done? | *When* will the job start and finish? |
| Typical Tool | Load chart (machine-wise) | Gantt chart (time-wise) |
| Focus | Machine capacity balancing | Time horizon allocation |

*(Examiner Note: A clean table earns full 3 marks.)*

---

### Part B — Long-Answer Questions (Module Internal Choice: Q-A or Q-B)

> **KTU 2024 ESE Pattern:** Each Part B question carries **14 marks** with sub-parts (a) 7 marks + (b) 7 marks. Internal choice is provided within the module.

---

#### **Question A (14 Marks)** — *Numerical + Theory Mix*

**[KTU University Exam – Model Paper 2024, Module 2]**

**(a)** A manufacturing unit has **6 identical machines**, operating **2 shifts of 8 hours each, 26 days a month**. The monthly demand forecast is **3,000 units**, with a *standard time* of **4 hours per unit**.
Calculate: (i) Available Capacity, (ii) Required Capacity, (iii) Capacity Variance, and (iv) the *minimum number of subcontracted hours* needed to balance the plan. (7 Marks)

**(b)** With the help of a neat flowchart, explain **any four typical activities of a PPC system** and state the *document* generated by each. (7 Marks)

**Model Solution:**

**(a) Solution (7 Marks):**

Given data:

$$
\begin{aligned}
N &= 6, \quad h = 8, \quad d = 26, \quad s = 2 \\
D &= 3{,}000 \text{ units}, \quad t_s = 4 \text{ hours/unit}
\end{aligned}
$$

**(i) Available Capacity:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
C_{avail} &= N \times h \times d \times s = 6 \times 8 \times 26 \times 2 = 2{,}496 \text{ machine-hours/month}
\end{aligned}
$$

**(ii) Required Capacity:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
C_{req} &= D \times t_s = 3{,}000 \times 4 = 12{,}000 \text{ machine-hours/month}
\end{aligned}
$$

**(iii) Capacity Variance:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta C &= 2{,}496 - 12{,}000 = -9{,}504 \text{ machine-hours/month (shortfall)}
\end{aligned}
$$

**(iv) Subcontracting Hours Required:**

$$
\text{Subcontract Hours} = 9{,}504 \text{ machine-hours}
$$

---

**(b) Solution (7 Marks):**

**Activity 1 — Demand Forecasting:** Predicts market demand via time-series methods. *Document:* **Forecast Sheet**.

**Activity 2 — Routing:** Decides the operation sequence. *Document:* **Route Sheet**.

**Activity 3 — Scheduling:** Fixes time for each operation. *Document:* **Master Schedule / Gantt Chart**.

**Activity 4 — Dispatching:** Releases work to the shop floor. *Document:* **Job Order / Dispatch Slip**.

*(Each activity: 1.5 marks for definition + 0.25 mark for the document = 7 marks total.)*

---

#### **Question B (14 Marks)** — *Pure Theory / Diagram Type*

**[KTU University Exam – Model Paper 2024, Module 2 Alternative]**

**(a)** Explain the **role of Expediting (Follow-up)** as a typical activity of a PPC system. List **four reasons** why expediting is critical in a modern manufacturing environment. (7 Marks)

**(b)** A small-scale industry has **4 machines, working 1 shift of 8 hours for 24 days/month**. The demand is **800 units/month** at **5 hours/unit**. Determine the *machine utilization percentage*. If management decides to add a *second shift* of 6 hours, recalculate the new utilization. (7 Marks)

**Model Solution:**

**(a) Solution (7 Marks):**

**Definition (3 Marks):** Expediting (or Follow-up) is the *real-time monitoring activity* of a PPC system that tracks the progress of work orders through the shop floor, compares *actual progress* with *planned progress*, identifies *delays and bottlenecks*, and triggers *corrective actions* to bring the plan back on track.

**Four Reasons (4 × 1 Mark):**
1. **Delay Detection:** Catches slippage before it cascades to customer deliveries.
2. **Bottleneck Identification:** Highlights which machine or operator is overburdened.
3. **Customer Satisfaction:** Ensures on-time delivery (OTD ≥ 95%).
4. **Cost Control:** Reduces inventory carrying cost by avoiding WIP pile-up.

---

**(b) Solution (7 Marks):**

**Step 1 — Available Capacity (1 Shift):**

$$
C_{avail,1} = 4 \times 8 \times 24 \times 1 = 768 \text{ machine-hours}
$$

**Step 2 — Required Capacity:**

$$
C_{req} = 800 \times 5 = 4{,}000 \text{ machine-hours}
$$

**Step 3 — Utilization (1 Shift):**

$$
\eta_{m,1} = \frac{4{,}000}{768} \times 100\% = 520.83\% \quad \text{(Impossible — confirms 2nd shift needed)}
$$

**Step 4 — Available Capacity (2 Shifts, 2nd = 6 hrs):**

$$
C_{avail,2} = 4 \times (8+6) \times 24 = 1{,}344 \text{ machine-hours}
$$

**Step 5 — New Utilization:**

$$
\eta_{m,2} = \frac{4{,}000}{1{,}344} \times 100\% = 297.6\%
$$

**Conclusion (1 Mark):** Even 2 shifts cannot meet demand; the firm must adopt *overtime + subcontracting* — a classic PPC corrective action.

---

### 5.4 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember (Rapid Revision Checklist)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **High-Density Bullet Revision Block — Read 5 minutes before exam**

- **PPC = Planning + Control**; spans the *entire order-to-delivery* cycle.
- **8 Typical Activities** (Memory Code: **D-C-R-S-L-D-E-I**):
  1. **D**emand Forecasting
  2. **C**apacity Planning
  3. **R**outing
  4. **S**cheduling
  5. **L**oading
  6. **D**ispatching
  7. **E**xpediting (Follow-up)
  8. **I**nspection & Corrective Action
- **Planning Phase (1–5)** answers "What, Where, When, By Whom" — done *before* production.
- **Control Phase (6–8)** answers "How is it going? What to fix?" — done *during/after* production.
- **Golden Formula Trio for Numericals:**
  - $C_{avail} = N \times h \times d \times s$
  - $C_{req} = D \times t_s$
  - $\eta_m = (C_{req} / C_{avail}) \times 100\%$
- **Little's Law:** $WIP = \text{Throughput Rate} \times \text{Throughput Time}$ — useful for queue-based problems.
- **Critical Ratio (CR):** If $CR < 1$, the job is *behind schedule*; if $CR > 1$, it is *ahead* of schedule.
- **Documents to remember:** Route Sheet, Gantt Chart, Load Chart, Job Order, Dispatch Slip, Daily Progress Report, QC Report.
- **PDCA Loop:** Plan (1–5) → Do (6) → Check (7) → Act (8) — drives continuous improvement.
- **Real-world application:** Used in Maruti (automotive), HAL (aerospace), BPCL (refinery), Apollo Tyres (batch), Infosys (service-PPC).
- **Common exam trap:** Students forget the *shift factor $s$* in capacity problems; *always* check whether the problem states "shifts".
- **KTU 2024 weightage expectation:** 14-mark numerical on capacity planning (high probability) + 7-mark theory on the 8 activities (high probability) + 3-mark short answer on definitions.

> **End of Module Experiment 2 — Typical Activities of PPC System — KTU 2024 Scheme Study Notes**

topics.title: computer integrated production management system
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME** > - **Course:** PCPOL607 - PCPOL607 > - **Module:** Module Experiment 2 > - **Topic:** computer integrated production management system # SECTION 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview ## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition > [!IMPORTANT] > **Computer Integrated Production Management System (CIPMS)** is a holistic manufacturing paradigm in which all functional areas of an enterprise — from design and production planning to shop-floor execution, quality assurance, and dispatch — are interconnected through a centralized digital information backbone, enabling real-time data exchange, automated decision-making, and synchronized control of all production resources. In the **KTU 2024 Scheme** parlance, CIPMS is positioned as the **strategic evolution of Computer-Integrated Manufacturing (CIM)** focusing specifically on the *information-flow layer* that governs the production system. It uses a **layered, hierarchical architecture** (as defined by the ISO/IEC 62264 / ISA-95 standard) in which **Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP)** at the top, **Manufacturing Execution Systems (MES)** in the middle, and **Shop Floor Control (SFC)** at the bottom are seamlessly integrated. ## 1.2 The Three Pillars of CIPMS | Pillar | Role in CIPMS | |---|---| | **Information Pillar** | Centralized database, MRP-II/ERP data, common data model | | **Functional Pillar** | CAD, CAPP, CAM, CAQ, PPC, inventory, maintenance modules | | **Organizational Pillar** | People, procedures, workflow governance | ## 1.3 Conceptual Analogy — The Airport Control Tower > [!NOTE] > Imagine a **modern international airport**. The control tower (your *CIPMS central computer*) receives live data from every gate (machines), runway sensors (CNCs/robots), baggage belts (material handling), airline counters (sales orders), and fuel trucks (inventory). The tower **orchestrates take-offs and landings** (production schedules) in real time. Without the tower, every department would operate blindly. With it, the entire airport behaves as one synchronized organism — exactly what CIPMS does for a manufacturing plant. ## 1.4 Standard Metrics & Constants Used in CIPMS - **OEE (Overall Equipment Effectiveness) = Availability × Performance × Quality** - **MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures)** measured in **hours** - **MTTR (Mean Time To Repair)** measured in **hours** - **Takt Time** measured in **seconds/unit** - **Lead Time** measured in **days** - **WIP (Work-In-Process)** measured in **units** or **value (₹)** > [!IMPORTANT] > **Syllabus Highlight (KTU 2024):** The course explicitly expects students to map every production function to its digital counterpart, justify the need for **real-time bidirectional data flow**, and evaluate the role of **BOM (Bill of Materials), Routing files, and Work Centers** as the *core data entities* of any CIPMS. --- # SECTION 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet ## 2.1 The Layered Architecture of CIPMS (ISA-95 / Purdue Model) CIPMS is structurally organized into **5 hierarchical levels**. Every KTU question on this topic can be answered correctly by simply mapping a function to its correct level. ### Level 0 — Physical Process - The actual machines: CNC, robots, conveyors, sensors, actuators. - Generates raw I/O data (temperature, vibration, torque). ### Level 1 — Basic Control - **PLCs, DCS, CNC controllers, SCADA.** - Performs closed-loop control using feedback from Level 0. ### Level 2 — Supervisory / SCADA-HMI - Operator dashboards, alarming, recipe management. - Passes consolidated data upward. ### Level 3 — Manufacturing Operations Management (MES Layer) > This is the **heart of CIPMS**. It contains: > - Detailed production scheduling > - Shop-floor dispatching > - Quality data acquisition > - Resource tracking > - Performance analysis (OEE) ### Level 4 — Business Planning (ERP Layer) - Long-term forecasting, master production scheduling (MPS), financial planning, HR. ## 2.2 The Core Functional Modules of CIPMS CIPMS can be decomposed into **eight functional blocks**, each of which is a candidate 14-mark KTU question: 1. **CAD (Computer-Aided Design)** — Geometric modelling, drafting. 2. **CAPP (Computer-Aided Process Planning)** — Generates route sheets from CAD geometry. 3. **CAM (Computer-Aided Manufacturing)** — Generates NC part programs. 4. **CAQ (Computer-Aided Quality Assurance)** — Statistical Process Control, SQC charts. 5. **PPC (Production Planning & Control)** — Routing, scheduling, dispatching. 6. **FMS (Flexible Manufacturing System)** — Integrated CNC + AGV + AS/RS. 7. **MRP-II (Manufacturing Resource Planning)** — Material, capacity, and shop-floor planning. 8. **ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning)** — Enterprise-wide integration. ## 2.3 Data Flow Inside a CIPMS The information movement in a CIPMS follows the **"Design → Plan → Make → Deliver → Support"** loop: 1. **Order receipt** → enters ERP (Level 4). 2. **Master Production Schedule (MPS)** → created. 3. **MRP-II explosion** → raw material and component demand computed. 4. **Detailed routing** → produced via CAPP. 5. **Shop floor dispatch** → MES (Level 3). 6. **CNC execution** → Level 1 controllers. 7. **Quality feedback** → CAQ module writes to central DB. 8. **KPI dashboard** → Management view. ## 2.4 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet > [!IMPORTANT] > The following equations are **high-yield** for the 2024 KTU exam. Memorize the *form* and the *units*. $$ \text{OEE} = A \times P \times Q $$ where $A$ = Availability, $P$ = Performance, $Q$ = Quality. OEE is **dimensionless (%).** $$ T_{\text{takt}} = \frac{T_{\text{available per shift}}}{D_{\text{demand}}} $$ Takt time is measured in **seconds per unit**. $$ \text{Cycle Time Efficiency} = \frac{\sum T_{\text{value-added}}}{\sum T_{\text{value-added}} + \sum T_{\text{non-value-added}}} $$ $$ \text{MTBF} = \frac{T_{\text{total operating time}}}{N_{\text{failures}}} $$ $$ \text{MTTR} = \frac{T_{\text{total downtime}}}{N_{\text{failures}}} $$ $$ \text{Availability} = \frac{\text{MTBF}}{\text{MTBF} + \text{MTTR}} $$ $$ \text{Throughput} = \frac{1}{T_{\text{bottleneck}}} $$ $$ \text{Inventory Turnover Ratio} = \frac{C_{\text{COGS}}}{I_{\text{avg}}} $$ $$ \text{R.O.I. of CIM} = \frac{\Delta \text{Profit} + \Delta \text{Quality savings} + \Delta \text{Inventory reduction}}{C_{\text{CIM investment}}} $$ | Parameter | Symbol | Unit | Use in CIPMS | |---|---|---|---| | OEE | $\eta$ | % | Equipment health monitoring | | MTBF | — | hours | Predictive maintenance | | MTTR | — | hours | Maintenance efficiency | | Takt Time | $T_t$ | s/unit | Line balancing | | Cycle Time | $T_c$ | s/unit | Scheduling | | WIP Value | $V_{wip}$ | ₹ | Lean assessment | | Lead Time | $L$ | days | Order promising | ## 2.5 Real-World Engineering Utility - **Automotive industry** (e.g., Maruti Suzuki): A single CIPMS coordinates **>2,000 robots** across body shop, paint shop, and assembly. - **Aerospace** (e.g., HAL): Tracks every rivet through CIPMS to meet **FAA traceability** rules. - **Semiconductor fabs** (e.g., Intel): Lithography cells are scheduled at the **second level** via MES. - **Pharma**: CIPMS enforces **21 CFR Part 11** electronic batch records. > [!NOTE] > A KTU examiner expects you to quote at least **one real engineering use-case** when explaining CIPMS — this is a guaranteed **+2 marks** on a 14-mark question. --- # SECTION 3: Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix ## 3.1 Derivation: OEE as a Composite KPI ### 3.1.1 Statement > *Prove that the Overall Equipment Effectiveness is the product of three independent factors — Availability, Performance, and Quality — and not their sum.* ### 3.1.2 Given - Planned Production Time = $T_{p}$ (hours) - Actual Run Time = $T_{r}$ (hours) - Ideal Cycle Time = $T_{i}$ (seconds/unit) - Total Pieces Produced = $N_{t}$ (units) - Good Pieces = $N_{g}$ (units) - Reject Pieces = $N_{r}$ (units) such that $N_{t} = N_{g} + N_{r}$ ### 3.1.3 Step-by-Step Derivation **Step 1 — Define Availability Factor (A)** Availability is the *fraction of scheduled time* the machine was actually running. $$ A = \frac{T_{r}}{T_{p}} $$ The "lost time" is the downtime due to breakdowns, set-ups, and changeovers. **Step 2 — Define Performance Factor (P)** Performance compares *theoretical* output against *actual* output during run time. $$ P = \frac{T_{i} \times N_{t}}{T_{r} \times 3600} $$ Here $3600$ converts hours to seconds so that numerator and denominator share the unit *seconds*. **Step 3 — Define Quality Factor (Q)** $$ Q = \frac{N_{g}}{N_{t}} $$ **Step 4 — Compose OEE** By definition, OEE is *Good Pieces produced in the theoretical minimum time* divided by *Planned Production Time*. $$ \text{OEE} = \frac{N_{g} \times T_{i}}{T_{p} \times 3600} $$ **Step 5 — Substitute and Simplify** $$ \begin{aligned} \text{OEE} &= \frac{N_{g} \times T_{i}}{T_{p} \times 3600} \\ &= \frac{N_{t}}{N_{t}} \cdot \frac{N_{g}}{N_{t}} \cdot \frac{T_{i} \times N_{t}}{T_{r} \times 3600} \cdot \frac{T_{r}}{T_{p}} \\ &= \underbrace{\left(\frac{N_{g}}{N_{t}}\right)}_{Q} \times \underbrace{\left(\frac{T_{i} \cdot N_{t}}{3600 \cdot T_{r}}\right)}_{P} \times \underbrace{\left(\frac{T_{r}}{T_{p}}\right)}_{A} \end{aligned} $$ **Step 6 — Conclude** $$ \boxed{\text{OEE} = A \times P \times Q} $$ This multiplicative form is *correct* because each factor is a **conditional probability** of the next event in the manufacturing chain. Adding them would double-count losses. > [!NOTE] > **Mark-Saver Tip:** Always convert *all times* to the **same unit (seconds)** before substituting. Examiners specifically deduct marks for unit mismatch in CIPMS calculations. ### 3.1.4 Numerical Verification A CNC turning cell has $T_{p}=8$ h, $T_{r}=6.5$ h, $T_{i}=45$ s, $N_{t}=500$, $N_{g}=475$. Calculate OEE. $$ A = \frac{6.5}{8} = 0.8125 $$ $$ P = \frac{45 \times 500}{6.5 \times 3600} = \frac{22500}{23400} = 0.9615 $$ $$ Q = \frac{475}{500} = 0.95 $$ $$ \text{OEE} = 0.8125 \times 0.9615 \times 0.95 = 0.7421 \;\;(74.21\%) $$ > **Interpretation:** World-class OEE benchmark is **≥ 85%**. A value of 74.21% indicates **availability loss is the biggest contributor** — the CIPMS dashboard should highlight the **downtime histogram** for corrective action. ## 3.2 Analytical Matrix — Mapping Functional Areas to Data Entities | Functional Area | Input Data Entity | Process Performed | Output Data Entity | |---|---|---|---| | Sales | Customer Order | Order promising | Confirmed Order | | Design (CAD) | Functional spec | 3-D modelling | Drawing + 3-D model | | Process Planning (CAPP) | CAD model | Variant/Generative planning | Route sheet + Operation sheet | | Manufacturing (CAM) | Route sheet | Tool-path generation | NC part program | | MRP-II | MPS + BOM | Explosion logic | Planned orders | | Shop Floor (MES) | Planned orders + Routing | Dispatching | WIP, Operation log | | Quality (CAQ) | Inspection data | SPC analysis | Control charts, Cp, Cpk | | Maintenance (CMMS) | Failure logs | Predictive analytics | PM schedules | | Finance (ERP) | All transactions | Cost roll-up | P&L, Balance sheet | > [!NOTE] > **KTU Examiner's Insight:** A 14-mark question on "Explain the architecture of CIPMS" must contain a **data-entity flow diagram** (like the table above) and the **hierarchical levels** (Levels 0–4). Missing one loses ~4 marks. --- # SECTION 4: Structural Diagrams & Schematics ## 4.1 ISA-95 / Purdue Reference Model for CIPMS ```mermaid flowchart TB L4["Level 4 - ERP
Finance MPS Forecasting"] L3["Level 3 - MES
PPC Dispatch Quality"] L2["Level 2 - SCADA HMI
Recipes Alarming"] L1["Level 1 - Basic Control
PLC CNC DCS"] L0["Level 0 - Physical Process
Sensors Actuators Machines"] L4 --> L3 L3 --> L4 L3 --> L2 L2 --> L3 L2 --> L1 L1 --> L2 L1 --> L0 L0 --> L1 ``` ## 4.2 Block-Level Functional Architecture of CIPMS ```mermaid flowchart LR CAD["CAD Module"] --> CAPP["CAPP Module"] CAPP --> CAM["CAM Module"] CAPP --> MES["MES - Shop Floor"] CAM --> MES ERP["ERP Module"] --> MRP2["MRP II Engine"] MRP2 --> MES BOM["Central BOM Database"] --> MRP2 ROUT["Routing Database"] --> MES MES --> SFC["Shop Floor Control"] SFC --> CNC1["CNC Machine 1"] SFC --> CNC2["CNC Machine 2"] SFC --> RBT["Industrial Robot"] CAQ["CAQ Module"] --> MES CNC1 --> CAQ CNC2 --> CAQ RBT --> CAQ MES --> KPI["KPI Dashboard OEE MTBF"] ERP --> KPI ``` ## 4.3 Information-Flow Sequence in a CIPMS ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant CUST as Customer participant ERP as ERP Level 4 participant MRP as MRP II Engine participant MES as MES Level 3 participant SHOP as Shop Floor Level 1 participant QA as CAQ Module CUST->>ERP: Purchase Order ERP->>MRP: MPS + Forecast MRP->>MES: Planned Order Release MES->>SHOP: Dispatch to CNC SHOP->>QA: Inline Inspection Data QA->>MES: SPC Cp Cpk MES->>ERP: Order Status + Cost ERP-->>CUST: Delivery Confirmation ``` ## 4.4 Closed-Loop Feedback Model ```mermaid flowchart LR PLAN["Plan - MPS"] --> DO["Do - MES Dispatch"] DO --> CHECK["Check - OEE SPC"] CHECK --> ACT["Act - CAPA Corrective Action"] ACT --> PLAN ``` > [!IMPORTANT] > **Diagram Reading Skill for KTU:** When asked to "draw the architecture of CIPMS", always include **bidirectional arrows** between ERP ↔ MES ↔ SCADA. Examiners mark **2 marks** specifically for showing *two-way data flow*. --- # SECTION 5: KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap ## 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each) ### Q1. `[KTU University Exam – May 2024]` **Define Computer Integrated Production Management System. List its four major functional subsystems.** **Model Answer:** > CIPMS is a manufacturing management philosophy in which all production-related functions — design, planning, execution, and quality — are integrated through a common digital information system to achieve synchronized, paperless, and data-driven production control. > > **Four major functional subsystems:** > 1. **CAD/CAPP/CAM** — product definition and process realization > 2. **MRP-II / ERP** — material and resource planning > 3. **MES / SFC** — shop-floor execution and dispatch > 4. **CAQ** — quality assurance and SPC *(3 marks: 1 mark for definition + 2 marks for listing & explaining subsystems.)* ### Q2. `[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]` **What is OEE? State the world-class benchmark value.** **Model Answer:** > OEE (Overall Equipment Effectiveness) is a composite Key Performance Indicator that measures the **percentage of planned production time** that is truly productive. > > $$ > \text{OEE} = A \times P \times Q > $$ > > **World-class benchmark:** $\geq$ **85%**. Typical discrete-industry average is **60%**. *(3 marks: 1 mark formula, 1 mark expansion, 1 mark benchmark.)* --- ## 5.2 Part B — 14-Mark Questions (Module Internal Choice) ### Question A `[KTU University Exam – Model Paper 2024]` **(a)** With a neat block diagram, explain the **hierarchical architecture of CIPMS** as per the **Purdue Reference Model**. Mention the function performed at each level. **(7 marks)** **(b)** Discuss the role of **MRP-II and MES** as the integrating software layers of CIPMS. Differentiate between MRP-II and ERP. **(7 marks)** ### Question B `[KTU University Exam – Model Paper 2024]` **(a)** Define **OEE**. Derive the expression $\text{OEE} = A \times P \times Q$ step by step. **(7 marks)** **(b)** A CNC cell operates 8 hours per shift. In one shift, the machine was unavailable for 1.5 hours due to breakdown and set-up. The ideal cycle time is 30 seconds. Total pieces produced = 700, of which 35 were rejected. Calculate **Availability, Performance, Quality, and OEE**, and comment on the result. **(7 marks)** --- ## 5.3 Model Solutions ### Solution to Question A #### (a) Hierarchical Architecture of CIPMS The Purdue Reference Model divides the enterprise into **five levels**: | Level | Name | Function | |---|---|---| | 0 | Physical Process | Sensors, actuators, machines, RFID | | 1 | Basic Control | PLC, CNC, DCS — closed-loop control | | 2 | Supervisory | SCADA, HMI, recipe management, alarming | | 3 | MES | Detailed scheduling, dispatch, traceability, OEE | | 4 | ERP | MPS, MRP-II, finance, HR, long-term planning | *Data flows bidirectionally between adjacent levels using standard protocols (OPC-UA, MQTT, ISA-95 messages).* #### (b) Role of MRP-II and MES - **MRP-II (Manufacturing Resource Planning):** Performs *explosion* of the BOM against the MPS, generates *planned orders*, performs *capacity planning* (CRP), and outputs *firm planned orders* to the shop floor. It is a **planning** function. - **MES (Manufacturing Execution System):** Receives firm planned orders, performs *detailed sequencing* on specific machines, *dispatches* operations, tracks *WIP*, captures *actual times and yields*, and feeds *shop-floor data* back to MRP-II. - **ERP** = MRP-II + **Finance + HR + Sales + CRM** (i.e., enterprise-wide scope). | Feature | MRP-II | ERP | |---|---|---| | Scope | Manufacturing | Enterprise-wide | | Time Horizon | Medium-term (weeks) | Long-term (years) | | Includes Finance | No | Yes | | Origin | 1970s | 1990s | ### Solution to Question B #### (a) OEE Derivation > *See full derivation in **Section 3.1** of these notes.* #### (b) Numerical Solution **Step 1 — Convert units.** Planned time $T_p = 8$ h, Downtime $=1.5$ h, $T_r = 8-1.5 = 6.5$ h. **Step 2 — Availability.** $$ A = \frac{T_r}{T_p} = \frac{6.5}{8} = 0.8125 \;(81.25\%) $$ **Step 3 — Performance.** $$ P = \frac{T_i \times N_t}{T_r \times 3600} = \frac{30 \times 700}{6.5 \times 3600} = \frac{21000}{23400} = 0.8974 \;(89.74\%) $$ **Step 4 — Quality.** $$ Q = \frac{N_g}{N_t} = \frac{700-35}{700} = \frac{665}{700} = 0.95 \;(95.00\%) $$ **Step 5 — OEE.** $$ \text{OEE} = 0.8125 \times 0.8974 \times 0.95 = 0.6926 \;(69.26\%) $$ **Step 6 — Comment.** The OEE of **69.26%** is **below the 85% world-class benchmark** and **below the 75% typical-lean benchmark**. The dominant loss is **Availability (18.75% downtime)** — the firm should invest in **TPM (Total Productive Maintenance)** to recover ~10% OEE. > [!WARNING] > **KTU Examiner's Valuation Pitfalls:** > 1. **Unit mismatch** — many students forget to convert $T_r$ from hours to seconds. **−2 marks**. > 2. **Confusing OEE formula** — writing $\text{OEE} = A + P + Q$ is **mathematically and conceptually wrong** (it is *multiplicative*). **−3 marks**. > 3. **Missing the conclusion** — examiners expect a one-line *comment* on the numerical result. **−1 mark** if omitted. > 4. **Drawing a flowchart without levels** — for the architecture question, mentioning *only* ERP and MES without Level 0–2 is **incomplete**. **−3 marks**. > 5. **Not mentioning ISA-95 / Purdue** by name — this is the *standard* and is expected in KTU 2024 answers. --- ## 5.4 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember (Rapid-Revision Checklist) > [!IMPORTANT] > **Pre-Exam Quick Recall — read this 30 minutes before the exam.** - **CIPMS = CIM + Production Management philosophy.** It is the *information + control backbone* of a modern factory. - **Purdue Model = 5 levels:** Level 0 (Process) → 1 (Control) → 2 (SCADA) → 3 (MES) → 4 (ERP). - **MRP-II explosion logic** uses the **BOM (Bill of Materials)** and the **MPS (Master Production Schedule)**. - **MES** sits at the **Level-3 boundary** — it is the *bridge* between business planning (ERP) and shop-floor execution (SFC). - **OEE = A × P × Q** (multiplicative, not additive). **World-class ≥ 85%.** - **MTBF ↑** = better reliability; **MTTR ↓** = better maintainability. - **BOM, Routing, Work Center** are the *three core data entities* of CIPMS. - **ERP scope > MRP-II scope**; ERP includes *Finance, HR, CRM*. - **CAPP** translates *what to make* (CAD) into *how to make* (Routing). - **CAQ** uses **SPC, Cp, Cpk** to drive **continuous improvement** (Deming cycle: PDCA). - **FMS** = CNC + AGV + AS/RS + central DNC computer — a *physical embodiment* of CIPMS at the cell level. - **Real-world examples** to quote: *Maruti Suzuki (automotive), Boeing (aerospace), Intel (semiconductors), Cipla (pharma).* - **Standard protocols**: *OPC-UA, MQTT, ISA-95 B2MML, ISO 10303 (STEP).* - **CIPMS benefits** (quote at least 4): ↓ WIP, ↓ Lead Time, ↑ Quality, ↑ Flexibility, ↑ OEE, ↓ Inventory, real-time traceability. - **CIPMS challenges** (quote at least 2): High CAPEX, change-management resistance, cybersecurity, legacy system integration. - **Always** show **bidirectional arrows** when drawing the architecture — fetch **+2 marks**. - **Always** add a **commentary line** at the end of any numerical answer — fetch **+1 mark**. - **The KTU 2024 examiner rewards** the use of **standard nomenclature** (ISA-95, MES, OEE, PDCA, TPM) — *never invent your own terms*.

topics.title: Material Requirement Planning
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PCPOL607 - PCPOL607
> - **Module:** Module Experiment 2
> - **Topic:** Material Requirement Planning

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### 1.1 Formal Academic Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus)

**Material Requirement Planning (MRP)** is a computer-based production planning and inventory control system used to manage **dependent demand** items — components, sub-assemblies, and raw materials — that are required to fulfil an independent demand for finished products listed in the **Master Production Schedule (MPS)**.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Definition (Verbatim):** MRP is a logic-based technique that translates the Master Production Schedule (independent demand) into a detailed schedule for the procurement of materials and components (dependent demand), using the Bill of Materials (BOM), Inventory Status File, and Lead Time information as primary inputs.

The system was pioneered by **Joseph Orlicky** in the 1960s at IBM and is governed by three foundational inputs and a structured set of outputs.

### 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — The "Restaurant Kitchen" Intuition

Imagine you run a large restaurant chain. Your **head chef** decides the menu for the week — that is your **Master Production Schedule** (e.g., 500 Biryani, 300 Pasta on Day 5). Now, the kitchen does not keep infinite stock of every spice. Before each day, the chef must:

1. Look at the **recipe book** (Bill of Materials — "Biryani needs 200g rice, 50g masala, 1 chicken leg").
2. Check the **pantry inventory** (Inventory Status File — "We have 5 kg rice, 800 g masala").
3. Know how long it takes the **supplier to deliver** (Lead Time — "Masala supplier needs 3 days").
4. Generate a **shopping list with dates** (Planned Order Releases — "Order 10 kg masala by Day 2").

MRP does exactly this — but for factories, machines, and thousands of components, computed instantly and accurately.

> [!NOTE]
> **Key Distinction for KTU Exams:** MRP is fundamentally different from Independent Demand systems (like EOQ/Reorder Point). MRP handles **dependent** demand (derived from parent item demand), whereas **EOQ** handles **independent** demand (raw market demand).

### 1.3 Standard MRP Terminology (KTU High-Frequency)

| Term | Meaning | Standard Metric |
|---|---|---|
| **Gross Requirement (GR)** | Total quantity needed in a period | Units (nos., kg, m) |
| **Scheduled Receipt (SR)** | Open orders already placed, expected arrival | Units |
| **Projected on Hand (POH)** | Expected inventory at end of period | Units |
| **Net Requirement (NR)** | Quantity that must be ordered after netting | Units |
| **Planned Order Receipt (POR)** | Quantity planned to be received | Units |
| **Planned Order Release (PORel)** | POR offset backward by lead time | Units |
| **Safety Stock (SS)** | Buffer against demand/supply variability | Units |
| **Lead Time (LT)** | Procurement or manufacturing time | Days / Weeks |

---

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### 2.1 Architectural Logic — The Three MRP Inputs

MRP operates on the **principle of dependent demand explosion**. The system requires three mandatory data files:

1. **Master Production Schedule (MPS)** — A time-phased plan stating *what* finished products are needed, *how many*, and *when*.
2. **Bill of Materials (BOM)** — A structured product tree showing *what* components and sub-assemblies make up each parent item, and in *what quantity*.
3. **Inventory Status File (ISF)** — A real-time record of current stock, open orders, lot sizes, lead times, and safety stock levels.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **BOM Levels:** Level 0 = Finished Product, Level 1 = Major Sub-assemblies, Level 2 = Components, etc. MRP explodes the BOM **level by level** from top to bottom.

### 2.2 The Five-Step MRP Computational Logic

For each component in the BOM, MRP performs the following algorithmic steps for every time period (week/day):

- **Step 1 — Gross Requirements (GR):** Calculate the total demand derived from the parent's planned order release × quantity per assembly.
- **Step 2 — Scheduled Receipts (SR):** Include any open purchase/manufacturing orders already scheduled to arrive in that period.
- **Step 3 — Projected on Hand (POH):** Previous POH + SR + POR − GR (must be ≥ Safety Stock, otherwise a net requirement arises).
- **Step 4 — Net Requirements (NR):** Triggered only when GR > (POH + SR). The standard rule is **NR = GR − (POH + SR)**.
- **Step 5 — Planned Order Release (PORel):** Offset the Planned Order Receipt (POR) **backward** by the lead time to determine *when* the order must be initiated.

### 2.3 Lot Sizing Techniques (KTU Favourite)

To determine the **quantity** of each planned order, MRP uses lot-sizing rules. The KTU 2024 syllabus emphasizes four standard techniques:

| Technique | Rule | Best Use Case |
|---|---|---|
| **Lot-for-Lot (L4L)** | Order quantity = Net Requirement exactly | Low holding cost, expensive items |
| **Economic Order Quantity (EOQ)** | Fixed Q based on cost minimisation | Stable, high-volume items |
| **Period Order Quantity (POQ)** | Covers demand for a fixed number of periods | Smooth demand patterns |
| **Minimum Order Quantity (MOQ)** | Round up to supplier's minimum | Restricted supplier constraints |

### 2.4 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

> [!NOTE]
> **All formulas below are high-yield and appear frequently in KTU University Exams (Module 2 / Production Planning).**

**A. Core MRP Balance Equation**

$$POH_t \;=\; POH_{t-1} \;+\; SR_t \;+\; POR_t \;-\; GR_t$$

**B. Net Requirement Rule**

$$NR_t \;=\; \max\!\left(0,\;\; GR_t \;-\; POH_{t-1} \;-\; SR_t \right)$$

**C. Planned Order Release (with Lead Time offset)**

$$PORel_t \;=\; POR_{t + LT}$$

**D. Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) — Lot Sizing**

$$Q_{EOQ} \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{2 \cdot D \cdot C_o}{C_h}}$$

where $D$ = annual demand, $C_o$ = ordering cost per order, $C_h$ = holding cost per unit per year.

**E. Period Order Quantity (POQ) Lot Size**

$$Q_{POQ} \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{k} D_i \quad \text{where k is chosen such that } \sum D_i \approx EOQ$$

**F. Average Inventory under Lot-for-Lot**

$$I_{avg} \;=\; 0 \;\; \text{(no carryover inventory)}$$

**G. Total Cost of Inventory (Lot Sizing Comparison)**

$$TC \;=\; \left(\frac{D}{Q}\right) \cdot C_o \;+\; \left(\frac{Q}{2}\right) \cdot C_h$$

**Standard Engineering Constants Used in MRP Problems:**

- **Default Planning Horizon (KTU):** 6 to 8 weeks
- **Standard Lead Time unit:** **weeks** (unless specified as days)
- **Safety Stock convention:** **0 units** unless explicitly given
- **Default Lot Size (if unspecified):** **Lot-for-Lot (L4L)**

### 2.5 Real-World Engineering Utility

MRP is the operational backbone of **discrete manufacturing industries** — automotive, electronics, aerospace, FMCG packaging. It enables:

- **Inventory reduction** of 20–35% by eliminating unnecessary safety stock on dependent items.
- **Improved customer service** by synchronising procurement with the MPS.
- **Production floor coordination** by issuing accurate work orders with **time-phased priorities**.
- **MRP II (Manufacturing Resource Planning)** extends MRP to include capacity, shop floor, and financial planning — a frequent advanced topic in KTU electives.

---

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
## 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

### 3.1 Solved Experiment Problem (KTU 2024 Style)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Problem Statement (Standard MRP Lab):** A company manufactures a **Table (T)** as the finished product. Each Table requires 1 **Tabletop (A)** and 4 **Legs (B)**. Each Tabletop requires 1 **Wooden Panel (C)** and 2 **Screws (D)**. The Master Production Schedule calls for **50 Tables in Week 4** and **75 Tables in Week 6**. Current inventory, lead times, and lot sizes are given below. Construct the complete MRP table for all components.

**Given Data Table:**

| Item | On Hand (OH) | Lead Time (LT) | Lot Size Rule | Safety Stock |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| T (Table) | 0 | 1 week | L4L | 0 |
| A (Tabletop) | 20 | 2 weeks | L4L | 0 |
| B (Leg) | 100 | 1 week | L4L | 0 |
| C (Wooden Panel) | 30 | 3 weeks | L4L | 0 |
| D (Screw) | 500 | 1 week | L4L | 0 |

### 3.2 Step-by-Step Solution

#### **Step 1 — Explode the Bill of Materials (BOM Structure)**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Level 0:} \quad & T \; (\text{Table}) \\
\text{Level 1:} \quad & T \rightarrow 1A + 4B \\
\text{Level 2:} \quad & A \rightarrow 1C + 2D
\end{aligned}
$$

**Multiplier Matrix (per parent unit):**

| Parent | Child | Quantity per Parent |
|---|---|---|
| T | A | **1** |
| T | B | **4** |
| A | C | **1** |
| A | D | **2** |

#### **Step 2 — MRP for Item T (Level 0 — Finished Product)**

| Week | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Gross Requirements** | 0 | 0 | 0 | **50** | 0 | **75** |
| Scheduled Receipts | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Projected on Hand (0) | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| **Net Requirements** | 0 | 0 | 0 | 50 | 0 | 75 |
| Planned Order Receipts | 0 | 0 | 0 | 50 | 0 | 75 |
| **Planned Order Releases** | 0 | 0 | **50** | 0 | **75** | 0 |

> **Logic:** With L4L, NR = POR. Release = POR offset by **1 week** backward. So POR 50 in Week 4 → Release 50 in Week 3. POR 75 in Week 6 → Release 75 in Week 5.

#### **Step 3 — MRP for Item A (Tabletop) — Level 1**

Multiplier: **1 A per T**. GR_A = PORel_T × 1.

| Week | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Gross Requirements** | 0 | 0 | 50 | 0 | 75 | 0 |
| Scheduled Receipts | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| On Hand Beginning | 20 | 20 | 20 | 20 | 20 | 20 |
| Projected on Hand | 20 | 20 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| **Net Requirements** | 0 | 0 | 30 | 0 | 75 | 0 |
| Planned Order Receipts | 0 | 0 | 30 | 0 | 75 | 0 |
| **Planned Order Releases** | 0 | **30** | 0 | **75** | 0 | 0 |

> **Logic Walkthrough (Week 3):** POH from Week 2 = 20. GR = 50. POH after consumption = 20 − 50 = −30 → NR = 30. L4L → POR = 30. Release offset by 2 weeks → Week 1. But Week 1 is in the past relative to NR occurring in Week 3, so release shifts to **Week (3 − 2) = Week 1** which is past, hence planner must expedite. For KTU lab, we record the release in the earliest feasible week: **Week 1**. For Week 5 NR = 75 → Release = Week 3. (Correction: LT = 2 weeks, so PORel Week 5 − 2 = **Week 3**, PORel Week 3 − 2 = **Week 1**).

> [!NOTE]
> **Correction in final tabular computation:** For A, LT = 2 weeks. POR in Week 3 → Release in Week 1. POR in Week 5 → Release in Week 3.

#### **Step 4 — MRP for Item B (Leg) — Level 1**

Multiplier: **4 B per T**. GR_B = PORel_T × 4.

| Week | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Gross Requirements** | 0 | 0 | 200 | 0 | 300 | 0 |
| Scheduled Receipts | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Projected on Hand | 100 | 100 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| **Net Requirements** | 0 | 0 | 100 | 0 | 300 | 0 |
| Planned Order Receipts | 0 | 0 | 100 | 0 | 300 | 0 |
| **Planned Order Releases** | 0 | **100** | 0 | **300** | 0 | 0 |

#### **Step 5 — MRP for Item C (Wooden Panel) — Level 2**

Driven by Item A's PORel. Multiplier: **1 C per A**.

| Week | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Gross Requirements** | 30 | 0 | 75 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Scheduled Receipts | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Projected on Hand | 30 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| **Net Requirements** | 0 | 0 | 75 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Planned Order Receipts | 0 | 0 | 75 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| **Planned Order Releases** | 0 | **75** | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |

> **Logic Walkthrough (Week 1):** GR = 30, POH before = 30 → POH after = 0. NR = 0. Week 3: GR = 75, POH before = 0 → NR = 75. Release = Week 3 − 3 = **Week 0** → which in KTU convention is written as **Week 0** or flagged as "expedite to Week 0" (i.e., immediate release at start of horizon). For exam simplicity, KTU accepts **Week 0** notation.

#### **Step 6 — MRP for Item D (Screws) — Level 2**

Driven by Item A's PORel. Multiplier: **2 D per A**.

| Week | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Gross Requirements** | 60 | 0 | 150 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Scheduled Receipts | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Projected on Hand | 500 | 440 | 290 | 290 | 290 | 290 |
| **Net Requirements** | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Planned Order Receipts | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| **Planned Order Releases** | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |

> **Logic Walkthrough:** On hand 500 is sufficient for all 210 screws required. **No planned orders needed.** This is a critical KTU learning — high safety stock on cheap items (screws) often negates the need for MRP releases.

### 3.3 Analytical Summary — Final Planned Order Release Matrix

| Item | Total Planned Order Releases (by Week) |
|---|---|
| T | 50 (W3), 75 (W5) |
| A | 30 (W1), 75 (W3) |
| B | 100 (W2), 300 (W4) |
| C | 75 (W0/immediate) |
| D | None required |

## 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics

### 4.1 MRP System Architecture (Block-Level Functional Flow)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    inputA[MPS Master Production Schedule] --> coreMRP[MRP Logic Engine]
    inputB[BOM Bill of Materials] --> coreMRP
    inputC[ISF Inventory Status File] --> coreMRP
    coreMRP --> step1[Step 1 Compute Gross Requirements]
    step1 --> step2[Step 2 Net Scheduled Receipts]
    step2 --> step3[Step 3 Calculate Projected on Hand]
    step3 --> decision{Net Requirement greater than zero}
    decision -- No --> skip[No Planned Order Generated]
    decision -- Yes --> step4[Step 4 Apply Lot Sizing Rule]
    step4 --> step5[Step 5 Generate Planned Order Receipt]
    step5 --> step6[Step 6 Offset by Lead Time]
    step6 --> outputA[Output Planned Order Releases]
    step6 --> outputB[Output Exception Reports]
    step6 --> outputC[Output Performance Reports]
    outputA --> explode[BOM Explosion to Next Level]
    explode --> coreMRP
```

### 4.2 BOM Tree Structure (Product Hierarchy)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    lvl0[Level 0 Table T] --> lvl1a[Level 1 Tabletop A]
    lvl0 --> lvl1b[Level 1 Leg B x 4]
    lvl1a --> lvl2a[Level 2 Wooden Panel C]
    lvl1a --> lvl2b[Level 2 Screws D x 2]
```

### 4.3 MRP Computational Cycle Flow

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    a[Gross Requirements GR] --> b[Add Scheduled Receipts SR]
    b --> c[Compute Projected on Hand POH]
    c --> d{NR triggered}
    d -- Yes --> e[Apply Lot Sizing L4L or EOQ]
    e --> f[Plan Order Receipt POR]
    f --> g[Offset by Lead Time]
    g --> h[Planned Order Release PORel]
    d -- No --> i[Continue to next period]
    h --> j[Explode BOM to Child Level]
    j --> a
```

> [!NOTE]
> **Reading the Diagram:** The MRP engine is iterative. Once a Planned Order Release is determined for a parent item, that release quantity is **multiplied by the BOM quantity per** to generate the Gross Requirements for the child item in the corresponding (lead-time-offset) week. This cascading explosion is the essence of MRP.

---
