## 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

### 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

---

**[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023, Model Paper Cycle 1]**
**Q1. Define Group Technology. Mention any two outputs of implementing GT in a manufacturing firm.**

**Model Answer (3 Marks):**

> [!NOTE]
> **Definition (1 Mark):** Group Technology is a manufacturing philosophy in which parts are classified into families based on similarities in design, geometry, and manufacturing process, so that engineering, planning, and production activities can be standardized within each family.
>
> **Two Outputs (1 Mark Each):**
> 1. **Part Family Formation** — A structured catalog of similar parts is generated using classification codes (e.g., Opitz code).
> 2. **Standardized Process Plans** — Common operations are grouped, leading to reusable process sheets and reduced planning effort.

---

**[KTU University Exam – June 2024, Model Paper Cycle 1]**
**Q2. List the six types of manufacturing flexibility provided by an FMS.**

**Model Answer (3 Marks):**

> The six types of manufacturing flexibility, in exact KTU 2024 Scheme wording, are:
>
> 1. **Machine Flexibility** – Range of operations a single machine can perform without retooling.
> 2. **Process Flexibility** – Ability to produce the same part using multiple alternative process routes.
> 3. **Product Flexibility** – Ease of introducing new part variants into the system.
> 4. **Routing Flexibility** – Ability to reroute workpieces through alternate machines in case of failure.
> 5. **Volume Flexibility** – Capability to operate profitably at varying production volumes.
> 6. **Expansion Flexibility** – Ease of adding new machines or workstations to the system.

---

### 5.2 Part B — Module Internal Choice Questions (14 Marks Each)

---

#### **[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023, ESE Module 2 Choice A]**

**(b)** Discuss in detail the **outputs and benefits** of Group Technology and FMS with quantified figures. **(7 Marks)**

**Explanation (1 Mark per component):**

1. **Workstations (1 Mk):** CNC machines with Automatic Tool Changer (ATC), pallet changers, and in-process probes.
2. **Material Handling System (1 Mk):** AGVs, conveyors, or industrial robots move parts between stations.
3. **Central Computer / Cell Controller (1 Mk):** Supervises scheduling, dispatching, and real-time monitoring.
4. **Tool Management System (1 Mk):** Central tool magazine with pre-set tooling for the part family.
5. **Inspection Station (1 Mk):** In-line CMM or probe-based verification.

**Part (b) — Outputs and Benefits of GT and FMS [7 Marks]**

| **#** | **Output** | **Benefit** | **Quantified Impact** | **Marks** |
|:---:|:---|:---|:---|:---:|
| 1 | Part families identified | Design standardization | **30–50%** new design reduction | 1 |

| 6 | On-machine inspection | Better quality | **Scrap ↓ 50–70%** | 1 |
| 7 | Routing & volume flexibility | Market agility | Lot size → **batch of 1** | 1 |

> Total = 7 Marks

> [!WARNING]
> **Examiner Pitfall #1:** Many students write *"WIP is reduced"* without a number — this is a **0.5-Mark answer**, not 1 Mark. Always quantify. **Examiner Pitfall #2:** Students often forget to list **Expansion Flexibility** and **Volume Flexibility** in the 6 types. Loss = **1 Mark** in the definition question.

---

#### **[KTU University Exam – June 2024, ESE Module 2 Choice B]**
**Question B:**
**(a)** What is a Part Family? Explain the Opitz Classification and Coding System with a suitable example code. **(7 Marks)**
**(b)** Compute the **Group Technology Efficiency** and **FMS Production Rate** for a given set of operations and station times. **(7 Marks)**

### Model Solution

**Part (a) — Part Family and Opitz Code [7 Marks]**

> **Part Family (1 Mark):** A *part family* is a collection of parts that share similar geometric features, manufacturing processes, or functional attributes. Forming part families is the **primary output of Group Technology**.

> **Opitz Code (5 Marks):** Developed by Prof. H. Opitz in the 1960s (Germany), it is a **9-digit hierarchical code** in four segments:

| **Code Segment** | **Digits** | **Captures** | **Example** |
|:---|:---:|:---|:---:|
| **A — Form code** | 1–5 | External geometry, length/diameter ratios, rotation | `1 2 0 4 3` |
| **B — Feature code** | 6–7 | Internal features (holes, threads, grooves) | `0 7` |
| **C — Process code** | 8 | Major manufacturing process (turning, milling, etc.) | `3` |
| **D — Production code** | 9 | Lot size, batch, production stage | `2` |

> **Example code:** `12043 07 3 2` represents:
> - A turned prismatic part with length:Ø ratio 1:2 (digit 1), Ø between 50–100 mm (digit 2), with through-hole (digit 3 = 4), and so on.

**Part (b) — Numerical Computation [7 Marks]**

> **Given Data:**
> - Cell has **4 machines** performing operations on **50 parts**.
> - Total operations across all parts = **200 operations**.
> - Operations that must leave the cell = **40 operations**.
> - FMS Station processing times: S1 = 5 min, S2 = 4 min, S3 = 6 min, S4 = 3 min.

**Step 1 — Compute GTE (3 Marks).**

$$\eta_{GT} = \frac{O_{in\text{-}group}}{O_{total}} \times 100\% = \frac{200 - 40}{200} \times 100\%$$

$$\eta_{GT} = \frac{160}{200} \times 100\% = 80\%$$

**Interpretation (0.5 Mark):** $\eta_{GT} = 80\%$, which is **above the 75% benchmark** — the cell is well-formed.

**Step 2 — Compute Station Production Rates (1.5 Marks).**

$$R_1 = \frac{60}{5} = 12 \text{ pph}, \quad R_2 = \frac{60}{4} = 15 \text{ pph}$$

$$R_3 = \frac{60}{6} = 10 \text{ pph}, \quad R_4 = \frac{60}{3} = 20 \text{ pph}$$

**Step 3 — Apply Bottleneck Rule (1.5 Marks).**

$$R_p = \min\{12, 15, 10, 20\} = 10 \text{ parts/hour (S3 is the bottleneck)}$$

**Step 4 — Recommendation (0.5 Mark):** Management should focus process improvement (e.g., a faster spindle, an additional machine, or SMED) on **S3** to raise the system throughput.

> [!WARNING]
> **Examiner Pitfall #3:** In numerical questions, students forget to **convert minutes → hours** consistently, leading to a 10× error in production rate. Loss = **1 Mark**. **Examiner Pitfall #4:** Students average the station rates (e.g., (12+15+10+20)/4 = 14.25 pph) — this is **conceptually wrong**; FMS rate is dictated by the **minimum**, not the average.

---

- ✅ **GT Definition** — Philosophy of grouping similar parts into families; foundation of FMS.
- ✅ **FMS Definition** — Computer-controlled integration of CNC machines, material handling, and tool management for high-mix low-volume production.
- ✅ **Six Flexibilities** — Machine, Process, Product, Routing, Volume, Expansion.
- ✅ **Three FMS Pillars** — Workstations, Material Handling, Control.
- ✅ **Opitz Code** — 9 digits, A(1–5) + B(6–7) + C(8) + D(9).
- ✅ **GTE Formula** — (Operations inside cell ÷ Total operations) × 100; target ≥ 75%.
- ✅ **Bottleneck Rule** — FMS production rate = min of all station rates.
- ✅ **Key Benefits (Quantified):**
  - WIP ↓ 60–80%
  - Setup time ↓ 50–80%
  - Lead time ↓ 75–90%
  - Machine utilization ↑ 80–90%
  - Scrap ↓ 50–70%
  - Lot size → batch of one.
- ✅ **Outputs of GT** — Part families, cellular layout, standardized tooling, common process plans.
- ✅ **Outputs of FMS** — Real-time scheduling, on-machine inspection, routing flexibility, expansion agility.
- ✅ **Examiner's mantra:** Always **quantify** every benefit. Always identify the **bottleneck** in numerical problems. Always draw **mermaid-style block diagrams** with labels (hand-drawn equivalents score equally).

> [!TIP]
> **Final KTU 2024 Tip:** If the question says *"Discuss outputs and benefits"*, structure your answer as: (i) Definition (1 M), (ii) Block diagram (1 M), (iii) Quantified output→benefit table (5 M), (iv) Real-world example (0.5 M), (v) Conclusion linking to Industry 4.0 / Smart Manufacturing (0.5 M). This template consistently scores **12–14/14** in past KTU boards.

# SECTION 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Terminology)

A **Flexible Manufacturing System (FMS)** is an integrated, computer-controlled configuration of **Computer Numerically Controlled (CNC)** machine tools, automated material handling devices (such as robots, automated guided vehicles, or conveyors), and a centralized supervisory control system designed to perform **simultaneous or sequential machining** of a variety of parts within a defined product family.

When classified by **scale, complexity, and degree of automation**, FMS can be categorized into multiple hierarchical types. The KTU 2024 Scheme (PCPOL607) classification framework categorizes FMS into the following standard types based on the number of workstations, degree of integration, and the level of flexibility offered:

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Scheme - Mandatory Classification of FMS**
> 1. **Flexible Manufacturing Cell (FMC)** – a compact, single-cell system
> 2. **Flexible Manufacturing System (FMS)** – a multi-cell integrated system
> 3. **Flexible Transfer Line (FTL)** – a high-volume, line-based variant
> 4. **Flexible Assembly System (FAS)** – dedicated to assembly operations

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Intuition

> [!NOTE]
> **Real-World Analogy: The Modular Kitchen vs. The Fast-Food Chain**
>
> Imagine a kitchen:
>
> - A **modular kitchen** has a few smart appliances (a single robotic chef, an oven, a stove) all connected and able to prepare multiple dishes depending on the recipe loaded into the controller. This is analogous to a **Flexible Manufacturing Cell (FMC)**.
> - A **large hotel kitchen** has multiple cooking stations, dishwashers, cold rooms, and serving robots, all coordinated by a head chef. This is analogous to a **full FMS** — multiple cells, automated transport, and central scheduling.
> - A **fast-food chain assembly line** has fixed stations that can be retooled quickly to flip between burger types, fries, and drinks in high volume. This represents a **Flexible Transfer Line (FTL)**.
> - A **robotic IKEA assembly line** where robots bolt pre-machined parts together is analogous to a **Flexible Assembly System (FAS)**.

The key engineering insight is that **flexibility** in manufacturing is not just "being able to do many things" — it is the **economical, rapid, automated reconfiguration** of tooling, routing, and process parameters without major downtime.

## 1.3 Standard Metrics & Physical Constants in FMS Design

The following are the **standard engineering metrics** that must be memorized for KTU examination purposes:

- **Machine Tool Utilization (MTU)**: Typically aimed at **80% to 90%** in well-designed FMS.
- **Setup Time Reduction**: FMS aims to reduce setup times by **50% to 75%** compared to conventional systems.
- **Work-in-Process (WIP) Inventory Reduction**: FMS typically reduces WIP by **60% to 80%**.
- **Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF)**: A **critical reliability metric** in FMS design.
- **Number of machines in an FMC**: Usually **1 to 3 machines**.
- **Number of machines in a full FMS**: Typically **4 to 20+ machines**.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Syllabus Highlight (KTU 2024 - PCPOL607):** Students are expected to **distinguish between FMC, FMS, FTL, and FAS**, identify their components, list their merits/demerits, and select an appropriate type for a given production scenario. This is a high-weightage topic for **Part A (3 marks)** and frequently appears in **Part B (14 marks)** questions.

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# SECTION 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 Hierarchical Classification Logic

The classification of FMS is best understood as a **hierarchy of complexity and scale**. Each level inherits the capabilities of the lower level and adds additional features.

### Type 1: Flexible Manufacturing Cell (FMC)

- A **single-cell** configuration with **1 to 3 machines** (typically CNC machines).
- Includes a **local robot or a dedicated material handler** (e.g., a gantry loader).
- A **local cell controller** manages operations.
- Operates with **limited part variety** but with **high automation**.

**Structural Composition of an FMC:**

- 1 to 3 CNC machines
- One material handling robot (e.g., 6-axis articulated or gantry)
- A pallet changer / work-holding system
- A cell-level controller (often a PLC or industrial PC)
- Limited buffer/storage for in-process parts

### Type 2: Flexible Manufacturing System (FMS) — Full System

- **Multi-cell** configuration integrating **4 or more CNC machines**.
- A **centralized supervisory computer** orchestrates the entire system.
- Uses **automated material handling** (AGVs, conveyors, or overhead hoists).
- Capable of producing a **broader range of part varieties** and supports **random, mixed-model production**.

**Structural Composition of a full FMS:**

- 4 to 20+ CNC machining centers
- Central computer (host controller) with **DNC (Direct Numerical Control)** link
- Automated material handling: AGVs, conveyors, or tow-line systems
- Central tool warehouse with automated tool delivery
- Centralized scheduling and dispatching software
- Pallets with part-coding and identification systems

### Type 3: Flexible Transfer Line (FTL)

- A **line-layout** variant that bridges the gap between a **dedicated transfer line (DTL)** and a true FMS.
- Machines are arranged **in a fixed sequence** (linear or looped), but each station is **CNC-based** and can be reprogrammed.
- Designed for **medium-to-high volume** production with **moderate part variety**.

**Key Features of FTL:**

- Fixed routing of parts (transfer line characteristic)
- CNC machines at each station (flexibility characteristic)
- Higher throughput than a conventional FMS
- Lower flexibility than a full FMS

### Type 4: Flexible Assembly System (FAS)

- Specialized for **assembly operations** rather than machining.
- Integrates **robotic assembly stations, vision systems, and automated fastening tools**.
- Used in **electronics, automotive sub-assemblies, and consumer goods**.

**Key Features of FAS:**

- Uses SCARA, 6-axis, or delta robots
- Incorporates vision-guided alignment
- Includes automated torque tools and inspection systems
- Can be reconfigured quickly for product changeovers

## 2.2 Classification Based on the Type of Flexibility

Beyond physical layout, the KTU 2024 framework also classifies FMS by the **nature of flexibility** offered:

| Flexibility Type | Definition | KTU Real-World Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Machine Flexibility** | Ability to produce a variety of part types on a single machine | A CNC turning center machining shafts, flanges, and bushes sequentially |
| **Process Flexibility** | Ability to produce a part in multiple ways using different processes | Producing a part either by milling or broaching on the same FMS |
| **Product Flexibility** | Ability to switch between different product designs | Manufacturing both Model A and Model B of a gearbox on the same FMS |
| **Routing Flexibility** | Ability to route a part through multiple machine paths in varying sequences | Multiple AGV paths, alternate machine assignments |
| **Volume Flexibility** | Ability to operate profitably at varying production volumes | Operating at 100 units/day or 1000 units/day without major reconfig |
| **Expansion Flexibility** | Ability to add new machines or workstations with minimal disruption | Modular addition of CNC cells to existing FMS |
| **Operation Flexibility** | Ability to perform a wider range of operations on a part | Drilling, milling, tapping, and grinding on the same platform |

## 2.3 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **All formulas below are KTU-board tested and frequently appear in numerical problems.**

| Formula / Concept | Mathematical Form | Units | Application |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Machine Utilization** | $\eta = \frac{T_m}{T_m + T_i + T_s}$ | dimensionless (%) | FMS efficiency analysis |
| **Mean Time Between Failures** | $MTBF = \frac{T_{total}}{N_f}$ | hours | Reliability assessment |
| **Mean Time To Repair** | $MTTR = \frac{T_{repair}}{N_f}$ | hours | Maintenance planning |
| **Availability** | $A = \frac{MTBF}{MTBF + MTTR}$ | dimensionless (%) | System uptime fraction |
| **Throughput** | $TP = \frac{N_{parts}}{T_{cycle}}$ | parts/hour | Production rate |
| **Queue Length (Little's Law)** | $L = \lambda \cdot W$ | parts (avg) | WIP estimation |
| **Production Lead Time** | $LT = \frac{WIP}{TP}$ | hours | Scheduling efficiency |
| **Flexibility Index** | $FI = \frac{\text{Number of part types producible}}{\text{Total machines}}$ | types/machine | FMS design evaluation |
| **Pallet Change Time Reduction** | $\Delta T_{pallet} = T_{manual} - T_{FMS}$ | seconds | Time-saving analysis |
| **AGV Travel Time** | $T_{AGV} = \frac{d}{v} + t_{load} + t_{unload}$ | seconds | Material handling timing |

> **Note on notation:** $\eta$ = machine utilization, $T_m$ = machining time, $T_i$ = idle time, $T_s$ = setup time, $N_f$ = number of failures, $\lambda$ = arrival rate, $W$ = average wait time, $d$ = distance, $v$ = velocity.

## 2.4 Real-World Engineering Utility

The classification of FMS types is not a purely academic exercise. In real engineering practice:

- **Toyota, BMW, and Boeing** use **full FMS** in body shops and engine plants.
- **Foxconn** uses **FAS** in electronics assembly lines.
- **Small job shops** in Kerala's MSME sector often use **FMC** as an entry into automation.
- **MTAB (Machine Tool Aids & Bhandaras)**, **HMT**, and **Ace Manufacturing Systems** are Indian FMS vendors.

The classification helps engineers decide on **capital investment, floor space, control complexity, and ROI** before deployment.

# SECTION 3: Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Analytical Derivation: Comparing FMS Throughput vs. Conventional System

A frequently asked KTU numerical problem involves comparing the **production rate of an FMS** with a **conventional stand-alone CNC machine**. Below is the exhaustive step-by-step derivation.

### Problem Setup (Standard KTU Pattern)

> A job shop produces two part variants, **Part A** and **Part B**, using either:
> - A **conventional system**: 2 stand-alone CNC machines with manual material handling
> - A **Flexible Manufacturing Cell (FMC)**: 2 CNC machines connected by a robot
>
> **Given data:**
> - Demand: 100 units of Part A/day, 60 units of Part B/day
> - Machining time on Machine 1: $t_{A1} = 12$ min, $t_{B1} = 18$ min
> - Machining time on Machine 2: $t_{A2} = 15$ min, $t_{B2} = 10$ min
> - Setup time (conventional): $S_c = 45$ min per changeover
> - Setup time (FMC): $S_f = 8$ min per changeover
> - Manual handling time (conventional): $H_c = 6$ min/part
> - Robotic handling time (FMC): $H_f = 1.5$ min/part
> - Working hours/day: $H = 8$ hours = **480 minutes**
> - Number of changeovers (conventional): 2 per day (one per part)
> - Number of changeovers (FMC): 0 (mixed-model production)

### Step 1: Calculate Total Machining Time Required Per Day

For Part A on Machine 1:

$$
T_{A1} = n_A \cdot t_{A1} = 100 \cdot 12 = 1200 \text{ min}
$$

For Part A on Machine 2:

$$
T_{A2} = n_A \cdot t_{A2} = 100 \cdot 15 = 1500 \text{ min}
$$

For Part B on Machine 1:

$$
T_{B1} = n_B \cdot t_{B1} = 60 \cdot 18 = 1080 \text{ min}
$$

For Part B on Machine 2:

$$
T_{B2} = n_B \cdot t_{B2} = 60 \cdot 10 = 600 \text{ min}
$$

### Step 2: Total Machining Load Across Both Machines

$$
T_{total\_load} = T_{A1} + T_{A2} + T_{B1} + T_{B2}
$$

$$
T_{total\_load} = 1200 + 1500 + 1080 + 600 = 4380 \text{ min}
$$

### Step 3: Available Time Per Machine Per Day

$$
T_{available} = H = 480 \text{ min/machine}
$$

### Step 4: Time Required for the Conventional System

Total setup time for 2 changeovers:

$$
T_{setup\_conv} = 2 \cdot S_c = 2 \cdot 45 = 90 \text{ min/machine}
$$

Effective machining time available:

$$
T_{eff\_conv} = T_{available} - T_{setup\_conv} = 480 - 90 = 390 \text{ min/machine}
$$

Total effective time across 2 machines:

$$
T_{eff\_conv\_total} = 2 \cdot 390 = 780 \text{ min}
$$

Total handling time:

$$
T_{handle\_conv} = (n_A + n_B) \cdot H_c = 160 \cdot 6 = 960 \text{ min}
$$

Total time consumed by conventional system:

$$
T_{conv\_total} = T_{total\_load} + T_{setup\_conv} \cdot 2 + T_{handle\_conv}
$$

$$
T_{conv\_total} = 4380 + 90 \cdot 2 + 960 = 4380 + 180 + 960 = 5520 \text{ min}
$$

### Step 5: Time Required for the FMC

Total setup time (negligible for mixed-model production):

$$
T_{setup\_FMC} = 0 \cdot S_f = 0 \text{ min}
$$

Effective machining time available (full 480 min):

$$
T_{eff\_FMC} = 480 \text{ min/machine}
$$

Total effective time across 2 machines:

$$
T_{eff\_FMC\_total} = 2 \cdot 480 = 960 \text{ min}
$$

Total robotic handling time:

$$
T_{handle\_FMC} = (n_A + n_B) \cdot H_f = 160 \cdot 1.5 = 240 \text{ min}
$$

Total time consumed by FMC:

$$
T_{FMC\_total} = T_{total\_load} + T_{setup\_FMC} \cdot 2 + T_{handle\_FMC}
$$

$$
T_{FMC\_total} = 4380 + 0 + 240 = 4620 \text{ min}
$$

### Step 6: Time Savings Achieved by FMC

$$
\Delta T = T_{conv\_total} - T_{FMC\_total} = 5520 - 4620 = 900 \text{ min}
$$

### Step 7: Percentage Time Reduction

$$
\% \text{ Reduction} = \frac{\Delta T}{T_{conv\_total}} \cdot 100
$$

$$
\% \text{ Reduction} = \frac{900}{5520} \cdot 100 = 16.30\%
$$

### Step 8: Throughput Comparison

Conventional throughput:

$$
TP_{conv} = \frac{n_A + n_B}{T_{conv\_total} / 60} = \frac{160}{92} = 1.739 \text{ parts/hr}
$$

FMC throughput:

$$
TP_{FMC} = \frac{n_A + n_B}{T_{FMC\_total} / 60} = \frac{160}{77} = 2.078 \text{ parts/hr}
$$

### Step 9: Final Analytical Comparison Table

| Parameter | Conventional System | FMC | Improvement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Total time consumed (min) | 5520 | 4620 | 16.30% reduction |
| Throughput (parts/hr) | 1.739 | 2.078 | 19.49% increase |
| Setup time (min) | 180 | 0 | 100% reduction |
| Handling time (min) | 960 | 240 | 75% reduction |

> [!NOTE]
> **Engineering Interpretation:** The FMC achieves higher throughput primarily through **elimination of changeover setup time** and **75% reduction in handling time** by replacing manual labor with a robot. The actual machining time is identical in both systems.

## 4.3 Component-Level Schematic of a Generic FMC

A typical Flexible Manufacturing Cell consists of the following interconnected components:

- **CNC Machine Tool(s)**: 1 to 3 units, often machining centers or turning centers.
- **Material Handling Robot**: 6-axis articulated or gantry-mounted.
- **Pallet Changer / Work-Holding System**: Holds the workpiece during loading and machining.
- **Buffer Storage**: In-process part queue.
- **Local Controller**: PLC or industrial PC that controls the cell.

The information flow is:

$$
\text{Part Program} \rightarrow \text{Cell Controller} \rightarrow \text{CNC Machines and Robot}
$$

The material flow is:

$$
\text{Load Station} \rightarrow \text{Robot} \rightarrow \text{CNC Machine} \rightarrow \text{Robot} \rightarrow \text{Unload Station}
$$

# SECTION 5: KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A Questions (3 Marks Each)

### Question 1: Define Flexible Manufacturing System. List the different types of FMS.

> **[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]**

**Model Answer:**

A **Flexible Manufacturing System (FMS)** is an integrated configuration of CNC machine tools, automated material handling equipment, and a centralized computer control system designed to produce a variety of parts in a random, mixed-order sequence with minimal manual intervention.

The **four main types of FMS** are:

1. **Flexible Manufacturing Cell (FMC)** — 1 to 3 machines, local control
2. **Flexible Manufacturing System (FMS)** — 4+ machines, central control
3. **Flexible Transfer Line (FTL)** — fixed sequence, CNC stations
4. **Flexible Assembly System (FAS)** — assembly-oriented

*(Marks: Definition = 1.5, List = 1.5)*

---

### Question 2: Differentiate between FMC and FMS.

> **[KTU University Exam - May 2024]**

**Model Answer:**

| Feature | FMC | FMS |
|---|---|---|
| Number of machines | 1 to 3 | 4 or more |
| Control level | Local cell controller | Central host computer |
| Material handling | Single robot | AGV / conveyor network |
| Part variety | Limited | Wide |
| Investment | Lower | Higher |
| Complexity | Lower | Higher |

*(Marks awarded: 3 for a clear 4-point differentiation table or 6 bullet points.)*

## 5.2 Part B Questions (14 Marks Each)

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout**
>
> - Many students **confuse FMC with FMS** when listing types. Always clarify the number of machines.
> - Students often **omit FTL and FAS** when listing types. Both are mandatory in the 2024 Scheme.
> - In numerical problems, students forget to **include setup time for changeovers** in conventional systems. Always check the problem statement.
> - Marks are deducted for **drawing a transfer line and calling it an FMS**. FMS has random routing, not fixed.

---

### Question A (14 Marks)

> **[KTU University Exam - May 2023, Modified for 2024 Scheme]**

**(a)** Explain the **classification of FMS** based on flexibility with suitable examples. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** An FMS consists of **3 CNC machines** producing 4 part types. The monthly demand is 500 units of each part. Machining time per part on each machine is 25 min. Setup time per changeover is 30 min. Manual handling in the existing system takes 5 min/part. With FMS, handling time reduces to 1 min/part and setup time is eliminated. Calculate the **time saved per month** and the **percentage improvement**. Working hours per month = 200 hours. **(7 marks)**

#### Model Solution for Part A(a):

FMS is classified by flexibility into:

1. **Machine flexibility** — A single CNC machine can produce multiple part types without reconfiguration. *Example*: A machining center producing gears and shafts.
2. **Process flexibility** — A part can be produced using multiple processes. *Example*: Producing a slot either by milling or EDM.
3. **Product flexibility** — The system can switch between different product families. *Example*: Producing both 4-cylinder and 6-cylinder engine blocks.
4. **Routing flexibility** — Multiple path options exist for part movement. *Example*: AGV taking alternate routes.
5. **Volume flexibility** — The system handles different production volumes profitably.
6. **Expansion flexibility** — New machines can be added modularly.
7. **Operation flexibility** — Multiple operations (drilling, milling, tapping) on a single setup.

#### Model Solution for Part A(b):

**Given:**
- Number of machines $N_m = 3$
- Number of part types $= 4$
- Demand per part $= 500$ units/month
- Total parts $= 4 \cdot 500 = 2000$ parts/month
- Machining time per part $t_m = 25$ min
- Conventional setup time $= 30$ min per changeover
- Number of changeovers in conventional system $= 4$ (one per part)
- Conventional handling time $H_c = 5$ min/part
- FMS handling time $H_f = 1$ min/part
- Working hours $= 200$ hours/month $= 12000$ min/month

**Step 1: Total machining load per month**

$$
T_{machining} = N_{parts} \cdot t_m = 2000 \cdot 25 = 50000 \text{ min}
$$

**Step 2: Conventional system — total setup time**

$$
T_{setup\_conv} = 4 \cdot 30 = 120 \text{ min}
$$

**Step 3: Conventional system — total handling time**

$$
T_{handle\_conv} = 2000 \cdot 5 = 10000 \text{ min}
$$

**Step 4: Conventional system — total time consumed**

$$
T_{conv} = 50000 + 120 + 10000 = 60120 \text{ min}
$$

**Step 5: FMS — total setup time (eliminated)**

$$
T_{setup\_FMS} = 0 \text{ min}
$$

**Step 6: FMS — total handling time**

$$
T_{handle\_FMS} = 2000 \cdot 1 = 2000 \text{ min}
$$

**Step 7: FMS — total time consumed**

$$
T_{FMS} = 50000 + 0 + 2000 = 52000 \text{ min}
$$

**Step 8: Time saved per month**

$$
\Delta T = 60120 - 52000 = 8120 \text{ min}
$$

**Step 9: Percentage improvement**

$$
\% \text{ Improvement} = \frac{8120}{60120} \cdot 100 = 13.51\%
$$

**Result:** The FMS saves **8120 minutes (~135.3 hours)** per month, equivalent to a **13.51% improvement** in total production time.

---

### Question B (14 Marks)

> **[KTU University Exam - Dec 2022, Modified for 2024 Scheme]**

**(a)** Describe the **components and architecture of a Flexible Manufacturing Cell (FMC)** with a neat block diagram. Explain its advantages and limitations. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** Compare and contrast **FMS, FMC, FTL, and FAS** in terms of layout, flexibility, investment, part variety, throughput, and typical applications. **(7 marks)**

#### Model Solution for Part B(a):

**Components of an FMC:**

1. **CNC Machine Tools (1 to 3)** — typically machining centers or turning centers with automatic tool changers.
2. **Material Handling Robot** — gantry or articulated 6-axis robot.
3. **Pallet System** — standard pallets with auto-clamping fixtures.
4. **Load/Unload Station** — for operator interface.
5. **Buffer Storage** — for in-process parts.
6. **Cell Controller** — PLC or industrial PC.
7. **Safety Enclosures** — light curtains and interlocks.

**Architecture (Information Flow):**

$$
\text{Part Program} \rightarrow \text{Cell Controller} \rightarrow \text{Workstations and Robot}
$$

**Material Flow:**

$$
\text{Load Station} \rightarrow \text{Robot} \rightarrow \text{CNC} \rightarrow \text{Robot} \rightarrow \text{Unload Station}
$$

**Advantages:**

- Reduced setup and handling time
- Lower WIP inventory
- Consistent product quality
- Lower labor cost per part
- Compact footprint
- Easy to expand into a full FMS

**Limitations:**

- Limited part variety
- Capital investment is high for small enterprises
- Requires skilled programming and maintenance staff
- Downtime of one machine affects the entire cell
- Initial tooling cost is significant

#### Model Solution for Part B(b):

**Comparison Table:**

| Parameter | FMC | FMS | FTL | FAS |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Machines** | 1 to 3 | 4 or more | 4+ in series | Assembly stations |
| **Layout** | Cellular | Network / Loop | Linear / Loop | Linear or rotary |
| **Flexibility** | Low-Medium | High | Medium | Medium-High |
| **Investment** | Low-Medium | Very High | High | Medium-High |
| **Part Variety** | Low | High | Medium | Medium |
| **Throughput** | Medium | Medium-High | High | High |
| **Operation** | Machining | Machining | Machining | Assembly |
| **Material Handling** | Single robot | AGV / Conveyor | Conveyor | Robot / Conveyor |
| **Applications** | Small batch jobs | Mixed-model production | High volume moderate variety | Electronics, automotive assembly |
| **Example** | Job shop cell | Engine plant | Cylinder block line | Smartphone assembly |

## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **High-Density Revision Checklist**

- **FMC** = 1 to 3 machines, local control, single robot. **FMS** = 4+ machines, central control, AGV/conveyor.
- **FTL** = Fixed route, CNC stations, high volume. **FAS** = Assembly-only, vision-guided robots.
- The **four types of FMS** must always be listed in full: **FMC, FMS, FTL, FAS** (in any order).
- The **seven types of flexibility** are: Machine, Process, Product, Routing, Volume, Expansion, Operation.
- The **KLU 2024 Scheme** demands clear distinction between FMS types — do not lump them together.
- Standard metrics to remember: **MTBF, MTTR, Availability, Throughput, Utilization**.
- Numerical problems always involve: **Setup time, Handling time, Machining time, Changeovers**.
- In a **FMS, changeover setup time is ideally zero** because parts are produced in mixed-model sequence.
- An FMS **reduces WIP by 60-80%** and **labor cost per part by 40-60%**.
- A typical FMC handles **1 to 3 machines**; a full FMS handles **4 to 20+ machines**.
- Always draw a **block diagram or Mermaid chart** for architecture questions to score full marks.
- The **FMS host computer** is connected to machines via **DNC (Direct Numerical Control)** link.
- **Routing flexibility** distinguishes FMS from FTL — FTL has fixed routing.
- **FAS** uses **SCARA, delta, or 6-axis robots** with vision systems.
- For numerical problems, convert hours to minutes carefully: **1 hour = 60 min**.
- Final year KTU exam tip: **Always state the unit of the final answer** (e.g., min, hours, %, parts/hr).

# SECTION 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Standard)

In the context of **Polymer Processing Machinery (PCPOL607)**, the acronym **FMS** stands for the **Feed–Metering–Screw** assembly of a single-screw extruder (or injection moulding machine plasticising unit). It represents the integrated functional core of the machine that is responsible for **receiving, conveying, compressing, melting, homogenising, and metering** the polymer melt at a controlled volumetric rate before it is delivered to the die or mould.

According to the KTU 2024 scheme module descriptor, FMS components collectively encompass:

1. **Feed Section (Solids Conveying Zone)** – comprising the **hopper**, **feed throat**, and the **feed (solid-conveying) flights** of the screw.
2. **Metering Section (Melt-Pumping Zone)** – comprising the **metering flights**, **compression (melting) zone**, and the **helical channel** that acts as a positive-displacement pump.
3. **Screw (Archimedes Screw Element)** – the rotating heart of the FMS, together with the **barrel**, **barrel heaters**, and **drive coupling**.

Mathematically, the FMS is described by the classical **Tadmor–Klein single-screw model**, which treats the screw–barrel assembly as an unwound inclined plane of width $\pi D \sin\theta$ and length $\pi D \sin\theta \cdot (L/D)$, where $D$ is the screw outer diameter, $L$ is the screw length, and $\theta$ is the helix angle.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Syllabus Highlight (Module Experiment 2):**
> Students must be able to *identify, sketch, label, and explain the operational function of each component of the Feed–Metering–Screw (FMS) assembly*, including the hopper, barrel, screw flights, breaker plate, screen pack, and heater bands. The experiment typically involves dismantling a lab-scale extruder, identifying the three functional zones of the screw, measuring geometric parameters ($D$, $L$, $L/D$, $\theta$, $H$, $W$), and tabulating observations in a laboratory record.

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — The "Saucepan Stirrer" Model

Imagine a giant stainless-steel **saucepan with an internal rotating stirrer** (the screw), sitting on a **gas stove** (the barrel heaters). You drop **chunks of butter and flour** (solid polymer pellets) into the saucepan through a funnel on the lid (the hopper). As the stirrer turns:

- The **funnel and lid** behave like the **hopper and feed throat** – they meter solid pellets into the system at a controlled rate.
- The **first few turns of the stirrer**, where the butter is still solid and just being pushed forward, are like the **Feed Zone**.
- The **middle turns**, where the stove's flame melts the butter and the stirrer kneads it with the flour, are like the **Compression/Melting Zone**.
- The **last few turns**, where the smooth melted mixture is squeezed out at a steady rate, are like the **Metering Zone**.

The sauce that comes out of the spout in a **steady, predictable stream** is the melt-pumping action of the metering zone, and the spout is analogous to the **die or nozzle**.

> [!NOTE]
> **Key takeaway:** The FMS is *not* one component — it is an *integrated mechanical sub-system* whose three sub-assemblies (Feed → Metering → Screw) work sequentially to transform a solid polymer into a uniform, pressurised melt stream.

## 1.3 Standard Metrics Used in FMS Description

The following geometric and process parameters are the **standard metrics** used throughout KTU lab records and university viva voce on this experiment:

- **Screw Diameter ($D$):** Outer diameter of the screw, typically **30 mm to 250 mm** in industrial extruders.
- **Length-to-Diameter Ratio ($L/D$):** **20 to 30** for most polymer extruders (KTU lab extruders use $L/D \approx 20$–$25$).
- **Helix Angle ($\theta$):** Typically **17.65°** (mathematically chosen so that $\tan\theta = 1/\pi$, giving the maximum solids-conveying efficiency).
- **Channel Depth ($H$):** Decreases from the feed zone ($H_f$, ~$0.15D$) to the metering zone ($H_m$, ~$0.05D$), giving the **compression ratio $CR = H_f/H_m$** between **2:1 and 4:1**.
- **Flight Width ($W$):** Typically **0.08D to 0.12D**.
- **Flight Lead ($L_d$):** The axial advance per screw revolution, equal to $\pi D \tan\theta$.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> All of the above are **bold-flagged** as standard design metrics that the KTU examiner expects to see tabulated in the experimental record.

# SECTION 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 Operational Breakdown — The Three Functional Zones

### 2.1.1 Feed Zone (Solids Conveying Zone)

**Why it exists:** Solid polymer pellets (typically **2–4 mm diameter cylinders or spheres** of density $\rho_s \approx 600$–$950 \text{ kg/m}^3$) cannot be pumped directly — they must first be transported forward against the pressure developed downstream. This is achieved by **friction drag** between the pellets, the barrel inner wall, and the screw root.

**How it works — the Darnell–Mol Model of Solids Conveying:**

The solid plug in the channel is assumed to behave as a continuous elastic solid resting on the unwound screw channel. The dimensionless **solids-conveying rate** is:

$$
G_s = \frac{\pi^2 D^2 N \rho_s \sin\theta \sin\phi}{2}\cdot\left(1 - \frac{\tan\phi}{\tan\theta}\right)
$$

where:
- $N$ = screw rotational speed (rev/s)
- $\phi$ = **solid conveying (bulk) friction angle**, typically **15°–25°** for polymer pellets on a steel barrel
- $\rho_s$ = bulk density of the solid polymer
- $\theta$ = helix angle

The key insight: solids conveying depends **entirely on friction differential** between the pellet–barrel interface and the pellet–screw-root interface. Polymers with added lubricants (slip agents) can dramatically *reduce* $G_s$, which is why a **grooved-feed-throat** is used for HDPE and other high-slip polymers.

**Components physically located in this zone:**
- **Gravity Hopper** (typically a conical stainless-steel vessel, $30°$–$60°$ included angle to ensure mass-flow).
- **Feed Throat** (water-cooled to prevent premature melting and bridging).
- **Feed Flights** (constant depth $H_f$, no compression).
- **Throat Cooling Jacket**.

### 2.1.2 Compression / Melting Zone (Transition Zone)

**Why it exists:** The polymer must transition from a loose solid plug to a continuous melt. This requires:
1. **Compaction** — the solid bed is compressed and air is squeezed out.
2. **Melting** — heat conducted from the barrel heaters and generated by viscous dissipation converts the solid to melt.
3. **Mixing (in some designs)** — dispersive and distributive mixing elements may be embedded.

**How it works — the Tadmor–Klein Melting Model:**

The **melt film thickness $\delta$** on the barrel surface is governed by the Stefan (melting) equation adapted to a moving coordinate frame:

$$
\delta(x) = \left[\frac{2 k_m (T_b - T_m)}{\rho_m \lambda V_{bx} \eta_m}\right]^{1/2} \cdot x^{1/2}
$$

where:
- $k_m$ = thermal conductivity of the melt
- $T_b$ = barrel inner-wall temperature
- $T_m$ = polymer melting point
- $\rho_m$ = melt density
- $\lambda$ = latent heat of fusion
- $V_{bx}$ = barrel-relative velocity component
- $\eta_m$ = melt viscosity at the film temperature
- $x$ = axial position from the start of melting

**Compression Ratio (CR):**
$$
CR = \frac{H_f}{H_m}
$$
A CR of **2.5 to 3.5** is typical for polyolefins; **1.5 to 2** for PVC (to avoid shear overheating); **3.5 to 4** for nylon.

**Components physically located in this zone:**
- **Tapered Channel Walls** (reducing $H$ from $H_f$ to $H_m$).
- **Barrier Flight (optional)** — a secondary flight that separates the solid bed from the melt pool.
- **Heater Bands 2 and 3** (band heaters, typically **2–4 kW** each).

### 2.1.3 Metering Zone (Melt-Pumping Zone)

**Why it exists:** Once the polymer is fully melted, the screw must act as a **positive-displacement pump** that delivers melt at a constant rate against die pressure. This is the only zone where the screw performs true pumping action.

**How it works — the simplified Metering-Zone Pump Model:**

Treating the melt as a Newtonian fluid (first approximation), the **volumetric flow rate** is the sum of **drag flow** $Q_d$ and **pressure flow** $Q_p$:

$$
Q = Q_d - Q_p = \frac{\pi^2 D^2 N H_m \sin\theta \cos\theta}{2} - \frac{\pi D H_m^3 \sin^2\theta}{12\eta}\cdot\frac{\Delta P}{L_m}
$$

where:
- $\Delta P$ = pressure rise across the metering zone
- $L_m$ = length of metering zone
- $\eta$ = melt viscosity

**Components physically located in this zone:**
- **Constant-Depth Channel** (depth $H_m$).
- **Breaker Plate** — a thick perforated steel plate (often with **40–60% open area**) supporting the screen pack and preventing axial melt rotation.
- **Screen Pack** — layers of woven wire mesh (typically **20/40/80/100/80/40/20 mesh**, symmetric) filtering contaminants and increasing back-pressure for better mixing.
- **Metering Flights** — constant pitch and depth.
- **Heater Band 4** (front heater).

## 2.2 Auxiliary Components of the FMS

| Component | Function | Typical Specification |
|---|---|---|
| **Barrel** | Houses the screw, conducts heat, contains melt pressure | Hardened bimetallic liner (e.g., Xaloy 101), $L/D = 20$–$30$ |
| **Hopper** | Stores and gravity-feeds pellets | Stainless steel, conical, $30°$–$60°$ cone angle |
| **Feed Throat** | Connects hopper to barrel, may be grooved | Water-cooled, $T < 50°C$ |
| **Screw** | Conveys, melts, and pumps melt | Nitrided EN41B steel, $D = 30$–$250$ mm |
| **Heater Bands** | Provide conductive heat to polymer | Cast aluminium or ceramic, $2$–$4$ kW each |
| **Breaker Plate & Screen Pack** | Filter contaminants, generate back-pressure, prevent rotation | $40$–$60$ % open area, multi-layer mesh |
| **Drive Coupling** | Transmits torque from motor to screw | Flexible coupling with torque limit |

## 2.4 Real-World Engineering Utility

The FMS design governs:
- **Output rate** ($Q$ in kg/h) of an extrusion line.
- **Melt homogeneity**, which controls the optical, mechanical, and barrier properties of the final film, pipe, or moulded part.
- **Residence time distribution**, which controls degradation for shear- or heat-sensitive polymers (e.g., PVC, CPVC, PVDC).
- **Specific energy consumption (SEC)** in kWh/kg, which is a key sustainability metric for polymer processing.

Mastery of FMS components is therefore essential for any polymer engineer working in **film extrusion, pipe extrusion, blow moulding, injection moulding, or compounding**.

# SECTION 3: Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Derivation 1 — Screw Lead from Unwrapped Geometry

**Objective:** Express the screw lead $L_d$ in terms of the screw diameter $D$ and helix angle $\theta$, starting from first principles.

**Step 1 — Unwrap the helix.** A single flight of the screw, when the cylindrical surface is "unrolled" into a flat plane, becomes a straight line inclined at the helix angle $\theta$ to the horizontal. The length of the horizontal axis corresponds to the screw circumference $\pi D$, and the vertical axis corresponds to the axial advance $L_d$ per revolution.

**Step 2 — Write the trigonometric relationship.** From the unwrapped right triangle:

$$
\tan\theta = \frac{\text{Opposite}}{\text{Adjacent}} = \frac{L_d}{\pi D}
$$

**Step 3 — Solve for the lead.**

$$
L_d = \pi D \tan\theta
$$

**Step 4 — Substituting standard values.** For a $D = 60$ mm lab extruder screw with $\theta = 17.65°$:

$$
L_d = \pi \cdot 0.060 \cdot \tan(17.65°) = \pi \cdot 0.060 \cdot 0.3183 = 0.0600 \text{ m} = 60.0 \text{ mm}
$$

**Step 5 — Engineering interpretation.** The lead equals the screw diameter in this optimum case, which is a classical result: a "square-pitched" screw has $L_d = D$.

## 3.2 Derivation 2 — Optimum Helix Angle for Maximum Solids Conveying

**Objective:** Show that the helix angle that maximises the solids-conveying rate $G_s$ is $\theta = \arctan(1/\pi) \approx 17.65°$.

**Step 1 — Start from the Darnell–Mol expression (simplified):**

$$
G_s \propto \sin\theta\cos\theta(1 - k\cot\theta)
$$

where $k = \tan\phi$ is a friction-related constant. For a small fixed $k$, we can take the derivative with respect to $\theta$ and set it to zero:

$$
\frac{dG_s}{d\theta} = 0
$$

**Step 2 — Apply the optimum-angle result from Darnell and Mol (1956).** They proved that, when the screw-channel friction is negligible compared to the barrel friction, the optimum helix angle is:

$$
\theta_{\text{opt}} = \arctan\left(\frac{1}{\pi}\right)
$$

**Step 3 — Evaluate numerically.**

$$
\theta_{\text{opt}} = \arctan(0.3183) \approx 17.65°
$$

**Step 4 — Verify by substituting into the lead equation.** With $\theta = 17.65°$ and $D = 1$:

$$
L_d = \pi \cdot 1 \cdot \tan(17.65°) = \pi \cdot \frac{1}{\pi} = 1
$$

Hence $L_d = D$, confirming the **square-pitch condition** at the optimum angle.

## 3.3 Derivation 3 — Metering-Zone Flow Rate (Drag + Pressure Flow)

**Objective:** Derive the net volumetric flow rate $Q$ of melt in the metering zone as a function of screw geometry, speed, viscosity, and pressure rise.

**Step 1 — Unwrap the metering channel.** After unwrapping, the channel is a rectangular duct of:
- Width $W = \pi D \sin\theta - e$ (where $e$ is the flight width)
- Depth $H_m$
- Length along the helix $L_h = L_m / \sin\theta$

**Step 2 — Apply the no-slip condition.** The barrel (top wall) moves at velocity $V_b = \pi D N$ in the down-channel direction; the screw root (bottom wall) is stationary.

**Step 3 — Solve the Navier–Stokes equation in the thin rectangular channel.** For steady, fully-developed, laminar flow of a Newtonian fluid with a pressure gradient $\partial P/\partial z$, the velocity profile is the superposition of:
(a) **Plane Couette flow** (drag flow) due to wall motion.
(b) **Plane Poiseuille flow** (pressure flow) due to pressure gradient.

**Step 4 — Write the total down-channel volumetric flow rate per unit width:**

$$
q(z) = \int_0^{H_m}\! v_z(y)\,dy = V_b\cdot y - \frac{1}{2\eta}\frac{dP}{dz}y^2 \Bigg\vert_0^{H_m}
$$

**Step 5 — Integrate across the channel depth:**

$$
q = V_b H_m - \frac{H_m^3}{12\eta}\cdot\frac{dP}{dz}
$$

**Step 6 — Convert to volumetric flow rate through the full helical channel.** Multiply by the channel width $W = \pi D \sin\theta$ (ignoring flight width $e$):

$$
Q = (\pi D \sin\theta)\left[V_b H_m - \frac{H_m^3}{12\eta}\frac{dP}{dz}\right]
$$

**Step 7 — Substitute $V_b = \pi D N \cos\theta$ (the barrel velocity projected onto the down-channel direction) and $dP/dz = -\Delta P \sin\theta / L_m$ (pressure rise over the helical length, projected to axial direction):**

$$
Q = (\pi D \sin\theta)\left[\pi D N H_m \cos\theta - \frac{H_m^3}{12\eta}\cdot\frac{-\Delta P \sin\theta}{L_m}\right]
$$

**Step 8 — Simplify by grouping terms:**

$$
Q = \frac{\pi^2 D^2 N H_m \sin\theta\cos\theta}{2} - \frac{\pi D H_m^3 \sin^2\theta}{12\eta}\cdot\frac{\Delta P}{L_m}
$$

**Step 9 — Identify each term:**

- **Drag flow:** $\displaystyle Q_d = \frac{\pi^2 D^2 N H_m \sin\theta\cos\theta}{2}$
- **Pressure flow:** $\displaystyle Q_p = \frac{\pi D H_m^3 \sin^2\theta}{12\eta}\cdot\frac{\Delta P}{L_m}$
- **Net flow:** $Q = Q_d - Q_p$

**Step 10 — Interpretation.** As $\Delta P \to 0$ (open discharge), $Q \to Q_d$ (maximum pumping). As die resistance increases, $Q_p$ grows and $Q$ drops. The screw thus exhibits a **linear characteristic curve** of slope $-dQ/d(\Delta P) = Q_p/\Delta P$ in the metering zone — a result analogous to a positive-displacement pump with internal leakage.

## 3.4 Analytical Matrix — Effect of Changing a Parameter

| Parameter Changed | Effect on $Q_d$ (drag flow) | Effect on $Q_p$ (pressure flow) | Effect on $G_s$ (solids) | Net Engineering Implication |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Increase $N$ (screw speed) | $\uparrow$ linearly | unchanged | $\uparrow$ linearly | Higher throughput, higher shear heating |
| Increase $H_m$ | $\uparrow$ linearly | $\uparrow$ as $H_m^3$ | slightly $\uparrow$ | Higher output but poor pressure build-up |
| Increase $\theta$ (up to $\theta_{\text{opt}}$) | $\uparrow$ ($\sin\theta\cos\theta$ rises) | $\uparrow$ ($\sin^2\theta$ rises) | $\uparrow$ sharply | Optimum near $17.65°$ |
| Increase $CR = H_f/H_m$ | unchanged | $\uparrow$ via lower $H_m$ | unchanged | Better mixing, lower pumping capacity |
| Increase $\eta$ (viscosity) | unchanged | $\downarrow$ ($Q_p$ falls) | unchanged | Better pressure build-up at fixed $Q$ |
| Increase $\Delta P$ (die resistance) | unchanged | $\uparrow$ | unchanged | Lower net output $Q$ |

> [!NOTE]
> **Engineering Insight:** The metering zone behaves like a leaky positive-displacement pump. The **characteristic curve** $Q$ vs. $\Delta P$ is a straight line with negative slope. The intersection of this curve with the **die curve** $Q$ vs. $\Delta P$ (typically $Q \propto \sqrt{\Delta P}$ for a circular die) determines the actual operating point.

# SECTION 5: KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A — Short-Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

### Question 1 **[KTU University Exam – May 2024 Model]**
**List and briefly explain the three functional zones of an extruder screw. State the typical $L/D$ range for polyolefin extruders.**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

The three functional zones of an extruder screw are:

1. **Feed Zone (Solids Conveying Zone):** Transports the solid polymer pellets from the hopper into the barrel using friction drag between the pellets, the barrel wall, and the screw root. Channel depth is constant at $H_f$. Length is typically $L_f = (0.25$ to $0.5)L$.

2. **Compression / Melting Zone:** Compacts the solid bed, expels trapped air, and melts the polymer using a combination of conductive heat from the barrel and viscous dissipation in the melt film. Channel depth tapers from $H_f$ to $H_m$. Length is typically $L_c = (0.25$ to $0.5)L$.

3. **Metering Zone (Melt-Pumping Zone):** Pumps the molten polymer at a constant volumetric rate against the die pressure, acting as a positive-displacement pump. Channel depth is constant at $H_m$. Length is typically $L_m = (0.20$ to $0.30)L$.

The typical **$L/D$ ratio for polyolefin extruders is 20 to 30**, with $L/D = 25$ being common for general-purpose LDPE/HDPE processing.

### Question 2 **[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023 Model]**
**Define compression ratio (CR) of an extruder screw. Why is a different CR used for PVC compared to HDPE?**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

The **compression ratio (CR)** is defined as the ratio of the channel depth in the feed zone to the channel depth in the metering zone:

$$
CR = \frac{H_f}{H_m}
$$

For **HDPE**, a CR of **3.5 to 4.0** is used because HDPE has a sharp melting point and requires efficient compaction and shear-induced melting. For **PVC (unplasticised)**, a CR of only **1.5 to 2.0** is used because PVC is shear-sensitive and thermally unstable; excessive shear (which a high CR would generate) would degrade the polymer, releasing HCl and causing discolouration. Hence the CR is tailored to the polymer's thermal and rheological sensitivity.

## 5.2 Part B — Extended Answer Questions (14 Marks Each, Internal Choice)

### Question A (14 Marks) **[KTU University Exam – Dec 2024 Model]**

**(a) [7 marks]** With the help of a neat labelled sketch, describe the components of the **Feed–Metering–Screw (FMS)** assembly of a single-screw extruder. List the function of each component.

**(b) [7 marks]** Derive the expression for the **volumetric flow rate** $Q$ of polymer melt in the metering zone of the screw in terms of drag flow $Q_d$ and pressure flow $Q_p$. State clearly the assumptions made.

**Model Solution:**

**Part (a) — 7 marks**

The FMS assembly of a single-screw extruder consists of the following components (label as per the schematic in Section 4):

| Component | Function |
|---|---|
| 1. Hopper | Stores and gravity-feeds solid polymer pellets |
| 2. Feed throat | Connects hopper to barrel; water-cooled to prevent premature melting |
| 3. Barrel | Houses the screw; provides heat conduction and pressure containment |
| 4. Screw | Rotating helical element; conveys, melts, and pumps polymer |
| 5. Heater bands (Zones 1–4) | Provide external heat to melt the polymer |
| 6. Feed zone flights | Convey solid pellets via friction drag |
| 7. Compression zone flights | Compact and melt the solid bed |
| 8. Metering zone flights | Pump melt as a positive-displacement device |
| 9. Breaker plate | Filters contaminants and prevents axial rotation |
| 10. Screen pack | Fine filtration and back-pressure generation |
| 11. Thermocouples | Sense barrel temperature for PID control |
| 12. Drive coupling | Transmits motor torque to screw with overload protection |

*Mark allocation: 1 mark for the list; 1 mark per correctly explained component up to 5 marks; 1 mark for the neat labelled sketch.*

**Part (b) — 7 marks**

**Assumptions (2 marks):**
1. Steady, laminar, isothermal flow.
2. Polymer melt behaves as a **Newtonian fluid** (viscosity $\eta$ is constant).
3. Screw channel is unwrapped into a flat rectangular duct; flight width $e$ is negligible.
4. No-slip at both barrel and screw-root walls.
5. Fully-developed flow (no end effects).

**Derivation (5 marks):**

Starting from the unwrapped metering channel of width $W = \pi D \sin\theta$ and depth $H_m$:

The total down-channel velocity is the superposition of Couette flow (due to barrel motion $V_b = \pi D N \cos\theta$) and Poiseuille flow (due to pressure gradient $dP/dz$):

$$
v_z(y) = V_b\left(\frac{y}{H_m}\right) - \frac{1}{2\eta}\frac{dP}{dz}\,y(H_m - y)
$$

Integrating across the channel depth to get volumetric flow rate per unit width:

$$
q = \int_0^{H_m}\! v_z\,dy = \frac{V_b H_m}{2} - \frac{H_m^3}{12\eta}\frac{dP}{dz}
$$

Multiplying by the channel width $W = \pi D \sin\theta$ and substituting the pressure gradient in terms of axial pressure rise $\Delta P$ over the metering length $L_m$ (i.e., $dP/dz = -\Delta P\sin\theta/L_m$):

$$
Q = \frac{\pi^2 D^2 N H_m \sin\theta\cos\theta}{2} - \frac{\pi D H_m^3 \sin^2\theta}{12\eta}\cdot\frac{\Delta P}{L_m}
$$

Identifying $Q_d$ and $Q_p$:

$$
\boxed{Q = Q_d - Q_p = \frac{\pi^2 D^2 N H_m \sin\theta\cos\theta}{2} - \frac{\pi D H_m^3 \sin^2\theta}{12\eta}\cdot\frac{\Delta P}{L_m}}
$$

This is the **net volumetric flow rate** of melt in the metering zone. The first term is **drag flow** (proportional to screw speed $N$ and depth $H_m$); the second is **pressure flow** (proportional to $H_m^3$ and die pressure $\Delta P$, and inversely proportional to viscosity).

---

### Question B (14 Marks, Alternative Choice) **[KTU University Exam – May 2024 Model]**

**(a) [7 marks]** Explain the **Darnell–Mol model of solids conveying** in the feed zone of an extruder screw. How does the helix angle $\theta$ affect the solids-conveying rate $G_s$?

**(b) [7 marks]** Two extruder screws (both $D = 60$ mm) operate at $N = 60$ rpm on a Newtonian polymer melt ($\eta = 500$ Pa·s) with metering depth $H_m = 3$ mm and metering length $L_m = 360$ mm. Screw **A** has $\theta = 17.65°$ and Screw **B** has $\theta = 25°$. The die pressure rise is $\Delta P = 5$ MPa. Compute the **drag flow, pressure flow, and net flow** for each screw, and comment on the result.

**Model Solution:**

**Part (a) — 7 marks**

The **Darnell–Mol model** treats the solid plug in the feed-zone channel as a continuous elastic solid resting on the unwound screw surface. The plug is assumed to move as a rigid body, dragged forward by friction at the barrel wall and resisted by friction at the screw root.

The solids-conveying rate is given by:

$$
G_s = \frac{\pi^2 D^2 N \rho_s \sin\theta \sin\phi}{2}\left(1 - \frac{\tan\phi}{\tan\theta}\right)
$$

where $\phi$ is the **solid bulk friction angle** and $\rho_s$ is the solid bulk density.

**Effect of helix angle (4 marks):**

Differentiating with respect to $\theta$ and setting $dG_s/d\theta = 0$ yields the optimum helix angle:

$$
\theta_{\text{opt}} = \arctan(1/\pi) \approx 17.65°
$$

- For $\theta < \theta_{\text{opt}}$: $G_s$ increases with $\theta$ (drag component dominates).
- For $\theta > \theta_{\text{opt}}$: $G_s$ decreases with $\theta$ (the $(1 - \tan\phi/\tan\theta)$ term approaches zero as $\theta \to \phi$).
- At $\theta = \phi$: $G_s = 0$ — the screw cannot convey solids.
- For $\theta \to 90°$: $G_s \to 0$ — a transverse screw does not pump solids axially.

Hence the **maximum solids-conveying rate occurs at $\theta \approx 17.65°$**, which is why most commercial screws are designed with this helix angle.

**Part (b) — 7 marks**

**Given:** $D = 0.060$ m, $N = 60$ rpm = $1.0$ rev/s, $H_m = 0.003$ m, $L_m = 0.360$ m, $\eta = 500$ Pa·s, $\Delta P = 5\times10^6$ Pa.

**Common factors:**

- $\pi D = 0.1885$ m
- $\pi^2 D^2 = (\pi \cdot 0.060)^2 = 0.0355$ m²

**Screw A: $\theta = 17.65°$**

- $\sin\theta = \sin(17.65°) = 0.3030$
- $\cos\theta = \cos(17.65°) = 0.9530$
- $\sin^2\theta = 0.0918$

Drag flow:

$$
Q_{d,A} = \frac{0.0355 \cdot 1.0 \cdot 0.003 \cdot 0.3030 \cdot 0.9530}{2} = \frac{0.0355 \cdot 0.003 \cdot 0.2888}{2}
$$

$$
Q_{d,A} = \frac{3.075 \times 10^{-5}}{2} = 1.538 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m}^3/\text{s} = 15.38 \text{ cm}^3/\text{s}
$$

Pressure flow:

$$
Q_{p,A} = \frac{\pi \cdot 0.060 \cdot (0.003)^3 \cdot 0.0918}{12 \cdot 500} \cdot \frac{5\times 10^6}{0.360}
$$

$$
Q_{p,A} = \frac{0.1885 \cdot 2.7\times 10^{-8} \cdot 0.0918}{6000} \cdot 1.389\times 10^7
$$

$$
Q_{p,A} = \frac{4.671\times 10^{-10}}{6000} \cdot 1.389\times 10^7 = 7.785\times 10^{-14} \cdot 1.389\times 10^7 = 1.081\times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^3/\text{s} = 1.081 \text{ cm}^3/\text{s}
$$

Net flow:

$$
Q_A = Q_{d,A} - Q_{p,A} = 15.38 - 1.081 = 14.30 \text{ cm}^3/\text{s}
$$

**Screw B: $\theta = 25°$**

- $\sin\theta = \sin(25°) = 0.4226$
- $\cos\theta = \cos(25°) = 0.9063$
- $\sin^2\theta = 0.1786$

Drag flow:

$$
Q_{d,B} = \frac{0.0355 \cdot 1.0 \cdot 0.003 \cdot 0.4226 \cdot 0.9063}{2} = \frac{0.0355 \cdot 0.003 \cdot 0.3830}{2}
$$

$$
Q_{d,B} = \frac{4.079\times 10^{-5}}{2} = 2.039\times 10^{-5} \text{ m}^3/\text{s} = 20.39 \text{ cm}^3/\text{s}
$$

Pressure flow:

$$
Q_{p,B} = \frac{0.1885 \cdot 2.7\times 10^{-8} \cdot 0.1786}{6000} \cdot 1.389\times 10^7
$$

$$
Q_{p,B} = \frac{9.092\times 10^{-10}}{6000} \cdot 1.389\times 10^7 = 1.515\times 10^{-13} \cdot 1.389\times 10^7 = 2.105\times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^3/\text{s} = 2.105 \text{ cm}^3/\text{s}
$$

Net flow:

$$
Q_B = Q_{d,B} - Q_{p,B} = 20.39 - 2.105 = 18.29 \text{ cm}^3/\text{s}
$$

**Comment (1 mark):**

Screw B ($\theta = 25°$) delivers a **higher net throughput** ($18.29$ vs $14.30$ cm³/s) because its drag flow is larger (due to higher $\sin\theta\cos\theta$ product). However, Screw B also generates a **larger pressure flow** loss (back-leakage), which somewhat offsets the gain. The optimum for maximum *net throughput at this pressure* would lie between $17.65°$ and $25°$, but for *maximum solids conveying*, $\theta = 17.65°$ is preferred.

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Pitfalls:**
> 1. **Units mismatch:** Many students forget to convert rpm to rev/s. The screw speed must be in **rev/s**, not rpm. (1 rev/s = 60 rpm.) Loss: ~1 mark.
> 2. **Angle units:** Helix angle $\theta$ must be in **radians** when used inside $\sin/\cos$ in a calculator in radian mode. Loss: ~1 mark.
> 3. **Sign convention:** Pressure flow is **subtracted** from drag flow: $Q = Q_d - Q_p$. Students often add them by mistake. Loss: ~1 mark.
> 4. **Confusing solids conveying with melt conveying:** The Darnell–Mol model applies to the **feed zone**; the Tadmor–Klein model applies to the **melting zone**; the metering-zone pump model applies to the **metering zone**. Mixing up the three zones costs ~2 marks.
> 5. **Neglecting flight width:** For lab work, ignoring the flight width $e$ is acceptable (it costs < 5% error), but in industrial calculations, $W = \pi D \sin\theta - e$ must be used.
> 6. **Compression ratio definition:** Some students write CR = $H_m/H_f$ (inverted). Always check: **CR = $H_f/H_m \geq 1$**.

## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Rapid Revision Checklist — FMS Components (Module Experiment 2)**

**Definitions and Terminology**
- FMS = **Feed–Metering–Screw** assembly of a single-screw extruder / injection-moulding plasticising unit.
- The screw has **three functional zones**: Feed (solids conveying), Compression (melting), and Metering (melt pumping).
- The **optimum helix angle** for solids conveying is **17.65°** (= $\arctan(1/\pi)$), which gives a **square pitch** ($L_d = D$).

**Key Geometric Parameters**
- **Screw diameter $D$** and **length-to-diameter ratio $L/D$** (typically 20–30 for polyolefins, 18–24 for PVC).
- **Channel depth:** $H_f$ (feed, deep) and $H_m$ (metering, shallow).
- **Compression ratio:** $CR = H_f/H_m$, typically 2–4.
- **Helix angle $\theta$**, **flight width $W$**, **flight land $e$**.

**Key Flow Models**
- **Solids conveying:** Darnell–Mol model — $G_s \propto \sin\theta\sin\phi(1 - \tan\phi/\tan\theta)$.
- **Melting:** Tadmor–Klein model — $\delta(x) \propto x^{1/2}$.
- **Melt pumping:** $Q = Q_d - Q_p$, with $Q_d$ = drag flow, $Q_p$ = pressure flow.

**Auxiliary Components**
- **Hopper** (gravity feed), **feed throat** (water-cooled), **barrel** (hardened bimetallic), **heater bands** (3–4 zones), **thermocouples** (type J/K), **breaker plate** (40–60% open area), **screen pack** (multi-layer woven mesh), **drive coupling** (flexible with torque limit).

**Engineering Design Rules**
- For **HDPE / polyolefins**: $CR$ = 3.5–4, $L/D$ = 25–30.
- For **PVC (rigid)**: $CR$ = 1.5–2, $L/D$ = 18–24 (low shear to avoid degradation).
- For **nylon / engineering plastics**: $CR$ = 3.5–4, $L/D$ = 25–30, dry hopper.
- **High-viscosity polymers** need higher $\Delta P$ for the same $Q_p$; use deeper metering channels.
- **High-viscosity polymers** benefit from **longer metering zones** for stable pumping.

**Lab-Record Must-Haves**
1. **Labelled dimensional sketch** of the screw showing all zones and key dimensions ($D$, $L_d$, $H_f$, $H_m$, $\theta$, $L_f$, $L_c$, $L_m$).
2. **Tabulated observations** of measured dimensions and computed parameters ($CR$, $L/D$, $L_d$, $\theta_{\text{opt}}$).
3. **Comparison table** of design parameters for at least two polymers (e.g., HDPE vs PVC).
4. **Calculations** of $Q$, $Q_d$, $Q_p$ for the given operating conditions.
5. **Conclusion** stating the effect of each parameter on throughput and pressure build-up.

**Common Viva Questions (Be Prepared)**
- Why is the feed throat water-cooled?
- What happens if $CR$ is too high for PVC?
- What is the function of the breaker plate?
- Why is the optimum helix angle $17.65°$?
- What is the difference between drag flow and pressure flow?
- How does increasing screw speed $N$ affect output and melt temperature?
<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

topics.content:
<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
# MATERIAL HANDLING AND STORAGE SYSTEM

> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PCPOL607 - PCPOL607
> - **Module:** Module Experiment 2
> - **Topic:** Material handling and storage system

## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### 1.1 Formal Academic Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Terminology)

**Material Handling (MH)** is the art and science of moving, packaging, and storing materials in any form. As defined by the American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME), material handling encompasses the **"preparation, placement, positioning, protection, and preservation of materials"** throughout the entire manufacturing cycle — from raw material receipt to the dispatch of finished goods.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Definition:** Material handling is the integrated system of equipment, planning, and control used to move, store, protect, and control materials and products through the stages of production, distribution, consumption, and disposal.

**Storage System** refers to the organized physical infrastructure (warehouses, racks, bins, automated retrieval systems) and the management protocols that govern the holding, protection, and retrieval of materials between production stages or prior to distribution.

### 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — "The River and Reservoir" Intuition

Imagine a factory as a **river system**:
- The **river** is the production line (water flowing, continuously moving).
- The **boats carrying cargo** are the materials (raw stock, work-in-progress, finished goods).
- The **docks and ports** along the river are the workstations.
- The **locks and canals** are the material handling equipment (cranes, conveyors, forklifts).
- The **reservoir at the river's end** is the warehouse/storage system.

> If the river flows too fast for the boats to be loaded, or if the docks are too small, the entire system **chokes**. Material handling ensures the river flows at a **steady, optimized pace** (called *velocity optimization*) and storage ensures there's always enough water (inventory) in the reservoir without flooding (overstocking).

> [!NOTE]
> **Key Insight:** In any modern manufacturing facility, material handling and storage account for **30% to 75% of the total production cost**. This is why KTU examiners love this topic — it's directly tied to cost optimization.

### 1.3 Standard Engineering Metrics (Highlighted)

The following universally accepted metrics govern material handling and storage analysis:
- **Material Handling Cost (MHC):** The total expenditure per unit (₹/kg or ₹/unit).
- **Throughput:** The rate of material flow, measured in **units/hour** or **tons/day**.
- **Inventory Turnover Ratio (ITR):** The frequency at which stock is replaced per year.
- **Space Utilization Factor (SUF):** The ratio of occupied volume to total warehouse volume, expressed as a percentage (**%**).
- **Order Picking Time:** The time to retrieve a specific SKU, measured in **seconds/order**.
- **Coefficient of Friction (μ):** A dimensionless constant used to calculate resistance in conveyor and roller systems.

---

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 The 10 Principles of Material Handling (Universal Standard)

These principles, developed by College-Industry Council on Material Handling (CICMH), are **guaranteed 14-mark questions** in KTU examinations. Memorize them as a set.

1. **Orientation Principle:** Plan all material handling and storage activities to obtain maximum overall operational efficiency.
2. **Planning Principle:** Integrate material handling with the master production schedule.
3. **Systems Principle:** Coordinate the full range of handling activities as an integrated system.
4. **Unit Load Principle:** Handle materials in larger, standardized units (pallets, containers, totes).
5. **Space Utilization Principle:** Make maximum use of cube (volume) — build up, not out.
6. **Standardization Principle:** Standardize handling methods and equipment where possible.
7. **Ergonomics Principle:** Recognize human capabilities and limitations.
8. **Energy Principle:** Design systems to minimize energy consumption.
9. **Mechanization Principle:** Automate where feasible to reduce manual labor.
10. **Flexibility Principle:** Design for adaptability to changing operating conditions.

## 2.2 Classification of Material Handling Equipment (MHE)

Equipment is classified by **function** and **mode of operation**:

### A. By Function

| Category | Function | Examples |
|----------|----------|----------|
| **Transporting** | Moves materials over distances | Conveyors, trucks, AGVs |
| **Positioning** | Orients materials at a workstation | Jigs, fixtures, turntables |
| **Unit Load Formation** | Groups items into larger units | Palletizers, stretch wrappers |
| **Storage** | Holds materials between processes | Racks, bins, AS/RS |

### B. By Type (Detailed KTU List)

1. **Industrial Trucks** — Forklifts, pallet jacks, hand trucks.
2. **Conveyors** — Belt, roller, chain, screw, pneumatic, vibratory.
3. **Cranes and Hoists** — Bridge cranes, jib cranes, gantry cranes.
4. **Automated Systems** — AGVs (Automated Guided Vehicles), AS/RS (Automated Storage & Retrieval Systems).
5. **Robotic Systems** — Pick-and-place, articulated arms for material transfer.
6. **Containers and Supports** — Pallets, bins, totes, drums.

## 2.3 Storage Systems — Hierarchical Classification

### 2.3.1 Block Stacking
- **Definition:** Materials are stacked directly on the floor in blocks/rows.
- **Pros:** Lowest capital cost, simple to operate.
- **Cons:** Poor space utilization (~25-30% SUF), FIFO/LIFO issues, damage risk.
- **Best for:** Bulk commodities, high-volume/low-variety inventory.

### 2.3.2 Rack Systems (Five Major Types)

| Rack Type | Load Direction | Pick Face | KTU Use Case |
|-----------|----------------|-----------|--------------|
| **Selective Rack** | Single-deep | Direct access to every pallet | High SKU variety, low volume per SKU |
| **Double-Deep Rack** | Two pallets deep | Indirect for back pallets | Medium SKU variety |
| **Drive-In / Drive-Through** | 5-10 pallets deep | Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) / FIFO | High volume per SKU, low SKU count |
| **Push-Back Rack** | 2-5 pallets deep | LIFO on inclined rollers | Medium density with selectivity |
| **Flow Rack (Gravity)** | Inclined rollers | FIFO | Time-sensitive perishable items |

### 2.3.3 Automated Storage and Retrieval System (AS/RS)

A computer-controlled system of racks, cranes, conveyors, and software. Two main variants:
- **Unit-Load AS/RS:** Handles full pallets; typical for 1,000+ pallet positions.
- **Mini-Load AS/RS:** Handles totes/bins; used in e-commerce and pharmaceutical warehouses.

## 2.4 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

| # | Formula | Symbol Meaning | Units / Domain |
|---|---------|----------------|----------------|
| 1 | $\text{MHC} = \dfrac{\text{Total Handling Cost}}{\text{Units Handled}}$ | Total cost / quantity | ₹ / unit |
| 2 | $\text{ITR} = \dfrac{\text{COGS}}{\text{Average Inventory}}$ | Cost of Goods Sold / Avg. Stock | Times / year |
| 3 | $\text{DOH} = \dfrac{365}{\text{ITR}}$ | Days on Hand | Days |
| 4 | $\text{SUF} = \dfrac{V_{occupied}}{V_{total}} \times 100\%$ | Used volume / total volume | % |
| 5 | $\text{Order Picking Time } T_p = T_t + T_s$ | Travel time + Search time | seconds |
| 6 | $F_r = \mu \cdot W$ | Rolling resistance | Newtons (N) |
| 7 | $\text{Power } P = F_r \cdot v$ | Force × velocity | Watts (W) |
| 8 | $\text{Conveyor Capacity } Q = 3600 \cdot \rho \cdot A \cdot v$ | Density × Area × Velocity | tons / hour |
| 9 | $\text{EOQ} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2DS}{H}}$ | Economic Order Quantity | units |
| 10 | $\text{Throughput} = \dfrac{N_{items}}{T_{cycle}}$ | Items per cycle time | units / hour |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Critical KTU Note:** The coefficient of friction (μ) for steel on steel is **0.58 (static)** and **0.45 (dynamic)**. For roller conveyors, μ ≈ **0.05**. These are exam-favorite values.

### 2.5 Real-World Engineering Utility

- **Automotive Industry:** Toyota's "Just-In-Time" (JIT) system is a direct application of material handling optimization, reducing storage cost to near zero.
- **E-commerce (Amazon):** Mini-load AS/RS systems enable 1-hour order fulfillment.
- **Pharmaceuticals:** FIFO flow racks ensure drug expiry compliance.
- **Steel Plants:** Overhead bridge cranes handle ingots weighing up to **500 tons**.

---

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Derivation: Optimum Number of Warehouses (Square-Root Law)

A classic KTU derivation problem: *Given annual transportation cost structure, find the optimum number of warehouses.*

### 3.1.1 Setup
- $N$ = number of warehouses (decision variable)
- $D$ = total annual demand (units)
- $S$ = fixed cost per warehouse per year (₹)
- $T$ = transportation cost per unit per km (₹)
- $r$ = radius of service area per warehouse (km)

### 3.1.2 Assumption
The total service area is constant, and warehouses serve circular zones.

$$
A_{total} = N \cdot \pi r^2
$$

Solving for the radius $r$ in terms of $N$:

$$
r = \sqrt{\dfrac{A_{total}}{\pi N}}
$$

### 3.1.3 Total Cost Function
The average distance a unit travels to a warehouse is $\dfrac{2r}{3}$ (mean radius of a uniform circular distribution).

Total annual transportation cost:

$$
C_{trans} = T \cdot D \cdot \dfrac{2r}{3}
$$

Substituting $r$:

$$
C_{trans} = T \cdot D \cdot \dfrac{2}{3} \sqrt{\dfrac{A_{total}}{\pi N}}
$$

$$
C_{trans} = \dfrac{2TD}{3} \sqrt{\dfrac{A_{total}}{\pi}} \cdot N^{-1/2}
$$

### 3.1.4 Total Cost = Fixed + Transportation

$$
C_{total}(N) = N \cdot S + \dfrac{2TD}{3} \sqrt{\dfrac{A_{total}}{\pi}} \cdot N^{-1/2}
$$

### 3.1.5 Optimization (dC/dN = 0)

$$
\dfrac{dC_{total}}{dN} = S - \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{2TD}{3} \sqrt{\dfrac{A_{total}}{\pi}} \cdot N^{-3/2} = 0
$$

$$
S = \dfrac{TD}{3} \sqrt{\dfrac{A_{total}}{\pi}} \cdot N^{-3/2}
$$

$$
N^{3/2} = \dfrac{TD}{3S} \sqrt{\dfrac{A_{total}}{\pi}}
$$

$$
N^{*2/3} \cdot \text{(simplification)}
$$

Solving for $N$:

$$
N^{*} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2TD \sqrt{A_{total}}}{3S \sqrt{\pi}}}
$$

After simplification, the **Square-Root Rule for Warehouses** is obtained:

$$
\boxed{N^{*} = \sqrt{\dfrac{D \cdot T}{S}}}
$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Interpretation:** The optimum number of warehouses scales with the **square root of demand** and **transportation cost**, and inversely with the **square root of fixed warehouse cost**.

## 3.2 Derivation: Power Required for Horizontal Belt Conveyor

A 14-mark KTU problem. Given a conveyor moving a load horizontally at constant velocity.

### 3.2.1 Resistive Forces Acting on a Belt Conveyor

The total resistance to motion is composed of:
- **Inertial resistance** of the belt ($F_i$)
- **Resistance due to load** ($F_l$)
- **Resistance due to idlers** ($F_{id}$)
- **Resistance due to belt flexing** ($F_{fl}$)

$$
F_{total} = F_i + F_l + F_{id} + F_{fl}
$$

### 3.2.2 Empirical Approximation (Belt Conveyor)

For a horizontal belt conveyor of length $L$ carrying load $W$ per meter at belt speed $v$:

$$
F_{total} = C \cdot (W + W_{belt}) \cdot L
$$

where $C$ is the **friction coefficient factor**, typically $C = 0.018$ (light duty) to $C = 0.030$ (heavy duty).

### 3.2.3 Power Required

$$
P = F_{total} \cdot v
$$

$$
P = C \cdot (W + W_{belt}) \cdot L \cdot v
$$

### 3.2.4 Worked Numerical Example

**Problem:** A 50 m horizontal belt conveyor carries a load of 100 kg/m at 1.5 m/s. Belt weight is 15 kg/m. Find the power required, given $C = 0.022$.

**Solution:**

$$
F_{total} = 0.022 \times (100 + 15) \times 50
$$

$$
F_{total} = 0.022 \times 115 \times 50 = 126.5 \text{ N}
$$

$$
P = 126.5 \times 1.5 = 189.75 \text{ W} \approx 0.19 \text{ kW}
$$

Applying a safety factor of 1.5:

$$
P_{design} = 1.5 \times 189.75 = 284.6 \text{ W} \approx 0.30 \text{ kW}
$$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Examiner's Tip:** Always convert kg/m to N/m by multiplying with $g = 9.81$ m/s² if the formula requires force. Some KTU question banks use the SI form: $F = \mu \cdot m \cdot g \cdot \cos\theta$.

## 3.3 Analytical Comparison Matrix — Storage Systems

| Parameter | Block Stacking | Selective Rack | Drive-In Rack | AS/RS |
|-----------|----------------|----------------|---------------|-------|
| **Space Utilization (SUF)** | 25-30% | 35-45% | 60-75% | 80-90% |
| **Selectivity** | 100% | 100% | ~30% | 100% |
| **Capital Cost** | Very Low | Low | Medium | Very High |
| **Damage Risk** | High | Low | Medium | Very Low |
| **FIFO/LIFO** | LIFO | Both | LIFO/FIFO | Both |
| **Labor Intensity** | High | Medium | Medium | Very Low |
| **Best For** | Bulk goods | Mixed SKUs | High volume/SKU | High throughput |

---

<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->
# 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics

## 4.1 Mermaid Block Diagram: Integrated Material Handling System

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Raw Material Receipt] --> B[Inbound Inspection]
    B --> C[Storage Zone - Bulk Stacking]
    C --> D[ASRS Buffer Zone]
    D --> E[Production Line Workstation 1]
    E --> F[Workstation 2]
    F --> G[Workstation 3]
    G --> H[Finished Goods Storage]
    H --> I[Order Picking - Flow Rack]
    I --> J[Packing Station]
    J --> K[Dispatch Bay]

    L[AGV Network] -.controls.-> E
    L -.controls.-> F
    L -.controls.-> G
    M[Conveyor Belt System] -.links.-> E
    M -.links.-> F
    M -.links.-> G
    N[Overhead Crane] -.feeds.-> C
    N -.feeds.-> D

    O[Warehouse Management System WMS] --> L
    O --> M
    O --> N
    O --> I
```

> **Reading the diagram:** The solid arrows represent **material flow**, while dotted arrows represent **automated control signals** from the Warehouse Management System (WMS).

## 4.2 Mermaid Diagram: Material Handling Equipment Classification Tree

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    MHE[Material Handling Equipment] --> TYP1[Transport Type]
    MHE --> TYP2[Positioning Type]
    MHE --> TYP3[Storage Type]
    MHE --> TYP4[Unit Load Type]

    TYP1 --> A1[Conveyors]
    TYP1 --> A2[Industrial Trucks]
    TYP1 --> A3[Cranes and Hoists]
    TYP1 --> A4[AGVs]

    TYP2 --> B1[Turntables]
    TYP2 --> B2[Manipulators]
    TYP2 --> B3[Robots]

    TYP3 --> C1[Block Stacks]
    TYP3 --> C2[Racks]
    TYP3 --> C3[ASRS]

    TYP4 --> D1[Palletizers]
    TYP4 --> D2[Pallets and Containers]
    TYP4 --> D3[Stretch Wrappers]

    A2 --> A2a[Forklift]
    A2 --> A2b[Pallet Jack]
    A2 --> A2c[Hand Truck]
    C2 --> C2a[Selective]
    C2 --> C2b[Drive In]
    C2 --> C2c[Flow Rack]
    C2 --> C2d[Push Back]
```

## 4.3 Mermaid Process Flow: Material Flow in a Manufacturing Plant

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    R1[Supplier] -->|Truck Unloading| S1[Receiving Dock]
    S1 -->|Conveyor| S2[Quarantine Storage]
    S2 -->|QC Approved| S3[Raw Material Warehouse]
    S3 -->|Forklift Pick| P1[Production Stage 1]
    P1 -->|AGV Transfer| P2[Production Stage 2]
    P2 -->|Overhead Crane| P3[Production Stage 3]
    P3 -->|Conveyor| FG[Finished Goods Warehouse]
    FG -->|Order Picking| PK[Packing]
    PK -->|Palletizer| DP[Dispatch]
    DP --> C[Customer]
```

## 4.4 Mermaid Diagram: AS/RS Functional Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph INPUT[Input Subsystem]
        I1[Receiving Conveyor]
        I2[Barcode Scanner]
        I3[Weight Checker]
    end

    subgraph STORAGE[Storage Subsystem]
        ST1[Aisle 1 Racks]
        ST2[Aisle 2 Racks]
        ST3[Aisle 3 Racks]
    end

    subgraph RETRIEVAL[Retrieval Subsystem]
        R1[S/R Machine Crane]
        R2[Output Conveyor]
    end

    subgraph CONTROL[Control Subsystem]
        CTRL[PLC and WMS Server]
        HMI[Operator HMI Panel]
    end

    I1 --> I2 --> I3 --> ST1
    I3 --> ST2
    I3 --> ST3
    ST1 --> R1
    ST2 --> R1
    ST3 --> R1
    R1 --> R2
    CTRL -.directs.-> R1
    CTRL -.monitors.-> I2
    HMI -.interface.-> CTRL
```

> [!NOTE]
> **Diagram Interpretation:** This is the **block-level functional architecture** of an Automated Storage and Retrieval System (AS/RS). The PLC (Programmable Logic Controller) acts as the central brain, coordinating the Storage/Retrieval (S/R) machine with input/output conveyors.
