<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### 1.1 Automated Storage and Retrieval System (AS/RS)

An **Automated Storage and Retrieval System (AS/RS)** is a computer-controlled, mechanized system that automatically stores and retrieves goods, parts, tools, and materials from defined storage locations, eliminating or drastically reducing the need for human intervention in warehouses and production stockrooms.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Syllabus Definition:** AS/RS is defined as a combination of equipment (silos, racks, cranes, conveyors) and controls (sensors, computers, software) working together to handle, store, and retrieve materials with maximum efficiency, minimum labour, and full inventory tracking.

**Conceptual Analogy:** Imagine a massive multi-storey library where instead of a librarian walking through aisles to find a book, a robotic crane on rails (like a tiny elevator-gantry hybrid) zooms in three dimensions — along the aisle (X-axis), across the rack (Y-axis), and up/down the height (Z-axis) — to deliver the exact box to the operator at a pickup station within seconds. That is an AS/RS.

### 1.2 Automatic Identification Systems (Auto-ID) and Data Capture

**Automatic Identification (Auto-ID)** refers to the technology used to identify objects, capture data about them, and enter that data directly into computer systems without human keystrokes. **Data Capture** is the broader process of recording the identified information into a digital database for tracking, billing, inventory, and production control.

> [!NOTE]
> **Core Barcode Equation of Information Density:**
> Data Density $= \dfrac{\text{Number of encoded characters}}{\text{Length of symbol (inches)}}$

**Conceptual Analogy:** Think of a supermarket checkout. The cashier simply passes the product over a laser scanner — a *beep* instantly identifies the item, its price, stock level, and expiry date. The cashier never types a number. That single *beep* is Auto-ID + Data Capture working in one second. In a factory, the same principle identifies bins, tools, WIPs, and finished goods moving on conveyors.

### 1.3 Computer Numerical Control (CNC) — Introduction

**Computer Numerical Control (CNC)** is a method of controlling machine tools (milling, turning, drilling, grinding, etc.) by means of a dedicated computer that executes pre-programmed sequences of machine control commands. The data fed into the computer is a **part program** containing G-codes (geometric codes) and M-codes (miscellaneous/machine functions).

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Highlight:** CNC is a *soft automation* technology where the same machine tool can manufacture different parts simply by changing the program — there is no need to physically retool the hard-wired logic, unlike traditional NC.

**Conceptual Analogy:** A traditional screw-cutting lathe requires a skilled operator turning handles continuously. A CNC lathe, in contrast, is like a *robotic chef*: you write a recipe (the part program) specifying "cut 2 mm depth at 0.5 mm/rev feed, then move to coordinate (X=50, Z=20)," and the chef (machine) executes it perfectly — 24/7, with no coffee breaks and no human error.

### 1.4 Standard Engineering Metrics

- **AS/RS Cycle Time:** typically **20 to 60 seconds** per transaction.
- **Barcode Standard Density:** Code 39 = **9.4 chars/inch**; Code 128 = **17 chars/inch**.
- **CNC Positioning Accuracy:** modern CNC machines = **$\pm$ 0.001 mm** (1 micron).
- **RFID Read Range:** passive tags = **up to 12 m**; active tags = **up to 100 m**.

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### 2.1 AS/RS — Operational Logic and Sub-Types

**Working Principle (Step-by-Step):**
- A central computer receives a **request** (order/withdrawal or storage instruction).
- The system determines the **optimal storage location** (often based on *random storage* or *closest-open-location* algorithms).
- The **storage/retrieval (S/R) machine** — either a crane, a car, or a robotic arm — travels along the rack aisle.
- Mechanical **extractor (telescopic fork or suction)** engages the pallet/box.
- The load is transported to the **input/output (I/O) station** for human or AGV pickup.
- Inventory database is updated in real time.

**Types of AS/RS (KTU-Mapped):**

| Type | Structural Layout | Typical Application |
|------|-------------------|---------------------|
| Unit-load AS/RS | Pallets on racks; heavy crane | Finished goods warehouse |
| Mini-load AS/RS | Bins/totes; lightweight crane | Pharmaceutical/electronic parts |
| Vertical Lift Module (VLM) | Single column, tray elevator | Tools, small parts |
| Carousel AS/RS | Rotating horizontal/vertical shelves | Order picking, kitting |
| Mobile Racking | Racks on wheeled bases | Long-span storage |

### 2.2 Automatic Identification Technologies — Analytical Breakdown

**Step-by-Step Classification Logic:**

- **Optical Technologies** — use light reflection patterns:
  - *Barcode (1D)* — parallel lines of varying width.
  - *2D Code (QR, Data Matrix)* — matrix of black/white cells.
  - *OCR (Optical Character Recognition)* — reads printed alphanumeric text.

- **Radio Frequency Technologies** — use electromagnetic coupling:
  - *RFID Passive* — no battery, powered by reader's field.
  - *RFID Active* — battery-powered transmitter.

- **Biometric Technologies** — fingerprint, iris, facial recognition (for personnel access).

- **Magnetic & Smart Card** — magnetic stripes, chip cards, NFC tokens.

- **Vision Systems** — machine vision cameras for shape, colour, defect detection.

### 2.3 CNC — Deep Theoretical Framework

**Core Components of a CNC System:**

| Component | Function | Real-World Example |
|-----------|----------|--------------------|
| Part Program | Sequence of instructions | Text file with G01, M08 etc. |
| Machine Control Unit (MCU) | Decodes program, generates axis motion | Fanuc / Siemens controller |
| Drive System | Powers the slides | Servo motors, stepper motors |
| Feedback System | Confirms actual position | Encoders (linear/rotary) |
| Machine Tool | Physical cutting action | Lathe, mill, EDM |
| Auxiliary Devices | Coolant, chip removal, tool changer | ATC, ATC arm, coolant nozzle |

**Coordinate System:** CNC uses the **Cartesian XYZ** convention, with **+Z always pointing away from the workpiece** toward the tool (milling) or toward the tailstock (turning).

### 2.4 KTU Formula Sheet (High-Yield for Numerical Problems)

> [!NOTE]
> **No vertical pipe `|` characters used in tables.** Absolute value and modulus are written as `\vert` or `\mid`.

| # | Formula / Parameter | Symbolic Expression | Units | Engineering Use |
|---|---------------------|---------------------|-------|-----------------|
| 1 | Spindle Speed | $N = \dfrac{1000 \cdot V}{\pi \cdot D}$ | rpm | Turning / Milling |
| 2 | Feed Rate | $f_r = N \cdot f \cdot z$ | mm/min | Multi-tooth cutters |
| 3 | Material Removal Rate (Turning) | $MRR = V \cdot f \cdot d$ | mm³/s | Productivity |
| 4 | Material Removal Rate (Milling) | $MRR = f_r \cdot a_p \cdot a_e$ | mm³/min | Productivity |
| 5 | Metal Removal Power | $P = \dfrac{MRR}{K \cdot 60}$ | kW | Machine selection |
| 6 | AS/RS Throughput | $T = \dfrac{3600}{t_c}$ | trans/hr | Warehouse design |
| 7 | Barcode Density | $\rho = \dfrac{n_{chars}}{L_{inch}}$ | chars/in | Scanner selection |
| 8 | RFID Read Range (Friis) | $R = \dfrac{\lambda}{4\pi}\sqrt{\dfrac{P_t G_t G_r}{P_{r,min}}}$ | m | Tag/reader design |
| 9 | Machining Time (Turning) | $t_m = \dfrac{L}{f_r}$ | min | Time estimation |
| 10 | Tool Life (Taylor's) | $V \cdot T^n = C$ | m/min · min | Tool economics |

Where: $V$ = cutting speed, $D$ = diameter, $f$ = feed/tooth, $z$ = number of teeth, $a_p$ = depth of cut, $a_e$ = width of cut, $t_c$ = cycle time, $\lambda$ = wavelength, $P_t$ = transmitted power, $G_t, G_r$ = antenna gains.

### 2.5 Real-World Engineering Utility

- **AS/RS** enables Industry 4.0 supply chains — used by Amazon, Bosch, Toyota, Apollo Tyres.
- **Auto-ID/RFID** is mandatory in aerospace parts tracking (FAA / DGCA mandates).
- **CNC** forms the backbone of FMS (Flexible Manufacturing Systems) and is a prerequisite for Smart Factories.

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
## 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

### 3.1 Derivation 1: CNC Spindle Speed and Feed Rate (Turning Operation)

**Given Data for a Typical KTU Numerical:**
- Workpiece diameter, $D = 60 \text{ mm}$
- Recommended cutting speed, $V = 30 \text{ m/min}$
- Feed per revolution, $f = 0.3 \text{ mm/rev}$
- Length of cut, $L = 120 \text{ mm}$

**Step 1 — Compute the Spindle Speed $N$:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
N &= \frac{1000 \cdot V}{\pi \cdot D} \\
  &= \frac{1000 \times 30}{\pi \times 60} \\
  &= \frac{30000}{188.4955} \\
  &= 159.1549 \text{ rpm}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Conversion logic:** The constant 1000 converts metres to millimetres because $V$ is in m/min while $D$ is in mm. The factor $\pi D$ gives the *circumferential distance* travelled by the tool per spindle revolution, so dividing $V \cdot 1000$ by $\pi D$ yields revolutions per minute.

**Step 2 — Compute the Feed Rate $f_r$:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_r &= N \cdot f \\
    &= 159.1549 \times 0.3 \\
    &= 47.7465 \text{ mm/min}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Conversion logic:** Each spindle revolution advances the tool by $f$ mm; over $N$ revolutions, the total advance per minute is $N \cdot f$.

**Step 3 — Compute the Machining Time $t_m$:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
t_m &= \frac{L}{f_r} \\
    &= \frac{120}{47.7465} \\
    &= 2.513 \text{ min}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4 — Add Approach and Overrun:**
A standard approach $L_a = 3 \text{ mm}$ and overrun $L_o = 2 \text{ mm}$ are added:

$$
\begin{aligned}
L_{total} &= L + L_a + L_o = 120 + 3 + 2 = 125 \text{ mm} \\
t_m &= \frac{125}{47.7465} = 2.618 \text{ min}
\end{aligned}
$$

### 3.2 Derivation 2: AS/RS Throughput Calculation

**Given Data:**
- Single-cycle time of S/R machine, $t_c = 45 \text{ seconds/transaction}$
- Operating hours per shift, $H = 8 \text{ hours}$
- Number of shifts per day, $s = 2$
- System availability / efficiency, $\eta = 0.90$

**Step 1 — Theoretical Maximum Throughput:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
T_{max} &= \frac{3600}{t_c} = \frac{3600}{45} = 80 \text{ transactions/hour}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2 — Effective Throughput (with efficiency):**

$$
\begin{aligned}
T_{eff} &= T_{max} \cdot \eta = 80 \times 0.90 = 72 \text{ transactions/hour}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3 — Daily Throughput:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
T_{daily} &= T_{eff} \cdot H \cdot s = 72 \times 8 \times 2 = 1152 \text{ transactions/day}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Conversion logic:** Hour-to-second conversion uses 3600; multiplying by operating hours and shifts gives daily capacity. The efficiency factor $\eta$ accounts for simultaneous storage/retrieval deadheading, maintenance, and indexing delays.

### 3.3 Derivation 3: RFID Link Budget (Friis Free-Space Equation)

**Given Data:**
- Reader transmit power, $P_t = 1 \text{ W} = 30 \text{ dBm}$
- Operating frequency, $f = 915 \text{ MHz}$ (UHF RFID)
- Transmitter antenna gain, $G_t = 6 \text{ dBi}$
- Receiver antenna gain, $G_r = 2 \text{ dBi}$
- Tag sensitivity, $P_{r,min} = -18 \text{ dBm}$

**Step 1 — Wavelength:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lambda &= \frac{c}{f} = \frac{3 \times 10^{8}}{915 \times 10^{6}} = 0.3279 \text{ m}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2 — Maximum Read Range (numerical Friis form):**

$$
\begin{aligned}
R &= \frac{\lambda}{4\pi} \sqrt{\frac{P_t \cdot G_t \cdot G_r}{P_{r,min}}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute (all linear, not dB):

$$
\begin{aligned}
P_t &= 1.0 \text{ W} \\
G_t &= 10^{0.6} = 3.981 \\
G_r &= 10^{0.2} = 1.585 \\
P_{r,min} &= 10^{-1.8} = 0.01585 \text{ W} \\
\frac{P_t G_t G_r}{P_{r,min}} &= \frac{1.0 \times 3.981 \times 1.585}{0.01585} = 398.2 \\
\sqrt{398.2} &= 19.955 \\
R &= \frac{0.3279}{4 \times 3.1416} \times 19.955 \\
  &= 0.02609 \times 19.955 = 0.521 \text{ m}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Conversion logic:** dB-to-linear conversion uses $10^{x/10}$ for power, $10^{x/10}$ for gains. The $\lambda / 4\pi$ factor is the free-space path loss constant.

### 3.4 Analytical Matrix — Comparison of AS/RS vs Auto-ID vs CNC

| Parameter | AS/RS | Auto-ID / Data Capture | CNC |
|-----------|-------|-------------------------|-----|
| Primary Function | Storage & Retrieval | Identification & Tracking | Manufacturing |
| Core Technology | Mechatronics, WMS, PLC | Barcode, RFID, Vision, OCR | Servo, MCU, G-code |
| Cycle Time Metric | 20–60 s | < 1 s read | Depends on part |
| Accuracy | 99.9% pick rate | 99.999% (RFID read) | $\pm$ 0.001 mm |
| ROI Payback | 2–5 years | 6–18 months | 1–3 years |
| Industry 4.0 Role | Smart Warehouse | Digital Twin Enabler | Smart Machine |
| Limitation | High capex, low flexibility | Tag cost, line-of-sight | Skilled programmer |

<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->
## 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics

### 4.1 Block-Level Architecture of a Complete AS/RS

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Central WMS Computer] --> B[Order / Instruction Dispatcher]
    B --> C[Path Optimizer Algorithm]
    C --> D[Storage Retrieval Machine Controller]
    D --> E1[Aisle X-Axis Drive Motor]
    D --> E2[Vertical Z-Axis Hoist Motor]
    D --> E3[Horizontal Y-Axis Telescopic Fork]
    E1 --> F1[Rack Aisle 1]
    E1 --> F2[Rack Aisle 2]
    E2 --> G1[Upper Rack Level]
    E2 --> G2[Middle Rack Level]
    E2 --> G3[Lower Rack Level]
    E3 --> H1[Load Pallet]
    E3 --> H2[Load Bin Tote]
    H1 --> I1[Input Output Station I/O]
    H2 --> I1
    I1 --> J[Conveyor or AGV Pickup]
    J --> K[Inventory Database Update]
    K --> A
```

**Reading the Diagram:** The flow starts at the Warehouse Management System (WMS) computer, which dispatches instructions, computes the optimal storage/retrieval path, and commands the S/R machine. The machine's three independent drives (X, Y, Z) move to the target cell, extract the load, and deliver it to the I/O station. The transaction is logged back to the inventory database, closing the feedback loop.

### 4.2 CNC Machine Tool — Block-Level Functional Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Part Program .nc file] --> B[Machine Control Unit MCU]
    B --> C1[X Axis Interpolator]
    B --> C2[Y Axis Interpolator]
    B --> C3[Z Axis Interpolator]
    C1 --> D1[Servo Drive X]
    C2 --> D2[Servo Drive Y]
    C3 --> D3[Servo Drive Z]
    D1 --> E1[Ball Screw and Slide X]
    D2 --> E2[Ball Screw and Slide Y]
    D3 --> E3[Ball Screw and Slide Z]
    E1 --> F1[Linear Encoder Feedback X]
    E2 --> F2[Linear Encoder Feedback Y]
    E3 --> F3[Linear Encoder Feedback Z]
    F1 --> B
    F2 --> B
    F3 --> B
    B --> G[Spindle Motor Controller]
    G --> H[Spindle with Cutting Tool]
    H --> I[Workpiece on Table or Chuck]
    I --> J[Chip Pan and Coolant System]
```

**Reading the Diagram:** This is a *closed-loop* CNC system. The part program enters the MCU; the MCU computes individual axis motions using interpolation; each axis has a dedicated servo drive, ball-screw mechanism, and linear encoder for position feedback. The encoder signal returns to the MCU for real-time error correction, achieving micron-level accuracy.

### 4.3 Automatic Identification and Data Capture — Functional Flow

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Object or Part Arrives at Read Point] --> B{Identification Technology}
    B -->|Optical| C1[Barcode 1D]
    B -->|Optical| C2[Data Matrix 2D]
    B -->|RF| C3[Passive RFID Tag]
    B -->|RF| C4[Active RFID Tag]
    B -->|Vision| C5[Machine Vision Camera]
    B -->|Magnetic| C6[Magstripe or Smart Card]
    C1 --> D[Reader / Scanner]
    C2 --> D
    C3 --> D
    C4 --> D
    C5 --> D
    C6 --> D
    D --> E[Decoder Unit]
    E --> F[Middleware Software]
    F --> G1[ERP System]
    F --> G2[Inventory Database]
    F --> G3[Production Tracking System]
    F --> G4[Quality Management QMS]
    G1 --> H[Closed Loop Real Time Control]
    G2 --> H
    G3 --> H
    G4 --> H
```

**Reading the Diagram:** Any object arriving at a checkpoint is interrogated by the appropriate Auto-ID technology. The raw signal (reflected light, RF backscatter, image) is decoded into a digital ID, pushed through middleware, and distributed to enterprise systems (ERP, WMS, MES, QMS). This closed loop enables real-time decision-making.

<!-- SECTION_4_END -->

<!-- SECTION_5_START -->
## 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

### Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

**Q1. [KTU University Exam — Dec 2023]**
Define Automated Storage and Retrieval System (AS/RS). List any four advantages of implementing AS/RS in a modern warehouse.

**Model Answer:**
AS/RS is a computer-controlled system that automatically stores and retrieves materials from defined storage locations using cranes, conveyors, and software controls, with minimal human intervention.

*Four advantages:*
- Maximises use of vertical space (saves floor area).
- Reduces labour cost and human error in picking.
- Improves inventory accuracy (99%+ via WMS integration).
- Enhances safety by removing workers from hazardous racking zones.

*(3 marks — 1 for definition, 2 for any four advantages)*

**Q2. [KTU University Exam — June 2024]**
What is the difference between a barcode and an RFID tag? Mention one specific industrial application of each.

**Model Answer:**

| Feature | Barcode | RFID Tag |
|---------|---------|----------|
| Read Mechanism | Optical (line-of-sight) | RF (no line-of-sight) |
| Read Speed | One at a time | Multiple simultaneously |
| Durability | Easily damaged | Encapsulated, rugged |
| Data Capacity | Limited (10–30 chars) | Larger (up to several KB) |
| Cost | Very low (< ₹5) | Higher (₹15–200) |

*Barcode application:* Point-of-sale billing in supermarkets.
*RFID application:* Toll collection (FASTag) and aerospace part tracking.

*(3 marks — 1 for differentiation, 2 for applications)*

---

### Part B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks Each — Internal Choice)

#### Question A (14 Marks)

**(a) [7 marks] [KTU University Exam — May 2024]**
Explain the working principle of a Unit-Load AS/RS with a neat block diagram. Discuss the role of the Warehouse Management System (WMS) software in coordinating storage and retrieval transactions.

**Model Solution:**

A Unit-Load AS/RS handles standard pallets (typically 1000 × 1200 mm, up to 1500 kg). The system consists of:

1. **Rack structure** — rows of vertical storage columns, typically 10–40 m high.
2. **Storage/Retrieval (S/R) crane** — a rail-mounted gantry that moves along the aisle (X-axis), hoists up/down (Z-axis), and extends a telescopic fork (Y-axis) into the rack cell.
3. **Input/Output (I/O) stations** — conveyor-fed pickup/delivery points at aisle ends.
4. **WMS software** — central computer managing inventory, locations, and transactions.

**Working sequence:**
- WMS receives a *put-away* or *pick* instruction.
- WMS assigns an *aisle, bay, level, and position* to the load.
- The S/R crane travels to that cell using optimised path algorithms (e.g., nearest-neighbour, dual-command cycles).
- The telescopic fork extends, engages the pallet, retracts, and the crane transports it to the I/O station.
- Transaction data is updated in the WMS database in real time.

**Role of WMS:**
- Tracks every pallet by unique ID (barcode/RFID).
- Optimises *dual-command cycles* (one S/R move stores one pallet *and* retrieves another).
- Manages FIFO/FEFO rotation, batch tracking, and lot genealogy.
- Interfaces with ERP for order fulfilment.

*(7 marks — 3 for description, 2 for diagram, 2 for WMS role)*

**(b) [7 marks] [KTU University Exam — May 2024]**
A turning operation is to be performed on a CNC lathe. The work-piece diameter is 80 mm, the recommended cutting speed is 25 m/min, the feed per revolution is 0.25 mm/rev, and the length of cut is 150 mm. Calculate: (i) the spindle speed, (ii) the feed rate in mm/min, and (iii) the machining time. Add an allowance of 3 mm for tool approach.

**Model Solution:**

**(i) Spindle Speed:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
N &= \frac{1000 \cdot V}{\pi \cdot D} \\
  &= \frac{1000 \times 25}{\pi \times 80} \\
  &= \frac{25000}{251.327} \\
  &= 99.47 \text{ rpm} \approx 100 \text{ rpm}
\end{aligned}
$$

**(ii) Feed Rate:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_r &= N \cdot f = 99.47 \times 0.25 = 24.87 \text{ mm/min}
\end{aligned}
$$

**(iii) Machining Time:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
L_{total} &= 150 + 3 = 153 \text{ mm} \\
t_m &= \frac{L_{total}}{f_r} = \frac{153}{24.87} = 6.15 \text{ min}
\end{aligned}
$$

*(7 marks — 2 for N, 2 for f_r, 3 for time including allowance)*

---

#### Question B (14 Marks) — Alternative Choice

**(a) [7 marks] [KTU University Exam — Dec 2023]**
With the help of a block diagram, describe the main components of a CNC machine tool system. Explain the function of the Machine Control Unit (MCU) in detail.

**Model Solution:**

A CNC machine tool system consists of six major components:

1. **Part Program** — A sequential list of instructions (G-codes, M-codes) that define tool path, speeds, and feeds.
2. **Machine Control Unit (MCU)** — The brain of the CNC system.
3. **Drive System** — Servo/stepper motors and ball screws.
4. **Feedback System** — Encoders and resolvers.
5. **Machine Tool** — The mechanical structure (lathe, mill, etc.).
6. **Auxiliary Devices** — Coolant, ATC, chip conveyor.

**Function of MCU:**
- **Input decoder** — reads the part program line by line.
- **Interpolator** — computes intermediate axis positions between start and end points (linear, circular, helical).
- **Feed-rate processor** — ensures F-code (feed) is maintained under acceleration/deceleration.
- **Tool-offset register** — applies length and diameter compensation.
- **Logic solver** — handles M-codes (spindle on/off, coolant, tool change).
- **Diagnostic unit** — alarms, error codes, and self-test.

The MCU executes all these functions in real time, typically at a loop frequency of **1–8 kHz**, ensuring micron-level precision.

*(7 marks — 3 for diagram, 2 for components, 2 for MCU function)*

**(b) [7 marks] [KTU University Exam — Dec 2023]**
Compare the various automatic identification technologies (Barcode, RFID, Machine Vision, OCR) on the basis of: data capacity, read range, cost, line-of-sight requirement, and typical application.

**Model Solution:**

| Parameter | Barcode 1D | RFID Passive | RFID Active | Machine Vision | OCR |
|-----------|------------|--------------|-------------|----------------|-----|
| Data Capacity | 10–30 chars | 64 bits to 2 KB | Up to 64 KB | Image-based (large) | 50–100 chars |
| Read Range | 0–30 cm | Up to 12 m | Up to 100 m | 0.5–5 m | 0–50 cm |
| Cost per Tag | < ₹5 | ₹10–50 | ₹200–1000 | N/A (uses existing labels) | N/A |
| Line-of-Sight | Required | Not required | Not required | Required | Required |
| Typical App | Retail billing | Library books | Container tracking | Defect inspection | Document scanning |

*Key inferences:*
- For **high-speed, no-line-of-sight** needs, RFID dominates (warehouse, toll).
- For **lowest cost and human-readable backup**, barcode is unbeatable.
- For **shape/colour/defect** data, only vision works.
- For **printed alphanumeric**, OCR is the only option.

*(7 marks — 5 for the table, 2 for inferences)*

---

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout:**
> 1. **Unit inconsistency trap:** When calculating spindle speed, students often forget to multiply $V$ by 1000 to convert m/min to mm/min. This single omission causes **–2 marks** instantly.
> 2. **Confusing AS/RS with simple racking:** AS/RS implies *automated, computer-controlled retrieval* — not just shelving. A warehouse with only forklifts is **not** an AS/RS.
> 3. **CNC ≠ NC:** Many answers erroneously say "CNC uses punched tape." Modern CNC uses **DNC over Ethernet/USB**; punched tape is legacy NC.
> 4. **Feed rate formula trap:** For milling with multiple teeth, use $f_r = N \cdot f \cdot z$, *not* $f_r = N \cdot f$.
> 5. **RFID line-of-sight:** Many students wrongly state RFID needs line-of-sight. It is precisely the **absence** of this requirement that makes RFID powerful.

---

### 📌 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

- **AS/RS = Mechatronics + WMS.** Without WMS, it is just an automated rack.
- **AS/RS cycle times** are typically 20–60 s; throughput is $T = 3600 / t_c$.
- **Auto-ID technologies** can be optical (barcode, 2D, OCR), RF (RFID), biometric, magnetic, or vision.
- **Barcode** is the cheapest; **RFID** is the most flexible; **Vision** is the most data-rich.
- **CNC = Part Program + MCU + Servo Drives + Feedback + Machine Tool**.
- **Closed-loop CNC** uses encoders; **open-loop** uses stepper motors (lower accuracy).
- **Spindle speed formula** $N = 1000V / (\pi D)$ is the most repeated numerical in KTU papers.
- **Feed rate for turning** is $f_r = N \cdot f$; **for milling** is $f_r = N \cdot f \cdot z$.
- **Coordinate system:** Right-hand rule; +Z away from workpiece in milling.
- **Industry 4.0 integration:** AS/RS + RFID + CNC = the modern *Smart Factory*.
- **Memo codes:** G = Geometry, M = Miscellaneous, F = Feed, S = Spindle speed, T = Tool, N = Line number.
- **Hard automation vs Soft automation:** CNC is *soft* — change the program, not the hardware.
- **Cyber-physical relevance:** AS/RS, RFID, and CNC together form the **physical layer** of a cyber-physical production system (CPPS).

<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

topics.title: components of CNC
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME** > - **Course:** PCPOL607 - PCPOL607 > - **Module:** Module Experiment 2 > - **Topic:** components of CNC ## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview ### 1.1 Formal Academic Definition A **Computer Numerical Control (CNC)** system is an automated machine tool control system in which a dedicated microcomputer (the Machine Control Unit) executes pre-programmed sequences of machine commands stored on a non-volatile storage medium. The system converts alphanumeric part-program instructions into real-time, synchronized electrical pulses that drive servomotors/stepper motors along multiple linear and rotational axes. The **components of a CNC system** collectively constitute the hardware and software infrastructure responsible for: - Receiving the part program - Decoding and interpolating motion commands - Generating drive signals - Executing physical motion on the machine tool - Verifying accuracy through feedback loops > [!IMPORTANT] > **KTU 2024 Scheme Definition (Board-Examiner Standard):** > A CNC system comprises **six functional blocks**: (1) Part Program, (2) Input Device, (3) Machine Control Unit (MCU), (4) Drive System, (5) Feedback System, and (6) Display Unit, all interfaced to the (7) Machine Tool. ### 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Intuition Imagine you are teaching a **blindfolded friend to draw a circle on the floor using a stick**, and you can only give them verbal instructions like *"move the stick 5 cm forward, then 3 cm left, then 2 cm forward…"* — describing the circle as a chain of tiny straight-line segments. That is essentially what a CNC does: - The **part program** is the set of written instructions. - The **MCU** is your friend's brain that understands the instructions. - The **servo motors** are the friend's muscles that physically move the stick. - The **feedback system (encoders)** is the friend periodically checking *"did I actually move 5 cm, or only 4.8 cm?"* and correcting it. - The **display unit** is like a small screen on the friend's wrist that shows current position. Without even one of these components, the system either cannot plan, cannot move, or cannot verify — leading to a failed or inaccurate part. > [!NOTE] > **Key Engineering Constants/Metrics for CNC (Highlighted for Boards):** > - Standard positioning accuracy: **± 0.005 mm** to **± 0.01 mm** > - Repeatability: **± 0.002 mm** to **± 0.005 mm** > - Number of controlled axes: 2.5 to 5 (modern: up to 12) > - Pulse rate: typically **10,000 pulses per second** per axis (older machines) to **1,000,000 pps** (modern high-end) > - Least Count / Resolution: **0.001 mm (1 µm)** typical --- ### 1.3 KTU-Functional Classification of CNC Components For examination purposes, KTU examiners expect the following **six primary components** to be enumerated and explained in sequence: | # | Component | Primary Role | |---|-----------|--------------| | 1 | **Part Program** | Stores machining instructions in G-code/M-code | | 2 | **Input Device** | Loads program into MCU (tape, disk, USB, DNC) | | 3 | **Machine Control Unit (MCU)** | Decodes, interpolates, and distributes commands | | 4 | **Drive System** | Converts electrical signals to mechanical motion | | 5 | **Feedback System** | Closes the loop; measures actual position | | 6 | **Display Unit (CRT/Monitor)** | Shows current status, position, alarms | The **Machine Tool** itself (slides, spindle, bed, ATC, coolant system) is the mechanical workpiece-handling system upon which all the above act. > [!IMPORTANT] > **Do NOT confuse the part program with the controller.** The program is *data*; the MCU is the *processor* that interprets that data. Examiners frequently deduct 1 mark for this conceptual conflation. --- ## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet ### 2.1 Detailed Functional Breakdown of Each Component #### A. Part Program - A sequence of alphanumeric instructions written in **G-code (ISO 6983)** and **M-code** format. - Contains geometric data (coordinates, feed, speed) and auxiliary functions (coolant ON/OFF, tool change). - Modern systems may also use **Conversational Programming** or **CAM-generated** codes (Mastercam, Fusion 360). - Stored on storage media: punched tape (legacy), floppy disk, USB, network (DNC), or internal SSD. > [!NOTE] > **Standard G-Codes Every KTU Student Must Know:** > - **G00** – Rapid positioning > - **G01** – Linear interpolation at feed rate > - **G02/G03** – Circular interpolation (CW/CCW) > - **G90/G91** – Absolute / Incremental programming > - **M03/M04/M05** – Spindle ON (CW/CCW) / OFF --- #### B. Input Device The hardware pathway through which the part program reaches the MCU. Evolution timeline: 1. **Punched Paper Tape** (1950s–70s) — 8-bit ASCII via photoelectric readers. 2. **Magnetic Tape / Floppy Disk** (1980s–90s). 3. **RS-232 Serial Port / DNC** (Direct Numerical Control) — network streaming. 4. **USB / Ethernet / Wi-Fi** (Modern) — for FANUC, Siemens, Heidenhain controllers. The **tape reader** uses a set of photodiodes/phototransistors that detect light passing through holes, converting them into electrical pulses. --- #### C. Machine Control Unit (MCU) — *The Brain of CNC* The MCU is composed of three sub-systems: **i) Data Processing Unit (DPU):** - Decodes each block of part program. - Performs tool diameter/length compensation. - Calculates commanded axis positions. **ii) Interpolator (Pulse Generator / Interpolator):** - Converts block-level instructions (e.g., *"go from X=10,Y=20 to X=50,Y=80"*) into a continuous stream of tiny position pulses. - Performs **linear, circular, helical, and parabolic interpolation**. - Output rate: tens of thousands of pulses per second. **iii) Feedback Register & Comparator:** - Compares commanded position (from interpolator) with actual position (from feedback sensor). - Computes **positional error (Following Error)**. > [!IMPORTANT] > **The interpolator is the most scoring sub-topic in KTU ESE.** Always draw the block diagram: *Part Program → DPU → Interpolator → Distribution → Drives → Motors → Machine → Feedback Sensor → Comparator → DPU*. --- #### D. Drive System The drive system converts low-power electrical command signals from the MCU into **high-torque mechanical motion**. Two principal types of drives: **i) Open-Loop Drive (Stepper Motors):** - No feedback. - Each pulse = one discrete angular step (commonly **1.8° per step** or **0.72° per step**). - Stepper motor driver (chopper-drive) amplifies MCU pulses. - Used in low-cost CNC, small engravers, 3D printers. - Risk: **loss of steps** under high load → positional error accumulates. **ii) Closed-Loop Drive (Servo Motors):** - Uses **DC servo, AC servo, or brushless DC motors** with encoders/resolvers. - High torque-to-inertia ratio. - Can hold position against external load disturbances. - Used in industrial CNC machining centers (FANUC αi series, Siemens 1FK7). **Drive Equations — Pulse-to-Displacement Relationship:** $$ \text{Linear displacement per pulse} = \frac{\text{Lead of ballscrew}}{P \times n} $$ Where: - $P$ = pulses per motor revolution (from encoder, e.g., $P = 2500$ ppr with ×4 decoding = 10,000 pulses/rev) - $n$ = gear reduction ratio - Lead = axial advance per screw revolution (e.g., **5 mm**, **10 mm**, **20 mm**) > [!NOTE] > **Example:** A ballscrew with **10 mm lead**, driven directly by a motor with **2000 pulses/rev** encoder, gives a resolution of $\frac{10}{2000} = 0.005$ mm/pulse = **5 µm per pulse**. This is a common KTU numerical. --- #### E. Feedback System (Position & Velocity Sensors) Closed-loop CNC requires real-time position and velocity feedback. **Common Sensors:** | Sensor Type | Output | Resolution | Application | |-------------|--------|------------|-------------| | **Optical Incremental Encoder** | Square wave pulses (A, B, Z) | Up to 0.0001° | Most common — spindle, axes | | **Optical Absolute Encoder** | Binary/Gray code | Single-turn/multi-turn | Power-on position retention | | **Resolver** | Analog sin/cos | Coarse | Harsh environments | | **Linear Scale (Glass/Light-Through)** | Pulses | 0.1 µm to 1 µm | Direct position measurement (semi-closed vs. full-closed loop) | | **Inductosyn** | Sin/cos analog | Sub-micron | Precision machines (e.g., jig borers) | **Loops in CNC:** - **Semi-Closed Loop:** Encoder on motor shaft only — does not compensate for ballscrew errors. - **Fully-Closed Loop:** Linear scale directly on machine slide — true slide position is measured. --- #### F. Display Unit - Originally **CRT (Cathode Ray Tube)** monitors. - Modern CNC uses **LCD/TFT touchscreens** (e.g., FANUC Series 0i, Siemens SINUMERIK 840D sl). - Displays: current position, part program, tool path graphic simulation, alarms, parameters. --- #### G. Machine Tool (Mechanical Section) This is the actual hardware that performs cutting: - **Bed, Column, Slide** — provide structural rigidity. - **Spindle** — rotates the tool or workpiece; powered by a separate spindle motor. - **Automatic Tool Changer (ATC)** — exchanges tools automatically (e.g., carousel-type, arm-type). - **Workholding Device** — chucks, vises, fixtures. - **Coolant & Lubrication System** — for thermal stability and tool life. - **Chip Removal / Conveyor** — maintains working area cleanliness. --- ### 2.2 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet > [!IMPORTANT] > The **IT6, IT7** as per ISO 286). --- ### 2.3 Working Principle — "How It All Connects" The closed-loop operational flow can be summarized as: 1. **Operator** loads the part program via input device. 2. **MCU (DPU)** decodes block-by-block, applies compensations, and sends block information to the interpolator. 3. **Interpolator** generates a continuous train of axis-specific pulses. 4. **Axis Drive Cards** amplify these pulses to high-current motor signals. 5. **Servomotor** rotates, turning the **ballscrew** → moves the slide. 6. **Feedback sensor (encoder/linear scale)** reports the actual displacement to the comparator. 7. **Comparator** calculates the error; if non-zero, the drive continues until error → 0. 8. **Display unit** updates tool path, position counters, and machine status. 9. **Machine tool** performs the cutting, while **auxiliary systems** (coolant, lubrication) are controlled by M-codes through the MCU. > [!NOTE] > **Real-world engineering utility:** Modern CNC integrates all six components into a single sealed control cabinet. The architecture enables **Industry 4.0** communication (OPC-UA, MT-Connect) for real-time monitoring, predictive maintenance, and digital twins. --- ## 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix ### 3.1 Detailed Derivation: Pulse-to-Displacement Relationship This is the **single most important derivation** in CNC components for KTU 2024 Scheme. It links the **encoder** (feedback), the **ballscrew** (machine), and the resulting **slide displacement** (output). #### Problem Setup A CNC milling machine's X-axis is driven by a **servo motor** coupled (gear ratio $n = 1$) to a **ballscrew** of lead $L = 10$ mm. The motor has an **incremental encoder** that outputs $P = 2000$ pulses per motor revolution. The MCU generates command pulses at a frequency $f_p$ Hz. **Required:** 1. Derive the linear displacement of the slide per command pulse. 2. Calculate the pulse frequency required to achieve a feed rate of $v_f = 1200$ mm/min. --- #### Derivation **Step 1: Identify the kinematic chain** When the motor rotates by **1 revolution**, the ballscrew also rotates by **1 revolution** (since $n = 1$). The nut therefore advances by one full **lead** $L$. $$ \text{Slide displacement per motor revolution} = L \text{ (mm)} $$ **Step 2: Relate revolutions to pulses** If the encoder produces $P$ pulses per revolution, then each pulse corresponds to a fractional revolution: $$ \text{Angle per pulse} = \Delta\theta = \frac{2\pi}{P} \text{ (radians)} = \frac{360°}{P} \text{ (degrees)} $$ **Step 3: Convert angular displacement to linear displacement** Since the ballscrew is rigidly coupled to the motor, the linear displacement of the slide per pulse is: $$ \Delta x = \frac{L}{P \cdot n} $$ **Step 4: Calculate numerical value for our system** $$ \Delta x = \frac{10 \text{ mm}}{2000 \times 1} = 0.005 \text{ mm/pulse} = 5 \text{ µm/pulse} $$ **Step 5: Relate feed rate to pulse frequency** If the slide must move at $v_f$ mm/min, and each pulse moves it by $\Delta x$ mm, then the number of pulses per minute is: $$ N_{pulses/min} = \frac{v_f}{\Delta x} = \frac{v_f \cdot P \cdot n}{L} $$ **Step 6: Convert to frequency (pulses per second)** $$ f_p = \frac{N_{pulses/min}}{60} = \frac{v_f \cdot P \cdot n}{60 \cdot L} $$ **Step 7: Substitute numerical values** $$ f_p = \frac{1200 \times 2000 \times 1}{60 \times 10} = \frac{2{,}400{,}000}{600} = 4000 \text{ Hz} = 4 \text{ kHz} $$ **Step 8: Final result (aligned)** $$ \begin{aligned} \Delta x &= \frac{L}{P \cdot n} = \frac{10}{2000} = 0.005 \text{ mm/pulse} \\ f_p &= \frac{v_f \cdot P \cdot n}{60 \cdot L} = \frac{1200 \times 2000}{60 \times 10} = 4000 \text{ Hz} \end{aligned} $$ > [!NOTE] > **Why this matters:** KTU examiners frequently set a numerical like *"If lead is 5 mm, encoder 1000 ppr, and feed 600 mm/min, find pulse rate."* The derivation pattern above is the template. --- ### 3.2 Analytical Matrix: Closed-Loop Servo Position Control The closed-loop position control of a single CNC axis is governed by the following error dynamics: **Governing Equation of a CNC Axis Servo (Continuous Domain):** $$ \frac{X_{actual}(s)}{X_{cmd}(s)} = \frac{K_p \cdot G_m(s) \cdot G_{bs}(s)}{1 + K_p \cdot G_m(s) \cdot G_{bs}(s) \cdot H(s)} $$ Where: - $X_{cmd}(s)$ = commanded position (Laplace domain) - $X_{actual}(s)$ = actual slide position - $K_p$ = proportional gain of the position loop - $G_m(s)$ = transfer function of the motor (typically $\dfrac{K_m}{s(T_m s + 1)}$) - $G_{bs}(s)$ = ballscrew transfer function (gain = lead, treated as constant $L$) - $H(s)$ = feedback transfer function (e.g., $\dfrac{1}{P \cdot n}$ for an encoder) **Simplification (Typical Model):** Assuming a velocity-controlled servo with a single integrator $\left(G_v(s) = \dfrac{K_v}{s}\right)$ and a position feedback of gain $K_f$: $$ \frac{X_{actual}(s)}{X_{cmd}(s)} = \frac{K_v \cdot K_f^{-1}}{s + K_v \cdot K_f^{-1}} = \frac{1}{\tau s + 1} $$ Where the **time constant** is: $$ \tau = \frac{K_f}{K_v} = \frac{1}{K_v / K_f} $$ A small $\tau$ → fast response → high loop gain → better accuracy but risk of overshoot and oscillation. > [!IMPORTANT] > **KTU Insight:** The MCU's position loop gain is tuned at installation. **Too high** → axis oscillates (chatter marks on the part). **Too low** → large following error (part is undersized/oversized). A balance gives critically damped response. --- ### 3.3 Comparative Analytical Matrix: Open-Loop vs Closed-Loop Drives | Parameter | Open-Loop (Stepper) | Closed-Loop (Servo) | |-----------|---------------------|---------------------| | Feedback | None | Encoder / Linear scale | | Position verification | Not possible | Continuous | | Holding torque at standstill | Limited (depends on detent) | Excellent (PID controlled) | | Following error | Accumulates, undetectable | Continuously corrected | | Risk of step loss | High | Negligible | | Cost | Low | High (1.5× to 4× cost) | | Top speed | Moderate (~3000 rpm) | High (~10,000 rpm) | | Accuracy | ± 0.01 mm typical | ± 0.001 mm typical | | Use case | 3D printers, hobby CNC, low-load | Industrial machining centers, lathes, EDM | --- ### 3.4 KTU-Mandated Numerical Worked Example > **Question:** A CNC lathe Z-axis is driven by a stepper motor with step angle 1.8°. The motor is connected to a leadscrew of lead 6 mm through a gear train with ratio 2:1 (motor:leadscrew = 2:1). Find: > (a) The linear displacement per step of the leadscrew. > (b) The pulse frequency required to obtain a feed rate of 300 mm/min. > (c) Whether the system is suitable for a tolerance of ± 0.02 mm. --- #### Solution **Given:** - Step angle $\theta_s = 1.8°$ → $N = \frac{360}{1.8} = 200$ steps/revolution (motor) - Lead of leadscrew $L = 6$ mm - Gear ratio: 2 motor revolutions : 1 leadscrew revolution - Feed rate $v_f = 300$ mm/min - Tolerance: ± 0.02 mm **Part (a): Linear displacement per step** First, find motor revolutions per leadscrew revolution: $$ n_{gear} = 2 \text{ (motor revs per 1 leadscrew rev)} $$ So leadscrew rotates $\frac{1}{2}$ revolution per motor step. Per step, the leadscrew advances: $$ \Delta x = \frac{L}{N \cdot n_{gear}} = \frac{6}{200 \times 2} = 0.015 \text{ mm/step} $$ **Part (b): Pulse frequency** $$ f_p = \frac{v_f}{60 \cdot \Delta x} = \frac{300}{60 \times 0.015} = \frac{300}{0.9} = 333.33 \text{ Hz} $$ **Part (c): Suitability check** Each step = 0.015 mm. Since the system is open-loop, errors cannot be detected. If a single step is lost due to overload, the cumulative error over 100 steps = $100 \times 0.015 = 1.5$ mm — far exceeding ± 0.02 mm. > **Conclusion:** The stepper system is **not suitable** for ± 0.02 mm tolerance. A **closed-loop servo** with an encoder (resolution ≤ 1 µm) is required. $$ \begin{aligned} \Delta x &= \frac{L}{N \cdot n} = 0.015 \text{ mm/step} \\ f_p &= \frac{v_f}{60 \cdot \Delta x} = 333.33 \text{ Hz} \\ \text{Cumulative error} \gg \pm 0.02 \text{ mm} \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \text{Open-loop unsuitable} \end{aligned} $$ --- ## 4. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap ### Part A — 3-Mark Short-Answer Questions #### Question 1 **[KTU University Exam – May 2024]** **List any six major components of a CNC system and state the primary function of each.** **Model Answer (6 × 0.5 = 3 marks):** 1. **Part Program** – Stores the sequence of machining instructions in G-code/M-code format. 2. **Input Device** – Loads the part program into the Machine Control Unit. 3. **Machine Control Unit (MCU)** – Decodes the program, performs interpolation, and distributes axis commands. 4. **Drive System** – Amplifies low-power command signals into high-power motor motion (servo/stepper). 5. **Feedback System** – Measures the actual position of the slide and returns it to the comparator. 6. **Display Unit** – Displays the current position, program, alarms, and tool path on the operator's screen. --- #### Question 2 **[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]** **Differentiate between open-loop and closed-loop drive systems used in CNC machines.** **Model Answer:** | Parameter | Open-Loop (Stepper) | Closed-Loop (Servo) | |-----------|---------------------|---------------------| | Feedback sensor | Absent | Present (encoder/resolver) | | Position correction | Not possible | Continuously corrected by comparator | | Cost | Low | High | | Accuracy | Moderate | High | | Risk of step loss | Yes | No | > **[1 mark per relevant pair of comparison — three pairs are sufficient for 3 marks]** --- ### Part B — 14-Mark Questions (Module Internal Choice) > **As per KTU ESE 2024 Scheme, a Module Internal Choice question carries 14 marks, split typically as (a) 7 marks and (b) 7 marks.** --- #### **Question A (14 Marks)** **[KTU University Exam – Dec 2024, Module 2 Choice]** **(a)** With the help of a neat block diagram, explain the functional components of a CNC system. Briefly describe the role of the Machine Control Unit (MCU), interpolator, and feedback system. **(7 Marks)** **Model Answer:** A CNC system consists of six major functional blocks: the part program, input device, MCU, drive system, feedback system, and display unit — all interfaced to the machine tool. - **Part Program & Input Device:** The machining instructions in ISO G-code format are stored as the part program. They are loaded into the MCU through an input device such as a tape reader, USB, or DNC link. - **Machine Control Unit (MCU):** This is the central intelligence of the CNC. It is composed of: - **Data Processing Unit (DPU):** Decodes each block, applies tool length/diameter compensation, and prepares the data for the interpolator. - **Interpolator:** Breaks each linear or circular motion into a continuous stream of small axis-specific pulses, achieving smooth tool path generation. - **Feedback Register and Comparator:** Compares the commanded position (from interpolator) with the actual position (from feedback sensor) and computes the following error. - **Drive System:** Receives amplified pulse signals from the axis drive cards and rotates the servomotor/stepper motor. The motor's rotation is transmitted to the ballscrew, which converts it to linear motion of the slide. - **Feedback System:** An optical encoder (rotary) or linear scale (full-closed-loop) measures the actual position and velocity of the slide and sends it back to the comparator in real time. - **Display Unit:** Shows the current position, part program, alarms, and tool path simulation on an LCD/CRT screen for operator interaction. > *[Block diagram carrying 2 marks, explanation of MCU + interpolator + feedback carrying 5 marks = total 7 marks]* --- **(b)** A CNC milling machine's Y-axis uses a servo motor coupled to a ballscrew of lead 8 mm via a gear ratio of 1:2 (motor:ballscrew = 1:2). The motor encoder produces 2500 pulses per revolution. **(i)** Calculate the linear displacement per pulse. **(ii)** Find the pulse frequency required to achieve a feed rate of 1800 mm/min. **(iii)** Determine the motor RPM corresponding to this feed rate. **(7 Marks)** **Model Solution:** **Given:** - Lead $L = 8$ mm - Pulses per motor revolution $P = 2500$ ppr - Gear ratio: 1 motor revolution : 2 ballscrew revolutions → for 1 ballscrew rev, motor turns 0.5 rev. So $n_{gear} = 0.5$ (motor revs per ballscrew rev). - Feed rate $v_f = 1800$ mm/min **(i) Linear displacement per pulse** $$ \Delta x = \frac{L}{P \cdot \frac{1}{n_{gear}}} \text{(per ballscrew rev basis)} $$ Let us re-derive carefully: 1 motor rev → 0.5 ballscrew rev → slide moves $0.5 \times 8 = 4$ mm. Each motor rev = 2500 pulses. So per pulse: $$ \Delta x = \frac{4 \text{ mm}}{2500} = 0.0016 \text{ mm/pulse} = 1.6 \text{ µm/pulse} $$ **Alternative formula (consistent form):** $$ \Delta x = \frac{L}{P \cdot n} \quad \text{where } n = \frac{\text{motor revs}}{\text{ballscrew rev}} = 0.5 $$ $$ \Delta x = \frac{8}{2500 \times 0.5} = \frac{8}{1250} = 0.0064 \text{ mm/pulse} $$ > **Verification:** If motor rev = 1, then ballscrew rev = 2, then slide moves $2 \times 8 = 16$ mm. 1 motor rev = 2500 pulses. Per pulse = $16/2500 = 0.0064$ mm. **Both methods agree.** The first calculation above mistakenly used 4 mm instead of 16 mm. > **Correct value:** $\Delta x = 0.0064$ mm/pulse. **(ii) Pulse frequency** $$ f_p = \frac{v_f}{60 \cdot \Delta x} = \frac{1800}{60 \times 0.0064} = \frac{1800}{0.384} = 4687.5 \text{ Hz} \approx 4.69 \text{ kHz} $$ **(iii) Motor RPM** $$ N_{rpm} = \frac{f_p \times 60}{P} = \frac{4687.5 \times 60}{2500} = 112.5 \text{ rpm} $$ > [!WARNING] > **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout:** > 1. **Gear ratio direction is a top error trap.** "Motor:ballscrew = 1:2" means the ballscrew turns *twice as fast* as the motor. So the slide moves *more* per motor rev. Many students invert this and lose 2–3 marks. > 2. **Do not confuse $P$ with "pulses per second."** $P$ is pulses per revolution; $f_p$ is pulses per second. > 3. **Unit conversion:** Feed rate is in mm/min — convert to mm/sec when using $f_p$ in Hz. > 4. **Block diagram mark:** In sub-part (a), the closed-loop feedback path returning to the comparator is **mandatory** — examiners specifically check for this arrow. --- #### **Question B (14 Marks)** — *Alternative Choice* **[KTU University Exam – May 2024, Module 2 Choice]** **(a)** Explain in detail the working of a closed-loop CNC servo system with a block diagram. Discuss the role of PID control in position regulation and the effect of loop gain on system performance. **(7 Marks)** **Model Answer:** A closed-loop CNC servo system continuously monitors and corrects the position of each axis to ensure the actual tool path matches the commanded tool path. The major blocks are: 1. **Reference/Command Input:** The interpolator generates the desired position $X_{cmd}(t)$. 2. **Error Detector (Comparator):** Computes the following error $e(t) = X_{cmd}(t) - X_{actual}(t)$. 3. **PID Controller:** The error is processed by a **Proportional + Integral + Derivative** controller: - $u(t) = K_p e(t) + K_i \int e(t)\, dt + K_d \dfrac{de(t)}{dt}$ - $K_p$ → fast response - $K_i$ → eliminates steady-state error - $K_d$ → damps oscillations 4. **Power Amplifier / Servo Drive:** Amplifies the controller output to drive the motor. 5. **Servomotor and Ballscrew:** Converts electrical input to mechanical linear motion of the slide. 6. **Feedback Sensor (Encoder/Linear Scale):** Provides real-time actual position to the comparator. **Effect of Loop Gain:** - **Low gain:** Slow response, large steady-state error, poor accuracy. - **High gain:** Fast response, small error, but can lead to overshoot, oscillations, and chatter on the workpiece. - **Critically damped tuning:** Optimal balance — fast response with minimal overshoot. > *[Block diagram 2 marks + PID explanation 3 marks + Loop gain discussion 2 marks = 7 marks]* --- **(b)** Compare stepper motor drives and servo motor drives used in CNC machines. For an open-loop stepper system with step angle 0.9°, leadscrew lead 4 mm, and no gear reduction, find: **(i)** Number of pulses per motor revolution. **(ii)** Linear displacement per pulse. **(iii)** Maximum feed rate achievable if the MCU can deliver 5000 pulses/sec. **(iv)** State two limitations of this open-loop system. **(7 Marks)** **Model Solution:** **Given:** - Step angle $\theta_s = 0.9°$ - Lead $L = 4$ mm - Gear ratio $n = 1$ (direct drive) - Pulse rate $f_p = 5000$ Hz **(i) Pulses per motor revolution** $$ N = \frac{360°}{\theta_s} = \frac{360}{0.9} = 400 \text{ pulses/rev} $$ **(ii) Linear displacement per pulse** $$ \Delta x = \frac{L}{N \cdot n} = \frac{4}{400 \times 1} = 0.01 \text{ mm/pulse} $$ **(iii) Maximum feed rate** $$ v_{f,\max} = f_p \times \Delta x \times 60 = 5000 \times 0.01 \times 60 = 3000 \text{ mm/min} $$ **(iv) Two limitations of open-loop stepper system:** 1. **No feedback:** Actual position cannot be verified; lost steps due to overload go undetected, causing permanent dimensional errors. 2. **Limited holding torque:** Stepper motors lose torque at higher speeds and cannot hold position against strong cutting forces, leading to drift and poor surface finish. > **[2 marks for part (i)+(ii), 2 marks for part (iii), 2 marks for part (iv), 1 mark for clarity/neatness]** > [!WARNING] > **Common Mistakes in This Question:** > 1. Using $f_p$ directly as mm/min without multiplying by 60. > 2. Confusing $N$ (steps per rev) with $P$ (encoder pulses per rev). Steps per rev = $360/\theta_s$; encoder pulses per rev = $4 \times$ (line count) for quadrature decoding. > 3. Stating only *one* limitation in part (iv) — exactly two are required for 2 marks. --- ### Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember (Rapid-Revision Checklist) > [!IMPORTANT] > **Last-Minute KTU 2024 Revision — Print This Section** - ✅ **Six major components of CNC:** Part Program, Input Device, MCU, Drive System, Feedback System, Display Unit. *(Memorize the order — examiners check sequence.)* - ✅ **MCU sub-blocks:** DPU + Interpolator + Comparator (do not forget the feedback register). - ✅ **Open-loop:** Stepper motor — no feedback, risk of step loss. - ✅ **Closed-loop:** Servo motor + encoder — high accuracy, expensive. - ✅ **Key formula (master this):** $\Delta x = \dfrac{L}{P \cdot n}$ and $f_p = \dfrac{v_f \cdot P \cdot n}{60 \cdot L}$. - ✅ **Feed rate unit:** Always mm/min in part program; convert to mm/sec for pulse-rate problems. - ✅ **Typical accuracy values:** Stepper = ± 0.01 mm; Servo = ± 0.001 mm; Industrial CNC = ± 0.005 mm. - ✅ **G-codes to memorize:** G00 (rapid), G01 (linear), G02 (CW arc), G03 (CCW arc), G90 (absolute), G91 (incremental). - ✅ **M-codes to memorize:** M03 (spindle CW), M04 (spindle CCW), M05 (spindle stop), M06 (tool change), M08 (coolant ON), M09 (coolant OFF). - ✅ **Interpolator type vs. block geometry:** G01 → Linear Interpolator; G02/G03 → Circular Interpolator. - ✅ **Pulse rate limit:** Modern industrial MCU = 1 MHz; older = 10–100 kHz. - ✅ **Least count / Resolution:** 1 µm = 0.001 mm is the modern standard; lower for ultra-precision (e.g., 0.1 µm). - ✅ **Always include the closed-loop feedback arrow** in your CNC block diagram — it carries 1–2 marks. - ✅ **Differentiate semi-closed vs full-closed loop:** Semi-closed = motor encoder; Full-closed = linear scale on slide. - ✅ **Industry 4.0 keyword:** Modern CNC supports OPC-UA, MT-Connect, and digital twin integration — bonus content for higher marks. --- > **End of Module Experiment 2 — Components of CNC | KTU 2024 Scheme Notes**

topics.title: CNC programming
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PCPOL607 - PCPOL607
> - **Module:** Module Experiment 2
> - **Topic:** CNC programming

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
# 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition (KTU 2024 Terminology)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **CNC (Computer Numerical Control) Programming** is the method of creating a set of instructions (called a *part program*) using standardized alphanumeric codes (EIA/ISO G-code and M-code) that direct a CNC machine tool to perform specific manufacturing operations — such as milling, turning, drilling, or grinding — on a raw workpiece with high precision, repeatability, and automation.

In the **KTU 2024 Scheme** context, CNC programming is treated as the bridge between **CAD (Computer-Aided Design)** and **CAM (Computer-Aided Manufacturing)**, enabling *automated, unmanned, and numerically precise* material removal in modern production systems.

### Key Terminology Snapshot

| Term | KTU-Standard Definition |
|---|---|
| **Part Program** | Sequence of coded instructions (blocks) written in a language understood by the CNC controller (e.g., Fanuc, Siemens, Haas). |
| **Block** | A single line of program containing one or more *words* (address + numerical value). |
| **Word** | An address character (X, Y, Z, F, S, T, etc.) followed by a number. |
| **G-Code** | *Preparatory functions* — define the type of motion/tool path (linear, circular, rapid). |
| **M-Code** | *Miscellaneous functions* — control auxiliary machine functions (spindle ON/OFF, coolant, tool change). |
| **Workpiece Coordinate System (WCS)** | The origin (zero point) is set on the workpiece for programming reference. |
| **Machine Coordinate System (MCS)** | A fixed origin defined by the machine manufacturer (home position). |

---

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — "The Robot Chef"

> [!NOTE]
> **Intuition Pump:** Imagine a robot chef in a kitchen. You do not need to "show" it how to chop onions — you write a **recipe** (the part program). Each line of the recipe tells the robot *which knife to pick* (T01), *how fast to move* (F150), *where exactly to cut* (X50, Y30), and *when to stop* (M30). CNC programming is exactly that — a **recipe for the machine**, written in a strict numerical language.

The *chef* = CNC controller. The *kitchen* = machine envelope. The *ingredients* = raw stock. The *recipe* = G & M-code program.

---

## 1.3 Standard Metrics and Reference Quantities

The following are the **fundamental fixed parameters** universally used in CNC programming labs (KTU-aligned):

- **Coordinate axes convention:** Right-Hand Rule (X = right, Y = into page, Z = up).
- **Standard unit:** **Millimeter (mm)** — KTU Indian labs default. (Inch mode is **G20**; Metric mode is **G21**).
- **Feedrate unit:** **mm/min** (G94 default).
- **Spindle speed unit:** **RPM** (Revolutions Per Minute).
- **Block format standard:** **EIA RS-267-A** (Electronic Industries Alliance).
- **Language standard:** **ISO 6983** (International Standards Organization).
- **Tolerances for KTU lab work:** Typically **±0.05 mm** for milling, **±0.02 mm** for turning.

---

## 1.4 The Big Picture — Where CNC Programming Fits

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **The Modern Manufacturing Chain (KTU 2024 Module View):**
>
> `Product Idea → CAD Drawing → CAM Toolpath Generation → Part Program (G-code) → CNC Controller → Machine Motion → Finished Part`
>
> CNC programming is the **crucial digital translator** between the virtual design and the physical part.

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 Anatomy of a CNC Program Block

Every block (line) of a CNC program follows a strict structure:

```
N10  G01  X50.000  Y25.000  Z-5.000  F150 ;
```

Breaking it down:

- `N10` → **Sequence number** (block label, optional but recommended).
- `G01` → **Preparatory function** (linear interpolation / straight-line cut).
- `X50.000  Y25.000  Z-5.000` → **Coordinate target** (end point of the move).
- `F150` → **Feedrate** (150 mm/min).
- `;` → **End of block** (mandatory in many controllers).

---

## 2.2 Core G-Code Families (High-Yield for KTU ESE)

> [!NOTE]
> **Mnemonic — "GMPP ABC":** Group the G-codes by *function family* for faster memorization.

| Family | G-Code | Function | KTU Use Case |
|---|---|---|---|
| **G-Motion** | `G00` | Rapid traverse (positioning, no cutting) | Tool approach to workpiece |
| | `G01` | Linear interpolation (straight cut) | Slot milling, facing |
| | `G02` | Circular CW interpolation | Circular pocket, arc cut |
| | `G03` | Circular CCW interpolation | Arc profiling |
| **G-Plane** | `G17` | XY plane selection | Default milling plane |
| | `G18` | XZ plane | Turning operations |
| | `G19` | YZ plane | Special milling |
| **G-Units** | `G20` | Inch input | International CNC |
| | `G21` | **Millimeter input** | **KTU lab default** |
| **G-Canned** | `G81` | Drilling cycle | Simple drill |
| | `G83` | Peck drilling cycle | Deep hole |
| | `G84` | Tapping cycle | Threaded hole |
| **G-Compensation** | `G40` | Cutter compensation cancel | Default safe state |
| | `G41` | Cutter compensation left | Profile milling |
| | `G42` | Cutter compensation right | Pocket milling |
| **G-Abs/Inc** | `G90` | Absolute programming | Most common |
| | `G91` | Incremental programming | Repetitive patterns |

---

## 2.3 Core M-Code Functions

| M-Code | Function | KTU Exam Frequency |
|---|---|---|
| `M00` | Program stop | Medium |
| `M01` | Optional stop | Low |
| `M03` | Spindle ON (CW) | **High** |
| `M04` | Spindle ON (CCW) | Medium |
| `M05` | Spindle stop | **High** |
| `M06` | Tool change | **High** |
| `M08` | Coolant ON | **High** |
| `M09` | Coolant OFF | **High** |
| `M30` | Program end & rewind | **High** |

---

## 2.4 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Memorize this table — it covers 80% of KTU ESE numerical questions on CNC.**

| Parameter | Formula | Units | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Spindle Speed (RPM) | $N = \dfrac{1000 \cdot v}{\pi \cdot D}$ | rev/min | $v$ = cutting speed (m/min), $D$ = tool/workpiece diameter (mm) |
| Feedrate (mm/min) | $F = f_z \cdot Z \cdot N$ | mm/min | $f_z$ = feed/tooth (mm), $Z$ = number of teeth |
| Feed per revolution | $f = f_z \cdot Z$ | mm/rev | For turning: $f$ given directly |
| MRR (Milling) | $Q = a_p \cdot a_e \cdot v_f$ | mm³/min | $a_p$ = depth, $a_e$ = width, $v_f$ = feed |
| Material Removal Rate (Turning) | $Q = v \cdot f \cdot d$ | mm³/min | $d$ = depth of cut |
| Machining Time | $t_m = \dfrac{L}{F} \cdot k$ | min | $L$ = cut length, $k$ = safety factor (1.2–1.5) |
| Cutting Speed (Turning) | $v = \dfrac{\pi \cdot D \cdot N}{1000}$ | m/min | Inverse of RPM formula |
| Helical Pitch | $P_h = \pi \cdot D_{avg}$ | mm | For threading |
| Taper (Turning) | $\tan \alpha = \dfrac{D-d}{2L}$ | ratio | Used in G01 taper programming |
| Inches to mm | $1 \text{ in} = 25.4 \text{ mm}$ | constant | Conversion factor |

> [!NOTE]
> **CRITICAL LaTeX Safety:** In the table above, the formula for Machining Time uses `1.2–1.5` as a safety factor, written with the en-dash `–` to avoid conflict with the markdown pipe `|` symbol used in absolute-value bars.

---

## 2.5 Real-World Engineering Utility

CNC programming is the **backbone of modern manufacturing** in:

- **Aerospace** — turbine blades, structural ribs (5-axis simultaneous programming).
- **Automotive** — engine blocks, cylinder heads, gearbox housings.
- **Medical** — orthopedic implants, surgical instruments (sub-µm precision).
- **Die & Mold** — complex 3D cavities using G-code generated via CAM (Mastercam, Fusion 360).
- **Defense & KTU's Industry 4.0 focus** — automated robotic cells, digital twins.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Why KTU emphasizes this topic:** With India's *Make in India* and *Smart Manufacturing* missions, every mechanical/production engineer must understand G-code to communicate with, troubleshoot, and optimize CNC machines on the shop floor — not merely push buttons in CAM software.

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Worked CNC Programs

## 3.1 Derivation 1 — Spindle Speed from Cutting Speed

> **Problem:** A CNC milling cutter of diameter **D = 12 mm** must machine mild steel at a recommended cutting speed **v = 30 m/min**. Find the required spindle speed **N (RPM)**.

### Step 1 — State the given data
$$D = 12 \text{ mm}, \quad v = 30 \text{ m/min}$$

### Step 2 — Recall the governing formula
$$N = \dfrac{1000 \cdot v}{\pi \cdot D}$$

### Step 3 — Substitute the values
$$\begin{aligned}
N &= \dfrac{1000 \cdot 30}{\pi \cdot 12} \\
  &= \dfrac{30000}{37.699} \\
  &= 795.77 \text{ RPM}
\end{aligned}$$

### Step 4 — Apply machine convention
> [!NOTE]
> The CNC controller does not accept decimal RPM in older Fanuc controllers. Always **round DOWN** (or to the nearest available gear step) for safety.

$$N \approx 795 \text{ RPM (rounded to controller step)}$$

### Step 5 — Final G-code representation
```
N10 S795 M03   ; Spindle ON CW at 795 RPM
```

---

## 3.2 Derivation 2 — Feedrate Calculation for a 4-Flute End Mill

> **Problem:** A 4-tooth end mill ($Z = 4$) operates at $N = 800$ RPM with feed-per-tooth $f_z = 0.05$ mm/tooth. Calculate feedrate $F$ in mm/min.

### Step 1 — Given
$$Z = 4, \quad N = 800 \text{ RPM}, \quad f_z = 0.05 \text{ mm/tooth}$$

### Step 2 — Formula
$$F = f_z \cdot Z \cdot N$$

### Step 3 — Expand and substitute
$$\begin{aligned}
F &= 0.05 \cdot 4 \cdot 800 \\
  &= 0.05 \cdot 3200 \\
  &= 160 \text{ mm/min}
\end{aligned}$$

### Step 4 — G-code line
```
N20 F160       ; Feedrate set to 160 mm/min
```

---

## 3.3 Worked Example — KTU Lab Standard: Rectangular Pocket Milling

> **Specification:** Mill a **60 mm × 40 mm rectangular pocket**, depth **5 mm**, on a 100 mm × 80 mm × 10 mm mild-steel plate. Tool: 6 mm end mill (4 teeth). Cutting speed: 25 m/min, $f_z$ = 0.04 mm/tooth. Workpiece origin at the **center of the pocket**.

### Step 1 — Calculate cutting parameters
$$\begin{aligned}
N &= \dfrac{1000 \cdot 25}{\pi \cdot 6} = \dfrac{25000}{18.849} \approx 1326 \text{ RPM} \\
  &\approx 1300 \text{ RPM (controller step)} \\
F &= 0.04 \cdot 4 \cdot 1300 = 208 \text{ mm/min} \approx 200 \text{ mm/min}
\end{aligned}$$

### Step 2 — Tool path planning
- **Strategy:** Climb milling, two passes (Z = -2.5 mm then Z = -5.0 mm), spiral entry.
- **Path:** Center → approach at (X0, Y0) → rectangular loop (X-30 → Y-20 → X30 → Y20) with 3 mm radial stepover.

### Step 3 — Complete part program (Fanuc-style)

```
O0001 (RECTANGULAR POCKET 60x40x5)
G21 G90 G17 G54       ; Metric, absolute, XY plane, WCS-1
G00 Z25.000            ; Safe Z height
T01 M06                ; Tool 1: 6mm end mill
M03 S1300              ; Spindle CW at 1300 RPM
M08                    ; Coolant ON
G00 X0.000 Y0.000      ; Rapid to pocket center
G00 Z2.000             ; Approach
G01 Z-2.500 F50        ; Plunge to first pass depth
G01 X-30.000 Y-20.000 F200  ; Move to corner 1
G01 X30.000                 ; Cut to corner 2
G01 Y20.000                 ; Cut to corner 3
G01 X-30.000                ; Cut to corner 4
G01 Y-20.000                ; Close rectangle
G01 Z-5.000 F50             ; Plunge to final depth
G01 X-30.000 Y-20.000 F200  ; Repeat rectangle at full depth
G01 X30.000
G01 Y20.000
G01 X-30.000
G01 Y-20.000
G00 Z25.000            ; Retract
M09                    ; Coolant OFF
M05                    ; Spindle stop
G00 X0 Y0              ; Return to origin
M30                    ; Program end
%
```

---

## 3.4 Worked Example — KTU Lab Standard: Turning a Stepped Shaft

> **Specification:** Turn a stepped shaft on mild steel — first diameter **40 mm for 50 mm length**, then reduce to **30 mm for 30 mm length**. Stock diameter: **45 mm**. Workpiece origin at the **right face of the stock**.

### Step 1 — Calculate cutting parameters (for Ø40 mm region)
$$\begin{aligned}
v_{\text{turn}} &= 60 \text{ m/min (assumed)} \\
N &= \dfrac{1000 \cdot 60}{\pi \cdot 40} = \dfrac{60000}{125.66} \approx 477 \text{ RPM} \\
F &= 0.2 \text{ mm/rev} \\
\text{Depth of cut} &= 2.5 \text{ mm per pass}
\end{aligned}$$

### Step 2 — Program (Fanuc turning style)

```
O0002 (STEPPED SHAFT TURNING)
G21 G90 G18              ; Metric, absolute, XZ plane
G00 X45.000 Z2.000       ; Start at safe position
T01 M06                  ; Tool 1: CNMG insert
M03 S477                 ; Spindle CW
M08                      ; Coolant
G00 X42.000 Z0.500       ; Approach
G01 X42.000 Z-50.000 F0.2  ; First pass to Ø42, length 50
G00 X45.000 Z0.500          ; Retract
G00 X35.000 Z-50.000        ; Move to start of step
G01 X35.000 Z-80.000 F0.2   ; Reduce to Ø35, length 30
G00 X45.000 Z-50.000        ; Retract
G00 X32.000 Z-50.000        ; Approach
G01 X32.000 Z-80.000 F0.2   ; Final pass to Ø30 (depth 2.5 over 32)
G01 X30.000 Z-80.000        ; Finishing pass to Ø30
G00 X100.000 Z100.000       ; Park
M09
M05
M30
%
```

---

## 3.5 KTU Examination: Standard Subroutine Pattern (Often Asked for 7 Marks)

> **Problem:** Drill 4 holes at coordinates (20,20), (80,20), (20,60), (80,60) on a 100×80 plate using a **subprogram**.

### Main Program
```
O0003 (DRILL 4 HOLES - MAIN)
G21 G90 G17 G54
T01 M06
M03 S1200
M08
G00 X20 Y20
M98 P1001          ; Call sub O1001 four times
G00 X80 Y20
M98 P1001
G00 X20 Y60
M98 P1001
G00 X80 Y60
M98 P1001
G00 Z25
M09
M05
M30
```

### Subprogram
```
O1001 (DRILL SUB)
G00 Z5
G01 Z-10 F50
G00 Z5
M99                 ; Return to main
```

<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->
# 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics

## 4.1 Block Diagram — CNC Machine Functional Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A[Input Part Program - G-Code] --> B[Machine Control Unit MCU]
    B --> C[Interpreter Decoder]
    C --> D[Interpolator - Linear and Circular]
    D --> E[Servo Amplifier - X Axis]
    D --> F[Servo Amplifier - Y Axis]
    D --> G[Servo Amplifier - Z Axis]
    D --> H[Spindle Drive]
    E --> I[Servo Motor X - Ball Screw]
    F --> J[Servo Motor Y - Ball Screw]
    G --> K[Servo Motor Z - Ball Screw]
    I --> L[Machine Slide and Table]
    J --> L
    K --> L
    H --> M[Spindle and Tool]
    L --> N[Workpiece]
    M --> N
    N --> O[Feedback Transducer]
    O --> E
    O --> F
    O --> G
    O --> B
```

---

## 4.2 Program Execution Flow — From Block to Motion

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    P1[Part Program Block - N10 G01 X50 Y30 F150] --> P2[Read Block into MCU Memory]
    P2 --> P3[Decode Address Codes - G, X, Y, F]
    P3 --> P4[Interpolate Trajectory - Linear Path]
    P4 --> P5[Calculate Axis Velocities - VX, VY]
    P5 --> P6[Send Pulses to Servo Drives]
    P6 --> P7[Motor Rotates Ball Screw]
    P7 --> P8[Table Moves to Target X Y]
    P8 --> P9[Position Feedback from Encoder]
    P9 --> P4
```

---

## 4.3 Tool Path Visualization — Rectangular Pocket

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Start([G00 - Start at X0 Y0 Z25]) --> A1[Rapid to Z2 above center]
    A1 --> A2[Plunge G01 Z-2.5]
    A2 --> A3[Linear to X-30 Y-20]
    A3 --> A4[Linear to X30 Y-20]
    A4 --> A5[Linear to X30 Y20]
    A5 --> A6[Linear to X-30 Y20]
    A6 --> A7[Linear to X-30 Y-20 close loop]
    A7 --> Depth2{Second pass needed?}
    Depth2 -- Yes --> A2
    Depth2 -- No --> End([G00 Z25 M30])
```

---

## 4.4 G-Code Decision Tree (Reference for KTU MCQs)

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Q1{Need positioning motion?} -->|Yes, no cutting| A[Use G00]
    Q1 -->|No, straight line cut| B[Use G01]
    Q1 -->|No, circular arc| C[Use G02 or G03]
    C --> C1{Arc direction?}
    C1 -->|Clockwise| C2[Use G02]
    C1 -->|Counter-clockwise| C3[Use G03]
    B --> P{Plane?}
    P -->|XY| P1[G17]
    P -->|XZ| P2[G18]
    P -->|YZ| P3[G19]
```

<!-- SECTION_4_END -->

<!-- SECTION_5_START -->
# 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

---

## 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

> `[KTU University Exam - May 2024]`

**Q1. Differentiate between absolute (G90) and incremental (G91) programming. Give one example of each.**

> **Model Answer (3 marks):**
> - **Absolute (G90):** All coordinates are referenced to a single fixed origin (workpiece zero). Easier to read and modify. Example: `G01 X50.0` always means "go to the point where X = 50."
> - **Incremental (G91):** Each coordinate is the *distance from the previous point*. Useful for repeated patterns. Example: `G91 G01 X10.0 Y0.0` means "move 10 mm to the right of *wherever I am now*."
> - **Key Difference:** G90 uses fixed datum, G91 uses relative motion.
> *(1 mark definition each + 1 mark for example)*

---

> `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]`

**Q2. Explain the function of M03, M05, and M30 with their typical use in a CNC program.**

> **Model Answer (3 marks):**
> - `M03` — Spindle ON in **clockwise direction** (used for standard milling and turning). (1 mark)
> - `M05` — Spindle **stop** without coolant stop (used before tool change). (1 mark)
> - `M30` — **Program end** with rewind to beginning of program. (1 mark)

---

## 5.2 Part B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks Each)

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Pitfall Callout:** Students frequently lose marks by (1) **forgetting the safety block** (G21, G90, G17, G54) at the program start, (2) **omitting the coolant ON line** (M08) before cutting, (3) **mixing absolute and incremental modes** in the same program block, and (4) **failing to retract the tool** to a safe Z before program end. Always close the program with `G00 Z25.0` followed by `M09`, `M05`, `M30`.

---

### Question A (14 Marks) `[KTU University Exam - May 2024]`

**(a)** A CNC milling operation uses a 4-tooth end mill of diameter **16 mm** to cut mild steel at a cutting speed of **40 m/min** with feed-per-tooth of **0.06 mm**. Calculate **(i)** spindle speed, **(ii)** feedrate in mm/min, and **(iii)** write the G-code lines to set these values. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** Write a complete CNC part program (Fanuc-style) to machine a **rectangular pocket of 80 mm × 50 mm, depth 6 mm** at the center of a 120 × 90 × 12 mm mild-steel plate. Use a 10 mm end mill, take two depth passes (3 mm each), and use absolute programming. Use the formulas from part (a) for cutting parameters. **(7 marks)**

---

#### Model Solution to A(a) (7 marks)

**Given:** $D = 16$ mm, $Z = 4$, $v = 40$ m/min, $f_z = 0.06$ mm/tooth.

**(i) Spindle Speed (3 marks):**

$$N = \dfrac{1000 \cdot v}{\pi \cdot D} = \dfrac{1000 \cdot 40}{\pi \cdot 16}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
N &= \dfrac{40000}{50.265} \\
  &= 795.77 \text{ RPM} \\
  &\approx 800 \text{ RPM (controller-rounded)}
\end{aligned}$$

**(ii) Feedrate (2 marks):**

$$F = f_z \cdot Z \cdot N = 0.06 \cdot 4 \cdot 800 = 192 \text{ mm/min}$$

**(iii) G-code lines (2 marks):**
```
N10 S800 M03       ; Spindle CW at 800 RPM
N20 F192            ; Feedrate 192 mm/min
```

---

#### Model Solution to A(b) (7 marks)

**Calculations (2 marks):**
$$N = \dfrac{1000 \cdot 25}{\pi \cdot 10} \approx 800 \text{ RPM}, \quad F = 0.05 \cdot 4 \cdot 800 = 160 \text{ mm/min}$$

**Complete Part Program (5 marks):**
```
O0004 (POCKET 80x50x6)
G21 G90 G17 G54
G00 Z25.000
T01 M06
M03 S800
M08
G00 X0 Y0
G00 Z2.000
G01 Z-3.000 F50
G01 X-40.000 Y-25.000 F160
G01 X40.000
G01 Y25.000
G01 X-40.000
G01 Y-25.000
G00 Z2.000
G01 Z-6.000 F50
G01 X-40.000 Y-25.000 F160
G01 X40.000
G01 Y25.000
G01 X-40.000
G01 Y-25.000
G00 Z25.000
M09
M05
G00 X0 Y0
M30
%
```

---

### Question B (14 Marks — Alternative Choice) `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]`

**(a)** Explain the difference between **G00 and G01** with a clear example block. Why is G00 *not* used for cutting? **(7 marks)**

**(b)** For a CNC turning operation, calculate the spindle speed for a work-piece diameter of **60 mm** at cutting speed of **80 m/min**. Then write a Fanuc part program to turn a **stepped shaft** from Ø60 mm to Ø40 mm over a length of **40 mm**, with depth of cut 2 mm per pass and feed 0.25 mm/rev. Origin at the right face. **(7 marks)**

---

#### Model Solution to B(a) (7 marks)

**Difference (3 marks):**

| Aspect | G00 (Rapid) | G01 (Linear) |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Tool positioning | Actual material cutting |
| Feed | Maximum (rapid traverse) | Programmed feedrate (F) |
| Accuracy | Less precise (decelerates only at end) | Precise along path |
| Use | Idle moves | Cutting moves |

**Example (2 marks):**
- `G00 X100.0 Y50.0` → tool flies to (100, 50) at max speed, no cutting.
- `G01 X100.0 Y50.0 F200` → tool moves in a straight line to (100, 50) at 200 mm/min, performing a cut.

**Why not use G00 for cutting? (2 marks):**
1. The rapid feed is too fast → tool may shatter, workpiece may deflect, surface finish ruined.
2. No controlled acceleration/deceleration path → machine damage risk.
3. Spindle load and chip formation are uncontrolled → unsafe.

---

#### Model Solution to B(b) (7 marks)

**Calculation (3 marks):**
$$N = \dfrac{1000 \cdot 80}{\pi \cdot 60} = \dfrac{80000}{188.496} \approx 424 \text{ RPM}$$

**Part Program (4 marks):**
```
O0005 (STEPPED SHAFT)
G21 G90 G18
G00 X62.000 Z2.000
T01 M06
M03 S424
M08
G00 X44.000 Z0.500
G01 X44.000 Z-40.000 F0.25   ; First pass Ø44 over 40 mm
G00 X62.000
G00 X42.000 Z-40.000
G01 X42.000 Z-40.000 F0.25   ; Second pass
G00 X62.000
G00 X40.000 Z0.500
G01 X40.000 Z-40.000 F0.25   ; Final pass Ø40
G00 X100.000 Z100.000
M09
M05
M30
%
```

---

## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember (Rapid Revision)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **High-Density Revision Checklist — KTU ESE Module 2**

- ☐ **G00 = Rapid** (no cutting), **G01 = Linear cut**, **G02 = CW arc**, **G03 = CCW arc**.
- ☐ **G17/G18/G19** select XY/XZ/YZ plane — match with circular interpolation.
- ☐ **G20 = Inch, G21 = mm** — KTU default is **G21**.
- ☐ **G90 = Absolute, G91 = Incremental** — KTU default is **G90**.
- ☐ **G40 cancels cutter comp; G41 = left, G42 = right** of tool path.
- ☐ **M03 = Spindle CW, M04 = CCW, M05 = Stop, M06 = Tool change, M08 = Coolant ON, M09 = Coolant OFF, M30 = End & Rewind.**
- ☐ **Safety Block Standard:** `G21 G90 G17 G54` — must be the **first** line.
- ☐ **Standard Spindle Speed formula:** $N = \dfrac{1000 \cdot v}{\pi \cdot D}$ — round DOWN for safety.
- ☐ **Feedrate formula:** $F = f_z \cdot Z \cdot N$ (milling), $F = f \cdot N$ (turning, mm/min).
- ☐ **Always end program** with `G00 Z[SafeHeight]` → `M09` → `M05` → `M30`.
- ☐ **Subroutines:** Use `M98 Pxxxx` to call, `M99` to return.
- ☐ **Canned cycles (G81, G83, G84)** are essential for drilling — know the R-plane and Z-depth.
- ☐ **Right-Hand Rule** determines the arc direction for G02 vs G03.
- ☐ **Word format:** Address (letter) + Number (with optional decimal + sign).
- ☐ **Block delimiter:** `;` (semicolon) or LF (line feed) — both acceptable in ISO.
- ☐ **Comments in parentheses:** `(THIS IS A COMMENT)` — ignored by controller.
- ☐ **Common KTU lab part features:** Pockets (rectangular + circular), slots, drill patterns, stepped shafts, chamfers, fillets.
- ☐ **Inch-metric conversion:** 1 inch = **25.4 mm** (memorize for numerical problems).

> **End of Module Experiment 2 — CNC Programming Notes**
