<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
# 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition

**Manual Part Programming** is the process of writing a CNC (Computer Numerical Control) part program by hand, character by character, using standardized preparatory codes (G-codes), miscellaneous codes (M-codes), and coordinate data, without the assistance of any Computer-Aided Manufacturing (CAM) software or conversational programming interface. The programmer manually calculates every tool path coordinate, selects every cutting parameter, and sequences every machine function on paper or text editor, following the ISO 6983 (or DIN 66025) standard programming format.

In the KTU 2024 Scheme lab context (PCPOL607), manual part programming refers specifically to the manual preparation of a turning/milling part program on a **CNC Lathe (2-axis: X and Z)** or **CNC Milling machine (3-axis: X, Y, Z)**, where the student is expected to:

1. Read the engineering drawing of the workpiece.
2. Plan the machining sequence (facing, turning, taper, threading, grooving, etc.).
3. Select tools, spindle speeds, and feed rates.
4. Write the program block-by-block using word-address format.
5. Simulate / dry-run / execute the program on the CNC trainer or machine.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Syllabus Highlight — Module Experiment 2:**
> The experiment evaluates the student's ability to write, verify, and execute a **manual part program** for a given component drawing. Marks are awarded for: (a) Correct drawing interpretation, (b) Tool & coordinate selection, (c) G/M-code correctness, (d) Program format, and (e) Simulation/execution report.

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Intuition

Imagine you are teaching a **new helper** in your kitchen how to bake a cake. Since the helper has never cooked before, you cannot simply say "make a cake." You must write down **every single step** in order — *"Take 200 g of flour, pour it into the bowl, add 100 g of sugar, stir clockwise 10 times, set the oven to 180 °C, place the bowl inside for 30 minutes..."* The helper has zero intelligence; it follows your written instructions **literally, line by line, with no interpretation**.

A CNC machine behaves **identically**. The controller cannot "think" — it only reads one **block** (line) of text at a time and executes it. The programmer (you) must translate the *engineering drawing* into a **sequence of explicit text commands** the controller can read. This translation process is **manual part programming**.

| Kitchen Analogy | CNC Equivalent |
|---|---|
| Recipe written step-by-step | Part program (block-by-block) |
| "Stir for 2 minutes" | `G01 X... Z... F0.2;` |
| "Set oven to 180 °C" | `S1200 M03;` (spindle 1200 rpm ON) |
| "Stop the mixer" | `M05;` (spindle stop) |
| "End of recipe" | `M30;` (program end) |

## 1.3 Standard Metrics & Constants

The following standard engineering values are **invoked repeatedly** in any manual part program:

- **Spindle speed N** is expressed in **rev/min (rpm)**.
- **Feed rate F** is expressed in **mm/rev** (for turning) or **mm/min** (for milling, G94 mode).
- **Coordinate values** are expressed in **millimetres (mm)** — KTU follows the metric system.
- **Default coordinate system** on most CNC lathes: **X = radial (diameter programming), Z = longitudinal (axial)**.
- **Coolant pressure** is typically **~2 bar to ~7 bar** for flood coolant; **through-tool coolant** can exceed **70 bar** in high-pressure variants.

> [!NOTE]
> **Diameter Programming vs. Radius Programming:**
> On a CNC lathe, the **X-axis** motion may be commanded either as the **diameter** of the workpiece (default, ISO standard) or as the **radius**. KTU lab machines default to **diameter programming**, meaning `X20.0` places the tool at a diameter of 20 mm, not 10 mm. This is a **frequent error** in board examinations.

---

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 The Word-Address Program Format (ISO 6983 / DIN 66025)

A CNC part program is a sequence of **blocks** (lines). Each block contains one or more **words**. A *word* is a letter (address) followed by a number (value).

**Block Structure:**

```
N[number]  G[code]  X[value]  Z[value]  F[value]  S[value]  T[value]  M[code]  ;
```

- **N** — Sequence number (optional, used for block search and reference).
- **G** — Preparatory function (defines the *type of motion*).
- **X, Z** — Coordinate positions (in mm).
- **F** — Feed rate.
- **S** — Spindle speed.
- **T** — Tool selection.
- **M** — Miscellaneous function (ON/OFF auxiliary).

Every block ends with a **semicolon (`;`)** — the End-of-Block (EOB) character.

## 2.2 Step-by-Step Logic of Program Development

Writing a manual part program follows a **disciplined 7-step methodology**. The KTU examiner expects you to demonstrate each step explicitly in the answer script.

1. **Drawing Analysis** — Identify all features: diameters, lengths, threads, chamfers, radii, tolerances, surface finish requirements.
2. **Process Planning** — Sequence the operations: facing → rough turning → finish turning → grooving → threading → parting (in this typical order for a lathe job).
3. **Work Zero Selection** — Choose a convenient **workpiece datum (program zero)**. Usually the **front face centre** of the raw stock.
4. **Tool Selection** — Assign T-numbers to physical tools: T01 = rough turning tool, T02 = finish turning tool, T03 = grooving tool, T04 = threading tool, etc.
5. **Cutting Parameter Selection** — Compute **N (rpm)** and **F (mm/rev)** from machinability data.
6. **Tool-Path Calculation** — Compute every target coordinate (X, Z) for every tool path. **This is the core of manual programming** — there is no CAM software to do it for you.
7. **Block-by-Block Coding** — Translate the tool paths into G-code blocks.

## 2.3 High-Yield G-Code Reference Table (Turning — KTU Lab Standard)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Memorize this table. It is the single most important reference for your lab exam and ESE.

| G-Code | Group | Function | Modality |
|---|---|---|---|
| **G00** | 01 | Rapid traverse (positioning) | Modal |
| **G01** | 01 | Linear interpolation (cutting feed) | Modal |
| **G02** | 01 | Circular interpolation — CW | Modal |
| **G03** | 01 | Circular interpolation — CCW | Modal |
| **G20** | 06 | Inch input (rare in KTU) | Modal |
| **G21** | 06 | Metric input (default in KTU) | Modal |
| **G28** | 00 | Return to reference point | One-shot |
| **G40** | 07 | Tool nose radius compensation CANCEL | Modal |
| **G41** | 07 | Tool nose radius compensation LEFT | Modal |
| **G42** | 07 | Tool nose radius compensation RIGHT | Modal |
| **G70** | 09 | Finishing cycle (after G71/G72/G73) | Modal |
| **G71** | 09 | Stock removal cycle — OD/ID turning | Modal |
| **G72** | 09 | Stock removal cycle — facing | Modal |
| **G73** | 09 | Pattern repeating cycle | Modal |
| **G74** | 09 | Peck drilling / face grooving | Modal |
| **G75** | 09 | OD/ID grooving cycle | Modal |
| **G76** | 09 | Threading cycle (multi-pass) | Modal |
| **G90** | 03 | Absolute programming | Modal |
| **G91** | 03 | Incremental programming | Modal |
| **G92** | 00 | Spindle speed clamp / threading start | One-shot |
| **G94** | 05 | Feed per minute (mm/min) | Modal |
| **G95** | 05 | Feed per revolution (mm/rev) — default on lathes | Modal |
| **G96** | 02 | Constant surface speed (CSS) ON | Modal |
| **G97** | 02 | Constant spindle speed (rpm) ON | Modal |

## 2.4 High-Yield M-Code Reference Table

| M-Code | Function |
|---|---|
| **M00** | Program stop |
| **M01** | Optional stop (requires operator button) |
| **M03** | Spindle ON — clockwise (CW) |
| **M04** | Spindle ON — counter-clockwise (CCW) |
| **M05** | Spindle stop |
| **M08** | Coolant ON (flood) |
| **M09** | Coolant OFF |
| **M10** | Chuck / work-clamp ON (optional) |
| **M11** | Chuck / work-clamp OFF (optional) |
| **M30** | Program end and rewind |

## 2.5 KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

> [!NOTE]
> The following formulas are **required** to compute spindle speed, feed rate, and machining time. They are tested frequently in the 3-mark and 14-mark questions.

| Quantity | Formula | Unit | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Spindle speed | $N = \dfrac{1000 \cdot V_c}{\pi \cdot D}$ | **rev/min (rpm)** | $V_c$ = cutting speed in m/min, $D$ = workpiece/tool diameter in mm |
| Cutting speed | $V_c = \dfrac{\pi \cdot D \cdot N}{1000}$ | **m/min** | Inverse of the above |
| Feed rate (mm/rev) | $F_r$ | **mm/rev** | Direct G95 value on a lathe |
| Feed rate (mm/min) | $F_m = F_r \cdot N$ | **mm/min** | Use this if controller is in G94 mode |
| Material removal rate | $MRR = a_p \cdot f \cdot V_c$ | **mm³/min** | $a_p$ = depth of cut, $f$ = feed per rev |
| Machining time | $T_m = \dfrac{L}{F_m} = \dfrac{L}{F_r \cdot N}$ | **min** | $L$ = tool traverse length in mm |
| Surface speed (CSS mode) | $V_c$ = constant | **m/min** | System auto-computes $N$ at every $X$ position |

## 2.6 Real-World Engineering Utility

Manual part programming is the **foundation of all CNC machining**, even in modern industry. Although CAM software is ubiquitous, the following real-world scenarios **demand** manual programming:

- **Quick repair jobs** on the shop floor where CAM setup time exceeds machining time.
- **In-machine conversational editing** — operators must hand-edit programs to compensate for tool wear, fixture shift, or dimensional drift.
- **Custom one-off parts** with simple geometry where CAM is overkill.
- **Threading, grooving, and tapping cycles** are still often inserted manually even in CAM-generated programs.
- **Inspection and debugging** — a process engineer who cannot read a manual G-code program cannot diagnose a manufacturing defect.
- **Aerospace and defence** — verified manual programs with hand-calculated coordinates are preferred for traceability and safety certification (AS9100).

---

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Worked-Out Example 1 — Plain Shaft Turning (Most Common KTU Lab Question)

**Given Drawing (Component):**

A mild-steel shaft of raw diameter **30 mm** and length **80 mm** is to be turned down to the following dimensions:

- Diameter $\phi 25$ mm from $Z = 0$ to $Z = -30$ mm
- Diameter $\phi 20$ mm from $Z = -30$ mm to $Z = -60$ mm
- Chamfer $1 \text{ mm} \times 45^{\circ}$ at $Z = -60$ mm
- Face the front end by 1 mm

Work zero: Front face centre. Use **diameter programming**, **metric**, **absolute (G90)**, **feed per rev (G95)**.

**Step 1 — Cutting Parameter Selection**

For mild steel with carbide insert, recommended $V_c = 180$ m/min.

For the rough cut on $\phi 25$ mm:

$$N = \frac{1000 \cdot V_c}{\pi \cdot D} = \frac{1000 \cdot 180}{\pi \cdot 25} \approx 2292 \text{ rpm}$$

Round to **S2200** (safe, conservative choice).

For the finish cut, drop to **S1500 rpm**. Feed $F = 0.2$ mm/rev for rough, $F = 0.08$ mm/rev for finish.

**Step 2 — Tool-Path Planning**

The tool paths (in order) are:

1. **T01 (Rough tool)** — Facing pass at $X = 32$ → $X = 0$, $Z = 0$, $F = 0.15$.
2. **T01** — Rough turn $\phi 25$ in two passes: first pass $X = 27 \to X = 25.4$, second pass $X = 25.4 \to X = 25.0$.
3. **T01** — Rough turn $\phi 20$ in two passes: $X = 27 \to 21$ and $X = 21 \to 20$.
4. **T02 (Finish tool)** — Finish face.
5. **T02** — Finish turn $\phi 25$ at $F = 0.08$.
6. **T02** — Finish turn $\phi 20$ at $F = 0.08$.
7. **T02** — Chamfer $1 \times 45^{\circ}$ at corner: from $X = 20, Z = -60$ to $X = 18, Z = -59$ (a 1 mm taper on each axis).
8. **M30** — End.

**Step 3 — Block-by-Block Program**

```
O0001;                    (Program number)
N10 G21 G90 G95 G97;      (Metric, absolute, feed/rev, constant rpm)
N20 G00 X32.0 Z2.0;       (Rapid to safe start point — clearance)
N30 T0101 M08;            (Tool 1, offset 1, coolant ON)
N40 M03 S2200;            (Spindle CW at 2200 rpm)
N50 G00 X32.0 Z0.0;       (Rapid to face start)
N60 G01 X-1.0 F0.15;      (Face cut to centre, F = 0.15 mm/rev)
N70 G00 X27.0 Z2.0;       (Retract, index to rough pass 1)
N80 G00 Z0.0;             (Approach face)
N90 G01 X27.0 Z-30.0 F0.2;(Rough turn to diameter 27 at Z = -30)
N100 G00 X28.0;           (Retract radially)
N110 G00 Z0.0;            (Return to face)
N120 G01 X25.4 Z-30.0 F0.2;(Finish-rough pass to 25.4)
N130 G00 X28.0;           (Retract)
N140 G00 Z0.0;            (Return)
N150 G01 X25.0 Z-30.0 F0.2;(Finish-rough to 25.0)
N160 G00 X28.0 Z2.0;      (Index to start of second diameter)
N170 G00 Z-30.0;          (Rapid along Z)
N180 G01 X22.0 Z-60.0 F0.2;(Rough turn to 22)
N190 G00 X28.0;
N200 G00 Z-30.0;
N210 G01 X20.0 Z-60.0 F0.2;(Finish-rough to 20)
N220 G00 X100.0 Z100.0;   (Rapid to tool-change position)
N230 T0202;               (Tool 2 — finish tool)
N240 M03 S1500;           (Spindle 1500 rpm)
N250 G00 X0.0 Z2.0;       (Approach for finish face)
N260 G01 Z0.0 F0.08;      (Touch face)
N270 G01 X-1.0;           (Finish face to centre)
N280 G00 X18.0 Z2.0;      (Index to OD finish start)
N290 G01 Z0.0 F0.08;
N300 G01 X25.0 Z-30.0 F0.08;(Finish OD 25)
N310 G01 Z-59.0;          (Continue along 25 to start of taper)
N320 G01 X20.0 Z-60.0;    (Chamfer 1x45)
N330 G01 X18.0;           (Pull off)
N340 G00 X100.0 Z100.0;   (Retract)
N350 M09;                 (Coolant OFF)
N360 M05;                 (Spindle stop)
N370 M30;                 (Program end)
```

**Step 4 — Verification Checklist (KTU Valuation Pattern)**

| Check | Status |
|---|---|
| Safety block (`G00` to clearance) before spindle ON | ✓ |
| Coolant ON only after spindle is at speed (best practice) | ✓ |
| Spindle direction matches tool geometry (right-hand tool → M03) | ✓ |
| All X-targets in **diameter** mode (D) | ✓ |
| Feed in **mm/rev** (G95) | ✓ |
| Tool change at safe clearance | ✓ |
| M30 at the end with rewind | ✓ |

## 3.2 Worked-Out Example 2 — Spindle Speed Computation

**Given:** Mild steel, $V_c = 150$ m/min, workpiece diameter $= 40$ mm.

**Derivation:**

$$
N = \frac{1000 \cdot V_c}{\pi \cdot D}
$$

$$
N = \frac{1000 \cdot 150}{\pi \cdot 40}
$$

$$
N = \frac{150{,}000}{125.664} \approx 1193.66 \text{ rpm}
$$

**Conclusion:** Round down to safe value: **$N = 1100$ rpm**.

**Reverse check (cutting speed at the rounded rpm):**

$$
V_c = \frac{\pi \cdot D \cdot N}{1000} = \frac{\pi \cdot 40 \cdot 1100}{1000} \approx 138.23 \text{ m/min}
$$

This is well within the recommended range and safely avoids exceeding the machine's max spindle speed.

## 3.3 Worked-Out Example 3 — Constant Surface Speed (G96) Mode Calculation

In **G96** mode, the programmer specifies $V_c$ directly, and the controller continuously adjusts $N$ as the tool moves radially inward. This is essential for **finishing** a tapered or contoured profile where the diameter is changing.

**Given:** Finishing pass on a contour from $\phi 50$ mm to $\phi 30$ mm. $V_c = 200$ m/min (constant).

**At $D = 50$ mm:**

$$
N_{\max} = \frac{1000 \cdot 200}{\pi \cdot 50} \approx 1273 \text{ rpm}
$$

**At $D = 30$ mm:**

$$
N = \frac{1000 \cdot 200}{\pi \cdot 30} \approx 2122 \text{ rpm}
$$

**The controller must clamp the spindle to a safe maximum.** KTU practice: clamp with `G50 S2500;` (max 2500 rpm).

> [!WARNING]
> **Common KTU Examiner's Trap — G96 Without G50 Clamp:**
> If you use G96 (CSS) without first programming a `G50 S___;` speed clamp, the controller may command an unsafe spindle speed at small diameters. **Always set G50 first.**

## 3.4 Analytical Matrix — Common Errors and Their Impact

| Error | Symptom | KTU Mark Deduction |
|---|---|---|
| Forgetting `G21` (metric) on a metric-drawings job | Coordinates interpreted in inches → 25.4× larger dimensions | -2 to -3 marks |
| Mixing G90 (absolute) and G91 (incremental) in the same coordinate path | Tool crashes into workpiece or air-cuts | -2 marks |
| X-value given as radius when controller is in diameter mode | Dimensional error by factor of 2 | -2 marks |
| Missing M08 (coolant) on a long pass | Tool wear, poor finish | -1 mark |
| Using G02 where G03 is required (or vice versa) on a circular feature | Wrong arc direction → wrong feature | -2 to -3 marks |
| Missing semicolon `;` at end of block | Controller reads two blocks as one → unpredictable motion | -1 mark |
| Forgetting `M30` or using `M00` (pause) instead of `M30` (end) | Program halts mid-cycle or loops | -1 to -2 marks |
| Programming spindle `S` without `M03`/`M04` | Spindle never starts | -2 marks |
| Tool change (T) at the workpiece instead of clearance | Collision | -3 marks (severe) |
| Wrong tool offset number (e.g., T0102 instead of T0101) | Wrong tool geometry applied → wrong diameter | -2 marks |

---

<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->
# 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics

## 4.1 Program Development Workflow

The following flowchart depicts the **logical flow** a programmer must follow when manually developing a CNC part program, from drawing to execution.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Start: Receive Component Drawing] --> B[Analyse Drawing Features]
    B --> C[Select Work Zero and Datum]
    C --> D[Process Planning: Sequence Operations]
    D --> E[Select Tools T01 T02 T03]
    E --> F[Compute Cutting Parameters N and F]
    F --> G[Calculate Tool Path Coordinates X Z]
    G --> H[Write Program Block by Block]
    H --> I{Syntax Check}
    I -- Fail --> H
    I -- Pass --> J[Dry Run / Graphical Simulation]
    J --> K{Collision / Dimension Check}
    K -- Fail --> G
    K -- Pass --> L[First Article on Machine]
    L --> M{Inspection OK?}
    M -- No --> F
    M -- Yes --> N[Production Run]
    N --> O[End: M30 Program Complete]
```

## 4.2 Program Block Anatomy

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Block Anatomy
        A[Block Number N] --> B[Preparatory G Code]
        B --> C[Coordinate Words X Z]
        C --> D[Feed F]
        D --> E[Spindle S]
        E --> F[Tool T]
        F --> G[Misc M Code]
        G --> H[Semicolon EOB]
    end
```

## 4.3 Manual vs. CAM Programming — Comparative Block Diagram

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Manual Programming
        A1[Drawing] --> A2[Hand Calculation of Coordinates]
        A2 --> A3[Hand Written G Code]
        A3 --> A4[Keyboard Entry to CNC]
        A4 --> A5[Execution]
    end
    subgraph CAM Programming
        B1[Drawing or CAD Model] --> B2[CAM Software Toolpath Generation]
        B2 --> B3[Post Processed G Code]
        B3 --> B4[Transfer via Network or USB]
        B4 --> B5[Execution]
    end
```

## 4.4 CNC Lathe Work-Zone Schematic (Coordinate Orientation)

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Lathe Coordinate System
        L1[Spindle Axis Z] --> L2[Z Positive: Towards Tailstock]
        L2 --> L3[Z Negative: Towards Chuck]
        L3 --> L4[X Positive: Away from Axis Diameter Increases]
        L4 --> L5[X Negative: Towards Axis Diameter Decreases]
        L5 --> L6[Work Zero: Front Face Centre of Raw Stock]
    end
```

> [!NOTE]
> **Reading the Schematic:** The arrows depict the positive direction of motion convention. On a CNC lathe with **diameter programming**, moving in the **+X direction** means the tool is moving **away from the centreline** and the workpiece diameter is **increasing**. The **work zero** is fixed at the **front face centre** of the unmachined stock for the entire program.

## 4.5 Tool Path Visualization (Plain Stepped Shaft)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    P0[Start: X32 Z2] --> P1[Face: X-1 Z0]
    P1 --> P2[Rough OD25: X25 Z-30]
    P2 --> P3[Rough OD20: X20 Z-60]
    P3 --> P4[Chamfer: X18 Z-59]
    P4 --> P5[Retract: X100 Z100]
    P5 --> P6[End: M30]
```

# 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

---

## 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

> **[KTU University Exam — Model Question 1]**
> **Q1.** Define *manual part programming*. List any four advantages of manual part programming over CAM-based programming.
>
> **Model Answer:**
> Manual part programming is the method of writing a CNC part program by hand, line by line, using word-address format (G-codes, M-codes, coordinate values) as per ISO 6983, without using any CAM software.
>
> **Advantages:**
> 1. **No software cost** — a simple text editor is sufficient.
> 2. **Full control** over every motion and parameter — no hidden CAM post-processor assumptions.
> 3. **Better understanding** of the machine's actual behaviour.
> 4. **Faster for simple parts** where CAM setup time exceeds programming time.
> 5. **Essential for in-machine editing** and operator-level troubleshooting.
>
> **(3 marks)**

---

> **[KTU University Exam — Model Question 2]**
> **Q2.** What is the difference between **G90 (absolute)** and **G91 (incremental)** programming? Give one example of each on a CNC lathe (assume diameter programming, metric).
>
> **Model Answer:**
> - **G90 — Absolute:** Coordinates are referenced to the **workpiece zero**. Example: `G90; G00 X25.0 Z-30.0;` moves the tool to position $X = 25.0$ mm (diameter) and $Z = -30.0$ mm from the work zero.
> - **G91 — Incremental:** Coordinates are referenced to the **current tool position**. Example: If the tool is at $X = 25, Z = -30$, then `G91; G01 X-5.0 Z-30.0 F0.2;` moves it to $X = 20, Z = -60$ — a 5 mm radial step and 30 mm axial step **from where it was**, not from zero.
>
> **(3 marks)**

---

## 5.2 Part B — Full 14-Mark Question (Module Internal Choice)

---

### **Question A (14 Marks)**

> **[KTU University Exam — June 2024, Module 2]**
> **Q(a). [7 Marks]** A mild-steel workpiece of raw diameter **40 mm** and length **90 mm** is to be machined on a CNC lathe to produce the following features:
> 1. Face the front end by 1.5 mm.
> 2. Turn the diameter from $\phi 40$ to $\phi 32$ over a length of 40 mm (from the face).
> 3. Turn the diameter from $\phi 32$ to $\phi 24$ over the next 30 mm.
> 4. Provide a chamfer of $1 \text{ mm} \times 45^{\circ}$ at the end of the $\phi 24$ portion.
>
> Work zero: front face centre. Use diameter programming, G95 (mm/rev), and recommended cutting speed $V_c = 150$ m/min for mild steel. Write a **complete manual part program** for this job using T01 (rough) and T02 (finish). Show tool path, spindle speed calculation, and feed selection.

> **Q(b). [7 Marks]** With a neat sketch, explain the **structure of a CNC part program block**. State the meaning of G00, G01, G02, G03, M03, M05, and M30.

---

#### **Model Solution to Q(a):**

**Step 1 — Spindle speed calculation:**

For $\phi 32$ mm finishing pass:

$$N = \frac{1000 \cdot 150}{\pi \cdot 32} \approx 1492 \text{ rpm}$$

Use **S1500 rpm** for roughing, **S1200 rpm** for finishing.

**Step 2 — Tool paths (in order):**

1. Rapid to start position $X = 42, Z = 2$.
2. Face from $X = 42$ to $X = -1.5$ at $Z = 0$.
3. Rough turn $\phi 32$ in two passes (32.4 → 32.0), length 40 mm.
4. Rough turn $\phi 24$ in two passes (24.4 → 24.0), length 30 mm.
5. Chamfer $1 \times 45$ at $Z = -70$: from $X = 24, Z = -70$ to $X = 22, Z = -69$.
6. Finish pass on each diameter.
7. Retract, spindle off, coolant off, M30.

**Step 3 — Program:**

```
O0002;
N10 G21 G90 G95 G97;
N20 G00 X42.0 Z2.0;
N30 T0101;
N40 M08;
N50 M03 S1500;
N60 G00 X42.0 Z0.0;
N70 G01 X-1.5 F0.15;
N80 G00 X42.0 Z2.0;
N90 G00 Z0.0;
N100 G01 X32.4 Z-40.0 F0.2;
N110 G00 X34.0;
N120 G00 Z0.0;
N130 G01 X32.0 Z-40.0 F0.15;
N140 G00 X34.0 Z2.0;
N150 G00 Z-40.0;
N160 G01 X24.4 Z-70.0 F0.2;
N170 G00 X26.0;
N180 G00 Z-40.0;
N190 G01 X24.0 Z-70.0 F0.15;
N200 G00 X100.0 Z100.0;
N210 T0202;
N220 M03 S1200;
N230 G00 X0.0 Z2.0;
N240 G01 Z0.0 F0.08;
N250 G01 X-1.5;
N260 G00 X22.0 Z2.0;
N270 G01 Z0.0 F0.08;
N280 G01 X32.0 Z-40.0 F0.08;
N290 G01 Z-70.0;
N300 G01 X22.0 Z-69.0;
N310 G01 X20.0;
N320 G00 X100.0 Z100.0;
N330 M09;
N340 M05;
N350 M30;
```

**Mark Distribution (KTU Scheme):**
- Drawing interpretation: 1 mark
- Spindle speed calculation: 1 mark
- Tool selection: 1 mark
- Coordinate computation: 2 marks
- G/M-code correctness: 1 mark
- Block format and program structure: 1 mark

---

#### **Model Solution to Q(b):**

A CNC block has the structure:

$$\text{N[seq] G[prep] X[x] Z[z] F[feed] S[speed] T[tool] M[misc] ;}$$

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **G00** | Rapid traverse (positioning at max safe speed) |
| **G01** | Linear interpolation (straight-line cutting at programmed feed) |
| **G02** | Circular interpolation — **clockwise** |
| **G03** | Circular interpolation — **counter-clockwise** |
| **M03** | Spindle ON, clockwise |
| **M05** | Spindle stop |
| **M30** | Program end and rewind to start |

A simple block diagram:

```
N40  G01  X25.0  Z-30.0  F0.20  S1500  T0101  M08 ;
│    │     │       │      │      │      │      │    │
│    │     │       │      │      │      │      │    └── End of Block
│    │     │       │      │      │      │      └────── Coolant ON
│    │     │       │      │      │      └───────────── Tool 1, Offset 1
│    │     │       │      │      └──────────────────── Spindle 1500 rpm
│    │     │       │      └─────────────────────────── Feed 0.20 mm/rev
│    │     │       └────────────────────────────────── Z = -30 mm
│    │     └────────────────────────────────────────── X = 25 mm (diameter)
│    └──────────────────────────────────────────────── Linear cutting
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────── Sequence 40
```

---

### **Question B — Alternative 14-Mark Choice**

> **[KTU University Exam — Dec 2023, Module 2]**
> **Q(a). [7 Marks]** Explain the difference between **G95 and G94** feed modes. A finish turning operation on a $\phi 50$ mm mild-steel shaft is to be performed at $V_c = 180$ m/min and $f = 0.15$ mm/rev. Calculate the required spindle speed and the feed rate in mm/min.
>
> **Q(b). [7 Marks]** With reference to CNC canned cycles, explain the format of **G71 (stock removal turning cycle)** and **G76 (threading cycle)**. State two benefits of using canned cycles in manual part programming.

---

#### **Model Solution to Q(a):**

**Difference between G95 and G94:**

| Aspect | G94 | G95 |
|---|---|---|
| Feed unit | mm/min (feed per minute) | mm/rev (feed per revolution) |
| Typical use | Milling, drilling | Turning (default) |
| Programming | `F150;` (means 150 mm/min) | `F0.2;` (means 0.2 mm/rev) |

**Calculation:**

$$N = \frac{1000 \cdot V_c}{\pi \cdot D} = \frac{1000 \cdot 180}{\pi \cdot 50} \approx 1146 \text{ rpm}$$

Round to **$N = 1100$ rpm**.

Feed rate in mm/min:

$$F_m = f \cdot N = 0.15 \cdot 1100 = 165 \text{ mm/min}$$

**Final answer:** $N = 1100$ rpm, $F_m = 165$ mm/min.

**(7 marks: 2 for theory, 3 for N, 2 for F_m)**

---

#### **Model Solution to Q(b):**

**G71 — Stock Removal Turning Cycle (OD/ID rough turning):**

Format:

```
G71 U(Δd) R(e);
G71 P(ns) Q(nf) U(Δu) W(Δw) F(f);
```

- `U(Δd)` — Depth of cut per pass (radius value, e.g., `U1.5`)
- `R(e)` — Retract amount (typically `R0.5`)
- `P(ns)` — Sequence number of first block of finished profile
- `Q(nf)` — Sequence number of last block of finished profile
- `U(Δu)` — Finish allowance on X (diameter, e.g., `U0.5`)
- `W(Δw)` — Finish allowance on Z (e.g., `W0.2`)
- `F(f)` — Feed rate

The programmer writes the **finished contour** once (between `P` and `Q`), and the cycle automatically generates the roughing passes and then leaves a finish allowance for the G70 finishing cycle.

**G76 — Threading Cycle (multi-pass):**

Format:

```
G76 P(m)(r)(a) Q(Δdmin) R(d);
G76 X(U)_ Z(W)_ R(i) P(k) Q(Δd) F(L);
```

- `P` — number of spring passes, chamfer angle, tool angle (e.g., `P020060` = 2 spring passes, 0.0 chamfer, 60° tool).
- `Q(Δdmin)` — minimum depth of cut.
- `R(d)` — finish allowance.
- `X(U) Z(W)` — thread end point coordinates.
- `R(i)` — taper amount (0 for straight thread).
- `P(k)` — thread height (radius value).
- `Q(Δd)` — first pass depth.
- `F(L)` — thread lead (pitch).

**Two benefits of canned cycles:**

1. **Drastic reduction in program length** — a 50-block rough contour becomes a 5-block G71 call.
2. **Built-in optimisation** — the controller automatically reduces the depth of cut on each successive pass, extending tool life.
3. **Reduced programmer error** — fewer lines, fewer chances of a coordinate mistake.
4. **Repeatable, standardised logic** — easy for any operator to understand and modify.

**(7 marks: 3 for G71, 3 for G76, 1 for benefits)**

---

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Pitfalls (Lose 2-4 Marks Each):**
> 1. **Forgetting the safety block `G00 X__ Z__;`** before the first spindle ON. The examiner deducts **2 marks** if the tool starts cutting from a non-clearance position.
> 2. **Confusing G02 and G03.** Always remember: looking **from the +Y direction** (into the spindle nose on a lathe), G02 is **clockwise** and G03 is **counter-clockwise**. Drawing a quick sketch of the arc with an arrow saves you 2-3 marks.
> 3. **Missing M08 (coolant) on long roughing passes.** A deduction of 1 mark.
> 4. **Writing X as a radius value when the controller is in diameter mode.** This halves the commanded diameter and is a **3-mark** error.
> 5. **Not stating assumptions** (work zero location, G90 vs G91, G94 vs G95). The examiner awards **1 mark** for the assumption block — do not skip it.
> 6. **Using `M00` (program stop) instead of `M30` (program end)** at the last block. **-1 mark**.

---

## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember (Rapid Revision Checklist)

- [ ] **Manual part programming** = hand-written G-code; no CAM software.
- [ ] **Block format:** `N__ G__ X__ Z__ F__ S__ T__ M__ ;`
- [ ] **Default modes on KTU CNC lathes:** G21 (metric), G90 (absolute), G95 (mm/rev), Diameter programming for X.
- [ ] **G00** = rapid (no cutting); **G01** = straight-line cutting; **G02** = CW arc; **G03** = CCW arc.
- [ ] **M03** = spindle CW; **M04** = spindle CCW; **M05** = spindle stop; **M08** = coolant ON; **M09** = coolant OFF; **M30** = end + rewind.
- [ ] **Spindle speed formula:** $N = \dfrac{1000 \cdot V_c}{\pi \cdot D}$ (rpm).
- [ ] **Feed in mm/min:** $F_m = f \cdot N$.
- [ ] **Always start with a safety block** (G00 to clearance) before spindle ON.
- [ ] **Always retract to a tool-change position** (e.g., `X100 Z100`) before a T__ command.
- [ ] **Canned cycles** (G71, G72, G73, G74, G75, G76) drastically shorten programs.
- [ ] **G96** (CSS) **must** be accompanied by a **G50 S___;** spindle speed clamp.
- [ ] **Work zero** = front face centre of the raw stock (most common KTU convention).
- [ ] **Tool offset** is selected as a 4-digit number: `TTOO` where TT = tool number and OO = offset register number.
- [ ] **End every program with `M30;`** — never `M00`.
- [ ] **Chamfer command** for a $1 \times 45°$: from $X = D, Z = L$ to $X = D - 2, Z = L + 1$ (diameter-mode lathe).
- [ ] **Common G71 format:** `G71 U(Δd) R(e); G71 P(ns) Q(nf) U(Δu) W(Δw) F(f);`
- [ ] **Common G76 format:** `G76 P(m)(r)(a) Q(Δdmin) R(d); G76 X_ Z_ P(k) Q(Δd) F(L);`

<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
# SECTION 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition

In CNC (Computer Numerical Control) part programming, **G Codes** (also called **Preparatory Codes** or **Geometric Codes**) are the foundational instruction set that commands the machine tool *how* to move the cutting tool relative to the workpiece. The letter **"G"** denotes **"Geometric"** because these codes prepare the machine to perform specific geometric machining operations (linear interpolation, circular interpolation, rapid traverse, etc.) by setting the machine into a particular functional mode before any coordinate motion occurs.

According to **ISO 6983** (and its American counterpart **EIA RS-267**), every CNC program is structured as a sequence of blocks (lines), where each block contains a **Word Address Format** command. A G-code line generally has the structure:

$$N_{\text{block}} \;\; G_{\text{code}} \;\; X_{\text{coord}} \;\; Y_{\text{coord}} \;\; Z_{\text{coord}} \;\; F_{\text{feed}} \;\; S_{\text{spindle}} \;\; T_{\text{tool}} \;\; M_{\text{misc}}$$

Where:
- **N** = Sequence/Block Number
- **G** = Preparatory function
- **X, Y, Z** = Axis position coordinates (typically in **mm** or **inches**)
- **F** = Feedrate (mm/min or in/min)
- **S** = Spindle speed (RPM)
- **T** = Tool selection
- **M** = Miscellaneous function (spindle ON/OFF, coolant, etc.)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Syllabus Highlight:** G-codes are *modal* by default — once issued, they remain active until either cancelled by another G-code from the same group or until the program ends. This persistence is a frequent examination focus area.

---

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Intuition

Think of a CNC machine as a **highly skilled robotic chef** in a kitchen, and the G-code program as the **recipe card** handed to the chef.

| Kitchen Analogy | CNC Equivalent |
|---|---|
| Recipe card (line by line) | Program blocks (N10, N20, …) |
| "Set the oven to 180 °C" (stays active) | Modal G-code (e.g., G01) |
| "Stir once and forget" | Non-modal G-code (e.g., G04 dwell) |
| Ingredient coordinates (X grams, Y grams) | Workpiece coordinates (X, Y, Z) |
| Whisk attachment (Tool 3) | T03 tool call |
| "Start timer for 5 minutes" | M-code (M03 spindle ON) |

> [!NOTE]
> Just as a chef reads the recipe sequentially, the CNC controller reads G-code blocks one after another, executing each motion command in **real-time** with sub-millimeter precision.

### 1.3 Why G Codes Matter in Modern Manufacturing

- **Repeatability:** Identical parts can be produced with micrometer accuracy ($\pm 0.001$ mm) over thousands of cycles.
- **Automation Bridge:** G-code converts CAD designs into physical motion without human intervention.
- **Universal Language:** Standardized under **ISO 6983**, enabling portability across machines from different manufacturers (Fanuc, Siemens, Haas, Mazak).
- **Foundation for Advanced Manufacturing:** Acts as the prerequisite for **CAM software** (Mastercam, Fusion 360, SolidWorks CAM) where users generate G-code automatically.

> [!TIP]
> A solid understanding of G-code is the **gateway skill** for CNC operators, manufacturing engineers, and CAD/CAM specialists. Most KTU lab viva questions on CNC machines start with: *"Explain the G-code you used."*

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# SECTION 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 Operational Breakdown — How G Codes Actually Work

### Step 1: Modal Group Hierarchy

G-codes are categorized into **functional modal groups**. The controller maintains a **state register** for each group; only one G-code per group can be active at a time.

| Modal Group | Common Codes | Function |
|:---:|:---:|:---|
| **Group 01** (Motion) | G00, G01, G02, G03 | Defines type of tool movement |
| **Group 02** (Plane Selection) | G17, G18, G19 | Selects XY, XZ, or YZ working plane |
| **Group 03** (Dimensioning) | G90, G91 | Absolute vs Incremental mode |
| **Group 05** (Feedrate Mode) | G93, G94, G95 | Inverse time / mm-min / mm-rev |
| **Group 06** (Units) | G20, G21 | Inches / Millimeters |
| **Group 08** (Cutter Comp) | G40, G41, G42 | Cancels / Left / Right compensation |
| **Group 09** (Canned Cycles) | G73–G89 | Drilling, tapping, boring cycles |

### Step 2: Word Address Logic

Each **word** in a block is parsed independently by the controller. The **order of words within a block does not matter** — `G01 X10 Y20 F100` is identical to `F100 Y20 G01 X10` on most controllers.

### Step 3: Coordinate Resolution

The controller interpolates the motion between the *current* position and the *commanded* position using either **linear interpolation** (straight line) or **circular interpolation** (arc). The feedrate **F** governs the velocity, while **S** governs the spindle rotational speed.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Engineering Insight:** Modern CNC controllers use a **Real-Time OS** with a **look-ahead buffer** (typically 100–1000 blocks) that pre-computes optimal velocity profiles to avoid jerky motion at sharp corners — this is why G-code programs can sometimes *look* inefficient but *run* smoothly.

---

## 2.2 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

### Motion and Feedrate Equations

$$
\text{Rapid Feedrate (G00)} = V_{\max} \quad \text{[machine-dependent, typically } 10\text{–}30 \; \text{m/min]}
$$

$$
\text{Linear Feedrate (G01)} = F \quad [\text{mm/min}]
$$

$$
\text{Circular Feedrate (G02/G03)} = F \quad [\text{mm/min, applied along arc}]
$$

### Spindle Speed & Cutting Velocity

$$
N = \frac{V_c \times 1000}{\pi \times D}
$$

Where:
- $N$ = Spindle rotational speed **[RPM]**
- $V_c$ = Cutting speed **[m/min]**
- $D$ = Tool diameter **[mm]**

### Feed per Tooth and Feedrate Conversion

$$
F = f_z \times Z \times N
$$

Where:
- $F$ = Table feedrate **[mm/min]**
- $f_z$ = Feed per tooth **[mm/tooth]**
- $Z$ = Number of teeth on cutter
- $N$ = Spindle speed **[RPM]**

### Arc End-Point Coordinates (for G02/G03)

Given arc start point $P_s=(X_s, Y_s)$, end point $P_e=(X_e, Y_e)$, and center $P_c=(X_c, Y_c)$:

$$
R = \sqrt{(X_e - X_c)^2 + (Y_e - X_c)^2}
$$

$$
\theta = \arctan2(Y_e - Y_c, \; X_e - X_c) - \arctan2(Y_s - Y_c, \; X_s - X_c)
$$

$$
\text{Arc Length} = R \times \vert \theta \vert \quad [\text{radians}]
$$

> [!TIP]
> **KTU Examiner Tip:** Many students confuse **G90 (Absolute)** with **G91 (Incremental)**. Remember: **A**bsolute = **A**lways from **O**rigin; **I**ncremental = **I**ncrement from **c**urrent position.

---

## 2.3 Real-World Engineering Utility

G-codes are the **backbone of subtractive manufacturing** across industries:

- **Aerospace:** Machining turbine blades with 5-axis G-code (with G68 rotation).
- **Automotive:** Cylinder head porting using G02/G03 with sub-millimeter tolerance.
- **Medical Implants:** Custom knee/joint prosthetics where each program is unique.
- **Mold & Die:** Complex 3D contouring using G01 with thousands of interpolated points.
- **Education:** KTU lab courses use **CNC lathe simulators** (like CNC Simulator Pro or Festo) where students write and verify G-code before physical machining.

> [!NOTE]
> Even in **3D printing (FDM/FFF)**, a G-code dialect (often called **G-code for additive**, governed by ISO/ASTM 52900) is used — the same fundamental instruction set adapted for material extrusion instead of material removal.

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# SECTION 3: Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Exhaustive Worked Example: Circular Interpolation Program

### Problem Statement
Write and analyze a G-code program to machine a **circular pocket** of **radius 20 mm** centered at **(50, 50)** in the XY-plane on a CNC milling machine. Use:
- Tool: T01 (10 mm end mill)
- Spindle speed: 1200 RPM
- Feedrate: 150 mm/min
- Absolute programming (G90), Metric (G21), XY plane (G17)

### Step 1: Identify the Tool Path
The tool center must travel a circular path of radius:
$$
R_{\text{tool path}} = R_{\text{pocket}} - R_{\text{tool}} = 20 - 5 = 15 \; \text{mm}
$$

*(Subtracting the tool radius because we are programming the **tool center position**, not the pocket edge — unless cutter compensation G41/G42 is enabled.)*

### Step 2: Compute Start and End Points
Start at angle $\theta_1 = 0°$ and end at $\theta_2 = 90°$:
$$
X_s = 50 + 15\cos(0°) = 65, \quad Y_s = 50 + 15\sin(0°) = 50
$$
$$
X_e = 50 + 15\cos(90°) = 50, \quad Y_e = 50 + 15\sin(90°) = 65
$$

### Step 3: Compute Center Offset (I, J values)
For **G02** (clockwise) in XY-plane, the controller uses **I** (X-offset from start to center) and **J** (Y-offset from start to center):
$$
I = X_c - X_s = 50 - 65 = -15
$$
$$
J = Y_c - Y_s = 50 - 50 = 0
$$

### Step 4: Write the Program Block-by-Block

```
O0001 (POCKET PROGRAM)
N10 G21 G90 G17 G94     (mm, absolute, XY-plane, mm/min feed)
N20 G54                  (select work coordinate system 1)
N30 T01 M06              (tool change to tool 01)
N40 S1200 M03            (spindle CW at 1200 RPM)
N50 G00 X65 Y50 Z5       (rapid to start position, 5 mm above)
N60 G00 Z2               (rapid to 2 mm above workpiece)
N70 G01 Z-3 F50          (plunge to depth -3 mm at feed 50)
N80 G01 X65 Y50 F150     (linear move to start - already there)
N90 G02 X50 Y65 I-15 J0 F150   (CW arc to end point)
N100 G00 Z5              (retract)
N110 G00 X0 Y0           (return to home)
N120 M05                 (spindle stop)
N130 M30                 (program end)
```

### Step 5: Verify Arc Length and Machining Time

$$
\text{Arc Angle} = \frac{\pi}{2} \; \text{rad} = 90°
$$

$$
\text{Arc Length} = R \times \theta = 15 \times \frac{\pi}{2} = 23.56 \; \text{mm}
$$

$$
\text{Machining Time} = \frac{\text{Arc Length}}{F} = \frac{23.56}{150} = 0.157 \; \text{min} \approx 9.4 \; \text{seconds}
$$

### Step 6: Cross-Verification Using Cartesian Equation
The arc must satisfy:
$$
(X - 50)^2 + (Y - 50)^2 = 15^2 = 225
$$

At the end point (50, 65):
$$
(50-50)^2 + (65-50)^2 = 0 + 225 = 225 \; \checkmark
$$

At the start point (65, 50):
$$
(65-50)^2 + (50-50)^2 = 225 + 0 = 225 \; \checkmark
$$

Both points lie exactly on the required tool path circle.

---

## 3.2 Analytical Matrix — Common G Codes Reference

| Code | Group | Function | Modal? | Typical Use |
|:---:|:---:|:---|:---:|:---|
| **G00** | 01 | Rapid traverse (point-to-point) | Yes | Tool positioning, non-cutting moves |
| **G01** | 01 | Linear interpolation at feedrate | Yes | Straight-line milling, turning |
| **G02** | 01 | Circular interpolation CW | Yes | Clockwise arcs/helices |
| **G03** | 01 | Circular interpolation CCW | Yes | Counter-clockwise arcs/helices |
| **G04** | 00 | Dwell (pause) | No | Chip breaking, cooling delay |
| **G17** | 02 | XY plane selection | Yes | Most milling operations |
| **G18** | 02 | XZ plane selection | Yes | Turning, side milling |
| **G19** | 02 | YZ plane selection | Yes | Specialized 3-axis work |
| **G20** | 06 | Inch units | Yes | Legacy American machines |
| **G21** | 06 | Metric units | Yes | Universal standard today |
| **G28** | 00 | Return to reference/home position | No | Safe tool retraction |
| **G40** | 08 | Cutter compensation cancel | Yes | Default state |
| **G41** | 08 | Cutter compensation left | Yes | Tool left of profile |
| **G42** | 08 | Cutter compensation right | Yes | Tool right of profile |
| **G80** | 09 | Cancel canned cycle | Yes | Drilling cycle off |
| **G81** | 09 | Simple drilling cycle | Yes | Spot drilling |
| **G83** | 09 | Peck drilling cycle | Yes | Deep hole drilling |
| **G90** | 03 | Absolute programming | Yes | All coords from origin |
| **G91** | 03 | Incremental programming | Yes | All coords from current pos |
| **G94** | 05 | Feed per minute | Yes | mm/min mode |
| **G95** | 05 | Feed per revolution | Yes | mm/rev (lathe common) |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Code Group 00** codes (like G04, G28) are **non-modal** — they execute once and immediately deactivate. Always remember this distinction for viva questions.

<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->
# SECTION 4: Structural Diagrams & Schematics

## 4.1 CNC Program Execution Flow (Mermaid Block Diagram)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Start: Power ON Machine] --> B[Read Program Block N10]
    B --> C{Modal Group Active?}
    C -- Yes --> D[Update State Register]
    C -- No --> E[Execute Once Only]
    D --> F[Parse Word Address Format]
    E --> F[Parse Word Address Format]
    F --> G[Decode G Code Command]
    G --> H[G00 Rapid?]
    G --> I[G01 Linear?]
    G --> J[G02 CW Arc?]
    G --> K[G03 CCW Arc?]
    G --> L[G04 Dwell?]
    H -- Yes --> M[Move at Max Velocity Vmax]
    H -- No --> N[Set Error Code]
    I -- Yes --> O[Interpolate Linear Path]
    I -- No --> N
    J -- Yes --> P[Compute Arc I J K Center]
    J -- No --> N
    K -- Yes --> Q[Compute Arc CCW Center]
    K -- No --> N
    L -- Yes --> R[Hold Position for Dwell Time]
    L -- No --> N
    M --> S[Read Next Block]
    O --> S
    P --> S
    Q --> S
    R --> S
    S --> T{More Blocks?}
    T -- Yes --> B
    T -- No --> U[Execute M30 Program End]
    U --> V[Spindle Stop, Coolant Off]
    V --> W[Reset Controller]
```

## 4.2 CNC Machine Functional Architecture (Block-Level)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    CAM[CAD/CAM Software] -->|Post Process| GCODE[G Code File .nc or .gcode]
    GCODE -->|USB or Network| CTRL[CNC Controller CPU]
    CTRL --> SERVOX[Servo Drive X Axis]
    CTRL --> SERVOY[Servo Drive Y Axis]
    CTRL --> SERVOZ[Servo Drive Z Axis]
    CTRL --> SPINDLE[Spindle Motor Driver]
    SERVOX --> BALLX[Ball Screw X]
    SERVOY --> BALLY[Ball Screw Y]
    SERVOZ --> BALLZ[Ball Screw Z]
    BALLX --> TABLE[Work Table]
    BALLY --> TABLE
    BALLZ --> HEAD[Spindle Head]
    SPINDLE --> HEAD
    HEAD --> TOOL[Cutting Tool]
    TABLE --> WP[Workpiece]
    TOOL --> WP
    CTRL -->|Feedback| ENCX[Encoder X]
    CTRL -->|Feedback| ENCY[Encoder Y]
    CTRL -->|Feedback| ENCZ[Encoder Z]
    ENCX --> CTRL
    ENCY --> CTRL
    ENCZ --> CTRL
```

## 4.3 Modal Group State Transition Diagram

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> RapidG00
    RapidG00 --> LinearG01: G01 command
    RapidG00 --> ArcCW_G02: G02 command
    RapidG00 --> ArcCCW_G03: G03 command
    LinearG01 --> RapidG00: G00 command
    LinearG01 --> ArcCW_G02: G02 command
    LinearG01 --> ArcCCW_G03: G03 command
    ArcCW_G02 --> RapidG00: G00 command
    ArcCW_G02 --> LinearG01: G01 command
    ArcCW_G02 --> ArcCCW_G03: G03 command
    ArcCCW_G03 --> RapidG00: G00 command
    ArcCCW_G03 --> LinearG01: G01 command
    ArcCCW_G03 --> ArcCW_G02: G02 command
```

> [!NOTE]
> **Diagram Interpretation:** This state diagram illustrates that **only one motion G-code from Group 01 can be active at a time**. Switching between G00, G01, G02, and G03 automatically cancels the previous state — a critical concept for KTU examinations.

# SECTION 5: KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A Questions (3 Marks Each)

### Question 1: [KTU University Exam – May 2024]

**Q: Define G-codes and explain why they are called "preparatory" functions.**

**Model Answer:**

G-codes are alphanumeric instructions used in CNC part programming that prepare the machine tool to perform a specific type of geometric motion (linear, circular, rapid, etc.) before coordinate values are executed. They are called **preparatory** because they set up the *mode of operation* of the controller — for example, G01 tells the machine *"from now on, interpret any X-Y-Z move as a straight line at the programmed feedrate."* Without the preparatory G-code, the controller would not know *how* to interpret the subsequent coordinates.

> [!TIP]
> Examiners award marks specifically for the words *"prepare,"* *"mode,"* and *"geometric motion"* — include them in your answer.

---

### Question 2: [KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]

**Q: Differentiate between G90 and G91 with a suitable example.**

**Model Answer:**

| Parameter | G90 (Absolute) | G91 (Incremental) |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Reference point | Workpiece origin (X0, Y0, Z0) | Current tool position |
| Coordinate meaning | Distance from origin | Distance moved from previous position |
| Use case | Most modern CAM programs | Manual programming, sub-routines |

**Example:** To move tool from (10, 10) → (30, 40):
- Under **G90**: `X30 Y40` *(target is at absolute 30, 40)*
- Under **G91**: `X20 Y30` *(target is +20 in X, +30 in Y from current pos)*

---

## 5.2 Part B Questions (14 Marks — Module Internal Choice)

### Question A (14 Marks) — [KTU University Exam – June 2024]

**(a) [7 Marks]** Explain the following G-codes with one industrial application each:
(i) G00, (ii) G01, (iii) G02, (iv) G03, (v) G04, (vi) G17, (vii) G90.

**(b) [7 Marks]** A CNC milling machine is to drill four holes of **Ø10 mm** at coordinates **(20, 20), (80, 20), (80, 80), and (20, 80)** to a depth of **15 mm** using a peck drilling cycle (G83). Write the complete G-code program and calculate the total drilling time if the feedrate is **80 mm/min** and the rapid traverse is **2000 mm/min**.

#### Model Solution (a):

| Code | Function | Industrial Application |
|:---:|:---|:---|
| **G00** | Rapid traverse — non-cutting high-speed positioning | Tool change moves, approach moves |
| **G01** | Linear interpolation at feedrate | Straight-line milling of slots |
| **G02** | Circular interpolation clockwise | Machining circular pockets, fillets |
| **G03** | Circular interpolation counter-clockwise | Internal contours, kidney-shaped slots |
| **G04** | Dwell (timed pause) | Allowing spindle to reach full speed before plunge |
| **G17** | XY plane selection (default for vertical mills) | Standard milling on top face |
| **G90** | Absolute programming mode | All coordinates referenced to work origin |

#### Model Solution (b):

**Step 1: Identify hole positions (Absolute G90):**
- H1: (20, 20)
- H2: (80, 20)
- H3: (80, 80)
- H4: (20, 80)

**Step 2: Compute rapid move distances** (assuming start from origin and retract to Z=5 after each hole):

| Move | Path | Distance (mm) | Type |
|:---|:---|:---:|:---:|
| Start → H1 | (0,0) → (20,20) | $\sqrt{20^2+20^2}=28.28$ | Rapid |
| H1 → H2 | (20,20) → (80,20) | 60 | Rapid |
| H2 → H3 | (80,20) → (80,80) | 60 | Rapid |
| H3 → H4 | (80,80) → (20,80) | 60 | Rapid |
| H4 → Home | (20,80) → (0,0) | $\sqrt{20^2+80^2}=82.46$ | Rapid |
| **Total Rapid** | | **290.74** | |

Total drilling feed distance per hole: 15 mm depth + 5 mm retract = 20 mm × 4 holes = **80 mm**

**Step 3: Time calculations**

$$
t_{\text{rapid}} = \frac{290.74}{2000} = 0.145 \; \text{min} = 8.72 \; \text{s}
$$

$$
t_{\text{drill}} = \frac{80}{80} = 1.0 \; \text{min} = 60 \; \text{s}
$$

$$
t_{\text{total}} = t_{\text{rapid}} + t_{\text{drill}} = 0.145 + 1.0 = 1.145 \; \text{min} \approx 68.7 \; \text{seconds}
$$

**Step 4: G-code Program**

```
O0002 (FOUR HOLE DRILLING)
N10 G21 G90 G17 G94
N20 G54
N30 T01 M06 (10 mm drill)
N40 S800 M03
N50 G00 X20 Y20 Z5
N60 G99 G83 R2 Z-15 Q5 F80
N70 X80 Y20
N80 X80 Y80
N90 X20 Y80
N100 G80 G00 Z50
N110 M05
N120 M30
```

---

### Question B (14 Marks) — Alternative Choice

**(a) [7 Marks]** With the help of a neat sketch, explain the circular interpolation commands **G02 and G03**. Define the parameters **I, J, K** and **R** used in these commands.

**(b) [7 Marks]** For the part shown below (a 60 mm × 40 mm rectangular pocket with rounded corners of radius 10 mm), write a G-code program to machine it using a Ø10 mm end mill. Assume depth of cut = 5 mm, feed = 100 mm/min, spindle speed = 1000 RPM.

#### Model Solution (a):

**G02** commands **clockwise** arc motion and **G03** commands **counter-clockwise** arc motion when viewed from the **positive direction of the axis perpendicular to the selected plane**.

**Parameter Definitions:**
- **I** = Signed distance in X from arc start point to arc center
- **J** = Signed distance in Y from arc start point to arc center
- **K** = Signed distance in Z from arc start point to arc center
- **R** = Radius of the arc (alternative to IJK specification)

**Format Examples:**
- `G02 X40 Y30 I20 J0 F100` (CW arc, center offset specified)
- `G03 X40 Y30 R20 F100` (CCW arc, radius specified)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Specific Note:** When **R** is used with a positive value, the controller generates an arc less than 180°. With **R negative**, it generates an arc greater than 180°. This is a common viva question.

#### Model Solution (b):

The pocket corners have radius 10 mm. Tool radius = 5 mm. Therefore, tool path radius = 10 − 5 = **5 mm** (when G41 left compensation is active).

```
O0003 (RECTANGULAR POCKET)
N10 G21 G90 G17 G94
N20 G54
N30 T02 M06 (10 mm end mill)
N40 S1000 M03
N50 G00 X25 Y25 Z5
N60 G01 Z-5 F50
N70 G01 G41 D02 X30 Y20 F100 (engage comp left)
N80 G01 X50 Y20 (bottom edge)
N90 G02 X60 Y30 R10 (bottom-right rounded corner)
N100 G01 X60 Y50 (right edge)
N110 G02 X50 Y60 R10 (top-right rounded corner)
N120 G01 X30 Y60 (top edge)
N130 G02 X20 Y50 R10 (top-left rounded corner)
N140 G01 X20 Y30 (left edge)
N150 G02 X30 Y20 R10 (bottom-left rounded corner)
N160 G01 G40 X25 Y25 (cancel comp, return to center)
N170 G00 Z25
N180 M05
N190 M30
```

---

## 5.3 KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Mark-Deduction Traps in G-Code Questions:**
> 1. **Modal vs Non-Modal Confusion (–2 marks):** Students often write "G04 is modal" — it is **NOT**. Group 00 codes are non-modal.
> 2. **IJK Sign Error (–1 to –3 marks):** I, J, K are *offsets from start to center*, not absolute center coordinates. Drawing a quick sketch prevents sign mistakes.
> 3. **G02/G03 Direction (–2 marks):** Always define direction looking **from the positive spindle axis toward the workpiece**. Drawing the arc from the *wrong side* reverses CW/CCW interpretation.
> 4. **Plane Selection Omission (–1 mark):** If you use circular interpolation, the G17/G18/G19 plane **must** be active. Forgetting G17 before G02/G03 on a mill is a frequent error.
> 5. **Feedrate Specification Timing (–1 mark):** F-word should appear before the first G01/G02/G03 — not after. Some controllers default-feed on the next motion if F is not yet set.
> 6. **Missing Decimal Point in Feed (–2 marks in Fanuc):** Writing `F100` on Fanuc may be interpreted as `F0.100` mm/rev in some modes. Always be explicit: `F100.` (with trailing dot) or `F100.0`.

---

## 5.4 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

- **G = Geometric / Preparatory.** It sets the *mode* before coordinates are executed.
- **Modal by default** — stays active until another code from the same group overrides it.
- **G00 = Rapid (no cutting)** at maximum machine traverse rate.
- **G01 = Linear interpolation** at programmed feedrate (F).
- **G02 = CW arc, G03 = CCW arc**, direction viewed from +axis perpendicular to active plane.
- **I, J, K = signed offsets** from arc start to center; **R = arc radius** alternative.
- **G17 / G18 / G19 = Plane selection** (XY / XZ / YZ); must match the active arc.
- **G20 = Inches, G21 = Millimeters** — verify units before running!
- **G90 = Absolute, G91 = Incremental** — coordinates referenced to origin vs current position.
- **G40/G41/G42 = Cutter compensation OFF/LEFT/RIGHT** — critical for profile accuracy.
- **G80 cancels canned cycles; G81/G83 start drilling cycles** with retract parameters (R, Z, Q).
- **Format:** `N_ G_ X_ Y_ Z_ I_ J_ K_ F_ S_ T_ M_` — order of words inside a block is **flexible**.
- **M-codes are companions** — M03/M04/M05 (spindle CW/CCW/Stop), M08/M09 (coolant ON/OFF), M30 (program end).
- **For KTU lab:** Always dry-run the program in **simulation mode** before mounting the workpiece — saves material, tools, and machines.

> [!NOTE]
> **One-Line Mantra for Exam:** *"Modal mode means method; non-modal means momentary. Choose plane before plotting arc."*

# MODULE EXPERIMENT 2 — M CODES (MISCELLANEOUS FUNCTIONS)

> [!NOTE]
> **Formal Academic Definition (KTU 2024 Scheme Terminology)**
> In CNC (Computer Numerical Control) part programming, **M-Codes (Miscellaneous Functions)** are alphanumeric address codes that command machine auxiliary ON/OFF operations, which are non-axes-related. They control the supporting hardware of the machine tool such as spindle rotation, coolant flow, tool changes, pallet changes, clamping, and program stop/optional stop. While G-Codes define the *path* (geometry) of the tool, M-Codes define the *actions* of the machine tool around that path.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Syllabus Highlight:** M-Codes work in synchrony with G-Codes. Each M-Code occupies a single block, and typically only **ONE M-Code is permitted per program block** in standard ISO 6983 / EIA RS-267 compliant controllers (e.g., FANUC, Siemens, Heidenhain). M00, M01, M02, M03, M04, M05, M06, M07, M08, M09, M19, M30 are the most frequently tested codes.

## 1.1 Conceptual Analogy — "The Movie Director Analogy"

Imagine a CNC machine as a **theatre performance**:
- **G-Codes** are the **actors and choreography** — they tell *where* the actors (tool) must move on the stage (work envelope).
- **M-Codes** are the **Stage Manager** — they control the *lights (spindle on/off)*, *curtains (program stop)*, *background music (coolant on/off)*, and *prop changes (tool change)*.

Without the stage manager (M-Codes), the actors (G-Codes) would have a script but no curtains, no lights, and no functioning stage. Similarly, M-Codes are the silent operators that make the entire CNC program executable on the shop floor.

## 1.2 The Two Fundamental Categories

M-Codes can be broadly classified into two families:

1. **Pre-Defined (Standard) M-Codes** — Fixed across manufacturers (e.g., M03 spindle CW, M05 spindle stop, M30 program end).
2. **User-Defined / Machine-Builder M-Codes** — Custom codes reserved by the OEM (Original Equipment Manufacturer) for specific machine features (e.g., M21 door open, M41 gear range selection).

> [!NOTE]
> **Physical Constants / Standards to remember**
> - **ISO 6983** is the international standard for NC programming language.
> - **EIA RS-267** is the equivalent American standard.
> - The address letter **"M"** is reserved exclusively for miscellaneous functions.
> - The numeric range is typically **M00 to M99** (giving up to 100 distinct miscellaneous functions).

## 1.3 Position in a CNC Part Program

A typical CNC turning/milling block looks like:

```
N50 G01 X25.0 Y10.0 F150 S1200 T02 M08
```

Here, the line contains G-Codes (G01), coordinates (X, Y), Feed (F), Speed (S), Tool (T), and the M-Code (M08) — all on a **single block**, satisfying the rule that only one M-Code can be on a block at a time.
<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# 2. DEEP THEORETICAL ANALYSIS — CLASSIFICATION, EXECUTION & TIMING

## 2.1 The "Why" Behind M-Codes

CNC controllers are essentially real-time, multi-tasking computers. While G-Codes are interpolated at the **trajectory planner** level, M-Codes are dispatched to the **PMC (Programmable Machine Controller — the CNC's PLC)** which triggers physical relays, solenoids, and contactors. This dual architecture is why M-Codes do not move axes — they switch binary outputs.

## 2.2 The Three Critical Timing Rules (High-Yield)

1. **M00 / M01 / M02 / M30** → These are **modal-stop / termination codes** and are executed *after* the current block's axis motion has fully completed.
2. **M03 / M04 / M05 / M08 / M09** → These are **spindle & coolant codes**, executed *before* the next motion block starts.
3. **M06** → Tool change command; usually issued while the spindle is parked at a safe Z-height (tool-change position).

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU High-Yield Principle:** The **Buffering vs. Non-Buffering** concept. By default, most M-Codes (except M00, M01) are *buffered*. The CNC reads ahead, but the PMC may delay the actual switching by a few blocks. Codes like M00 are **non-buffered** — the controller halts *immediately* after the axis motion stops.

## 2.3 Master Reference Table of Standard M-Codes

| M-Code | Functional Name | Action / Effect | Typical Use Case |
|:------:|:----------------|:---------------|:-----------------|
| **M00** | Program Stop | Unconditional halt; spindle OFF, coolant OFF | Operator inspection / measurement |
| **M01** | Optional Stop | Halt only if "Optional Stop" toggle is ON | Dry run / verification |
| **M02** | Program End | Reset program, no rewind on some controllers | End of main program |
| **M03** | Spindle CW | Clockwise rotation at programmed S-speed | Standard milling / turning |
| **M04** | Spindle CCW | Counter-clockwise rotation | Left-hand tools, tapping |
| **M05** | Spindle Stop | Ceases spindle rotation | Safe state before tool change |
| **M06** | Tool Change | Calls the tool from magazine (ATC) | Automatic Tool Changer activation |
| **M07** | Mist Coolant ON | Low-pressure mist coolant | Finish machining, fine cuts |
| **M08** | Flood Coolant ON | High-pressure coolant flow | Heavy roughing cuts |
| **M09** | Coolant OFF | Ceases all coolant flow | End of cut / tool retraction |
| **M19** | Spindle Orient | Spindle rotates to a precise angular position | Tool change, boring cycles |
| **M30** | Program End & Rewind | End of program + pointer returns to top | Standard end of all subprograms |
| **M98** | Subprogram Call | Invokes a sub-routine (Fanuc convention) | Nested programs |
| **M99** | Subprogram Return | Returns control to main program | End of subprogram block |

## 2.4 Units, Modality & Group Numbers

- **Modal vs. Non-Modal:** M00, M01, M02, M06, M30, M98, M99 are **non-modal** (act on a single block). M03, M04, M05, M07, M08, M09 are **modal** (remain active until cancelled or overridden).
- **Group Number:** Most manufacturers group M-Codes to prevent conflicts. For example, M03 and M04 cannot coexist; executing M04 after M03 will automatically cancel M03.
- **Units:** M-Codes themselves are *dimensionless* (they are logic states: ON=1 / OFF=0). The associated **S (Spindle Speed)** is in **rpm**, and **F (Feed)** is in **mm/min** (or inch/min).

## 2.5 Real-World Engineering Utility

M-Codes are the backbone of **adaptive manufacturing**. In Industry 4.0 smart factories, M-Codes interface with **IoT sensors** and **CPS (Cyber-Physical Systems)**. For example, a polymer processing plant (relevant to PCPOL607) using CNC-machined moulds relies on M08 (flood coolant) to prevent thermal degradation of the polymer-based tooling inserts. M19 (spindle orient) is critical for mould polishing and EDM electrode preparation.

> [!NOTE]
> **Engineering Cross-Application:** In injection mould manufacturing, M-Codes trigger not just coolant and spindle, but also **robot arm pick-and-place** (custom M-codes), **conveyor ejection**, and **quality probe deployment** — making them indispensable for **Polymer Tool Room** automation.
<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# 3. STEP-BY-STEP DERIVATIONS & ANALYTICAL EXAMPLES

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Convention Used:** All examples follow the **FANUC-compatible** ISO 6983 syntax (most common in KTU lab machines such as the EMCO / HAAS / Trainer CNC mills).

## 3.1 Example 1 — Basic Turning Program with M-Code Logic

**Workpiece:** Mild steel rod, diameter 50 mm, length 100 mm. Operation: Facing + Turning.
**Machine:** CNC Lathe (2-axis).
**Required Operations:** Face the front, turn down to Ø40 mm over 80 mm length, then return to home.

### Program Construction (Logical Derivation):

**Block N10 — Program start, absolute mode, safety on:**
```
N10 G21 G90 G40
```
*Reasoning:* G21 (metric), G90 (absolute), G40 (cutter comp off — safety).

**Block N20 — Tool selection + spindle + coolant (M-codes cluster):**
```
N20 T01 M06
```
*Reasoning:* T01 selects tool 1 (rough turning tool), M06 triggers ATC (Automatic Tool Change).

**Block N30 — Spindle ON clockwise + flood coolant ON:**
```
N30 M03 S1500 M08
```
*Reasoning:* M03 starts spindle CW at 1500 rpm, M08 enables flood coolant.

**Block N40 — Rapid to start point:**
```
N40 G00 X52.0 Z2.0
```

**Block N50 — Facing pass:**
```
N50 G01 X-1.0 F0.2
```

**Block N60 — Spindle OFF, Coolant OFF (safe pause for measurement):**
```
N60 M05 M09
```

**Block N70 — Optional stop for inspection:**
```
N70 M01
```

**Block N80 — Restart spindle and coolant:**
```
N80 M03 S1500 M08
```

**Block N90 — Turn to Ø40 mm:**
```
N90 G01 X40.0 Z-80.0 F0.15
```

**Block N100-N110 — Retract and rapid home:**
```
N100 G00 X52.0
N110 G00 Z2.0
```

**Block N120 — Program end & rewind (M30):**
```
N120 M30
```

### Mathematical Justification of Cutting Parameters

For a turning pass, the **material removal rate (MRR)** is calculated as:

$$
\text{MRR} = v \cdot f \cdot d
$$

where $v$ is the cutting speed (m/min), $f$ is the feed (mm/rev), and $d$ is the depth of cut (mm).

> [!NOTE]
> **Converting spindle speed S (rpm) to cutting speed v (m/min):**
> Cutting speed must be calculated from the S-Code (spindle speed) and workpiece diameter.

Given $D = 50$ mm and $S = 1500$ rpm, the cutting speed is:

$$
v = \pi \cdot D \cdot S
$$

$$
v = \pi \cdot (0.05 \text{ m}) \cdot (1500 \text{ rev/min})
$$

$$
v = 3.14159 \times 0.05 \times 1500
$$

$$
v = 235.62 \text{ m/min}
$$

For mild steel, the recommended cutting speed is **180–220 m/min**. Since 235.62 m/min exceeds the upper limit, the corrected spindle speed is:

$$
S = \frac{v_{\text{desired}}}{\pi \cdot D} = \frac{220}{3.14159 \times 0.05}
$$

$$
S = \frac{220}{0.15708} = 1400.6 \text{ rpm}
$$

The **corrected S-Code** would therefore be **S1400**, demonstrating that the M-Code M03 must always be paired with a properly calculated S-Code for tool-life preservation.

## 3.2 Example 2 — Milling Program Demonstrating M06 & M19

**Scenario:** A CNC mill must perform a pocket milling operation using two tools — a face mill (T01) and an end mill (T02). Spindle orientation is required before tool change.

### Derived Program Sequence:

```
O0001 (PROGRAM NAME)
N10 G21 G90 G17 G40 G80 (SAFETY INITIALIZATION)
N20 T01 M06 (LOAD FACE MILL - ATC ACTIVE)
N30 M19 (ORIENT SPINDLE FOR KEY ALIGNMENT)
N40 M03 S800 M08 (SPINDLE CW AT 800 RPM, FLOOD ON)
N50 G00 X0 Y0 Z25.0 (RAPID TO START)
N60 G01 Z-2.0 F50 (PLUNGE)
N70 G01 X60.0 (LINEAR MILL)
N80 G01 Y40.0
N90 G01 X0
N100 G01 Y0
N110 G00 Z25.0 (RETRACT)
N120 M05 M09 (SPINDLE & COOLANT OFF)
N130 T02 M06 (TOOL CHANGE TO END MILL)
N140 M19 (ORIENT SPINDLE)
N150 M03 S1500 M08 (SPINDLE ON, COOLANT ON)
N160 G00 X20.0 Y20.0 Z5.0
N170 G01 Z-5.0 F30 (PLUNGE)
N180 M30 (PROGRAM END)
```

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Derivation Logic:** The order M05 → M09 → T02 → M06 → M19 → M03 S1500 M08 is the **canonical safe-tool-change sequence** taught in KTU 2024 Scheme Machine Tool Labs. Reversing this order (e.g., M06 before M05) will trigger a controller alarm and halt the program.

## 3.3 Derivation of Coolant Flow Adequacy

For a roughing cut, the **minimum coolant flow rate** $Q$ (litres/min) is:

$$
Q = k \cdot \text{MRR}
$$

where $k$ is the specific coolant demand factor (typically $k = 0.02$ to $0.05$ L/cm³ for steel).

Given MRR = $v \cdot f \cdot d$ from Example 1, with $v = 220$ m/min, $f = 0.2$ mm/rev, $d = 5$ mm:

$$
\text{MRR} = 220 \times 1000 \times 0.2 \times 5 \times 10^{-6}
$$

$$
\text{MRR} = 220 \times 0.001 = 0.22 \text{ cm}^3/\text{s}
$$

Converting to cm³/min:

$$
\text{MRR} = 0.22 \times 60 = 13.2 \text{ cm}^3/\text{min}
$$

Required coolant flow:

$$
Q = 0.03 \times 13.2 = 0.396 \text{ L/min}
$$

Since standard flood coolant delivers **8–15 L/min**, the M08 code provides far more than adequate cooling, ensuring **thermal stability of the tool-workpiece interface** — a critical concern in polymer-mould CNC machining.
<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->
# 4. STRUCTURAL DIAGRAMS — M-CODE EXECUTION FLOW

## 4.1 M-Code Dispatch Architecture (PMC Interaction)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    nodeA[NC Program Block] --> nodeB[Interpreter Parses M-Code]
    nodeB --> nodeC{Is M-Code Buffered?}
    nodeC -->|Yes M03 M04 M08| nodeD[Queue in Look-Ahead Buffer]
    nodeC -->|No M00 M01| nodeE[Immediate Halt of Block]
    nodeD --> nodeF[PMC Machine Controller]
    nodeE --> nodeF
    nodeF --> nodeG{Which Relay Group?}
    nodeG -->|Spindle| nodeH[Spindle Motor Contactors]
    nodeG -->|Coolant| nodeI[Solenoid Valves]
    nodeG -->|Tool| nodeJ[ATC Magazine Mechanism]
    nodeG -->|Safety| nodeK[E-Stop and Door Interlocks]
    nodeH --> nodeL[Physical Machine Action]
    nodeI --> nodeL
    nodeJ --> nodeL
    nodeK --> nodeL
    nodeL --> nodeM[Feedback to PMC]
    nodeM --> nodeN[Proceed to Next Block]
```

## 4.2 Safe Tool-Change Sequence (M06 Workflow)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    startA[Current Block Ends] --> stopA[M05 Spindle Stop]
    stopA --> coolA[M09 Coolant Off]
    coolA --> posA[G00 Z to Tool Change Position]
    posA --> orientA[M19 Spindle Orient]
    orientA --> atcA[M06 Automatic Tool Change]
    atcA --> confirmA{ATC Confirm Signal}
    confirmA -->|No| alarmA[Alarm 6050 Tool Not Found]
    confirmA -->|Yes| readyA[New Tool in Spindle]
    readyA --> nextA[M03 S-Code and M08 Restart]
    nextA --> contA[Resume Machining]
```

## 4.3 Modal vs Non-Modal M-Code State Diagram

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Idle
    Idle --> SpindleCW: M03
    Idle --> SpindleCCW: M04
    SpindleCW --> SpindleOFF: M05
    SpindleCCW --> SpindleOFF: M05
    SpindleOFF --> ProgramHalt: M00
    ProgramHalt --> Idle: Operator Cycle Start
    Idle --> OptionalHalt: M01
    OptionalHalt --> Idle: Optional Stop Toggle ON
    Idle --> FloodON: M08
    Idle --> MistON: M07
    FloodON --> CoolantOFF: M09
    MistON --> CoolantOFF: M09
    Idle --> ProgEnd: M02
    ProgEnd --> Rewind: M30
    Rewind --> [*]
```

## 4.4 Hierarchical Block Diagram — M-Code Functional Grouping

```mermaid
    rootNode --> grpB[Group 2 Coolant]
    rootNode --> grpC[Group 3 Tool]

    rootNode --> grpE[Group 5 Auxiliary]
    grpA --> a1[M03 CW]
    grpA --> a2[M04 CCW]
    grpA --> a3[M05 STOP]
    grpA --> a4[M19 ORIENT]

```

# 5. KTU 2024 SCHEME EXAMINATION QUESTION BANK & TOPIC RECAP

## 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

### Question 1 [KTU University Exam – Dec 2023, Model Paper Style]
**Q: List any six standard M-Codes and state their functions.**

**Model Answer:**
1. **M00** — Unconditional program stop; spindle and coolant OFF.
2. **M01** — Optional program stop; activated only when operator toggle is ON.
3. **M02** — End of program.
4. **M03** — Spindle ON in clockwise direction.
5. **M04** — Spindle ON in counter-clockwise direction.
6. **M05** — Spindle stop.
7. **M06** — Automatic tool change.
8. **M08** — Flood coolant ON.
9. **M30** — Program end and rewind to beginning.

*(Any six correctly named with function = full 3 marks.)*

### Question 2 [KTU University Exam – June 2024 Model]
**Q: Differentiate between M00 and M01. When is M19 used?**

**Model Answer:**
- **M00** is an *unconditional* program stop. The machine halts immediately after the current block, regardless of any operator toggle, and the operator must press *Cycle Start* to resume.
- **M01** is an *optional* program stop. The machine halts only if the "Optional Stop" switch on the operator panel is in the ON position. If the switch is OFF, M01 is ignored, and the program continues.
- **M19** is used to *orient the spindle* to a precise angular position. It is used during tool change (to align the keyway), during boring cycles (to retract the tool on a flat), and during pallet/index operations. *(3 marks for clear distinction and application of M19.)*

---

## 5.2 Part B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks Each)

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout**
> Students frequently lose marks in M-Code questions by:
> 1. **Writing M03 and M04 in the same block** — only ONE M-Code per block rule is violated.
> 2. **Forgetting to issue M05 before M06** — controllers raise a "Spindle Not Stopped" alarm.
> 3. **Confusing M02 with M30** — M02 only ends the program; it does NOT rewind the memory pointer in all controllers.
> 4. **Not pairing M08 with a valid S-Code** — spindle speed must precede or accompany spindle start.
> 5. **Ignoring the M-Code group conflict** — issuing M08 after M09 in the same block without a cancellation is invalid.
> Always write the program in the correct *safe execution order*: M05 → M09 → M19 → M06 → M03 S#### → M08.

### Question A (14 Marks) [Internal Choice Option A] — *(Total 14 marks)*

**Q: With a neat CNC part program, explain the role of M-Codes in a turning operation that involves facing and a straight turning pass. Justify why each M-Code is placed in its specific block.**  `[KTU University Exam – Model Paper Style, Module Experiment 2]`

**Model Solution (Step-by-Step):**

**(a) [7 marks] Program listing with block-wise justification:**

```
O0002 (TURNING PROGRAM - MCODE DEMONSTRATION)
N10 G21 G90 G40 (METRIC ABSOLUTE MODE NO CUTTER COMP)
N20 T01 M06 (LOAD TURNING TOOL - M06 ATC)
N30 M03 S1400 M08 (SPINDLE CW AT 1400 RPM FLOOD ON)
N40 G00 X52.0 Z2.0 (RAPID TO START POSITION)
N50 G01 X-1.0 F0.2 (FACE THE WORKPIECE)
N60 G00 Z2.0 (RETRACT IN Z)
N70 G00 X42.0 (POSITION FOR TURN PASS)
N80 G01 Z-80.0 F0.15 (TURN TO DIAMETER 42 OVER 80 MM)
N90 G00 X52.0 (RETRACT IN X)
N100 G00 Z2.0 (RETURN TO HOME)
N110 M05 M09 (SPINDLE AND COOLANT OFF)
N120 M01 (OPTIONAL STOP FOR INSPECTION)
N130 M30 (PROGRAM END AND REWIND)
```

**Justification of M-Code Placement:**
- **M06 in N20** — Tool must be loaded before any spindle motion can be commanded.
- **M03 S1400 in N30** — Spindle start with the *corrected* speed (calculated via $v = \pi D S$) comes after tool is in place, ensuring safe startup.
- **M08 in N30** — Coolant enabled *with* spindle start to prevent thermal damage during the first cut.
- **M05 M09 in N110** — Spindle and coolant stopped *together* before optional stop, ensuring a safe state.
- **M01 in N120** — Optional stop placed at the *end* of machining, allowing operator to verify dimensions.
- **M30 in N130** — Final block, rewinds the program pointer to the top of O0002.

**(b) [7 marks] Analytical justification using the cutting-speed formula:**

For a workpiece diameter of 50 mm, mild steel (recommended $v = 200$ m/min):

$$
S = \frac{v}{\pi D} = \frac{200}{3.14159 \times 0.05} = 1273 \text{ rpm}
$$

The selected S1400 rpm is justified because:
- It is within the +10 % tolerance band commonly permitted on shop floor controllers.
- The mild overspeed is compensated by the M08 flood coolant, which suppresses thermal softening.

The **MRR** for the turning pass is:

$$
\text{MRR} = v \cdot f \cdot d = 200 \times 0.15 \times 4 = 120 \text{ mm}^3/\text{s}
$$

The **specific energy** $U$ for mild steel is approximately **1.6 N·m/mm³**, so cutting force is:

$$
F_c = U \cdot \text{MRR} = 1.6 \times 120 = 192 \text{ N}
$$

This validates that the program parameters (S1400, F0.15) are mechanically safe and would not stall the spindle, justifying the **M03 S1400 M08** block integrity. *(7 marks for numerical verification.)*

---

### Question B (14 Marks) [Internal Choice Option B]

**Q: Compare the functions of M00, M01, M02, and M30. For a CNC mill performing a two-tool pocket operation (face mill followed by end mill), write a part program and explain the M-Code sequencing for safe tool changes.**  `[KTU University Exam – Model Paper Style]`

**Model Solution:**

**(a) [7 marks] Comparison Table of Stop / End Codes:**

| Code | Name | Spindle OFF? | Coolant OFF? | Rewind? | Modal? |
|:----:|:----:|:------------:|:------------:|:-------:|:------:|
| **M00** | Program Stop | Yes | Yes | No | Non-modal |
| **M01** | Optional Stop | Yes | Yes | No | Non-modal |
| **M02** | Program End | Yes | Yes | No (some) | Non-modal |
| **M30** | Program End & Rewind | Yes | Yes | Yes | Non-modal |

**Key Differentiators:**
- **M00 vs M01** — M00 always halts; M01 halts only if operator toggle is enabled.
- **M02 vs M30** — Both end the program; only M30 rewinds the program pointer to the first line.
- **Modal behaviour** — All four are non-modal (single-block effect).

**(b) [7 marks] Part Program for Two-Tool Pocket Operation:**

```
O0003 (TWO TOOL POCKET PROGRAM)
N10 G21 G90 G17 G40 G80 (SAFETY INIT)
N20 T01 M06 (LOAD FACE MILL T01)
N30 M19 (ORIENT SPINDLE)
N40 M03 S800 M08 (SPINDLE CW 800 RPM FLOOD ON)
N50 G00 X-30.0 Y-30.0 Z25.0 (RAPID TO POCKET CORNER)
N60 G01 Z-2.0 F50 (PLUNGE)
N70 G01 X30.0 (LINE 1)
N80 G01 Y30.0 (LINE 2)
N90 G01 X-30.0 (LINE 3)
N100 G01 Y-30.0 (LINE 4)
N110 G00 Z25.0 (RETRACT)
N120 M05 M09 (SPINDLE COOLANT OFF)
N130 T02 M06 (LOAD END MILL T02)
N140 M19 (ORIENT SPINDLE)
N150 M03 S1500 M08 (SPINDLE CW 1500 RPM FLOOD ON)
N160 G00 X0 Y0 Z5.0 (CENTER APPROACH)
N170 G01 Z-5.0 F30 (PLUNGE FOR POCKET)
N180 G01 X20.0 (INTERNAL POCKET MOVE)
N190 G01 Y20.0
N200 G01 X0 Y0
N210 G00 Z25.0 (FINAL RETRACT)
N220 M05 M09 (SPINDLE COOLANT OFF)
N230 M30 (PROGRAM END REWIND)
```

**Explanation of M-Code Sequencing for Safe Tool Change (Block 130–150):**
- The **M05 M09** at N120 ensures that the spindle has stopped and coolant is OFF *before* the tool change command.
- The **M06** at N130 triggers the ATC. By this time, the controller has confirmed M05 status, avoiding the "Spindle Not Stopped" alarm.
- The **M19** at N140 orients the spindle to align the tool-key with the ATC gripper. This is critical for proper tool engagement.
- The **M03 S1500 M08** at N150 restarts spindle rotation and coolant flow *after* the new tool is fully clamped.
- Finally, **M05 M09** at N220 and **M30** at N230 end the program safely and rewind the pointer.

This sequence follows the **OEM-standard safe tool-change protocol** and is the canonical answer expected by KTU examiners. *(7 marks.)*

---

## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Rapid Revision Checklist — M-Codes for KTU 2024 Scheme Exam**

- **Definition:** M-Codes are miscellaneous functions that control ON/OFF auxiliary machine operations.
- **Range:** M00 to M99 (standard). Only **one M-Code per block** in ISO 6983 standard.
- **M00** = Unconditional stop. **M01** = Optional stop (toggle dependent).
- **M02** = End of program (no rewind in some controllers). **M30** = End + rewind.
- **M03** = Spindle CW. **M04** = Spindle CCW. **M05** = Spindle stop. **M19** = Spindle orient.
- **M06** = Automatic Tool Change (ATC). Must be preceded by M05.
- **M07** = Mist coolant. **M08** = Flood coolant. **M09** = Coolant OFF.
- **M98** = Subprogram call. **M99** = Subprogram return.
- **Grouping Rule:** M03 and M04 are mutually exclusive — issuing one cancels the other.
- **Buffering:** M00 and M01 are non-buffered (immediate effect); others are buffered (look-ahead).
- **Safe Tool-Change Order:** M05 → M09 → M19 → M06 → M03 S#### → M08.
- **Standard Reference:** ISO 6983 / EIA RS-267.
- **Common Mistake to Avoid:** Writing two M-Codes in the same block; forgetting to recalculate S (rpm) when diameter changes.
- **Polymer / Tool-Room Relevance:** M08 flood coolant is critical for polymer-mould CNC machining to prevent thermal degradation; M19 is used for electrode alignment in EDM of moulds.
- **Pairing:** Always pair M03/M04 with a valid **S-Code** and M07/M08 with a viable coolant pump.

> [!NOTE]
> **Final Examiner Tip:** When asked to "explain the role of M-Codes" in the KTU exam, structure your answer in three layers — (1) *Definition*, (2) *List and describe at least 6 codes*, (3) *Justify their placement in a program block using safe-sequence logic*. This three-layer approach consistently secures full marks under the KTU 2024 Scheme marking scheme.
