## SECTION 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### 1.1 Formal Academic Definition

**CNC Turning Programming** is the process of creating a sequence of coded instructions (known as a part program) that directs a Computer Numerically Controlled (CNC) lathe to perform turning operations such as facing, straight turning, taper turning, contouring, grooving, and threading on a cylindrical workpiece.

According to the **ISO 6983 (DIN 66025)** standard adopted by KTU 2024 scheme, a CNC turning part program is composed of:

- **G-codes (Preparatory codes):** Define the *type of motion* (linear, circular, rapid, etc.).
- **M-codes (Miscellaneous functions):** Define *auxiliary machine actions* (spindle ON/OFF, coolant ON/OFF, tool change, program end).
- **Coordinate words (X, Z):** Define the *tool position* in the turning coordinate system.
- **Feed (F)** and **Spindle Speed (S):** Define the *cutting parameters*.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Definition:** *Programming of simple components in turning* refers to the manual part-programming (also called G-code programming) of axisymmetric parts requiring standard operations like facing, straight turning, taper turning, and grooving on a 2-axis CNC lathe (X-axis = diameter/cross slide, Z-axis = longitudinal axis).

### 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Intuition

Think of writing a CNC program like writing a **recipe for a very literal robot chef**:
- The **G-code** is the *instruction* ("stir clockwise", "cut straight").
- The **X, Z coordinates** are the *exact spot* in the kitchen ("3 cm from the bowl edge").
- The **M-code** is the *kitchen helper's task* ("turn on the stove", "stop the mixer").
- The **F (feed)** is *how fast* you stir, and **S (spindle speed)** is *how fast* the blender rotates.

The machine reads each line (called a **block**) one by one, exactly like following a recipe line-by-line. If you skip a step or give wrong dimensions, the "dish" (your component) will be ruined.

### 1.3 Key Terminology (KTU Board Standard Vocabulary)

| Term | Full Form | KTU Standard Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **NC** | Numerical Control | Hard-wired numeric control (older generation) |
| **CNC** | Computer Numerical Control | Software-based numeric control (modern) |
| **APT** | Automatically Programmed Tools | High-level programming language |
| **DNC** | Distributed Numerical Control | Network-based program transfer |
| **MCP** | Machine Control Panel | Operator interface on the CNC |
| **APC** | Automatic Pallet Changer | Used in advanced turning centers |
| **O-word** | Program Number | Identifies the program (e.g., O0001) |
| **Block** | Line of Program | One complete instruction line |

> [!NOTE]
> **KTU 2024 Exam Tip:** Always begin your program with the **program number (O0001)**, end with **M30**, and include a **safety block** (G21, G40, G80, G99) at the start. Examiners often allocate 2 marks just for the safety block.

### 1.4 Turning Coordinate System (KTU Convention)

The standard CNC turning coordinate system follows the **Right-Hand Rule**:
- **Z-axis:** Along the spindle axis (positive direction = away from chuck towards tailstock).
- **X-axis:** Perpendicular to Z-axis (positive direction = away from the part centerline). Diameter programming is used.
- **X-axis diameter programming:** The value of X represents the **diameter** (2 × radius), not the radius. This is a unique feature of turning.

```
       Z+ (away from chuck)
        ───────────────►
        │
        │ X+ (away from center)
        │
        ▼
       Chuck (Headstock)
```

---

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
## SECTION 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### 2.1 Structural Breakdown of a CNC Turning Program

A standard KTU-style CNC turning part program follows this structure:

1. **Program Header Block** (`O0001`)
2. **Safety / Initialization Block** (`G21 G40 G80 G99`)
3. **Tool Selection Block** (`T0101`)
4. **Coordinate System Selection** (`G54` or `G50`)
5. **Spindle & Coolant ON** (`M03 S1500`, `M08`)
6. **Tool Movement to Start Position** (`G00 X... Z...`)
7. **Cutting Blocks** (`G01`, `G02`, `G03` operations)
8. **Coolant & Spindle OFF** (`M09`, `M05`)
9. **Return to Home / Tool Change** (`G00 X100 Z100`, `T0000`)
10. **Program End** (`M30`)

### 2.2 High-Yield G-Codes for Turning (KTU 2024)

| G-Code | Function | KTU Use Case |
|---|---|---|
| **G00** | Rapid Traverse (non-cutting) | Tool positioning between cuts |
| **G01** | Linear Interpolation (with feed) | Straight turning, facing, taper |
| **G02** | Circular CW interpolation | Convex radii on turned parts |
| **G03** | Circular CCW interpolation | Concave radii on turned parts |
| **G20** | Inch input | Imperial measurements |
| **G21** | Metric input | **Standard in KTU labs** |
| **G28** | Return to Reference Point | Home position return |
| **G40** | Tool Nose Radius Compensation Cancel | Default state |
| **G41** | Tool Nose Radius Compensation Left | Finishing passes |
| **G42** | Tool Nose Radius Compensation Right | Finishing passes |
| **G54-G59** | Work Coordinate System Selection | Multiple set-ups |
| **G90** | Absolute Programming | **Default in KTU 2024** |
| **G91** | Incremental Programming | Sometimes used for roughing |
| **G94** | Feed per Minute (mm/min) | Turning default |
| **G95** | Feed per Revolution (mm/rev) | Turning default on lathes |
| **G96** | Constant Surface Speed | Facing and tapering |
| **G97** | Constant Spindle Speed | **Default for turning** |
| **G98** | Feed per minute (combined with G96) | Used in milling/lathe |
| **G99** | Feed per revolution | **KTU turning default** |

### 2.3 High-Yield M-Codes for Turning (KTU 2024)

| M-Code | Function | When Used |
|---|---|---|
| **M00** | Program Stop | Manual intervention required |
| **M01** | Optional Stop | Operator-activated |
| **M03** | Spindle ON (CW) | Main cutting direction |
| **M04** | Spindle ON (CCW) | Reversed direction (rare) |
| **M05** | Spindle Stop | End of cutting |
| **M06** | Tool Change | For lathes with ATC |
| **M08** | Coolant ON (Flood) | During cutting |
| **M09** | Coolant OFF | After cutting |
| **M10** | Chuck Clamp | Workpiece clamping |
| **M11** | Chuck Unclamp | Workpiece release |
| **M30** | Program End & Rewind | **Always last block** |

### 2.4 KTU Formula Sheet for Turning Calculations

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The following formulas are **mandatory** for any CNC turning problem in KTU 2024 exams.

| Parameter | Formula | Units | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Spindle Speed | $N = \dfrac{V_c \times 1000}{\pi \times D}$ | rpm | $V_c$ in m/min, $D$ in mm |
| Cutting Speed | $V_c = \dfrac{\pi \times D \times N}{1000}$ | m/min |  |
| Feed Rate | $V_f = f \times N$ | mm/min | $f$ in mm/rev |
| Material Removal Rate | $MRR = V_c \times f \times d$ | mm³/min | $d$ = depth of cut |
| Machining Time (Turning) | $t_m = \dfrac{L}{f \times N}$ | min | $L$ = length of cut |
| Machining Time (Facing) | $t_m = \dfrac{\pi (D_i^2 - D_f^2)}{4 \times V_c \times f}$ | min | $D_i$ = initial, $D_f$ = final dia |
| Taper Angle | $\tan \alpha = \dfrac{D_1 - D_2}{2 \times L}$ | degrees |  |
| Chamfer Length | $C = \sqrt{x^2 + z^2}$ | mm | For 45° chamfer, $x = z$ |

**Standard Cutting Parameter Ranges (Mild Steel on HSS):**
- Cutting speed $V_c$ = **25–35 m/min** (HSS) or **150–250 m/min** (Carbide)
- Feed rate $f$ = **0.1–0.5 mm/rev**
- Depth of cut $d$ = **0.5–3 mm**

> [!NOTE]
> **Why these matter in engineering:** In real production, incorrect calculation of spindle speed leads to **tool failure**, **poor surface finish**, or **chatter**. KTU expects students to compute these before writing the program.

---

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
## SECTION 3: Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

### 3.1 Derivation 1: Spindle Speed (N)

The spindle speed is derived from the basic definition of cutting speed: the linear velocity at which the cutting edge engages the workpiece surface.

**Step 1 — Definition:** Cutting speed is the peripheral speed of the workpiece at the cutting point.

$$V_c = \pi \times D \times N$$

where:
- $V_c$ = cutting speed (m/min)
- $D$ = workpiece diameter at cutting point (m)
- $N$ = spindle rotational speed (rpm)

**Step 2 — Unit Conversion:** Since $D$ is given in mm in KTU problems, convert to meters:

$$D_{m} = \dfrac{D_{mm}}{1000}$$

**Step 3 — Substituting into the original equation:**

$$V_c = \pi \times \dfrac{D_{mm}}{1000} \times N$$

**Step 4 — Solving for N:**

$$\boxed{N = \dfrac{V_c \times 1000}{\pi \times D_{mm}}}$$

**Worked Example (KTU Style):** Calculate spindle speed for turning mild steel of 50 mm diameter with carbide insert, $V_c$ = 200 m/min.

$$\begin{aligned}
N &= \dfrac{200 \times 1000}{\pi \times 50} \\
  &= \dfrac{200000}{157.08} \\
  &= 1273.24 \text{ rpm}
\end{aligned}$$

The machine will accept **S1273** (rounded to nearest integer on most controllers).

### 3.2 Derivation 2: Feed Rate ($V_f$)

Feed rate is the linear speed at which the tool advances along the cutting direction.

**Step 1 — Definition:** Feed per revolution ($f$) is the distance the tool moves in one spindle rotation.

**Step 2 — Total linear travel per minute:**

$$V_f = f \times N$$

**Step 3 — Substituting N from Derivation 3.1:**

$$\begin{aligned}
V_f &= f \times \dfrac{V_c \times 1000}{\pi \times D} \\
    &= \dfrac{f \times V_c \times 1000}{\pi \times D}
\end{aligned}$$

**Worked Example:** For $f = 0.2$ mm/rev and $N = 1273$ rpm:

$$\begin{aligned}
V_f &= 0.2 \times 1273 \\
    &= 254.6 \text{ mm/min}
\end{aligned}$$

The CNC will accept **F254.6** (or rounded **F255**).

### 3.3 Derivation 3: Machining Time for Straight Turning

For a simple straight turning operation from diameter $D_i$ to $D_f$ over length $L$:

**Step 1 — Length traversed per revolution:** $f$ mm

**Step 2 — Number of revolutions required:** $\dfrac{L}{f}$

**Step 3 — Time per revolution:** $\dfrac{1}{N}$ minutes

**Step 4 — Total machining time:**

$$\boxed{t_m = \dfrac{L}{f \times N}}$$

**Worked Example:** $L = 100$ mm, $f = 0.2$ mm/rev, $N = 1273$ rpm:

$$\begin{aligned}
t_m &= \dfrac{100}{0.2 \times 1273} \\
    &= \dfrac{100}{254.6} \\
    &= 0.393 \text{ min} \\
    &= 23.55 \text{ seconds}
\end{aligned}$$

### 3.4 Derivation 4: Machining Time for Facing

For facing from initial diameter $D_i$ to final diameter $D_f$:

**Step 1 — Area of material removed:**

$$A = \dfrac{\pi}{4} (D_i^2 - D_f^2)$$

**Step 2 — Using MRR relationship:** $MRR = V_c \times f \times d$

The depth of cut $d$ for facing = radial step. In a single pass from edge to center:

**Step 3 — Time:**

$$\boxed{t_m = \dfrac{\pi (D_i^2 - D_f^2)}{4 \times V_c \times f}}$$

### 3.5 Analytical Decision Matrix: When to Use Each Code

| Scenario | Recommended Code | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Tool needs to move fast, no cutting | **G00** | Saves time, no feed engaged |
| Straight cutting at controlled rate | **G01** | Maintains constant feed |
| External convex arc | **G02** (CW) | Direction matches spindle CW + tool outside |
| External concave arc | **G03** (CCW) | Direction matches spindle CW + tool inside |
| Programming from part zero | **G90** | KTU default for clarity |
| Taper or chamfer | **G01** with X & Z both | Single linear move |
| Final finishing pass | **G41/G42** | Compensates for tool nose radius |
| Multi-rep operations | **Subprograms (M98/M99)** | Modular programming |

### 3.6 Complete Worked Program — Simple Stepped Shaft

**Component:** Mild steel shaft, Ø40 mm × 80 mm long.
**Operations:** Face one end, turn Ø30 from Z=0 to Z=40, then Ø25 from Z=40 to Z=70, chamfer at Z=70, part off.

**Calculations:**
- $D = 40$ mm, $V_c = 200$ m/min → $N = \dfrac{200000}{\pi \times 40} = 1591.5$ → **S1600**
- $f = 0.2$ mm/rev → $V_f = 0.2 \times 1600 = 320$ → **F0.2** (G99 mode)

**Part Program (ISO Format):**

```
O0001;
G21 G40 G80 G99;          (SAFETY BLOCK)
T0101;                     (T01: RH Turning Tool, Offset 01)
M03 S1600;                 (SPINDLE CW AT 1600 RPM)
M08;                       (FLOOD COOLANT ON)
G00 X42.0 Z2.0;            (RAPID TO START POINT)
G01 X-1.0 Z0 F0.2;         (FACE TO CENTRE, FEED 0.2)
G00 X40.0 Z2.0;            (RETRACT)
G01 Z-40.0 F0.2;           (TURN Ø40 to length 40mm)
G00 X32.0;                 (STEP TO Ø32 APPROACH)
G01 Z-40.0 F0.2;           (TURN Ø30 from Z=-40 to Z=0) [note: X30 means diameter 30]
G00 X32.0;                 (RETRACT IN X)
G00 Z2.0;                  (RETURN ALONG Z)
G01 X30.0;                 (APPROACH Ø30)
G01 Z-40.0 F0.2;           (TURN Ø30)
G00 X32.0;                 (RETRACT)
G00 Z-35.0;                (APPROACH FOR Ø25)
G01 X27.0;                 (APPROACH Ø27 BEFORE Ø25)
G01 X25.0 Z-70.0 F0.2;     (TURN Ø25 OVER 35MM LENGTH)
G01 X30.0 Z-72.0 F0.1;     (45° CHAMFER 2×2)
G00 X100.0 Z100.0;         (GO HOME)
M09;                       (COOLANT OFF)
M05;                       (SPINDLE STOP)
M30;                       (PROGRAM END)
```

## SECTION 5: KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

### 5.1 Part A Questions (3 Marks Each)

**Q1. [KTU University Exam – May 2024]**
*Define part programming. List any four preparatory codes used in CNC turning.*

**Model Answer:**
Part programming is the process of preparing a coded list of instructions (the part program) that a CNC controller interprets to perform machining operations on a workpiece.

Four preparatory G-codes used in CNC turning:
1. **G00** – Rapid traverse (positioning at maximum rate).
2. **G01** – Linear interpolation with controlled feed (straight cutting).
3. **G02** – Circular interpolation, clockwise direction.
4. **G03** – Circular interpolation, counter-clockwise direction.

(Other valid: G21, G40, G90, G94, G95, G96, G97, G99.)

---

**Q2. [KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]**
*State the functions of the following codes: (i) M03 (ii) M08 (iii) M30.*

**Model Answer:**
- **(i) M03** – Spindle ON in clockwise (forward) rotation. Used during all normal turning operations.
- **(ii) M08** – Flood coolant ON. Activates the coolant pump for cutting fluid delivery.
- **(iii) M30** – Program end and rewind. Stops program execution, rewinds to start, and resets registers.

---

### 5.2 Part B Questions (14 Marks Each — Internal Choice)

#### **Question A (14 Marks) [KTU University Exam – May 2024 Model]**

**(a)** A mild steel component of initial diameter 50 mm and length 120 mm is to be turned to a final diameter of 40 mm over a length of 80 mm. Calculate the following for an HSS tool: cutting speed $V_c = 30$ m/min and feed $f = 0.25$ mm/rev. **(7 marks)**
   (i) Spindle speed N
   (ii) Feed rate $V_f$ in mm/min
   (iii) Machining time $t_m$
   (iv) Material removal rate MRR (depth of cut = 5 mm)

**(b)** Write a complete ISO part program to perform the above turning operation. Use safety block, tool T0101, and follow the program structure taught in KTU Module 2. **(7 marks)**

---

##### **Model Solution for Question A (a):**

**(i) Spindle Speed N:**

$$N = \dfrac{V_c \times 1000}{\pi \times D}$$

For the initial diameter $D = 50$ mm (roughing):

$$\begin{aligned}
N &= \dfrac{30 \times 1000}{\pi \times 50} \\
  &= \dfrac{30000}{157.08} \\
  &= 191 \text{ rpm}
\end{aligned}$$

For the final pass at $D = 40$ mm:

$$\begin{aligned}
N &= \dfrac{30 \times 1000}{\pi \times 40} \\
  &= \dfrac{30000}{125.66} \\
  &= 238.7 \approx 239 \text{ rpm}
\end{aligned}$$

Average N ≈ **215 rpm** (or design uses N = 191 rpm for safety).

**(ii) Feed Rate $V_f$:**

$$V_f = f \times N = 0.25 \times 191 = 47.75 \text{ mm/min}$$

**Answer: $V_f = 47.75$ mm/min**

**(iii) Machining Time $t_m$:**

$$t_m = \dfrac{L}{f \times N} = \dfrac{80}{0.25 \times 191}$$

$$t_m = \dfrac{80}{47.75} = 1.676 \text{ min} \approx 100.5 \text{ seconds}$$

**(iv) Material Removal Rate MRR:**

$$\begin{aligned}
MRR &= V_c \times f \times d \\
    &= 30000 \text{ mm/min} \times 0.25 \text{ mm/rev} \times 5 \text{ mm} \\
    &= 37500 \text{ mm}^3/\text{min}
\end{aligned}$$

(Note: $V_c$ converted to mm/min = 30000.)

##### **Model Solution for Question A (b):**

```
O0001;
G21 G40 G80 G99;              (Safety Block - Metric, No Comp, No Cycle, Feed/rev)
T0101;                          (Select RH Turning Tool, Offset 01)
M03 S191;                       (Spindle CW at 191 rpm)
M08;                            (Coolant ON)
G00 X52.0 Z2.0;                 (Rapid to start, X = 52 i.e. 2mm above Ø50)
G01 X50.0 Z0 F0.25;             (Approach face at Ø50)
G01 Z-80.0 F0.25;               (Turn Ø50 → wait, this is wrong)
```

**CORRECTED PROGRAM:**

```
O0001;
G21 G40 G80 G99;              (Safety Block)
T0101;                          (Turning Tool)
M03 S191;
M08;
G00 X52.0 Z2.0;                 (Approach start position)
G00 X50.0 Z0;                   (Move to face at Ø50)
G01 X40.0 Z0 F0.25;             (Face to Ø40 if facing included - optional)
G00 X52.0 Z2.0;                 (Retract for turning pass)
G00 X42.0;                      (Approach Ø42)
G01 X40.0 Z-80.0 F0.25;         (Turn from Ø50 to Ø40 over 80mm)
G00 X52.0;                      (Retract)
G00 Z2.0;                       (Return to Z start)
G00 X100.0 Z100.0;              (Home position)
M09;
M05;
M30;
```

---

#### **Question B (14 Marks) [KTU University Exam – Dec 2023 Model]**

**(a)** Explain with a neat sketch the **CNC turning coordinate system**. State the difference between **G90 and G91** programming modes. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** For a taper turning operation, the start diameter is 60 mm at Z = 0 and the end diameter is 40 mm at Z = -50 mm. Calculate the taper ratio and the included angle. Also, write the corresponding G-code block using G01. **(7 marks)**

---

##### **Model Solution for Question B (a):**

**CNC Turning Coordinate System:**
The standard CNC turning machine follows the right-hand rule with two linear axes:
- **Z-axis**: Lies along the spindle centerline. Positive direction is **away from the chuck**, towards the tailstock.
- **X-axis**: Perpendicular to the Z-axis. Positive direction is **radially outward** from the part centerline. **X is programmed as diameter.**

Origin (Program Zero) is typically set at the **center of the finished face** of the workpiece.

**Diagram (described):**
```
                    Z+
        ───────────────────────────►
        │         Tailstock
        │           ┃
   X+   │           ┃
   ┌────┤       ┌───┴───┐
   │    │       │PART   │
   │    │       │ Ø=Dia │ (Spindle & Chuck on left)
   ▼    │       └───────┘
  Chuck │           Z=0 (origin at face center)
```

**Difference between G90 and G91:**

| Aspect | G90 (Absolute) | G91 (Incremental) |
|---|---|---|
| Reference | All coordinates from **program zero** | All coordinates from **current tool position** |
| Programming | Easier to read and debug | Compact for repeated moves |
| Error propagation | Errors do not accumulate | Errors accumulate move-to-move |
| KTU 2024 default | **Default mode** | Used in special cases |
| Example | G01 X30.0 Z-40.0 | G01 U-20.0 W-40.0 |

##### **Model Solution for Question B (b):**

**Taper Ratio:**
Taper per unit length = $\dfrac{D_1 - D_2}{L} = \dfrac{60 - 40}{50} = \dfrac{20}{50} = 0.4$ mm/mm

Or expressed as **1 in 2.5** (since $\dfrac{L}{D_1 - D_2} = \dfrac{50}{20} = 2.5$).

**Included Taper Angle:**

$$\begin{aligned}
\tan \alpha &= \dfrac{D_1 - D_2}{2L} \\
\tan \alpha &= \dfrac{60 - 40}{2 \times 50} = \dfrac{20}{100} = 0.2
\end{aligned}$$

$$\alpha = \tan^{-1}(0.2) = 11.31°$$

**Included angle** (full taper, both sides) = $2\alpha = 22.62°$.

**G-code Block (Absolute Programming, G90):**

```
G01 X40.0 Z-50.0 F0.2;
```

(Start at X60 Z0, move to X40 Z-50 in a single linear interpolation.)

**Incremental version (G91):**
```
G91;
G01 U-20.0 W-50.0 F0.2;
G90;
```

---

### 5.3 KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Mistakes Where KTU Students Lose Marks:**
>
> 1. **Forgetting the safety block** (G21 G40 G80 G99) at the start — examiners deduct **2 marks** consistently. Always include it.
>
> 2. **Confusing G02 and G03 direction** in turning. For turning with **spindle CW (M03)**, an *external* convex curve uses **G02**. Internal concave curve also uses **G02**. The direction is judged by looking **along the +Z axis** (from tailstock towards chuck).
>
> 3. **Wrong unit usage:** Mixing inches and metric. **Always state G21** explicitly. Don't assume default.
>
> 4. **Forgetting to retract the tool** before returning to home — causes **tool-workpiece collision** in lab exams.
>
> 5. **Not specifying the feed mode** (G98/G99). KTU turning default is **G99 (feed per revolution)**. Without this, the F value is interpreted as mm/min.
>
> 6. **Writing only M30 without prior M05 and M09** — program ends abruptly. Always stop spindle and coolant first.
>
> 7. **Spelling errors in M-codes** like M8 instead of M08 — most controllers reject the program. Always use **two-digit codes**.
>
> 8. **Decimal point errors:** Writing X40 instead of X40.0. Modern controllers may interpret as 40 microns if decimal point is omitted — disaster in exams.

---

### 5.4 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!NOTE]
> **Rapid Revision Checklist — Programming of Simple Components in Turning**
>
> ✅ **Standard Program Order:** Safety Block → Tool Selection → Spindle & Coolant ON → Rapid Approach → Cutting → Retract → Spindle & Coolant OFF → Home → M30.
>
> ✅ **Always include safety block:** `G21 G40 G80 G99` (metric, no comp, no canned cycle, feed/rev).
>
> ✅ **X-axis is diameter-programmed** in turning (not radius) — unique to lathes.
>
> ✅ **Tool nose radius compensation (G41/G42):** Use only for finishing passes, not roughing.
>
> ✅ **Standard feeds for turning:** 0.1–0.5 mm/rev (roughing: high; finishing: low).
>
> ✅ **Standard cutting speeds:** HSS = 25–35 m/min, Carbide = 150–250 m/min (for mild steel).
>
> ✅ **M30 is mandatory last block** — never use M00 or M01 as program end.
>
> ✅ **G02 = CW** and **G03 = CCW** when viewed from the **+Z direction** (looking from tailstock to chuck).
>
> ✅ **Taper angle formula:** $\tan \alpha = \dfrac{D_1 - D_2}{2L}$ — divide by 2 because X is diameter.
>
> ✅ **Spindle speed calculation:** Always round DOWN to nearest available machine rpm — never round up (causes tool wear).
>
> ✅ **Chamfer block:** For 2 mm × 45° chamfer ending at X = 30, Z = -70, write: `G01 X30.0 Z-72.0 F0.1` (if coming from Ø25).
>
> ✅ **Tool position home:** Standard is **X100 Z100** — confirm with your lab machine manual.
>
> ✅ **MRR formula:** $MRR = V_c \times f \times d$ — multiplied in consistent units (mm³/min if all in mm and min).

---

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
# 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Drilling — Formal Definition

> [!NOTE]
> **Drilling** is a **subtractive machining process** that uses a **multi-point cutting tool** (typically a *twist drill*) to produce a **cylindrical hole** of a specified diameter and depth in a solid workpiece by a combination of **rotary motion** (primary motion) and **axial linear motion** (secondary motion/feed).

In KTU 2024 scheme terminology, drilling is classified under the umbrella of **hole-making operations** in conventional machining. It is the most common secondary operation performed on cast, forged, or rolled stock components.

**Conceptual Analogy (Intuition):**
Imagine a carpenter using a hand auger to bore a hole into a wooden plank. He rotates the handle (rotary motion) while simultaneously pushing downward along the axis (feed motion). The cutting lips at the tip scrape away chips, and a continuous spiral groove carries the chips upward and out of the hole. A **drilling machine** does exactly the same thing — but with rigid precision, calibrated feeds, and far greater power. The *twist drill* is essentially the engineered, industrial counterpart of the carpenter's auger.

## 1.2 Milling — Formal Definition

> [!NOTE]
> **Milling** is a **subtractive machining process** that uses a **rotating multi-point cutter** (having one or more teeth) to progressively remove material from the surface of a workpiece. The cutter rotates about a fixed axis (primary motion), while the workpiece is fed against it (secondary motion) along one or more axes.

Milling is the **most versatile** of all conventional machining processes because, by changing the cutter geometry and feed direction, almost any profile — flat surfaces, slots, gears, splines, helical grooves — can be generated.

**Conceptual Analogy (Intuition):**
Picture a circular saw blade spinning rapidly. As you push a log into the spinning blade, the teeth of the blade shave off thin layers of wood one after another. Each tooth acts as a tiny single-point cutter. A **milling cutter** is essentially a multi-toothed circular blade on a rigid arbor, and the **workpiece** (held on a moving table) is the "log" that gets progressively shaped.

## 1.3 Key Physical Constants & Standard Metrics

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The two dominant kinematic quantities in any drilling or milling operation are:
> - **Cutting Speed (V)** — measured in **m/min** or **m/s**
> - **Feed (f)** — measured in **mm/rev** (drilling) or **mm/tooth** (milling)
>
> These are the **inputs** that a KTU examiner expects you to compute first; all downstream quantities (spindle speed, MRR, power, time) follow from them.

| Quantity | Symbol | Standard Unit | KTU 2024 Notation |
|----------|--------|---------------|-------------------|
| Cutting Speed | $V$ | m/min | m/min |
| Spindle Speed | $N$ | rev/min (rpm) | rpm |
| Feed per revolution | $f_r$ | mm/rev | mm/rev |
| Feed per tooth | $f_z$ | mm/tooth | mm/tooth |
| Depth of cut | $d$ | mm | mm |
| Diameter | $D$ | mm | mm |
| Number of teeth | $Z$ | — | — |
| Material Removal Rate | $Z_w$ (MRR) | mm³/min | cm³/min or mm³/s |

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 Drilling — Operational Breakdown

A **twist drill** is the standard drilling tool. It consists of three functional zones:

1. **Point / Cutting End** — Contains the cutting lips (shearing) and the chisel edge (extrusion). The point angle is typically **118°** for general-purpose steels, **135°** for hardened alloys.
2. **Body / Flute Region** — Contains helical flutes (helix angle ≈ **24°–32°**) that evacuate chips and admit cutting fluid.
3. **Shank / Tang** — Provides holding (straight shank for small drills, Morse taper shank for larger drills).

### 2.1.1 Drilling Kinematic Logic (Step-by-Step)

- **Step 1:** The workpiece is clamped on the drill press table (or a vice).
- **Step 2:** The drill is held in the spindle chuck and rotated at a calculated spindle speed $N$.
- **Step 3:** The drill is fed axially downward at a prescribed feed rate.
- **Step 4:** The two cutting lips engage the workpiece; the chisel edge pushes material aside, generating continuous spiral chips that travel up the flutes.
- **Step 5:** A through hole (or blind hole) of diameter $D$ and depth $L$ is produced.

> [!NOTE]
> **Why is the cutting speed measured at the drill periphery?**
> Because that is where the actual cutting occurs. The point and the central chisel edge move much slower (the centre is at zero velocity). All KTU spindle-speed calculations therefore use the **diameter $D$** at the outer cutting lip.

### 2.1.2 Types of Drilling Machines (KTU Syllabus Highlight)

| Type | Typical Use | KTU Exam Note |
|------|-------------|---------------|
| **Bench drilling machine** | Small workpieces, light duty | Max spindle speed ≈ 3000 rpm |
| **Upright / Pillar drill** | Medium workpieces | Vertical column with table |
| **Radial drilling machine** | Large/heavy workpieces | Spindle slides along radial arm |
| **Gang drill** | Multi-operation production | Multiple spindles on one column |
| **Multi-spindle drill** | Mass production | Several drills operate in parallel |
| **Deep-hole drilling machine** | L/D > 10 (gun barrels) | High-pressure coolant through tool |

## 2.2 Milling — Operational Breakdown

Milling cutters have **multiple teeth** arranged around the periphery (and sometimes the face) of a cylindrical body. Each tooth engages and disengages the workpiece **cyclically** as the cutter rotates.

### 2.2.1 The Two Cardinal Milling Modes (HIGH-YIELD KTU TOPIC)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Up Milling (Conventional Milling):**
> - Cutter rotation **opposes** feed direction.
> - Tooth starts cutting with **maximum chip thickness** and ends with **zero chip thickness**.
> - Chip slides **up** the tooth face → rubbing → poor surface finish.
> - Tends to lift the workpiece off the table → safer for **clamped / no-zero-clearance** setups.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Down Milling (Climb Milling):**
> - Cutter rotation **matches** feed direction.
> - Tooth starts with **zero chip thickness**, ends with maximum.
> - Shear starts cleanly → better surface finish, lower power.
> - Pulls the workpiece **into** the cutter → **requires backlash-free table** (only on CNC/KK machines in KTU labs).

### 2.2.2 Types of Milling Machines

| Type | Feature | Typical Application |
|------|---------|---------------------|
| **Column-and-knee type** (Plain/Horizontal/Universal) | Knee moves table vertically; overarm supports arbor | Tool-room, batch production |
| **Bed-type / Fixed-bed** | Table slides on a fixed bed; rigid | Heavy-duty production |
| **Turret-type / Ram-type** | Spindle mounted on ram; versatile head orientation | Tool-room, die making |
| **Planer-type (double-column)** | Large table, vertical spindles | Machining long, flat surfaces |
| **CNC milling centre** | 3+ axes computer-controlled | Modern industry (KTU 2024 emphasis) |

### 2.2.3 Common Milling Cutters (KTU Identification)

- **Plain milling cutter** — Cylindrical periphery teeth → produces flat surfaces parallel to the cutter axis.
- **Side-and-face milling cutter** — Teeth on periphery **and** both sides → slots, deep slots.
- **End mill** — Teeth on periphery **and** end face → pockets, slots, profiling.
- **Face milling cutter** — Large diameter, inserts on face → facing flat surfaces.
- **Slot drill (two-lip end mill)** — End-cutting, plunge-capable → key slots, T-slots.
- **Form milling cutter** — Tooth profile matches desired profile → gear teeth, splines.
- **Fly cutter** — Single-point tool on a holder → large-diameter facing.

## 2.3 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **The "Golden Four" Formulas for Both Drilling and Milling** (Every KTU problem starts here.)

| # | Quantity | Formula | Units | Notes |
|---|----------|---------|-------|-------|
| 1 | Cutting speed | $V = \dfrac{\pi D N}{1000}$ | m/min | $D$ in mm, $N$ in rpm |
| 2 | Spindle speed | $N = \dfrac{1000 \, V}{\pi D}$ | rpm | Inverse of #1 |
| 3 | Feed rate | $V_f = f_r \times N$ (drilling) or $f_z \times Z \times N$ (milling) | mm/min | $Z$ = no. of teeth |
| 4 | Material Removal Rate | $\text{MRR} = \pi/4 \cdot D^2 \cdot f_r \cdot N$ (drilling); $\text{MRR} = w \cdot d \cdot V_f$ (milling) | mm³/min | $w$ = width, $d$ = depth |

### 2.3.1 Extended Formula Table — Machining Time & Power

| Quantity | Formula | Units |
|----------|---------|-------|
| **Machining time (drilling)** | $T_m = \dfrac{L}{f_r \cdot N} = \dfrac{L}{V_f}$ | min |
| **Machining time (milling)** | $T_m = \dfrac{L + l_a + l_o}{V_f}$ | min |
| **Specific cutting energy** | $K_c$ (given in tables) | N·mm⁻² or J/mm³ |
| **Power at cutter** | $P_c = \dfrac{\text{MRR} \times K_c}{60 \times 10^3}$ (for mm³/s MRR) | kW |
| **Total power / motor power** | $P_m = \dfrac{P_c}{\eta}$ | kW |
| **Feed force (milling)** | $F_f \approx \text{MRR} \times k_c$ / (peripheral) | N |
| **Average chip thickness** | $h_m = \dfrac{2 \, V_f}{N \, Z \, \sqrt{D^2 - D \cos\theta}}$ ... use $h_m = \dfrac{f_z \sin\kappa}{\cos\lambda}$ for face milling | mm |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Key Engineering Constants to Memorise:**
> - $\pi \approx 3.1416$
> - Mechanical efficiency of machine tool: **$\eta \approx 0.7$ to $0.85$** (use **$\eta = 0.8$** if not specified)
> - Standard drill point angle: **118°** (general), **135°** (hardened)
> - Standard helix angle: **30°** (general)

## 2.4 Real-World Utility

- **Drilling** is the workhorse for assembly — every bolted joint in a car, aircraft, or machine originates from a drilled hole.
- **Milling** is the workhorse for **shape generation** — engine blocks, gear blanks, mould cavities, aerospace structural components.
- In modern KTU-aligned industry, both processes are dominated by **CNC machining centres**, but the underlying kinematic formulas are **unchanged**.
- These processes determine **cycle time, energy consumption, tool life, and surface integrity** — directly impacting manufacturing cost and quality.

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Derivation of Cutting Speed (V) and Spindle Speed (N)

### 3.1.1 Starting Concept

When a cutter of diameter $D$ rotates at $N$ revolutions per minute, a point on the periphery traces a circular path of circumference $\pi D$ per revolution.

### 3.1.2 Derivation (Exhaustive, Line-by-Line)

**Step 1:** Distance travelled by the periphery in **one revolution** = circumference of the cutter.

$$
\text{Distance per rev} = \pi D
$$

**Step 2:** Distance travelled in **$N$ revolutions** (i.e., 1 minute).

$$
\text{Distance per min} = N \times \pi D
$$

**Step 3:** This distance is the **cutting speed** $V$ (defined as the linear velocity of the cutter periphery relative to the workpiece), but $D$ is in mm and $N$ is in rpm. To express $V$ in **m/min**, divide by 1000.

$$
V_{\text{(m/min)}} = \frac{\pi D_{\text{(mm)}} \times N_{\text{(rpm)}}}{1000}
$$

**Step 4:** Rearranging for spindle speed $N$ (used when cutting speed is specified).

$$
N = \frac{1000 \, V}{\pi D}
$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Dimensional Check:** $D$ in mm, $N$ in rev/min. The product $\pi D N$ gives mm/min. Dividing by 1000 converts to m/min. ✓

## 3.2 Derivation of Feed Rate

### 3.2.1 Drilling — Feed Rate

In drilling, **$f_r$** is the **feed per revolution** in mm/rev. In one revolution, the drill advances axially by $f_r$. In $N$ revolutions (one minute), the axial advance is:

$$
V_f = f_r \times N \quad [\text{mm/min}]
$$

### 3.2.2 Milling — Feed Rate

In milling, **$f_z$** is the **feed per tooth** in mm/tooth. In one revolution, the cutter has $Z$ teeth engaging, each feeding $f_z$, so the feed per revolution is $f_r = f_z \cdot Z$. In one minute:

$$
V_f = f_r \times N = f_z \times Z \times N \quad [\text{mm/min}]
$$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Common KTU Trap:** Students often confuse $f_r$ (mm/rev) and $f_z$ (mm/tooth). In **drilling**, you are given $f_r$ directly. In **milling**, you are usually given $f_z$.

## 3.3 Derivation of Material Removal Rate (MRR)

### 3.3.1 MRR in Drilling

The drill sweeps an annular footprint, but the actual undeformed chip cross-section per revolution equals the **area of the cylindrical hole** produced per revolution.

$$
\text{Area} = \frac{\pi}{4} D^2
$$

Volume removed per revolution = Area × axial advance per rev:

$$
\text{Volume/rev} = \frac{\pi}{4} D^2 \times f_r
$$

Volume removed per minute (multiply by $N$):

$$
\boxed{\text{MRR}_{\text{drill}} = \frac{\pi}{4} \, D^2 \, f_r \, N \quad [\text{mm}^3/\text{min}]}
$$

**Numerical Example (KTU-style):**
Given: $D = 20$ mm, $f_r = 0.2$ mm/rev, $N = 500$ rpm.

$$
\text{MRR} = \frac{\pi}{4} \times 20^2 \times 0.2 \times 500
$$

$$
= \frac{3.1416}{4} \times 400 \times 0.2 \times 500
$$

$$
= 0.7854 \times 400 \times 100
$$

$$
= 31416 \text{ mm}^3/\text{min} \approx 31.4 \text{ cm}^3/\text{min}
$$

### 3.3.2 MRR in Milling

In peripheral milling (up or down), the cutter removes a chip of **width $w$** (radial depth, perpendicular to feed) and **thickness determined by feed/tooth $f_z$**. The undeformed chip cross-section per tooth per revolution ≈ $w \times h_m$, where $h_m$ is the average chip thickness. The standard KTU formula is:

$$
\boxed{\text{MRR}_{\text{mill}} = w \times d \times V_f \quad [\text{mm}^3/\text{min}]}
$$

where:
- $w$ = width of cut (mm)
- $d$ = depth of cut (mm)
- $V_f$ = table feed (mm/min)

**Derivation logic:** In one minute, the workpiece advances $V_f$ mm. The cutter is removing a "strip" of width $w$ and thickness $d$. The volume of that strip = cross-sectional area × length = $w \times d \times V_f$.

## 3.4 Derivation of Machining Time

### 3.4.1 Drilling

The drill must travel an axial distance equal to the **hole depth $L$** at a feed rate $V_f$ mm/min.

$$
\boxed{T_m = \frac{L}{V_f} = \frac{L}{f_r \cdot N} \quad [\text{min}]}
$$

### 3.4.2 Milling (with Approach and Overrun)

In milling, the cutter is circular and must "engage" before the workpiece reaches the desired length $L$ and "disengage" after. An **approach distance $l_a$** and **overrun distance $l_o$** must be added.

$$
\boxed{T_m = \frac{L + l_a + l_o}{V_f} \quad [\text{min}]}
$$

Approximation for a plain milling cutter of diameter $D$ and depth $d$:

$$
l_a \approx \sqrt{d(D - d)} \quad \text{[mm]}
$$

## 3.5 Analytical Matrix — Quick Lookup (Drilling vs Milling)

| Parameter | Drilling | Milling |
|-----------|----------|---------|
| Primary motion | Drill rotates | Cutter rotates |
| Secondary motion | Drill feeds axially | Workpiece (or cutter) translates |
| Multi-point? | Yes (2 lips) | Yes (Z teeth) |
| Typical cutting speed $V$ | 20–80 m/min (steel) | 20–200 m/min (steel) |
| Typical feed | $f_r = 0.05$–$0.5$ mm/rev | $f_z = 0.05$–$0.5$ mm/tooth |
| MRR formula | $\frac{\pi}{4} D^2 f_r N$ | $w \cdot d \cdot V_f$ |
| Time formula | $L / V_f$ | $(L + l_a + l_o) / V_f$ |
| Chip flow | Up the flutes (continuous spiral) | Discontinuous (per-tooth) |

# 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics

## 4.1 Drilling — Block-Level Functional Architecture

The following Mermaid block diagram maps the **functional architecture** of a typical drilling system, including the kinematic chain from motor to cutting edge.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    M[Electric Motor] -->|P_m kW| GB[Gearbox]
    GB -->|Spindle N rpm| SP[Spindle + Chuck]
    SP -->|Torque + Rotation| DR[Twist Drill]
    DR -->|Cutting at lips| WK[Workpiece]
    AX[Feed Lever / Rack] -->|Axial feed f_r| SP
    CL[Coolant Pump] -->|Cutting fluid| DR
    WK -.->|Chips + heat| CL
```

**Reading the diagram:**
- The **Motor** provides raw mechanical power $P_m$.
- The **Gearbox** reduces speed and multiplies torque, outputting spindle rotation $N$.
- The **Spindle + Chuck** holds the drill and provides the rotational primary motion.
- The **Feed Lever / Rack** converts manual/auto input into axial feed.
- The **Coolant Pump** circulates cutting fluid to reduce heat and flush chips.

## 4.2 Milling — Block-Level Functional Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    M2[Main Motor] --> TR[Transmission Box]
    TR --> AR[Arbor / Spindle]
    AR --> CUT[Milling Cutter Z teeth]
    CUT -->|Rotates at N rpm| WP[Workpiece on Table]
    TB[Table Feed Drive] -->|V_f mm/min| TBL[Sliding Table]
    TBL --> WP
    CL2[Coolant Nozzle] --> CUT
    WP -.->|Generated chips| CHIP[Chip Pan + Conveyor]
```

## 4.3 Up Milling vs Down Milling — Cutter–Workpiece Geometry

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph UM["UP MILLING Conventional"]
        U1[Workpiece moves RIGHT] --> U2[Cutter rotates COUNTER-CLOCKWISE]
        U2 -.Thick-to-thin chip.-> U3[Lift on entry]
    end
    subgraph DM["DOWN MILLING Climb"]
        D1[Workpiece moves RIGHT] --> D2[Cutter rotates CLOCKWISE]
        D2 -.Thin-to-thick chip.-> D3[Pull on entry]
    end
```

## 4.4 Drill Geometry — Anatomy of a Twist Drill

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    PT[Point - 118 deg point angle] --> LP[Cutting Lips - 2]
    LP --> CE[Chisel Edge - centre]
    PT --> FL[Flutes - helical 30 deg]
    FL --> MR[Margins - guidance]
    MR --> BK[Body]
    BK --> SH[Shank - Tang or Taper]
    SH --> TL[Tolerance Land]
```

# 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

### Q1. `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]`

**Differentiate between up-milling and down-milling. State any two advantages of down-milling.**

**Model Answer:**
In **up milling (conventional milling)**, the cutter rotates against the direction of feed; chip thickness decreases from maximum to zero per tooth engagement; the tooth tends to rub against the machined surface, producing poorer surface finish; the cutter tends to lift the workpiece — safer with backlashy machines.

In **down milling (climb milling)**, the cutter rotates in the same direction as feed; chip thickness increases from zero to maximum; shearing action is cleaner producing **better surface finish**; **lower power consumption**; longer tool life; chips are thrown behind the cutter. Disadvantage: requires backlash-free table to avoid workpiece being pulled into the cutter.

**Advantages of Down Milling:**
1. Better surface finish (clean shearing, no rubbing).
2. Lower power consumption due to thinner initial chip and reduced rubbing.

*(Marks split: 1.5 for difference + 1.5 for advantages)*

### Q2. `[KTU University Exam - May 2024]`

**List the various types of drilling machines used in the industry. Mention any two specific applications.**

**Model Answer:**
1. **Bench-type drilling machine** — small holes, light-duty work, instrument components.
2. **Upright / pillar drill** — medium-size workpieces, general workshop.
3. **Radial drilling machine** — large and heavy workpieces, e.g., boiler shells, large flanges.
4. **Gang drilling machine** — multi-operation production (drill, ream, tap in sequence).
5. **Multi-spindle drill** — mass production (automotive cylinder blocks).
6. **Deep-hole drilling machine** — long, slender holes (gun barrels, oil-pipe strings).
7. **CNC drilling/tapping centre** — automated production lines.

*(Any two specific applications earn full credit.)*

---

## 5.2 Part B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks, Internal Choice)

### Question A (14 Marks) — **[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023, Modified]**

**(a)** A hole of **25 mm diameter** and **60 mm depth** is to be drilled in a mild-steel workpiece using a HSS twist drill. The recommended cutting speed is **$V = 25$ m/min** and the feed is **$f_r = 0.15$ mm/rev**. Calculate:
1. Spindle speed $N$ in rpm.
2. Feed rate $V_f$ in mm/min.
3. Material removal rate (MRR) in mm³/min and cm³/min.
4. Machining time $T_m$ in seconds.
5. Theoretical power required if the unit cutting energy for mild steel is **$K_c = 2000$ N/mm²** and machine efficiency is **$\eta = 0.8$**.

**(b)** With a neat sketch, explain the **geometry of a twist drill** and label the **point angle, lips, chisel edge, flutes, helix angle, and shank**.

---

### Step-by-Step Model Solution to Q-A

**(a) Solution:**

**Step 1: Spindle speed**

$$
N = \frac{1000 \, V}{\pi D} = \frac{1000 \times 25}{\pi \times 25}
$$

$$
N = \frac{25000}{78.54} \approx 318.3 \text{ rpm}
$$

Rounded to **$N \approx 318$ rpm** (or 320 rpm in practical use).

**Step 2: Feed rate**

$$
V_f = f_r \times N = 0.15 \times 318.3
$$

$$
V_f \approx 47.75 \text{ mm/min} \approx 47.8 \text{ mm/min}
$$

**Step 3: Material Removal Rate**

$$
\text{MRR} = \frac{\pi}{4} D^2 f_r N = \frac{\pi}{4} \times 25^2 \times 0.15 \times 318.3
$$

$$
= 0.7854 \times 625 \times 0.15 \times 318.3
$$

$$
= 0.7854 \times 625 = 490.87
$$

$$
490.87 \times 0.15 = 73.63
$$

$$
73.63 \times 318.3 \approx 23{,}433 \text{ mm}^3/\text{min}
$$

Converting to cm³/min (divide by 1000):

$$
\text{MRR} \approx 23.43 \text{ cm}^3/\text{min}
$$

**Step 4: Machining time**

$$
T_m = \frac{L}{V_f} = \frac{60}{47.75} \approx 1.257 \text{ min}
$$

Convert to seconds:

$$
T_m = 1.257 \times 60 \approx 75.4 \text{ s}
$$

**Step 5: Theoretical Power**

Convert MRR to mm³/s:

$$
\text{MRR}_{s} = \frac{23{,}433}{60} \approx 390.55 \text{ mm}^3/\text{s}
$$

Cutting power:

$$
P_c = \frac{\text{MRR}_s \times K_c}{10^6} \quad \text{[kW] if $K_c$ in N/mm²}
$$

Wait — careful with units. $P$ [W] = MRR [mm³/s] × $K_c$ [N·mm/mm³ = N/mm²] × 1 mm = N·mm/s = mW × 10³. Using:

$$
P_c \; [\text{W}] = \text{MRR}_s \times K_c = 390.55 \times 2000 = 781{,}100 \text{ W}
$$

Converting to kW:

$$
P_c \approx 781.1 \text{ kW}
$$

That is unrealistic for a single drill; the issue is using $K_c$ in N/mm² directly with mm³/s. The proper form is:

$$
P_c \, [\text{kW}] = \frac{\text{MRR}\, [\text{mm}^3/\text{min}] \times K_c\, [\text{N/mm}^2]}{60 \times 10^6}
$$

Let me re-derive cleanly:

$$
1 \text{ N·mm} = 10^{-6} \text{ kJ}; \quad 1 \text{ min} = 60 \text{ s}
$$

$$
P_c = \frac{23{,}433 \times 2000}{60 \times 10^6} \text{ kW} = \frac{46{,}866{,}000}{60{,}000{,}000} \approx 0.781 \text{ kW}
$$

Motor power:

$$
P_m = \frac{P_c}{\eta} = \frac{0.781}{0.8} \approx 0.976 \text{ kW}
$$

**Final answers to (a):**
1. $N \approx 318$ rpm
2. $V_f \approx 47.75$ mm/min
3. MRR $\approx 23{,}433$ mm³/min $= 23.43$ cm³/min
4. $T_m \approx 75.4$ s
5. $P_m \approx 0.98$ kW

**(b) Model Sketch Description:**

The twist drill consists of the following labelled parts:
- **Point** with **point angle = 118°** (for general steels)
- **Cutting lips** (two lips, parallel to each other for a balanced cut)
- **Chisel edge** at the centre connecting the two lips
- **Flutes** — helical grooves (helix angle ≈ 30°) that evacuate chips
- **Body / lands** — bearing surfaces that provide guidance in the hole
- **Shank** — straight (small drills) or Morse taper (large drills)
- **Tang** — small projection on tapered shank to prevent slippage in spindle

*(Award: 7 marks for (a) calculation breakdown; 7 marks for (b) labelled sketch with clear descriptions.)*

---

### Question B (14 Marks) — **Internal Choice Alternative**

**(a)** A horizontal plain-milling cutter of **60 mm diameter** with **8 teeth** is used to machine a mild-steel workpiece. The recommended cutting parameters are: **cutting speed $V = 30$ m/min**, **feed per tooth $f_z = 0.1$ mm/tooth**, **radial depth (width) $w = 50$ mm**, and **axial depth $d = 4$ mm**. The length of the workpiece is **200 mm**. Calculate:

1. Spindle speed $N$
2. Table feed rate $V_f$
3. Material removal rate (MRR)
4. Approximate approach distance $l_a$ and machining time $T_m$

**(b)** With the help of a neat diagram, explain the **principle and operation of a radial drilling machine**. State any **two advantages** of using it over a pillar drill.

---

### Step-by-Step Model Solution to Q-B

**(a) Solution:**

**Step 1: Spindle speed**

$$
N = \frac{1000 \, V}{\pi D} = \frac{1000 \times 30}{\pi \times 60} = \frac{30{,}000}{188.5} \approx 159.15 \text{ rpm}
$$

$$
N \approx 159 \text{ rpm}
$$

**Step 2: Feed per revolution**

$$
f_r = f_z \times Z = 0.1 \times 8 = 0.8 \text{ mm/rev}
$$

**Step 3: Table feed rate**

$$
V_f = f_r \times N = 0.8 \times 159.15 \approx 127.3 \text{ mm/min}
$$

**Step 4: Material removal rate**

$$
\text{MRR} = w \times d \times V_f = 50 \times 4 \times 127.3
$$

$$
= 200 \times 127.3 = 25{,}460 \text{ mm}^3/\text{min} = 25.46 \text{ cm}^3/\text{min}
$$

**Step 5: Approach distance**

$$
l_a = \sqrt{d(D - d)} = \sqrt{4 \times (60 - 4)} = \sqrt{4 \times 56} = \sqrt{224}
$$

$$
l_a \approx 14.97 \text{ mm} \approx 15 \text{ mm}
$$

**Step 6: Machining time**

$$
T_m = \frac{L + l_a + l_o}{V_f}
$$

Assume overrun $l_o \approx l_a \approx 15$ mm:

$$
T_m = \frac{200 + 15 + 15}{127.3} = \frac{230}{127.3} \approx 1.807 \text{ min}
$$

$$
T_m \approx 108.4 \text{ seconds} \approx 1 \text{ min } 48 \text{ s}
$$

**Final answers to (a):**
1. $N \approx 159$ rpm
2. $V_f \approx 127.3$ mm/min
3. MRR $\approx 25{,}460$ mm³/min
4. $l_a \approx 15$ mm; $T_m \approx 1.81$ min ≈ 108 s

**(b) Radial Drilling Machine — Operating Principle:**

A **radial drilling machine** consists of a heavy vertical **column** mounted on a base. A horizontal **arm (radial arm)** can swing 360° around the column and can be raised or lowered. The **spindle head**, carrying the drill spindle, slides along the radial arm.

**Operation:** The radial arm is positioned so that the drill spindle is directly above the desired hole location on the workpiece (which remains stationary). The arm is clamped, the spindle head is fed down, and the drill enters the workpiece. The arm can then be repositioned for the next hole — multiple holes can be drilled without re-clamping the workpiece.

**Two Advantages over Pillar Drill:**
1. **Heavy, large workpieces** can be drilled at multiple locations without re-positioning — saves time and improves accuracy.
2. The radial arm accommodates **drilling at various angles** and at large radii from the column base — versatile for big fabrications like boiler shells, large gear blanks, and structural frames.

*(Award: 7 marks for (a) calculations; 7 marks for (b) explanation and advantages.)*

---

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Pitfall Callout — Where Students Commonly Lose Marks:**
> 1. **Forgetting the 1000 factor** in $V = \pi D N / 1000$ → answer in **wrong order of magnitude** → -2 to -3 marks.
> 2. **Unit confusion** between $f_r$ (mm/rev) and $f_z$ (mm/tooth). Drilling = $f_r$; Milling = $f_z$. Mixed-up → entire MRR wrong.
> 3. **Not converting MRR to consistent units** before computing power. Use mm³/s with $K_c$ in N/mm² to get W → divide by $10^3$ for kW. Showing power in W when kW is asked → -1 mark.
> 4. **Ignoring approach/overrun** in milling time calculation. Examiner gives 1–2 marks for that step.
> 5. **Wrong sign in $l_a$ formula**: It is $\sqrt{d(D-d)}$, **NOT** $\sqrt{d \cdot D - d^2}$ (same mathematically but students often write it incorrectly).
> 6. **Forgetting the machine efficiency $\eta$** in the power question → -1 mark.
> 7. **Confusing direction of milling**: Examiners will deduct 1 mark if "up milling" and "down milling" are interchanged in a labelling question.

---

## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Rapid-Revision Checklist for Drilling and Milling Systems**

- **Drilling** uses a **multi-point twist drill** with rotary + axial feed; produces cylindrical holes.
- **Milling** uses a **multi-tooth rotating cutter** with workpiece/cutter translation; produces flat surfaces, slots, pockets, profiles.
- **Universal cutting-speed formula:** $V = \pi D N / 1000$ (m/min). Always remember the **1000**.
- **Spindle speed (most-used reverse):** $N = 1000 \, V / (\pi D)$.
- **Feed rate:** Drilling — $V_f = f_r \cdot N$; Milling — $V_f = f_z \cdot Z \cdot N$.
- **MRR:** Drilling — $\frac{\pi}{4} D^2 f_r N$; Milling — $w \cdot d \cdot V_f$.
- **Time:** Drilling — $L / V_f$; Milling — $(L + l_a + l_o) / V_f$ with $l_a = \sqrt{d(D-d)}$.
- **Power:** $P_c = \text{MRR} \cdot K_c$ (in consistent units); $P_m = P_c / \eta$, with $\eta \approx 0.8$.
- **Up milling = conventional** (chip thick→thin); **Down milling = climb** (chip thin→thick, better finish).
- **Drill geometry:** point 118°, helix 30°, two cutting lips, one chisel edge.
- **Tool materials:** HSS for low-speed general use; Carbide / Coated carbide for high-speed CNC.
- **Coolant:** Always use cutting fluid — extends tool life, improves finish, evacuates chips.
- **KTU golden rule:** Always **state given data, the formula, the substitution, and the boxed answer** in every calculation.

# SECTION 1: CORE TECHNICAL DEFINITION & INTUITIVE OVERVIEW

## 1.1 Canned Cycles in CNC Programming

### Formal Academic Definition
A **canned cycle** is a pre-programmed, standardized sequence of machine tool movements stored in the CNC controller's firmware that combines multiple conventional machining operations (such as rapid traverse, plunge cut, feed cut, and retract) into a **single, compact G-code instruction**. These are officially classified by ISO 6983 and standardized under **G-codes G81 through G89**, and they are fundamentally used to reduce programming complexity for repetitive hole-making operations like drilling, tapping, boring, and reaming.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Syllabus Highlight:** Canned cycles are *factory-defined subprograms* embedded in the CNC machine's controller. Students must remember that they are activated by a single line of code but execute multiple sequential moves internally.

### Conceptual Analogy (Plain English)
Think of a **canned cycle as a "shortcut button"** on your TV remote. Instead of pressing 5 separate buttons to change inputs, adjust volume, set the channel, and confirm — you just press one "Watch Movie" button. The canned cycle is that single button: you write **one line of G-code**, but the machine silently performs the **approach → plunge → feed → retract** sequence that would otherwise require **6–8 separate lines** of manual programming.

### Standard Canned Cycle Categories
| G-Code | Operation Type | Common Application |
|--------|---------------|--------------------|
| **G81** | Drilling cycle (simple) | Spot drilling, shallow holes |
| **G82** | Drilling with dwell | Counter-boring, flat-bottomed holes |
| **G83** | Peck drilling (deep hole) | Deep holes (depth/diameter > 5) |
| **G84** | Tapping cycle (right-hand) | Threaded holes |
| **G85** | Boring (feed in / feed out) | Precision finishing |
| **G86** | Boring (feed in / rapid out) | Medium-finish boring |
| **G87** | Back boring | Internal grooves on back side |
| **G88** | Boring with manual retract | Inspection bore |
| **G89** | Boring with dwell | Finishing with chip break |

---

## 1.2 Cutter Radius Compensation (CRC)

### Formal Academic Definition
**Cutter Radius Compensation (CRC)** is a real-time, controller-driven offset function — invoked by **G41 (Left)** or **G42 (Right)** and cancelled by **G40** — that shifts the *programmed tool path* laterally by an amount equal to the cutter's nose radius (or half-diameter) so that the **actual machined contour** matches the **engineering drawing dimensions**. The offset is stored in the controller's **offset register** (typically the Geometry Offset Table: D01–D99 or H-codes depending on the controller — Fanuc uses D, Siemens uses D, Heidenhain uses TOFF).

> [!NOTE]
> **Definition Callout:** CRC is a *contour-shifting algorithm*, not a tool-length change. It manipulates the *X-Y coordinate trajectory* of the tool's center, not the Z-axis spindle position.

### Conceptual Analogy (Plain English)
Imagine you are **painting a wall with a wide paint roller**. If you want the *edge of the paint* to align with a tape line, you must hold the **center** of the roller a small distance away from the tape — otherwise the roller's edge will smudge onto the tape. **Cutter Radius Compensation does exactly this**: the controller automatically keeps the *cutter's center* at a calculated offset distance from the programmed path so that the *outer edge of the cutter* produces the desired shape on the workpiece.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Standard Engineering Metric:** The cutter radius is most commonly in the range of **0.4 mm to 12.0 mm** for end mills, and the offset is always **half the cutter diameter** (r = D/2). The KTU examiner may test the sign convention: G41 = Tool **Left** of workpiece direction, G42 = Tool **Right** of workpiece direction.

---

## 1.3 Robot Technology — Robot Anatomy

### Formal Academic Definition
A **robot's anatomy** refers to the **physical structural architecture** of an industrial robot, comprising the **manipulator (mechanical arm)**, the **end-effector (gripper/tool)**, the **actuator system**, the **sensor system**, the **controller**, and the **power supply unit**. The anatomy is classified by the **type of joint (Revolute 'R' or Prismatic 'P')** and the **sequence of joint axes** (e.g., RRP, RRR, PPR), as standardized by **ISO 8373:2021** and the **ANSI/RIA R15.05** industrial robot safety standard.

### Conceptual Analogy (Plain English)
Picture a **human arm picking up a glass of water**. The **shoulder**, **elbow**, and **wrist** are like robot joints; the **upper arm** and **forearm** are the links; your **hand** is the end-effector; your **brain** is the controller; and your **muscles and nerves** are the actuators and sensors. A robot is essentially a *mechanical skeleton* powered by motors and governed by software — performing the same kinematic chain a human performs, but with **higher repeatability (±0.02 mm)** and **greater payload capacity**.

> [!NOTE]
> **Key Performance Metrics (per KTU Board standards):**
> - **Degrees of Freedom (DOF):** Typically **6** for industrial manipulators (3 for positioning + 3 for orientation).
> - **Payload:** From **3 kg (SCARA)** to **>1000 kg (heavy-payload arms)**.
> - **Repeatability:** Usually **±0.02 mm to ±0.1 mm** (high-precision class).
> - **Reach:** From **0.5 m** to **>3.5 m** for standard industrial arms.

---

# SECTION 2: DEEP THEORETICAL ANALYSIS & KTU HIGH-YIELD FORMULA SHEET

## 2.1 Canned Cycle — Operational Logic Breakdown

Every canned cycle follows a **6-stage operational sequence** that the controller executes internally once a single block is encountered:

1. **Initial Point → R Plane (Rapid Traverse — G00):** The tool moves from its current position to a point directly above the hole location at the **R-plane** (clearance plane) height. This is the safe approach.
2. **R Plane → Z Target (Plunge — G01 with feedrate F):** The tool plunges from the R-plane to the final **Z-depth** at the programmed feed rate. This is the cutting motion.
3. **Dwell at Bottom (Optional — G04 P__):** The tool pauses at the bottom of the hole for a specified time (e.g., for chip breaking, hole bottom finishing, or spring-back relief).
4. **Retract to R Plane (G00 or G01 depending on cycle):** The tool retracts either by **rapid traverse** (drilling cycles) or by **controlled feed** (boring/tapping cycles).
5. **Return to Initial Point (Optional):** If the **G98 modal command** is active, the tool returns to the initial point; if **G99** is active, it returns to the R-plane.
6. **Cycle Cancellation (G80):** Cancels the active canned cycle and restores the controller to normal G-code mode.

> [!NOTE]
> **Canned Cycle Format (Fanuc-style):**
> `G81 X__ Y__ Z__ R__ F__ ;`
> - **X, Y** = Hole center coordinates
> - **Z** = Final depth (negative value, e.g., Z-15.0)
> - **R** = R-plane height (positive value above workpiece, e.g., R2.0)
> - **F** = Feed rate (mm/min)

---

## 2.2 Cutter Radius Compensation — Operational Logic

CRC is governed by three primary states:

| G-Code | Function | Tool Path Behavior |
|--------|----------|---------------------|
| **G40** | Cancel CRC | Tool center follows programmed path exactly |
| **G41** | CRC Left | Tool is **left** of workpiece when looking in the direction of tool travel |
| **G42** | CRC Right | Tool is **right** of workpiece when looking in the direction of tool travel |

### Lead-In and Lead-Out Behavior
- **Lead-In (Approach Block):** A 2–5 mm linear or arc motion is required *before* the compensation becomes fully active. This is called the **lead-in distance**.
- **Lead-Out (Departure Block):** Similarly, a lead-out motion is required to *deactivate* compensation.
- The controller automatically computes the **intersection point** (also called the **tool offset intersection**) and offsets the path by **r = D/2**.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **The sign convention for KTU board problems:**
> - **External machining (profiling outside the part):** Use **G42** (tool to the right, conventional climb milling).
> - **Internal machining (pocketing inside the part):** Use **G41** (tool to the left, conventional climb milling).

---

## 2.3 Robot Anatomy — Joints, Links & Kinematic Chain

An industrial robot is built from a **serial kinematic chain** of rigid bodies (links) connected by actuated joints.

### Joint Types
| Joint Type | Symbol | Motion Description | Typical Application |
|------------|--------|--------------------|--------------------|
| **Revolute** | R | Rotation about a fixed axis | Shoulder, elbow, wrist joints |
| **Prismatic** | P | Linear sliding along an axis | Telescopic arm, gantry columns |
| **Cylindrical** | (deprecated) | R + P combined | Older designs |
| **Spherical** | (deprecated) | 2R + 1R combined | Ball-joint wrists |

### Standard Robot Configurations (per KTU 2024 syllabus)
| Configuration | Joint Sequence | Typical Use |
|---------------|----------------|-------------|
| **Cartesian (PPP)** | 3 Prismatic | Pick-and-place, CNC loading |
| **Cylindrical (RPP)** | 1 Rev + 2 Prism | Assembly, machine tending |
| **Spherical (RRP)** | 2 Rev + 1 Prism | (Historical) Welding, painting |
| **Articulated (RRR)** | 3 Revolute | Automotive welding, sealing |
| **SCARA (RRP)** | Selective Compliance | PCB assembly, high-speed pick |
| **Delta (3R parallel)** | Parallelogram | Packaging, food industry |

### Work Envelope Equations

The **work envelope (workspace)** of a 2-link planar arm is defined by **forward kinematics**:

$$r = \sqrt{(L_1 \cos\theta_1 + L_2 \cos(\theta_1 + \theta_2))^2 + (L_1 \sin\theta_1 + L_2 \sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2))^2}$$

And the inverse relation:

$$\theta_2 = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{r^2 - L_1^2 - L_2^2}{2 L_1 L_2}\right)$$

The **workspace boundary** is governed by the constraint:

$$L_1 - L_2 \le r \le L_1 + L_2$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Engineering Utility:** Knowing the work envelope is critical in **cell layout design**. A KTU examiner may ask you to compute the *dead-zone* (region unreachable by the end-effector) for a given L₁, L₂ pair.

---

# SECTION 3: STEP-BY-STEP DERIVATIONS & ANALYTICAL MATRIX

## 3.1 Worked Example: Drilling 6 Holes Using G81 Canned Cycle

**Problem Statement (KTU Board Style):**
A 100 mm × 80 mm mild steel plate (thickness 12 mm) is to be drilled with **6 through-holes** of diameter 8 mm arranged in a **3 × 2 grid** with 40 mm X-spacing and 50 mm Y-spacing. The hole origin is at the **lower-left corner of the plate** at coordinates (10, 10). Write a CNC program using the **G81 canned cycle** with a feed rate of 120 mm/min and a spindle speed of 800 rpm. The R-plane is 2 mm above the workpiece top surface (Z = 0).

### Step-by-Step Solution

**Step 1 — Identify Hole Coordinates (in mm):**

For a 3 × 2 grid starting at (10, 10) with ΔX = 40, ΔY = 50:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Row 1 (Y = 10):} \quad & (10,\ 10),\ (50,\ 10),\ (90,\ 10) \\
\text{Row 2 (Y = 60):} \quad & (10,\ 60),\ (50,\ 60),\ (90,\ 60)
\end{aligned}
$$

**Reasoning:** We use the canonical grid formula $X_i = X_0 + (i-1) \cdot \Delta X$, with i = 1, 2, 3 (since we have 3 columns). Similarly, $Y_j = Y_0 + (j-1) \cdot \Delta Y$, with j = 1, 2 (since we have 2 rows).

**Step 2 — Set the Z-Depth:**
Since the plate is 12 mm thick and the holes are through-holes, we add 1 mm for breakthrough. The drill point reaches the bottom of the workpiece at Z = –13.0 mm (assuming Z = 0 is the top surface).

**Step 3 — Build the Program (Fanuc-style):**

```text
O0001 (DRILLING PROGRAM FOR 3X2 GRID)
G21 G90 G17 G54        (Metric, Absolute, XY plane, Work offset 1)
G00 Z50.0              (Safe Z height)
M03 S800               (Spindle CW, 800 rpm)
G00 X10.0 Y10.0        (Position over hole #1)
G99 G81 R2.0 Z-13.0 F120   (Activate G81, R-plane = 2, depth = -13, feed = 120)
X50.0 Y10.0            (Hole #2)
X90.0 Y10.0            (Hole #3)
Y60.0                  (Hole #4 — Y jumps, X stays)
X50.0 Y60.0            (Hole #5)
X10.0 Y60.0            (Hole #6)
G80                    (Cancel canned cycle)
G00 Z50.0              (Retract to safe Z)
M05                    (Spindle off)
M30                    (Program end, rewind)
```

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Examination Note:** Notice how **only 6 lines** (the X-Y positions) are needed for the actual hole operations. Without canned cycles, the same program would require **at least 18–24 lines** (one rapid + one feed + one rapid per hole). This is the **5x–6x code-reduction** advantage.

---

## 3.2 Worked Example: Cutter Radius Compensation Calculation

**Problem Statement:**
A pocket of dimensions **50 mm × 30 mm** is to be machined inside a workpiece using a **10 mm diameter end mill** (cutter radius = 5 mm). The pocket has **square corners**. Using CRC, determine:
1. The **tool path coordinates** for a clockwise (CW) milling direction.
2. The **lead-in/lead-out distance** required.

### Step-by-Step Solution

**Step 1 — Identify the Cutter Radius:**
Given cutter diameter D = 10 mm, so cutter radius r = 5 mm.

**Step 2 — Determine the Offset Direction:**
For a **pocket (internal milling)** with **CW tool motion**, the tool must be on the **left** of the workpiece contour when looking in the direction of travel. Therefore we use **G41**.

**Step 3 — Compute the Offset Tool Path:**
The cutter center must travel on a path that is **offset inward by r = 5 mm** from the actual pocket wall.

The original pocket is 50 × 30 mm. The tool center path becomes:

$$
\begin{aligned}
X_{\text{tool path}} &= 50 - 2(5) = 40 \text{ mm} \\
Y_{\text{tool path}} &= 30 - 2(5) = 20 \text{ mm}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Reasoning:** The tool center path forms a *concentric rectangle* inside the original pocket. The amount of inset is **2r = 10 mm** total (5 mm on each side).

**Step 4 — Set the Lead-In Distance:**
The standard lead-in is **1.5 × r to 3 × r**. For r = 5 mm:

$$L_{\text{lead-in}} = 2 \times r = 10 \text{ mm (commonly used)}$$

**Step 5 — Build the Program (relevant section):**

```text
G90 G54 G00 X-10.0 Y5.0   (Position outside pocket, lead-in start)
G01 Z-2.0 F60              (Plunge to depth)
G41 D01 X0 Y5.0 F100       (Activate G41 with offset register D01 = 5.0)
X40.0                      (Mill along bottom of pocket)
Y20.0                      (Mill up right side)
X0                         (Mill along top)
Y5.0                       (Mill down left side)
G40 X-10.0 Y5.0            (Deactivate CRC on lead-out)
```

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Student Mistake:** Forgetting that the **offset value (D01) is loaded into the offset register** as a *positive* value (5.0), and the controller automatically decides the sign based on G41/G42.

---

## 3.3 Worked Example: Robot 2-Link Arm Workspace Calculation

**Problem Statement:**
A 2-link planar robot arm has link lengths L₁ = 400 mm and L₂ = 300 mm. The joint angles θ₁ and θ₂ can each vary from 0° to 150°. Determine:
1. The **maximum reach** of the end-effector.
2. The **minimum reach** (dead-zone boundary).
3. The **workspace area** (approximate).

### Step-by-Step Solution

**Step 1 — Maximum Reach:**
Maximum reach occurs when the arm is **fully extended** (θ₂ = 0°). Using the triangle rule:

$$r_{\max} = L_1 + L_2 = 400 + 300 = 700 \text{ mm}$$

**Step 2 — Minimum Reach:**
Minimum reach occurs when the arm is **folded back on itself** (θ₂ = 180°, theoretical limit):

$$r_{\min} = L_1 - L_2 = 400 - 300 = 100 \text{ mm}$$

> [!NOTE]
> Since θ₂ is limited to 150° (not 180°), the *true* minimum reach is slightly larger than 100 mm, but for KTU calculation purposes, the formula $r_{\min} = L_1 - L_2$ is the standard.

**Step 3 — Workspace Area:**
The workspace is an **annular sector** with inner radius 100 mm, outer radius 700 mm, and angular sweep of 150°.

$$
A_{\text{workspace}} = \frac{\theta_{\text{sweep}}}{360°} \times \pi (r_{\max}^2 - r_{\min}^2)
$$

Substituting the values:

$$
\begin{aligned}
A_{\text{workspace}} &= \frac{150°}{360°} \times \pi \times (700^2 - 100^2) \\
&= \frac{5}{12} \times \pi \times (490000 - 10000) \\
&= \frac{5}{12} \times \pi \times 480000 \\
&= 200000 \pi \\
&\approx 628318.5 \text{ mm}^2 \\
&\approx 0.628 \text{ m}^2
\end{aligned}
$$

**Reasoning:** We convert angular degrees to a fraction of a full circle ($\frac{150}{360} = \frac{5}{12}$), then apply the area formula for an annular sector. The annulus area is $\pi (R^2 - r^2) = \pi (r_{\max}^2 - r_{\min}^2)$.

---

# SECTION 4: STRUCTURAL DIAGRAMS & SCHEMATICS

## 4.1 Canned Cycle Operational Flow (Mermaid Block Diagram)

    F --> G[G98 or G99 active?]

    G -- G98 --> I[Retract to Initial Point]

    I --> J
    J --> K{More holes in program?}
    K -- Yes --> B
    K -- No --> L[Encounter G80: cancel cycle]

# SECTION 5: KTU 2024 SCHEME EXAMINATION QUESTION BANK & TOPIC RECAP

## Part A — 3-Mark Questions

**Q1. [KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]**
*Define a "canned cycle" in CNC programming. List any **four** standard G-codes used for canned cycles and state their applications.*

**Model Answer:**
A canned cycle is a pre-defined sequence of machine tool motions stored in the CNC controller that simplifies repetitive hole-making operations. Each canned cycle replaces multiple manual programming lines with a single G-code block.

| G-Code | Application |
|--------|-------------|
| G81 | Simple drilling / spot drilling |
| G82 | Drilling with dwell (counterbore) |
| G83 | Peck drilling for deep holes |
| G84 | Tapping (right-hand threads) |

---

**Q2. [KTU University Exam – June 2024]**
*What is the difference between **G41** and **G42** in cutter radius compensation? State the sign convention with a neat sketch description.*

**Model Answer:**
- **G41 (Cutter Compensation Left):** The tool is positioned on the **left** side of the programmed path when looking in the direction of tool travel. Used for **internal milling (pockets)**.
- **G42 (Cutter Compensation Right):** The tool is positioned on the **right** side of the programmed path when looking in the direction of tool travel. Used for **external profiling (contours)**.

The **cancellation code is G40**, which returns the tool center to the exact programmed path.

---

## Part B — 14-Mark Questions (Module Internal Choice)

### Question A (14 Marks)

**[KTU University Exam – Model Paper 2024]**
**(a)** [7 Marks] Describe the **G81 drilling cycle** with a neat block diagram. Explain the role of the **R-plane**, the **G98** and **G99** return commands, and the function of the **G80** cancellation code. Write a sample program to drill **4 holes** at coordinates (20, 20), (60, 20), (20, 50), and (60, 50) on a 10 mm thick plate using G81, with R = 3 mm, Z = –12 mm, F = 100 mm/min, and S = 1000 rpm.

**(b)** [7 Marks] Explain the **anatomy of a 6-DOF articulated robot** in detail. Sketch a labeled diagram (using a block diagram if physical drawing is not feasible) showing the **base, shoulder, elbow, and three wrist joints**. State the **DH parameters** used for forward kinematics and define the **work envelope** of such a robot.

### Model Solution to Question A (a)

The **G81 drilling cycle** is the simplest canned cycle, used for **shallow, straight drill holes** without dwell. Its operational sequence is:

1. The tool moves in **rapid traverse (G00)** from its current position to the (X, Y) coordinates of the hole center, then to the **R-plane** height (e.g., R = 3 mm).
2. The tool plunges from the R-plane to **Z = –12 mm** at the programmed **feed rate (F = 100 mm/min)**.
3. **Return behavior:**
   - **G99 active:** Tool retracts to the R-plane.
   - **G98 active:** Tool retracts to the **Initial Point** (the position before the cycle started).
4. **G80** cancels the canned cycle; subsequent X-Y moves are no longer treated as hole centers.

**Sample Program:**

```text
O0002 (DRILL 4 HOLES WITH G81)
G21 G90 G17 G54
G00 Z50.0
M03 S1000
G00 X20.0 Y20.0
G99 G81 R3.0 Z-12.0 F100
X60.0 Y20.0
X20.0 Y50.0
X60.0 Y50.0
G80
G00 Z50.0
M05
M30
```

### Model Solution to Question A (b)

A **6-DOF articulated robot** (also called an **anthropomorphic arm** or **jointed-arm robot**) consists of:

| Joint # | Name | Type | Axis of Motion |
|---------|------|------|----------------|
| 1 | Waist (Base) | Revolute (R) | Rotation about vertical Z |
| 2 | Shoulder | Revolute (R) | Rotation about horizontal axis |
| 3 | Elbow | Revolute (R) | Rotation about horizontal axis |
| 4 | Wrist Roll | Revolute (R) | Rotation about forearm axis |
| 5 | Wrist Pitch | Revolute (R) | Rotation about wrist axis |
| 6 | Wrist Yaw | Revolute (R) | Rotation about tool axis |

**Denavit-Hartenberg (DH) Parameters** are used to describe each joint: **link length (aᵢ), link twist (αᵢ), joint offset (dᵢ), and joint angle (θᵢ)**. The **forward kinematics** of the manipulator is computed by the homogeneous transformation matrix:

$$
^{i-1}T_i = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta_i & -\sin\theta_i \cos\alpha_i & \sin\theta_i \sin\alpha_i & a_i \cos\theta_i \\ \sin\theta_i & \cos\theta_i \cos\alpha_i & -\cos\theta_i \sin\alpha_i & a_i \sin\theta_i \\ 0 & \sin\alpha_i & \cos\alpha_i & d_i \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
$$

The **work envelope** is the **3D region of space that the Tool Center Point (TCP) can reach**. For a typical 6-DOF articulated robot with reach R = 1.5 m, the envelope is roughly **spherical with a hollow interior** (unreachable dead-zone near the base of radius ≈ 0.3 m).

---

### Question B (14 Marks) — Alternative Choice

**[KTU University Exam – Model Paper 2024]**
**(a)** [7 Marks] Explain the concept of **Cutter Radius Compensation (CRC)**. Differentiate between **G40, G41, and G42** with their applications. Describe the necessity of **lead-in and lead-out motions** with a simple example where a 6 mm end mill is used to machine a square pocket of 40 mm × 40 mm.

**(b)** [7 Marks] With a neat sketch, explain the **basic anatomy of an industrial robot** listing the following components: (i) Manipulator, (ii) End Effector, (iii) Actuators, (iv) Sensors, (v) Controller, (vi) Power Supply. State the **degrees of freedom (DOF)** of a typical industrial robot and explain why 6 DOF is considered the standard.

### Model Solution to Question B (a)

**Cutter Radius Compensation (CRC)** is a real-time tool path offset that allows the programmer to write the part geometry directly into the program while the controller automatically adjusts the *tool center path* by the **cutter radius (r)** to produce the correct machined feature.

**G-code Commands:**

| G-Code | Function | Common Use |
|--------|----------|------------|
| G40 | Cancel CRC | End of compensation region |
| G41 | CRC Left (tool on left) | Internal pockets, climb milling inside |
| G42 | CRC Right (tool on right) | External profiles, climb milling outside |

**Worked Example — 40 × 40 mm Square Pocket, 6 mm End Mill:**

Cutter diameter D = 6 mm, so radius r = 3 mm. The tool center path is offset **inward by 3 mm** on all four sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}
X_{\text{tool path}} &= 40 - 2(3) = 34 \text{ mm} \\
Y_{\text{tool path}} &= 40 - 2(3) = 34 \text{ mm}
\end{aligned}
$$

A lead-in of **2 × r = 6 mm** is required before activating G41, and a lead-out of the same length before calling G40.

**Sample Program Segment:**

```text
G00 X-6.0 Y3.0          (Lead-in start position)
G01 Z-2.0 F50           (Plunge to depth)
G41 D01 X0 Y3.0 F80     (Activate CRC, D01 = 3.0)
X34.0                   (Mill bottom edge)
Y34.0                   (Mill right edge)
X0                      (Mill top edge)
Y3.0                    (Mill left edge)
G40 X-6.0 Y3.0          (Deactivate CRC, lead-out)
```

### Model Solution to Question B (b)

The **basic anatomy of an industrial robot** consists of six major subsystems:

**(i) Manipulator (Mechanical Arm):** The serial kinematic chain of links and joints that physically moves the end-effector through space. Comprises base, arm (shoulder + elbow), and wrist.

**(ii) End Effector:** The tool mounted at the wrist — grippers, welding torches, paint sprayers, vacuum cups, or specialized tools. The **Tool Center Point (TCP)** is the reference origin of the end-effector.

**(iii) Actuators:** The "muscles" of the robot. Typical types:
- **Servo motors** (electric, most common)
- **Pneumatic cylinders** (low-cost pick-and-place)
- **Hydraulic actuators** (heavy-payload robots, > 500 kg)

**(iv) Sensors:** The "nervous system":
- **Position encoders** (one per joint)
- **Force/torque sensors** (wrist-mounted)
- **Proximity sensors, vision cameras**

**(v) Controller:** The "brain" — a microprocessor-based computer with a **teach pendant** for programming, **servo amplifiers** for motor control, and a **safety PLC** for emergency stops and interlocks.

**(vi) Power Supply:** Converts AC mains to the **DC bus voltage** required by the servo drives, with **UPS backup** for controlled shutdown.

**Degrees of Freedom (DOF):** A standard industrial robot has **6 DOF** — **3 for position** (X, Y, Z location in Cartesian space) plus **3 for orientation** (roll, pitch, yaw of the end-effector). This is sufficient to place a rigid tool at **any desired position with any desired orientation** within the workspace, satisfying the **Pieper's criterion** for a solvable closed-form inverse kinematics solution.

---

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Common Pitfall Alert:**
> 1. **Confusing G98 and G99:** Many students write G99 when they mean G98 and lose 2–3 marks. Remember: **G99 → R-plane** (shorter retract, faster), **G98 → Initial Point** (longer retract, used when obstacles are between holes).
> 2. **Wrong CRC sign convention:** Writing **G42 for a pocket** (when G41 is correct) is a 3-mark penalty in KTU valuation. Memorize: **G41 = left, used inside; G42 = right, used outside.**
> 3. **Offset value sign:** The cutter radius in the offset register is always loaded as a **positive** value; the controller determines the sign. Loading a negative value is a common mistake.
> 4. **Robot anatomy completeness:** Listing only 3–4 components instead of all 6 leads to partial credit. KTU expects the full **6-subsystem** answer.
> 5. **DOF reasoning:** Stating "6 DOF" without justifying **why** (3 position + 3 orientation) is considered a 1-mark deduction. Always justify!

---

## 📋 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **High-Density Rapid Revision Checklist:**

### Canned Cycles
- ✅ Canned cycles are **single-line G-code instructions** (G81–G89) that replace 5–8 manual programming lines.
- ✅ The **R-plane** is the safe rapid-approach height above the workpiece.
- ✅ **G98** returns to the Initial Point; **G99** returns to the R-plane.
- ✅ **G80** cancels the canned cycle.
- ✅ **G83** is used for **deep holes** (peck drilling); **G84** is for **tapping**.

### Cutter Radius Compensation
- ✅ CRC offsets the **tool center path** by **r = D/2** (half the cutter diameter).
- ✅ **G41 = Left (internal pockets), G42 = Right (external profiles), G40 = Cancel.**
- ✅ A **lead-in motion of 2×r to 3×r** is mandatory before activating CRC.
- ✅ The offset value is stored in **register D01–D99** (Fanuc) as a **positive** value.

### Robot Anatomy
- ✅ Six major subsystems: **Manipulator, End Effector, Actuators, Sensors, Controller, Power Supply.**
- ✅ Joint types: **R (Revolute)** and **P (Prismatic).**
- ✅ Standard industrial robot = **6 DOF** (3 position + 3 orientation).
- ✅ Standard configurations: **Cartesian (PPP), Cylindrical (RPP), Spherical (RRP), Articulated (RRR), SCARA.**
- ✅ **Repeatability** is in the range **±0.02 mm to ±0.1 mm**; **payloads** range from **3 kg to >1000 kg**.
- ✅ **Workspace** for a 2-link arm: $r_{\max} = L_1 + L_2$, $r_{\min} = L_1 - L_2$.
