> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PCPOL607 - PCPOL607
> - **Module:** Module Experiment 2
> - **Topic:** processing and assembly and inspection. 9 Course Assessment Method (CIE: 40 marks

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
# SECTION 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Defining the Module Experiment

**Module Experiment 2** in a polymer processing laboratory is a hands-on synthesis-and-evaluation exercise in which a polymer matrix composite (PMC) or moulded polymer product is **processed**, **assembled**, and subjected to **inspection** to validate the product against engineering specifications. The three pillars of this experiment are tightly coupled: *processing* determines internal structure, *assembly* determines geometric integrity, and *inspection* validates that the finished artefact satisfies the design intent.

> [!NOTE]
> **Syllabus Highlight (KTU 2024 Scheme):** The Continuous Internal Evaluation (CIE) for laboratory courses is fixed at **40 marks**, distributed across *regular lab performance, record submission, viva-voce, model practical examination, and attendance* as per the 2024 academic regulations.

### 1.2 The Three Pillars at a Glance

| Pillar | What it does | In-lab deliverable |
|---|---|---|
| **Processing** | Converts raw polymer/resin/ fibre system into a shaped body | A defect-free cured/moulded specimen |
| **Assembly** | Joins, fits, and aligns the processed part with mating components | A functionally integrated sub-assembly |
| **Inspection** | Verifies geometry, surface, mechanical and dimensional attributes | A signed inspection report & test record |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Examiner Anchor:** When asked to "explain the experiment" in the viva, always narrate the workflow in the order **Processing → Assembly → Inspection** and conclude with the CIE mark distribution. Examiners reward a *structured* answer.

### 1.3 Conceptual Analogy (Plain-English Intuition)

Think of the experiment like **baking a layered cake for a customer**:

- **Processing** is *baking the sponge* — you mix the batter (resin + hardener), pour it into a greased pan (mould), and bake (cure) at the right temperature and time. If the oven is too hot or you open it too early, the cake collapses.
- **Assembly** is *stacking and icing the layers* — you trim rough edges, place one layer on top of another, and bind them with frosting (adhesive/fastener), making sure the layers are aligned.
- **Inspection** is the *quality check before delivery* — you measure the height with a ruler (vernier), check the surface for cracks (visual), and tap-test for hollow regions (NDT).

The same logic — *make → fit → verify* — governs every polymer product lab in the KTU curriculum.

### 1.4 Physical Constants and Standard Metrics

The following constants and metrics must be memorised for the viva and the record book:

- **Standard test temperature:** $23 \pm 2 \text{ °C}$
- **Standard relative humidity:** $50 \pm 5 \text{ \% RH}$
- **Standard curing pressure (hand lay-up):** $\approx 0.1$ to $0.5 \text{ MPa}$ (roller/brush consolidation)
- **Standard curing pressure (compression moulding):** $5$ to $15 \text{ MPa}$
- **Typical cure cycle:** $80 \text{ °C}$ for **2 h** + post-cure at $120 \text{ °C}$ for **4 h** (epoxy systems, indicative)
- **CIE total:** **40 marks** | **ESE (lab exam) total:** typically **60 marks** for a 100-mark combined course

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# SECTION 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 Pillar I — Processing (Composite / Moulded Part Fabrication)

Processing in a polymer lab is the controlled transformation of a liquid/granular feed into a solid artefact. For a typical **glass-fibre reinforced epoxy laminate** (the most common KTU lab specimen), the steps are:

1. **Mould preparation** — release-agent application, surface cleaning, edge damming.
2. **Resin system preparation** — mixing epoxy resin with hardener in a stoichiometric ratio (commonly 10 : 1 by weight for general-purpose systems).
3. **Lay-up** — placing reinforcement plies (chopped strand mat / woven roving) on the mould and impregnating with resin.
4. **Consolidation & cure** — removing entrapped air with rollers, then curing at ambient or elevated temperature.
5. **De-moulding & post-cure** — careful extraction followed by elevated-temperature post-cure to maximise $T_g$ and cross-link density.

> [!NOTE]
> **Why cure at elevated temperature?** A higher cure temperature drives the cross-linking reaction closer to completion, increasing the **glass-transition temperature** $T_g$, reducing residual stresses, and improving mechanical performance. This is the *thermodynamic* foundation of the lab.

### 2.2 Pillar II — Assembly

Assembly joins two or more processed parts. Common KTU-lab techniques:

- **Adhesive bonding** — surface roughening → solvent wipe → adhesive application → clamping → cure.
- **Mechanical fastening** — drilling pilot holes → countersinking → bolt/screw insertion → torque-tightening to a specified preload.
- **Press/ snap-fit** — geometric interference fit (no fastener).
- **Hybrid assembly** — adhesive + fastener for safety-critical joints.

The governing design equation for a single-lap adhesive joint (Volkersen-type analysis) is:

$$\tau = \frac{P}{b \cdot L} \left[ \frac{\cosh(\lambda x)}{\cosh(\lambda L / 2)} \right]$$

with the auxiliary parameter:

$$\lambda = \sqrt{\frac{G_a}{t_a} \cdot \left( \frac{1}{E_1 t_1} + \frac{1}{E_2 t_2} \right)}$$

where $P$ is the axial load, $b$ the joint width, $L$ the overlap length, $G_a$ and $t_a$ the adhesive shear modulus and thickness, and $E_1 t_1$, $E_2 t_2$ the tensile stiffness of the two adherends.

### 2.3 Pillar III — Inspection

Inspection verifies that the product meets specifications. The methods are tiered:

| Tier | Method | What it checks |
|---|---|---|
| **Dimensional** | Vernier / micrometer / CMM | Linear dimensions, tolerances |
| **Visual** | Magnifier, dye-pen, naked eye | Surface cracks, voids, porosity |
| **Physical** | Density (Archimedes), hardness (Shore A/D, Barcol) | Degree of cure, void content |
| **Mechanical** | Tensile / flexural / impact (Izod/Charpy) | Strength, modulus, toughness |
| **NDT** | Ultrasonic C-scan, tap-test, radiography | Internal delamination, voids |

The **void content** of a laminate is a high-yield viva question and is computed as:

$$V_v = \frac{\rho_{th} - \rho_{ex}}{\rho_{th}} \times 100 \, \%$$

where the *theoretical* density is obtained from the rule of mixtures:

$$\rho_{th} = \frac{1}{\dfrac{W_f}{\rho_f} + \dfrac{W_m}{\rho_m}}$$

with $W_f$, $W_m$ the weight fractions of fibre and matrix, and $\rho_f$, $\rho_m$ their respective densities.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Engineering Utility:** Void content $> 2 \text{ \%}$ in a structural composite significantly degrades interlaminar shear strength (ILSS) and fatigue life. Hence inspection is not just a regulatory step — it is a *gate-keeper* for the part's in-service performance.

## 2.4 The 9th Component: Course Assessment Method (CIE: 40 marks)

As per the KTU 2024 Scheme, the **Continuous Internal Evaluation (CIE)** for the laboratory component carrying 40 marks is distributed as follows (typical, scheme-aligned):

| Sl. No. | CIE Component | Marks (out of 40) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Regular performance in lab sessions & punctuality | 10 |
| 2 | Laboratory record / observation notebook | 10 |
| 3 | Model practical examination (internal) | 10 |
| 4 | Viva-voce & oral assessment | 05 |
| 5 | Attendance (≥ 90 % → full; 85–89 % → 80 % marks; < 85 % → not eligible) | 05 |
|  | **Total CIE** | **40** |

The **End Semester Evaluation (ESE)** for the lab is a **separate practical examination of 60 marks**, conducted by an external examiner. The final certification requires:

$$\text{Total Lab Marks} = \text{CIE} + \text{ESE} = 40 + 60 = 100$$

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Mistake:** Many students confuse CIE (40) with the *theory* CIE of a lecture course. The 40-mark figure here is **specifically for the laboratory CIE** of PCPOL607. A 75 % minimum in CIE and 75 % attendance are mandatory eligibility conditions for appearing in ESE.

## 2.5 KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

| # | Formula / Rule | Meaning / Use | Units |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $V_f = \dfrac{\rho_{c} - \rho_{m}}{\rho_{f} - \rho_{m}}$ | Volume fraction of fibre (density method) | dimensionless |
| 2 | $W_f = \dfrac{w_f}{w_f + w_m}$ | Weight fraction of fibre | dimensionless |
| 3 | $\rho_{th} = \left( \dfrac{W_f}{\rho_f} + \dfrac{W_m}{\rho_m} \right)^{-1}$ | Theoretical composite density | g/cc |
| 4 | $V_v = \dfrac{\rho_{th} - \rho_{ex}}{\rho_{th}} \times 100$ | Void content (vol %) | % |
| 5 | $\sigma_t = \dfrac{P}{A}$ | Tensile stress in inspection coupon | MPa |
| 6 | $\varepsilon = \dfrac{\Delta L}{L_0}$ | Engineering strain | dimensionless |
| 7 | $E = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon}$ | Young's modulus from inspection test | GPa |
| 8 | $\sigma_{flex} = \dfrac{3PL}{2bd^2}$ | Flexural stress (3-point bend) | MPa |
| 9 | $\text{CIE total} = 40$ | Internal marks for lab course | marks |
| 10 | $\text{ESE total} = 60$ | External lab exam marks | marks |

> **Pipe-safe note:** In the table above, $\rho_{c}$ is the *measured* composite density; subscripts $f$ and $m$ denote fibre and matrix respectively. All fractions are dimensionless, stresses are in MPa, and moduli are in GPa.

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# SECTION 3: Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Exhaustive Derivation 1 — Theoretical Density via Rule of Mixtures

The rule of mixtures for density assumes the constituent volumes are *additive* (no voids) and the weights are conserved.

**Given:** $W_f$ = weight fraction of fibre, $W_m$ = weight fraction of matrix, $W_f + W_m = 1$. Densities $\rho_f$ and $\rho_m$.

**Step 1** — Express weight fractions in terms of a reference mass $M_{total}$:

$$m_f = W_f \cdot M_{total}, \quad m_m = W_m \cdot M_{total}$$

**Step 2** — Convert masses to volumes using $\rho = m / V \implies V = m / \rho$:

$$V_f = \frac{W_f \cdot M_{total}}{\rho_f}, \quad V_m = \frac{W_m \cdot M_{total}}{\rho_m}$$

**Step 3** — Total volume (assuming no voids):

$$V_c = V_f + V_m = M_{total} \left( \frac{W_f}{\rho_f} + \frac{W_m}{\rho_m} \right)$$

**Step 4** — Theoretical density (mass per unit volume):

$$\rho_{th} = \frac{M_{total}}{V_c} = \frac{1}{\dfrac{W_f}{\rho_f} + \dfrac{W_m}{\rho_m}}$$

> This is the inverse-rule-of-mixtures form, which always yields the correct theoretical density from weight-fraction inputs. The result is dimensionally consistent: numerator is **1**, denominator has units of $1/\rho$ → so $\rho_{th}$ carries the units of density. ✓

## 3.2 Exhaustive Derivation 2 — Void Content from Theoretical vs Experimental Density

**Given:** A processed composite specimen of measured (experimental) density $\rho_{ex}$ and theoretical density $\rho_{th}$ computed above.

**Step 1** — Define the *missing* density as the gap between theoretical and experimental values. Since voids reduce mass but not volume of the mould cavity:

$$\Delta \rho = \rho_{th} - \rho_{ex}$$

**Step 2** — Define the void fraction as the *ratio* of missing density to the theoretical upper bound:

$$V_v = \frac{\rho_{th} - \rho_{ex}}{\rho_{th}}$$

**Step 3** — Express as a percentage (the standard reporting form in lab records):

$$V_v (\%) = \frac{\rho_{th} - \rho_{ex}}{\rho_{th}} \times 100$$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Sign Convention:** $\rho_{th} \ge \rho_{ex}$ is *always* true for a real specimen (voids always reduce mass). If your lab data shows the opposite, you have either a measurement error (e.g. trapped air bubble in water-displacement) or a recording mistake. Recheck before submitting the record.

## 3.3 Exhaustive Derivation 3 — Volume Fraction from Density Method

**Given:** Measured composite density $\rho_c$, fibre density $\rho_f$, matrix density $\rho_m$.

**Step 1** — Mass balance: $m_c = m_f + m_m$ and volume balance (no voids): $V_c = V_f + V_m$.

**Step 2** — Divide the volume equation by $V_c$:

$$1 = \frac{V_f}{V_c} + \frac{V_m}{V_c} = V_{f,\text{vol}} + V_{m,\text{vol}}$$

**Step 3** — Use $m_i = \rho_i V_i$ to express masses in terms of volumes:

$$\rho_c V_c = \rho_f V_f + \rho_m V_m = \rho_f V_{f,\text{vol}} V_c + \rho_m V_{m,\text{vol}} V_c$$

**Step 4** — Cancel $V_c$ and substitute $V_{m,\text{vol}} = 1 - V_{f,\text{vol}}$:

$$\rho_c = \rho_f V_{f,\text{vol}} + \rho_m (1 - V_{f,\text{vol}})$$

**Step 5** — Solve for the fibre volume fraction $V_f$:

$$V_f = \frac{\rho_c - \rho_m}{\rho_f - \rho_m}$$

> The numerator captures the *excess* density of the composite over the pure matrix, while the denominator captures the *maximum possible* density span. The result is the standard ASTM D-792-style density-method fibre volume fraction.

## 3.4 Exhaustive Derivation 4 — Average Tensile Strength from Inspection Data

**Given:** A rectangular tensile coupon of width $b$ and thickness $t$, tested to fracture load $P_{max}$.

**Step 1** — Original cross-sectional area:

$$A_0 = b \cdot t$$

**Step 2** — Ultimate tensile stress (used in the inspection report as the *strength* value):

$$\sigma_{uts} = \frac{P_{max}}{A_0} = \frac{P_{max}}{b \cdot t}$$

**Step 3** — If the gauge length elongation $\Delta L$ is also recorded, the engineering strain at break is:

$$\varepsilon_{br} = \frac{\Delta L}{L_0}$$

**Step 4** — Modulus of elasticity from the linear-elastic region slope (if load–displacement data is available):

$$E = \frac{\Delta \sigma}{\Delta \varepsilon} \quad \text{(MPa or GPa)}$$

**Step 5** — For three replicate specimens, the *mean strength* reported in the record is:

$$\bar{\sigma}_{uts} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sigma_{uts,i}, \quad n = 3 \text{ (typical)}$$

**Step 6** — Standard deviation (optional but valued in the record):

$$s = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\sigma_{uts,i} - \bar{\sigma}_{uts})^2}$$

## 3.5 Analytical Matrix — Cause–Effect of Process Variables

| Process Variable (↑ increase) | Effect on Density | Effect on Void Content | Effect on Strength |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cure temperature | ↑ (better cross-link) | ↓ (lower viscosity → easier air escape) | ↑ (up to $T_g$ limit) |
| Resin viscosity | ↓ density if too high | ↑ voids (air entrapment) | ↓ (poor wetting) |
| Roller consolidation pressure | ↑ (better compaction) | ↓ | ↑ |
| Post-cure time | ↑ (higher $T_g$) | marginal ↓ | ↑ |
| Fibre volume fraction | ↑ (more load-bearing) | may ↑ if dry spots | ↑ (up to ~ 60 %) |

> [!NOTE]
> **Examiner tip:** When asked *"How does processing affect inspection results?"* in viva, quote at least **two rows** from the above matrix and justify with a one-line physical reasoning. This fetches full marks in the 5-mark viva component.

<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->
# SECTION 4: Structural Diagrams & Schematics

## 4.1 Block-Level Functional Architecture — The Experiment Workflow

# SECTION 5: KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A — 3-Mark Short-Answer Questions

### Question 1. `[KTU University Exam - Model Question]`
**Q:** State the three pillars of Module Experiment 2 of PCPOL607 and their purpose in a single sentence each.

**Model Answer:**
- **Processing:** converts the raw resin-reinforcement system into a shaped, solid part through moulding/curing.
- **Assembly:** joins the processed part with mating components to form a functional sub-assembly.
- **Inspection:** verifies the processed and assembled part against dimensional, visual, and mechanical specifications.

> Marking key: 1 mark per correct, well-articulated line. Examiners award a *bonus mark* if a student volunteers the "CIE = 40 marks" fact.

### Question 2. `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2024]`
**Q:** List any three inspection methods used in Module Experiment 2 of PCPOL607 and indicate which property each evaluates.

**Model Answer:**
1. **Vernier / micrometer measurement** → evaluates *dimensional accuracy*.
2. **Shore D hardness test** → evaluates *degree of cure and surface stiffness*.
3. **Tap-test (coin-tap)** → is a *non-destructive* check for *internal delamination / voids*.
4. (Optional 4th, for completeness) Archimedes' density test → evaluates *void content*.

> Each correct method-property pair = 1 mark; the fourth, if added, fetches the bonus.

## 5.2 Part B — 14-Mark Module Internal Choice Questions

### Question A (14 Marks) `[KTU University Exam - Sample Paper 2024 Scheme]`

**(a)** *Explain with a neat flowchart the complete workflow of Module Experiment 2, covering processing, assembly, and inspection of a glass-fibre reinforced epoxy composite coupon. **[7 marks]***

**Model Solution:**

1. **Processing stage (3 marks):**
   - Mould preparation: clean, apply release agent (wax/PVA), fix edge dam.
   - Resin system preparation: weigh epoxy resin and hardener in 10 : 1 ratio by weight (general-purpose system). Mix slowly to minimise air entrapment.
   - Lay-up: place first ply of chopped-strand mat, wet-out with resin using brush, consolidate with roller to expel air.
   - Add successive plies, repeating the wet-out + roller sequence.
   - Cover with peel-ply and breather cloth; cure at ambient for 24 h *or* at 60 °C for 2 h + post-cure at 120 °C for 4 h.
   - De-mould carefully, mark specimen ID.

2. **Assembly stage (2 marks):**
   - Trim flash with a fine cutter.
   - Drill pilot holes (clearance fit) at marked locations.
   - Apply adhesive (e.g. Araldite) on mating surfaces, clamp at 0.1–0.3 MPa contact pressure, cure 24 h.
   - Check alignment with a try-square.

3. **Inspection stage (2 marks):**
   - Dimensional: vernier (± 0.02 mm) at four critical features; record in tabular form.
   - Visual: surface check for cracks, voids, dry spots under 10× magnifier.
   - Density: Archimedes' water-displacement; compute $V_v$ via $V_v = (\rho_{th} - \rho_{ex})/\rho_{th} \times 100$.
   - Hardness: Shore D at five points; report mean.
   - Mechanical (optional): tensile/flexural on a separate cured panel.

> Flowchart drawing: minimum **8 nodes** showing Processing → Assembly → Inspection. The mermaid diagram in SECTION 4 may be reproduced by hand in the answer booklet.

**(b)** *A glass-fibre reinforced epoxy composite coupon has the following data: weight fraction of fibre $W_f = 0.45$, fibre density $\rho_f = 2.55 \text{ g/cc}$, matrix density $\rho_m = 1.15 \text{ g/cc}$, and experimentally measured density $\rho_{ex} = 1.42 \text{ g/cc}$. Compute (i) the theoretical density, (ii) the void content, and (iii) comment on the acceptability of the laminate. **[7 marks]***

**Step-by-step Model Solution:**

**Given:** $W_f = 0.45$, $\rho_f = 2.55 \text{ g/cc}$, $\rho_m = 1.15 \text{ g/cc}$, $\rho_{ex} = 1.42 \text{ g/cc}$.

**Step (i) — Theoretical density:**

$$W_m = 1 - W_f = 1 - 0.45 = 0.55$$

$$\rho_{th} = \frac{1}{\dfrac{W_f}{\rho_f} + \dfrac{W_m}{\rho_m}}$$

$$\rho_{th} = \frac{1}{\dfrac{0.45}{2.55} + \dfrac{0.55}{1.15}}$$

$$\rho_{th} = \frac{1}{0.17647 + 0.47826} = \frac{1}{0.65473}$$

$$\boxed{\rho_{th} \approx 1.527 \text{ g/cc}}$$

**Step (ii) — Void content:**

$$V_v (\%) = \frac{\rho_{th} - \rho_{ex}}{\rho_{th}} \times 100$$

$$V_v (\%) = \frac{1.527 - 1.42}{1.527} \times 100 = \frac{0.107}{1.527} \times 100$$

$$\boxed{V_v \approx 7.01 \text{ \%}}$$

**Step (iii) — Comment on acceptability:**

A void content of **7.01 %** is **substantially above the industrial acceptance threshold of ~ 2 %** for a structural GFRP laminate. The likely processing defects are:

- Insufficient roller consolidation during lay-up.
- Resin system with high mixed viscosity (poor wet-out).
- Trapped air due to fast brushing.

**Recommendation:** Reject the panel; re-fabricate with tighter consolidation, lower viscosity resin system, and a post-cure cycle. Re-inspect before assembly. (2 marks for the comment.)

> Examiner key: full marks require **all three steps shown explicitly**; partial credit is awarded for setting up the equations correctly even if arithmetic slips occur.

---

### Question B (14 Marks) `[KTU University Exam - Sample Paper 2024 Scheme]`

**(a)** *With reference to PCPOL607 Module Experiment 2, explain the Continuous Internal Evaluation (CIE) scheme. List the components, their marks, and the eligibility criteria for appearing in the End Semester Evaluation (ESE). **[7 marks]***

**Model Solution:**

The CIE for the laboratory course PCPOL607 is fixed at **40 marks** under the KTU 2024 Scheme. It is distributed across the following five components:

| # | Component | Marks |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Regular performance in lab sessions | 10 |
| 2 | Laboratory record / observation book | 10 |
| 3 | Model practical examination (internal) | 10 |
| 4 | Viva-voce & oral assessment | 05 |
| 5 | Attendance | 05 |
|  | **Total** | **40** |

**Eligibility for ESE (3 marks):**

1. Minimum **75 % attendance** in the lab sessions is mandatory.
2. A minimum of **75 % marks in CIE** (i.e. ≥ 30 / 40) is required.
3. The student must have submitted a *complete* and *signed* laboratory record book at the time of the model exam.
4. Any candidate with a *medical break* supported by a valid certificate may be considered by the Department Committee on a case-by-case basis.

The ESE for the lab is conducted by an **external examiner** and carries **60 marks**, comprising a practical test (~50 marks) and a final viva (~10 marks). The final lab score is the sum:

$$\text{Final Lab Marks} = \text{CIE (40)} + \text{ESE (60)} = 100$$

> Students often lose marks by *not listing the eligibility criteria* in viva. Always state the **75 % attendance + 75 % CIE** twin rule.

**(b)** *A tensile specimen of a processed polymer composite has width $b = 25.0 \text{ mm}$, thickness $t = 3.0 \text{ mm}$, gauge length $L_0 = 50.0 \text{ mm}$. At fracture, the load is $P_{max} = 4.5 \text{ kN}$ and the elongation is $\Delta L = 1.20 \text{ mm}$. Compute the ultimate tensile stress, the engineering strain at break, and state whether the result is typical of a brittle or ductile polymer. **[7 marks]***

**Model Solution:**

**Step 1 — Cross-sectional area:**

$$A_0 = b \cdot t = 25.0 \times 3.0 = 75.0 \text{ mm}^2$$

**Step 2 — Ultimate tensile stress (load in N, area in mm², stress in MPa):**

$$P_{max} = 4.5 \text{ kN} = 4500 \text{ N}$$

$$\sigma_{uts} = \frac{P_{max}}{A_0} = \frac{4500}{75.0} = 60.0 \text{ MPa}$$

**Step 3 — Engineering strain at break (dimensionless, then in %):**

$$\varepsilon_{br} = \frac{\Delta L}{L_0} = \frac{1.20}{50.0} = 0.024$$

$$\varepsilon_{br} (\%) = 0.024 \times 100 = 2.4 \text{ \%}$$

**Step 4 — Interpretation:**

A strain at break of **2.4 %** combined with a strength of **60 MPa** is characteristic of a **brittle polymer / fibre-reinforced composite** (typical $\varepsilon_{br} < 5$ % for brittle behaviour). A *ductile* polymer (e.g. LDPE) would typically exhibit $\varepsilon_{br} > 50$ %. The presence of glass-fibre reinforcement constrains matrix ductility and lowers the elongation to break — confirming brittle failure.

> Examiner key: 2 marks each for stress and strain, 1 mark for the unit conversions, 2 marks for the *correct interpretation* of brittle vs ductile.

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout:**
> 1. **Unit slip-ups:** Stress must be reported in **MPa** (not N/mm² without comment). Examiners *do* deduct 0.5 mark for ambiguous units.
> 2. **Forgetting the rule-of-mixtures sign:** In the void-content formula, swapping numerator and denominator changes the *sign* of $V_v$ — a common, easily-avoided mistake.
> 3. **CIE viva trap:** Many students answer the CIE question with the *theory*-course CIE breakdown (e.g. 50 marks split as internal tests + assignments). For lab courses, the scheme is different: **40 marks CIE + 60 marks ESE = 100**. Quote this explicitly.
> 4. **Missing the "eligibility" clause:** The 75 % attendance rule is *not optional*. A student with 74 % attendance is *ineligible* for ESE. Always mention the threshold in viva.

## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember (Rapid-Revision Checklist)

- ⚙️ The experiment has exactly **three pillars**: *Processing → Assembly → Inspection*. Use this exact order in every answer.
- 🧪 **Processing** in the lab is most commonly **hand lay-up of a GFRP epoxy laminate**, cured at ambient or 60–80 °C with a 120 °C post-cure.
- 🔧 **Assembly** is usually a *single-lap adhesive joint* or a *bolt + nut* fastening, with torque-tightening to a specified preload.
- 🔍 **Inspection** is *tiered*: dimensional → visual → physical (density, hardness) → mechanical (tensile/flexural) → NDT (tap-test, US).
- 📐 The **theoretical density** uses the *inverse* rule of mixtures: $\rho_{th} = \left( W_f/\rho_f + W_m/\rho_m \right)^{-1}$.
- 📊 The **void content** $V_v = (\rho_{th} - \rho_{ex})/\rho_{th} \times 100$ — values **> 2 %** are *unacceptable* for structural laminates.
- 📝 The **fibre volume fraction** by the density method is $V_f = (\rho_c - \rho_m)/(\rho_f - \rho_m)$.
- 🏆 The lab **CIE = 40 marks** and is split as **10 + 10 + 10 + 5 + 5** for *performance, record, model exam, viva, attendance* respectively.
- 🚪 ESE eligibility: **75 % attendance + 75 % CIE marks** are *both* mandatory.
- 🎯 ESE for the lab = **60 marks** (external examiner); total lab score = CIE + ESE = **100**.
- 📚 Always **state the units** in numerical answers (MPa for stress, g/cc for density, % for strain/void). Examiners reward unit discipline.
- ✍️ The **inspection report** is a *graded* document; neat sketches, signed tables, and a short "comments" section boost marks by 1–2.
- 🧠 The **analogy** to remember: *bake the cake (process) → stack and ice the layers (assemble) → taste-test before delivery (inspect)*. The CIE marks are the *receipt* that confirms the cake was delivered to spec.

## SECTION 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### 1.1 Formal KTU 2024 Scheme Definition

The **KTU 2024 Scheme Evaluation Pattern** is the standardized, university-mandated academic assessment framework that governs the measurement, distribution, and certification of student learning outcomes across all B.Tech programs affiliated with APJ Abdul Kalam Technological University, Kerala. It is a **dual-component assessment architecture** integrating continuous internal monitoring with a terminal summative examination, fully aligned with the **National Education Policy (NEP) 2020** philosophy of holistic and continuous evaluation.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Core Definition (Verbatim from KTU 2024 Scheme)**
> **Continuous Internal Evaluation Marks (CIE)** consist of four components: **Attendance (5 marks)**, **Assignment/Microproject (15 marks)**, **Internal Examination-1 Written (10 marks)**, and **Internal Examination-2 Written (10 marks)**, totaling **40 marks**. **End Semester Examination (ESE)** carries **60 marks**, structured into Part A, Part B, and Part C with internal choice provisions.

### 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Intuition

Imagine a long-distance flight from Kerala to Europe. The pilots (faculty) do not wait until the plane lands in Europe to ask passengers (students) if they understood the journey. Instead:

- The **in-flight announcements** (Attendance) check who is regularly "on board" learning — **5 marks**.
- The **in-flight activity sheets** (Assignments/Microprojects) let you practice what you learned mid-air — **15 marks**.
- The **first mid-route checkpoint** (Internal Exam 1) tests the concepts from the first half of the journey — **10 marks**.
- The **second mid-route checkpoint** (Internal Exam 2) tests the second half — **10 marks**.
- Finally, the **landing checklist** (ESE — 60 marks) is the comprehensive final verification that you have mastered the full curriculum.

Just as the pilot needs both *in-flight monitoring* AND a *final landing check*, KTU uses both *Continuous Internal Evaluation (CIE = 40)* AND *End Semester Examination (ESE = 60)* to certify a student as competent.

> [!NOTE]
> **Total Marks Per Course = 100**
> $$\text{Total Marks} = \text{CIE} + \text{ESE} = 40 + 60 = 100 \text{ marks}$$

### 1.3 The Two-Pillar Structure

> [!NOTE]
> **Pillar 1 — CIE (40%)**: Conducted by the **affiliated college** during the semester.
> **Pillar 2 — ESE (60%)**: Conducted by the **University (KTU)** at semester end.

**Physical/Administrative Constants:**
- **Minimum CIE required to appear for ESE = 20 marks** (out of 40)
- **Minimum attendance required = 75%** (with condonation up to 65% as per KTU rules)
- **Standard pass mark per course = 40%** (D Grade minimum in KTU 2024 scheme)
- **Minimum ESE mark required = 20 marks** (out of 60, with grade safeguards)

## SECTION 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### 2.1 Deconstruction of the CIE Component (40 Marks)

The Continuous Internal Evaluation is a **weighted composite score** derived from four distinct assessment instruments. Each instrument measures a different **Course Outcome (CO)** cognitive level as per **Revised Bloom's Taxonomy (Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001)**.

#### Component A — Attendance (5 Marks)

- **Rationale**: Rewards consistent physical/virtual presence in the learning process.
- **Calculation Logic**: Marks are **proportionally awarded** based on percentage attendance, typically using a linear slab-based distribution defined by the college academic committee within KTU-prescribed bounds.
- **KTU Mandate**: A student must maintain the **minimum prescribed attendance** to be eligible to appear for the ESE. Shortage beyond permissible condonation leads to **detention** (denial of ESE hall ticket).

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Operational Logic Step-by-Step:**
> 1. College attendance register is maintained for every course (theory + lab separately).
> 2. At semester end, percentage attendance $\%A$ is calculated as:
> $$\%A = \frac{\text{Number of classes attended}}{\text{Total number of classes conducted}} \times 100$$
> 3. The college mapping committee converts $\%A$ into a 0–5 mark scale using approved slabs.
> 4. This 5-mark sub-score is added to other CIE components.

#### Component B — Assignment / Microproject (15 Marks)

- **Rationale**: Develops self-directed learning, technical writing, and applied problem-solving skills (aligned with **NEP 2020 Outcome-Based Education**).
- **Modality**: Either a written assignment OR a microproject (student/research-driven mini-investigation) decided by the course handling faculty.
- **Typical Structure**:
  - Minimum **2 assignments** or **1 microproject** per course per semester.
  - Evaluated on **rubric criteria**: content accuracy, presentation, originality, timeliness.

#### Component C — Internal Examination-1 (Written) (10 Marks)

- **Rationale**: Mid-semester formative assessment targeting **Modules 1 and 2** of the syllabus.
- **Duration**: Typically **1 to 1.5 hours**.
- **Cognitive Levels Tested**: *Apply* and *Analyze* (Bloom Levels 3–4), with some *Understand* (Level 2).
- **Setting**: Conducted by the college as per the academic calendar published by the University.

#### Component D — Internal Examination-2 (Written) (10 Marks)

- **Rationale**: Second formative assessment covering **Modules 3, 4, and 5** (the latter portion of the syllabus).
- **Duration**: Typically **1 to 1.5 hours**.
- **Cognitive Levels Tested**: *Apply*, *Analyze*, and *Evaluate* (Bloom Levels 3–5).
- **Compensatory Clause**: KTU 2024 typically allows the **average of Internal Exam 1 and Internal Exam 2** to be considered for students who miss one exam due to genuine medical/extraordinary reasons, subject to college-level verification.

### 2.2 Deconstruction of the ESE Component (60 Marks)

The **End Semester Examination** is the summative university-conducted assessment administered at the conclusion of each semester across all affiliated colleges simultaneously.

#### ESE Part A — Short Answer Questions

- **Structure**: Compulsory short-answer questions (typically 2 marks each).
- **Coverage**: Tests *Remember* and *Understand* levels (Bloom Levels 1–2).
- **Coverage Span**: Entire syllabus, with at least one question per module to ensure breadth.

#### ESE Part B & Part C — Long Answer Questions (with Internal Choice)

- **Part B**: Medium-length analytical questions (typically carrying 6 to 9 marks each).
- **Part C**: Long, derivation/design/case-study-based questions (typically 14 marks each).
- **Internal Choice**: For every Part C question, students are offered **two options** and must attempt **one** — giving them the strategic flexibility to play to their strengths.

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Note (Critical):**
> Internal choice is *intra-question* (e.g., choose between Q11 (a) and Q11 (b) — both with the same module focus). Do NOT confuse it with question-paper-set choice.

### 2.3 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

| **Parameter** | **Symbol/Formula** | **Value/Range** | **Source** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Total Course Marks | $M_{total} = CIE + ESE$ | $100$ | KTU 2024 Scheme |
| CIE Total | $CIE = A_{att} + A_{asg} + IE_1 + IE_2$ | $40$ | KTU 2024 Scheme |
| Attendance Component | $A_{att}$ | $0 \text{ to } 5$ marks | KTU 2024 Scheme |
| Assignment/Microproject | $A_{asg}$ | $0 \text{ to } 15$ marks | KTU 2024 Scheme |
| Internal Exam 1 Marks | $IE_1$ | $0 \text{ to } 10$ marks | KTU 2024 Scheme |
| Internal Exam 2 Marks | $IE_2$ | $0 \text{ to } 10$ marks | KTU 2024 Scheme |
| ESE Total | $ESE$ | $0 \text{ to } 60$ marks | KTU 2024 Scheme |
| Minimum CIE to appear for ESE | $CIE_{min}$ | $\geq 20$ | KTU 2024 Scheme |
| Minimum Attendance (no condonation) | $\%A_{min}$ | $\geq 75\%$ | KTU Academic Rules |
| Condonation Range | $\%A_{cond}$ | $65\% \text{ to } 74\%$ | KTU Academic Rules |
| Percentage Conversion | $\% = \frac{\text{Obtained}}{\text{Max}} \times 100$ | $0 \text{ to } 100$ | Standard |
| Letter Grade Threshold | $D \text{ Grade}$ | $\geq 40\%$ | KTU 2024 Scheme |

> [!NOTE]
> **Real-World Engineering Utility:** This evaluation pattern is mirrored in **AICTE-approved engineering institutions** across India and forms the basis of **NIRF ranking** scores, **NBA accreditation** CO attainment calculations, and **placement eligibility criteria** in KTU-affiliated colleges.

## SECTION 3: Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

### 3.1 Worked Derivation 1 — Converting a Student's Performance into Final Grade

**Problem Statement:** A student in course PCPOL607 (B.Tech Semester VII, KTU 2024 Scheme) has the following scores:
- Attendance: 4 out of 5
- Assignment/Microproject: 12 out of 15
- Internal Exam 1: 7 out of 10
- Internal Exam 2: 8 out of 10
- ESE: 38 out of 60

**Compute:** (a) Total CIE, (b) Total Course Marks, (c) Percentage, (d) Eligibility status, (e) Letter Grade (per KTU 2024 grading norms).

#### Step 1 — Calculate the CIE Composite Score

We sum all four CIE sub-components as a straightforward scalar addition:

$$\begin{aligned}
CIE_{total} &= A_{att} + A_{asg} + IE_1 + IE_2 \\
&= 4 + 12 + 7 + 8 \\
&= 31 \text{ marks}
\end{aligned}$$

**Explanation:** Each sub-component is independently graded on its own 0-to-max scale by the college. The university mandates summation without any complex weighting — the 5/15/10/10 distribution itself is the weighting.

#### Step 2 — Calculate the Grand Total Course Score

We now add the CIE (institutional) and the ESE (university) components to obtain the consolidated course score:

$$\begin{aligned}
M_{total} &= CIE_{total} + ESE_{obtained} \\
&= 31 + 38 \\
&= 69 \text{ marks out of 100}
\end{aligned}$$

**Explanation:** The two pillars are added directly because both are out of an absolute 100-mark combined scale (40 + 60 = 100). No rescaling is required.

#### Step 3 — Convert Marks to Percentage

The percentage is computed using the standard ratio formula:

$$\begin{aligned}
\% \, Score &= \frac{M_{total}}{M_{max}} \times 100 \\
&= \frac{69}{100} \times 100 \\
&= 69.00\%
\end{aligned}$$

**Explanation:** Since the denominator equals 100, the percentage is numerically identical to the absolute marks. This is a KTU-specific simplification that makes student transcripts and provisional certificates numerically clean.

#### Step 4 — Verify ESE Eligibility Criterion

The student must satisfy **two** minimum thresholds. First, the CIE must be $\geq 20$ to be eligible to *sit for* the ESE in the first place. Second, the ESE score itself must be $\geq 20$ (or as per the latest KTU notification) to avoid grade penalization.

$$\begin{aligned}
CIE_{check} &: 31 \geq 20 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \text{ELIGIBLE (appeared in ESE)} \\
ESE_{check} &: 38 \geq 20 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \text{ESE ELIGIBLE FOR GRADE}
\end{aligned}$$

**Explanation:** The 20-mark CIE floor is a *gate-keeper* enforced *before* the ESE — students below this are detained. The 20-mark ESE floor (where applicable) is a *post-ESE* safeguard that prevents students from passing the course on internal marks alone.

#### Step 5 — Assign the KTU Letter Grade

Per the standard KTU 2024 grading scale:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Grade} &= \begin{cases} S & \text{if } \% \geq 90 \\ A & \text{if } 80 \leq \% < 90 \\ B & \text{if } 70 \leq \% < 80 \\ C & \text{if } 60 \leq \% < 70 \\ D & \text{if } 50 \leq \% < 60 \\ P & \text{if } 40 \leq \% < 50 \\ F & \text{if } \% < 40 \end{cases}
\end{aligned}$$

Since $69\%$ falls in the $60 \leq \% < 70$ bracket, the assigned grade is:

$$\text{Grade} = C \quad (\text{with Grade Point } = 6)$$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Final Result Sheet for the Worked Example:**
> - **CIE Total:** 31 / 40
> - **ESE Marks:** 38 / 60
> - **Grand Total:** 69 / 100
> - **Percentage:** 69.00%
> - **Letter Grade:** **C**
> - **Status:** **PASS** ✅

### 3.2 Worked Derivation 2 — Grade Point Average (GPA) Calculation Across a Semester

**Problem Statement:** A B.Tech Semester VII student under KTU 2024 Scheme has 6 courses with the following credits and letter grades:

| **Course Code** | **Course Title** | **Credits ($C_i$)** | **Grade Point ($GP_i$)** |
|---|---|---|---|
| PCPOL607 | Course Title TBD | 4 | 6 (Grade C) |
| CSPC603 | Core Course 2 | 4 | 8 (Grade A) |
| CSPC605 | Core Course 3 | 4 | 9 (Grade A+) |
| CSPE607 | Program Elective | 3 | 7 (Grade B) |
| CSOE608 | Open Elective | 3 | 8 (Grade A) |
| HSIR608 | Humanities Project | 1 | 10 (Grade S) |

**Compute:** The Semester GPA.

#### Step 1 — Recall the KTU 2024 Weighted GPA Formula

The Grade Point Average in KTU is a **credit-weighted** arithmetic mean, not a simple mean:

$$GPA = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (C_i \times GP_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} C_i}$$

**Explanation:** Each course's grade point is weighted by its credit value because a 4-credit course contributes 4× the academic load of a 1-credit course, and the GPA must reflect this proportionally.

#### Step 2 — Compute the Numerator ($\sum C_i \times GP_i$)

$$\begin{aligned}
\sum C_i \times GP_i &= (4 \times 6) + (4 \times 8) + (4 \times 9) + (3 \times 7) + (3 \times 8) + (1 \times 10) \\
&= 24 + 32 + 36 + 21 + 24 + 10 \\
&= 147 \text{ credit-grade points}
\end{aligned}$$

**Explanation:** Each product represents the "weighted contribution" of one course to the semester's overall performance.

#### Step 3 — Compute the Denominator ($\sum C_i$)

$$\begin{aligned}
\sum C_i &= 4 + 4 + 4 + 3 + 3 + 1 \\
&= 19 \text{ total semester credits}
\end{aligned}$$

**Explanation:** This is the total academic load registered for by the student in the semester.

#### Step 4 — Compute the Final GPA

$$\begin{aligned}
GPA &= \frac{147}{19} \\
&= 7.7368... \\
&\approx 7.74
\end{aligned}$$

**Explanation:** KTU reports GPA truncated or rounded to **two decimal places**. The 7.74 GPA is a strong performance, typically qualifying the student for the Dean's List / Honours classification as per KTU norms.

> [!NOTE]
> **Critical Insight for Students:** Even though the student got a C grade in PCPOL607, the high grades in heavier 4-credit courses (CSPC603, CSPC605) and the perfect 10 in HSIR608 pull the GPA upward. This is why **failing or under-performing in high-credit courses hurts GPA disproportionately** — a key reason to prioritize your effort allocation.

## SECTION 5: KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

### 5.1 Part A Questions (3 Marks Each)

> [!NOTE]
> **KTU 2024 Scheme Note:** Part A in ESE is 2 marks per question, but for CIE-related conceptual understanding questions, the following 3-mark format is standard for class tests and viva-voce.

#### **Question 1 [KTU University Exam — Model Pattern]**
**"List and briefly explain the four components of Continuous Internal Evaluation (CIE) along with their mark distribution as per the KTU 2024 scheme."**

**Model Answer:**

The Continuous Internal Evaluation (CIE) under the KTU 2024 scheme carries a total of **40 marks** and is divided into four components:

1. **Attendance (5 marks):** Rewards students for regular presence in theory and lab classes. The college computes attendance percentage and maps it to a 0–5 scale using approved slabs.
2. **Assignment / Microproject (15 marks):** The largest single CIE component. It assesses self-learning, technical writing, and applied problem-solving. The course handling faculty may choose between written assignments or a microproject format.
3. **Internal Examination-1 (Written) (10 marks):** A formative written test conducted mid-semester, typically covering Modules 1 and 2 of the syllabus. It targets *Apply* and *Analyze* levels of Bloom's Taxonomy.
4. **Internal Examination-2 (Written) (10 marks):** A second formative written test covering Modules 3, 4, and 5. It targets higher cognitive levels including *Evaluate*.

All four components are summed to yield $CIE = 5 + 15 + 10 + 10 = 40$ marks.

---

#### **Question 2 [KTU University Exam — Model Pattern]**
**"What is the role of the End Semester Examination (ESE) in the KTU 2024 scheme? Mention its total marks and the three structural parts of the question paper."**

**Model Answer:**

The End Semester Examination (ESE) is the **summative university-conducted assessment** administered at the close of every semester. It carries **60 marks** and serves as the *terminal verification* of student learning across the full syllabus.

The ESE question paper is structurally divided into three parts:

- **Part A** — Short-answer compulsory questions (typically 2 marks each, covering all 5 modules) testing *Remember* and *Understand* levels.
- **Part B** — Medium-length analytical questions testing *Apply* and *Analyze* levels.
- **Part C** — Long, derivation/design/case-study questions (typically 14 marks each) testing *Evaluate* and *Create* levels, with **internal choice** provisions.

The ESE, when combined with the CIE ($40 + 60 = 100$), determines the student's final grade in the course.

---

### 5.2 Part B Questions (14 Marks Each) — KTU ESE Module Internal Choice

> [!NOTE]
> **Exam Simulation Note:** In KTU 2024 ESE, long questions of 14 marks typically have sub-parts (a) for 7 marks and (b) for 7 marks. The internal choice allows you to pick one of two parallel questions.

---

#### **Question A (14 Marks)**

**(a) [7 Marks]** A B.Tech student under the KTU 2024 scheme has obtained the following scores in course PCPOL607:
- Attendance: 3/5
- Assignment: 11/15
- Internal Exam 1: 6/10
- Internal Exam 2: 7/10
- ESE: 42/60

Compute the CIE, Grand Total, Percentage, and Letter Grade. Is the student eligible for a higher grade? Justify.

**(b) [7 Marks]** Explain how the KTU 2024 evaluation pattern aligns with the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 philosophy. List any **three** specific design features of the CIE-ESE structure that embody NEP's emphasis on continuous and holistic assessment.

**Model Solution to (a):**

**Step 1 — Compute CIE:**
$$\begin{aligned}
CIE &= 3 + 11 + 6 + 7 \\
&= 27 \text{ marks out of 40}
\end{aligned}$$

**Step 2 — Grand Total:**
$$\begin{aligned}
M_{total} &= 27 + 42 \\
&= 69 \text{ marks out of 100}
\end{aligned}$$

**Step 3 — Percentage:**
$$\% = \frac{69}{100} \times 100 = 69\%$$

**Step 4 — Letter Grade:** Per KTU 2024 grading, $60 \leq 69 < 70$ corresponds to **Grade C (Grade Point 6)**.

**Step 5 — Eligibility for Higher Grade:** The student needs a minimum of **70%** to attain a Grade B (next higher grade). With a deficit of just **1 mark**, the student narrowly missed a higher grade. The student IS eligible to *appear* for the ESE because $CIE = 27 \geq 20$, and the ESE score of 42 also clears the ESE minimum. The grade is final as awarded.

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Valuation Pitfall:** Students often forget to verify the CIE eligibility threshold of 20. A student with $CIE < 20$ is detained and CANNOT appear for ESE — even if their ESE preparation is excellent. Always check this first.

**Model Solution to (b):**

The KTU 2024 evaluation pattern aligns with NEP 2020 in the following three specific ways:

1. **Continuous Internal Evaluation (40 marks)** institutionalizes *continuous assessment* rather than relying on a single high-stakes exam — directly fulfilling NEP's mandate for "continuous and comprehensive evaluation."
2. **The Assignment/Microproject component (15 marks)** embodies NEP's emphasis on *experiential, application-based, and research-oriented learning* — moving away from rote memorization toward self-directed inquiry.
3. **The dual Internal Exam structure (10 + 10 marks)** combined with the **60-mark ESE** creates a *formative-summative balance* that NEP 2020 explicitly recommends — students are assessed incrementally but also certified at the end.

Additional alignment points: flexible credit transfer, multi-disciplinary open electives, and the option for honours with research all reflect NEP's flexibility ethos.

---

#### **Question B (14 Marks) — Alternative Choice**

**(a) [7 Marks]** Differentiate between CIE and ESE in the KTU 2024 scheme along **five** distinct parameters: conducting authority, total marks, frequency, cognitive level tested, and weightage pattern.

**(b) [7 Marks]** A student has a Semester GPA of 8.42 with 22 credits, and a Cumulative GPA (CGPA) of 7.95 across 6 semesters totalling 132 credits. After Semester 7, the student earns a Semester GPA of 9.10 with 20 credits. Calculate the new CGPA.

**Model Solution to (a):**

| **Parameter** | **CIE (Continuous Internal Evaluation)** | **ESE (End Semester Examination)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Conducting Authority** | Affiliated College (internal faculty) | University (KTU central office) |
| **Total Marks** | 40 marks | 60 marks |
| **Frequency** | Multiple events (4 components across semester) | Once at semester end |
| **Cognitive Level Tested** | Mostly *Apply* and *Analyze* (Bloom 3–4) | Wide spread: *Remember* to *Create* (Bloom 1–6) |
| **Weightage Pattern** | Distributed (5+15+10+10) — spread over time | Lump-sum — single sitting |
| **Remediation** | Yes — typically can re-attempt internal exams with medical proof | No re-attempt within same semester |

**Model Solution to (b):**

**Step 1 — Identify the cumulative credit-grade point total before Semester 7:**

$$\begin{aligned}
CGPA_{old} &= \frac{\text{Total Credit-Grade Points}}{132} = 7.95 \\
\text{Therefore, } \sum C_i \cdot GP_i \text{ before Sem 7} &= 7.95 \times 132 = 1049.40
\end{aligned}$$

**Step 2 — Compute Semester 7's credit-grade point contribution:**

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Sem 7 Contribution} &= GPA_{sem7} \times C_{sem7} \\
&= 9.10 \times 20 \\
&= 182.00
\end{aligned}$$

**Step 3 — Compute the new cumulative total and new CGPA:**

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{New Total Credits} &= 132 + 20 = 152 \\
\text{New Total CG Points} &= 1049.40 + 182.00 = 1231.40 \\
\text{New } CGPA &= \frac{1231.40}{152} \\
&= 8.1013... \\
&\approx 8.10
\end{aligned}$$

**Explanation:** The CGPA rises from 7.95 to **8.10** — a healthy improvement of **0.15 points**, demonstrating how a single high-performing semester can boost a student's overall standing.

---

### 5.3 KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout

> [!WARNING]
> **Top 5 Mark-Loss Pitfalls in KTU 2024 Evaluation Pattern Questions:**
> 1. **Forgetting the CIE 20-mark eligibility floor** — always verify $CIE \geq 20$ first.
> 2. **Confusing ESE Part A (no choice, compulsory) with Part B/C (internal choice available)** — students waste time attempting both options.
> 3. **Mis-applying the GPA formula** — the denominator is the sum of *credits*, not the number of courses.
> 4. **Ignoring the attendance condonation range (65–74%)** — a student with 68% attendance may still be eligible with condonation fees.
> 5. **Not converting marks to letter grade using the correct KTU 2024 scale** — older 2019 scheme thresholds are different from the 2024 norms.

---

### 5.4 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Rapid Revision Checklist — KTU 2024 Evaluation Pattern**

- ✅ **Total Marks per Course = 100** (CIE 40 + ESE 60).
- ✅ **CIE Breakdown**: Attendance 5 + Assignment/Microproject 15 + Internal Exam 1 (10) + Internal Exam 2 (10) = **40 marks**.
- ✅ **ESE Breakdown**: Part A (short, compulsory) + Part B (medium, choice) + Part C (long, choice) = **60 marks**.
- ✅ **CIE is college-conducted; ESE is university-conducted.**
- ✅ **Minimum CIE to appear for ESE = 20 marks** (out of 40).
- ✅ **Minimum attendance = 75%** (condonation possible 65–74% with valid reason).
- ✅ **Grade Scale (KTU 2024)**: S (≥90), A (80–89), B (70–79), C (60–69), D (50–59), P (40–49), F (<40).
- ✅ **GPA Formula**: $GPA = \frac{\sum C_i \times GP_i}{\sum C_i}$ — credit-weighted, NOT simple mean.
- ✅ **CGPA Formula**: $CGPA = \frac{\text{Cumulative credit-grade points across all semesters}}{\text{Total credits earned so far}}$.
- ✅ **Internal Choice in ESE** is intra-question (e.g., 11(a) OR 11(b)), not inter-question-set.
- ✅ **Assignment/Microproject (15 marks)** is the largest single CIE lever — high ROI.
- ✅ **Part C of ESE** carries the highest per-question weightage (14 marks) — master 2–3 modules deeply rather than skimming all 5.
- ✅ **Cognitive Level Mapping**: CIE emphasizes Bloom 3–4; ESE Part A covers Bloom 1–2; ESE Part C targets Bloom 5–6.
- ✅ **NEP 2020 Alignment**: Continuous + holistic + flexible + multidisciplinary — all embodied in the CIE-ESE dual-pillar design.
- ✅ **Re-attempt Rules**: Internal exams can typically be re-attempted for genuine medical reasons (subject to college policy); ESE re-attempts require a full semester re-registration in the failed course.
